## 1. Kāliṅga Vagga
## 1. Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka
## A Husband if Laywomen, a Teacher if Nuns

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha, the Teacher who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Vivara-thima-saṃ,' concerning the ordination of four female wanderers (paribbājikā).

In the city of Vesālī, there lived seven thousand seven hundred and seven Licchavī princes. All these princes delighted in asking and answering questions. At that time, a Nigaṇṭha (Jain) skilled in five hundred views arrived in Vesālī. The Licchavī princes honored that Nigaṇṭha.

A female Nigaṇṭha of similar character also arrived. The Licchavī princes had the two, the male Nigaṇṭha and the female Nigaṇṭha, engage in a debate. The two were equal in their abilities.

Then, the Licchavī princes thought that a child born of these two would be exceptionally wise. Having thought so, they arranged a marriage between the male and female Nigaṇṭhas and had them live together.

In due course, through their union, four daughters and one son were born to the Nigaṇṭhas. They named the daughters Saccā, Lolā, Avadhārikā, and Paṭicchādā. They named the son Saccaka.

When these five children reached the age of wisdom, they learned one thousand views—five hundred from their mother and five hundred from their father. The parents instructed the daughters: 'If any layperson can defeat your views, you must become his servants (wives); if a monk defeats your views, you must ordain under him.'

Later, the parents passed away. After their death, Saccaka Nigaṇṭha remained in Vesālī, teaching the Licchavī princes. The four sisters, however, traveled from city to city for the purpose of debate, carrying rose-apple (jambu) branches. Upon reaching Sāvatthī, they planted a rose-apple branch at the city gate and told the youths: 'Whoever is able to answer our questions, whether a layperson or a monk, let them scatter the dust with their feet and trample this branch.' Having said this, they entered the city to collect alms.

At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, after sweeping the unswept areas, filling empty water pots, and attending to sick monks, entered Sāvatthī for alms late in the morning. Seeing the rose-apple branch and questioning the youths, he learned the reason. The Elder Sāriputta then had the youths destroy the branch and told them: 'Tell those who placed this branch to come and see me at the gate of Jetavana Monastery after they have finished their meal.' He then entered the city for alms and, after eating, sat at the monastery gate.

The female wanderers, returning from their alms round, saw that the branch had been trampled and asked who had done it. When the youths told them it was the Elder Sāriputta and that they should go to the Jetavana gate if they wished to debate, the sisters entered the city again, gathered a crowd, and went to the Jetavana gate to ask the Elder Sāriputta about the thousand views.

The Elder Sāriputta answered all thousand views and then asked, 'Do you know anything beyond these views?' They replied, 'No, Venerable Sir.' He then said, 'I shall ask you one question.' They replied, 'Ask, Venerable Sir; if we know, we shall answer.'

The Elder Sāriputta asked, 'What is the One?' The wanderers did not know. The Elder Sāriputta then provided the answer. The female wanderers said, 'Venerable Sir, defeat is ours; victory is yours.' The Elder Sāriputta asked, 'What will you do now?'

They replied, 'Venerable Sir, our parents instructed us: "If any layperson defeats your views, become his wives; if a monk defeats them, ordain under him." We shall ordain.'

The Elder Sāriputta agreed and had them ordain under the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā. Before long, all the nuns attained the Fruit of Arahantship.

One day, the monks in the Dhamma Hall began a conversation: 'Friends, the Elder Sāriputta became the refuge of the four female wanderers and led them to the Fruit of Arahantship.'

The Buddha arrived and asked, 'Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?' When they informed him, he said, 'Monks, not only now has Sāriputta been their refuge; he was their refuge in the past as well. Now he has given them the consecration of monkhood; in the past, he placed them in the position of queens.' Having said this, he remained silent. At the request of the monks, he related the past story.

In the past, when King Kāliṅga reigned in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kāliṅga, King Assaka reigned in the city of Pāṭali in the kingdom of Assaka. King Kāliṅga possessed a great army and was as strong as an elephant. He saw no rival for battle. Desiring war, he asked his ministers, 'I wish to fight, but I see no rival. What should I do?'

The ministers replied, 'Great King, there is a way. Your Majesty has four daughters of supreme beauty. Let them be adorned, placed in a covered carriage, and escorted by a large retinue through the villages, towns, and royal capitals. Whichever king desires to take these princesses, we shall wage war against him.' King Kāliṅga did as the ministers suggested.

Wherever the princesses arrived, the kings, out of fear, would not allow them to enter the cities. They sent gifts but kept them outside the city walls. Thus, they traveled throughout the whole of Jambudīpa until they reached the city of Pāṭali in the kingdom of Assaka. King Assaka also closed the city gates and sent gifts.

King Assaka had a minister named Nandisena, who was wise, skillful, and resourceful. Nandisena thought, 'These princesses have traveled all over Jambudīpa and found no rival. If this continues, Jambudīpa will be considered empty of heroes. I shall fight King Kāliṅga.' Having thought so, Nandisena went to the city gate, called the gatekeeper, and spoke this first verse to open the gate for the princesses:

1. Open this gate; let them enter the city of King Aruṇa,
Which is well-guarded by Nandisena, a lion among men.

Having said this, Nandisena had the gate opened, took the princesses, and presented them to King Assaka, saying, 'Great King, do not be afraid. If there is a war, we shall be victorious. These princesses are of supreme beauty. Make them your chief queens.' He then had them consecrated and told their attendants, 'You may return. Inform your king that King Assaka has placed the princesses in the position of queens.' He then dismissed them.

They returned and reported to King Kāliṅga. King Kāliṅga said, 'King Assaka must not know my power,' and immediately set out with a vast army.

Nandisena, learning of King Kāliṅga's approach, sent word: 'Let him stay within his own borders; do not let him cross into our king's territory. The battle shall take place between the borders of the two kingdoms.'

King Kāliṅga, hearing this, stayed within his own borders. King Assaka also stayed within his own borders.

At that time, the Bodhisatta had become an ascetic and built a hermitage between the two kingdoms. King Kāliṅga thought, 'Ascetics are somewhat knowledgeable. Who can know what will happen? Which king will win and which will lose? I shall ask the ascetic.' Disguised, he approached the Bodhisatta, exchanged greetings, and asked, 'Venerable Sir, King Kāliṅga and King Assaka wish to fight and are stationed at their borders. Among them, who will win and who will lose?'

'Great Layman, I do not know this victory or defeat. However, Sakka, the King of Gods, comes here. I shall ask him and tell you. Come back tomorrow.'

Sakka came to the Bodhisatta, and the Bodhisatta asked him about the matter. Sakka said, 'Venerable Sir, King Kāliṅga will win, and King Assaka will lose. This omen will also appear.'

When King Kāliṅga returned the next day and asked, the Bodhisatta informed him. Without even asking what the omen would be, King Kāliṅga went away rejoicing, thinking, 'I shall win.' The news spread.

Hearing this, King Assaka called Nandisena and said, 'King Kāliṅga will win, and we shall lose. What shall we do?' Nandisena replied, 'Great King, who can know who will win or lose? Do not worry.' He comforted the king and then approached the Bodhisatta, paid respects, and sat down.

He asked, 'Venerable Sir, who will win and who will lose?' The Bodhisatta replied, 'King Kāliṅga will win, and King Assaka will lose.' Nandisena asked, 'Venerable Sir, what will be the omen for the winning king, and what will be the omen for the losing king?' The Bodhisatta said, 'Great Layman, the guardian deity of the winning king will be a pure white bull. The guardian deity of the losing king will be a pure black bull. The guardian deities of the two kings will fight to determine victory and defeat.'

Upon hearing this, Nandisena left and called a thousand great warriors who were friends of the king. He led them up a nearby mountain and asked, 'Friends, will you be able to give your lives for our king?' They replied, 'We will.' 'If so, throw yourselves down this precipice,' he said. The thousand warriors prepared to jump.

He then stopped them, saying, 'There is no need to throw yourselves down this precipice. Fight with love for our king and without retreating.' The thousand warriors agreed.

When the battle began, King Kāliṅga, thinking 'I shall win,' became lax in his efforts. His troops also became lax, thinking their king would win; they did not maintain formation and moved about as they pleased. They did not exert effort when effort was needed.

The two kings approached each other on horseback to fight. Their guardian deities appeared in front of them. King Kāliṅga's guardian deity was a pure white bull, and King Assaka's was a pure black bull. These deities approached each other to fight. Only the two kings could see the bulls; others could not.

Nandisena asked King Assaka, 'Great King, do you see the guardian deities?' The king replied, 'I do.' 'In what form do they appear?' the minister asked. The king said, 'King Kāliṅga's guardian deity appears as a pure white bull, and mine appears as a pure black bull. Seeing this, I stand dejected.'

'Great King, do not be afraid. We shall be victorious. King Kāliṅga will lose. Dismount from your horse, hold this spear, and while firmly grasping the side of your well-trained Sindh horse with your left hand, go quickly with these thousand warriors and strike King Kāliṅga's guardian deity with the spear to bring him down. Then, we thousand shall strike with a thousand spears. When struck thus, King Kāliṅga's guardian deity will perish. Then King Kāliṅga will lose, and we shall win.'

King Assaka agreed and, following Nandisena's signal, struck with his spear. The thousand ministers also struck with their thousand spears. The guardian deity died right there. At that very moment, King Kāliṅga was defeated and fled. Seeing him flee, the thousand ministers proclaimed loudly, 'King Kāliṅga is fleeing!'

As King Kāliṅga fled in fear of death, he wished to reproach the ascetic and spoke this second verse:

2. Victory to the Kāliṅgas, who endure the unendurable,
Defeat and ruin to the Assakas.
Thus was it spoken by you, O holy one;
The upright do not speak falsehood.

Thus, reproaching the ascetic, King Kāliṅga fled quickly to his own city, not even daring to look back. Two or three days later, Sakka came to the ascetic. The ascetic, wishing to speak with Sakka, spoke this third verse:

3. The gods have transcended falsehood,
Truth is their supreme wealth, O Sakka.
That was spoken falsely by you, O King of Gods.
Depending on what did you speak untruth, O Maghavā, O Mahinda?

Hearing this, Sakka spoke the fourth verse:

4. Have you not heard it said, O Brahmin,
That the gods do not envy human effort?
Self-control, concentration, an unbreakable mind,
Steadfastness, and timely exertion,
Firm energy and human perseverance—
By these alone was the victory of the Assakas.

When King Kāliṅga fled, King Assaka took the spoils and returned to his city. Nandisena sent word to King Kāliṅga: 'Send the inheritance portion for these four princesses. If you do not, I shall do what must be done.' King Kāliṅga, hearing this and being greatly terrified, sent the inheritance due to the princesses. From then on, the two kings lived in harmony.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Buddha identified the birth: 'At that time, these young nuns were the daughters of King Kāliṅga. Sāriputta was the minister Nandisena. And I myself was the ascetic.'

## With a retinue of followers, strict discipline, a firm mind, and striving even unto death, one can surely drink the draught of victory.
The Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Mahāassāroha Jātaka
## The King and the Forest Dweller

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha, the Teacher who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Mahāassāroha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Adeyyesu dadaṃ dānaṃ,' concerning the Elder Ānanda.

(The present story has been told below.) In this Mahāassāroha Jātaka, the Teacher said, 'In the past, the wise also showed gratitude based on the help they received,' and related the past story.

In the past, the Bodhisatta was the King of Bārāṇasī and reigned righteously. He gave alms and observed the precepts. That King of Bārāṇasī, intending to suppress a rebellion in the border region caused by thieves, set out surrounded by his army. When the battle was lost, he fled on horseback and reached a certain border village.

In that border region, thirty royal servants lived. These royal servants had gathered early in the center of the village to attend to village affairs. At that moment, the king, riding a horse equipped with armor and himself fully adorned, entered the village through the gate. The villagers, terrified and wondering what was happening, fled and entered their respective houses.

Among those people, one man did not go to his house but went to welcome the king. He asked, 'I heard our king went to the border region. Who are you, friend? A royal official or a thief?' The king replied, 'Friend, I am a royal official.' 'If so, come,' the man said, and led the king to his house, seated him on his own bench, and told his wife, 'Lady, come and wash the feet of our friend.' He had her wash the king's feet, provided food according to his means, and spread a bed, saying, 'Rest for a while.' The king lay down.

The householder removed the horse's trappings, walked the horse to and fro, gave it water, rubbed its back with oil, and gave it grass. Having thus attended to the king for three or four days, when the king said, 'Friend, I shall go,' the man again did everything necessary for both the king and the horse. The king, being pleased, said as he was leaving, 'Friend, I am known as Mahāassāroha (the Great Horseman). My house is in the center of the city. If you come to the city for any reason, stand at the south gate and ask the gatekeeper, "In which house does Mahāassāroha live?" Then, bring the gatekeeper and come to my house.' Having said this, he departed.

The king's army, not finding the king, had set up camp outside the city. Seeing the king, they went to welcome him and surrounded him.
9:
When the King entered the city, he stood at the gate and called the gatekeeper. Having the people move aside, he said, "My dear, a certain border villager will come, wishing to see me, and will ask, 'Where is the house of the Great Horse-Rider?' You should take that border villager by the hand and bring him to me. At that time, you shall receive a thousand pieces of money."

When that border villager did not come to the city, the King demanded taxes from the village where that man lived. Even when the taxes were demanded in this way, the man did not come. In the same manner, he had taxes demanded a second and a third time. Yet, the man did not come.

Then the villagers gathered and said to that man, "Sir, since the time your friend the Great Horse-Rider came, we have been oppressed by taxes and are unable to lift our heads. Sir, please go; speak to your friend the Great Horse-Rider and have him release us from the taxes."

The man said, "Very well, I shall go. However, it is not proper for me to go empty-handed. My friend has two young sons. Prepare clothing, wraps, and ornaments for those young sons, for his wife, and for my friend." The villagers replied, "Very well, we shall prepare them," and they prepared all the gifts.

That man took those gifts and the cakes fried in his own house, went to the city, reached the south gate, and asked the gatekeeper, "Friend gatekeeper, where is the house of the Great Horse-Rider?"
10:
5. He who gives to those unworthy of gifts, and gives not to those worthy of gifts, finds no friend when he falls into misfortune and ruin.

6. He who gives not to those unworthy of gifts, and gives to those worthy of gifts, finds a friend when he falls into misfortune and ruin.

7. The sight of the special benefit of association and mutual enjoyment perishes among those of ignoble nature and the deceitful. But even a small favor done for the noble and the upright, for such as these, is of great fruit.

8. One who has previously done a kindness, performing what is very difficult in the world, is worthy of supreme honor, whether he performs a favor later or not.

He spoke these verses.

Tāta, my dear. Yo, whichever person. Adeyyesu, to those to whom gifts should not be given. Dānaṃ, a gift. Dadaṃ, gives. Deyyesu, to those to whom gifts should be given. Nappavecchati, does not give. Āpāsu, when dangers arise. So, that person. Byasanaṃ, into ruin. Patto, having fallen. Sahāyaṃ, a friend. Nādhigacchati, does not find.

Yo, whichever person. Adeyyesu, to those to whom gifts should not be given. Dānaṃ, a gift. Na dadaṃ, does not give. Deyyesu, to those to whom gifts should be given. Pavecchati, gives. Āpāsu, when dangers arise. So, that person. Byasanaṃ, into ruin. Patto, having fallen. Sahāyaṃ, a friend. Adhigacchati, finds.

Anariyadhammesu, among those who have the conduct of the ignoble. Saṭhesu, among the deceitful. Kataṃ, that which is done. Saññogasambhogavisesadassanaṃ, seeing the special benefit of association and mutual enjoyment. Nassati, perishes. Ariyesu, among the noble. Ajjavaesu, among the upright. Tādisu, among such as these. Aṇumpi, even a small. Kataṃ, favor done. Mahapphalaṃ, of great fruit. Hoti, is.

Yo, whichever person. Pubbe, in the past. Katakalyāṇo, having done a kindness. Loke, in the world. Sudukkaraṃ, that which is very difficult to do. Akā, performed. So, that person. Pacchā, at a later time. Kayirā vā, whether he does a favor. Na kayirā vā, or whether he does not do a favor. Accantaṃ, certainly. Pūjanāraho, is worthy of honor.

That gatekeeper said, "Come, I will show you," and taking the man by the hand, went to the palace gate and announced, "The gatekeeper has arrived, bringing a certain border villager."

The King, hearing these words, rose from his seat and said, "Let my friend and those who have come with him enter." He went out to welcome him, showing his affection, and asked, "Are my friend's wife and the children free from illness?" Taking him by the hand, he ascended to the magnificent upper terrace, seated him on the royal throne under the white parasol, and summoned the Chief Queen, saying, "O Queen, wash the feet of my friend." The Queen washed the feet of that border villager. The King poured water from a golden pitcher. The Queen also washed his feet and anointed them with scented oil.

The King asked, "Friend, is there any snack brought for us?" The man said, "There is," and took the cakes out of his bag. The King, receiving them in a golden bowl and wishing to show hospitality to the man, said, "Eat the snacks brought by my friend," and had the Queen and the ministers eat, and he himself ate as well.

The border villager also showed other gifts. To honor the man, the King removed his Kāsika garments and wore the pair of clothes brought by the border villager. The Queen also removed her Kāsika garments and ornaments and wore the clothes brought by the border villager.

Then the King had the border villager eat food fit for a king and commanded an official, "Go, have this man's beard and hair groomed in the same manner as mine, have him bathed in scented water, have him dressed in Kāsika cloth worth a hundred thousand, and have him adorned with royal ornaments and bring him back." That official did exactly as the King commanded.
11:
The King had the drums sounded to assemble the ministers. In the middle of the white parasol, he had a line drawn with pure vermilion and granted him half of the kingdom. From that time on, the two kings ate and slept together. Their intimacy was very firm, and no one could break it.

At that time, he also had the man's wife and children summoned, and had a house built for them within the city. The two kings reigned in harmony and joy.

The ministers were angry and said to the Prince, "Your Highness, the King has given half of the kingdom to a commoner. He eats, drinks, and sleeps with that commoner. He even makes the young ones pay respect to him. We do not understand the King's actions. What is the King doing? We are ashamed. You, Prince, should speak to the King."

The Prince agreed, reported all these words to the King, and said, "Great King, do not do this."

The King said, "My dear, do you truly know where I stayed when I lost the war?"

"Great King, I do not know," the Prince replied.

"I stayed in that man's house, recovered from my illness, and returned to rule. Why should I not give wealth to such a person who has done me a great favor?" To show that one who gives to those who should not be given to, but fails to give to those who deserve it, will find no one to help them when they encounter danger, the Bodhisatta spoke—

Upon hearing these words, neither the ministers nor the Prince said anything further.
12:
The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the villager from the border region, and I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī."

## When favors exist, return them; such people are noble
The Mahāassāroha Jātaka ends.

9. "In supreme sensual pleasures, well-endowed,
You lived before as the Sole King (Ekarāja).
Now cast into a miserable pit,
Why do you not lose your former complexion and strength?"

Thus he spoke this first verse.

Ekarāja: O King Ekarāja. So tvaṃ: You. Pubbe: In the past. Anuttare: In very noble. Samiddhe: In complete. Kāmaguṇe: In sensual pleasures. Bhutvāna: Having enjoyed. Vasi: You lived. Dāni: Now. Dugge: In an uneven. Narakamhi: In a pit. Khitto: Being suspended. Purāṇaṃ: Former. Vaṇṇabalaṃ: Complexion and strength. Nappajjahe: Why do you not lose?

## 3. Ekarāja Jātaka
## The Righteous King

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Ekarāja Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Anuttare kāmaguṇe samiddhe," concerning an obscure courtier who served the King of Kosala.

(The present story is told below in the Seyya Jātaka.) In this Ekarāja Jātaka, the All-Knowing Buddha said, "Lay follower, it is not only you who have brought benefit through misfortune; wise men of old also brought benefit through their own misfortune," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, a courtier of the King of Bārāṇasī committed an offense in the palace. The King, seeing the courtier's fault with his own eyes, banished him from the country. That courtier then served the King of Kosala named Dubbhisena.

(The full account is told in the Mahāsīlava Jātaka.)

In this Ekarāja Jātaka, King Dubbhisena captured the King of Bārāṇasī, who was sitting among his ministers on the magnificent terrace, placed him in a sling, and hung him upside down from the lintel of the north gate. The King of Bārāṇasī, focusing on the rebel king, developed loving-kindness (mettā), performed the preparatory work for kasiṇa meditation, and attained jhāna. His bonds were severed. Then, the King sat cross-legged in the air.
13:
A burning sensation arose in the body of the rebel king, and he cried out, "I am burning, I am burning!" as he rolled to and fro on the ground. When he asked, "What is this?" they replied, "Great King, you have hung such a righteous and innocent king upside down from the lintel of the north gate." He then said, "If that is so, go quickly and release him."

The King's men went and saw the King of Bārāṇasī sitting cross-legged in the air, and they returned to report this to King Dubbhisena. King Dubbhisena went quickly, paid homage to the King of Bārāṇasī, and in order to ask for forgiveness—

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta spoke these verses:

10. "Patience and austerity were previously desired by me, O Dubbhisena.
Now having attained them, O King,
Why should I lose my former complexion and strength?

11. All things are indeed thus accomplished,
For the glorious, the wise, and the enduring.
Having attained great former glory,
Why should one lose their former complexion and strength?

12. O Lord of men, one should dispel pleasure with pain,
Or pain with pleasure, through endurance.
In both states, the wise, being perfectly at peace,
Remain equal in both pleasure and pain."

Dubbhisena: O King Dubbhisena. Pubbeva: Even before. Mayhaṃ: By me. Khantī ca: Both patience. Tapo ca: And austerity. Sampatthitā: Were desired. Ahosi: It was so. Rāja: O King Dubbhisena. Idāni: Now. Ahaṃ: I. Taṃ: That desired patience and austerity. Laddhāna: Having attained. Purāṇaṃ: Former. Vaṇṇabalaṃ: Complexion and strength. Kathaṃ nu: For what reason. Jahe: Should I abandon?

Sabbā-sabbāni: All matters of giving, virtue, meditation, and observing the uposatha. Evaṃ pariniṭṭhitāni kira: Are indeed thus accomplished. Yasassinaṃ-yasassī: One who has a retinue. Paññavantaṃ-paññavā: One who is wise. Visayha: O King who can endure what is difficult to endure. Yaso ca: Even a person of wealth and status.
14:
Not obtained before; never obtained in the past. Noble, sublime happiness. Having obtained. Former; that which occurred in the past. Complexion and strength; should not abandon.

O King Dubbhisena, having discarded the royal happiness due to the suffering caused by you... or having discarded the suffering caused by you with the happiness of Jhana, one endures that which is difficult to endure. The virtuous ones, being of a peaceful nature, are equal in both happiness and suffering. They become the same.

Hearing these words, King Dubbhisena apologized to the Bodhisatta and said, "Your Majesty, please rule your own country yourself; I shall ward off your enemies," and after handing over the royal authority to that wicked minister, he departed.

The Bodhisatta also handed over the kingship to his ministers, renounced the world as an ascetic, and was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jataka: "At that time, Dubbhisena was Ānanda, and I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī."

## Loving-kindness, when practiced and developed, can lead to the attainment of Jhana.

The Ekarāja Jātaka ends.

## 4. Daddara Jātaka

## Living in a Dunghill for Three Years

The Present Story: While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Daddara Jātaka, starting with the verse "Imāni maṃ," concerning a certain wrathful monk.

(The present story is mentioned below.) At that time, while the monks were discussing that monk's wrathful nature in the Dhamma Hall, the Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what subject are you gathered here discussing now?" When they replied, "With such and such a subject," He had that monk summoned and asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are wrathful?"

When the monk replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Buddha said, "Monks, not only now is this monk wrathful; in the past too, he was wrathful. Because of his wrathful nature, the wise ones of old, even while established in the state of pure Naga kings, had to live for three years in an unclean place filled with excrement." Having said this, He brought forth the past story.
15:
13. These harsh words in the human world distress me, O Daddara.
Non-venomous ones insult me, a venomous snake,
calling me a frog-eater and a water-dweller.

He spoke this first verse.

Brother Daddara, elder brother Daddara. In the human world. These harshly spoken words. Me. Distress. Non-venomous village boys. A snake with swift poison. Me. Calling me a frog-eater. Or calling me a water-dweller. While saying so. They insult.

14. One banished from one's own country and gone to another land
should make a large granary to store harsh words.

15. Where people do not know a person by birth or conduct,
one should not be proud while living among strangers.

16. A wise man living in a foreign land should endure
even the threats of a slave, as if enduring fire.

He spoke these verses.

From one's own country. Being banished. To another land. One who has arrived. Harshly spoken words. To store. Large. Granary. Should make.

Where. A person. By birth. Or by conduct. They do not know. There. Pride, the thought of "I". Should not make. Among people who do not know one's virtues. One who lives. Should endure.

Living in a foreign land. One who lives. A wise man. Even of a slave. Even like fire. Threatening. Should endure.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a Naga named Mahādaddara, the son of the Naga King Daddara, who ruled in the Daddara Naga realm at the foot of Mount Daddara in the Himavant region. The younger brother of that Mahādaddara was named Cūḷadaddara.

Cūḷadaddara was wrathful and harsh. He went about insulting and striking the young Nagas. The Naga King, knowing his harsh nature, ordered Cūḷadaddara to be banished from the Naga realm. Mahādaddara, however, asked his father for forgiveness and prevented it. A second time, the King became angry with Cūḷadaddara, and a second time, Mahādaddara asked for forgiveness.

On the third occasion, the King said, "You prevent me from banishing this ill-behaved Naga. Both of you, leave this Naga realm and live in the dunghill in Bārāṇasī for three years." Thus, he banished them from the Naga realm.

Those two, Mahādaddara and Cūḷadaddara, went there and lived. At that time, while they were searching for food at the water's edge in the dunghill, village boys saw them and, striking them and throwing sticks and clods at them, insulted them, saying, "Friends, these water-snakes that eat green frogs have large heads and tails like needles," and so on.

Cūḷadaddara, because of his fierce and harsh nature, being unable to endure their contempt, spoke to his brother, saying, "Brother, these boys are insulting us. They do not know our nature as venomous snakes. I cannot endure their contempt. I will destroy them with the breath of my nostrils."
16:
Hearing the words of Cūḷadaddara, Mahādaddara said:

Thus, the two Nāgas, Mahādaddara and Cūḷadaddara, lived in the cesspool of Bārāṇasī for three years. After three years had passed, their father sent for the two brothers. From that time onwards, they were free from pride.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the angry monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmī-phala). To identify the Jātaka: "At that time, the angry monk was Cūḷadaddara, and I myself was Mahādaddara."

## Forbearing with those who do not know, one will surely find peace.

The Daddara Jātaka ends.

## 5. Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka
## Marrying the daughter to the virtuous one

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Teacher, the instructor of the world including the devas, told this Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Natthi loke raho nāma," concerning the suppression of defilements.

(The present story will become clear in the Pānīya Jātaka of the Ekādasaka Nipāta.) In this Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka, the summary of the story should be understood as follows:
17:
17. "There is no such thing as a secret place in the world for one who commits an evil deed.
Beings of the forest see it; the fool thinks it is a secret."

18. "I see no secret place, nor does a void exist.
Where I see no other person, that place is not empty of me."

He spoke these stanzas.

In the world, for one who commits an evil deed, there is no such thing as a secret place. The devas who dwell in the forest see it. The fool thinks of that evil deed, "It was done by me in secret."

I see no secret place. A place void of beings does not exist. Where I see no other person, that place is not empty of me, who committed the deed.

Five hundred monks, while residing within Jetavana Monastery, entertained sensual thoughts during the three watches of the night. The All-Enlightened Teacher, during all six portions of the day and night, constantly watches over the monks, just as a one-eyed man guards his eye with diligence, or as a father with an only son guards that son, or as a yak (camarī) guards its tail.

When the All-Enlightened Teacher looked over Jetavana with his divine eye during the night, he saw those monks like thieves who had appeared in the palace of a Universal Monarch. He opened the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), called the Elder Ānanda, and said, "Ānanda, assemble the monks who reside within Jetavana, which was purchased by spreading crores of coins, and prepare a seat at the door of the Perfumed Chamber."

Elder Ānanda did as the Buddha commanded and informed the Teacher. The All-Enlightened Teacher sat upon the prepared seat and, addressing all the monks collectively, said, "Monks, the wise of old did not commit evil, saying 'There is no secret place in the commission of evil.'" Being requested by those monks, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he came of age, he became the senior student among five hundred youths under a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) in that very city of Bārāṇasī.

The teacher had a daughter who had reached marriageable age. He thought, "I will test the virtue of these youths and give my daughter only to the one who is perfect in virtue." One day, he called the youths and said, "My sons, I have a daughter who has come of age. I wish to arrange her marriage. It is proper to obtain clothes and ornaments. Go and steal clothes and ornaments when your relatives are not looking. I will only accept what is taken when no one sees; I will not accept what is brought after being seen."

The disciples agreed, saying "Very well," and from then on, they stole clothes, ornaments, and so forth when their relatives were not looking and brought them. The teacher kept the items brought by each student separately.
18:
The Bodhisatta, however, did not bring any garment or ornament. Then the teacher said to the Bodhisatta, "Dear son, did you not bring any garment or ornament?" He replied, "Teacher, I did not." "Dear son, why did you not bring any?" he asked.

Wishing to show that he saw no place secret for doing evil, while the others brought garments and ornaments that were taken while someone was looking, he said:

The teacher, being pleased with the Bodhisatta, said, "Dear son, it is not that there is no wealth in my house. However, wishing to give my daughter to one endowed with virtue, I did this to test these youths. This daughter is a suitable match for you alone." Having adorned his daughter, he gave her to the Bodhisatta. To the remaining youths, he said, "Take back to your own houses the garments and ornaments you have brought, just as you brought them."

The Teacher, the Buddha, said, "Thus, monks, those immoral youths did not obtain that woman because of their own lack of virtue, while the wise youth obtained her because of being endowed with virtue." Having become fully enlightened, he spoke these verses:

19. "Dujjacca, Sujacca, Nanda, and Sukhavaddhita,
Vajja and Adhuvasīla—desiring the woman, they abandoned the Dhamma.

20. "How could a Brahmin, a master of all Dhammas,
Who protects the Dhamma, being firm and striving for truth, abandon it?"

[Explanation:] Dujjacca, Sujacca, Nanda, Sukhavaddhita, Vajja, and Adhuvasīla—these are the names of the six eldest youths. "They abandoned the Dhamma" means all those youths, being desirous of the woman, abandoned the nature of obtaining the woman [through virtue].

"How could a Brahmin" refers to the other Brahmin who was endowed with virtue. For what reason would he abandon the nature of obtaining the woman? "Master of all Dhammas" means one who has reached the further shore of all Dhammas, which in this context refers to the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the three types of right conduct. "Protects the Dhamma" means he guards the Dhamma. "Firm" means he possesses the firmness of guarding virtue. "Striving for truth" means he is endowed with exertion in the true nature of the aforementioned Dhamma of virtue. "How could that Brahmin abandon the nature of obtaining the woman?"
19:
Identifying the Birth: The Omniscient Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the five hundred monks were established in Arahantship. How did he identify the Birth? "At that time, Sāriputta was the teacher, and I myself was the wise youth." Thus he identified the Birth.

## For an evil deed, look closely; there is no secret place.

The Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka is concluded.

## 6. Sujāta Jātaka

## What fruit is this?

The Present Account: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Sujāta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kimaṇḍakā", concerning Queen Mallikā.

One day, a dispute arose between King Kosala and Queen Mallikā regarding their glory. (It is also said to be a "bedroom quarrel".) The King, being angry, ignored Mallikā's very existence. Queen Mallikā thought, "The Buddha probably does not know that the King is angry with me."

The Omniscient Buddha, knowing this and thinking, "I will bring about their reconciliation," dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robes, and entered Sāvatthī accompanied by five hundred monks, proceeding to the palace gate. The King took the Tathāgata's bowl, led him into the palace, and seated him on the prepared seat. Having poured the water of donation for the community of monks headed by the Buddha, he served rice gruel and hard food.
20:
21. "What are these eggs, O Lord, placed in a golden dish?
Reddish in color and beautiful—tell me when I ask."

[Explanation:] "O Lord, King. These fruits of reddish color and without impurity are placed in a golden dish. These fruits, round like eggs—what fruits are they? O King, being asked, please tell me about those fruits."

22. "Those which you formerly, O Queen, with hair disheveled and wearing rags,
Gathered with your hands into your lap—those are the jujube fruits of your kind.

23. "This wretched woman burns while living in the royal house and finds no delight;
Royal enjoyments are leaving her. Take her back to that very house
Where she will live by gathering jujubes."

[Explanation:] "O Queen, formerly, those jujubes which you gathered with your hair hanging down, wearing worn-out rags, and putting them into your lap with your hands—this fruit that I am eating is the jujube fruit given by your own kind. This wretched woman, while living in the royal palace, is feverish and finds no delight. The King's enjoyments are abandoning her. Take this wretched woman back to that very house where she will live by selling jujubes."

The Omniscient Buddha covered his bowl with his hand and asked, "Great King, where is the Queen?" The King replied, "Venerable Sir, what is the use of that woman who is intoxicated by her own glory and retinue?" The Omniscient Buddha said, "Great King, it is not right for you, who yourself gave her glory and raised her up, to be intolerant of a fault committed by that woman."

The King, having heard the Buddha's advice, had Queen Mallikā summoned. Queen Mallikā then attended to the Buddha. The Omniscient Buddha, having preached on the benefits of harmony, saying, "You should be in harmony with one another," departed. From then on, the King and Queen lived in harmony.

The monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the Omniscient Buddha, with just a single word, brought about reconciliation between the King and Queen." 

The Omniscient Buddha came and asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered now?" When they replied, "For such and such a conversation," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have reconciled them with a single word; in the past also, I reconciled them with just a single instruction." Being requested by the monks, he brought forth the past story.
21:
24. These faults of negligence, O Great King, occur in a woman who has attained prosperity. Forgive Queen Sujāta, O Lord; do not be angry with her, O Chief of Charioteers.

Thus he spoke this verse.

Mahārāja, O Great King. Iddhippattāya, to a woman who has attained fame and followers. Nariyā, of a woman. Ete pamādadosā, these faults of negligence. Honti hi, indeed occur. Mahārāja, O Great King. Sujātāya, to Queen Sujāta. Khama, please be patient and forgive. Rathesabha, O Lord, most excellent among those who ride chariots. Assā, to that Queen Sujāta. Mā kujjha, do not be angry.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a minister who advised the King on matters of welfare. One day, the King opened the wind-window and stood looking at the palace courtyard.

At that time, a beautiful young woman named Sujāta, a vegetable seller's daughter, was walking through the palace courtyard carrying a basket of jujubes on her head, calling out, "Buy jujubes! Buy jujubes!" The King, hearing Sujāta's voice, became infatuated with her. Learning she was unmarried, he had her summoned, appointed her as his Chief Queen, and gave her great wealth.

The King loved Sujāta dearly. One day, the King was eating jujubes from a golden dish. Queen Sujāta, seeing the King eating jujubes, and wishing to ask, "O Great King, what kind of fruit are you eating?"—

The King became angry and said, "You daughter of a vegetable seller, a jujube seller! Do you not even recognize the jujubes that were the property of your own kinsfolk?"

The Bodhisatta thought, "Except for me, no one else will be able to reconcile this King and Queen. I will appease the King and prevent him from expelling the Queen." He then spoke the verse.

By the words of the Bodhisatta, the King forgave the Queen's fault and restored her to her former position. From then on, the King and Queen lived together in harmony.

Identifying the Birth: The Omniscient Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Birth: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was the King of Kosala, Sujāta was Mallikā, and I myself was the minister."

## Forgetting one's past and being arrogant leads to danger.

The Sujāta Jātaka is concluded.

## 7. Palāsa Jātaka

## The Benefit of Service

The Present Account: The Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Palāsa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Aceṭanaṃ brāhmaṇa assuṇantaṃ", while lying on his deathbed at the time of his Parinibbāna, concerning the Elder Ānanda.

The Venerable Elder Ānanda, knowing that the Buddha would attain Parinibbāna at dawn, was overcome with grief, thinking, "I am still a trainee (sekha) with work yet to be done, and my Teacher is about to pass away. My twenty-five years of service to the Omniscient Buddha will be in vain." He stood leaning against the doorpost of a garden cell and wept.
22:
"My service has been in vain," he thought, overcome with grief, and leaning against the doorpost of the garden cell, he wept. The Teacher, not seeing him, asked the monks, "Monks, where is Ānanda?" Having heard the reason and having him summoned, he said, "Ānanda, you have performed merit. Strive with great effort, and you will soon become an Arahant. Do not worry, Ānanda. Why should your service to me be in vain now? Even in the past, when I was still subject to passion, your service to me was not without benefit." Then he told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a tree deity in a Palāsa tree not too far from Bārāṇasī. At that time, the people of Bārāṇasī were worshippers of deities and were constantly engaged in making offerings.

At that time, a poor Brahmin thought, "I too will serve a deity." He cleared the grass around the base of a large Palāsa tree on high ground, scattered sand, swept it, marked the tree with scented five-finger marks, worshipped it with flowers, scents, and incense, lit a lamp, said "May you sleep well," circumambulated the tree, and left. On the second day, he went early and asked if the tree had slept well.

One day, the tree deity thought, "This Brahmin serves me very much. I will test him and find out why he serves me, and then I will give him what he desires."

25. Acetanaṃ brāhmaṇa assuṇantaṃ,
Jāno ajānantamimaṃ palāsaṃ.
Āraddhavīriyo dhuvaṃ appamatto,
Sukhasayyaṃ pucchasi kissa hetu.

He spoke this first verse:

"O Brahmin, for what reason do you, knowing it is insentient, ask this Palāsa tree—which cannot hear because it lacks consciousness and does not know—if it has slept well, with such persistent effort and constant diligence?"

26. Dūre suto ceva brahā ca rukkho,
Dese thito bhūtanivāsarūpo.
Tasmā namassāmi imaṃ palāsaṃ,
Ye cettha bhūtā te dhanassa hetu.

He spoke this second verse:

"O Brahmin, this tree is famous even from afar and it is large. It stands on high, level ground and is a dwelling place for spirits. Therefore, I pay homage to this Palāsa tree. And the powerful spirits who dwell here, I pay homage to them too, for the sake of wealth."

When the Omniscient Buddha did not see Ānanda, he asked the monks, "Where is Ānanda?" and had him summoned to advise him, saying, "Ānanda, you have performed merit in the past. Strive with great effort, and you will soon become an Arahant. Ānanda, do not worry. Why should your service to me be in vain now? Even in the past, when I was still subject to passion, your service to me was not without benefit." Then he told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a tree deity in a Palāsa tree not too far from Bārāṇasī. At that time, the people of Bārāṇasī were worshippers of deities. They were constantly engaged in making offerings to the deities.

At that time, a poor Brahmin thought, "I too will serve a deity." He cleared the grass around the base of a large Palāsa tree on high ground, scattered sand, swept it, marked the tree with scented five-finger marks, worshipped it with flowers, scents, and incense, lit a lamp, said "May you sleep well," circumambulated the tree, and left. On the second day, he went early and asked if the tree had slept well.

One day, the tree deity thought, "This Brahmin serves me very much..."
23:
27. "I will do for you according to my power,
O Brahmin, seeing your gratitude.
How could your efforts in the presence of the virtuous,
Be in vain?"

28. "Beyond the Tinduka tree is a Pilakkha tree,
Surrounded, an ancient place of sacrifice, and grand.
At its root, this treasure is buried,
With no heir; go and dig it up."

Thus, the deity spoke these verses.

Brahmin, O Brahmin. *So ahaṃ*, I. *Kataññutaṃ*, the state of knowing the favor you have done. *Pekkhamāno*, seeing. *Yathānubhāvaṃ*, according to my ability. *Te*, to you. *Karissāmi*, I shall do a favor. *Hi-saccaṃ*, that word is true. *Sataṃ*, of the virtuous. *Sakāse*, in the presence. *Kataṃ*, having reached the performance of service. *Te*, your. *Pariphanditāni*, efforts made by body and speech. *Moghāni*, in vain and without benefit. *Kathaṃ assu*, how could they be?

*Samma brāhmaṇa*, friend Brahmin. *Tindukarukkhassa*, of the Tinduka tree. *Paro*, standing behind. *Yo pilakkho*, which Pilakkha tree. *Atthi*, there is. *Tasseva*, of that very Pilakkha tree. *Mūlasmiṃ*, at the root. *Parivārito*, surrounding the Pilakkha tree. *Pubbayañño*, having been a place of sacrifice in the past. *Uḷāro*, great. *Nikhāto*, buried. *Esa- eso nidhi*, this pot of gold. *Adāyādo*, now has no heir. *Gaccha*, go. *Taṃ*, that treasure. *Uddharāhi*, dig up and take.

Thinking, "I will test this Brahmin and give him the reason for which he serves me," the tree deity, at that moment when the Brahmin came and swept, stood nearby in the form of an old Brahmin and—

Hearing those words, the Brahmin—

Hearing those words, the tree deity, being pleased with the Brahmin, comforted him saying, "Brahmin, I am the deity born in this Butea tree; do not be afraid, I shall give you wealth," and standing in the sky by great divine power at the door of his celestial mansion—

Having spoken thus, the tree deity said, "Brahmin, if you dig up and take that treasure pot, you will be exhausted; you go ahead,"
24:
"I myself will carry those treasures to your house and bury them in such and such a place. Use that wealth throughout your life, give alms, and keep the precepts," thus advising the Brahmin, the deity established that wealth in the Brahmin's house by his own power.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, the Brahmin was Ānanda, and the tree deity was I myself."

## By honoring a noble deity, prosperity can arise.
The Palāsa Jātaka ends.

## 8. Sakuṇa Jātaka
## The Ungrateful Lion

While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the All-Knowing Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, spoke this Sakuṇa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ," concerning the ingratitude of Devadatta.

"Monks, not only now is Devadatta ungrateful; in the past also, he was indeed ungrateful," the Teacher said, and brought forth the past story.

In the past, monks, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a woodpecker in the Himālaya region. At that time, a bone got stuck in the throat of a certain lion while he was eating meat. His throat became swollen. He was unable to take food. Severe pain set in.

Then, the woodpecker, while searching for food, saw the lion and, perching on a branch, asked, "Friend lion, what is your suffering?" The lion told him the matter. "Friend lion, I would remove that bone stuck in your throat, but I do not dare enter your mouth because I am afraid of you; you might eat me," said the woodpecker. "Friend woodpecker, do not be afraid, I will not eat you; give me my life," said the lion.
25:
30. "To me who feeds on blood,
And always performs cruel deeds,
That you are alive after entering between my teeth,
Is a great favor to you."

Thus, he spoke this second verse.

*Bho sakuṇa*, O bird. *Dantantaragato*, having reached between the teeth. *Santo*, being. *Tvaṃ*, you. *Yampi jīvasi*, that you still live. *Taṃ*, that living. *Lohitabhakkhassa*, for me who drinks and eats blood. *Niccaṃ*, always. *Luddāni*, cruel deeds. *Kubbato*, for me who performs. *Mama*, my. *Bahuṃ*, is a great honor (favor) to you.

31. "One who is ungrateful and does nothing,
Who makes no return for what was done,
In whom gratitude does not exist,
Service to him is useless."

32. "One from whom friendship is not gained,
Despite favors done in his presence,
Without envying or abusing him,
One should slowly depart from him."

Thus, he spoke these two verses.

*Yasmiṃ*, in whom. *Kataññutā*, the state of knowing gratitude. *Natthi*, does not exist. *Tassa*, to that ungrateful person. *Sevanā*, association/service. *Niratthā*, is useless. *Mittadhammo*, a person who does favors. *Yassa*, of whom. *Sammukhaciṇṇena*, by favors done in his presence. *Na labbhati*, does not receive benefit. *Katassa*, to the one who has done a favor. *Akataññuṃ*, one who does not know the favor. *Akattāraṃ*, one who does nothing. *Appaṭikārakaṃ*, one who does not return the favor. *Anusūyaṃ*, without envying. *Anakkosaṃ*, without abusing. *Tamhā*, from that ungrateful person. *Saṇikaṃ*, slowly and gently. *Apakkame*, one should depart.

The woodpecker, saying "Very well," made the lion lie on his right side. Thinking, "Who knows what might happen?" he placed a stick between the lion's lower and upper lips so that he could not close his mouth. He then entered the mouth and struck the end of the bone with his beak. The bone fell out. After making the bone fall, as he was exiting the lion's mouth, he struck the propped stick with his beak to make it fall and then flew out to perch on a tree branch.

The lion, having recovered, one day killed a forest buffalo and was eating it. The woodpecker, wishing to test the lion, perched on a branch above him and, desiring to speak with the lion—

29. "We have done your task,
As much as was in our power.
O King of Beasts, salutation to you!
May we receive something?"

Thus, he spoke this first verse.

*Migarāja*, King of Beasts. *Te*, to you. *Namo*, salutation. *Atthu*, let there be. *Yaṃ balaṃ*, whatever power. *Amhākaṃ*, to us. *Ahuvamhase-ahosi*, there was. *Tena balena*, by that power. *Te*, your. *Kiccaṃ*, task. *Mayaṃ*, we. *Akaramhasa*, have done. *Mayaṃ*, we. *Kiñci api*, even a little meat. *Labhāmahse*, shall we receive?

Hearing those words, the lion—

Hearing those words, the woodpecker—

Having spoken thus, the woodpecker departed.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, the lion was Devadatta, and the woodpecker was I myself."

## The ungrateful person who discards favors is indeed a base person.
The Sakuṇa Jātaka ends.
26:
## 9. Chava Jātaka
## Educating by Choosing the Right Place

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Chava Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sabbamidam carimam katam," concerning the Chabbaggiya monks.

(The story of the present is found in detail in the Vinaya. In this Chava Jātaka, only the summary should be known.)

The All-Knowing Buddha summoned the Chabbaggiya monks and asked, "Monks, is it true that you sit on low seats and preach the Dhamma to those sitting on high seats?" When they replied, "It is true, Bhante," He rebuked them, saying, "Monks, it is improper to show disrespect to the Dhamma. Wise men of old also rebuked those who taught the Vedas while sitting on low seats." He then told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Caṇḍāla family. When he reached maturity, he earned his wealth. The Bodhisatta's wife had a pregnancy craving and said to the Bodhisatta, "My lord, I wish to eat a mango." The Bodhisatta replied, "Dear lady, there are no mangoes at this time. I will bring you some other sour fruit." She said, "My lord, I will live only if I get a mango; if I do not, I shall die."

The Bodhisatta, with a heart attached to the woman, thought, "Where can I find a mango?" At that time, there was a mango tree in the King of Bārāṇasī's garden that bore fruit constantly. Thinking, "I will take a ripe mango from there and satisfy her craving," he went to the garden at night, climbed the mango tree, and hid, looking among the branches for fruit. While he was doing this, dawn broke. He thought, "If I descend and leave now, they will see me and catch me as a thief. I will leave at night." Having thought so, he climbed into a fork of the tree and remained hidden.

At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī entered the garden to learn the Vedas from the Chaplain. He sat on a high seat at the foot of the mango tree and made the teacher sit on a low seat to teach him the Vedas.

The Bodhisatta, hiding above, thought, "This King who sits on a high seat to learn the Vedas is unrighteous. This Brahmin who sits on a low seat to teach the Vedas is also unrighteous. I, too, am unrighteous, for I follow the will of a woman and steal mangoes without regard for my own life." Thinking thus, as he descended from the mango tree, he held onto a low-hanging branch and stood between the King and the Brahmin, saying, "O Great King, I am ruined, you are deluded, and the Chaplain is dead (to virtue)."
27:
33. "All this is done basely; both do not see the Dhamma.
Both have fallen from their natural state—he who teaches the mantras,
And he who learns the mantra."

34. "I eat the meal of Sāli rice, pure and seasoned with meat.
Therefore, I do not practice this Dhamma practiced by the sages."

He spoke this second verse.

I (Aham), the Brahmin, eat (bhuñje) the King's (rañño) property (santakam), the pure (sucim) rice (odanam) of Sāli (sālīnam) seasoned with meat (maṃsūpasecanaṃ). Therefore (tasmā), I do not practice (na sevāmi) that Dhamma (etaṃ dhammaṃ) practiced (sevitaṃ) by the sages (isīhi), the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas.

35. "Go forth, the world is large; other beings also cook food.
Do not let the unrighteousness you practice break you like a stone breaks a pot."

36. "Fie upon that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O Brahmin,
Which is obtained by downfall or by unrighteous conduct."

He spoke these two verses.

Brahmin (brāhmaṇa), the world (loko nāma) is vast (mahā). Go to another place (paribbaja). Other beings (aññepi pāṇino) besides the King also cook rice (pacanti). Just as a stone (asmā) breaks (bhindati iva) a pot (kumbhaṃ), do not let the unrighteousness (adhammo) you have practiced (ācarito) break (mā abhidā) you (taṃ).

Brahmin (brāhmaṇa), whether by falling into the woeful states (vinipātena vā) or by practicing unrighteousness (adhammacaraṇena vā), whatever gain of prosperity (yā vutti) arises (uppajjati), we censure (dhiratthu-garahāma) that gain of fame (taṃ yasalābhañca) and that gain of wealth (taṃ dhanalābhañca).

When asked by the King why he spoke thus, the Bodhisatta spoke this first verse:

"And he who learns the mantra."

All (sabbaṃ) this action (idaṃ kiccaṃ) performed by the three of us is a base deed (carimaṃ kataṃ). This Brahmin (yo cāyaṃ) who sits on a low seat (nīcāsane nisīditvā) and teaches the mantras (mantre ajjhapeti), and this King (yo ca) who sits on a high seat (ucce āsane nisīditvā) and learns the mantra (mantaṃ adhīyati)—both (ubho) of you do not see (na passare) the Dhamma (dhammaṃ). Both (ubho) of you have fallen away (cutā) from the natural state of Dhamma (pakatiyā).

Hearing this, the Brahmin said:
28:
36. "Fie upon that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O Brahmin,
Which is obtained by downfall or by unrighteous conduct."

Hearing these words, the Bodhisatta spoke:

At that time, the King was pleased with the Bodhisatta's Dhamma talk and asked, "Good man, of what caste are you?" "I am a Caṇḍāla, O King," he replied. "Good man, if you were of noble birth, I would give you the kingship. From this day forth, I shall be the King by day, and you shall be the King by night." So saying, the King took the flower garland from his own neck and placed it on the Bodhisatta's neck, appointing him as the City Guard (Nagarguttika).

This practice of wearing a flower garland on the neck became the tradition of City Guards wearing red flower garlands. From then on, the King remained established in the Bodhisatta's advice, showed respect to his teacher, and sat on a low seat to learn the Vedas.

Identification of the Birth: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King was Ānanda, and the Caṇḍāla's son was I myself."

## When it comes to the Dhamma, be truly respectful.

The Chava Jātaka ends.
29:
## 10. Seyya Jātaka
## Renouncing Status for the Forest

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Seyya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sasamuddapariyāyaṃ," concerning a dissatisfied monk.

While that monk was wandering for alms in the city of Sāvatthī, he saw a beautiful, well-adorned woman and became dissatisfied with the Sasana (the holy life). Then, the monks informed the Omniscient Buddha. The Omniscient Buddha asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha asked, "Who has made you dissatisfied?" and the monk reported the matter.

The Omniscient Buddha said, "Monk, why are you dissatisfied with such a Sasana that leads out of the suffering of Saṃsāra? In the past, wise men, even when they obtained the position of Chaplain (Purohita), rejected that position and became monks." Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the Chaplain's wife and was born on the same day as the King's son. The King asked his ministers, "Is there any child born on the same day as my son?" They replied, "Great King, there is the son of the Chaplain."

The King had the Chaplain's son brought and gave him to the nurses to be raised together with the Prince. The ornaments, drinks, and food for both boys were identical.

When they reached the proper age, they went together to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and returned. The King appointed his son as the Viceroy (Uparāja), and the Viceroy possessed great wealth and retinue. From that time on, the Bodhisatta ate, drank, and slept together with the Prince. Their intimacy was firm.

Later, when the Prince ascended to the throne upon his father's passing, he enjoyed great prosperity. The Bodhisatta thought, "My friend is ruling the country. At the moment he remembers me, he will surely give me the position of Chaplain. What is the use of me living in a house? I will become a monk and cultivate seclusion (viveka)."

Having so thought, the Bodhisatta paid respects to his parents, asked for their permission to become a monk, abandoned his great wealth, and departed alone for the forest. Entering the Himālaya, he built a hermitage in a delightful spot, became an ascetic, attained the supernormal powers (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and lived enjoying the bliss of Jhāna.
30:
37. Sasamuddapariyāyaṃ, mahiṃ sāgarakuṇḍalaṃ.
Na icche saha nindāya, evaṃ seyya vijānahi.
38. Dhiratthu taṃ yasalābhaṃ, dhanalābhañca brāhmaṇa.
Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena vā.
39. Api ce pattamadāya, anagāro paribbaje.
Sāyeva jīvikā seyyo, yā cādhammena esanā.
40. Api ce pattamadāya, anagāro paribbaje.
Aññaṃ ahiṃsayaṃ loke, api rajjena taṃ varaṃ.

He spoke these verses:

Seyya, O Minister Seyya! Because it is accompanied by blame, I do not desire the earth (mahiṃ) which is surrounded by the oceans (sasamuddapariyāyaṃ) and which has the sea as its earring (sāgarakuṇḍalaṃ). Know this (vijānāhi) to be so (evaṃ).

Brahmin! Whether it be by falling into the lower realms (vinipātena) or by unrighteous conduct (adhammacaraṇena), whatever gain of wealth (yā vutti) arises, we despise (dhiratthu) that gain of fame (taṃ yasalābhaṃ) and that gain of wealth (taṃ dhanalābhaṃ).

Rather than the search for wealth (yā ca esanā) through unrighteousness (adhammena), it is better (seyyo) to live that very life (sāyeva jīvikā) of wandering for alms (paribbaje) taking a bowl (pattama dāya) as a homeless one (anagāro).

If one wanders for alms (paribbaje) taking a bowl (pattama dāya) as a homeless one (anagāro), without harming others (aññaṃ ahiṃsayaṃ) in the world (loke), that life is more excellent (varaṃ) even than kingship (rajjena api).

At that time, the King remembered the Bodhisatta and asked, "My friend is not seen. Where is he?" The ministers informed him of the Bodhisatta's renunciation, saying, "He is living in a delightful forest grove." The King asked for the Bodhisatta's location and said to the minister named Seyya, "Go, bring my friend back. I will give him the position of Chaplain."

That minister Seyya agreed, saying "Very well," and departed from Bārāṇasī. In due course, he reached the border country, established a camp in a village there, and went with forest-dwellers to the Bodhisatta's dwelling place. Seeing the Bodhisatta sitting at the door of his leaf-hut like a golden statue, he paid respects, sat in a suitable place, and after exchanging greetings, said, "Bhante, the King wishes to give you the position of Chaplain and desires your return."

The Bodhisatta replied, "Let alone the position of Chaplain, even if I were to receive the kingship of the entire Jambudīpa, including the Kāsi and Kosala kingdoms, or the glory of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), I would not go. Indeed, wise men do not take back the defilements (kilesa) once they have been discarded. That which has been discarded once is like a gob of spit."

In this way, although the minister repeatedly entreated him, the Bodhisatta rejected that entreaty.
31:
The minister Seyya, not having won the mind of the Bodhisatta, paid homage to him and departed, then reported the Bodhisatta's refusal to return to the King.

Identifying the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the monk who was dissatisfied with the Dispensation was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Many other monks also realized the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. How did he identify the Jātaka? At that time, Ānanda was the King, Sāriputta was the minister named Seyya, and I myself was the ascetic, the son of the chaplain. Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Renouncing the Mundane, Seeking the Supramundane for Refuge

The Seyya Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Pucimanda Vagga
## 1. Pucimanda Jātaka
## The Neem Tree Deity

The Present Story: While the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, he told this Pucimanda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Uṭṭhehi cora", concerning the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna.

While the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna was staying in a forest hut near Rājagaha, a certain thief broke into a house in a village at the city gate, took the valuables, and fled. He entered the precinct of the Elder's hut, thinking, "Here I will be protected," and lay down at the entrance of the Elder's dwelling.

The Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, knowing that the thief was sleeping at the entrance, felt apprehensive about him. Thinking, "Association with a thief is not proper," he went out and drove him away, saying, "Do not sleep here." The thief left the dwelling, obscured his tracks, and fled.
32:
1. "Rise up, thief! Why do you sleep? What use is sleep to you? Let not the King's men catch you, the evildoer in the village."

He spoke this first verse. 
Thief (cora), rise up (uṭṭhehi). Why (kiṃ) do you sleep (sesi)? What use (ko attho) is sleep (supanena) to you (te)? Let not the King's men (rājāno) catch (mā gahesuṃ) you (taṃ), the one who commits a cruel act (kibbisa-kārakaṃ) in the village (gāme).

2. "Whatever thief they may catch, the evildoer in the village, what is that to the Neem tree deity standing in the forest?"

He spoke this second verse.
Whatever (yaṃ) catching they will do to the thief (coraṃ), the evildoer (kibbisa-kārakaṃ) in the village (gāme). When that thief is caught (tattha), what is it (kiṃ nu) to the Neem tree deity (pucimandassa) who is born (jātassa) and stands (tiṭṭhato) in the forest (vane)?

People, taking torches and following the thief's tracks, came to that dwelling. Seeing the places where the thief had come, stood, sat, and slept, they said, "The thief came from here, stood here, sat here, slept here, and fled from this place. We do not see him." They searched here and there, and not seeing him, they returned.

The next day, the Elder Mahā Moggallāna, having wandered for alms in Rājagaha in the morning and returned from his alms round, went to the Veḷuvana Monastery and reported the matter to the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Moggallāna, it is not only you who felt apprehension for one who should be suspected; the wise of old also felt apprehension." Being requested by the Elder, he brought forth the past.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a Neem tree deity (Nimba) in the city's cemetery forest. At that time, one day, a thief who had committed a crime in a village at the city gate entered the cemetery forest. In that cemetery, there were two large trees: a Neem tree and a Sacred Fig tree (Assattha). The thief placed his bundle of goods at the foot of the Neem tree and lay down.

At that time, they used to catch thieves and impale them on Neem-wood stakes. Then the Neem tree deity thought, "If people come and catch this thief, they will cut a branch of this Neem tree, make a stake, and impale him. If that happens, the tree will be destroyed. Now, I will drive the thief away from this Neem tree." Having thought so, the Neem tree deity, wishing to speak with the thief—
33:
3. "You do not know, O Assattha, the relation between me and the thief. When the King's men catch the thief, the evildoer in the village, they impale him on a Neem stake. At that, my mind is apprehensive."

He spoke this third verse.
O Assattha tree deity (assattha), you (tvaṃ) do not know (na jānāsi) the reason (antaraṃ) why I (mama ca) and the thief (corassa ca) should not stay together. When the King's men (rājāno) catch (gahetvā) the thief (coraṃ), the evildoer (kibbisa-kārakaṃ) in the village (gāme), they impale him (appenti) on a Neem-wood stake (nimbasūlasmiṃ). At that act (tasmiṃ), my (me) mind (mano) is apprehensive (saṅkate).

4. "One should suspect what is to be suspected; one should guard against future danger. Fearing future danger, the wise man looks to both worlds."

He spoke this fourth verse.
A wise man (dhīro) should suspect (saṅkeyya) what is to be suspected (saṅkitabbāni). One should guard against (rakkheyya) future danger (anāgataṃ bhayaṃ). Because of future danger (anāgatabhayā), he looks to (avekkhati) both worlds (ubho loke).

Having said this to the thief, the deity frightened him, saying, "Go elsewhere before the King's men catch you," and made him flee. When the thief had fled, the Assattha tree deity [spoke the second verse].

Hearing that, the Neem tree deity [spoke the third verse].

While the tree deities were thus conversing with each other, the owners of the goods, carrying torches and following the tracks, arrived. Seeing the place where the thief had slept, they said, "Friends, the thief has just risen and fled. We have not caught the thief. If we catch him, we will impale him on a stake of this very Neem tree or hang him from a branch and then go." They searched here and there, and not seeing the thief, they departed.

Hearing their words, the Assattha tree deity spoke the fourth verse.
34:
The Master, having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, identified the birth-story: "At that time, Ānanda was the deity of the Assattha tree, and I myself was the deity of the Nimba tree."

## Foreseeing danger from all sides, avoidance is not difficult.

The Pucimanda Jātaka is concluded.

## 2. Kassapamandiya Jātaka

## Patience towards Elders

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kassapamandiya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Api Kassapa mandiyā," concerning an elderly monk.

In Sāvatthī, a certain son of a good family, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, ordained in the presence of the Buddha. While practicing meditation, he soon attained the fruit of Arahantship. Later, his mother passed away.

Upon his mother's death, he ordained his father and younger brother. While living at Jetavana Monastery, hearing that robes and requisites were easily obtainable at a certain village monastery as the time for the rains retreat approached, the three of them went there to observe the retreat. After the retreat, they returned to Jetavana. At a place near Jetavana, the young monk said, "Novice, let the Elder rest and then bring him along; I will go ahead to clean the living quarters," and he entered Jetavana.

The elderly monk walked slowly. The novice, as if repeatedly pushing him with his head, forced him along, saying, "Go, Bhante! Go, Bhante!" The Elder, saying, "You are bringing me under your own will," turned back and started walking again from the beginning. While the father and son were thus quarreling with each other, the sun set and it became dark.

The other monk, having swept the precincts and prepared the water, did not see them coming. He took a torch and went out to meet them. Seeing them approaching, he asked, "Why are you so late?" The elderly monk told him the reason. The young monk then let both the Elder and the novice rest and brought them along gently. On that day, they did not get the opportunity to attend upon the Buddha.
35: On the second day, when they came to the Buddha, paid homage, and sat down, the Omniscient Buddha asked the monk, "Monk, when did you arrive?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, we arrived yesterday." "Having arrived yesterday, do you only now come to attend upon me?" the Buddha asked. The monk replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir," and explained the reason. The Omniscient Buddha rebuked the elderly Elder, saying, "Monk, not only now has this old man acted in such a way; he did so in the past as well. Now he has troubled you, but in the past, he troubled the wise." At the monk's request, the Buddha related the past story. The Past Account: Long ago, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a village of Kāsi. When he reached maturity, his mother died. After performing the funeral rites for his mother, and after a month or half a month had passed, he gave away the wealth in the house as alms. Taking his father and younger brother, he went to the Himalayan region, took up the ascetic life with bark garments given by the devas, and lived in a pleasant forest grove, subsisting on roots and wild fruits. In the Himalayas, during the rainy season when it rains incessantly, it is not possible to dig for roots, and fruits and leaves fall. Most ascetics leave the Himalayas and live in human habitations. At that time, the Bodhisatta took his father and brother to live in the human world. When the Himalayas were again full of flowers and fruits, he took them both and returned to his own hermitage in the Himalayas. As the sun was setting near the hermitage, he said, "You two come slowly;"
36:
5. Even if, Kassapa, out of ignorance, a youth insults or strikes,
the wise man forgives all; the sage endures it.
6. If the virtuous quarrel, they are soon reconciled again.
Fools break like clay pots; they do not find peace.
7. These [virtuous] ones come together again; their bond does not decay.
He who knows his own fault, and he who knows how to accept an apology.
8. He is indeed superior, a bearer of the burden, a sustainer of the yoke,
who is able to reconcile himself with others who have offended.
These four verses were spoken.

Kassapa, O Kassapa. Api, indeed. Mandiyā, because of being foolish or ignorant. Yuvā, a youth. Sapati vā, may insult. Hanti vā, or may strike. Dhīro, the wise man. Taṃ sabbaṃ, all that. Khamate, forgives. Paṇḍito, the sage. Taṃ, that insult or assault. Titikkhati, endures.

Santo, the virtuous. Sacepi vivadanti, even if they quarrel. Puna, again. Khippaṃ, quickly. Sandhīyare, they are reconciled. Bālā, fools. Pattāva, like clay pots. Bhijjanti, are easily broken. Te, those fools. Samathaṃ, towards peace/reconciliation. Na ajjhagū, do not reach.

Yo ca, and he who. Adhipannaṃ, the fault. Jānāti, knows. Yo ca, and he who. Desanaṃ, the confession or apology. Jānāti, knows [how to accept]. Ete, these people. Bhiyyo, again. Samāyanti, are united. Tesaṃ, of them. Sandhi, the bond of affection. Na jīrati, does not decay.

Yo, he who. Adhipannānaṃ, towards those who have committed a fault. Paresaṃ, others. Sayaṃ, himself. Sandhātuṃ, to reconcile. Arahati, is worthy. Eso, that person. [Is] uttaritaro, more excellent than those previously mentioned. Bhāravaho dhuraddharo, a bearer of the burden and sustainer of the yoke of friendship.

Saying, "I will go ahead and clean the monastery," the Bodhisatta left the father and son behind and departed.

As the young ascetic walked slowly with the elder ascetic, he walked as if pressing the elder's head with his own head two or three times. The elder ascetic said, "You are leading me according to your own will," and they turned back to start from the beginning. While the elder and younger ascetics were thus quarreling, it became dark.

The Bodhisatta, having swept the monastery, fetched water, and holding a torch, came to meet them on the road. Seeing the young and elder ascetics, he asked, "What have you been doing for so long?" The young ascetic told him what the father had done.

The Bodhisatta gently led both ascetics, stored their requisites, let the father bathe, washed his feet, performed massages such as rubbing with a stone, and provided a charcoal brazier to relieve his fatigue. Then, sitting near the father, he thought of admonishing him, saying, "Father, those who are like children are like clay pots; they break in an instant, and once broken, they cannot be mended. Even if children insult them, elders should endure it." Thus, wishing to advise the father, he said:
37:
In this way, the Bodhisatta gave advice to his father. From that time on, the father became disciplined and well-trained.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the elderly monk was the father ascetic. The novice was the young ascetic. I myself was the ascetic who gave advice to the father."

## Whether caused by oneself or others, many suffer.
The Kassapa-Mandiya Jātaka ends.

## 3. Khantivādī Jātaka
## Incomparable Patience

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Khantivādī Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yo te hatthe ca pāde ca," concerning a certain wrathful monk.

(The story of the present has been told below.) The All-Knowing Buddha said to that monk, "Bhikkhu, why do you give way to anger after ordaining in the Dispensation of the Buddha who is free from anger? Sages of old did not show anger toward others even when they were struck with a thousand blows, or when their hands, feet, ears, and noses were severed." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Kalābu reigned in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family with eighty crores of wealth. His name was young Kuṇḍala. When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and accumulated wealth. After his parents passed away, he looked at the pile of wealth and thought, "My relatives have departed without taking this wealth. I, however, should take it with me [by way of merit]." He then distributed all the wealth through discerning charity to whoever brought it. He entered the Himavantā, became an ascetic, and lived for a long time subsisting on wild fruits. Later, to seek salt and acidic foods, he returned to the world of men and eventually reached Bārāṇasī. He stayed in the royal garden, and the next day, while wandering for alms in the city, he reached the gate of the General's (Senāpati) house.
