The General, impressed by the Bodhisatta's deportment, invited him inside, fed him with food prepared for himself, received a promise from him to stay, and settled him in that very royal garden.

Then one day, King Kalābu, intoxicated with liquor and surrounded by a large retinue of skilled dancers, went to the garden. He had a bed spread on the auspicious stone slab and slept on the lap of a beloved woman. The dancing women, skilled in singing and music, performed their arts. It was a scene of great luxury, like the splendor of Sakka, King of Devas. The King fell into a deep sleep.
38:
Then those women thought, "For whose sake are we performing music and song? That King has fallen asleep. What is the use of singing and playing?" They abandoned their musical instruments right there and wandered through the garden. Enticed by the flowers, fruits, and tender leaves, they enjoyed themselves in the park.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was staying at the foot of a well-blossomed Sal tree in that garden, passing the time in the bliss of monkhood like a noble elephant in rut. The women wandering in the garden saw the Bodhisatta and said, "Ladies, an ascetic is sitting at the foot of that tree. Let us sit near him and listen to some Dhamma until the King wakes up." They went, paid homage, surrounded him, and said, "Please preach to us some Dhamma that is suitable to be preached." The Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to them.

Then, that beloved woman moved her body and woke the King. When the King woke up and did not see those women, he asked, "Where have those wretches gone?" They said, "Great King, they have gone and are sitting surrounding an ascetic." King Kalābu became angry, seized his sword, and went quickly, saying, "I will kill that false ascetic!"

Then, seeing the King coming in anger, those women who were most intimate with him went, took the sword from the King's hand, and calmed the King's anger.

King Kalābu came and stood near the Bodhisatta and said, "Monk, what is your doctrine?" "Great King, I have the doctrine of patience (Khantivāda)," he said. He asked, "What is this thing called patience?" "The state of not being angry toward those who revile or strike you is called patience," he replied.

The King said, "Now I shall know the fact of your having patience," and summoned the executioner. The executioner, by his custom, took an axe and a thorny whip, dressed in saffron-colored clothes, wearing a red garland, came and paid homage to the King, saying, "Great King, what shall I do?"
39:
9. "He who cut off your hands and feet, and your ears and nose—be angry with him, O Great Hero; do not destroy this kingdom."

He spoke this first verse.

O Great Hero, ascetic of great effort. Yo, which King. Te, your. Hatthe ca, hands. Pāde ca, feet. Kaṇṇanāsañca, ears and nose. Chedayi, cut. Tassa, with that King. Kujjha, be angry. Idaṃ raṭṭhaṃ, this kingdom. Mā vinasā, do not destroy.

"Drag this thief, this failed ascetic, and throw him on the ground. Take the thorny whip and give him two thousand lashes on the four sides: front, back, and both sides," the King said. The executioner did as the King said. The Bodhisatta's outer skin and inner skin were torn. The flesh was cut. Blood flowed.

The King said again, "Monk, what is your doctrine?" "Great King, I have the doctrine of patience. You, King, think that my patience is between my skin. My patience is not between my skin. You, King, are not able to see patience. Great King, my patience is established within my heart," he said.

The executioner asked again, "Great King, what shall I do?" "Cut off both hands of this false ascetic," he said. The executioner took the axe, placed the hands on the chopping block, and cut them off. Then he said, "Cut off the feet." He cut off the feet as well. From the severed ends of the hands and feet, blood flowed like liquid lac.

Again the King asked, "Monk, what is your doctrine?" "Great King, I have the doctrine of patience. You, King, think that my patience is in the ends of my hands and feet. This patience of mine is not in the ends of my hands and feet; it is established in a deep place," he said.

The King said, "Cut off the ascetic's ears and nose." The executioner cut off the ears and nose. Blood flowed from the entire body. Again he asked, "Monk, what is your doctrine?" "Great King, I have the doctrine of patience," he said. "Do not think, King, that the ascetic's patience is established in the tips of the ears and nose. My patience is established deep within the heart," he said. The King said, "False ascetic, you yourself carry your patience and stay!" and after kicking the Bodhisatta's chest with his foot, he departed.

When the King had gone, the General wiped the blood from the Bodhisatta's body, placed the severed ends of the hands, ears, and nose in a fold of his garment, and after making the Bodhisatta sit up gently and paying homage, he sat in a suitable place and pleaded, "Venerable Sir, if you wish to be angry, be angry only with the King who committed the offense against you. Do not be angry with the other citizens of the country."

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta spoke this second verse:

10. "May that King who cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose, live long; for those like me do not get angry."
40:
11. "In the past, there was a recluse who taught patience. The King of Kāsi cut him, who was established in patience alone."
12. "The result of that harsh deed was bitter, which the King of Kāsi experienced, being cast into hell."
He preached these two verses.
'Atītamaddhānaṃ' means in the past. 'Khantidīpano' means one who is endowed with patience. 'Samaṇo' means a recluse. 'Ahu' means there was. 'Khantiyāyeva' means in patience alone. 'Ṭhitaṃ' means established. 'Taṃ' means that recluse. 'Kāsirājā' means the King of Kāsi. 'Achedayi' means caused to be cut.
Whatever deed the King of Kāsi did, the result of that harsh deed was bitter. The King of Kāsi, being cast into hell, experienced suffering.
"May the king who cut my hands, my feet, and my ears and nose, live long. Wise ones like me do not get angry."
When the king left the garden and passed out of the Bodhisatta's sight, this great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, split like a garment stiffened with starch. Flames from Avīci emerged and seized the king, wrapping him as if with a red woolen blanket given by his family. That King Kalābu entered the earth right at the garden gate and was established in the Avīci Great Hell.
The Bodhisatta also passed away on that very day. The king's retinue and the citizens came with perfumes, flowers, incense, and fragrances in their hands and performed the funeral rites for the Bodhisatta's body.
Some teachers say, "The Bodhisatta went back to the Himālaya." That is not true.
After becoming the Buddha, the Fully Enlightened One said:
Some teachers say, "The Bodhisatta's hands, feet, ears, and nose were reattached." That also is certainly not true.
The Master, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the angry monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). Many others attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and so forth. As for the identification of the Jātaka: "At that time, King Kalābu was Devadatta, the general was Sāriputta, and the ascetic Khantivādī was I myself."
## Great karma will befall the fool who wrongs the virtuous.
The Khantivādī Jātaka is finished.
41:
## 4. Lohakumbhi Jātaka
## Du, Sa, Na, So
The Master, the Fully Enlightened One, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Lohakumbhi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Dujjīvitaṃ ajīvimha," concerning the King of Kosala.
At that time, it is said that the King of Kosala heard the voices of four beings in hell during the night. One being said only the syllable "Du". One said the syllable "Sa". One said the syllable "Na". One said only the syllable "So".
In a past life, those beings in hell were princes in Sāvatthī who committed adultery with others' wives. Those princes transgressed against women who were protected and guarded by others, and they indulged in sensual play. Having committed much evil, when they were cut by the wheel-weapon of the King of Death, they were reborn in the four Lohakumbhī (Iron Cauldron) hells near Sāvatthī. Having been boiled in those Lohakumbhī hells for sixty thousand years, when they rose up and saw the rim of the Lohakumbhī hell's mouth, the four of them cried out in a great voice in succession, "When shall we be released from this suffering?"
The king, hearing the voices of those beings in hell and being terrified by the fear of death, stayed awake until dawn while sitting.
At the time of sunrise, the Brahmins came and asked the king if he had slept well. The king said, "Teachers, how could there be a happy sleep for me? Today I heard four such terrifying sounds."
The Brahmins shook their hands. When asked, "What is it, teachers?", they said, "Great King, these are violent sounds." He asked, "Are they sounds that can be remedied or not?" They said, "Great King, they are certainly sounds that cannot be remedied. However, we are well-trained in our arts." He asked, "How will you ward them off?" They said, "Great King, it is not possible to perform a great remedy easily. We shall remedy it by offering a 'Sacrifice of All Fours' (Sabbacatukka-yañña)."
"In that case, quickly take four elephants, four horses, four bulls, four humans, and so on, taking four of each kind of creature starting from quails, and perform the Sacrifice of All Fours to ensure my well-being." They accepted, saying, "Very well, Great King," and taking what they needed, they prepared the sacrificial pit. They brought many living beings and tied them to the sacrificial posts. Thinking, "We shall eat much fish and meat, and we shall obtain much wealth," they became enthusiastic and kept coming back and forth, saying, "Your Majesty, it is proper to obtain this; Your Majesty, it is proper to obtain that."
Queen Mallikā approached the king and asked, "Great King, why are the Brahmins wandering about with such great enthusiasm?" The king said, "Queen, what is this to you? You are intoxicated and heedless with your own glory; you do not know our suffering." She asked, "Great King, what suffering?"
42:
"O Queen, I have heard such sounds as have never been heard before. I asked the Brahmins, 'What will happen to me because of hearing these sounds?' The Brahmins said, 'Great King, danger to your kingship, your wealth, or your life is apparent. We will perform a sacrifice of all fours (sabbacatukka-yañña) to ensure your well-being.' I told them to proceed. Taking my word, those Brahmins prepared a sacrificial pit and are coming for whatever items they need," he said.

"Great King, have you asked the Supreme Brahmin in the world including the devas about the origin of these sounds?" she asked. "O Queen, who is this Supreme Brahmin in the world including the devas?" "The Great Gotama, the Fully Enlightened One, Great King." "O Queen, I have not asked the Fully Enlightened One." "Then, Great King, go and ask him."

The King, taking the words of Queen Mallikā, ate his breakfast, mounted his noble chariot, went to the Jetavana monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked: "Venerable Sir, during the night I heard four sounds and asked the Brahmins. The Brahmins said, 'We will perform a sacrifice of all fours to ensure well-being,' and they are working at the sacrificial pit. What will happen to me because of hearing those sounds?"

"Great King, no danger at all will occur. Beings in hell, undergoing suffering, cried out in this way," the Buddha said. "These sounds were not heard by you alone now; they were heard by ancient kings as well. Those ancient kings also asked the Brahmins and, wishing to perform a sacrifice involving the slaughter of animals, heard the words of the wise and did not do so. The wise explained the meaning of those sounds, caused the great multitude of beings to be released, and ensured well-being." Having said this, being requested by King Kosala, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in an obscure Kāsi village. When he came of age, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he renounced them, became an ascetic, attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and lived in a delightful forest grove in the Himālaya, sporting in jhāna.
43:
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, having heard the sounds of the four beings in hell, was terrified. When the Brahmins said, "One of three dangers will occur; we shall appease it with a sacrifice of all fours," he consented. The chaplain (purohita), together with the Brahmins, prepared the sacrificial pit. A great number of creatures were led to the sacrificial posts.

Then the Bodhisatta, making loving-kindness (mettā) his precursor, looked upon the world with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Seeing this matter, he thought, "Today I should go; well-being will come to the great multitude of beings." By the power of his psychic potency, he flew through the air, descended into the park of the King of Bārāṇasī, and sat upon the auspicious stone slab like a golden image.

Then the senior pupil of the chaplain approached his teacher and said, "Teacher, is it not true that in our Vedas there is no such thing as ensuring well-being by killing others?" The chaplain rebuked him, saying, "You are guarding the King's wealth. We shall eat much fish and meat and obtain wealth. Be silent!"

The pupil thought, "I will not be a companion in this matter," and leaving, he went to the royal park. Seeing the Bodhisatta, the young Brahmin paid homage, and after exchanging greetings, sat down at a respectful distance. The Bodhisatta asked, "Young man, does the King rule the kingdom righteously?"

"Venerable Sir, the King rules righteously. However, during the night he heard the sounds of four persons and asked the Brahmins. The Brahmins said, 'We will perform a sacrifice of all fours to ensure well-being.' The King, wishing to ensure his own well-being by performing an act of slaughtering creatures, has had a great number of creatures led to the sacrificial posts. Venerable Sir, it is proper for virtuous ones like you to explain the origin of those sounds and release the creatures from the jaws of death."

"Young man, the King does not know me, and I do not know the King. But we do know the origin of these sounds. If the King were to approach and ask us, we would speak so as to leave him with no doubt." "In that case, Venerable Sir, stay here for a moment; I will bring the King." "Very well, young man," he said. The young man went and informed the King of the matter and brought him.

Then the King paid homage to the Bodhisatta, sat at a respectful distance, and asked, "Is it true, Venerable Sir, that you know the origin of the sounds I heard?" "Yes, Great King, it is true." "Please tell me, Venerable Sir."

"Great King, in a previous life, these men committed misconduct with the wives of others who were protected and guarded. They were reborn in the four iron cauldrons (lohakumbhī) near Bārāṇasī. Boiling in the frothing, caustic molten metal, they spent thirty thousand years going down to the bottom of the cauldron and thirty thousand years rising up. Seeing the mouth of the cauldron and looking outside, the four persons wished to recite four complete verses, but being unable to do so, they uttered only a single syllable each and sank back into the iron cauldrons. Among them, the being who sank after saying the syllable 'Du' wished to say this—"
44:
13. We lived a wretched life, we who gave not when things were at hand. Though wealth existed, we made no refuge for ourselves.
14. Sixty thousand years have been fully completed in every way. For us being cooked in hell, when will there be an end?
15. There is no end, whence an end? No end is seen. For then, evil was done, by me and by you, friend.
16. I, surely, having gone from here and obtained a human birth, being one who knows the words of the good and endowed with virtue, will do much merit.

Saying that they were unable to complete these verses, the Bodhisatta, through his own wisdom, completed and preached them. (The same method should be understood for the remaining verses.)

The verse intended by the one who said the syllable 'Sa' is as follows:
[Verse 14 above]

The verse intended by the one who said the syllable 'Na' is as follows:
[Verse 15 above]

The verse intended by the one who said the syllable 'So' is as follows:
[Verse 16 above]

13. *Ye mayaṃ*, we who; *sante*, while gifts and recipients were present; *na dadamhase*, did not give. *Duj jīvitaṃ*, a wretched life; *ajīvimha*, we lived. *Bhogesu*, while wealth; *vijjamānesu*, existed; *attano*, for ourselves; *dīpaṃ*, a refuge; *nākamma*, we did not make.
14. *Niraye*, in hell; *paccamānānaṃ*, for us who are being cooked; *sabbaso*, in every way; *saṭṭhivassasahassāni*, sixty thousand years; *paripuṇṇāni*, are completed. *Kadā*, when; *anto*, the end; *bhavissati*, will there be?
15. *Mārisa*, friend who is like me; *mama ca*, by me; *tuyhañca*, and by you; *tadā hi*, at that time; *pāpaṃ*, evil; *pakataṃ*, was done in abundance. *Anto*, an end; *natthi*, there is not. *Kuto*, by what reason; *anto*, an end; *atthi*, would there be? *Anto*, the end; *na paṭidissati*, is not seen.
45:
16. *So ahaṃ*, I; *ito*, from this hell; *gantvā*, having escaped; *mānusiṃ yoniṃ*, a human birth; *laddhāna*, having obtained; *vadaññū*, one who knows the words of the good; *sīlasampanno*, endowed with virtue; *hutvā*, becoming; *nūna*, surely; *bahuṃ*, much; *kusalaṃ*, merit; *kāhāmi*, will do.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having spoken each verse, said: "Great King, that hell-being, though wishing to speak this verse in full, was unable to do so because of the greatness of his own evil. Thus, that hell-being lamented while experiencing the result of his own karma. There is no danger to you, Great King, because of hearing that sound. Do not be afraid."

The King released many beings, had the golden drum beaten, and destroyed the sacrificial pit. The Bodhisatta, having ensured the welfare of many beings, stayed in that garden for two or three days, then went to the Himalayas and, with undiminished jhāna, was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the senior pupil of the chaplain was Sāriputta, and I myself was the ascetic."

## For sexual misconduct, they suffer; remember Du-Sa-Na-So.

The Lohakumbhi Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Sabba-maṃsa-lābha Jātaka

## Sweet words bring benefit.

The Teacher, the Omniscient One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Sabba-maṃsa-lābha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Pharusā vata te vācā," concerning the meat-broth alms-food given by the Venerable Sāriputta to monks who had taken purgatives.

At that time, some monks at Jetavana took purgatives. They needed meat-broth. The attendant monks, thinking "We will bring meat-broth," entered Sāvatthī and wandered for alms in the street of the rice-sellers' houses, but returned without obtaining any.

The Venerable Sāriputta, entering for alms later in the day, saw those monks and asked, "Friends, why have you returned so early?" They told him the matter. The Venerable Sāriputta said, "In that case, come," and taking those monks, went to that very street. The people filled their bowls and offered meat-broth. The attendant monks brought the meat-broth and gave it to the sick monks, who then consumed it.
46:
17. Harsh indeed is your speech, you are a beggar for meat.
Your speech is like the membrane; I give you the membrane, friend.

Thus he spoke this first verse.
Friend, you are a beggar for meat. Your speech is indeed harsh. Your speech is like the membrane. Friend, I give you the membrane.

18. In this world, a brother is called a limb of men.
Your speech is like a limb; I give you a limb, friend.

Thus he spoke this second verse.
In the world, people call a brother a limb. Your speech is like a limb. Friend, I give you a limb.

At that time, one day, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised a discussion: "Friends, the Venerable Sāriputta, seeing sick monks who had taken purgatives and had not received meat-flavored alms, called the attendants of those monks and went for alms in the street of the rice-sellers, and having obtained much meat-flavored alms, had it sent to the monastery."

The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your present discussion?" When they replied, "With such a subject, Lord," he said, "Monks, not only now has Sāriputta obtained meat; in the past, wise men skilled in speaking pleasant and endearing words also obtained it." He then told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a merchant's son. One day, a hunter obtained much meat, filled a cart, and came to the city to sell it.

At that time, four merchant sons living in Bārāṇasī left the city and sat at a crossroads, chatting about things they had seen or heard. One of those four merchant sons saw the meat cart and said, "I will make that hunter give me a piece of meat." The others said, "Go and get it."

He approached the hunter and said, "Hey, hunter! Give me a piece of meat." The hunter replied, "Sir, one who begs from another should speak pleasant words. You shall receive a piece of meat suitable for the words you spoke."

Saying, "Take this membrane; I give you the membrane that is like your speech," he took a piece of membrane, devoid of flesh and blood, and gave it to him. Then another merchant son asked him, "How did you ask for it?" He replied, "I said 'Hey'." The second son said, "I too will ask him," and went and said, "Big brother, give me a piece of meat." The other replied, "You shall receive a piece of meat suitable for your words."
47:
Thus he spoke and gave him a piece of a limb. Another merchant son asked him, "How did you ask for it?" He replied, "I called him 'Brother'." The third son said, "I too will ask the hunter," and went and said, "Father, give me a piece of meat." The hunter replied, "You shall receive a piece of meat suitable for your words."

19. A son saying "Father" makes a father's heart tremble.
Your speech is like the heart; I give you the heart, friend.

Thus he spoke this third verse.
Son, the one who says "Father" makes a father's heart tremble. Friend, your speech is like the heart. I give you the heart.

Thus he spoke and gave him the heart along with sweet meat. The fourth merchant son asked him, "How did you ask for it?" He replied, "I called him 'Father'." The fourth son said, "I too will ask," and went and said, "Friend, give me a piece of meat." The hunter replied, "You shall receive a piece of meat suitable for your words."

20. For him who has no friend in the village, it is just like the forest.
Your speech is like the whole; I give you the whole, friend.

Thus he spoke this fourth verse.
For whom there is no friend in the village, that village is just like a forest. Friend, your speech is like my whole self. I give you all the meat.

Thus he spoke and said, "Friend, come, I will bring all this meat on the cart to your house." The merchant son had the hunter drive the cart to his house, had the meat unloaded, and showed great honor and hospitality to the hunter. He also sent for the hunter's wife and children, made him give up the hunter's trade, and settled him in the midst of his own wealth. He remained inseparable friends with the hunter and lived in harmony for the rest of his life.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, the Buddha identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the hunter was Sāriputta, and the merchant son who obtained all the meat was I myself."

## Speak pleasantly and endearingly; be loved by many humans and devas.

Here ends the Sabbamaṃsalābha Jātaka.
48:
## 6. Sasa-Paṇḍita Jātaka
## The Sacrifice of Life

The Present Story: While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, who is the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sasa-Paṇḍita Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Satta me rohitā macchā," concerning the offering of all requisites (sabbaparikkhāra-dāna).

In Sāvatthī, a certain householder prepared an offering of all requisites for the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head. He erected a pavilion at the door of his house, invited the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head, and seated them on the noble seats prepared in the well-decorated pavilion. Having given an excellent offering of various exquisite flavors, he invited them again for the sake of the next day's benefit for seven days. On the seventh day, he offered all requisites to the five hundred monks with the Buddha at their head.

At the conclusion of the meal, while performing the Anumodanā, the Omniscient Buddha said, "Lay devotee, you should feel joy and gladness. This offering is indeed the lineage of the wise of old. The wise of old, having sacrificed their lives for the sake of beggars who came to them, even gave their own flesh." At the request of that householder, He brought forth the past.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the species of hares and lived in a forest. At that time, on one side of the forest was the foot of a mountain, on another side a river, and on another side a border village. The Bodhisatta, the King of Hares, had three friends: a monkey, a jackal, and an otter.

These four wise ones, living together, would each take food in their respective feeding grounds and assemble together in the evening. The Wise Hare would preach the Dhamma by way of admonishing his three friends, saying, "Alms should be given. Virtue should be observed. The Uposatha should be kept." Those three friends, having accepted the advice of the Wise Hare, would enter their respective dwellings and live there.

One day, the Bodhisatta looked at the sky and, seeing the moon, knew that the next day would be the Uposatha day. He said to his three friends, "Tomorrow is the Uposatha. You three should also undertake the precepts and observe the Uposatha. An offering given while established in virtue is of great fruit. Therefore, when beggars arrive, you should give an offering from the food you were to eat, and then eat." Those three friends agreed, saying, "Very well," and stayed in their respective places.
49:
21. Seven red fish are mine,
Taken from the water to the land.
This, O Brahmin, I possess;
Eat this and dwell in the forest.

He spoke this first verse.

Brāhmaṇa: O Brahmin. Me: To me. Udakā: From the water. Thalaṃ: To the dry land. Ub bhatā: Pulled up by a fisherman. Satta: Seven. Rohitā macchā: Red fish (carp). Santi: There are. Idaṃ: This property. Me: To me. Atthi: There is. Taṃ: This property. Bhutvā: Having eaten. Vane: In the forest. Vasa: Dwell.

On the next day, among those friends, the otter went early to the bank of the Ganges to search for food. At that time, a fisherman had pulled up seven red fish, strung them on a creeper, and buried them in the sand on the bank of the Ganges, then went downstream to catch more fish. The otter, smelling the fish, dug up the sand, saw the fish, and pulled them out. He cried out three times, "Is there an owner of these?" and seeing no owner, he bit the creeper, took them to his dwelling in a bush, and lay down reflecting on his virtue, thinking, "I will eat them only at the proper time (before noon)."

The jackal also came out from his dwelling to search for food and saw two meat skewers, a roasted lizard, and a jar of curd in a field-watcher's hut. He cried out three times, "Is there an owner of these things?" and seeing no owner, he put the string of the curd jar around his neck, took the two meat skewers and the roasted lizard in his mouth, brought them to his dwelling in a bush, and lay down reflecting on his virtue, thinking, "I will eat them only at the proper time."

The monkey also came out from his dwelling, entered a grove, took a bunch of mangoes, placed them in his dwelling, and lay down reflecting on his virtue, thinking, "I will eat them only at the proper time."

The Bodhisatta, however, lay in his own dwelling in a bush, reflecting on his virtue and thinking, "I will go out at the proper time and eat Dabba grass. It is not possible to give grass to the beggars who come to me. I have no sesame, rice, or such things. If a beggar comes to me, I will give my own flesh."

By the power of the Bodhisatta's virtue, Sakka's Paṇḍukambala stone throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, upon reflecting, saw the reason and, wishing to test the King of Hares, first went to the otter's dwelling and stood in the guise of a Brahmin.

When asked, "Brahmin, for what purpose do you stand there?", he said, "O wise one, if I get some food, I will observe the Uposatha and stay here."
50:
23. "Ripe mangoes, cool water, and delightful cool shade. I have these, O Brahmin; eat them and dwell in the forest."

Thus, he spoke this third verse.

Brahmaṇa, O Brahmin. Me, to me (I have). Ambapakkaṃ, ripe mangoes. Sītaṃ, cool. Dakaṃ-udakaṃ, water from the Gaṅgā. Manoramā, delightful to the heart. Sītacchāyā, cool shade. Idaṃ, these aforementioned things. Me, to me. Atthi, there are. Etaṃ, those ripe mangoes and Gaṅgā water. Bhutvā, having eaten and drunk. Vane, in the forest which has delightful shade. Vasa, dwell.

The otter, saying "Very well, I shall give you food," wishing to speak with Sakka—

The Brahmin said, "Let it be for now, it is still early; I shall know later," and went to the jackal. When the jackal asked, "For what purpose do you stand here?", he spoke in the same way as before. The jackal, saying "Very well, I shall give," wishing to speak with Sakka, spoke this second verse:

22. "The night meal of a field-watcher named Dussa has been brought by me. Two meat-skewers, a roasted lizard, and a jar of curds. I have these, O Brahmin; eat them and dwell in the forest."

Brahmaṇa, O Brahmin. Dussa, of the one with this name. Khettapālassa, of the field-watcher. Rattibhattaṃ, the night meal. Me, by me. Apābhataṃ, has been brought. Dve, two. Maṃsasūlā ca, meat-skewers. Godhā ca, a roasted lizard. Ekaṃ, one. Dadhi-vārakanca, jar of curds. Idaṃ, these things. Me, to me. Atthi, there are. Etaṃ, those things. Bhutvā, having eaten. Vane, in the forest. Vasa, dwell.

The Brahmin said, "Let it be for now, it is still early; I shall know later," and went to the monkey. When the monkey asked, "For what purpose have you come and stood here?", he spoke in the same way as before. The monkey, saying "Very well, I shall give," wishing to speak with Sakka—

The Brahmin said, "Let it be for now, it is still early; I shall know later," and went to the Wise Rabbit. When the rabbit asked, "For what purpose have you come and stood here?", he spoke in the same way as before.

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta was filled with joy and said, "O Brahmin, you have done well in coming to me for food."
51:
24. "A rabbit has no sesame, no mung beans, nor rice. Having eaten me, roasted by this fire, dwell in the forest."

Thus, he spoke this fourth verse.

Brahmaṇa, O Brahmin. Sasassa, to a rabbit. Tilā, sesame seeds. Na atthi, do not exist. Muggā, mung beans. Na atthi, do not exist. Taṇḍulā, rice grains. Napi atthi, also do not exist. Iminā agginā, by this fire. Pakkaṃ, roasted. Mamaṃ, me. Bhutvā, having eaten. Vane, in the forest. Vasa, dwell.

"Today I shall give a gift that I have never given before. You are virtuous and will not commit the taking of life. Go, Brahmin, gather various kinds of wood, make a fire of coals, and inform me. I shall sacrifice my body and jump into the heap of coals. When my body is roasted, you may eat the meat and perform your ascetic duties," he said, wishing to speak with Sakka.

Sakka, hearing the rabbit's words, created a heap of coals by his supernatural power and informed the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta rabbit rose from his bed of dabba grass, went to the heap of coals, and thinking, "If there are small insects between my hairs, may they not die," he shook his body three times. Offering his entire body as a gift, he jumped into the heap of coals with a joyful heart, like a royal swan descending into a lotus pond. However, that fire was unable to heat even a single pore of the Bodhisatta's body. It was as if he had entered a chamber of snow.

Then, addressing Sakka, he asked, "Brahmin, the fire you have made is extremely cold; it cannot heat even a single pore of my body. What is the reason for this?" Sakka replied, "Wise Rabbit, I am not a Brahmin; I am Sakka. I have come to test you." The Bodhisatta let out a lion's roar, saying, "Sakka, let alone you, even if the entire world were to test me with a gift, they would not find in me any unwillingness to give."

Then Sakka, saying, "Wise Rabbit, let your virtue be known throughout the entire aeon," squeezed a mountain, took the essence of the mountain, and drew the sign of a rabbit on the orb of the moon. He then took the Bodhisatta and placed him on the young dabba grass in that same forest thicket and returned to his own abode. Those four wise ones, living in harmony and joy, fulfilled their virtue, gave alms, observed the Uposatha, and passed away according to their kamma.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder who had given all the requisites was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. As for the identification of the Jātaka: At that time, Ānanda was the otter, Moggallāna was the jackal, Sāriputta was the monkey, Anuruddha was Sakka, and I, the Buddha, was the Wise Rabbit. Thus, He identified the Jātaka.
52:
## The Scene of Giving, the Act of Donation, the Example of the Hare King

Here ends the Sasa-paṇḍita Jātaka.

## 7. Matarodana Jātaka

## Worldly Conditions

**The Present Account**

The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Matarodana Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Mataṃ mataṃ eva rodatha,' concerning a certain householder living in Sāvatthī.

It is said that the brother of that householder had passed away. Overcome by grief due to his brother's death, that householder did not bathe, did not eat, and did not apply perfumes. Early in the morning, he would go to the cemetery and weep, consumed by sorrow.

At dawn, as the Omniscient Buddha surveyed the world, He saw that this householder possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He thought, 'Except for Me, there is no one else capable of quenching his sorrow and granting him the Fruit of Stream-entry by relating an account of the past. I must certainly be a refuge for this householder.' The next day, after returning from His alms round and finishing His meal, He took a companion monk and went to the door of the householder's home. Hearing that 'The Teacher has arrived,' the householder had a seat prepared and said, 'Please enter the house.' When invited, the Buddha entered and sat upon the prepared seat.

The householder also came, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat in a suitable place. Then the Omniscient Buddha asked him, 'Householder, are you grieving?' He replied, 'Yes, Venerable Sir, I have been grieving since the time of my brother's death.'

'Lay disciple, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are impermanent. That which is subject to destruction must decay. One should not grieve over it. Even the wise of old did not grieve when their brothers died, knowing that what is subject to destruction must decay.' Having said this, and being requested by the householder, He related the account of the past.

**The Account of the Past**

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family with a wealth of eighty crores. When he reached maturity, his parents passed away. After their death, the Bodhisatta's older brother managed the household affairs, and the Bodhisatta lived depending on him. Later, the older brother passed away due to a certain disease. Relatives, friends, and companions gathered, raised their arms, and wailed. Not a single person was able to maintain their composure. However, the Bodhisatta neither wailed nor wept. People criticized the Bodhisatta, saying, 'Look, friends!'
53:
'When his brother died, there was not even a frown on his face. He is extremely hard-hearted. He probably desired his brother's death, thinking, "I alone shall enjoy both portions of the wealth."' Thus they criticized the Bodhisatta. Even his relatives criticized him, saying, 'You do not weep even though your brother has died.'

Hearing their words, the Bodhisatta said, 'Because of your extreme foolishness, you do not know the eight worldly conditions (aṭṭha lokadhamma) and thus weep because "my brother is dead." I too shall die; therefore, I do not weep. You too shall die. Therefore, do not weep, reflecting that "we too shall die." All conditioned things, having arisen, cease. There is not a single formation capable of remaining in its own nature. You fools weep because you are ignorant and do not know the eight worldly conditions. Why should I weep?' He then spoke these verses:

25. You weep only for the dead, for those who have already passed; you do not weep for the one who is yet to die. All those who bear a body must gradually give up their lives.

26. Devas, humans, four-footed animals, flocks of birds, snakes, and those with great bodies—none are masters of their own bodies. Even while enjoying themselves in their respective places of birth, they give up their lives.

27. Having observed such instability and lack of permanence, and the pleasure and pain among men, weeping and shedding tears is useless. Why do masses of sorrow overwhelm you?

28. Those who are profligate, drunkards, unvirtuous, foolishly bold in wrong thoughts, and not engaged in the practice of merit—those fools who are unskilled in the eight worldly conditions—consider a wise man like me, who does not weep at the death of relatives, to be a fool.

Thus he spoke these verses.

(Exegesis): You weep for the dead, for each one who dies. You do not weep for the one who will die. All beings who carry a body must gradually give up their lives. Devas, humans, animals, birds, and snakes, though possessing wealth and bodies, are not masters of their own bodies; they give up life while delighting in their existence. Seeing the instability of pleasure and pain among men, weeping is fruitless. Why does sorrow oppress you? The profligate, the drunkards, those who do not practice virtue, those bold in improper thoughts, and those not striving in good deeds—these fools, unskilled in the eight worldly conditions, regard the wise man who does not grieve as a fool.

'One should not grieve over the destruction of conditioned things. Even the wise of old did not grieve when their brothers died, knowing that what is subject to destruction must decay.' Having said this, and being requested by the lay disciple, He related the account of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family with a wealth of eighty crores. When he reached maturity, his parents passed away. After their death, the Bodhisatta's older brother managed the wealth. The Bodhisatta lived depending on his brother. Later, the Bodhisatta's brother fell ill and died. Relatives and friends gathered, raised their arms, and wailed. Not a single person was able to maintain their composure. The Bodhisatta, however, did not weep.

People said, 'Look, friends! When his brother died, this man does not even have a frown on his face. He is very hard-hearted. He seems to have wanted his brother's death so that he alone could enjoy the two portions of wealth.' Thus they criticized the Bodhisatta. Relatives also criticized him, saying, 'Why do you not weep when your brother has died?'

Hearing their words, the Bodhisatta said, 'Because of your extreme foolishness, you do not know the eight worldly conditions and thus weep when a brother dies. I too shall die; therefore, I do not weep. You too shall die. Therefore, do not weep, reflecting that "we too shall die."'
54:
"All formations are impermanent; they arise and pass away. There is no other formation capable of remaining in that state. You, who are extremely foolish and ignorant, do not understand the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma) and thus weep. For what purpose should I weep?"

Having said this, the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to them and freed them all from sorrow.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). As for the identification of the Birth: "At that time, I myself was the wise man who preached the Dhamma to the people and made them free from sorrow."

## Formations are truly perishable; they will surely perish.

The Matarodana Jātaka is concluded.

## 8. Kaṇavera Jātaka
## The Oleander Flower

The Present Story: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kaṇavera Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Yaṃ taṃ vasanta samaye,' concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

(The present story will become clear in the Indriya Jātaka of the Aṭṭhakanipāta.)

The Fully Enlightened Buddha said to that monk, "Monk, in the past, you also suffered decapitation by a sword because of that woman." Being requested by the monk, He brought forth the past.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born under a thief's star in the house of a certain householder in a village of Kāsi. When he came of age, he made his living by committing robbery and became famous in the world. He was brave and possessed the strength of an elephant. No one was able to capture him.

One day, the Bodhisatta broke into a merchant's house through a breach and stole a great deal of wealth.
55:
The citizens approached the King and said, "Great King, a great thief is plundering the city; please have him captured." Hearing this, the King ordered the city guard to capture the thief. The city guard, having stationed men in groups here and there during the night, captured the thief along with the stolen goods and informed the King. The King ordered the city guard, "Cut off the thief's head."

The city guard had the thief's hands bound tightly behind his back, hung a wreath of red oleander flowers around his neck, sprinkled brick dust on his head, and led him to the execution ground, beating him with rods at every crossroads to the sound of a harsh-toned drum. The whole city was in an uproar, saying, "The thief who plundered this city has been caught!"

At that time, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a courtesan named Sāmā who earned a thousand pieces [per night]. She was a favorite of the King and had a retinue of five hundred slave girls.

Standing at the window on the upper floor of her palace, she saw the thief being led away. The thief was very handsome, pleasing to look at, possessed of great beauty, and appeared to everyone as if he were of divine form. Upon seeing the thief, Sāmā's heart was filled with passion, and she thought, "By what means can I make this man my husband?" Thinking that there was a way, she gave a thousand pieces of money into the hands of a woman who served her interests and sent her, saying, "This thief is Sāmā's brother. Apart from Sāmā, he has no other refuge. Take this thousand pieces and release the thief."

The woman went and did as Sāmā had said. The city guard said, "This thief is well-known in the city; it is not possible to release him. However, if I get another man, I can place this thief in a covered carriage and release him." The woman went back and informed Sāmā.

At that time, a certain merchant's son was infatuated with Sāmā and would give her a thousand pieces every day. On that day too, at sunset, he took a thousand pieces and went to Sāmā's house.

Sāmā took the thousand pieces, placed them on her lap, and sat weeping. When asked, "What is the matter?" she replied, "My lord, this thief is my brother. He does not come to me because he says, 'I do a lowly job.' When I sent word to the city guard, he sent back a message saying, 'I will release him only if I receive a thousand pieces.' Now, I cannot find anyone to take this thousand pieces to the city guard."

Because of his infatuation with Sāmā, the merchant's son said, "I will go." She said, "If that is so, take the money you brought and go." The merchant's son took the money and went to the city guard's house.
56:
The city guard kept the merchant's son in a hidden place and had the thief ride in a covered carriage to be sent to Sāmā. He made a pretense, saying, 'This thief is well-known in the country; let it be dark first. When it is dark and people are quiet, I will have him executed.' After waiting for a moment until the people were quiet, he took the merchant's son to the execution ground under heavy guard. There, he beheaded him with a sword, impaled the body on a stake, and re-entered the city.

From that time on, Sāmā took nothing from the hands of others. She lived in delight only with that thief. The great thief thought, 'If this Sāmā becomes attached to another man, she will have me killed as well and then delight with that person. This Sāmā is truly one who betrays her friends. It is best for me not to stay with her and to flee quickly. However, I should not go empty-handed; I will take her ornaments and jewelry and then go.'

Having thought thus, one day he said to Sāmā, 'Sister, we are always in the house like chickens kept in a cage. I wish to go and play in the garden for a day.' Sāmā agreed, saying, 'Very well.' She prepared all the provisions, such as hard and soft food, and adorned herself with all her ornaments. She then rode with the great thief in a covered carriage and went to the garden.

While playing with Sāmā in the garden, the great thief thought, 'Now is the time for me to flee.' As if wishing to delight in sensual pleasure with her, he entered a thicket of Kaṇavera (oleander) bushes. There, as if embracing her, he squeezed her until she fainted, struck her, took off all her ornaments, wrapped them in her upper garment, slung the bundle over his shoulder, leaped over the garden fence, and fled.
57:
29. They sang this first song:

'That which happened in the spring season,
Among the bright Kaṇavera blossoms,
You squeezed Sāmā by her arms;
She sends you word of her health.'

(Explanation:) 'In the spring season' means during the springtime. 'Among the bright Kaṇavera blossoms' refers to the oleander flowers endowed with the radiance of red color. 'Sāmā' is the woman of that name. 'Squeezed' means he squeezed her while embracing her as if wishing to delight in sensual pleasure. 'She sends you word' means that Sāmā is well; you fled out of fear, thinking 'she is dead,' but she spoke of her own health and informed you.

30. He spoke this second verse:

'O friend, it is surely not to be believed,
That the wind could carry away a mountain.
If the wind could carry a mountain,
It could carry the whole earth as well.
Where Sāmā has died,
How could she send me word of her health?'

(Explanation:) 'O dancer, this is surely not to be believed, nor should it be believed. Just as the wind might carry a mountain like grass and leaves—if it could carry a mountain, it could carry the whole earth—this word is just as unbelievable. Since Sāmā is dead, for what reason should I believe she sends word of her health? The dead do not send messages to anyone.'

When Sāmā regained consciousness, she stood up, went to her attendants, and asked, 'Where is the master?' They replied, 'Mistress, we do not know.' Thinking, 'He must have fled in fear, believing I was dead,' she became dejected. She went home directly from the garden and vowed, 'From the time I no longer see my beloved husband, I shall not sleep on an adorned bed,' and she slept on the ground. From then on, she did not wear pleasant clothes, did not eat pleasant food, and did not use perfumes or garlands.

Thinking, 'I will search for and summon the master by some means,' she called for actors and gave them a thousand pieces of money. When they asked, 'Mistress, what shall we do?', she instructed them, 'There is no place you cannot reach. While traveling through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, hold festivals, and in the midst of the assembly, sing this song first.' She taught the actors the first verse and said, 'When you sing this song, if the master is within that assembly, he will speak with you. Then, tell him of my health and bring him back. If he does not come, send word.' Giving them provisions, she sent the actors away.

Leaving Vārāṇasī and holding festivals in various places, they went to a border region. The great thief had fled and was living in that border village. While the actors were holding a festival there—

The great thief, hearing those words, approached the actor and said, 'You say Sāmā is alive, but I do not believe it.' Wishing to speak with the actor—

Hearing the words of the great thief, the actor—
58:
31. He spoke this third verse:

'She is not dead,
Nor does she desire another.
Sāmā is devoted to one alone,
And she longs only for you.'

(Explanation:) 'She does not desire another man; she longs for, desires, and wishes only for you.'

Hearing this, the thief said, 'Whether she lives or dies, I have no need of her,' and spoke the fourth verse:

32. 'Sāmā exchanged me, a stranger,
For one long known;
She exchanged the unstable for the stable.
Sāmā might exchange me for another too;
I will go far away from here.'

(Explanation:) 'Sāmā exchanged me, with whom she had no prior acquaintance, for the merchant's son with whom she had long association. She gave a thousand to the city guard to take me, exchanging me, the unstable one, for that stable husband. Sāmā might likewise exchange me for another husband. I will go to a place so far away that it is impossible to hear news or tidings of her.' Having said, 'Tell her of my departure from here to another place,' he fastened his loincloth very firmly while they were watching and fled with great speed.

The actors went and told her of his actions. Sāmā became full of remorse and spent the rest of her time in her natural state.

The Teacher (the Buddha), having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Birth Story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. How did he identify the Birth Story? 'The dissatisfied monk of today was the merchant's son of that time. The former wife of this monk was Sāmā of that time. And I myself was the great thief of that time.'

## Pursuing lust, behaving corruptly, one meets with misery and trouble.

The Kaṇavera Jātaka ends.
59:
## 9. Tittira Jātaka
## The Decoy Partridge
The Present Story: While the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at the Badarikārāma monastery near the city of Kosambī, he told this Tittira Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Susukhaṃ vata jīvāmi,' concerning the Venerable Rāhula Thera.
(The Present Story is detailed in the Tippallattha Jātaka below.)
In the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, Venerable Rāhula is desirous of training, scrupulous, and amenable to advice." When this conversation about the virtues of Venerable Rāhula Thera had arisen, the Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such a subject," the Buddha said, "Monks, not only now is Rāhula amenable to advice; in the past too, he was indeed amenable to advice." Having said this, he brought forth the past.
The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. When he reached maturity, he went to the city of Takkasilā, learned all the arts, renounced the world, and became an ascetic in the Himavanta region. Having attained the direct knowledges and meditative attainments, and sporting in jhāna, he lived in a pleasant forest grove. Later, he went to an obscure border village to seek salt and vinegar.
The people living in that village, seeing the Bodhisatta, were filled with faith. They built a hermitage for him in an obscure forest and supported him with the requisites, inviting him to stay.
At that time, a bird hunter in that village caught a decoy partridge, trained it well, and kept it in a cage to look after it. That hunter would take the partridge to the forest and, by its cry, catch the partridges that came, selling them to make a living.
60:
33. "I live very happily indeed, and I get food to eat.
Yet I stand in a trap; what, Bhante, will be my destiny?"
He spoke this first verse.
Bhante, Venerable Sir. Ahaṃ, I. Imaṃ sākuṇikaṃ, this bird hunter. Nissāya, relying on. Vata, indeed. Susukhaṃ, very happily. Jīvāmi, live. Bhuñjituṃ, to eat. Labhāmi ceva, I also get as I desire. Api ca kho, nevertheless. Paripanthe ca, in danger too. Tiṭṭhāmi, I stand. Bhante, Venerable Sir. Mama, my. Gati, destiny. Kā nu, what will it be?
34. "If your mind does not incline, O bird, towards an evil deed,
No evil clings to the one who is not involved and is pure."
He spoke this second verse.
Pakkhi, bird. Pāpassa kammuno, for the sake of an evil deed. Te, your. Mano, mind. Ce nappaṇamati, if it does not incline. Abyāvaṭassa, to one who is not involved. Bhadrassa, to one who is good. Pāpaṃ, evil. Na upalimpati, does not smear.
35. "'Our kinsman is sitting there,' thinking thus, many birds come.
The hunter incurs the act because of me; my mind is suspicious of that."
He spoke this third verse.
Bhante, Venerable Sir. No, our. Ñātako, kinsman. Nisinnoti, is sitting, thinking thus. Bahujano, many partridges. Āgacchate, come. Paṭicca, because of me. Kammaṃ, the act of taking life. Luddo, the hunter. Phusati, incurs. Tasmiṃ, in that evil of the hunter. Me, my. Mano, mind. Saṅkate, is suspicious, wondering 'is it my evil?'
The partridge thought, "Because of me alone, my kinsmen are perishing; this evil is indeed mine." Having thought so, it did not make a sound. It remained silent. Then the hunter, knowing the partridge's silence, struck the partridge on the head with a bamboo splinter. The partridge made a sound due to the oppression of suffering. In this way, that hunter, relying on that partridge, caught partridges and made a living.
Then that partridge thought, "I have no intention that these kinsmen of mine should die; however, the hunter incurs the act of taking life because of me. If I do not make a sound, those partridges do not come; only when I make a sound do they come. This hunter catches all the partridges that come and brings them to the end of their lives. In this matter, is there evil in me or not?" Having thought so, from that time on, that partridge went about considering, "Who indeed can dispel this doubt of mine?" looking for a wise person of such nature.
Then one day, that bird hunter, taking many partridges, went to the Bodhisatta's hermitage to drink water. He placed the cage near the Bodhisatta, drank water, and fell asleep while lying on the sandy ground.
The partridge, knowing that the hunter had fallen asleep, thought, "I will ask the ascetic about my doubt; if he knows, he will answer me." While staying in the cage, it wished to ask the Bodhisatta—
61:
36. If the mind is not corrupted, the action dependent [on one] does not touch [one]. To the one who is unconcerned and auspicious, evil does not cling.

He spoke this fourth verse:

Bird, if your mind is not corrupted, the act of killing living beings committed by the hunter depending on you does not touch you. To you who are unconcerned and good, evil does not smear.

Then, wishing to solve the problem, the Bodhisatta—

Hearing those words, the partridge—

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta—

Thus, the Bodhisatta made the partridge understand. The partridge, relying on the Bodhisatta, became free from remorse. When the hunter woke up, he paid homage to the Bodhisatta, took the cage, and departed.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, identified the birth: "At that time, Rāhula was the partridge, and I myself was the ascetic."

## Volition is Kamma, the Root; Explaining to Clear Doubts and Remorse

The Tittira Jātaka is finished.

## 10. Succaja Jātaka

## Sharing Joy and Sorrow

Present Story: While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Succaja Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Succajaṃ vata naccaji," concerning a certain householder.

That householder, intending to collect a debt in a small village, went there with his wife. Having made them pay the debt and taking the money, he left it with a family to bring later. While returning to Sāvatthī, they saw a mountain on the way.

Then the wife said to the householder, "Lord, if this mountain were made of gold, would you give me a little?" He replied, "What kind of woman are you? I will give you nothing." The wife was displeased, thinking, "This man is so hard-hearted that even if this mountain were gold, he would give me nothing."

Those two came near the Jetavana Monastery and, thinking they would drink water, entered the monastery and drank water.
62:
The All-Knowing Buddha, having seen at dawn the supporting condition for the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) of those two people, sat in the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) emitting the six-colored rays, awaiting their arrival. Those two, after drinking water, came and paid homage to the Buddha and sat down.

The All-Knowing Buddha exchanged friendly greetings with them and asked, "Where have you been?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we went to a small village to settle a debt," He asked, "Laywoman, does your husband desire your welfare? Does he do you favors?"

"Venerable Sir, I love this man, but he does not love me. Today, when I saw a mountain and asked, 'If this mountain were gold, would you give me a little?', he said, 'What kind of woman are you? I will give nothing.' This man has such a hard heart," she reported.

"Laywoman, although this man says this now, in the past, when he remembered your virtues, he gave you all his sovereignty," the Buddha said. Being requested by the lay disciples, "Venerable Sir, please tell us," He brought up the past.

Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a minister who conducted all the king's affairs. Then one day, the king saw his son, the viceroy, coming to pay attendance and thought, "This prince might act treacherously in my palace." He called the viceroy and said, "My son, as long as I live, you shall not stay in the city. Live elsewhere and become king after my passing."

The viceroy said, "Very well," paid homage to his father, and left the city of Bārāṇasī with his chief wife. He went to the border regions, entered the forest, built a leaf-roofed hut, and lived there subsisting on forest roots and fruits. Later, the king passed away. The viceroy, observing the stars and knowing the fact of the king's death, was returning to Bārāṇasī when he saw a mountain on the way.
63:
At that time, the wife said to the prince, "Great King, if this mountain were to become gold, would you give me even a little?" He replied, "What kind of woman are you? I shall give nothing." That woman felt unhappy, thinking, "I entered the forest because I could not break my love for this man, yet he speaks thus. He has a very hard heart. Even if he becomes king, what good will he do for me?"

When the prince returned and was established in the kingship, he gave that woman only the luxury of the position of Chief Queen. Beyond that, there was no affection or generosity. He did not even acknowledge her presence.

The Bodhisatta thought, "This queen was helpful to this king; she lived in the forest, enduring suffering. But this king neglects her and enjoys himself with other women. I will act in such a way that this queen receives all prosperity." Thinking thus, one day he approached the queen, paid respects, and said, "Great Queen, we do not receive even a morsel of food from you. Why do you neglect us? Are you so hard-hearted?"

"Father, if I were to receive anything myself, I would give it to you. But if I receive nothing, what can I give? What wealth will the king give me now? When he was on the journey, I asked him, 'If this mountain were to become gold, would you give me even a little?' and he replied, 'What kind of woman are you? I shall give nothing.' Since he would not give even what is easy to give, what will he give me now?"

The Bodhisatta asked, "Great Queen, would you be able to say these words in the presence of the king?" The queen replied, "Father, I would be able to." "In that case," said the Bodhisatta, "I will stand in the king's presence and ask you; then you should speak." The queen agreed, saying, "Very well, father."

When the Bodhisatta came to serve the king and the queen was present, he said, "Great Queen, do we not receive anything from you?" She replied, "Father, when I receive nothing myself, what can I give you? When that king was coming from the forest, he saw a mountain and I asked, 'If this mountain were to become gold, would you give me even a little?' He replied, 'What kind of woman are you? I shall give nothing.' Thus, he did not give even what is easy to give. What wealth will he give me now?" Wishing to explain this meaning, she spoke this first verse:

37. Succajaṃ vata naccaji, vācāya adadaṃ giriṃ.
Kiṃ hi tassa cajantassa, vācāya adada pabbataṃ.

(Indeed, he did not give what is easy to give; he did not give the mountain even by word. For one who does not give that which I requested, what would he give? He did not give the mountain even by word.)

Tāta: Father. Giriṃ: the mountain. Vācāya: by word. Adadaṃ: the king who did not give. Vata: indeed. Succajaṃ: that which is easy to give. Naccaji: did not give, did not sacrifice. Mayā: by me. Yācitassa: requested. Tassa: that useless mountain. Acajantassa: while not giving. Kiṃ hi cajeyya: what indeed would he give? Pabbataṃ: the mountain. Vācāya: even by mere word. Adadaṃ: did not give.
64:
38. Yañhi kayirā tañhi vade, yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade.
Akaroṃtaṃ bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitā.

(One should say only what one would do; one should not say what one would not do. The wise recognize one who speaks but does not act.)

Paṇḍito: the wise man. Yañhi: that which. Kayirā: should do. Tañhi: that indeed. Vade: should say. Yaṃ: that which. Na kayirā: should not do. Taṃ: that. Na vade: should not say. Bhāsamānaṃ: speaking. Akaroṃtaṃ: one who does not act. Paṇḍitā: the wise. Parijānanti: recognize.

39. Rājaputta namo tyatthu, sacce dhamme ṭhito casi.
Yassa te byasanaṃ patto, saccasmiṃ ramate mano.

(O Prince, homage to you; you stand in truth and righteousness. Even having reached ruin, your mind delights in truth.)

Rājaputta: Prince. Te: to you. Namo: homage. Atthu: may there be. Tvaṃ: you. Sacce ca: in truth. Dhamme ca: in Dhamma (righteousness). Ṭhito: stand. Asi: are. Byasanaṃ: ruin, called being banished from the country. Patto: having reached. Yassa te: of you. Mano: the mind. Saccasmiṃ: in truth. Ramate: delights.

40. Yā daliddī daliddassa, aḍḍhā aḍḍhassa kittimā.
Sā hissa paramā bhariyā, sahiraññassa itthiyo.

(She who is poor when the husband is poor, and rich when the husband is rich, O famous King; she alone is his supreme wife. For a man with wealth, there are always women.)

Kittima: O famous Great King. Yā bhariyā: which wife. Daliddassa: when the husband is poor. Daliddī: herself is also poor. Aḍḍhassa: when the husband is wealthy. Aḍḍhā: herself is also wealthy. Sā hi bhariyā: that wife alone. Assa: of that man. Paramā bhariyā: is the supreme wife. Sahiraññassa: to one who has gold, silver, and wealth. Itthiyo: women. Hontiyeva: always exist. Anaccharriyā: they are not a wonder.

Hearing those words, the king—

Hearing those words, the queen raised her hands in salutation to the king—

Hearing the queen's words praising the king's virtues, the Bodhisatta, wishing to speak of the queen's virtues—

Having said this, the Bodhisatta spoke of the queen's virtues: "Great King, this queen lived in the forest during your time of hardship and suffered together with you. You should honor and support this queen."
65:
Having remembered the Queen's virtues through the Bodhisatta's words, the King said, "O wise one, through your words I have remembered the Queen's virtues," and he granted her full sovereignty. He also bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta, saying, "You, wise one, have made me remember the Queen's virtues."

Identifying the Jātaka: The Omniscient Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the husband and wife were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. To identify the Jātaka: "At that time, the householder was the King of Bārāṇasī, the female lay devotee was the Queen, and I myself was the wise minister."

## The Noble Wife, Constant in Both Adversity and Prosperity
The Succaja Jātaka is concluded.

## 3. Kuṭidūsaka Vagga
## 1. Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka
## The Monkey Who Destroyed the Hut

The Present Story: While dwelling at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Manussasseva te sīsaṃ," concerning a young monk who set fire to the leaf-hut of the Elder Mahākassapa.

(The story originated in Rājagaha.) At that time, the Elder Mahākassapa was living in a forest hut near Rājagaha. Two young monks were attending to him. Of these two, one was helpful to the Elder, while the other was difficult to admonish. Whatever the helpful monk did, the other would act as if he had done it himself.

When the helpful monk prepared the water for washing the face and so on, the other would go to the Elder, pay homage, and say, "Venerable Sir, the water is ready; please wash your face," and so forth. When the helpful monk rose early and swept the Elder's precinct, the other, at the time the Elder came out, would strike the broom here and there, making it appear as if he himself had swept the entire precinct. The dutiful monk thought, "This difficult monk acts as if he has done whatever I have done. I will make his deceitful behavior known."
66:
Having thought thus, while the difficult monk had returned from the village after his meal and was sleeping, the dutiful monk heated the bath water and placed it outside the bathhouse, but left only a ladleful of hot water in a pot on the stove. When the difficult monk woke up and saw the steam rising, he thought, "He must have heated the water and placed it in the bathhouse." He went to the Elder and said, "Venerable Sir, the bath water is ready in the bathhouse; please bathe."

The Elder, intending to bathe, came with the young monk, but seeing no water in the bathhouse, he asked, "Where is the water?" The young monk quickly went to the fire-room and lowered the ladle into the empty pot. The ladle struck the bottom of the empty pot and made a "tata" sound. From then on, that young monk became known by the name Uḷuṅkasaddaka.

At that moment, the dutiful monk brought the water from outside the bathhouse and said, "Venerable Sir, please bathe." After bathing, the Elder reflected and realized the difficult nature of Uḷuṅkasaddaka. When Uḷuṅkasaddaka came to attend to him in the evening, the Elder admonished him, saying, "Friend, a monk should only say 'I have done it' for what he has actually done. To say 'I have done it' for what one has not done is a conscious lie. From this day forward, do not do such a thing."

Uḷuṅkasaddaka became angry with the Elder and did not go for alms with him the next day. The Elder went for alms with the dutiful disciple. Uḷuṅkasaddaka went to the house of the Elder's supporters. When asked, "Venerable Sir, where is the Elder?" he replied, "He is unwell and staying at the monastery." When they asked, "Venerable Sir, what food would be suitable for him?" he said, "Give such and such food," took it, went to a place of his liking, ate it, and then returned to the monastery.

The next day, the Elder went to that house and sat down. The people asked, "Venerable Sir, what illness did you have? We heard you stayed at the monastery yesterday. We sent food with such-and-such young monk; did you receive it, Venerable Sir?" The Elder remained silent, finished his meal, and returned to the monastery.

In the evening, when Uḷuṅkasaddaka came to attend to him, the Elder called him and said, "Friend, I hear you went to such-and-such a village and house, requested such-and-such food for the Elder, and ate it yourself. Making requests (viññatti) is not proper. Do not perform such improper conduct again."

Uḷuṅkasaddaka harbored a grudge against the Elder because of this, thinking, "Yesterday, he quarreled with me over some hot water, and today he quarrels because he cannot tolerate a handful of food I ate at the supporters' house. I will show him what I can do." The next day, while the Elder was away for alms, he took a mallet, smashed the utensils, set fire to the leaf-roofed hut, and fled.
67:
If a traveler does not find a companion who is better or equal to himself, let him resolutely pursue a solitary life; there is no fellowship with a fool.

Monks, if a practitioner does not find one better than himself or equal to himself, he should firmly practice living alone. There is no friendship with a fool.

1. O monkey, your head is like a human's, and your hands and feet too. Then for what reason do you have no house?

He spoke this first verse. O monkey, your head is like a human's head. Your hands and feet are also like a human's hands and feet. This being so, for what reason do you have no house?

That Uḷuṅkasaddaka, while still alive, became a human-peta (human-ghost), withered away, and upon death, was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell. The misconduct committed by that Uḷuṅkasaddaka became well-known among the people.

Then, some monks went from the city of Rājagaha to Sāvatthī, and after putting away their bowls and robes in a suitable place, they went to the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. The Blessed Teacher exchanged friendly greetings with them and asked, "Where have you come from?" They replied, "From Rājagaha, Venerable Sir." "Who is the teacher there who gives exhortation?" "The Elder Mahākassapa, Venerable Sir." "Is Kassapa well, monks?" "Yes, Venerable Sir, the Elder is well. However, his resident pupil, when given an exhortation, became angry, set fire to the Elder's leaf-hut, and fled."

Hearing this, the Teacher said, "Monks, rather than living with such a fool, it is better for Kassapa to live alone," and he spoke this verse from the Dhammapada.

After saying this, he addressed those monks again, "Monks, not only now has he destroyed a hut; in the past too, he destroyed a hut. Not only now is he angry with his exhorter; in the past too, he was angry," and being requested by them, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the form of a Singila bird. When he reached maturity, he built a pleasant, rain-proof nest and lived in the Himalayan region.

Then, during the rainy season, while the rain was falling in an incessant stream, a certain monkey, oppressed by the cold and with teeth chattering, sat near the Bodhisatta.
68:
2. O Singila, my head is like a human's, and my hands and feet too. But that wisdom which is called supreme among humans, that wisdom I do not possess.

He spoke this second verse. O Singila, Singila. My head is like a human's head. My hands and feet are also like a human's hands and feet. That wisdom which is said to be supreme among humans, that wisdom I do not possess.

3. For one with an unsteady mind, a light mind, a betrayer of friends, and one whose virtue is always inconstant, there is no state of happiness.

4. So exert your power, overcome your habits. Build a hut, O monkey, to protect against the cold and wind.

He spoke these two verses. For one with an unsteady mind, a light mind, a betrayer of friends, and one whose virtue is always inconstant, there is no state of happiness. O monkey, you should exert your power. Overcome the habit called immorality. Build a house that can protect against the cold and wind.

The Bodhisatta, seeing that exhausted monkey and wishing to converse with him—

Hearing those words, the monkey—

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta—

The monkey thought, "This bird insults me because he is sitting in a place where the rain does not soak him. I will not let him stay in this nest." Having so thought, wishing to catch the Bodhisatta, he rushed forward. The Bodhisatta flew up and went elsewhere. The monkey destroyed the nest, crushing it to pieces, and went away.
69:
Having brought this Dhamma teaching to a close, the Omniscient Buddha identified the birth-story: "At that time, the young monk who burnt down the hut was the monkey. I myself was the singila bird."

## If you advise a fool, you will only bring ruin upon yourself

The Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka is concluded.

## 2. Duddubha Jātaka

## The Earth is Collapsing

The Story of the Present: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Duddubha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Duddubhāyati bhaddante," concerning the ascetics of other sects (titthiyas).

It is said that those ascetics slept on beds of thorns in various places near Jetavana Monastery. They practiced the "five-fold heat" (pañcātapa) penance and various kinds of false asceticism.

Then, many monks, while returning to Jetavana Monastery after collecting alms in Sāvatthī, saw those ascetics practicing false penances along the way. They approached the Buddha and asked, "Venerable Sir, is there any essence in the practices observed by these ascetics of other sects?"

The Omniscient Buddha said, "Monks, there is neither essence nor special benefit in the practices of those ascetics. When examined, their practices are like a path smeared with excrement, or like the 'duddubha' sound heard by the little hare." Requested by the monks to explain the matter of the little hare's 'duddubha' sound, he related the story of the past.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of a lion and, upon reaching maturity, lived in the forest. At that time, there was a grove of palms mixed with vilva trees near the Western Ocean. In that palm grove, a certain little hare lived under a palm leaf near a vilva tree.

One day, after returning from foraging, the little hare lay under the palm leaf and thought, "If this earth were to collapse, where would I go?" At that moment, a ripe vilva fruit fell onto the palm leaf. Hearing the sound of the vilva fruit, the little hare thought, "The earth is surely collapsing!" and he jumped up and fled without even looking back.
70:
Another hare saw him fleeing in great haste out of fear of death and asked, "Sir, why are you fleeing in such terror?" "Do not ask me, sir," he replied. When the other hare persisted, asking, "What is it, sir? What is it?", the fleeing hare, without looking back, said, "The earth is collapsing here!" Then the hare who had asked also fled after him.

In the same way, another hare saw them, and then another. Thus, a thousand little hares fled together. A deer saw them and joined the flight.

A wild boar saw them, then a sambar deer, a buffalo, a gayal, a rhinoceros, a tiger, a lion, and an elephant. When they asked what was happening and were told, "The earth is collapsing here," they all fled. In this manner, a host of animals stretching for a league (yojana) was formed.

Then the Bodhisatta saw the host of animals fleeing and asked, "What is the matter?" Hearing that the earth was collapsing, he thought, "The collapse of the earth has never happened before. Surely these creatures must have misunderstood some sound. If I do not make an effort, all these beings will perish. I shall save their lives."

Having so thought, he went with the speed of a lion to the foot of a mountain ahead of them and roared the lion's roar three times. Terrified by the lion's roar, the animals turned back and gathered together. The lion went among the creatures and asked, "For what reason are you fleeing?" When they said, "The earth is collapsing," he asked, "Who saw the earth collapsing?" When they said, "The elephants know," he questioned the elephants.

The elephants said, "We do not know; the lions know." The lions said, "We do not know; the tigers know." The tigers said, "The rhinoceroses know." The rhinoceroses said, "The gayals know." The gayals said, "The buffaloes know." The buffaloes said, "The sambar deer know." The sambar deer said, "The wild boars know." The wild boars said, "The deer know." The deer said, "We do not know; the little hares know."
71:
5. 'It makes the sound "duddubh", venerable sir, in the place where I dwell. I do not know what it is that makes this "duddubh" sound.'

He spoke this first verse.

'Sāmi', lord. 'Te', to you. 'Bhaddaṃ', good fortune. 'Atthu', may there be. 'Yasmiṃ dese', in which place. 'Ahaṃ', I. 'Vasāmi', dwell. 'Tattha', there. 'Duddubhāyati', it makes the sound 'duddubh'. 'Kiṃ', why. 'Etaṃ-etasmiṃ padese', in that place. 'Duddubhāyati', it makes the sound 'duddubh'. 'Etaṃ', that matter. 'Ahaṃ', I. 'Na jānāmi', do not know.

When the other rabbits were questioned, they pointed to this rabbit, saying, 'This rabbit said it.' Then [the Lion] asked that rabbit, 'Friend, is it true that the earth is collapsing?' 'Lord, it is true; I saw it,' he replied. 'Where were you staying when you saw it?' he asked. 'Lord, I saw it while staying in a palm grove mixed with wood-apple trees near the Western Ocean. While I was lying under a small palm tree at the foot of a wood-apple tree in that forest, I thought, "If the earth collapses, where shall I run?" At that very moment, I heard the sound of the earth collapsing and ran,' he said.

The Lion thought, 'In truth, a ripe wood-apple fell upon a palm leaf and made the sound "duddubh". This rabbit, hearing that sound, imagined the earth was collapsing and fled. I will find out the truth of this matter.'

Having so thought, the Lion took the rabbit, comforted the multitude of animals, and said, 'Stay here until I return after finding out the truth of whether the earth collapsed or not at the place where this rabbit saw it.' He then placed the rabbit on his back, ran with the speed of a lion, and upon reaching the palm grove, set the rabbit down and said, 'Come, friend, show me the place you saw.' 'Lord, I do not dare to show it,' he said.
