When told, 'Friend, do not be afraid,' the rabbit, not daring to approach the wood-apple tree, stood not far off and said, 'Lord, this is the place where the "duddubh" sound occurred.'

When he said this, the Lion went to the foot of the wood-apple tree and saw the place where the rabbit had lain under the palm tree and the ripe wood-apple that had fallen onto the palm leaf. Realizing the truth that the earth had not collapsed, he placed the rabbit on his back, returned quickly with the speed of a lion to the presence of the multitude of animals, reported the whole matter, and comforted the herd of animals, saying, 'Do not be afraid,' and then dismissed them.

At that time, had the Bodhisatta not existed, all the animals would have entered the ocean and perished. Because of the Bodhisatta, all the animals gained their lives.

The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this past story, and having attained Enlightenment, spoke these three verses:

6. 'Hearing the wood-apple fall, the rabbit ran, thinking "duddubh". Hearing the rabbit's word, the herd of animals was terrified.

7. Not reaching a clear understanding of the facts, following the reports of others, fools who take rumors as the highest truth fall under the influence of others.

8. But those who are endowed with virtue, who delight in the peace of wisdom, who are far from and refrain [from evil], those wise ones do not fall under the influence of others.'

'Saso', the rabbit. 'Duddubhanti', making the sound 'duddubh'. 'Patitaṃ', fallen. 'Beluvaṃ', hearing the sound of the ripe wood-apple. 'Sutvā', having heard. 'Javi', ran. 'Migavāhinī', the herd of animals. 'Sasassa', of the rabbit. 'Vacanaṃ', the word.
72:
'Sutvā', having heard. 'Santattā', being terrified. 'Javi', ran.

'Ye bālā', those fools. 'Padaviññāṇaṃ', not reaching the aggregate of ear-consciousness [clear understanding]. 'Appatvā', not having reached. 'Paraghosānusārino', following the sounds of others. 'Panādaparamā', regarding the noise of others as the highest truth. 'Te bālā', those fools. 'Parapattiyā', they become believers in others' words. 'Honti', they are.

'Ye dhīrā', those wise ones. 'Sīlena ca', endowed with the virtue of the Noble Path. 'Sampannā', are endowed. 'Paññāya ca', endowed with the wisdom of the Noble Path. 'Sampannā', are endowed. 'Upasame', delighting in the stilling of defilements. 'Ratā', they delight. 'Ārakā', far from committing evil. 'Viratā', refraining from evil. 'Te dhīrā', those wise ones. 'Parapattiyā', believing the words of others. 'Na honti', they are not.

Identifying the birth-story: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth-story: 'At that time, I myself was the Lion.'

## Believe only what is worthy of belief; consider all things with wisdom.

The Duddubha Jātaka ends.

## 3. Brahmadatta Jātaka

## To Beg is to be Disliked

The Present Story: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at the Aggāḷava Shrine near the city of Āḷavī, told this Brahmadatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Dvayaṃ yācanako', concerning the training rule on building huts.

(The present story is the same as that in the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka below.)

In this Brahmadatta Jātaka, the All-Knowing Buddha asked, 'Monks, is it true that you live making many requests and many intimations?' When they replied, 'It is true, Blessed One,' He rebuked those monks of Āḷavī and said, 'Monks, in former times, wise men, even when invited by a king who ruled the earth and water, desired to ask for a leaf-umbrella and a pair of single-layered sandals, yet out of fear of breaking their sense of shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa), they did not speak in the midst of the people but spoke in private.' Having said this, He brought forth the past.
73: In the past, when King Uttarapañcāla was reigning in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the kingdom of Kapila, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a market town. Upon reaching maturity, he learned all the arts in the city of Takkasilā. Later, he was ordained as an ascetic and lived for a long time in the Himalayas, subsisting on forest roots and various wild fruits. To partake of salt and vinegar, he wandered into the human realm and reached the city of Uttarapañcāla, where he stayed in the royal garden. The next day, while seeking alms, he entered the city and arrived at the palace gate. The King, being pleased with the Bodhisatta’s calm demeanor, invited him to sit on the magnificent terrace, served him food fit for a king, and after receiving his consent, had him reside in the garden. The Bodhisatta ate at the palace every day. When the rainy season had passed, he wished to return to the Himalayas and thought, "For me, who will be traveling, it is proper to obtain a pair of single-layered sandals and a leaf umbrella. I shall ask the King." Having thought so, one day he went to the garden, and seeing the King who had come to pay respects and was seated, he thought, "I will ask for the sandals and the umbrella." Then he thought again, "A person who asks another, saying 'Give me this,' is said to be crying. The owner of the wealth who says 'I have nothing' is also said to be crying back. Let not the many people see me crying, nor let them see the King crying back. In a secluded place, let both of us cry and then remain silent." Having thought thus, he then said to the King, "Great King, I desire a private audience." Hearing this, the King dismissed his attendants. The Bodhisatta thought, "If I ask and the King does not give, our friendship will be broken. Therefore, I will not ask." Being unable to mention the name of the sandals that day, he said, "Go for now, Great King, I will let you know another day." On another day, when the King came to the garden, he said the same thing. Again and again, he did the same. While the Bodhisatta was thus unable to make his request, twelve years passed. Then the King thought, "My master says, 'Great King, I desire a private audience,' but when the assembly has departed, he does not dare to say anything. Twelve years have passed for my master who wishes to speak. Perhaps my master, who has practiced the holy life for a long time, has become weary and wishes to enjoy sensual pleasures and desires the kingship. Yet, being unable to utter the word 'kingship,' he remains silent. Today, I will offer him whatever he desires, starting with the kingship." Having thought thus, the King went to the garden, paid his respects, and sat down.
74: 12. "I give to you, O Brahmin, a thousand red cows along with a bull. For how could a noble person, having heard your verses endowed with Dhamma, not give to another noble person?" He spoke this fourth verse. Brahmin: O ascetic who has put away evil. To you. Along with a bull. A thousand red cows. I give. Truly. Endowed with Dhamma: your words which are consistent with the truth. Having heard. A noble person: one endowed with noble conduct. To a noble person: to one endowed with noble conduct. How could he not give? Why would he remain without giving? When the Bodhisatta said he desired privacy, the King dismissed the assembly, and to the Bodhisatta who was unable to say anything, he said, "Bhante, for twelve years you have said you desire privacy, but even when privacy is gained, you are unable to say anything. I offer you everything, starting with the kingship. Being without fear, ask for whatever you desire." "Great King, will you give what I ask?" he said. "Bhante, I will give," the King replied. "Great King, for me who will be traveling, it is proper to obtain a pair of single-layered sandals and a leaf umbrella." "Bhante, were you unable to ask for this much for twelve years?" the King asked. "Great King, it is true that I was unable," he said. "Bhante, why did you do this?" the King asked. "Great King, one who asks, 'Please give me this thing,' is said to be crying. One who says, 'I have nothing,' is said to be crying back. If you, being asked, were not to give, let not the many people see that crying of mine and that crying back of yours, O King. Thus I desired privacy," he said, and to show this, he spoke these verses: 9. O King Brahmadatta, a beggar meets with two things: The loss of wealth or the gain of wealth. For such is the nature of begging. 10. They say that begging is crying, O Chief of Charioteers of the Pañcālas. He who refuses a request, they say that is crying back. 11. Let not the assembled Pañcālas see me crying, Nor you crying back. Therefore, I desire privacy. He spoke these verses. King Brahmadatta: King Brahmadatta. A beggar. The loss of wealth or the gain of wealth. Thus. Two things. Meets with. Truly. Begging. Has the nature of gain and loss. Chief of Charioteers of the Pañcālas: The King who is the supreme head of the Pañcāla kingdom. Begging. The wise. Crying. They say. He who. Begging. Refuses. That refusal. The wise. Crying back. They say. Me who is crying. You who are crying back. Well-assembled: those who have come together in harmony. The Pañcālas: the people of the Pañcāla kingdom. Let them not see. I keep in mind. Therefore. I. Privacy. I desire. The King, being pleased with the Bodhisatta's mark of respect, wished to give a boon.
75:
The Bodhisatta said, "Great King, I have no need for sensual desires or material objects. Give me only the umbrella and sandals I requested." Taking the single-layered sandals and the leaf umbrella, he advised the king, "Great King, be diligent, practice giving, keep the precepts, and observe the Uposatha." After advising the king, even as the king was pleading with him, he went to the Himalayas. There, he attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti) and was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the ascetic was I myself."

## One who begs, one who refuses, and one who cries; if one begs often, they are much disliked.

The Brahmadatta Jātaka is finished.

## 4. Cammasāṭaka Jātaka

## The Ram-Butted Wanderer

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who instructs the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Cammasāṭaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kalyāṇarūpo vatayaṃ," concerning a wanderer named Cammasāṭaka.

That wanderer, it is said, wore clothing made of leather. One day, leaving the wanderers' park and walking for alms in Sāvatthī, he reached a place where rams were fighting. A ram, seeing the wanderer and wishing to strike him, backed away. The wanderer, thinking, "This ram is showing me respect," did not move back. The ram ran with great speed, struck him on the thigh, and knocked him down. This act of the wanderer showing favor to an unworthy ram became well-known among the Saṅgha of monks.

The monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the wanderer Cammasāṭaka met his destruction by showing favor to an unworthy ram." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he met his destruction by showing favor to an unworthy ram," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family and, upon reaching maturity, engaged in trade.
76:
13. Truly, this four-footed creature is of beautiful form,
Excellent, and very well-behaved;
This noble ram of great fame
Pays respect to a Brahmin endowed with birth and mantras.

He spoke this first verse.

(Gloss:) Yasassī: of great fame. Yo meṇḍavaro: which noble ram. Jātimantūpapannaṃ: endowed with noble birth and knowledge of the Vedas. Brāhmaṇaṃ: to the Brahmin. Apacāyati: pays respect. Catuppado: four-footed. Yo meṇḍavaro: which noble ram. Kalyāṇarūpo vata: is indeed of beautiful form. Subhaddako ceva: and is indeed of excellent virtue. Supesalo ca: and is indeed very fond of virtue.

15. The thigh bone is broken, the basket of requisites is overturned and rolled away,
And all the belongings of the Brahmin are shattered.
Lifting both arms, he wails,
"Run here! The practitioner of the holy life is being struck!"

He taught this third verse.

(Gloss:) Brāhmaṇassa: of the wanderer. Ūruṭṭhi: the thigh bone. Bhaggam: is broken. Khāribhāro: the load full of requisites. Vaṭṭito: is overturned and rolled away. Sabbañca: and all. Bhaṇḍaṃ: the belongings. Bhinnaṃ: are shattered. Brahmacārī: the wanderer. Hañyate: is struck and killed. Tumhe: you all. Abhidhāvatha: run here! Iti: thus saying. Ubhopi: both. Bāhā: arms. Paggayha: lifting up. Kandati: he wails.

At that time, a certain wanderer named Cammasāṭaka, while walking for alms in Benares, saw a ram backing away and, thinking, "This ram is honoring me," did not step aside. Thinking, "Among all these people, this one ram knows my virtue," he stood there with hands clasped in salutation and spoke the first verse.

A wise merchant sitting in a shop there, wishing to stop the wanderer, spoke the second verse:

14. Do not, O Brahmin, because of a brief sight,
Place trust in a four-footed beast.
Desiring to deliver a hard blow,
It backs away to give a powerful strike.

(Gloss:) Brāhmaṇa: O Brahmin wanderer. Ittaradassanena: by seeing it at that moment. Catuppadassa: of the four-footed ram. Vissāsaṃ: trust. Mā āpajji: do not place. Daḷhappahāraṃ: a hard blow. Abhikankhamāno: desiring. Avasakkati: it backs away. So: that ram. Suppahāraṃ: a powerful strike. Dassati: will give.

The Cammasāṭaka Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Godharāja Jātaka

## The Lizard-Eating Ascetic

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who instructs the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Godharāja Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Samaṇaṃ taṃ maññamāno," concerning a hypocritical monk. (The introductory story is detailed below.)

In this Godharāja Jātaka as well, they brought that monk and showed him to the Teacher, saying, "Venerable Sir, this monk is a hypocrite." The Teacher said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he was a hypocrite," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in the species of lizards (iguanas) and, upon reaching maturity, was endowed with physical strength. He lived in the forest.
78:
17. Thinking you were an ascetic, I approached you, one who is unrestrained. You struck at me with a club, just as one who is not an ascetic would do.

18. What use is your matted hair, O witless one? What use is your antelope skin? Your interior is a jungle, while you polish the exterior.

A certain immoral ascetic built a leaf-hut near that iguana and lived there. The Bodhisatta, while wandering for food, saw that ascetic's hut and, thinking, "This must be the hut of a virtuous ascetic," went there, paid respects to the ascetic, and then returned to his own dwelling.

Then one day, that rogue ascetic received some well-prepared and delicious lizard meat at the house of a supporter. Having asked, "What kind of meat is this?" and hearing that it was lizard meat, he was overcome by the craving for its taste. Thinking, "I will kill the iguana that constantly comes to my hermitage, cook it as I please, and eat it," he took ghee, curds, and spices, went to the hut, took a club, and hid it under his saffron robe. He then sat at the door of the leaf-hut, appearing very peaceful, watching for the Bodhisatta's arrival.

The Bodhisatta arrived and, seeing that the ascetic's faculties were disturbed, thought, "This ascetic must have eaten the meat of my kinsmen. I shall investigate him." Standing downwind, he caught the scent of the body and, realizing that lizard meat had been eaten, he did not approach the ascetic but retreated and went away.

The ascetic, realizing that the Bodhisatta was not coming, threw the club. The club did not hit the body but reached the tip of the tail. The rogue ascetic said, "Hey, iguana! Go! I have missed you."

The Bodhisatta replied, "You have missed me for now, but you will not miss the four states of misery (apāya)," and he fled, entering a termite mound at the end of the cloister walk. He then poked his head out of another hole and, wishing to speak with that rogue ascetic, uttered these two verses:

I, thinking you were an ascetic, approached you, who are unrestrained in body, speech, and mind. In such a manner as one who is not an ascetic, you threw a club at me.

O witless one, what use are your matted hair to you? What use is your antelope skin to you? Your interior is a jungle of defilements, while you polish the exterior.
79:
19. "Come, lizard, turn back; eat the rice of the hill paddy. I have oil and salt, and I have plenty of long pepper."

He spoke this third verse.

Godha: Lizard. Ehi: Come. Nivattassu: Turn back. Sālīnaṃ: Of the hill paddy. Odanaṃ: Rice. Bhuñja: Eat. Me: To me. Telañca: Oil. Loṇañca: Salt. Atthi: There is. Mayhaṃ: To me. Pahūtaṃ: Plenty. Pipphali: There is also a commodity spiced with asafoetida, cumin, ginger, garlic, pepper, and long pepper.

20. "I will enter even deeper into the anthill, a hundred men deep. You speak of oil and salt, but long pepper is harmful to me."

He spoke this fourth verse.

Duṭṭhatāpasa: Wicked ascetic. So ahaṃ: That I. Sataporisaṃ: A hundred men deep. Vammikaṃ: Into the anthill. Bhiyyo: Further. Pavekkhāmi: Will enter. Tvaṃ: You. Telañca: Oil. Loṇañca: Salt. Kittesi: Speak of. Mayhaṃ: To me. Pipphali: Spices such as long pepper. Ahitaṃ: Are unsuitable.

Within, there is a jungle of defilements. Without, you smooth yourself over.

Hearing these words, the ascetic—

Hearing these words, the Bodhisatta—

Having said this, he threatened him: "You wicked false ascetic, if you stay here, I will have the people in the village where you collect alms catch you, saying 'This ascetic is a thief,' and bring you to ruin. Flee quickly!" The false ascetic fled from that place.

The Master, having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, identified the birth-story: "At that time, this monk who performs wonders was the false ascetic, and I myself was the Lizard King."

## Associate with consideration; only when goodness is known should one befriend.

The Godharāja Jātaka is concluded.

## 6. Kakkāru Jātaka

## The Celestial Flower

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Kakkāru Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kāyena yo nāvahare," concerning Devadatta.

When Devadatta caused a schism in the Saṅgha and the assembly departed along with the Chief Disciples, hot blood gushed from Devadatta's mouth. Then, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, Devadatta told lies and split the Saṅgha; now he is ill and suffering great pain."
80:
21. He who does not steal with his body, nor speak lies with his speech, and who, having gained fame, does not become intoxicated—he indeed is worthy of the Kakkāru flower.

He uttered this first verse:

He who does not steal another's property, even a blade of grass, with his body; who does not speak a lie with his speech even at the cost of his life; and who, having obtained wealth and status, does not become negligent—that person is truly worthy of the divine flower called Kakkāru.

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?" When they replied, "It is this subject," He said, "Monks, not only now is Devadatta a liar; in the past too, he was a liar. Not only now does he suffer great pain for telling lies; in the past too, he suffered it," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a certain deity in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. At that time, a great festival was held in Bārāṇasī. Many Nāgas, Garuḍas, and terrestrial deities came to watch the festival. From the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, four deities also came to see the festival, wearing wreaths made of divine flowers called Kakkāru. The city of Bārāṇasī, twelve leagues in extent, became filled with the single scent of those flowers. People wandered about, wondering, "Who is wearing these flowers?"

Those deities, knowing that the people were observing them, flew to the royal courtyard and stood in the air by their great divine power. A great crowd gathered. The King also went there with the Crown Prince and others. Then they asked the deities, "Lord, from which deva world do you come?" "We come from the Tāvatiṃsa deva world." "For what purpose have you come?" "To see the festival." "What are these flowers called?" "They are called divine Kakkāru flowers." "Lord, you may wear other flowers in the deva world; please give these to us." The deities said, "Divine Kakkāru flowers possess great power and are suitable only for devas. They are not suitable for base, witless, low-aspiring, and immoral humans in the human world. However, for those humans who are endowed with such and such virtues, these are suitable."
81:
22. "One should seek wealth righteously; one should not take wealth by fraud. Having obtained riches, one should not be intoxicated; he indeed is worthy of the Kakkāru flower."

He spoke this second verse. 

"One should seek wealth righteously. One should not take wealth by fraud. Having obtained riches, one should not be negligent. That person indeed is worthy of the celestial flower called Kakkāru."

23. "Whose mind is not like turmeric, and whose faith is unwavering. One should not eat delicious food alone; he indeed is worthy of the Kakkāru flower."

He spoke this third verse. 

"Whose mind does not fade quickly like the liquid of dyed turmeric, but remains firm. And whose faith—whether believing in kamma and its results or the words of a trustworthy person—does not fade or break even by a little. One who does not eat delicious food alone, excluding beggars or others worthy of sharing, but eats only after sharing with them; he indeed is worthy of these flowers."

Then they asked those deities, "Sirs, from which deva world have you come?" "We have come from the Tāvatiṃsa deva world," they replied. "For what purpose have you come?" they asked. "We have come to see the festival," they said. "What are the names of these flowers?" they asked. "They are celestial flowers called Kakkāru," they replied. "Sirs, please wear other flowers in the deva world and give these flowers to us," they requested.

The deities said, "The Kakkāru celestial flowers possess great power; they are suitable only for devas. They are not suitable for those in the human world who are wicked, lacking in wisdom, of evil intent, and devoid of virtue. They are suitable for those humans who are endowed with such and such virtues." Having said this, the eldest among the deities spoke:

Hearing those words, the chaplain thought, "I do not possess even one of these virtues. However, I will tell a lie, take those flowers, and wear them. When I wear them thus, the multitude will know me as 'this brahmin is endowed with virtues'." Having thought so, the chaplain said, "I am endowed with those virtues," and having the Kakkāru flowers brought to him, he wore them and then requested the second deity. That deity also spoke:

The chaplain said, "I am endowed with these virtues," and having the flowers brought to him, he wore them and requested the third deity. The third deity also spoke:

The chaplain said, "I am endowed with these virtues," and having the flowers brought to him, he wore them and requested the fourth deity. That deity also spoke:

The chaplain said, "Give them; I am endowed with these virtues," and having the flowers brought to him, he wore them.
82:
24. "Whether to one's face or behind one's back, one who does not revile the virtuous. One who acts as he speaks; he indeed is worthy of the Kakkāru flower."

He spoke this fourth verse. 

"Whether in one's presence or behind one's back, one who does not revile the virtuous. One who acts in the same manner as he speaks (one whose words and deeds are in harmony); he indeed is worthy of the celestial flower called Kakkāru."

The four deities gave the four flower wreaths to the chaplain and went to the deva world.

At the time of the deities' departure, a great pain arose in the chaplain's head. His head felt as if it were being cut by a sharp-edged chisel or pressed by an iron band. Reaching such agony, the chaplain rolled to and fro and cried out with a loud voice.

When asked, "What is this matter?", he said, "I told a lie, saying I possessed virtues that I did not have within me, and requested those flowers from the deities. Now I have reached this pain and my whole body trembles. Please remove these flower wreaths from my head." They were unable to remove those flower wreaths. They became as if fastened with iron bands. Then, they lifted the chaplain and carried him to his house. Seven days passed while the chaplain was crying out in his house.

The King consulted with his ministers, saying, "The immoral brahmin will die; what shall we do?" They replied, "Great King, if a festival is held again, the deities will return." The King had the festival held, and the deities returned. Making the entire city filled with the single scent of the flowers, they stood in the palace courtyard as before.

The multitude gathered, brought the immoral brahmin, and laid him on his back in front of the deities. That immoral brahmin entreated the deities, "Sirs, please give me my life."

The deities said, "These flowers are not suitable or fitting for you, who are immoral and of evil nature. You had the intention to deceive us; you have received the fruit of your own lying." Thus, having censured the immoral brahmin in the midst of the multitude, they removed the flower wreaths from his head, gave an exhortation to the multitude, and went back to their own place.
83:
The Omniscient Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the Brahmin was Devadatta, one of those deities was Kassapa, one was Moggallāna, one was Sāriputta, and I myself was the eldest deity.”

## False speech, for the speaker, brings great danger
The Kakkāru Jātaka ends.

## 7. Kāka-vatī Jātaka
## The Garuda who stole a wife
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kāka-vatī Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Vāti cāyaṃ tato gandho,” concerning a dissatisfied monk.

The Omniscient Buddha asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?” When the monk replied, “It is true, Venerable Sir,” the Buddha asked, “By what power are you dissatisfied?” The monk replied, “By the power of defilements (lust), Venerable Sir.” The Buddha then said, “Monk, women are indeed difficult to guard; they cannot be guarded. Even the wise men of old, though they made a woman live in a silk-cotton tree mansion in the middle of the great ocean, were unable to guard her,” and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the king's chief queen. When he came of age, he became king upon his father's passing. His chief queen was named Kāka-vatī, and she was as beautiful as a goddess.

(This account of the past story in this Kāka-vatī Jātaka is a brief summary. The detailed past story will be made clear in the Kunāla Jātaka.)

At that time, a certain Garuda king came in human form and played dice with the king. Having become infatuated with Queen Kāka-vatī, he took her and carried her away to the Garuda realm, where he enjoyed her company.

When the king did not see his queen, he said to a musician named Naṭakuvera, “Go and search for her.” While investigating, the musician discovered the truth. He climbed onto the Garuda king, hid between his wings, and when the Garuda rested in a grove of reeds by a lake, he stayed there. When the Garuda departed from that grove, the musician again sat between the wings and reached the Garuda realm. Emerging from the wings, he committed misconduct with Queen Kāka-vatī through the power of lust. Then, sitting between the Garuda’s wings once more, he returned. When the Garuda king was playing dice with the King of Bārāṇasī, the musician took his lute, went to the dice-playing circle, and standing near the king, sang this first verse:
84:
25. "The scent wafts from where my beloved dwells;
KākavatĢ is far from here, where my heart delights."
This was the first verse he spoke.

(Commentary): *Yattha* means in the Garuda realm. *Me* means my. *Piyā* means wife. *Vasati* means dwells. *Tato* means from that Garuda realm. *Ayaṁ gandho* means this scent of Queen KākavatĢ's body, who is anointed with divine perfumes. *Vāti ca* means it wafts indeed. *Yattha* means in which Queen KākavatĢ. *Me* means my. *Mano* means mind. *Nirato* means delights. *Sā KākavatĢ* means that Queen KākavatĢ. *Itō* means from this city of BārāṇasĢ. *Dūre* means in the distant Garuda realm. *Vasati* means she dwells.

This was the second verse spoken.

By you the seven seas; by you I climbed the silk-cotton tree."
This was the third verse spoken.

(Commentary): *Ahaṁ* means I. *Tayā* means by you. *Samuddaṁ* means the ocean. *Atariṁ* means I crossed. *Tayā* means by you. *Kepukaṁ* means the river named Kepuka. *Atariṁ* means I crossed. *Tayā* means by you. *Satta samuddāni* means the seven SĢdā oceans. *Atikkamitvā* means having passed. *Tayā* means by you. *Simbaliṁ* means the silk-cotton tree. *Aruhiṁ* means I climbed.

Hearing these words, the Garuda king—
Hearing these words, the musician Naṡakuvera—
Thereafter, the Garuda king—

That Garuda king brought Queen KākavatĢ back, gave her to the King of BārāṇasĢ, and never returned to the city of BārāṇasĢ again.
85:
The Omniscient Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). As for the identification of the birth: "At that time, the discontented monk was the harpist named Naṭakuvera, and I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī."

## Difficult to Guard is a Woman; Do Not Cling to Her Despite Repeated Warnings

The Kāka-jātaka is concluded.

## 8. Ananusociya-jātaka

## Distraught Over the Death of a Wife

While the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, He told this Ananusociya-jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Bahūnaṃ vijjatī bhotī," concerning a certain householder whose wife had died.

When his wife passed away, that householder did not bathe, drink, anoint himself, eat, or perform any work. Overwhelmed by grief, he merely wandered about the cemetery weeping. However, within the householder, the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) shone like a lamp inside a jar.

At dawn, the Omniscient Buddha, surveying the world, saw that householder and thought, "Except for Me, there is no one else who can remove this householder's grief and grant him the Path of Stream-entry. I shall be his refuge." After returning from the alms round and finishing His meal, He took an attendant monk and went to the householder's door. When the householder came out to welcome Him and performed the customary honors, the Buddha sat on the prepared seat. When the householder approached, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place, the Buddha asked, "Lay follower, why are you silent?" He replied, "Yes, Bhante, it is as You say. My wife has died, and I remain silent, grieving for her."

The Buddha said, "Lay follower, that which is of a nature to break must surely break. It is not proper to grieve over such a nature. Even the wise of old did not grieve when their wives died, saying, 'That which is of a nature to break has broken.'" Being requested by the householder, He brought forth the past story.

(The past story will be clearly explained in the Cūḷabodhi-jātaka of the Dasaka-nipāta; here in this Ananusociya-jātaka, the following is a summary of the past story.)

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. When he came of age, he learned all the arts in the city of Takkasilā and returned to his parents.
86:
(In this Ananusociya-jātaka, the Bodhisatta practiced the holy life from his youth.)

Then his parents informed him, "We shall search for a wife for you." The Bodhisatta replied, "I have no desire for household life. I shall become an ascetic after you have passed away." Though he said this, they pleaded with him again and again. So, he had a golden statue made and said, "If I find a maiden like this, I shall take her." The Bodhisatta's parents placed that golden statue in a covered carriage and sent people with a large retinue, saying, "Go, wander throughout the land of Jambudīpa. Wherever you see a Brahmin maiden of such a nature, give this golden statue and bring her back."

At that time, a meritorious being, having passed away from the Brahma realm, was reborn as a maiden in the house of a Brahmin possessing eighty crores of wealth in a market town in the kingdom of Kāsi. They gave her the name Sammillabhāsinī.

When she reached the age of sixteen, she was exceedingly beautiful, pleasing to behold, like a celestial nymph, and endowed with all auspicious marks. In that maiden named Sammillabhāsinī, no sensual thought had ever arisen; she practiced the supreme holy life.

The people wandering with the golden statue reached that village. When the people there saw the golden statue, they said, "Why is Sammillabhāsinī, the daughter of such-and-such a Brahmin, standing here?"

Hearing these words, the people went to the Brahmin's house and asked for Sammillabhāsinī. Sammillabhāsinī sent word to her parents, "I shall become a nun after you have passed away; I have no desire for household life." Her parents, wondering what the maiden would do, accepted the golden statue and sent Sammillabhāsinī away with a large retinue. Although neither the young man nor the young woman desired it, the marriage ceremony was performed.

Even though the two lived in the same room and slept on the same bed, they never looked at each other with lust. They lived together in one place like two monks or two Brahmas.

Later, the Bodhisatta's parents passed away. After performing their funeral rites, the Bodhisatta called Sammillabhāsinī and said, "Lady, take this wealth—eighty crores from my family and eighty crores from yours—and manage the household. I shall become an ascetic."
87:
29. She exists among many; what will she be to me? Therefore, I do not grieve for her, the dear one with the gentle smile.

30. If one should grieve for that which is no longer there, one should rather grieve for oneself, who is always falling into the power of death.

Sammillahasini said, "If you, my lord, become a monk, I too shall become a nun; I cannot bear to leave you."

Saying, "If that is so, then come," the Bodhisatta gave away all his wealth in charity and, renouncing his possessions like a glob of spit, entered the Himavanta. Both of them became ascetics and lived there for a long time, subsisting on forest roots and fruits. Later, to seek salt and vinegar, they descended from the Himavanta and eventually reached Vārāṇasī, where they stayed in the royal park.

While they were staying in the royal park, the female ascetic, being delicate, suffered from bloody dysentery after consuming unwholesome mixed food. Failing to get suitable medicine, she became weak.

At the time for alms-round, the Bodhisatta took her and brought her to the city gate. He laid her on a bench in a rest house and went for alms himself. Before the Bodhisatta could even leave the city, the female ascetic passed away. Seeing the beauty of the female ascetic, a great crowd gathered around her, weeping and wailing.

When the Bodhisatta returned from his alms-round and learned of her death, he thought, "That which is subject to decay has decayed; all formations are impermanent and of such a nature." He then sat on the very bench where she lay, ate his mixed food, and rinsed his mouth.

The crowd standing around asked, "Venerable sir, what was this female ascetic to you?" He replied, "When I was a layman, she was my wife (attendant at my feet)." They asked, "Venerable sir, even we cannot restrain ourselves and are weeping and wailing; why do you not weep?"

The Bodhisatta, wishing to preach the Dhamma to the people, said, "While she was alive, she was something to me; now that she has passed to the other world, she is nothing. She has gone under the power of death; why should I weep?" and spoke these verses:

31. Life-force does not follow one who is standing, sitting, lying, or walking. Even in the time it takes to open or shut an eye, age decays.

32. In this self which is thus failing, and where separation is certain, one should have compassion for the remaining living beings; one should not grieve for the one who is gone.
88:
Regarding those verses:

"She exists among many" (bahūnaṃ vijjatī bhotī) means this lady, having left us, now exists and is found among many hundreds of others who have died. "What will she be to me?" (tehi me kiṃ bhavissati) means what relation will she have with me now that she is among the dead? Or, what extra connection could she have with me—will she be a wife or a sister? There is also a reading "tehi mekaṃ," meaning this body of mine will also become one with those dead ones. "Therefore" (tasmā) means because she has been numbered among the dead and is nothing to me, I do not grieve for her.

"For that which is no longer there" (yaṃ yaṃ tassa) means if one should grieve for that being who is dead and ceased, and who no longer exists for the one grieving. There is also a reading "yassā." "Falling into the power of death" (maccuvasaṃ pataṃ) means in such a state, one should rather grieve for oneself who is constantly falling and going into the power of death; in that case, there would be no time for not grieving.

In the third verse, "Life-force does not follow one who is standing, sitting, lying, or walking" (na heva ṭhitaṃ nāsīnaṃ, na sayānaṃ na paddhagūṃ) implies that the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) does not merely follow a being in one posture. "Paddhagūṃ" means one who is walking or moving about. This means that while beings live heedlessly in all four postures, the life-force remains heedful day and night in all postures, performing only the work of its own exhaustion. "As long as it opens" (yāva vyāti) means as long as the eye opens. This was a common expression at that time. It means that even in the brief moment of opening and shutting the eyes, the age (vayo) of these beings decays; in all three stages of life, that particular age only diminishes and never increases.

"In this self which is thus failing" (tattrattani vata ppaddhe) means in this very self. It means that while age is thus decaying, this physical body, which is called "self," is failing; it is made incomplete or halved by age.
89:
Tattha, in the decline of that age. Vata, indeed. Attani, in the self/body. Paddhe, in deficiency and attachment. Vinābhāve, in separation. Asaṃsaye, there should be no doubt. Sesam bhūtaṃ, the remaining living beings should be pitied and loved. Vītaṃ, the dead should not be grieved for repeatedly.

Thus the Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma, showing the nature of impermanence with four verses. The people performed the funeral rites for the female wanderer. The Bodhisatta entered the Himalayas, developed the Jhanas, Abhiññas, and Samāpattis, and was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Omniscient Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He identified the Jātaka thus: “At that time, Sammillabhāsinī was the mother of Rāhula, and I myself was the ascetic.”

## Decay is natural, many should remember, do not grieve
The Ananusociya Jātaka ends.

## 9. Kāḷabāhu Jātaka
## Blackie of the Forest
While staying at Veḷuvana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kāḷabāhu Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Yaṃ annapānassa,” concerning Devadatta who had lost his gain and honor.

Devadatta, having harbored malice against the Tathāgata where it was undeserved, sent archers and released the elephant Nālāgiri, making his guilt evident. Then, the people stopped providing the regular alms-food and other offerings they had established for Devadatta. Even the king no longer looked upon him with favor. Having lost his gain and honor, Devadatta went about begging for food from families.

The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, Devadatta, wishing to produce gain and honor, was unable to make even what he had gained remain stable.” The Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they replied, “For such a discussion,” He said, “Monks, not only now has he lost his gain and honor; in the past also, he lost his gain and honor,” and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Dhanañjaya was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a parrot named Rādha. He had a large and well-proportioned body. His younger brother was named Poṭṭhapāda. A hunter caught the two parrot brothers, adorned them, and presented them to the King of Bārāṇasī.

## 10. Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka
## Sensual Pleasures are Like a Piece of Meat

**The Present Account**
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇaṃ," concerning a Brahmin who tested his own virtue.

(Both the Present and Past Accounts have already been related below.)

Specifically, in this Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka, the Bodhisatta was the chaplain (purohita) to the King of Bārāṇasī. Wishing to test his own virtue, for three days he took kahāpaṇa coins from a goldsmith's board. They seized the Bodhisatta, calling him a thief, and presented him to the King. Standing in the presence of the King, the Bodhisatta recited this first stanza:

37. Sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇaṃ, sīlaṃ loke anuttaraṃ.
Passa ghoraviso nāgo, sīlavāti na haññati.

Virtue indeed is good; virtue is supreme in the world. Behold, even a snake with deadly venom is not harmed because it is virtuous.

Having praised virtue with this stanza and obtained the King's permission to become an ascetic, he departed to ordain. Then one day, a hawk seized a piece of meat from a meat market and flew into the sky. Other birds surrounded that hawk and attacked it with their claws and beaks. Unable to endure the pain, the hawk dropped the piece of meat. Another hawk seized it.

That hawk which took the piece of meat was likewise attacked by the other birds and dropped it as before. Then another hawk seized it. Among those birds, whichever one held the meat was pursued by the others. Whichever one dropped it became happy.

Seeing this occurrence, the Bodhisatta reflected, "These sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat; only those who carry them experience suffering, while those who let go find happiness." He then recited this second stanza:

38. Yāvadēvassahū kiñci, tāvadeva akhādisuṃ.
Saṅgamma kulalā loke, na hiṃsanti akiñcanaṃ.

As long as that hawk had even a little piece of meat held in its beak, the hawks in this world gathered and pecked at it. But the other birds do not harm the one who has nothing, having released the meat.

Leaving the city, the Bodhisatta slept at a man's house in a village along the way in the evening. In that house, a maidservant named Piṅgalā had made an appointment with a man, saying, "Come at such and such a time."
93:
40. Na samādhiparo atthi, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.
Na paraṃ nāpi attānaṃ, vihiṃsati samāhito.

He recited this fourth stanza:

In this present world and in the world hereafter, there is no happiness superior to concentration (samādhi). One who is composed and concentrated harms neither others nor himself.

That maidservant named Piṅgalā, after washing her masters' feet, sat at the threshold while they slept, watching for the man's arrival, thinking, "He will come now, he will come now," passing the first and middle watches of the night. At dawn, realizing "He will not come now," her expectation ceased, and she lay down and fell into a deep sleep.

Seeing this, the Bodhisatta reflected, "This maidservant sat for this long thinking that the man would come. Now, knowing he will not come, her expectation is broken and she sleeps happily. In the context of defilements, expectation (desire) is suffering; only the state of being without expectation is happiness." He then recited this third stanza:

39. Sukhaṃ nirāsā supati, āsā phalavatī sukhā.
Āsaṃ nirāsaṃ katvāna, sukhaṃ supati piṅgalā.

One who is free from expectation sleeps happily. The fulfillment of expectation is happy. Piṅgalā, having turned her expectation into non-expectation, now sleeps happily.

The next day, as the Bodhisatta entered the forest from that village, he saw another hermit absorbed in meditative absorption (jhāna). Reflecting that there is no happiness in this world or the next that surpasses the bliss of jhāna, he recited [the fourth stanza mentioned above].

The Bodhisatta then entered the forest, ordained as a hermit, developed meditative absorptions and higher knowledges (abbiññā), and was destined for the Brahma realm.

Having delivered this discourse, the Omniscient Buddha identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the Brahmin chaplain."

## Like a piece of meat, in sensual pleasures, if one clings, suffering follows.

The Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka ends.
The third chapter, Kuṭidūsaka Vagga, is complete.

## 4. Kokila Vagga
## 1. Kokila Jātaka
## Speaking Excessively Leads to Ruin

**The Present Account**
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kokila Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Yo ve kāle asampatte," concerning Kokālika. (The Present Account has been detailed in the Takkāriya Jātaka.) The Omniscient Buddha then related the past.

**The Past Account**
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was an official who advised the King. The King was very talkative. The Bodhisatta wandered about seeking a metaphor to restrain the King's talkativeness.

One day, the King went to the park and sat on the royal stone slab. Above the slab was a mango tree. In a crow's nest in that tree, a female cuckoo (kokila) laid her egg and left. The female crow looked after the cuckoo's egg. Later, a young cuckoo hatched from that egg. Thinking "This is my son," the female crow brought food in her beak and raised the young cuckoo. While its wings were not yet grown, the young cuckoo cried out with the sound of a cuckoo out of season. The female crow thought, "Even now this young bird makes a different sound; what will it do when it grows up?" She pecked it to death with her beak and threw it out of the nest. The young cuckoo fell at the King's feet.

The King asked the Bodhisatta, "Friend, what is the meaning of this?" The Bodhisatta, who had been searching for a metaphor to restrain the King, thought, "Now I have found that metaphor." He said, "Great King, those who are very harsh-tongued and speak excessively out of season meet with such suffering."

"Great King, this young cuckoo, raised by the female crow, cried out with a cuckoo's sound out of season before its wings were grown. Therefore, the female crow, realizing 'This bird is not my son,' pecked it to death and threw it from the nest. Whether they be humans or animals, those who speak excessively out of season undergo such suffering," and he recited these stanzas:

2. Indeed, a well-sharpened sword or halāhala poison does not strike down as instantly as a poorly spoken word.

3. Therefore, a wise person should guard their speech, whether at the right time or the wrong time. One should not speak excessively, even with one's equals.

4. He who speaks moderately at the right time, being circumspect and guided by wisdom, overcomes all enemies, just as a Garuḍa captures a snake.

He spoke these verses.

O Great King! Indeed, if a person speaks excessively before the proper time for speaking arrives, they lie defeated like the offspring of a cuckoo. Just as a poorly spoken word kills in an instant, a well-sharpened sword does not. Just as a poorly spoken word kills in an instant, halāhala poison, which causes immediate death, does not.

Therefore, a wise person should guard their speech at the right time or the wrong time. Even with one's equals, one should not speak excessively.

Just as a Garuḍa king captures a snake, so too a wise person, guided by wisdom, who speaks moderately at the proper time, can capture and control all enemies.

The King, having heard the Bodhisatta's teaching, became moderate in speech from then on. He increased the Bodhisatta's prosperity and gave him much.

Identifying the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the young cuckoo was Kokālika, and the wise minister was I myself."

## If one speaks before the time is right, one will meet with danger

The Kokila Jātaka ends.

## 2. Rathalaṭṭhi Jātaka
## Blaming others for one's own mistake

The Teacher, the Omniscient One who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Rathalaṭṭhi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Api hantvā hato brūti," while staying at Jetavana Monastery, concerning King Kosala's chaplain (purohita).

While that chaplain was going to his revenue village in a chariot, he drove the chariot on a narrow road and saw a caravan leader. He shouted, "Move your caravan!" and proceeded. When the caravan did not move aside, he became angry and struck the carter of the lead wagon with his goad. The goad hit the chariot's yoke, bounced back, and struck the chaplain's own forehead. At that moment, a lump swelled up on his forehead. The chaplain returned and reported to the king, "I was struck by the carters." When the carters were summoned and questioned, only the chaplain's fault was seen.

Then one day, the monks discussed in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, it is said that the King's chaplain, while bringing a case saying 'I was struck by the carters,' was himself defeated."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing as you sit here?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now has he done such a thing; in the past too, he did exactly the same," and he brought forth the past story.

The Past Story: In the past, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a judge for that king.

## 3. Pakkagodha Jātaka
## Run Away, Roasted Iguana!

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the Teacher of the world including the devas, told this Pakkagodha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Tadeva me tvaṃ," concerning a certain householder.

(The story is detailed below.) Specifically, in this Pakkagodha Jātaka, while a householder and his wife were returning after collecting a debt, a hunter gave them a roasted iguana on the way, saying, "Both of you may eat this." The man sent his wife to fetch water, ate the entire roasted iguana himself, and when his wife returned, he said, "My dear, the roasted iguana ran away." She replied, "Very well, lord; if the roasted iguana has run away, what can be done?"

Thus, the husband and wife drank water at Jetavana Monastery and sat in the presence of the Blessed One. The Fully Enlightened One asked, "Laywoman, does this lay disciple desire your welfare? Does he love you?" The woman replied, "Venerable Sir, I desire his welfare and I love him, but he does not love me."

The Fully Enlightened One said, "Laywoman, let it be as you say; do not worry. This man indeed acts in such a way. However, when he remembers your virtue, he will give you all his wealth, just as he did in the past." Being requested by the two of them, He brought forth the past story.

In the past (the past story is identical to the one mentioned below). Specifically, while a prince and princess were returning to Bārāṇasī, a hunter, seeing their exhaustion, gave them a roasted iguana, saying, "Both of you may eat this." The princess tied the roasted iguana with a creeper and carried it as they traveled.

Seeing a lake, the prince and princess turned off the path and sat at the foot of an Asattha tree. The prince said, "My dear, go and fetch water with a lotus leaf; we shall eat the iguana meat." The princess hung the roasted iguana on a branch of the Asattha tree and went to fetch water. The prince ate the entire roasted iguana, held the tip of its tail, and sat facing away.

When the princess returned with the water, the prince said, "My dear, the iguana climbed down from the branch and entered an anthill. I ran and grabbed the tip of its tail, but the part I held broke off in my hand, and it entered the hole." The princess said, "My Lord, let it escape. If the roasted iguana has run away, what can we do? Come, let us go." After drinking water, the two went to Bārāṇasī.

## 4. Rājovāda Jātaka

## A good leader brings happiness to all

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Rājovāda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Gavaṃ ce taramānānaṃ," concerning the admonition of a king.

(The story will become clear in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka.) Specifically, in this Rājovāda Jātaka, the Omniscient Buddha said, "Great King, wise kings of old, having heard the words of the wise and ruling with righteousness and justice, went on to fill the celestial realm," and being requested by the King, He brought forth the past.
101: The Atīta-vatthu: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. Having learned all the arts and reached maturity, he renounced as a hermit and attained the direct knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti). He lived in a pleasant region of the Himalayas, subsisting on forest roots and fruits. At that time, the King, being one who sought his own faults, searched, thinking, 'Is there anyone who speaks of my faults?' Finding no one among the inner circle, the outer circle, inside the city, or outside the city who spoke of his faults, he wondered, 'What about the country folk?' and traveled through the countryside in disguise. Finding no one there either who spoke of his faults, and hearing only praise of his virtues, he thought, 'What about the Himalayan region?' and entered the forest. While wandering, he reached the Bodhisatta's hermitage, paid homage to him, and after receiving friendly greetings, sat in a suitable place. Then the Bodhisatta brought ripe banyan fruits from the forest and ate them. Those ripe banyan fruits were sweet, flavorful, and like powdered sugar. The Bodhisatta addressed the King, saying, 'O meritorious donor, eat this ripe banyan fruit and drink water.' The King did as the Bodhisatta said and asked, 'Venerable sir, why is this ripe banyan fruit so very sweet?' 'O meritorious donor, the King must be ruling righteously and justly; therefore, it is sweet.' 'Venerable sir, does it become unsweet when the King is unrighteous?' 'Yes, O meritorious donor, it is just as you say. When kings are unrighteous, oil, honey, molasses, and the like, as well as forest roots and fruits, become unsweet and lose their essence. Not only these, but the entire country becomes essence-less and tasteless. But when they are righteous, all those foods are sweet and flavorful, and the entire country becomes full of essence.' The King said, 'Venerable sir, let it be as you have said.' Without revealing his identity as the King, he paid homage to the Bodhisatta and returned to Bārāṇasī. Thinking, 'I will test the hermit's words,' he ruled unrighteously. Thinking, 'Now I shall know,' he let some time pass and then went back to that hermitage, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and sat in a suitable place.

The Bodhisatta said, "O King of great merit, the King must be unrighteous. In times when kings are unrighteous, everything from the large and small forest fruits becomes unsweet and flavorless."

Among the cattle crossing the river, if the lead bull goes straight, when the leader has gone straight, all the cows go straight.

In the same way, among men, he who is designated as the chief—if that king practices righteousness, what need is there to speak of the other people? If the king is righteous, the entire realm dwells in happiness.

Having heard the Bodhisatta's words, the King made his kingship known and said, "Venerable sir, previously I myself made the sweet banyan fruit bitter; now I shall make it sweet again." Having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, he went to the city and ruled righteously. The ripe banyan fruit returned to its natural state.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King was Ānanda, and the ascetic was I myself."

## If one rules with righteousness, the country and its people will be prosperous and abundant

The Rājovāda Jātaka ends.

## 5. Jambuka Jātaka
## Crushed to Death by an Elephant due to Great Pride

While residing at the Jetavana monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Jambuka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Brahā pavaḍḍhakāyo so,” concerning Devadatta’s imitation of the Buddha.

(The present story has been detailed below. Specifically, in this Jambuka Jātaka, the summary should be understood as follows:)

When the Omniscient Buddha asked, “Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do when he saw you?” the Venerable Sāriputta Thera replied, “Venerable Sir, imitating You, he lay down after giving a fan into my hand. At that time, Kokālika struck Devadatta in the chest with his knee. Thus, by imitating You, Devadatta suffered pain.”

Upon hearing these words, the Omniscient Buddha said, “Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta suffers pain by imitating me; he also suffered in the past,” and at the request of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the family of lions and lived in a cave in the Himālaya. One day, after killing a buffalo, eating its meat, and drinking water, he returned to his cave.

A certain jackal, seeing the lion and being unable to flee, lay down on its chest. When asked, “Jackal, what are you doing?” it replied, “Lord, I wish to serve you.” The lion said, “In that case, come,” and taking the jackal to his dwelling place, he fed it by bringing meat every day. Having reached a state of being fat and stout by eating the lion’s leftovers, pride arose in that jackal one day.
104:
18. He who is not a lion, yet through a lion's pride transforms himself, lies on the ground moaning, like a jackal that has attacked an elephant.

19. Without considering the strength and lineage of the glorious, supreme person of great power and well-formed shoulders, this jackal lies killed by the elephant.

20. He who performs a task here with measurement, knowing his own strength and power, through study, counsel, and well-spoken words, being circumspect, wins great success.

That jackal approached the lion and said, "Lord, I serve you at all times. You always bring prey and feed me. Today, you stay here; I will kill an elephant, eat its meat, and bring some for you."

The lion said, "Jackal, do not take pleasure in that task. You were not born of a race that kills elephants and eats their meat. I will kill an elephant and give it to you. An elephant has a large body; do not try to catch one. Listen to my words."

Despite the lion's warning, the jackal left the cave, howled three times like a jackal, and standing on the mountain peak, looked down at the foot of the mountain. Seeing a black elephant coming along the foot of the mountain, he jumped, thinking, "I will land on its frontal lobes," but he tumbled and fell at the elephant's feet.

The elephant raised its front feet and stepped on the jackal's head. The head was crushed to pieces. The jackal lay there moaning. The elephant went away trumpeting like a crane.

The Bodhisatta went and stood on the mountain peak, and seeing the destroyed jackal, he said, "The jackal is ruined because of his own pride," and spoke these three verses:

Like a jackal reaching an elephant, moaning and lying on the ground as if sleeping; he who is not a lion but acts with a lion's pride, transforming himself, such a person is like this jackal.

This jackal, [without considering] the glorious, supreme person...
105:
...the supreme person, with well-formed large shoulders, the lion king of great strength. Without considering the manifestation of power and lineage, he lies dead, killed by the elephant.

In this world, he who is circumspect and wise, who acts with measurement, knowing his own physical and intellectual strength, through mantras (study), through consultation with the wise, and through well-spoken words, that person wins great benefit.

Thus, the Bodhisatta spoke of the proper conduct in this world through these three verses.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, and the lion was I myself."

## Pride overwhelms, overestimation leads to ruin

The Jambuka Jātaka ends.

## 6. Brahāchatta Jātaka

## Carrying wisdom, wealth is regained

The Teacher, who is the guide of the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Brahāchatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Tiṇaṃ tiṇanti lapasi," concerning a deceitful monk. (The present story has been told).

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a minister who advised him on matters of welfare and Dhamma. The King of Bārāṇasī went with a great army against the King of Kosala, reached Sāvatthī, entered the city through battle, and captured the king.

The King of Kosala had a son named Chatta. He fled in disguise and went to Takkasilā, where he learned the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge. Leaving Takkasilā, he continued his studies and reached a border village.
106:
Depending on that border village, five hundred ascetics lived in leaf-huts in the forest. Prince Chatta approached those five hundred ascetics, thinking, "I shall learn some art from these ascetics as well," and ordained as a monk. He learned all the arts that the ascetics knew and later became the leader of the group.

Then one day, he addressed the group of ascetics, "Sirs, why do you not go to the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa)?" They replied, "Friend, the people in the Middle Country are wise. They will ask questions, they will request discourses (anumodanā), they will ask for the recitation of blessings (maṅgala), and they will criticize those who are unable to do so. Out of fear of such things, we do not go."

Prince Chatta said, "Sirs, do not be afraid. I will handle all of those things." The ascetics said, "In that case, let us go," and each taking their various requisites, they eventually reached the city of Bārāṇasī.

The King of Bārāṇasī had brought the King of Kosala under his power. Leaving royal officials in the city of Sāvatthī, he himself took the wealth that was in Sāvatthī and went to Bārāṇasī. He filled copper pots with it, buried them in the garden, and resided only in Bārāṇasī.

Then, the ascetics stayed in the royal garden at night, and the next morning, they entered the city of Bārāṇasī for alms and reached the palace gate. The King, being pleased with the deportment of those ascetics, had them invited in and seated on the magnificent terrace. He offered the ascetics gruel and snacks and asked various questions until the meal was finished. Prince Chatta alone, pleasing the King's heart, answered all the questions and, at the end of the meal, gave a wonderful discourse. The King was exceedingly pleased, took their promise to stay, and had all the ascetics reside in the garden.

Prince Chatta knew a mantra for uncovering treasure pots. While residing in the garden, he recited the mantra to discover where the King of Bārāṇasī had buried his father's wealth. Knowing that it was buried in the garden, he thought, "I will take this wealth and reclaim my kingdom." He then called the ascetics and said, "Sirs, I am the son of the King of Kosala. When the King of Bārāṇasī took our kingdom, I fled in disguise and have protected my life for this long. Now I have obtained my father's wealth. I will take that wealth, go, and reclaim my own country. What will you sirs do?" They replied, "We too will follow along with you."

The Bodhisatta thought, "The King has great grief and wanders about lamenting. Except for me, no one else is able to dispel this King's sorrow. I shall make the King free from grief." Having so thought, one day while the Bodhisatta was sitting comfortably with the King, at the time when the King was lamenting—

Upon hearing these words—

The King spoke in reproach of Prince Chatta, and through the words spoken by the Bodhisatta, he became free from sorrow and ruled the kingdom righteously.

Identifying the Birth: The Omniscient Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the monk who performs wonders was Brahāchatta. I myself was the wise minister at that time.”

## Skilled in Wisdom, Possessor of Wealth, He Takes Over the Realm

The Brahāchatta Jātaka ends.

## 7. Pīṭha Jātaka
## One's Own Error, Blaming Others
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Pīṭha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na te pīṭhamadāyimha," concerning a certain monk.

That monk went from the countryside to Jetavana Monastery, put away his bowl and robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and asked the novices and junior monks, "Friends, who are the benefactors of visiting monks in Sāvatthī?" They replied, "Friend, the great treasurer named Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay devotee named Visākhā are the benefactors of the Saṅgha; they stand in the place of parents to the Saṅgha."

The monk said, "Very well," and the next morning, even before any other monk had entered, he went to the door of Anāthapiṇḍika's house. Because he arrived too early, no one noticed him. Obtaining nothing from Anāthapiṇḍika's house, he went to Visākhā's house. There too, because he arrived too early, he obtained nothing.

Wandering from house to house, he returned only after the rice gruel was finished. Again, he wandered here and there and returned only after the meal was finished. Going back to the monastery, he went about disparaging those families, saying, "Both families are without faith and devotion. Yet these monks say they are 'faithful and devoted.' What kind of people are they?"

Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, it is said that a certain monk from the countryside went to the doors of the donors' houses too early, and when he did not receive alms, he went about disparaging the donors." The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they told him, he summoned that monk and asked, "Is it true, monk, that you disparaged the donors because you did not receive alms?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "Monk, why are you angry? In the past, before the Buddha arose, even ascetics did not get angry when they went to the doors of donors and did not receive alms," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā. Later, he renounced the world as an ascetic and lived for a long time in the Himalayas. To seek salt and vinegar, he went to Bārāṇasī, stayed in a park, and the next day entered the city for alms.

At that time, the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī was full of faith and devotion.

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. To identify the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the merchant of Bārāṇasī, and I myself was the ascetic."

## Even if one is a monk, one should not harbor resentment toward others.

## 8. Thusa Jātaka
## The Verse of Life-Saving
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world, told this Thusa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Viditaṃ thusaṃ," concerning King Ajātasattu.

When King Ajātasattu was conceived in the womb of his mother, Queen Videhī, the daughter of the King of Kosala, the queen had a pregnancy craving to drink the blood from the right knee of King Bimbisāra, and she became pale in complexion. When asked by her attendants, she informed them of the matter.

The King also heard of it, summoned the soothsayers, and asked, "The Queen has such a pregnancy craving; what will be the result of this craving?" The soothsayers said, "The being born from the Queen's womb will kill you, Great King, and take the kingdom."
112:
The King thought, 'If this son of mine should kill me and take the kingship, what fault would there be in me?' He had his right thigh cut with a knife, collected the blood in a golden bowl, and gave it to the Queen to drink.

The Queen thought, 'If the son born in my womb should kill his father, what use is that son to me?' and had her belly massaged to induce an abortion. King Bimbisāra, upon learning this, summoned the Queen and said, 'Dear, it is said my son will kill me and take the kingship. I am not one who will live forever without aging or dying. Let me see my son's face; do not do such a thing from this day forward.'

From then on, the Queen went to the garden and had her belly massaged. The King, learning of this, forbade her from going to the garden. When her pregnancy was full-term, she gave birth to a son. On the naming day, they named the prince Ajātasattu, because even before he was born, he was his father's enemy.

The King, having served the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with choice food and offerings, sat listening to the Dhamma after paying homage to the Buddha. At that moment, they dressed the prince and presented him to the King. Out of great affection, the King took the son and placed him on his lap. Because of his love for his son, he cherished him so much that he could not listen to the Dhamma.

The All-Enlightened Buddha, knowing the King's state of negligence, said, 'Great King, in the past, kings who were suspicious of their sons kept them in hiding and commanded, "Only after my passing shall you bring him out and establish him in the kingship."' At King Bimbisāra's request, the Buddha then related a story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā, teaching the arts to many princes and brahmins.
113:
29. The chaff is known to the rats; the rice grain is also known.
Rejecting the chaff, they eat the rice.
He recited this first verse.

'To the rats' (undurānaṃ); 'the chaff' (thusaṃ)—even in the darkness, it is known (viditaṃ) as chaff. 'The rice grain' (taṇḍulaṃ)—it is also known (viditaṃ) as rice. 'Rejecting' (vivajjetvā) every bit of chaff, they 'eat' (khādare) only the rice.

The son of the King of Bārāṇasī also went to the Bodhisatta when he was sixteen years old, learned the three Vedas and all the arts, and having mastered them, took leave of his teacher.

The teacher, observing the prince through the science of physiognomy (Angavijjā), thought, 'A danger to this prince is apparent because of his son. I shall avert that danger through my own power.' He composed four verses and gave them to the prince. He instructed him thus:

'Dear, when you are established in the kingship and your son is sixteen years old, recite the first verse while eating your meal. Recite the second verse during a great audience. Recite the third verse while ascending the palace, standing at the head of the stairs. Recite the fourth verse while entering the royal bedchamber, standing on the threshold.'

The prince agreed, paid homage to the teacher, and left. He was established as the heir apparent and, upon his father's passing, became King. When his son reached sixteen years of age, seeing the royal glory and wealth as the King went out for garden sports and such, he desired to kill his father and take the kingship. He spoke to his attendants. Those attendants said, 'Very well, O Prince. What is the use of power obtained in old age? It is proper to kill the King by some means and take the kingship.'

The prince thought, 'I will kill him by making him eat poison.' While having dinner with his father, he sat holding the poison. Before the King's hand even touched the food in the bowl to eat—
