30. Whatever counsel was held in the forest, and whatever whispering in the ear in the village; and this 'thus and so'—all this is known by me.

He recited this second verse.

*Araññasmiṃ ca*, in the garden; *gāme ca*, in the village; *nikaṇṇikā*, whispering in the ear; *yā mantanā ca*, whatever counsel there was. *Iti*, thus, in every such counsel to kill me; *yañcetaṃ iti cီti ca*, and this present seeking of an opportunity to kill me here and there; *atthi*, there is. *Etampi*, all that too; *mayā*, by me; *viditaṃ*, is known.

31. By nature, it is said, a monkey is a father to his son; while he is still young, he bites off the seeds with his teeth.

He recited this third verse.

*Pitā*, the father; *makkaṭo*, monkey; *jātassa*, born of himself; *puttassa*, to the young monkey son; *phalaṃ*, the seed; *dhammena*, by nature; *daharasseva santassa*, while still young; *dantehi*, with teeth; *acchidā*, cuts off; *purisabhāvaṃ*, manhood; *nāseti*, destroys.

Thinking 'The King has found out,' and being afraid, the prince did not dare to put poison in the rice bowl; he rose, paid homage to the King, and fled from that place. He reported the matter to his attendants and asked, 'He has found out today; how shall we kill him now?' From that time on, those attendants hid in the garden and, whispering in his ear, counseled him: 'There is one way; when you are girded with your sword and have reached the great audience, stay among the ministers, and knowing the King's moment of negligence, you should strike and kill him with the sword.' They made him take note of this.

The prince agreed, saying 'Very well,' and being girded with his sword during the great audience, he went and moved here and there, seeking an opportunity to kill. At that moment, the King—

The prince, thinking 'My father the King knows of my enmity,' fled from that place and reported it to his attendants. When seven or eight days had passed, they said, 'Prince, your father does not know of your enmity; you only imagined it so by your own thinking. Kill him!'

One day, the prince took his sword and stood at the head of the stairs. The King, standing at the head of the stairs—

The prince, fearing 'My father wants to have me seized,' fled and reported to his attendants, 'My father has threatened me.' When half a month had passed, they said, 'Prince, if the King knew, he would have destroyed you in all this time; you only said so by your own imagination. Kill the King!'

One day, the prince took his sword, entered the royal bedchamber on the upper palace, and sat under the couch, thinking, 'I will kill him as soon as he comes.' The King, having finished his evening meal, dismissed his retinue and, intending to sleep, entered the royal chamber and, standing on the threshold—
115:
32. As you slink about like a blind goat in a mustard field, and as you lie here beneath [the couch]—all this is known by me.

He recited this fourth verse.

*Tvaṃ*, you; *sāsape*, when entering a mustard field; *ajakāṇova*, like a blind goat; *bhayena*, out of fear; *yametaṃ parisappasi*, that which you slink here and there. *Idāni*, now; *māressāmīti*, thinking 'I will kill'; *heṭṭhato*, under the couch; *yo pāyaṃ seti*, that which you lie; *etampi*, all that too; *mayā*, by me; *viditaṃ*, is known.

When the King, after dinner, had dismissed the assembly and was about to enter the royal chamber to sleep, he stood at the threshold—

Thus, even though the King did not know [the prince was there], his verse revealed those various meanings to the prince. The prince thought, 'My father knows me; now he will destroy me.' Terrified, he came out from under the couch, dropped his sword at the King's feet, and prostrated himself with his chest on the ground at the King's feet, saying, 'Forgive me, O Great King!'

The King threatened the prince, saying, 'You thought, "Who will know of my deed?"' He had him bound in chains, sent to prison, and placed under guard. At that time, the King remembered the virtues of the Bodhisatta. Later, that King passed away. After performing the funeral rites for the King, they released the prince from prison and established him in the kingship.

The Teacher, having brought forward this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, I myself was the world-renowned teacher in the city of Takkasilā.'

## An enemy fool should be kept far away

End of the Thusa Jātaka.

## 9. Bāveru Jātaka

## The Crow and the Peacock

The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Bāveru Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Adassanena morassa,' concerning the heretics whose gain and honor had vanished.
116:
These ascetics (titthiyas) received gains before the Buddha appeared. However, when the Buddha appeared, their gains and honors vanished, and they became like fireflies at sunrise. Regarding this matter of the ascetics, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall.

The All-Enlightened Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit here?" When they replied, "It is such and such a subject," he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past also, before those with merit appeared, those without merit received the highest gains and fame. But when those with merit appeared, those without merit lost their gains and honors." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the peacock species. When he grew up, he was endowed with great beauty and wandered in the forest.

At that time, some merchants took a direction-finding crow (disākāka) and went to the Kingdom of Bāveru by ship. At that time, it is said, there were no birds in the Kingdom of Bāveru.

The inhabitants, whenever they came, saw the direction-finding crow sitting in its cage and said, "Look at the color of this bird's skin up to its neck, its beak, and its eyes which are like spheres of jewels!" They praised only the crow and said to the merchants, "Sirs, give us this bird. We have need of it. You can get another one in your own country."

The merchants said, "Then take it for a price." The inhabitants said, "Give it to us for one kahāpaṇa." The merchants said, "We will not give it." Gradually increasing the price, when they said, "Give it for a hundred kahāpaṇas," the merchants said, "This bird is very useful to us, but let there be friendship with you," and they took the hundred kahāpaṇas and gave it away.
117:
33. Through the non-seeing of the peacock, the crested one, the sweet-voiced one, they honored the crow there with meat and fruit.

34. But when the peacock, endowed with a sweet voice, came to Bāveru, then the gains and honors of the crow vanished.

35. As long as the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, the Light-maker, does not arise, so long do they honor other numerous recluses and brahmins.

36. But when the Buddha, endowed with a sweet voice, preached the Dhamma, then the gains and honors of the ascetics (titthiyas) vanished.

Thus he spoke these verses.

*Sikhino*: endowed with a crest. *Mañjubhāṇino*: having a sweet voice. *Morassa*: the peacock. *Adassanena*: because of not seeing. *Tattha*: in that Kingdom of Bāveru. *Kākaṃ*: the crow. *Maṃsena ca*: with meat. *Phalena ca*: with large and small fruits. *Apūzesuṃ*: they honored.

*Yadā ca*: but when. *Sarasampanno*: endowed with a [sweet] voice. *Moro*: the peacock. *Bāveruṃ*: to the Kingdom of Bāveru. *Āgamā*: arrived. *Atha*: then. *Vāyasassa*: for the crow. *Lābho ca*: gains. *Sakkāro ca*: and honors. *Ahāyatha*: vanished.

*Yāva*: for as long as. *Dhammarājā*: he who pleases the assembly with the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. *Pabhaṅkaro*: the light-maker in the three worlds. *Buddho*: the Buddha. *Nuppajjati*: does not arise. *Tāva*: for that long. *Aññe*: other. *Puthū*: many. *Samaṇabrāhmaṇe*: recluses and brahmins. *Apūzesuṃ*: they honored.

*Yadā ca*: but when. *Sarasampanno*: endowed with a voice like that of the Great Brahma. *Buddho*: the Buddha. *Dhammaṃ*: the Dhamma of the Four Truths. *Adessayi*: preached. *Atha*: then. *Titthiyānaṃ*: for the ascetics. *Lābho ca*: gains. *Sakkāro ca*: and honors. *Ahāyatha*: vanished.

They put [the crow] in a golden cage and fed it with various kinds of fish, meat, and large and small fruits. In a place where no other birds existed, the crow, though possessed of ten unwholesome qualities, reached the pinnacle of gains, honors, and fame.

On another occasion, those merchants caught a peacock king and trained it to cry at the snap of fingers and to dance at the clap of hands, and then went to the Kingdom of Bāveru. When a great crowd had gathered, the peacock king stood on the prow of the ship, flapped its wings, uttered a sweet sound, and danced.

The people, seeing the peacock king, were filled with joy and said, "Sirs, give us this bird king, who is endowed with great beauty and is well-trained."

The merchants said, "First we brought a crow, and you took it. Now we have brought a peacock king, and you ask for it too. It is not possible to keep bringing birds to your country." The people said, "Let it be as you say, sirs; you will get another in your own country. Give this one to us." They increased the price and bought it for a thousand kahāpaṇas.

Then they placed the peacock king in a cage adorned with the seven jewels and fed it with fish, meat, large and small fruits, honey, parched rice, sugar, drinks, and so on. The peacock king was endowed with the highest gains, honors, and fame. From the time the peacock king arrived, the gains and honors of the crow vanished. No one even wanted to look at it.

The crow, unable to get food and snacks, went away crying "Caw, caw," and alighted on a dunghill to find its food.

The All-knowing Buddha, having connected the two stories, and being the Fully Enlightened One—

Having preached these four verses and connecting the Jātaka, he said: "At that time, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was the crow, and I, the Buddha, was the peacock king."

## When the virtuous arrive, the meritless vanish, like the crow when the peacock came.

Bāveru Jātaka is finished.
118:
## 10. Visayha Jātaka
## The Great Alms-giving
The Omniscient Buddha, who is the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Visayha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Adāsi dānāni,' concerning the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. (The story has been detailed below in the Khadirangāra Jātaka.)

In this Visayha Jātaka, the Omniscient Buddha called the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and said, 'Householder, in the past, wise men also gave alms, rejecting Sakka, King of the Devas, who stood in the air and forbade them, saying, "Do not give alms."' Having been requested by the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, He brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta became a merchant named Visayha, possessing eighty crores of wealth. He was endowed with the five precepts, desired to give alms, and delighted in alms-giving.

That merchant Visayha built alms-halls in six places: at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the gate of his own house, and he distributed alms. Every day, he spent six hundred thousand pieces of money. The food of the Bodhisatta and the food of the beggars were exactly the same. Because of the power of the alms-giving of the merchant Visayha, who gave alms as if plowing the whole of Jambudīpa, the abode of Sakka trembled. The Paṇḍukambalasilāsana of Sakka showed signs of heat.
119:
37. Adāsi dānāni pure visayha,
Dadatō ca tē khayadhammō ahōsi.
Itō paraṃ cē na dadeyya dānaṃ,
Tiṭṭheyyuṃ tē saṃyamantassa bhōgā.

He spoke this first verse.

Visayha: O Merchant Visayha. Tvaṃ: You. Pure: In the past. Dānāni: Alms. Adāsi: Gave. Dadatō: While giving. Tē: To you. Bhōgānañca: Of wealth also. Khayadhammō: The nature of exhaustion. Ahōsi: Occurred. Itō: From this time. Paraṃ: Hereafter. Dānaṃ: Alms. Cē na dadeyya: If you do not give. Saṃyamantassa: Of you who restrains (from giving). Tē: Your. Bhōgā: Wealth. Tiṭṭheyyuṃ: Shall remain.

When Sakka reflected, 'Who indeed wishes to displace me from my position?' he saw the great merchant and thought, 'This merchant Visayha is giving alms so extensively, as if plowing the whole of Jambudīpa. By this alms-giving, he likely wishes to displace me and become Sakka himself. I will destroy his wealth, make him poor, and act so that he cannot give alms.' Thinking thus, he caused all the wealth, grain, oil, honey, molasses, syrup, sugar, and so forth, and even the multitude of slaves and laborers, to disappear.

Then, those who were diligent in giving alms came and reported, 'Lord, the collection of things prepared in the alms-hall is exhausted. We see nothing in any of the places where they were kept.' He sent for his wife and said, 'You all must bring provisions from this house; do not cut off the alms-giving. Dear lady, continue the alms-giving.'

The wife searched the entire house and, not seeing even half a māsaka of wealth, said, 'Lord, except for the clothes we are wearing on our bodies, I see no other wealth. The whole house is empty.' He had the doors of the chambers containing the seven kinds of jewels opened, but even upon looking, he saw no wealth. Except for the merchant and his wife, other slaves and laborers were also not to be seen. Again, the Bodhisatta called his wife and said, 'Dear lady, I cannot stop the alms-giving. Search the whole house and look for any wealth.'

At that moment, a grass-cutter threw down a sickle, a carrying pole, and a grass-binding rope between the doors and fled. The merchant's wife saw that sickle, carrying pole, and rope, and bringing them, she gave them to him, saying, 'Lord, except for these objects, I see no other wealth.'
120:
38. O Thousand-eyed One, the noble say that even for the extremely poor, unrighteousness is a deed not to be done. O King of Devas, let not that wealth be ours, for the sake of which we would abandon faith.

39. Where one chariot goes, another chariot follows. The ancient practice I have established, O Vāsava, let it indeed continue.

40. If there be wealth, we shall give; if there is none, how shall we give? Even being in such a state, we shall give; let us not be negligent in giving.

Thus, he spoke these three verses.

O Sahassanetta, King Sakka. O Ariya, one of pure conduct. Even the extremely poor (suduggatena). The noble ones, such as the Buddha, say that the base act of not giving alms is a deed not to be done (akiccaṃ). O King of Devas. If we were to abandon faith (saddhā) for the sake of any wealth or possessions, let that wealth not be ours.

O Vāsava, King Sakka. By whichever path one chariot goes, another subsequent chariot follows by that same path. The ancient practice (vattaṃ) that I have established—let that practice of mine continue. May it not cease.

If there be wealth, we shall give. If there is no wealth, how could we give? Even being in this state of cutting grass, we shall give. Let us not forget the act of giving alms.

The Bodhisatta said, "My lady, I have never cut grass in all this time. From today onwards, I shall cut grass, carry it, and sell it, and give alms according to what I earn." Fearing that his almsgiving would be interrupted, he took a sickle, a carrying pole, and a rope, went out of the city to the grasslands, and cut grass. Thinking, "This much grass shall be for us, and this much I shall give in alms," he tied the grass into two bundles, hung them on the pole, carried them away, and sold them at the city gate. Obtaining a small coin (māsa), he gave one portion of the money to beggars.

The beggars were many. To the beggars who cried, "Give to me! Give to me!" he gave the other portion as well, and spent that day without food along with his wife. In this manner, six days passed.

Then, on the seventh day, as the heat of the sun touched the forehead of the merchant Visayha—who had been without food for seven days and was carrying very fine grass—his eyes began to swim. Being unable to maintain his mindfulness, he leaned against the grass and fell.

At that moment, Sakka, wishing to test the merchant who acted thus, arrived and stood in the air.

The Bodhisatta, hearing Sakka's words, asked, "Who are you?" "I am Sakka," he replied. Hearing Sakka's words, the Bodhisatta said, "One becomes Sakka by personally giving alms, undertaking virtue, observing the Uposatha, and fulfilling the seven vows. But you, you forbid the giving of alms which is the cause of your own sovereignty. You are performing an ignoble act."

Sakka, being unable to stop the Bodhisatta, asked, "For what purpose do you give alms?" The Bodhisatta replied, "I do not give alms desiring the status of Sakka, nor do I give alms desiring the status of Brahma. I give alms desiring only Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)."
121:
Sakka, hearing the Bodhisatta's words, was pleased and rubbed his back with his hand. At that very moment, as if he had just eaten, the Bodhisatta's entire body was restored. By the power of Sakka, all the Bodhisatta's wealth and possessions returned to their original state.

Sakka said, "Great Merchant, from this day forward, give alms by spending one million two hundred thousand coins every day." Having filled the Bodhisatta's house with immeasurable wealth, he sent him off and returned to his own abode.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the merchant's wife was the mother of Rāhula, and the merchant Visayha was I myself."

## The Bodhisatta certainly performs almsgiving
The Visayha Jātaka ends.

## 5. Cūḷakuṇāla Vagga
## 1. Kaṇḍarī Jātaka
The detailed story of this Kaṇḍarī Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Narānamārāmakarāsu', will become clear in the Kuṇāla Jātaka of the Asīti Nipāta.

The Kaṇḍarī Jātaka ends.

## 2. Vānara Jātaka
## The Heart
The Teacher, the Omniscient One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Vānara Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Asakkhiṃ vata attānaṃ', concerning Devadatta's attempt to kill the Buddha.

(The story has been detailed below in the Susumāra Jātaka.) The Omniscient Buddha brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the monkey species in the Himālaya region. When he reached maturity, he lived by the banks of the Gaṅgā.

At that time, a female crocodile in the Gaṅgā river conceived a longing for the Bodhisatta's heart and told the male crocodile. The male crocodile, planning to drown the Bodhisatta monkey in the water, take his heart, and give it to the female crocodile, said to the Bodhisatta, "Friend, come! Let us go to the small island in the middle of the river to eat large and small fruits."
122:
1. I have indeed been able to lift myself from the water to the dry land. No more, O water-born one, will I come under your power again.
2. Enough of these mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits that are on the other side of the ocean; better for me is the fig tree.

"Friend, how shall I go?" said the Bodhisatta. "I will carry you on my back and take you," said the crocodile. Not knowing the crocodile's intention, the Bodhisatta jumped and sat on the crocodile's back. After going a little way, the crocodile began to dive into the water.

Then the Bodhisatta said to the crocodile, "Friend, why are you sinking me in the water?" "I will kill you and give your heart to my wife," said the crocodile. "O crocodile of little wisdom, do you think my heart is within my chest?" said the Bodhisatta.

"If there is no heart in your chest, where do you keep it?" asked the crocodile. "Do you not see that heart hanging on the fig tree (udumbara)?" said the Bodhisatta. "I see it; will you give it to me?" asked the crocodile. "I will give it," said the Bodhisatta.

Because of his dull wit, the crocodile took the Bodhisatta and went to the foot of the fig tree by the riverbank. The Bodhisatta jumped from the crocodile's back and, sitting on the fig tree, spoke these four verses:

3. He who does not quickly understand the matter that has arisen, follows the will of the enemy and later regrets it.
4. He who quickly understands the matter that has arisen, is freed from the oppression of the enemy and does not regret it later.

O water-born one (vārija), crocodile. I (ahaṃ). From the water (udakā). To the dry land (thalaṃ). Myself (attānaṃ). To lift (uddhātuṃ). I have indeed been able (asakkhiṃ vata). Now (dāni). Again (puna). I (ahaṃ). Under your power (tuyhaṃ vasaṃ). I will not go (na gacchāmi).

To the other side (pāraṃ) of the river/ocean (samuddassa). Having gone (gantvā). Which are to be eaten (khāditabbāni). Those mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits (yāni amba-jambu-panasāni). They exist (santi). With those mangoes (etehi ambehi ca). With those rose-apples (etehi jambūhi ca). With those jackfruits (etehi panasehi ca). To me (mayhaṃ). There is no need (alaṃ). To me (mayhaṃ). The fig tree (udumbara). Is better (varaṃ).

And he who (yo ca). The matter (atthaṃ). That has arisen (uppatitaṃ). Quickly (khippaṃ). Does not understand (na anubujjhati). That person (so). Follows (anveti) the will of the enemy (amittavasaṃ). And later (pacchā ca). Regrets (anutappati).

And he who (yo ca). The matter (atthaṃ). That has arisen (uppatitaṃ). Very quickly (khippameva). Understands (nibodhati). That person (so). From the oppression of the enemy (sattusambādhā). Is freed (muccate). And later (pacchā ca). Does not regret (na anutappati).
123:
...does not regret.

In this way, the Bodhisatta explained the cause of the accomplishment of human affairs through these four verses and entered the forest.

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, and I myself was the monkey king."

## Wisdom alone is the way to escape everything.

The Vānara Jātaka ends.

## 3. Kuntinī Jātaka
## The Heron

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kuntinī Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Avasimha tava āgāre," concerning a heron bird living in the palace of King Kosala.

That heron bird performed the duties of a messenger for the king. She had two young ones. The king sent the heron bird to another king, carrying a letter.

While she was away, children in the king's house crushed the two young ones with their hands and killed them. When the heron returned and did not see her young ones, she asked, "Who killed my children?" They said, "Such and such a person killed them."

At that time, there was a tiger raised in the king's house. It was fierce and rough, kept by the power of bonds. Then those children went to see the tiger. The heron bird also went together with those children, thinking, "Just as these children killed my sons, so will I do to them." She took the children and threw them at the tiger's feet. The tiger crunched and ate them. The heron bird, thinking "Now my heart's desire is fulfilled," flew away to the Himalayas.
124:
5. "We have lived in your house, always honored and worshipped.
Now you yourself have caused this; behold, O King, I depart."

She spoke this first verse.

O King, we have lived in your house, always honored and worshipped. Now you yourself have caused the reason for my sorrow. Behold, I shall go.

6. "When an evil deed is done, and a return evil deed is done,
In this way, the enmity is settled; stay, O Kuntinī, do not go."

He spoke this second verse.

O Kuntinī, when a cruel deed such as killing a young one is done by another, and a retaliatory cruel deed such as killing in return is done by oneself, one knows, 'I have retaliated.' By this much, that enmity is settled and appeased. Therefore, stay, O Kuntinī, do not go.

Hearing this, the monks in the Dhamma Hall started a conversation: "Friends, in the King's palace, a Kuntinī bird of such a name, having caused the boys who killed her young ones to be killed by a tiger, has gone to the Himalayas."

The Blessed Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit gathered here?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now has this Kuntinī bird taken the boys who killed her young ones, placed them at the feet of a tiger, and gone to the Himalayas; she did the same in the past as well." Then he related the story of the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta ruled righteously. In that King's palace, a Kuntinī bird performed the duties of a messenger.

(The entire story is the same as before; what follows is the specific detail.)

This Kuntinī bird, after having the tiger kill the boys, thought, "Now it is not possible for me to live in this place. I will go. But if I go, I should not go without informing the King; I will go only after informing him." Having so thought, she approached the King, paid homage, and standing in a suitable place, said, "Lord, due to your negligence, the boys killed my young ones. I, being under the influence of anger, have caused those boys to be killed in return. Now it is not possible for me to live in this place."

Hearing those words, the King—

Hearing those words, the Kuntinī bird—

7. "Between the victim and the perpetrator, friendship is not joined again.
The heart does not consent; I go indeed, O Lord of Chariots."

She spoke this third verse.

O Lord of Chariots, noble among kings who ride chariots. Between the one who was oppressed and the one who is the oppressor, friendship—
125:
8. "Between the victim and the perpetrator, friendship is joined again
Among the wise, but not among fools; stay, O Kuntinī, do not go."

He spoke this fourth verse.

O Kuntinī, between the one who was oppressed and the one who is the oppressor, if friendship is broken, it is joined again among the wise, but not among fools. Stay, O Kuntinī, do not go.

Again, it is not joined. My heart does not consent. I shall go indeed.

The King, hearing those words—

The Kuntinī bird said, "Great King, even though it be so, it is not possible for me to live in this place." She paid homage to the King, flew up, and went to the Himalayas.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Kuntinī was the present Kuntinī, and the King of Vārāṇasī was I myself."

## One should not continually harbor enmity with those who are great and cruel.

Kuntinī Jātaka is finished.

## 4. Amba Jātaka

## The Ascetic and the Young Women

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Amba Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yo nīliyaṃ maṇဍayati," concerning a certain Elder who guarded a mango grove.

That Elder, having ordained in his old age, built a leaf-hut in a mango grove on the outskirts of Jetavana. He lived there guarding the mango grove and eating the fallen ripe mangoes. He also gave mangoes to the people who came to him.

While that Elder was away for alms, mango thieves would knock down the mangoes, eat them, and take them away. At that moment, four daughters of a merchant, who were wandering about after bathing in the Aciravatī River, entered that mango grove.
126:
9. He who dyes his hair blue, and is troubled by tweezers;
May she follow the will of such a man, she who carried away your mangoes.

This was the first verse spoken.

Venerable Sir, may the woman who stole your mangoes follow the will of that old man who adorns his hair with blue dye and is troubled by plucking out the grey hairs found among the dark ones with tweezers.

The elder monk, seeing the merchant's daughters, said, "You have eaten my mangoes." They replied, "Venerable Sir, we have just arrived; we did not eat your mangoes." "In that case, swear an oath," said the elder. "Venerable Sir, we shall swear," they said and took the oath. The elder made the merchant's daughters swear, shamed them, and let them go.

Upon hearing of this deed of the elder monk, the monks in the Dhamma Hall began a discussion: "Friends, the elder of such-and-such a name made the merchant's daughters, who entered his mango grove, swear an oath, shamed them, and let them go."

The Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "We are discussing such-and-such a matter," the Buddha said, "Monks, not only now has this elder been a mango-guard and made the four merchant's daughters swear, shaming them before letting them go; he did the same in the past." Having said this, he related the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. At that time, a fraudulent matted-hair ascetic lived in a leaf hut in a mango grove by the river near Bārāṇasī. He guarded the mangoes, ate the fallen ripe ones, gave some to people who came to him, and lived by various forms of wrong livelihood.

At that time, Sakka, King of Devas, while surveying the world to see who supports their parents, who respects the elders in the family, who gives alms, who keeps the precepts, who observes the Uposatha, and which recluses are devoted to their duties or who live improperly, saw this fraudulent ascetic living improperly while guarding the mango grove. "This fraudulent ascetic has abandoned his recluse duties, such as the meditation on kasinas, and spends his time guarding a mango grove. I will shock him." While the ascetic was in the village for alms, Sakka, by his power, made the mangoes fall as if they had been plundered by thieves.

Then, four daughters of a merchant from Bārāṇasī entered the mango grove. The fraudulent ascetic saw them and said, "You have eaten my mangoes." They said, "Venerable Sir, we have just arrived; we do not eat your mangoes."
127:
10. Twenty, or twenty-five, or even twenty-nine years of age;
May she reach such an age without obtaining a husband, she who carried away your mangoes.

This was the second verse spoken.

Venerable Sir, may the woman who stole your mangoes reach the age of twenty, twenty-five, or twenty-nine, and though she has reached such a mature age, may she not obtain a husband.

11. May she travel a long distance, alone as an abhisārikā;
May she not see her husband at the rendezvous, she who carried away your mangoes.

This was the third verse spoken.

Venerable Sir, may the woman who stole your mangoes, being an abhisārikā (a woman going to meet a lover) out of desire for a husband, travel alone for a long distance of one or two gāvutas; and even after going, may she not see that husband at the place appointed, where he said, 'Come to such-and-such a place.'

12. Adorned, well-dressed, wearing garlands, and anointed with sandalwood;
May she sleep alone on her bed, she who carried away your mangoes.

This was the fourth verse spoken.

Venerable Sir, may the woman who stole your mangoes, though adorned, well-dressed, wearing garlands, and anointed with sandalwood, sleep alone on her bed.

"In that case, swear an oath," he said. "Venerable Sir, if we swear, will we be allowed to go?" they asked. "Yes, you will," he replied. "Very well, Venerable Sir," they said, and the eldest among them, wishing to swear the oath, spoke the first verse.

The fraudulent ascetic told her, "You stand to one side," and made the second daughter swear. As she swore, she spoke the second verse.

When she had sworn and stood in a suitable place, the third daughter spoke the third verse.

When she had sworn and stood in a suitable place, the fourth daughter spoke the fourth verse.

The fraudulent ascetic said, "You have sworn very heavy oaths. Others must have eaten the mangoes. You may go now," and he dismissed the merchant's daughters. Sakka then showed a terrifying sight and drove the fraudulent ascetic away from that place.
128:
Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, identified the birth-story: "At that time, this elderly monk who guards the mango grove was the rogue ascetic. The four daughters of the merchant were the same four daughters. I myself was Sakka, the King of Devas."

## If one becomes a monk, one should practice the Dhamma clearly

The Amba Jātaka is concluded.

## 5. Rājakumbha Jātaka

## The Very Lazy Person

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Rājakumbha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Vanaṃ yadaggi dahati," concerning a certain lazy monk.

That monk was a son of a good family living in Sāvatthī. Although he had renounced his life to ordain in the Dispensation, he was lazy. He remained outside the practices of learning the Pali texts, learning the commentaries, wise reflection, and performing major and minor duties, and was overcome by the hindrances (nīvaraṇas). In all postures, such as sitting and standing, he was merely lazy.

Concerning that monk's state of laziness, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, such a monk, having ordained in this Dispensation that leads out of suffering, lives lazily, overcome by the hindrances."

The All-Knowing Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," He said, "Monks, not only now is this monk lazy; in the past too, he was indeed lazy," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister. The King of Bārāṇasī was lazy by nature. The Bodhisatta traveled about seeking a metaphor to awaken the King.

Then one day, while the King was wandering in the park surrounded by his ministers, he saw a lazy man named Rājakumbha. Such was his lazy nature that even if he walked the whole day, he would only move an inch or two. He was lazy in this manner.
129:
13. "When the fire, the black-pathed one, burns the forest,
How do you act, Pacalaka, with such slow effort?"

He spoke this first verse.

(The meaning is:) Pacalaka, you who are constantly lazy. You have such feeble effort. When the fire, which reaches everywhere and has a black path of smoke, burns the forest, what will you do then?

14. "There are many tree hollows and holes in the ground,
If we do not reach them, it will be our time (death)."

He spoke this second verse.

(The meaning is:) There are many tree hollows and holes in the ground. If we cannot reach those tree hollows and holes, then death alone will come to us.

15. "He who hurries when it is time to be slow, and is slow when he should hurry,
Destroys his own welfare, like one treading on and crushing a dry leaf.

16. "He who is slow when it is time to be slow, and hurries when he should hurry,
His welfare is fulfilled, like the moon dividing the nights."

He spoke these two verses.

(The meaning is:) Whoever acts quickly at a time when one should act slowly and gently, and acts slowly at a time when one should act quickly—that person destroys his own welfare, just as one destroys a dry palm leaf by treading on it.

Whoever acts slowly at a time when one should act slowly, and acts quickly at a time when one should act quickly—that person's welfare is fulfilled, just as the new moon reaches fullness day by day as it passes from night to night.

Seeing that lazy man, the King asked the Bodhisatta, "Friend, who is this person?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, this man is named Rājakumbha. He is lazy by nature. Even if he walks the whole day, he only moves an inch or two. Such is his lazy nature." Desiring to speak with that lazy man, he said, "Friend Rājakumbha, your movement is very slow. When a forest fire burns this forest, what will you do?"

Hearing those words, Rājakumbha spoke (the second verse).

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta spoke (the last two verses).

After hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the King became diligent from that time onwards.
130:
Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the All-Knowing Buddha identified the birth-story: "At that time, Rājakumbha was the lazy monk. I myself was the wise minister."

## If one nurtures laziness, for many people, their welfare is destroyed

The Rājakumbha Jātaka is concluded.

## 6. Kesava Jātaka

## Food Given in Trust Keeps Illness Away

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kesava Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Manussindaṃ jahitvāna," concerning food given in trust (vissāsabhojana).

In the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, five hundred monks were regularly fed. The merchant's house was always like a well or a pond for the Saṅgha of monks. It glowed with the radiance of saffron robes and was filled with the breeze caused by the monks' movements.

Then one day, while the King was circumambulating the city to the right, he saw the Saṅgha of monks at the merchant's house and thought, "I too will regularly offer alms-food to the Noble Saṅgha." He went to the monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and requested to regularly feed five hundred monks.

From that time on, fragrant and excellent rice-food, which had been stored for three years, was regularly offered at the King's palace. However, there were no donors who offered with their own hands out of trust and affection; the King had his officials give the food. The monks did not wish to sit and eat at the King's house.

They would take the various kinds of excellent-tasting food and go to the houses of their own supporters. They would give that food to their supporters and eat whatever food—whether coarse or fine—was given by those supporters.
131:
Then one day, many large and small fruits were offered to the King. The King said, "Offer these fruits to the Saṅgha." The people went to the dining hall, but seeing no monks, they reported back to the King, "There are none." The King asked, "Is it not the time for the meal?"

"Great King, it is indeed the time for the meal. However, the monks take the food from your palace and go to the houses of their trusted attendants, give it to them, and then eat the coarse or fine food provided by those attendants," they replied.

The King thought, "Our food is excellent. Why do they not eat it and instead eat other food? I will ask the Buddha." He went to the monastery, paid respects to the Buddha, and asked.

The Omniscient Buddha said, "Great King, food given by those who are trusted is the best. Because there is no intimacy in your house and no one who gives with affection, the monks take the food and eat it in places where they have trust. Great King, there is no flavor equal to that of trust.

That is true. Even the four-sweet medicine (catumadhura) given by one who is not trusted is not worth as much as millet rice given by one who is trusted. In the past, when wise men fell ill, even though the King had five families of physicians treat them, the illness did not subside. Only when they went to their trusted friends and consumed unsalted gruel made of crushed millet and wild grain, and leaves boiled in plain water, did they become free from disease." Having said this, and being requested by King Kosala, He brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. They named him Young Kappa. When Young Kappa reached the age of maturity, he learned all the arts in Takkasilā and later became an ascetic.
132:
17. Having left the Lord of Men, who is successful in all desires,
How does the Blessed Kesī delight in Kappa’s hermitage?
This was the first verse spoken.

Blessed (Bhagavā): the venerable Kesava. Lord of Men (Manussinda): the King of Bārāṇasī, who is endowed with all desirable things. Having left (Jahitvāna): having abandoned. In Kappa’s hermitage (Kappassa assame): why does he delight there?

18. There are pleasant and delightful trees, Nārada;
The well-spoken words of Kappa delight me.
This was the second verse spoken.

Nārada: the minister Nārada. In Kappa’s hermitage, there are trees (vakkhā) that are good, delightful, and pleasing to the mind. The well-spoken words (subhāsitāni) of the ascetic Kappa delight me.

At that time, the ascetic named Kesava lived in the Himavanta as a teacher of a group, surrounded by five hundred ascetics. The Bodhisatta went to Kesava and lived as his senior disciple. Kesava desired the welfare of Kappa and loved him dearly. The teacher and disciple were extremely close to each other.

Later, Kesava took his disciples to the human realm to seek salt and acidic foods. Arriving at Bārāṇasī, they stayed in the royal park. The next day, they entered the city for alms and reached the palace gate. Seeing the group of ascetics, the King invited them, fed them in the palace, and having received their consent, had them stay in the park.

When the rainy season passed, Kesava took leave of the King. The King said, "Venerable sir, you are old. Please stay depending on us; send only the young ascetics to the Himavanta." Kesava agreed, sent the young ones to the Himavanta with his senior disciple, and remained alone. Kappa went to the Himavanta and lived with the other ascetics.

Living without Kappa, Kesava became weary and, longing to see him, could not sleep. Because he could not sleep, his food did not digest properly. He developed dysentery and suffered great pain. The King called five families of physicians to treat the ascetic, but the illness did not subside.

The ascetic said to the King, "Great King, do you desire my death, or do you desire my recovery?" The King replied, "Venerable sir, I desire your recovery." "In that case, send me to the Himavanta." The King said, "Very well, venerable sir," and called a minister named Nārada, saying, "Nārada, take our venerable teacher and go to the Himavanta along with the forest-dwellers."

Nārada took him there and returned. As soon as Kesava saw Kappa, his mental illness was cured, and his weariness subsided. Then Kappa gave him gruel made of millet and wild grain, along with leaves boiled in plain water without salt. At that very moment, Kesava’s dysentery was cured.
133:
19. "You eat rice of the finest sort, with clean meat sauce; how then does this saltless millet and wild rice please you?"

He spoke this third stanza.

"Venerable sir, you eat rice of the finest sort, with clean meat sauce. How then does this saltless food of millet and wild rice please and satisfy you?"

Then the King sent the minister Nārada, saying, "Go and find out about the condition of the hermit Kesava." The minister Nārada went and, seeing the hermit Kesava free from illness, said, "Venerable sir, the King of Bārāṇasī took five physicians to treat you, but they could not cure your illness. How did the hermit Kappa treat you?"

Thus, as if speaking with others, he asked about the reason for the hermit Kesava's contentment. Hearing those words, the hermit Kesava said:

"The hermit Kappa, who makes me contented in this way, gave me leaves and a gruel of millet and wild rice boiled in unsalted water to drink. By drinking that gruel, the illness in my body was appeased."

Hearing those words, the minister Nārada spoke. Hearing those words, the hermit Kesava spoke this fourth stanza:

20. "Whether it be tasty or not, whether it be little or much, where one eats with trust, trust is the highest flavor."

"Nārada, in whatever place one eats with trust, whether the food be delicious or not, whether it be little or much, the food eaten in such a place is indeed tasty. Why is it tasty? Because among flavors, trust is the highest and most excellent. Therefore, it is tasty."

The minister Nārada, having heard the words of the hermit Kesava, went to the King and reported, "The hermit Kesava spoke these words."

Establishing the connection of the Jātaka, the All-Enlightened Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, the King was Ānanda, Nārada was Sāriputta, Kesava was Baka Brahmā, and Kappa was I myself."

## One who loves and cares, through such treatment, the illness is cured.

The Kesava Jātaka is finished.

He spoke this first stanza.

"Rakkhasa, you stand in the air holding a huge hammer made entirely of iron. Today, are you appointed to protect me, or are you making an effort to kill me?"

## 7. Ayakūṭa Jātaka
## The Ogre with the Iron Hammer

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Ayakūṭa Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with 'Sabbāyasaṃ', concerning the practice for the welfare of the world.

(The story will become clear in the Mahākaṇha Jātaka of the Dvādasaka Nipāta.) The All-Enlightened Buddha brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the King's chief queen. When he reached maturity, having mastered all the arts, he was established in the kingship upon his father's death and ruled righteously.

At that time, people were devoted to the worship of gods and performed sacrifices to them by killing many goats, sheep, and other animals. The Bodhisatta had the drum beaten, proclaiming, "No living being shall be killed."

The yakkhas (ogres), no longer receiving their sacrifices, became angry with the Bodhisatta. They went to a gathering of yakkhas in the Himālaya and sent a fierce yakkha to kill the Bodhisatta. That yakkha took a huge, glowing iron hammer as large as a mountain peak and came, thinking, "I will kill him by striking him with this hammer." He stood above the Bodhisatta's bed at the end of the middle watch of the night.

At that moment, Sakka's throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting on the cause, understood it. He took his thunderbolt (Vajira) and went to stand above the yakkha.

The Bodhisatta saw the yakkha and, wishing to speak with him, wondered, "Does he stand here wishing to protect me, or does he wish to kill me?"

The Bodhisatta saw only the yakkha, not Sakka. The yakkha, out of fear of Sakka, did not dare to strike the Bodhisatta.

Hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the yakkha, wishing to explain the matter, said, "Great King, I do not stand here to protect you. I came to kill you by striking you with this glowing iron hammer, but out of fear of Sakka, I do not dare to strike you." He then spoke the second stanza:
135:
23. "If the king of gods, Maghavā, the husband of Sujā, the lord of the devas, protects me, let all the Pisācas roar as they wish; I do not fear the race of Rakkhasas."

24. "Let the Kumbhaṇḍas and all the dust-Pisācas cry out as they please; the Pisācas are not enough for a fight; that is just a great intimidation."

He spoke these two stanzas.

"Rakkhasa, if the king of gods, Maghavā, the husband of Sujā, who rules over the devas, protects me, let all the Pisācas roar openly as they wish; I am not at all terrified of the race of Rakkhasas."

"Let all the Kumbhaṇḍas, who have secret organs as large as pots, and the dust-Pisācas who live in rubbish heaps, certainly cry out. The Pisācas are not capable of fighting. That great terrifying display may occur, but I am not afraid."

22. "I am a messenger of the Rakkhasas, sent here to kill you. But Indra, the king of gods, protects you; therefore, I shall not split your head."

He spoke this second stanza.

"Great King, I am a messenger of the Rakkhasas here. I have been sent to kill you. But Indra, the king of gods, protects you. Therefore, I shall not split your head."

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta spoke.

Sakka drove the yakkha away and, after advising the Great Being, said, "Do not fear, Great King; from this day forth, your protection is my responsibility," and returned to his own place.

Establishing the connection of the Jātaka, the All-Enlightened Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha, and the King of Bārāṇasī was I myself."

## For the welfare of the world, one carries the burden; the king of gods, Indra, must provide protection.

The Ayakūṭa Jātaka is finished.
136:

He spoke this first verse.

Dear son (Tāta). That man (Yo puriso). You (Taṃ). Should inspire confidence (Vissāsaye). Your (Te). Confidence (Vissāsañca). Should tolerate (Khameyya). Willing to listen to words of confidence (Sussūsī ca). Patient with faults (Titikkhī ca). Should be (Bhaveyya). From here (Ito). Having gone (Gato). That man (Taṃ purisaṃ). Associate (Bhajehi).

That man's (Yassa purisassa). By body (Kāyena). By speech (Vācāya). By mind (Manasā). Wrongdoing (Dukkaṭaṃ). Is not (Natthi). From here (Ito). Having gone (Gato). That man (Taṃ purisaṃ). On the breast (Urasi). Resting (Patiṭṭhāya). Like a grown son (Vaḍḍhito iva). Associate/Attend to (Bhajehi).

Dear son (Tāta). Like turmeric dye, having an unstable mind (Haliddirāgaṃ). Like a monkey, having a quick mind (Kapicittaṃ). In a moment, being passionate and dispassionate (Rāgavirāginaṃ). Such a nature (Tādisaṃ). Man (Purisaṃ). The whole (Sakalaṃ). Surface of Jambudīpa (Jambudīpatalaṃ). Empty of people (Nimmanussampi). Even if (Ce siyā). You (Tvaṃ). Do not associate (Mā sevi).

## 8. Arañña Jātaka
## A True Friend

The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Arañña Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with "Araññā gāmamāgamma", concerning a monk tempted by a fat maiden.

(The story will become clear in the Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka.) The All-Knowing Buddha brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, having completed his education in Takkasilā, and after his wife passed away, he took his son and became an ascetic. Living in the Himavanta, he would leave his son at the hermitage and go out in search of various fruits.

At that time, thieves raided a border village and took captives. One young woman escaped and reached that hermitage. She tempted the young ascetic and caused him to break his virtue. She said, "Come, let us go."

The young ascetic said, "Let my father come first; I will go only after seeing my father." She said, "In that case, come after seeing him," and leaving the hermitage, she waited on the road. When the father arrived, the young ascetic—
137:
Then the father, wishing to give advice to the young ascetic—

Hearing those words, the young ascetic said, "Dear father, where shall I find a man endowed with these qualities? I will not go; I will live only in your presence," and he turned back from going to the village. Then the father taught the young ascetic the kasiṇa meditation. Both of them, without losing their jhāna, were destined for the Brahma realm.

Identification of the Jātaka: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the son and the maiden were these two (the monk and the maiden), but the father ascetic was I myself."

## If the mind is not stable, one should avoid many people and not associate with them.

The Arañña Jātaka ends.

## 9. Sandhibheda Jātaka
## The Slandering Jackal

The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sandhibheda Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with "Neva itthīsu sāmaññaṃ", concerning the precept against backbiting (pesuñña-sikkhāpada).
138:
At one time, the Blessed One, hearing that the Chabbaggī monks were carrying backbiting talk, summoned them and asked, "Monks, is it true that you carry backbiting talk to various monks who are quarreling and disputing, so that new quarrels arise and existing ones increase even further?" When they replied, "It is true," he rebuked them and said:

"Monks, backbiting talk is like a strike from a sharp sword. Even a long-standing intimacy is quickly destroyed by such talk. One who takes up backbiting talk and causes the destruction of their own friendship is like the lion and the bull." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as his son. When he reached maturity, he completed his education in Takkasilā, and upon his father's passing, he reigned righteously.

At that time, a certain cowherd, while tending cattle in the forest pens, failed to notice a pregnant cow and left her behind. That cow developed an intimacy with a lioness. Both became firm friends and wandered together.

Later, the cow gave birth to a calf, and the lioness gave birth to a lion cub. These two young animals also became firm friends through the friendship inherited from their families and wandered together.

Then, a hunter entered the forest and, seeing the intimacy between the bull and the lion, took forest produce to Bārāṇasī and presented it to the King. When the King asked, "Friend hunter, have you seen anything extraordinary in the forest?" he replied, "Your Majesty, I saw nothing else extraordinary, but I did see a lion and a bull wandering together in mutual intimacy."

"If a third party appears among them, there will be danger. When you see a third party among them, inform me," the King said. "Very well, Your Majesty," the hunter replied.
139:
29. Neither in females is there commonality,
Nor in food, O Charioteer.
Yet, see how well-planned was the scheme
Of this breaker of friendship.

30. Like a sharp sword in the flesh,
Slander circulates.
Wherein the lowest of beasts
Devour both the bull and the lion.

31. He lies in this bed [of death],
Which you see here, O Charioteer,
Who listens to the words of a slanderer,
A breaker of friendship.

32. Those people prosper in happiness,
Like humans who have gone to heaven,
Who do not listen to the words
Of a breaker of friendship, O Charioteer.

"When a third companion appears for the lion and the bull, there will be danger. When you see that third companion of the lion and the bull, inform me," the King had said. The hunter agreed.

When the hunter went to Bārāṇasī, a jackal was serving both the lion and the bull. The hunter went to the forest, saw the jackal, and returned to the city to inform the King that a third companion had appeared.

The jackal thought, "Except for the meat of a lion and a bull, there is no other meat I have not eaten. I will cause these two to break their friendship and eat their meat." Having so planned, the jackal slandered them to each other, saying, "The bull said this about you," and "The lion said this about you," causing them to quarrel and soon bringing them to their death.

The hunter went and informed the King, "Your Majesty, a third companion has appeared for the lion and the bull." "Who is that companion?" the King asked. "A jackal, Your Majesty," he replied.

The King said, "The jackal will break the friendship of the two friends and have them killed. We shall arrive at the time of the death of the lion and the bull." Mounting his chariot and traveling with the hunter as his guide, he arrived just as the lion and the bull had quarreled and lost their lives. The jackal, joyful and delighted, ate the lion's meat at one time and the bull's meat at another.

Seeing the lion and the bull who had reached the end of their lives, the King, while standing in his chariot, spoke these four verses to his charioteer:

*Sārathi*, Charioteer. *Imesaṃ*, for this lion and bull. *Itthīsu*, in females. *Sāmaññaṃ*, commonality. *Neva atthi*, there is none at all. *Bakkhesupi*, and in food. *Sāmaññaṃ*, commonality. *Na atthi*, there is none at all. *Atha*, yet. *Assa sandhibhedassa*, of that jackal who breaks friendships. *Yāva*, how very. *Sucintitaṃ*, well-planned [the scheme]. *Passa*, behold.

*Yattha*, wherein [slander]. *Parivattamāne*, when it circulates. *Adhamā*, the low. *Migā*, jackals. *Usabhañca*, the bull. *Sīhañca*, and the lion. *Bakkhayanti*, devour. *Maṃsamhi*, in the flesh. *Tikkho*, sharp. *Asiva*, like a sword. *Taṃ pesuññaṃ*, that slander. *Mittabhāvaṃ*, the state of friendship. *Chindantameva*, only by cutting. *Parivattati*, circulates.

*Sārathi*, Charioteer. *Yamimaṃ*, this [lying in death of the two creatures]. *Passasi*, do you see? *Yo*, whoever. *Sandhibhedassa*, of a breaker of friendship. *Pisuṇassa*, of a slanderer. *Vācaṃ*, the words. *Nibodhati*, takes up. *So*, that person. *Imaṃ sayanaṃ*, this bed [of death]. *Seti*, lies in.

*Sārathi*, Charioteer. *Ye janā*, those people who. *Sandhibhedassa*, of a slanderer. *Vācaṃ*, the words. *Nāvabodhanti*, do not take up. *Te janā*, those people. *Saggagatā*, endowed with celestial bliss. *Narā iva*, like humans. *Sukhaṃ*, happiness. *Edhanti*, attain.
140:
The King, having spoken these verses, had the lion's mane, skin, claws, and fangs taken, and then returned to the city.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was I myself."

## Slanderers cause loved ones to hate and part
The Sandhibheda Jātaka ends.

## 1. Maṇikuṇဍala Jātaka
## The King of Kosala and the King of Bārāṇasī
Regarding the present story, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Maṇikuṇဍala Jātaka while staying at Jetavana Monastery, adorned with the verse beginning with "Jino rathassaṃ maṇikuṇဍale ca," concerning a corrupt official in the palace of the King of Kosala.
141: The story is expanded in the Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka below.
142:
2. Wealth leaves a mortal first,
Or the mortal leaves wealth first.
Possessors of wealth are impermanent, O seeker of sensual pleasures,
Therefore, I do not grieve in the time of sorrow.

3. The moon rises, becomes full, and wanes;
The sun, having dispelled the darkness, sets.
The worldly conditions, O enemy, are known to me,

He spoke these two verses.

Pubbataraṃ: even earlier. Jahāti: leaves. Bhoggino: the possessors of wealth. Asassatā: are impermanent. Tasmā: therefore. Ahaṃ: I. Sokakāle: in the time when sorrow might occur. Suriyo: the sun. Andhaṃ: the darkness. (Dhamento: destroying.) Tapetvāna: having made it shine. Paleti: sets. (Evameva: in this same way. Bhoggā: riches. Uppajjanti ca: both arise. In this Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka of the past, the Bodhisatta was the King of Bārāṇasī. A corrupt minister brought the King of Kosala to seize the kingdom of Kāsi and had the King of Bārāṇasī bound and cast into prison. The King, having developed meditative absorption (jhāna), sat cross-legged in the air. A burning sensation arose in the body of the robber king. The robber king approached the King of Bārāṇasī and spoke the first verse:

1. You have lost your chariots and horses, and your jeweled earrings,
You have likewise lost your sons and your wives.
In the face of losing all your wealth without exception,
Why do you not burn with grief in the time of sorrow?

Mahārāja: Great King. Tvaṃ: you. Rathassaṃ: chariots and horses. Maṇikuṇḍale ca: and jeweled earrings. Jīno: have lost/been deprived of. Asi: you are. Tatheva: likewise. Putte ca: sons. Dāre ca: and wives. Jīno: have lost. Asi: you are. Asesakesu: without exception. Sabbesu: in all. Bhogesu: wealth. Jīno: have lost. Asi: you are. Kasmā: why. Sokakāle: in the time of sorrow. Na santappasi: do not you burn with grief?

## Living Free from Sorrow

Having heard those words, the Bodhisatta—
143:
3. The moon rises, becomes full, and wanes;
The sun, having dispelled the darkness, sets.
The worldly conditions, O enemy, are known to me,
Therefore, I do not grieve in the time of sorrow.

In that context, 'pubbeva maccaṃ' means wealth leaves the mortal first, or the mortal leaves that wealth even earlier. 'Kāmakāmī' is an address to the robber king. O you who desire sensual pleasures, those who possess wealth in the world are impermanent; either they become poor while still alive when wealth is lost, or they themselves perish leaving wealth behind. Therefore, I do not grieve even in the time of sorrow for the great multitude—this is the meaning. 'Viditā mayā sattuka lokadhammā' is an address to the robber king. O enemy, the worldly conditions such as gain and loss, fame and obscurity, are known to me. Just as the moon rises, becomes full, and then wanes again; and just as the sun, destroying the darkness and shining with great light, sets again in the evening and is not seen; in the same way, riches arise and perish. What is the use of sorrow there? Therefore, I do not grieve—this is the meaning.

Thus the Great Being, having preached the Dhamma to the robber king, now spoke rebuking that very robber king:

4. A lazy layman who enjoys sensual pleasures is not good,
An unrestrained monk is not good.
A king who acts without consideration is not good,
A wise man who is angry is not good.

5. A kshatriya should act after consideration, not without consideration, O Lord of the Land.
For one who acts after consideration, O King, fame and glory increase.

These two verses have already been explained in detail below.

## 2. Sujāta Jātaka

## A Father's Happiness Due to a Wise Son

The Story of the Present: The All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sujāta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kiṃ nu santaramānova," concerning a householder whose father had died.

It is said that when his father passed away, that householder went about weeping, unable to dispel his sorrow. The All-Enlightened Buddha, seeing that householder's potential for the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), went for alms in Sāvatthī and then, taking a regular attendant monk with him, went to the householder's home. Sitting on the prepared seat, He asked the householder who sat after paying homage, "Lay follower, are you grieving?" When the householder replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "Lay follower, in the past, wise men did not grieve when their fathers passed away after hearing the words of the wise." Being requested by the householder, He brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in a householder's family. They named him "Young Sujāta." When Sujāta reached the age of maturity, his grandfather passed away.

Then Sujāta's father, overcome by sorrow from the time of his father's death, brought the bones from the cemetery, built an earth stupa in his own garden, and buried those bones in that earth stupa. Every time he arrived there, he honored the stupa with flowers and wept while reflecting. He did not bathe, did not anoint himself, did not eat or drink, and did not manage his affairs.

7. "A dead ox cannot rise through food or drink. You lament in vain, just like a fool."
He spoke these two verses.
Sujāta, Sujāta. You, to a dead old ox, as if in a hurry, having mown green grass, why do you say "Eat, eat"?
Neither by giving food nor by giving water does a dead ox rise. Just as a person without wisdom would speak such words, so too do you speak empty words.

## Removing Grief
The Bodhisatta, seeing his father, thought: "Since my grandfather died, my father has been overwhelmed by grief. There is no one but me who can understand and remove my father's grief. I shall remove his grief by means of a certain device." Seeing a dead ox outside the village, he brought grass and water, placed them before the dead ox, and said, "Eat! Drink!"

Everyone who passed by saw the Bodhisatta and said, "Friend Sujāta, you are giving grass and water to a dead ox; why are you acting like a madman?" Sujāta said nothing. Then they went to Sujāta's father and said, "Your son has gone mad; he is giving grass and water to a dead ox."

Hearing this, the householder's grief for his father subsided, and concern for his son took its place. The householder went quickly and said, "Sujāta, are you not a wise man? Why do you give grass and water to a dead ox?"

Father, the head remains just as it was before. The hands and feet also remain just as they were. The tail remains just as it was before. The ears also remain just as they were. Therefore, I think this ox might rise.
But of my grandfather, the head, hands, and feet are not seen at all. Therefore, you who weep at a mound of earth, are you not indeed the one without wisdom?

Hearing these words, the Bodhisatta's father thought, "My son is wise; he knows the affairs of this world and the next. He did this to make me understand." He thought, "Dear Sujāta, you are wise. I have realized that 'all conditioned things are impermanent.' From today, I shall not grieve. A son who removes a father's grief should be like you." Wishing to praise his son, he said:

## 3. Venasākha Jātaka
## The Ruin of Sovereignty through Cruelty
The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Bhesakaḷāvana near Saṃsumāragiri in the Bhagga country, told this Venasākha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Nayidaṃ niccaṃ bhavitabbaṃ," concerning Prince Bodhi.

Prince Bodhi was the son of King Udena. At that time, Prince Bodhi, residing in the city of Saṃsumāragiri, summoned a master carpenter who was perfect in his craft and had him build a palace called Kokanada, which was unlike any other king's palace. After it was built, he became stingy, thinking, "This carpenter might build such a palace for another king," and he had the carpenter's eyes plucked out.

The fact that Prince Bodhi had the carpenter's eyes plucked out became well-known among the community of monks. Therefore, in the Dhamma hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, Prince Bodhi had the eyes of such a master carpenter plucked out; he is indeed cruel, harsh, and oppressive."

The doer of good receives good, and the doer of evil receives evil.

When a man performs deeds and receives their results, he sees those deeds in himself. A doer of good sees good; a doer of evil sees evil. Whatever kind of seed one sows, that is the kind of fruit one reaps.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā. Young princes and Brahmins from all over Jambudīpa learned the arts from him. ## The Teacher's Advice

The Bodhisatta, knowing the prince's cruel, harsh, and oppressive nature through the science of body marks (aṅgavijjā), advised him: "My dear, you are cruel, harsh, and oppressive. Power gained through cruelty does not last long; sovereignty is easily destroyed. Such a cruel person finds no footing, like one with a broken boat in the ocean. Therefore, do not be so cruel and harsh." To advise the prince, he said:

That Prince Brahmadatta paid homage to his teacher, went to Bārāṇasī, demonstrated his learning to his father, was established as the heir apparent, and upon his father's death, became king. He had a chaplain named Piṅgala.

That cruel, harsh, and oppressive chaplain Piṅgala, being greedy for wealth, thought, "It would be good if I could make this King Brahmadatta capture all the kings in the whole of Jambudīpa..."

The Bodhisatta repaired the city and made it impregnable to others.

## Sacrifice of a Thousand Kings

The King of Bārāṇasī halted by the banks of the Ganges, having a curtain-wall set up at the foot of a great banyan tree, a canopy hung above, and a bed prepared. Although he had captured a thousand kings across the surface of Jambudīpa and fought, he was unable to take Takkasilā. He asked his chaplain, 'Teacher, though we have come with all these kings, we cannot take Takkasilā. What should be done?'

'Great King, let us pluck out the eyes of the thousand kings, kill them, rip open their bellies, take the choice flesh, and make an offering to the deity dwelling in this banyan tree. Let us encircle the tree with their entrails and mark it with bloody five-finger prints. If we do this, our victory will come quickly,' the chaplain replied.

The King agreed, saying 'Very well.' He stationed powerful wrestlers inside the curtain-wall, summoned the kings one by one, had them subdued until they were unconscious, plucked out their eyes, took their flesh, and cast their bodies into the Ganges. Having performed the sacrifice as described, he beat the war-drum and went forth to battle.

## 4. Uraga Jātaka

## Five Who Do Not Weep for the Dead

The All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Uraga Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Uragova tacaṃ jiṇṇaṃ,' concerning a householder whose son had died.

The present story is just like the story of the one whose wife died or the one whose father died.

In this Uraga Jātaka as well, the All-Knowing Buddha went to the house of that householder whose son had died, and as the householder sat after paying homage, He asked, "Lay disciple, are you grieving?" When the householder replied, "Yes, Bhante, it is as you say. I have been grieving since the time my son died,"—
151:
“Lay devotee, that which is of a nature to break, breaks; that which is of a nature to perish, perishes. Such destruction does not occur in only one house. Indeed, throughout the infinite universes and the three realms, there is no such thing as a being who is undying. There is not even a single conditioned thing (saṅkhāra) that is capable of remaining permanent in that state. All beings are subject to death. All conditioned things are subject to dissolution.

Wise men of old, when a son died, did not grieve, saying: ‘That which is subject to death has died; that which is subject to destruction has perished.’” Having said this, and being requested by the householder, the Teacher brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a Brahmin family in a gate-village of Bārāṇasī. Having established his household, he made his living by farming. 

## The Six Members of the Household
The Bodhisatta had two children: a son and a daughter. When the son reached the proper age, the Bodhisatta brought a young woman from a similar family and gave her to him. Thus, there were six people in the household: the Bodhisatta, his wife, his son, his daughter, his daughter-in-law, and a female servant. They lived together in harmony, joy, and loving companionship.

## The Practice of the Virtuous
The Bodhisatta gave this advice to the other five: “Give alms according to what you have acquired, keep the precepts, observe the Uposatha duties, develop mindfulness of death, and contemplate your own mortality. For all these beings, death is certain, but life is uncertain. All conditioned things are impermanent and subject to decay and dissolution. Be diligent both by night and by day.” They accepted his advice, saying, “Very well,” and diligently practiced mindfulness of death (maraṇassati).

## The Death of the Son
Then one day, the Bodhisatta went to the field with his son to plow. The son gathered rubbish and set it on fire. In an ant-hill near that pile of rubbish, there lived a venomous snake. The smoke struck the snake's eyes. Enraged, thinking, “Because of this man, I am in danger,” it came out of the ant-hill and bit the man, sinking its four fangs into him. The man turned over and fell dead.

The Bodhisatta, seeing his son fall, left his oxen and went to him. Realizing his son was dead, he lifted him up, laid him at the foot of a tree, covered him with a cloth, and neither wept nor lamented. He only contemplated impermanence, thinking: “That which is of a nature to break has broken; that which is of a nature to die has died. All conditioned things are impermanent and end in death.” Then he continued plowing.

## The Family Does Not Weep
Seeing a neighbor passing near the field, the Bodhisatta asked, “Friend, are you going home?” When the man replied, “Yes,” the Bodhisatta said, “In that case, please go to our house and tell the Brahmin lady: ‘Today, do not bring food for two as before, but bring food for only one person. And whereas previously only the servant girl came alone with the food, today let all four of you come, dressed in clean clothes and carrying perfumes and flowers.’”
152:
The neighbor went and delivered the message to the Brahmin lady exactly as the Bodhisatta had instructed. She asked, “Friend, who gave you this message?” When he replied, “The Brahmin gave it,” she knew, “My son is dead.” Yet, there was not even a tremor of emotion in her. Having thus well-developed her mind, she dressed in clean clothes, took perfumes and flowers, and having the servant girl carry the food, she went to the field with the others. Not a single person wept or lamented.

The Bodhisatta sat in the very shade where his son lay and ate his meal. After the meal, they all gathered wood, placed the body on the pyre, honored it with perfumes and flowers, and cremated it. Not a single person shed even a drop of a tear. All of them had well-developed mindfulness of death.

## Why the Father Did Not Weep
By the power of their virtue, the throne of Sakka, King of Devas, showed signs of heat. Sakka reflected, “Who is it that wishes to displace me from my seat?” and realized it was due to the power of their merit. With a heart full of devotion, he thought, “I should go to them, have them utter a lion’s roar, and at the end of that lion’s roar, fill their house with the seven kinds of treasures before returning.” He quickly went there, stood by the side of the cemetery, and asked, “Friends, what are you doing?” “We are cremating a human being, Lord,” they replied. “You are not cremating a human; I think you have killed a deer and are roasting it,” said Sakka. “It is not so, Lord; we are indeed cremating a human,” they replied. “In that case, he must have been your enemy,” Sakka said. Then the Bodhisatta said, “Lord, he was my own son, not an enemy.” “Then he must have been a son you did not love?” “He was a very dear son, Lord.” “Then why do you not weep?” To explain the reason for not weeping, the Bodhisatta spoke the first verses:

Therefore, I do not grieve for him; he has gone according to his destiny (gati).”
