## 5. Ghaṭa Jātaka

## The Enemy's Distress due to Loving-kindness Jhāna
The Teacher, the one who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Ghaṭa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Aññe socanti rodanti," concerning a certain minister of the King of Kosala.

The story is similar to the one told below.

## Profit from Misfortune
In this Ghaṭa Jātaka, the King of Kosala gave great wealth to a minister who had been helpful to him, but later, listening to the words of slanderers, he had him bound and cast into prison. While sitting in that prison, the minister attained the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). The King, recognizing the minister's virtue, had him released.

The minister took perfumes and flowers, went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. Then the Teacher asked him, "Lay follower, did misfortune befall you?" When he replied, "Venerable Sir, misfortune did occur, but through that misfortune, benefit came to me; I have attained the Path of Stream-entry," the Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not only you who brought benefit out of misfortune; the wise of old also brought benefit out of misfortune." At the minister's request, the Teacher brought forth the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the womb of the Chief Queen. They named him Prince Ghaṭa. Later, having mastered the arts at Takkasilā, Prince Ghaṭa ruled righteously. A certain minister in King Ghaṭa's palace committed an offense. The King, knowing the offense firsthand, banished him from the country.

## Holding a Grudge
At that time, a king named Dhaṅka was reigning in Sāvatthī. The banished minister went to King Dhaṅka and served him. Following the method mentioned below, the minister made King Dhaṅka believe his words and led him to seize the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. King Dhaṅka, having taken the kingdom, had the Bodhisatta bound in chains and cast into prison. The Bodhisatta, having developed jhāna, sat cross-legged in the air. A burning sensation arose in King Dhaṅka's body.

## Why Do You Not Grieve?
King Dhaṅka went and saw the Bodhisatta's face, which was as radiant as a golden mirror or a blooming lotus, and wishing to question the Bodhisatta, he spoke the first verse:

29. "Others grieve and weep, others have tearful faces. But your complexion is serene; why, Ghaṭa, do you not grieve?"
157:
30. Sorrow brings back nothing of the past, nor does it bring future happiness.
Therefore, Dhanka, I do not grieve; there is no companionship in sorrow.

31. One who grieves becomes pale and thin, and loses his appetite for food.
Enemies are delighted when one is afflicted, pierced by the arrow of grief.

32. Whether in a village or in a forest, in a valley or on a plateau,
[Misery] will not come to me who stands [firm]; thus have I seen the path.

33. For one whose own self is not enough to bring the flavor of all desires,
Even the entire earth will not bring him happiness.

He spoke these verses.

Dhanka: King Dhanka. Sorrow: Grieving does not bring back past happiness. Nor does it bring future happiness. Therefore: For that reason. I: I. Do not grieve: I do not sorrow. Companionship: Because of the companion of jhāna. In sorrow: In grieving. Is not: There is none.

One who grieves: A person who sorrows. Pale: Has a pale complexion. Becomes: It happens. Thin: Becomes emaciated. Becomes: It happens. His: That grieving person's. Food: Even the meal. Is not liked: He has no appetite for it. Pierced by the arrow: When the arrow of sorrow has entered. Afflicted: To one who is distressed. Enemies: Foes. Are delighted: They become joyful. Are: They become so.

In a village: Also in the village. If: That city. In a forest: Also in the woods. In a valley: Also in a low-lying place. If: That city. On a plateau: Also on high ground. Stands: Who is established. Me: To me. (That: That destruction rooted in sorrow.) Will not come: It shall not arrive. I: I. Thus: In this way. Have seen the path: Possess the jhāna that has been seen.

To whom: To which king. Self: Friends who bring about one's welfare. Are: There are; among those friends. Even one: Even a single friend. To bring the flavor of all desires: To bring all the desired flavors known as the bliss of jhāna. Enough: Is capable. Not: Is not. Even the entire earth: All the land as well. To him: To that king. Happiness: The bliss of jhāna. Will not bring: It shall not carry.

He spoke this first verse:

Ghaṭa: King Ghaṭa. Others: Other people. Grieve: They sorrow. Weep: They cry. Other: Other. People: Humans. With tearful faces: Have faces wet with tears. You: You. Have a bright complexion: Have a clear facial appearance. Are: You are. Why: For what reason. Do you not grieve: Why do you not sorrow?

## No Benefit in Grieving
At that time, the Bodhisatta, wishing to explain the reason for not grieving to King Dhanka—
158:
King Dhanka, having heard these four verses, apologized to the Bodhisatta, handed over the kingdom, and departed. The Bodhisatta also handed over the kingdom to the ministers, went to the Himalayan region, ordained as a hermit, and with undiminished jhāna, was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was King Dhanka, and I myself was King Ghaṭa."

## Grieving and Lamenting Bring Only Suffering
The Ghaṭa Jātaka ends.

## 6. Koraṇḍiya Jātaka

## Giving to Those Who Do Not Want Reduces the Value of the Gift
While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who is capable of disciplining the world including the devas, told this Koraṇḍiya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Eko araññe," concerning the Venerable Sāriputta Thera.

The Venerable Sāriputta Thera, whenever he saw immoral people such as hunters and fishermen who came to him, would say, "Take the precepts, take the precepts," and give them the moral precepts (sīla). Out of respect for the Thera, those people did not dare to break his word and took the precepts. However, after taking them, they did not observe the precepts. They only performed their own [sinful] works. The Thera called his resident disciples and said, "Friends, such and such people took the precepts from me, but after taking them, they do not observe them."

"Venerable Sir, you give the precepts to those people even though they do not desire them. Those people do not dare to break your word and thus take the precepts. From this day forward, please do not give the precepts to such people," the disciples submitted. The Thera was displeased.

Having heard about this matter, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised a discussion: "Friends, it is said that the Venerable Sāriputta gives the precepts to every person he sees."

The All-Knowing Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," He said, "Monks, not only now has Sāriputta given the precepts to those who do not ask in every place he sees them; in the past also, he gave the precepts to those who did not ask in every place he saw them," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family and was named "Koraṇḍiya." When Koraṇḍiya reached the age of maturity, he became the senior student of a world-renowned teacher in the city of Takkasilā.
159:
34. "Alone in the forest, in a mountain ravine,
Lifting and lifting, you throw a stone.
Repeatedly, with a hurried appearance,
Koraṇḍiya, what indeed is your purpose here?"
This was the first verse he spoke.
Koraṇḍiya, Koraṇḍiya. You, in the forest, alone, repeatedly, with a hurried manner, take stones and throw them into the mountain ravine. What benefit is there for you in filling this ravine?

35. "I shall make this ocean-bounded earth
As level as the palm of my hand.
Scattering the peaks and the mountains,
Therefore, I throw stones into the ravine."

## Giving Precepts to Everyone
At that time, the world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) gave the precepts (sīla) to those who did not ask, wherever he saw them, saying, "Take the precepts, take the precepts." Those people, having taken them, did not guard them. The teacher informed his students of this matter.

The students said, "Teacher... you give the precepts to those people even though they do not desire them. Therefore, they break them. From today onwards, give the precepts only to those who ask. Do not give them to those who do not ask." The world-renowned teacher felt regret. Even so, he continued to give the precepts wherever he saw people.

## Ending the Teacher's Habit
Then one day, people came and invited the teacher to recite blessings for the brahmins. The world-renowned teacher called the young man Koraṇḍiya and said, "Dear boy... I will not go. You take these five hundred young men, go there, receive the offerings for the recitation, and bring back our share."

Koraṇḍiya said, "Very well," and while returning, he saw a ravine on the way and thought, "Our teacher gives the precepts to those who do not ask wherever he sees them. From today onwards, I will act so that he gives the precepts only to those who ask." Having thought so, while the other young men were resting comfortably, Koraṇḍiya got up, lifted a large stone, and threw it repeatedly into the ravine.

## Argument Between Teacher and Student
Then the other young men asked Koraṇḍiya, "Teacher... why do you do this?" Koraṇḍiya did not say anything. Those young men went quickly and informed the teacher. The teacher came and, wishing to speak with Koraṇḍiya—

Koraṇḍiya, hearing those words and wishing to make the teacher understand, spoke—
Scattering the peaks and the mountains,
Therefore, I throw stones into the ravine.
160:
A single man is not fit to make
This earth level like the palm of his hand.
I think you will leave this world of the living,
Koraṇḍiya, while still desiring to fill this ravine.
This was the third verse he spoke.

Koraṇḍiya, Koraṇḍiya. A single man is not able to make this earth level like the palm of a hand. I think you will leave this world of the living while searching for stones and seeking a way to fill this ravine.

This was the second verse he spoke.
Teacher, I shall make this earth, which is bounded by the oceans, level like the palm of a hand, by breaking down the hills of earth and the mountains of rock. Therefore, I throw stones into the ravine.

Hearing those words, the brahmin teacher—
36. "A single man is not fit to make
This earth level like the palm of his hand."

Hearing those words, the young man Koraṇḍiya—
37. "If I, a single man, am unable
To make this earth-bearer (the earth) level,
Even so, O Brahmin, you will not be able to lead
These people of various views to your will."
This was the fourth verse he spoke.

O Brahmin teacher. If I, being a single man, am unable to make the earth level, even so, you, teacher, will not be able to bring these people of various views to your own will.

Hearing those words, the teacher thought, "Koraṇḍiya... you speak what is fitting. Now I will not do such a thing," and realizing his own error, he spoke—
161:
38. "In a concise form, you have told me
My own benefit, Koraṇḍiya; it is just so.
Just as the earth cannot be made level
By a single man, so it is with people."
This was the fifth verse he spoke.

Koraṇḍiya, young man. You have told me the benefit through a concise analogy. This word of yours is true as you say. Just as this earth cannot be made level, so too a man cannot make all people uniform.

Thus the teacher praised the young man. Having done so, and understanding the meaning of what the student said, he took him home.

The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, Sāriputta was the brahmin teacher, and I myself was the young man Koraṇḍiya."

## The Earth is Not Level, and People Cannot Be Made Uniform
The Koraṇḍiya Jātaka ends.

## 7. Laṭukika Jātaka
## One Should Not Oppress the Weak
The All-Knowing Buddha, who is the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Laṭukika Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Vandāmi taṃ kuñjara saṭṭhiဟာယနံ," concerning Devadatta.

One day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma hall: "Friends... Devadatta is harsh, cruel, and violent. He does not have even a bit of compassion for living beings."

The All-Knowing Buddha came and asked, "Monks... what conversation are you gathered for now?" When they replied, "For such a conversation," he said, "Monks... it is not only now that Devadatta is without compassion; in the past too, he was without compassion," and he brought the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the elephant species. When he reached maturity, he was inspiring and had a large body. He became the leader of a herd, surrounded by eighty thousand elephants, and lived in the Himalayan region.

## The Little Bird's Plea and Escape
At that time, a female quail (laṭukika) laid her eggs in the place where the elephants roamed. When the eggs matured, the young birds hatched. While those young birds were still unable to fly because their wings had not yet grown, the Bodhisatta, surrounded by eighty thousand elephants, arrived at that place while searching for food.
162:
39. Vandāmi taṃ kuñjara saṭṭhihāyanaṃ,
Āraññakaṃ yūthapatiṃ yasassiṃ.
Pakkhehi taṃ pañjalikaṃ karomi,
Mā me vadhī puttake dubbalāya.

She spoke this first stanza.

Kuñjara: O king elephant. Saṭṭhihāyanaṃ: one whose strength declines at sixty years of age. Āraññakaṃ: one who roams the forest. Yūthapatiṃ: the leader of the elephant herd. Yasassiṃ: one with a great following. Taṃ: you. Ahaṃ: I. Vandāmi: salute. Pakkhehi: with my wings. Pañjalikaṃ: the act of saluting with joined palms. Karomi: I perform. Dubbalāya: of me, who am weak. Me: my. Puttake: little young ones. Mā vadhī: do not kill.

40. Vandāmi taṃ kuñjara ekacāriṃ,
Āraññakaṃ pabbatasanugocaraṃ.
Pakkhehi taṃ pañjalikaṃ karomi,
Mā me vadhī puttake dubbalāya.

She spoke this second stanza.

Kuñjara: O king elephant. Ekacāriṃ: one who roams alone. Āraññakaṃ: one who lives in the forest. Pabbatasanugocaraṃ: one who seeks food on rocky mountains and earthen hills. Taṃ: you. Ahaṃ: I. Vandāmi: salute. Pakkhehi: with my wings. Ahaṃ: I. Pañjalikaṃ: the act of saluting with joined palms. Karomi: I perform. Dubbalāya: of me, who am weak. Me: my. Puttake: little young ones. Mā vadhī: do not kill.

41. Vadhissāmi te laṭukike puttakāni,
Kiṃ me tuvaṃ kāhasi dubbalāsi.
Sataṃ sahassānipi tādhisīnaṃ,

The mother quail saw the Bodhisatta and thought, 'This king elephant will trample and kill my young. Now, for the sake of my young ones' protection, I will ask the king elephant for righteous protection.' Having thought so, she folded her wings and stood before the king elephant.

The Bodhisatta said, 'Little quail, do not worry. I will protect your young.' He stood over the young birds until the eighty thousand elephants had passed. Then he called the quail and said, 'Little quail, behind us comes a lone rogue elephant. He will not listen to our words. When he comes, entreat him also to ensure the safety of your young.' Then he departed.

## Harm Despite Entreaty

The little quail went to meet that elephant and, paying homage with her wings, [spoke].

The elephant, hearing the little quail's words, [spoke].
163:
42. Na heva sabbattha balena kiccaṃ,
Balañhi bālassa vadhāya hoti.
Karissāmi te nāgarāja anatthaṃ,
Yo me vadhī puttake dubbalāya.

She spoke this fourth stanza.

Nāgarāja: O king elephant. Sabbattha: in all matters. Balena: by strength. Kiccaṃ: that which is to be done. Na heva: is not so. Hi saccaṃ: it is true. Balaṃ: physical strength. Bālassa: for the fool. Vadhāya: for destruction. Hoti: it is. Yo tvaṃ: you who. Dubbalāya: of me, who am weak. Me: my. Puttake: little young ones. Vadhī: killed. Te: your. Anatthaṃ: ruin. Karissāmi: I shall bring about.

Vāmena pādena papothayeyyaṃ.

She spoke this third stanza.

Laṭukike: O little quail. Te: your. Puttakāni: little young ones. Vadhissāmi: I shall kill. Tvaṃ: you. Dubbalā: weak. Asi: are. Tvaṃ: you. Me: to me. Kiṃ kāhasi: what can you do? Tādhisīnaṃ: of those like you. Sata-sahassānipi: even a hundred thousand quails. Vāmena pādena: with my left foot alone. Papothayeyyaṃ: I shall kill.

Having said this, the elephant crushed the quail's young underfoot, washed them away with urine, and went off trumpeting.

## The Quail's Threat

The little quail perched on a branch and threatened him, saying, 'Now you go away trumpeting. In a few days, you shall see my deed. You may not know that the power of wisdom is greater than physical strength, but I shall make you know!'

## Forming Alliances and Seeking Help

Having said this, the little quail served a crow for a few days. The crow, being pleased, asked, 'What shall I do for you?' She replied, 'Master, I have no other task. I desire that you peck and break the eyes of a certain rogue elephant with your beak.' The crow agreed, saying 'Very well.'

She then served a bluebottle fly. The fly also asked, 'What task of yours shall I perform?' She said, 'When the rogue elephant's eyes are broken for this reason, I wish for you to drop maggots into those eyes.' The fly also said 'Very well.' Then she served a frog...
164:
43. Behold the crow and the quail, the frog and the blue fly.
These killed the elephant; behold the result of enmity.
Therefore, one should not create enmity with anyone, even an unpleasant person.

Having preached this verse, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

Monks. Behold the crow. Behold the female quail. Behold the frog. Behold the blue fly. These four creatures were able to kill the elephant. Behold the course of the enemy's enmity. Therefore, one should not create enmity with anyone, even with one who is not loved.

When a certain frog was approached and asked, "What shall I do for you?", [the quail] said, "When that rogue elephant becomes blind and seeks water, stay on the mountain top and croak. When that elephant climbs the mountain top, descend and croak at the precipice; I desire this service from you." The frog agreed, saying "Very well."

## The Foolish Elephant is Dead

Then one day, the crow pecked both eyes of the elephant with its beak. The blue fly released maggots [into the wounds]. The elephant, being bitten by the maggots and reaching a state of agony, became thirsty and went searching for water. At that time, the frog stayed on the mountain top and croaked. The elephant, thinking there would be water in that place, climbed the mountain top. Then the frog descended, stood at the mountain precipice, and croaked. The elephant, thinking there would be water in that place, came towards the precipice, fell, and died.

The little female quail, knowing the fact that the elephant was dead, was delighted and joyful, saying, "I have seen the back of my enemy." She walked back and forth on the elephant's back and then went according to her karma.

## Do Not Make Enmity

The Omniscient Buddha, in order to show that "Monks, one should not create what is called enmity with anyone; in this way, four creatures being united caused even a powerful elephant to reach the end of its life," said:

As for how the Jātaka was identified: At that time, Devadatta was the rogue elephant. I, the Buddha, was the leader of the herd. Thus, He identified the Jātaka.

## Crow, Fly, Bird, Frog; the four were united, the big elephant died.

The Latukika Jātaka ends.
165:
## 8. Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka
## The Bodhisatta who did not cry even when his hands and feet were severed

The Present Story: While the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, he told this Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Aham-eva dūsiyā bhūnahatā," concerning Devadatta’s attempts to kill him.

In other Jātakas, Devadatta was unable to even frighten the Bodhisatta. However, in this Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, when the Bodhisatta was only seven months old, Devadatta had his hands, feet, and head severed, creating what is called a "wreath of swords" (asimālaka).

In the Daddara Jātaka, he also killed him by grabbing his neck, then cooked and ate his flesh on a stove. In the Khantivādī Jātaka, he had him beaten with a thousand strokes of two whips, had his hands, feet, ears, and nose severed, had him dragged by his matted hair, laid him on his back, and stomped on his chest before leaving. The Bodhisatta passed away on that very day. In the Cūḷanandiya Jātaka and the Mahākapi Jātaka as well, he caused the Bodhisatta's death. In this same way, even during the time he became a Buddha, Devadatta long persisted in his efforts to kill him.

One day, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised a discussion: "Friends, Devadatta is making every effort to kill the Buddha. He employed archers to kill the Fully Enlightened One, rolled a rock down, and released the elephant Nālāgiri."

The All-Knowing Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what subject are you gathered here discussing now?" When they replied, "With such a subject," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has attempted to kill me; he did so in the past as well. Now, however, he cannot even cause me to be frightened. In the past, when I was Prince Dhammapāla, he brought about the end of my life, even though I was his own son, and made a wreath of swords." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Mahāpatāpa was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the King’s chief queen, named Candādevī. They named him Dhammapāla. When Prince Dhammapāla was seven months old, his mother bathed him in scented water and sat playing with him.
166:
The King went to the Queen's quarters. While the Queen was playing with her son, she was so filled with love for him that she did not stand up from her seat even upon seeing the King. The King thought, "Even now, this Queen is arrogant because of her son. She regards me as nothing. When the son grows up, she will not even recognize me as a human being. I will kill this prince right now." Having thought this, the King returned and sat on his throne, then summoned the executioner, saying, "Come according to your duty."

The executioner came wearing saffron-dyed clothes, adorned with red flowers, with an axe on his shoulder, and carrying a block and a stick for placing hands and feet. He bowed to the King and stood there, asking, "What shall I do, O King?" The King said, "Go to the royal bedchamber and bring Dhammapāla."

The Queen, knowing that the King had returned in anger, sat crying with the Bodhisatta lying on her breast. The executioner went and struck the Queen on her back, snatched the prince from her hands, and brought him before the King, asking, "What shall I do, O King?" The King had a wooden board brought and placed before him, saying, "Lay Dhammapāla on this board." He did so.

Candādevī followed behind her son, weeping. Again, the executioner asked, "What shall I do, O King?" "Sever Dhammapāla’s hands," the King replied.

Candādevī, wishing to show that "Great King, my son is only a seven-month-old infant and knows nothing; he has no fault. If there be a fault, let it be mine. Therefore, sever my hands instead," spoke this first verse:

44. Aham-eva dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassa.
Etaṃ muñcatu dhammapālaṃ, hatthe me deva chedehi.

I alone am the offender, the destroyer of prosperity, against King Mahāpatāpa. Release this Dhammapāla; O King, sever my hands.

[Word-for-word meaning:] Aham-eva: I alone. Mahāpatāpassa rañño: against King Mahāpatāpa. Dūsiyā: have committed an offense. Bhūnahatā: have destroyed prosperity. Deva: O King. Etaṃ Dhammapālaṃ: this Dhammapāla. Muñcatu: release. Me: my. Hatthe: hands. Chedehi: have them severed.

The King looked at the executioner. "Great King, what shall I do?" asked the executioner. "Do not delay; sever the hands," the King said. At that moment, the executioner took a sharp axe and severed the prince's two hands as if they were the tender shoots of a bamboo.

Even as his hands were being severed, the prince did not shed a tear nor cry; he endured it, placing patience (khanti) and loving-kindness (mettā) at the forefront. Candādevī, however, took the severed stumps of the hands, placed them in her lap, and went about crying, covered in blood.
167:
45. "I alone am the wrongdoer, the destroyer of prosperity for King Mahāpatāpa. Release this Dhammapāla; O King, cut off my feet instead."
She spoke this second verse.
O King! I alone have committed the fault. I have destroyed the prosperity of King Mahāpatāpa. Release this Dhammapāla. Cut off my feet.

46. "I alone am the wrongdoer, the destroyer of prosperity for King Mahāpatāpa. Release this Dhammapāla; O King, cut off my head instead."
She spoke this third verse.
O King! I alone have committed the fault. I have destroyed the prosperity of King Mahāpatāpa. Release this Dhammapāla. Cut off my head.

Again, the executioner asked, "O Great King, what shall I do?" He said, "Cut off both feet." Hearing this, Candādevī—

The King again commanded the executioner. The executioner cut off both feet. Candādevī took the feet into her lap, and covered in blood, she wept, saying, "Lord Mahāpatāpa, a mother must care for children whose hands and feet are severed. I will work for hire to support my son. Give this son to me!"

The executioner asked, "O King, is my task finished?" "It is not yet finished," he replied. "Then what shall I do, O Great King?" "Cut off Dhammapāla's head," he said. Hearing this, Candādevī—

## The Mother's Heart-Wrenching Lament

Having said this, she bowed her own head to receive the blow. Again, the executioner asked, "O Great King, what shall I do?" "Cut off Dhammapāla's head," he said. The executioner cut off the head and asked, "O King, is my task finished?" "It is not yet finished," he replied. "Then what shall I do, O Great King?" "Catch Dhammapāla on the point of a sword and make what is called a 'garland of swords' (asimālaka)."

The executioner threw the prince's body into the air, caught it on the point of a sword, made a 'garland of swords', and scattered the pieces across the palace floor.

Queen Candādevī placed the flesh of the Bodhisatta in her lap and, weeping on the palace floor, spoke these verses:
168:
49. "The arms of Dhammapāla, anointed with the essence of sandalwood, are severed. For the heir to the earth, my life, O King, is coming to an end."
She spoke this verse.
On the surface of the earth, which is his father's property, the arms of Dhammapāla, the heir, which were anointed with the essence of sandalwood, are severed. O King, my life is ceasing.

47. "Surely this king has no friends or ministers who are kind-hearted, who do not tell the king: 'Do not kill your own son.'"

48. "Surely this king has no relatives or friends who are kind-hearted, who do not tell the king: 'Do not kill your own son born of yourself.'"
She spoke these two verses.
Those people—friends or ministers with soft hearts—who do not say to the king, "O King, do not kill your own son," surely they do not exist for this King Mahāpatāpa.
Those people—friends or relatives with soft hearts—who do not say to the king, "O King, do not kill your own son born of yourself," surely they do not exist for this King Mahāpatāpa.

After Queen Candādevī spoke these two verses, she lifted her breast with both hands—
As Queen Candādevī lamented thus, her heart broke like a bamboo in a burning bamboo grove. She passed away right there.

## The King Swallowed by the Earth

The King fell from the high palace to the ground. Then, the thick earth, two hundred and forty thousand leagues in depth, unable to bear the wickedness of King Mahāpatāpa, split in two and provided an opening. Flames from Avīci rose up, and as if wrapping him in a woolen blanket provided by his kin, seized King Mahāpatāpa and cast him into Avīci.

The ministers performed the funeral rites for Queen Candādevī and the body of the Bodhisatta.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King was Devadatta, Candādevī was Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, and Prince Dhammapāla was I myself."

## Obsessed with Lust, Cruel to his Son, Wrongly Acting, Sent to Avīci

The Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka ends.

## 9. Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka
## Exchanging One's Life for the Husband's Life

**The Present Account**
While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the Teacher of the world including the devas, told this Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Vikkama re haripāda,” concerning a certain daughter of a family.

That woman was a daughter of a family in Sāvatthī who served the two Chief Disciples. She was endowed with faith and devotion, a lover of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. She was perfect in conduct, wise, and delighted in meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna).

## A Buddhist Woman
A family of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) of the same class in Sāvatthī asked for her hand in marriage. At that time, her parents said: “Our daughter is endowed with faith and devotion; she cherishes the Triple Gem and delights in meritorious deeds such as giving. You hold wrong views. You will not allow this young woman to give alms as she wishes, to hear the Dhamma, to go to the monastery, to observe the precepts, or to perform the Uposatha duties. Therefore, we will not give her to you. You should take a maiden from a family of wrong view similar to yourselves.”

When they were thus rejected, the family of wrong view said: “Let your daughter come to our house and perform all those meritorious deeds you mentioned as she desires; we shall not prevent her. Please give her to us.” When they were told, “If that is so, take her,” they performed the wedding ceremony under a favorable constellation and took the woman to their home.

## Converting the Husband of Another Faith
That woman was perfect in her duties and conduct. She served her husband like a deity. She performed the duties toward her father-in-law, mother-in-law, and husband. One day, she said to her husband: “My lord, I wish to give alms to the Elders who are our family mentors.” He replied: “Very well, lady, give alms as you desire.”

She invited the Elders, made great offerings, served them choice food, and after they had eaten, she sat in a suitable place and said: “Venerable sirs, this family holds wrong views and lacks faith; they do not know the virtues of the Triple Gem. I request you, noble sirs, please accept alms at this very house until this family comes to know the virtues of the Triple Gem.” The Elders consented and regularly took their meals there.

Later, she said to her husband: “My lord, the Elders regularly come to our house; why do you not see them?” The husband replied: “Very well, I shall see them.” The next day, after the Elders had finished their meal, she informed her husband. He approached, exchanged friendly greetings with the Elders, and sat in a suitable place.

## Attaining the Path and Fruit
Then, the Venerable Sāriputta preached the Dhamma to that man. The man, having gained faith in the Dhamma discourse and the deportment of the Venerable Sāriputta, began from that time to prepare seats for the Elders, strain the drinking water, and listen to the Dhamma during the intervals of the meal. Subsequently, his wrong views were dispelled.
170:
Then one day, the Elder, while preaching the Dhamma to the couple, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, both husband and wife were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

From that time onward, starting from the man’s parents down to the lowest servants and laborers, all dispelled their wrong views and became devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. 

Then one day, the woman said to her husband: “My lord, I have no desire for household life; I wish to ordain.” He replied: “Very well, lady, I too shall ordain.” With a large retinue, he escorted her to the nunnery and had her ordained. He himself approached the Teacher and requested ordination. The Teacher ordained him. Both of them developed insight (vipassanā) and before long attained the Fruit of Arahantship.

One day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, the young nun of such-and-name has been a support both to herself and to her husband. Having ordained herself and attained Arahantship, she also led her husband to Nibbāna.”

The All-Knowing Buddha arrived and asked: “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they replied, “With such a discussion,” He said: “Monks, not only now has this young nun released her husband from the snare of passion; in the past, she also released the wise from the snare of death.” Having said this, He brought forth the past account.

**The Past Account**
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a deer. When he reached maturity, he was beautiful and pleasing to behold. He was golden-hued, with limbs as if polished with lac, horns like silver threads, eyes like jewel orbs, and a face like the color of a red blanket.

His wife, a young doe, was also beautiful and pleasing to behold. They lived together in harmony, and eighty thousand variegated deer attended upon the Bodhisatta. At that time, hunters set snares in the deer tracks. One day, the Bodhisatta, walking at the head of the deer, was caught in a snare by his foot. He pulled, thinking, “I will break it,” but the skin was cut. Pulling again, the flesh was cut, and then the tendon was cut, until the snare reached the bone and stayed there. Unable to break the snare and terrified by the fear of death, he uttered a cry of capture. Hearing it, the frightened herd of deer fled. But his wife, looking back among the deer as she fled and not seeing him, thought, “This danger must have befallen my dear husband.” She quickly went to him, weeping with a face full of tears.

The leather snare is strong; it cuts all around my foot.

52. Spread the leaves, O hunter; draw your sword from its scabbard.
Kill me first, and then kill the great deer.

She spoke this third verse. 

Luddaka, hunter. Tvaṃ, you. Palāsāni, leaves of the flame-of-the-forest tree. Attharassu, spread them out. Asiṃ, the sword. Nibbaāha, draw it from its scabbard. Paṭhamaṃ, first. Maṃ, me. Vadhitvāna, having killed. Pacchā, afterwards. Mahāmigaṃ, the great deer. Hana, kill.

The wife of that Bodhisatta was also young and beautiful, and she was lovely to behold. Those two lived together in perfect harmony. Eighty thousand deer of various kinds attended to the Bodhisatta.

## The Deer King Caught in a Snare

At that time, hunters set snares on the paths of the deer. One day, while the Bodhisatta was walking at the head of the deer, his foot got caught in a snare. Thinking, "I will break the snare," he pulled. The skin was cut. When he pulled again, the flesh was cut. When he pulled once more, the tendon was cut. The snare reached the bone and stayed there. The Bodhisatta, unable to bite through it and fearing death, let out the cry of one caught in a snare.

Hearing that sound, the herd of deer fled. But the Bodhisatta's wife, after fleeing, looked among the deer and, not seeing the Bodhisatta, thought, "This danger must have befallen my beloved husband." She quickly went to the Bodhisatta and, with a tearful face, weeping, said, "Lord, you are of great strength. This snare will not be able to hold you. Exert your strength and break that snare." Wishing to encourage him, she spoke the first verse:

50. Strive, O golden-footed one! Strive, O great deer!
Break the leather snare; I cannot enjoy the forest alone.

Re haripāda, O you with feet like the color of gold. Mahāmiga, noble deer. Vikkama, strive. Re haripāda, O you with feet like the color of gold. Mahāmiga, noble deer. Vikkama, strive. Vārattikaṃ pāsaṃ, the leather snare. Chinda, break it. Ahaṃ, I. Ekā, alone. Vane, in the forest. Na rame, cannot be happy.

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta stag spoke the second verse:

## The Queen Doe's Plea

Then the doe comforted the Great Being, saying, "Lord, do not fear. I will plead with the hunter using my own power to save your life. If I cannot succeed by pleading, I will give my own life to save yours." Having comforted the Great Being, she stood supporting the blood-stained Bodhisatta. 

The hunter, taking his sword and spear, approached like the fire at the end of an eon. Seeing him, the doe comforted the stag, saying, "Lord, the hunter is coming. I will use my power; do not fear." She went to meet the hunter, stood respectfully to one side, saluted him, and praised the Bodhisatta's virtues: "Lord, my husband, the golden-colored deer king, is endowed with virtue and conduct; he is the king of eighty thousand deer." Desiring to offer her own life while the deer king stood there, she spoke the third verse:

May you be happy, O blessed one, and may this great deer be happy too.

He spoke this fourth verse.

Bhaddē, O noble and wise lady. Me, by me. Ito pubbe, before this time. Mānuusiṃ, human speech. Bhāsantiṃ, speaking. Migiṃ, a doe. Sutaṃ vā, having heard. Diṭṭhaṃ vā, having seen. Na, there is not. Tvañca, may you also. Sukhī, happy. Hohi, be. Eso cāpi mahāmigo, and may this great deer also. Sukhī, happy. Hotu, be.

Just as I rejoice today, seeing the great deer released.

She spoke this fifth verse.

Luddaka, hunter. Ajja, today. Ahaṃ, I. Muttaṃ, released. Mahāmigaṃ, the deer king. Disvā, having seen. Yathā nandāmi, just as I rejoice. Evaṃ tathā, in the same way. Tvaṃ, may you. Sabbehi ñātibhi saha, together with all your kinsfolk. Nandassu, rejoice.

## The Hunter Releases and Heals

Hearing her words, the hunter thought, "Even human women do not sacrifice their lives for their husbands' sake, but this doe, though an animal, gives up her life. She also speaks with a sweet human voice. Today, I shall give life to both this doe and her husband."

Having thus comforted the doe, the hunter went to the Bodhisatta, cut the leather snare with a knife, gently removed the snare caught in the foot, and joined the tendons to tendons, flesh to flesh, and skin to skin, and massaged the foot with his hand.

At that moment, through the power of the perfections fulfilled by the Great Being, the power of the hunter's heart of loving-kindness, and the power of the doe's virtue in protecting her friend, the tendons, flesh, and skin were joined together. The Bodhisatta stood up, healthy and free from pain.

## The Doe's Blessing

Seeing the Bodhisatta healthy, the doe was filled with joy and, wishing to express her appreciation to the hunter, spoke the fifth verse.

## The Deer King's Sermon

The Bodhisatta thought, "This hunter has become my refuge; I too should be a refuge for him." He gave the hunter a certain jewel found in the feeding ground and said, "Friend, from this day forward, do not commit killing and other such acts."
173:
"With this ruby, establish your wealth, support your children and wife, and perform meritorious deeds such as giving and virtue." Having given this advice to the hunter, he entered the forest.

Identifying the birth-story, the All-Knowing Buddha brought forth this Dhamma teaching and said: "At that time, Channa was the hunter, the young nun was the doe, and I myself was the King of the Deer."

## A wise wife brings happiness to her husband.

The Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka ends.

## 10. Suyonandī Jātaka

## On the Inability to Guard Women

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Suyonandī Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Vāti gandho timirānaṃ," concerning a monk who was dissatisfied with the holy life.

The All-Knowing Buddha asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When he replied, "It is true," the Teacher asked, "What did you see that made you dissatisfied?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I saw an adorned woman and became dissatisfied."

"Monk, it is impossible to guard women. Even the wise men of old, though they kept a woman in the abode of the Supaṇṇas and guarded her, were unable to do so," the Teacher said. At the monk's request, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Tamba reigned in Bārāṇasī, he had a chief queen named Suyonandī, who possessed supreme beauty.

## The Supaṇṇa King Abducts the Queen

At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the realm of the Supaṇṇas. In those days, Nāgadīpa was known as Sedumadīpa. The Bodhisatta lived in the Supaṇṇa abode on that island. He would go to Bārāṇasī and play dice with King Tamba in the guise of a young man.

Seeing the beauty of his form, the attendants told Queen Suyonandī, "A young man of such appearance is playing dice with our king." Hearing this, she wished to see him. One day, she adorned herself and went to the dice-playing area, standing among her attendants to look at him. The Bodhisatta also looked at the queen. Both became infatuated with each other.
174:
The Supaṇṇa king, by his power, caused a wind to arise in the city of Bārāṇasī. Fearing the palace would collapse, the people fled from the royal residence. The Supaṇṇa king, by his power, created darkness, seized the queen, and flew through the air to his abode on Sedumadīpa. No one knew where Queen Suyonandī had gone. That Supaṇṇa king, while enjoying himself with Queen Suyonandī, would go to Bārāṇasī to play dice with the king.

## The Musician Sagga Reaches the Supaṇṇa Realm

King Tamba had a musician named Sagga. Since the king did not know where the queen had gone, he summoned the musician and sent him, saying, "Friend, go and search all the land and sea routes to find where the queen has gone."

Taking provisions, the musician searched from the village gates onwards and reached the port of Bharukaccha. At that time, merchants were sailing from Bharukaccha to Suvaṇṇabhūmi. The musician approached them and said, "Sirs, I am a musician. I will play the lute for you in exchange for my passage. Please take me with you." The merchants agreed, took him aboard, and set sail.

Desiring to listen on the boat, the merchants called the musician and said, "We wish to listen; play the lute." He replied, "If I play the lute, the fish will be stirred, and then your ship will be destroyed." The merchants said, "There is no such thing as fish being stirred when a lute is played among humans. Play the lute!"

"If that is the case, do not be angry with me," he said. He tuned the lute and played, matching the sound of the strings with his voice and his voice with the strings. Intoxicated by the sound, the fish were stirred. Then a sea monster (makara) leaped and fell onto the ship, causing it to break apart.

## The Musician and Suyonandī

When Queen Suyonandī went down from the abode to wander on the shore while the Garuḍa king went to play dice, she saw the musician named Sagga. Recognizing him, she asked, "How did you come here?" The musician told her the whole story.

"If that is so, do not be afraid," she said, comforting the musician. She embraced him with both arms, carried him to the abode, and laid him on the bed. When his exhaustion was relieved, she gave him celestial food, bathed him with celestial scented water, dressed him in celestial garments, adorned him with scented flowers, and again laid him on a celestial bed. Thus, she looked after him during the day, and when the Garuḍa king returned, she hid him. When the king left, she enjoyed herself with the musician through the power of passion.

## Found the Queen

Then, after a month and a half had passed, merchants living in Bārāṇasī arrived at the foot of the banyan tree on Seduma Island to collect wood and water. That musician boarded the ship with the merchants and went to the city of Bārāṇasī. Seeing the king, while he was playing dice, he took his lute and played it in the presence of the king—

Hearing those words, the Garuḍa king—

O King Tamba. That Queen Suyonandī, who is always anointed with the scent of sandalwood, who is beautiful and pleasing to behold, [treated] me with tenderness, with softness,

## Returning the Queen
The Garuda King, becoming remorseful while the musician was singing, thought, "Even though I live in the Garuda realm, I am unable to protect this woman. What use have I for this unvirtuous woman?" He then took the woman, gave her back to the King, and departed. From that time on, he never returned.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Fully Enlightened One revealed the Truths, and at the end of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*). To identify the birth: At that time, Ānanda was the King, and I myself was the Garuda King. Thus He identified the Jātaka.

## Women's Nature: Even when Guarded, They Go Astray
The Suyonandī Jātaka ends.

## 2. Vaṇṇārohavagga
## 1. Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka
## About the Slandering Jackal
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Vaṇṇārohena," concerning the two Chief Disciples (*Aggasāvaka*).

## How the Two Elders were Slandered
On one occasion, the two Elders, thinking, "During this rainy season (*vassa*), we shall develop meditation in a secluded place," took leave of the Fully Enlightened One, left their retinue, took their bowls and robes themselves, and departed from Jetavana. They stayed in a forest near a border village. A certain scavenger (*viqhāsāda*) stayed nearby in a suitable spot in that forest, serving the Elders.

That scavenger, seeing the harmonious living of the Elders, thought, "These Elders live in great harmony. Would it be possible to divide them from one another?" He approached the Venerable Sāriputta and asked, "Venerable Sir, is there any grudge between you and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna?" The Venerable Sāriputta asked, "Why, lay follower?"
177:
60. "By appearance and stature, by birth, and by strength and exertion,
Subāhu is not superior to me, O Sudāṭha—thus you speak."

He spoke this first verse.

Sudāṭha: the lion king. Subāhu: the tiger. By appearance and stature: by color, form, and height. By birth: by lineage. By strength and exertion: by power and effort. Than me. Not superior: not better or more excellent. Thus. You. Speak: do you say so?

"Venerable Sir, when I came, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said: 'What is special about Sāriputta in terms of birth, age, clan, and lineage, or in terms of learning, mastery of scriptures, realization of the Dhamma, and psychic powers and meditative attainments?' Thus he spoke only of your lack of virtue." The Venerable Sāriputta smiled and said, "Go, lay follower."

## The Slanderer Had to Flee
Later, on another day, he approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and spoke in the same way. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also smiled and said, "Go, lay follower." Then he approached the Venerable Sāriputta and asked, "Friend, did this scavenger say anything in your presence?" "Yes, friend, he spoke in my presence too," he replied. "It is proper to expel this scavenger," the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said. When he said, "Very well, friend, expel him," the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna snapped his fingers and drove the scavenger away, saying, "Do not stay here!"

The two elders lived together in harmony, went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. The All-Enlightened One greeted them and asked, "Did you spend the rainy season happily?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, a certain scavenger wished to divide us, but being unable to do so, he fled," the Buddha said:

"Sāriputta, it is not only now that this scavenger wished to divide you and fled because he was unable to do so; he has done so before." Being requested by them, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in the forest. At that time, a lion and a tiger lived in a mountain cave in that forest.

## How the Tiger and Lion were Slandered
A certain jackal, serving the lion and the tiger and eating their leftovers, grew large in body. One day he thought, "I have never eaten the meat of a lion or a tiger. It is proper for me to cause a rift between these two. Then, when they have quarreled and died, I shall eat their meat."

Having so thought, the jackal approached the lion and asked, "Lord, is there any enmity between you and the tiger?" "Friend jackal, there has never been any enmity," the lion replied. "Lord, when I came, this tiger said: 'In terms of physical appearance, stature, birth, strength, or energy, the lion does not even reach a sixteenth part of me.' Thus he spoke only of your lack of virtue."
178:
Then the lion said to the jackal, "Go, that tiger would not speak such things." The jackal then approached the tiger and spoke in the same manner.

## The Tiger and Lion Consult Each Other
Hearing those words, the tiger also approached the lion and, wishing to ask, "Friend, did you say this?" spoke the following.

Hearing those words, the lion spoke these four verses:

Sudāṭha is not superior to me, O Subāhu—thus you speak.

62. If you, friend Subāhu, wrong me who lives thus in harmony with you,
I no longer take pleasure in living together with you.

63. Whoever believes the words of others as the truth
Will soon be divided from his friend and produce much enmity.

But he in whom one rests like a son on his mother's breast,

Friend Subāhu: the tiger of equal age. Thus. Me, who lives in harmony with you. The jackal's. Words. Taking. You. If you wrong [me]. I. Now. With you. Together. Living. Do not take pleasure.

Whoever. Others'. Words. As the truth. Should believe. In that fool. Friend. Quickly. Would be broken. Much. Enmity. Increases.

Whoever. Always. Being heedful [in a guarded sense]: not giving trust to a friend. Suspecting a rift: fearing the destruction of the friendship. Looking only for flaws: searching for a gap or opening. He. A friend: is called a friend. A son. On the breast: as if sleeping on a mother's breast without suspicion or fear. In whom. Rests. And whoever. By others: because of others. Cannot be divided. He. Truly. Is called a friend.

## The Jackal Had to Flee

When the lion had spoken of the virtues of a friend with these four verses, the tiger apologized to the lion, saying, "It was my fault." Those two, the tiger and the lion, lived together in harmony just as before. But the jackal fled and went elsewhere.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the All-Enlightened Buddha identified the Jātaka: "The one who was then the scavenger is now the jackal; Sāriputta was then the lion; Moggallāna was then the tiger; and I myself was the tree deity dwelling in that forest who witnessed that event with my own eyes."

## Do Not Let Slander Destroy Friendship

The Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka

## How Virtue is Superior to Knowledge and Wisdom

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Sīlaṃ seyyo," concerning a certain Brahmin who was testing virtue.

The King regarded this Brahmin as superior to other Brahmins, thinking, "This one is endowed with virtue." The Brahmin thought, "Does the King regard me as superior to others because I am endowed with virtue, or because I am possessed of great learning? I will first test the greatness of virtue and learning."

Having thought so, one day he took a coin from a goldsmith. Out of respect, the goldsmith said nothing. Even when he took it a second time, he said nothing. But on the third time, he had him seized, saying, "He is a plunderer," and showed him to the King.
180:
## Virtue is Superior to Learning

When asked, "What did the Brahmin do?", he replied, "He plundered wealth." When asked, "Brahmin, is it true?", he said, "Great King, I did not plunder wealth. I had a doubt: Is virtue superior, or is learning superior? Wishing to test which of these two is superior, I took the coins three times."

"The goldsmith bound me and showed me to Your Majesty. Now I have known the greatness of virtue over learning. I have no need for household life; I shall go forth as a monk." Having obtained permission to go forth, without even looking back at his house door, he went to Jetavana Monastery and requested the Teacher for ordination.

The Teacher granted him the novice ordination and the higher ordination. Not long after becoming a monk, he developed insight and attained the fruit of Arahantship.

The monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the Brahmin of such-and-such a name tested his own virtue, went forth, practiced insight, and attained the fruit of Arahantship."

The All-Enlightened Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?" When they replied, "With such-and-such a subject," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that this Brahmin tested his virtue, went forth, and established his own refuge; in the past, the wise also tested their virtue, went forth, and established their own refuge." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. When he came of age, he learned all the arts in Takkasilā, came to Bārāṇasī, and saw the King. The King gave the Bodhisatta the position of chaplain. The Bodhisatta observed the five precepts. The King also regarded the Bodhisatta with respect, thinking, "He is a virtuous man."

The Bodhisatta thought, "Does he regard me so because I am endowed with virtue, or because I am possessed of great learning?" All the details are just like the present story.

## The Excellence of Virtue

In this Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka, the Brahmin said, "Now I have known the greatness of virtue over learning," and spoke these five verses:

65. Sīlaṃ seyyo sutaṃ seyyo, iti me saṃsayo ahu.

Great King! To me, is virtue superior? Is learning superior? Thus, I had a doubt. Now, virtue is indeed superior to learning. Thus, I have known. I have no doubt.

## Useless Without Virtue

Great King! Birth and...
181:
Lineage is of no use, and appearance is of no use. Only virtue is said to be supreme. For one who is not endowed with virtue, learning is of no benefit.

An unrighteous Khattiya (king) and an unrighteous Vessa (merchant)—both of them, having left the worlds of humans and devas, are reborn in a state of misery.

## Equal if Virtuous
Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, Suddas, Caṇḍālas, and Pukkusas—having practiced the Dhamma here in this life, they become equal in the celestial realm.

## Only Virtue for the Afterlife
The Vedas do not provide wealth and happiness in the afterlife. Neither lineage nor relatives provide wealth and happiness in the afterlife. Only one's own pure virtue leads to the benefit of happiness in the afterlife.

Thus, the Bodhisatta praised the attributes of virtue, spoke to the king, and having obtained permission to ordain, entered the Himālaya on that very day. He became an ascetic, attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and passed away to the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I was the brahmin who tested virtue and became an ascetic."

## Great Knowledge, but Virtue is Higher
The Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka is finished.

## Words Alone Do Not Make a Friend
One who transgresses shame (hiri) and loathes the state of friendship, who says only in words, "I am your friend," but does not perform noble deeds—know him as "This person is not my friend."

One should speak of what one would do; one should not speak of what one would not do. The wise recognize one who speaks but does not act.
183:
## A True Friend Acts
One who is always diligent and does not allow a friend's ruin, who dreads the breaking of friendship and looks for the cause of its preservation—he is a friend. Just as a child sleeps without fear on its mother's breast, so does a friend sleep without fear with such a person. One who cannot be divided from others by others is truly a friend.

## Four Duties of a Friend
One who sees the benefits and carries the fourfold burden of a man—giving, virtue, meditation, and friendship—cultivates the ground for joy, praise, and happiness.

## Three Tastes of the Deathless
Having drunk the taste of joy arising from physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka), and having drunk the taste of joy obtained through the stilling of defilements, and drinking the taste of liberation called the joy of Dhamma—one becomes free from the distress of defilements and free from evil.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having become weary of associating with bad friends, reached the deathless Nibbāna through the power of seclusion and reached the climax of the teaching.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I was the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī."

## Distinguish Bad and Good Friends, Associate Appropriately
The Hiri Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Ahituṇḍika Jātaka
## About the Snake Charmer who Kept a Monkey

**The Present Story**
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Ahituṇḍika Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Dhutto'mhi", concerning a certain elderly monk.

The story is detailed in the Sālūka Jātaka below. In this Ahituṇḍika Jātaka as well, that elderly monk ordained a certain village boy and then abused and beat him. The novice fled and returned to lay life. For a second time, he had the boy ordained and treated him the same way. After returning to lay life a second time, when he was pleaded with again, he did not even wish to look at the monk.

In the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, this elderly monk named so-and-so can neither live with his novice nor live without him. The novice, having seen his faults, does not even wish to look back at him; the novice is wise."

The Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such-and-such a subject," He said, "Monks, it is not only now that this novice is wise and, having seen faults once, does not wish to look back; he was the same in the past." Then He brought forth the past story.

**The Past Story**
Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of grain merchants and earned his living by selling grain.

## The Snake Charmer's Monkey
At that time, a snake charmer took a monkey, trained it, and made it play with a snake. When a festival was proclaimed in Bārāṇasī, he left the monkey with the grain merchant and went about for seven days making the snake perform. The merchant gave the monkey food and snacks. On the seventh day, the snake charmer returned from the festival, beat the monkey three times with a bamboo split, took him to a park, tied him up, and fell asleep.

## The Monkey Escaped
The monkey untied his bonds, climbed a mango tree, and sat there eating mangoes.

## Flattering to Call Back
The snake charmer woke up, saw the monkey in the tree, and thought, "I should coax this monkey to catch him." Desiring to speak with the monkey, he spoke this first stanza:

75. I am a gambler, friend Handsome-face, defeated at the dice. Bring down some ripe mangoes; let us eat the fruit of your effort.

[Gloss:] Samma Sumukha, friend monkey with a handsome face. Ahaṃ, I. Jūte, in gambling. Dhutto, am a rogue. Amhi, I am. Akkhaparājito, defeated by the dice. Ambapakkāni, the ripe mangoes. Harehi, drop them down. Te, your. Vīriyaṃ, ripe mangoes obtained through effort. Bhakkhayāmase, let us eat.

78. I remember that painful sleep. Even if you were to make me a king, I would not give to you even if asked; for I am terrified by fear.

## Knowing Enemy and Friend

## 6. Gumbiya Jātaka
## About the Ogre who Poisoned Food

**The Present Story**
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Gumbiya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Madhuvaṇṇaṃ madhurasaṃ," concerning a dissatisfied monk.

The Teacher asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher asked, "What did you see that made you dissatisfied?" The monk replied, "Bhante, I saw a decorated woman."

The Teacher said, "Monk, these five sensual pleasures are like the honey-taste mixed with deadly poison placed on the road by an ogre named Gumbiya." Having said this, and being requested by the monk, he brought forth the past story.

**The Past Story**
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of caravan traders. When he came of age, he took five hundred wagons of goods from Bārāṇasī for trade. Upon reaching the entrance of a great forest, he assembled the caravan members and said:

"Friends, on this road there are poisonous leaves, flowers, fruits, and so on. Also, non-humans (ogres) place rice-packets, honey, and fruits mixed with poison on the path. If you wish to eat anything you have not eaten before, do not eat it without asking me."

Having given this advice, he proceeded on the journey.

## Do not eat food recklessly

At that time, an ogre named Gumbiya spread leaves on the path in the middle of the forest and placed honeycombs mixed with deadly poison. He himself wandered nearby, striking trees as if he were collecting honey. Those who did not know, thinking, "These must have been placed for the sake of merit," ate them and met their end. The non-humans would then come and eat the corpses. Some of the Bodhisatta's caravan members, being of a greedy nature, saw the honey and, unable to restrain themselves, ate it. Those of a wise nature, thinking, "We will eat after asking [the leader]," took some and waited.
187:
80. Honey-colored, sweet-tasting, and honey-scented was the poison. Gumbiya, seeking food, placed the poison in the forest.

81. Thinking "It is honey," those who ate that poison experienced its bitterness and met their death.

82. But those who, after reflection, avoided that poison, remained happy among the suffering and were at peace among those being burned.

83. In the same way, among humans, sensual pleasures are like poison that has been prepared. They are a bait and a bond, the guise of Death lurking in the cave.

84. In the same way, those who always avoid these sensual pleasures, which are like a sickness and a servant, cross over the attachment in the world.

Having taught these verses, the Teacher declared the Truths and identified the birth story.

When the Bodhisatta's caravan members saw the honey that had been placed, some of a frivolous nature could not restrain themselves and ate it. The wise ones, thinking, "We will eat after asking the Bodhisatta," took it and stood waiting.

The Bodhisatta, seeing those people, made them discard the honey in their hands. Those who had eaten first died. To those who had eaten only half, he gave emetics, and after they had vomited, he gave them *catumadhura* (the four sweet things). Thus, by the power of the Bodhisatta, they regained their lives. The Bodhisatta safely reached his destination, sold his goods, and returned to his home.

The Teacher, having brought this past story, and having become the Buddha, said:

## Avoid the Poisoned Honey of Sensual Pleasures

*Evameva*: in the same way. *Manussesu*: among humans. *Kāmā samohitā*: the collection of the five sensual pleasures. *Visaṃ*: is called poison. *Etaṃ*: these five sensual pleasures which are poison. *Āmisañca*: are bait. *Bandhanañca*: are bonds. *Guhāsayo*: lurking in the cave of the body.

At the end of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

As for the identification of the birth story: "At that time, I myself was the caravan leader." Thus he identified the birth story.

## The five sensual pleasures are like poisoned honey; they cause death quickly.

## Envy of others brings no benefit to oneself

At that time, a certain poor physician, having found no work in the village, was leaving when he reached that spot. He saw a snake sleeping with its head protruding from a fork in the tree. He thought, "I have found nothing in any village. I will trick these boys, have them bitten by the snake, then treat them and get something."

## 8. Tacasāra Jātaka

## One should not worry even when facing death

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, who is the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana monastery, spoke this Tacasāra Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Amittahatthathagatā," concerning the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now is the Tathāgata wise and skillful in means; in the past also he was wise and skillful in means," and he brought the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy family in a small village. All the details should be understood as in the previous Sāḷiya Jātaka.

In this Tacasāra Jātaka, when the doctor died, the villagers bound the children with bamboo strips as "murderers" and took them to Bārāṇasī to show the King.

On the way, the Bodhisatta gave advice to the other children: "Do not be afraid. Even when you see the King, be unafraid and have pleasant faculties. The King will speak to you first. From then on, I will speak." They agreed and did as the Bodhisatta said.

## Why are they not afraid?

The King, seeing the children unafraid and with pleasant faculties, thought: "These children are bound with loathsome bamboo strips and brought here, yet even in such suffering they are not afraid and remain pleasant. What is the reason for their lack of sorrow?" Wishing to ask them, he spoke the first verse:

90. Having fallen into the hands of enemies, bound with bamboo strips, your faces are bright and clear. Why do you not grieve?

Children, though you have fallen into the hands of enemies and are bound with bamboo strips, you have clear complexions. Why do you not worry?
191:
## Sorrow and lamentation bring only suffering

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta spoke these verses:

91. By sorrowing and lamenting, not even a little benefit is gained. Seeing him sorrowing and suffering, enemies become delighted.

92. When dangers arise, the wise man who knows how to determine what is beneficial does not tremble. Seeing his face unchanged as before, his enemies become distressed.

93. By incantations, by consultation, by well-spoken words, by giving gifts, or by lineage—wherever and however one might gain a benefit, there and in that way one should strive.

94. When one knows that this benefit is unattainable by oneself or another, one should endure without sorrowing, thinking, "It is firm karma; what can I do now?"

Great King, by sorrowing and lamenting, not even a small benefit is obtained. Seeing one sorrowing and suffering, enemies become joyful.

When dangers arise, the wise man who knows how to determine the benefit does not tremble. Seeing his face unchanged, those enemies become distressed.

## Five Ways to Resolve Problems

By incantations (manta), by consulting with the wise, by pleasant speech, by giving bribes to the ministers of justice, or by mentioning one's lineage, enemies should be overcome. Among these five means, by whichever means and in whichever matter a benefit may be gained, one should exert effort in that way and in that matter.

## Attaining Office
The King, having heard the Bodhisatta's Dhamma discourse, investigated the case and, realizing his innocence, ordered the removal of the punishments. He bestowed great wealth upon the Great Being and appointed him as a precious minister, an advisor on worldly and spiritual matters. He also gave wealth and various positions to the other boys.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda. The boys were the elder and junior monks. I myself was the wise boy."

## 10. Palāsa Jātaka

## Encountering Danger by Not Fearing What Should Be Feared
The Present Story: While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Palāsa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Haṃso palāsamavaca," concerning the suppression of defilements.

The story will become clear in the Paññāsa Jātaka. In this Palāsa Jātaka, the Teacher addressed the monks: "Monks, even a small defilement should be feared. Defilement, like a banyan tree, leads to destruction. The wise of old also feared what should be feared." Having said this, he brought the past story.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a golden goose. Living in a golden cave on Mount Cittakūṭa, he would go to eat self-sown rice in the Jātassara Lake in the Himālaya region.

On the Bodhisatta's path of travel, there was a large Palāsa tree. He would rest there while going and also while returning. At that time, the Bodhisatta became well-acquainted with the tree-deity residing in that Palāsa tree.

## 3. Aḍḍha Vagga

## 1. Dīghītikosala Jātaka

## On the Necessity of Listening to Parents' Words

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Dīghītikosala Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Evaṃbhūtassa te rāja," while staying at Jetavana Monastery, concerning the quarreling monks of Kosambī.

When those Kosambī monks came to Jetavana and paid their respects, the All-Knowing Buddha called them and said, "Monks, you are my heart-born sons, born from my mouth. It is not proper for those called sons to break the advice given by their father. But you have not followed my advice.

Wise men of old, even when the enemies who had killed their parents and seized their kingdom fell into their hands in the forest, they thought, 'It is not proper to break the advice given by our parents; we shall not break the advice,' and they did not kill them." Having said this, he related the past story.

In this Jātaka, both the present and past stories will be clearly explained in detail in the Saṅghabhedaka Khandhaka.

## How the Parents' Words Were Followed

That Prince Dīghāvu, holding the topknot of the King of Bārāṇasī who was sleeping on his lap in the forest, thought, "Now, holding the topknot of the enemy who killed my parents, I shall cut him into pieces." ## 3. Mūsika Jātaka

## Escaping death by listening to the teacher's words

The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Mūsika Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kuhiṃ gatā kattha gatā," concerning Ajātasattu.
202:
The story is expanded in the Thusa Jātaka below. In this Mūsika Jātaka as well, the All-Knowing Buddha, seeing King Bimbisāra at one time playing with his son and at another time listening to the Dhamma, realized that danger would arise for King Bimbisāra because of his son. He said, "Great King, ancient kings, suspecting what was to be suspected, used to place their sons in a suitable location, saying, 'Let him rule the kingdom after my death,'" and he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the city of Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha). A prince of the King of Bārāṇasī named Yava studied all the arts under the Bodhisatta. Having completed his studies, he wished to depart and took leave of his teacher.

The teacher, knowing through the power of the science of body signs (Angavijjā) that danger would arise for Prince Yava because of his son, strove to find a simile to avert that danger for the prince.

## The First Verse to Save Life

At that time, the Bodhisatta had a horse. A wound had formed on the horse's leg. To care for the wound, they kept the horse inside the house. Then, a mouse came out of the house and nibbled at the wound on the horse's leg. The horse was unable to endure it.

One day, unable to bear the pain, the horse kicked the mouse as it came to nibble, causing it to fall into a well and die. When the grooms did not see the mouse, they said, "On other days, the mouse would come and nibble the wound. Now it is not seen; where has it gone?"

The Bodhisatta, witnessing this event, thought, "Others do not know and ask, 'Where has the mouse gone?' I alone know that the mouse was killed and thrown into the well." Using this very incident as a simile, he composed the first verse and gave it to the prince.

The attendants said, "Prince, it is not possible to go to the border and act as a rebel. Kill your father by some means and take the kingship."

The prince agreed, saying, "Very well." In the evening, he went near the king's bathing pool within the palace grounds and stood holding a sword (khagga), intending to kill the king there.

## 4. Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka

## Concerning the Handing of the Sword-Hilt to the Thief

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ," concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

When that monk reported, "Venerable Sir, my former wife causes me to be dissatisfied with the holy life," the All-Knowing Buddha said, "Monk, this woman is one who habitually works for your disadvantage. In the past, too, you died because of her; your head was cut off with a sword." Having said this, and being requested by the monk, He brought forth the past.
206:
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. At that time, a certain Brahmin youth living in Benares learned all the arts in Takkasilā and reached perfection in the art of archery. He became known as "Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise."

## The Teacher Gives His Daughter

Then the teacher, saying, "This man has learned the art as well as I," gave him his daughter. Cūḷadhanuggaha took the young woman and set out on the journey, saying, "I will go to Benares."

## Handing the Sword-Hilt to the Thief

On the way, an elephant had made a certain area desolate. No one dared to go to that place. Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise, even while people were watching and warning him, took his wife and entered the forest.

Then, in the middle of the forest, the elephant charged at Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise. Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise shot the elephant in the frontal globes with an arrow. The arrow pierced through and came out the back. The elephant fell right there.

Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise made that place safe and reached another forest ahead. In that forest, fifty robbers were plundering travelers on the road. Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise, though warned by people, entered that forest as well and reached the place where the robbers were staying, having killed animals and roasting the meat to eat near the road.

The robbers, seeing Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise coming with his well-adorned wife, made an effort, saying, "Let us capture him." The robber leader was skilled in the marks of a great man. Looking at Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise, he knew, "This is an excellent man," and did not allow even a single person to rise against him.

Cūḷadhanuggaha the Wise sent his wife to the robbers, saying, "Go and say, 'Give us a spit of meat,' and bring the meat." She went and said, "They say, give them a spit of meat." The robber leader, thinking he was a priceless man, had a spit of meat given. The robbers, saying, "The cooked meat was eaten by us," gave a spit of raw meat. Cūḷadhanuggaha, thinking highly of himself, became angry at the robbers for giving him raw meat. The robbers also became angry, saying, "Is he the only man? Are we women?" and rose up. Cūḷadhanuggaha shot forty-nine men with forty-nine arrows and brought them down. There was no arrow left to shoot the robber leader. It is said that in his quiver there were exactly fifty arrows. Among them, he shot the elephant with one, and with forty-nine arrows he shot the robbers. Having brought down the robber leader, he sat on his chest and had his wife bring the sword from her hand, saying, "I will cut off his head." At that very moment, she felt lust for the robber leader and placed the hilt in the hand of the robber, and in the hand of her husband...
207:
19. "Taking all the goods, you have crossed to the other shore, O Brahmin.
Come back quickly, and take me across from here now."

She spoke this first verse.
Brahmin, O Brahmin. Tvaṃ, you. Sabbaṃ, all. Bhaṇḍaṃ, goods. Samādāya, taking. Pāraṃ, to the other shore. Tiṇṇo, have crossed. Asi, you are. Lahuṃ, quickly. Paccāgaccha, come back. Idāni, now. Ito, from here. Khippaṃ, quickly. Mampi, me also. Tārehi, take across.

The robbers said, "We shall eat cooked meat," and gave him a spit of uncooked meat. The wise Cūḷadhanuggaha praised himself and was angry with the robbers, saying, "They give me a spit of uncooked meat."

The robbers threatened him and rose up, saying, "This man is but one, what can he do? We are not women." The wise Cūḷadhanuggaha shot forty-nine arrows and laid them low. He had no arrow left to shoot the chief robber.

In the quiver of the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha, there were only fifty arrows. Among those arrows, he shot an elephant with one. With the remaining arrows, he shot forty-nine robbers. Having laid the chief robber low, he climbed onto the robber's chest and asked his wife to give him the sword to cut off the robber's head.

The wife, becoming infatuated with the chief robber she saw at that moment, placed the hilt in the robber's hand and the blade in her husband's hand. The robber, grasping the hilt of the sword, drew it out and cut off the head of the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha.

## The Sorrow of the Husband-Deserter

When the chief robber had killed the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha and taken the woman, he asked about her lineage. The woman said, "I am the daughter of a world-renowned teacher in the city of Takkasilā." He asked, "By what means did this man obtain you?" She replied, "My father was pleased, thinking, 'This man learns the arts just like me,' and gave me to him. Because I loved you, I caused the husband given to me by my family to be killed."

The chief robber thought, "This woman killed even the husband given by her father; if she sees another man, she will do the same to me. It is proper to abandon her." As he went along, he saw a shallow river filled with water that had just arrived, and said, "Lady, in this river, the crocodiles are fierce and cruel. What shall we do?"

The woman said, "Lord, wrap all the jewelry and goods in my upper robe, take them to the other shore, and then come back to take me and go."

The chief robber agreed, took all the jewelry and goods, entered the river, and as if crossing, reached the other shore, abandoned the woman, and went on. Seeing him, she spoke with the chief robber, saying, "Lord, why do you go as if abandoning me? Why do you do this? Come, take me also and go."

The robber, hearing those words and standing on the other shore, spoke this second verse:

20. "You exchanged a long-standing acquaintance for me, an unknown, O lady;
The stable for the unstable.
