You might exchange me for another too;
I will go far away from here."

Bhotī, O lady. Tvaṃ, you. Cīrasanthutena, for the husband of long acquaintance. Asanthutaṃ, me, the unacquainted one. Nimīni, you have exchanged. Dhuvena, for the stable husband. Addhuvaṃ, me, the unstable one. Nimīni, you have exchanged. Bhotī, O lady. Tvaṃ, you. Mayāpi, even for me. Aññaṃ, another husband. Nimineyya, might exchange. Ahaṃ, I. Ito, from here. Dūrataraṃ, to a very distant place. Gamissaṃ, shall flee.

The chief robber said, "You stay here," and while the woman was weeping, he took the bundle of goods he was carrying and fled.
208:
21. "Who is this making a great laugh in the clump of Eḷagala grass?
There is no dancing or singing here, nor well-timed clapping.
Why do you laugh, O fair-waisted one, in a time for weeping?"

He spoke this third verse.
Eḷagala-gumbe, in the clump of Eḷagala grass. Ayaṃ, this woman. Ahu-hāsiaṃ, a great laugh. Karoti, makes. Kā, who is this woman? Idha, here. Nacca-gītaṃ vā, dancing and singing. Susamāhitaṃ, well-performed. Tāḷaṃ vā, music or clapping. Na, there is not. Susoṇi, O one with a beautiful waist. Sobhane, O beautiful lady. Tvaṃ, you. Anamhī-kāle, in a time when one should weep. Kinnu, why. Jagghasi, do you laugh so loudly?

## Dropping the Roasted Fish upon Seeing the Fresh Fish

That foolish woman, due to her excessive greed, reached such a state of ruin and, being helpless, approached a clump of Eḷagala grass nearby and sat weeping.

At that moment, Sakka, the King of Devas, looking down upon the world of men, saw the woman who had lost both her husband and her lover due to her excessive greed and was weeping. Thinking, "I will rebuke her, make her ashamed, and then return," he took the young devas Mātali and Pañcasikha, went to that place, and stood by the riverbank.

He commanded, "Mātali, you become a fish. Pañcasikha, you become a bird. I will become a fox and, carrying a piece of meat in my mouth, will go before that woman. When I reach there, you, Mātali, jump out of the water and fall in front of me. Then I will drop the piece of meat I am carrying in my mouth and run to catch the fish. At that moment, you, Pañcasikha, pick up that piece of meat and fly into the sky. You, Mātali, fall back into the water."

Saying, "Very well, O King," Mātali transformed into a fish. Pañcasikha transformed into a bird. Sakka transformed into a fox and, carrying a piece of meat in his mouth, came before the woman. The fish jumped out of the water and fell in front of the fox. The fox dropped the piece of meat from his mouth and ran to catch the fish. The fish jumped and fell back into the water. The bird picked up the piece of meat and flew into the sky.
209:
22. "O jackal, fool, ignorant one, you are of little wisdom, Jambuka. Having lost both the fish and the piece of meat, you brood like a wretched man who has lost a thousand pieces of gold."

This is the fourth verse she spoke.

*Bāla*: fool. *Dummedha*: ignorant. *Jambuka*: greedy one. *Singāla*: jackal. *Tvaṃ*: you. *Appapañño*: are of little wisdom. *Asi*: are. *Macchañca*: both the fish. *Pesiñca*: and the meat. *Jīno*: having lost. *Kapaṇo viya*: like a wretched man who has lost a thousand pieces of gold. *Jhāyasi*: you brood.

23. "The faults of others are easily seen, but one's own are hard to see. Having lost both your husband and your lover, I think you are the one who should brood more than I."

This is the fifth verse he spoke.

*Pāpadhamme*: O woman of evil conduct. *Dussīle*: O immoral woman. *Aññesaṃ*: of others. *Vajjaṃ*: the fault. *Sudassaṃ*: is easy to see. *Attano vajjaṃ pana*: but one's own fault. *Duddasaṃ*: is hard to see. *Tvaññeva*: you alone. *Patiñca*: both the husband given by your parents. *Jārañca*: and the paramour. *Jīna*: having lost. *Jhāyasi maññe*: I think you brood more than I.

The jackal, having obtained neither the fish nor the piece of meat, sat looking at the clump of kusa grass with a dejected face.

## From Crying to Laughing

Seeing that jackal, she laughed loudly, like a pot breaking, saying, "This jackal, oppressed by great greed, has obtained neither the meat nor the fish."

## Hey, Who is Laughing?

Hearing that laughter, the jackal said—

## How Foolish!

Hearing those words, the woman said—

## You are More Foolish

Then the jackal said—

## I Regret It Now

Hearing the jackal's words, the woman spoke this sixth verse:

24. "It is just as you say, O king of beasts, Jambuka. I shall go from here and surely become an obedient wife to my husband once more."

*Migarāja*: O king of beasts. *Jambuka*: O jackal. *Tvaṃ*: you. *Yathā bhāsasi*: as you say. *Evameva*: it is exactly so. *Ahaṃ*: I. *Ito*: from here. *Gantvā*: having gone. *Puna*: again. *Yaṃ bhattāraṃ*: whatever husband. *Labhitvā*: I obtain. *Nūna-ekanteneva*: most certainly. *Tassa bhattū*: of that husband. *Vasānugā*: obedient to his will. *Hessaṃ*: I shall be.

## Once a Fence-Jumper, Always a Fence-Jumper

Then, hearing the words of that immoral woman, Sakka, King of Gods, spoke this final verse:

25. "He who would steal a clay bowl would also steal a bronze bowl. You have already committed this sin, and you will surely do so again."

*Anācare*: O woman of immoral conduct. *Tvaṃ*: you. *Kiṃ kathesi*: what are you saying? *Yo*: he who. *Mattikaṃ thālaṃ*: a clay bowl. *Hare*: steals. *So*: he. *Kaṃsathālampi*: even a bowl made of bronze, gold, or silver. *Hare*: would certainly steal. *Tayā*: by you. *Idaṃ pāpaṃ*: this evil. *Katañceva*: has already been done. *Punapi*: again. *Tvaṃ*: you. *Evaṃ*: in this way. *Karissasi*: will do it again."
210:
In this way, Sakka shamed that woman, caused her to fall into a state of misery, and then returned to his own place.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). How did he identify the Jātaka? — "The discontented monk of today was then the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha. The former wife of the discontented monk was then the wife of Cūḷadhanuggaha. I myself was then Sakka, King of Gods."

## Discarding the Stream to Seek the River, Finding Only Water and No Fish

The Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka is concluded.

## 5. Kapota Jātaka

## Ruined by Fickleness

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Kapota Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Idāni khomhi," concerning a certain greedy monk.

The story of the greedy monk has been explained in detail elsewhere. The Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are greedy?" When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, you are not greedy only now; in the past also you were greedy, and because of your greed, you met your end," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a pigeon and lived in a nesting basket in the kitchen of a merchant in Bārāṇasī.
211:
26. Now I am happy and free from illness, the pigeon, who was like a thorn to me, has departed. Now I will satisfy my heart's desire.

27. Who is this crested crane, this thief who has stolen the nest? Come closer, O crane; my friend the crow is fierce.

This is the second verse he spoke.

Sikhinī: having a crest. Corī: one who steals the nesting place. Laṅghipitāmahā: having the value of rain (as an ancestor). Ayaṃ balākā: this female crane. Kā: which female crane? Balāke: O female crane. Oraṃ: into this place. Āgaccha: come. Me: my. Sakhā: friend. Vāyaso: the crow. Caṇḍo: is fierce.

## The Misery of the Foolish Crow who Stole Curry

At that time, a certain crow became attached to fish and meat, befriended that pigeon, and lived in that very nesting basket. One day, seeing a large amount of fish and meat, the crow thought, "I shall eat that fish and meat," and moaning greatly, he lay in the nesting basket.

Although the pigeon said, "Friend crow, come, let us go to seek food," the crow replied, "I am lying down because of indigestion; you go alone." Thus, he did not go to seek food. When the pigeon had gone, he thought, "My enemy, who was like a thorn, has gone; now I shall eat the fish and meat as I desire," and he spoke this first verse:

"Tathāhi maṃ maṃsasākaṃ baleti."

(Meaning:) I am now indeed happy. I am free from illness. I am free from thorns. The pigeon has departed. Now I will perform that which pleases my heart. Therefore, the meat and the curry remaining from the meat give me strength and effort.

The cook, having cooked the fish and meat, came out of the kitchen and stood wiping the sweat from his body. The crow came out of the basket, ate the meat until his belly was full, and then perched on the basket where the meat was kept, making the sound "Kiri, kiri."

The cook came quickly, caught the crow, plucked out all its feathers, and having ground fresh ginger and mustard seeds, mixed them with sour buttermilk and smeared it over the crow's entire body. Then, he ground a potsherd, pierced it, tied it around the crow's neck with a string, placed him back in the nesting basket, and left.

## The Pigeon's Mockery

The pigeon returned and, seeing the crow, wished to mock him, saying: "A crane is lying in my friend crow's basket. What crane is this? My friend the crow is fierce; if he comes, he might even kill you."

## Do Not Mock Me, Dear Pigeon

Hearing those words, the crow spoke this third verse:

28. It is not fit for you to laugh, seeing me in such a state, plucked by the cook's son and smeared with the dregs of flour and buttermilk.

Samma: friend. Sūdaputtena: by the cook. Vilūnaṃ: having the feathers plucked. Piṭṭhamaṇḍena: with the clear liquid of buttermilk mixed with ginger and mustard powder. Makkhitaṃ: smeared. Edisaṃ: having such a nature of suffering. Mamaṃ: me. Disvāna: having seen. Te: for you. Jagghitāye: to mock. Alaṃ hi: it is truly not fit.
212:
The pigeon, still wishing to mock him, spoke the fourth verse:

29. You are well-bathed and well-anointed, satiated with food and drink. And on your neck, you wear a beryl; did you go to Kajangala?

Samma: friend. Tvaṃ: you. Sunhāto: are well-cleansed. Suvilitto: are well-anointed. Annapānena: with food and drink. Tappito: are satiated. Asi: you are. Te kaṇṭhe ca: and on your neck. Veḷuriyo: a beryl gem is adorned. Tvaṃ: you. Kajangalaṃ: into the city of Bārāṇasī. Agamā nu: did you go?

30. May neither friend nor foe of yours go to Kajangala. There they pluck the feathers and bind a potsherd to the neck.

Pārāvata: O pigeon. Te: your. Mitto vā: whether a friend. Amitto vā: or a bird who is not a friend. Kajangalaṃ: to the city of Bārāṇasī. Mā agamāsi: let them not go. Tattha: in that city of Bārāṇasī. Piñchāni: the feathers. Lāyitvā: having plucked. Kaṇṭhe: to the neck. Vaṭṭanaṃ: a potsherd. Bandhanti: they are known to bind.

31. You will fall into such misery again, friend, for such is your character. Human enjoyments are not easily enjoyed by birds.

Samma: friend. Tvaṃ: you. Punapi: again. Evarūpaṃ: such a state of suffering. Āpajjasi: will reach. Hi saccaṃ: it is true. Tava: your. Sīlaṃ: habit/character. Tādisaṃ: is of such a kind. Manusakā bhogā: human possessions and enjoyments. Pakkhinā: by a bird. Subhuñjā: easily enjoyed. Na honti: are truly not.

## You are all dressed up

The pigeon, wishing to mock him again—

## I am in trouble

Then the crow—

## Still wanting to eat the best

Hearing those words, the pigeon—

Thus the Bodhisatta, having admonished the crow, did not remain in that house, but spreading his wings, he flew away to another place. The crow also reached the end of his life in that very house.

As for the connection of the Jātaka: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the fruit of Anāgāmi. As for how the Jātaka was identified: "The greedy monk of that time was the crow of then, and I, the Buddha, was the pigeon of then."
213:
## Desiring what is unsuitable, the foolish crow has died

Here ends the Kapota Jātaka.

Summary of the Jātakas:
Maṇikuṇḍala, Sujātā, Veṇasākha, Uraga,
Ghaṭa, Koraṇḍi, Laṭukika, Dhammapāla, and Miga.
Suyonandī, Vaṇṇāroha, Sīla, Hirī, Khajjopana,
Ahi-gumbiya, Sāḷiya, Tacasāra, Mittavinda,
Palāsa, Dīghīti, Migapotaka, Mūsika,
Dhanuggaha, and Kapota—these are the twenty-five Jātakas.

The commentary on the Pañcakanipāta is finished.
214:
## 1. Avāriya Vagga
## 1. Avāriya Jātaka
## The Reason for Not Knowing the Noble and the Base

The Present Story: While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, who teaches the world including the devas, told this Avāriya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Māsu kujjha bhūmipati," concerning a certain ferryman at a landing place.

That ferryman was said to be foolish. He did not know the virtues of the Triple Gem, such as the Buddha, nor did he know the virtues of other persons. He was fierce, harsh, and violent.

## The Harassment of the Monk

At that time, a certain monk living in the countryside, thinking, "I will pay homage to the Buddha," arrived at the landing of the Aciravatī River in the evening and said to the ferryman, "Lay follower, I wish to go to the other side; please give me a boat." The ferryman replied, "Venerable sir, it is not the right time now; stay in a certain place for a while." The monk said, "Lay follower, where shall I stay here? Please take me across."

The ferryman became angry and said, "Come, monk!" He took the elder onto the boat, but instead of going straight, he steered the boat downstream, caused waves to rock the boat, soaked the monk's bowl and robes, exhausted him, and finally let him off in the dark.

Then the monk went to the monastery, but having no opportunity to attend upon the Buddha that day, he approached the Teacher the next day, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Buddha, having exchanged friendly greetings, asked, "When did you arrive?" The monk replied, "I arrived yesterday, Bhante."

"If you arrived yesterday, why have you come to see me only today?" the Buddha asked. The monk then related the incident.

Hearing this, the Buddha said, "Monk, not only now is this ferryman fierce, harsh, and violent; in the past also, he caused suffering to the wise." Having said this, at the monk's request, he brought forth the past.
215:
1. Māsu kujjha bhūmipati, māsu kujjha rathesabha.
Kuddhaṃ appaṭikujjhanto, rājā raṭṭhassa pūjito.
2. Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale.
Sabbattha anusāsāmi, māsu kujjha rathesabha.

He preached these two verses:

Bhūmipati, O Great King who rules the earth, do not be angry. Rathesabha, O Great King, noble among those who ride chariots, do not be angry. The king who does not return anger to one who is angry is honored by the people of the country.

Rathesabha, O Great King, noble among those who ride chariots, whether in the village or in the forest, whether in the lowlands or on the uplands, in all places, I advise you: do not be angry. Thus I instruct you.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he studied all the arts at Takkasilā, became an ascetic, and for a long time lived on wild fruits in the Himālaya. To seek salt and vinegar, he reached Bārāṇasī, stayed in the royal park, and entered the city for alms the next day.

## The Ascetic Revered by the King

At that time, the king saw the ascetic who had arrived at the palace courtyard and, being pleased with his deportment, invited him into the palace, fed him, received his consent to stay, and had him reside in the royal park, visiting him once a day to pay respects.

The Bodhisatta ascetic said to the king, "Great King, one called a king should avoid the four wrong paths (agati) and, being diligent, should rule with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion." Wishing to advise him daily:

In this way, the Bodhisatta spoke these verses to the king every day he came. The king, with a devoted heart, offered the Bodhisatta a choice village yielding a revenue of one hundred thousand. The Bodhisatta refused it.

## The Foolish Ferryman

Thus the Bodhisatta lived in that very park for twelve years. Thinking, "I have lived here for a very long time; I will first wander through the countryside and then return," he did not tell the king but called the gardener and said, "Lay follower, I feel weary. I will wander through the countryside and then return; you go and tell the king." After departing, he reached a ferry landing on the Ganges.

At that ferry landing, there was a ferryman named Avāriyapitā. That ferryman was foolish. He did not know the virtues of those possessed of virtue, nor did he know his own advantage or disadvantage. He used to ferry people who wanted to cross the Ganges first and then ask for the fare. He would quarrel with those who did not pay, and he mostly received only abuse and blows. His profit was small.
216:
3. There was a ferryman on the Gaṅgā named Avāriyapitā.
Having first ferried people across, he later asks for the fare.
Because of that, he has quarrels and does not prosper in wealth.

He [the Buddha] spoke this third verse.
On the Gaṅgā, there was a ferryman. He was known as Avāriyapitā, the father of Avāriya. That ferryman, having first ferried the multitude of people who use the ferry, asks for the fare afterwards. Therefore, quarrels arise for him. He does not prosper with wealth at all.

4. Ask while they are still uncrossed, O dear ferryman.
For the mind of one who has crossed is one thing,
And the mind of one seeking the other shore is another.

He spoke this verse.
O dear ferryman, ask for the fare while people are still on the near shore, before they have crossed to the other side. Having received and kept the fare in a secure place, you should ferry the people to the other side afterwards. In this way, your wealth will increase. Indeed, O dear ferryman, the mind of one who has reached the other shore is different; he desires to leave without paying. However, the mind of one who is a shore-seeker, desiring to reach the other side, is different; he is willing to pay even extra to go. Therefore, you should ask while they are still uncrossed. This is the increase of your wealth.

Having heard this, the ferryman thought, "This is just his advice; now he will surely give me something else." Then the Bodhisatta, saying, "This, friend, is the increase of your wealth; now listen to the increase of your welfare and Dhamma," and desiring to advise him, said:

## Asking for the Fare After Crossing
The Bodhisatta approached that ferryman and said, "Friend, take me to the other side." Hearing this, the ferryman said, "Monk, will you give me the boat fare?" "Friend, I will tell you what is called the increase of wealth, the increase of welfare, and the increase of Dhamma," he replied. Hearing this, the ferryman thought, "This monk will certainly give me something," and he carried the hermit to the other side and said, "Give me the boat fare."

## Teaching for the Increase of Wealth
The hermit said, "Friend, very well," and first desiring to speak the words that are the cause for the increase of wealth:

## Social Conduct
Hearing these words, the ferryman thought, "This hermit has first given me an advice; now he will give me something other than this advice." Then the Bodhisatta said to the ferryman, "Friend, these words which are the cause for the increase of wealth have been spoken to you; now listen to the words which are the cause for the increase of welfare and Dhamma," and desiring to advise him:

## Striking the Monk
Having thus spoken to the ferryman with this verse the words that cause the increase of welfare and Dhamma, he said, "These words spoken to you are the words that cause welfare and Dhamma to increase."
217:
5. Whether in a village or in the forest,
In the lowlands or on the highlands,
I instruct you everywhere: do not be angry, O ferryman.

He spoke this verse.
O ferryman, whether in a village, or in a town, or in the forest, or in a low-lying place, or in a town, or on the highlands, I instruct you: do not be angry in any place.

That wicked man, not considering that advice as something to be respected, said, "Monk, is this the boat fare you give me?" When the hermit replied, "Yes, friend," he said, "I have no need for these words; give me something else."

"Friend, I have nothing else," the hermit said. "If you have nothing, why did you ride the boat?" he said, and making the hermit fall by the bank of the Gaṅgā, he sat on his chest and struck the hermit's face.

## Not Everyone Should Be Instructed
The Omniscient Buddha said, "Monks, in this way, by giving that advice, the hermit received a choice village from the king. By speaking that very same advice to the extremely foolish ferryman, he received a striking on the face. Therefore, one who gives advice should give it only to a suitable person, and not to an unsuitable person." Having said this, and having become fully enlightened, he spoke the following verse:

6. By the same instruction the king gave a choice village;
By that very same instruction the ferryman struck the face.

By the very instruction through which the king gave a choice village, by that same instruction, the ferryman struck the face.

## Receiving the King's Punishment
While the ferryman was striking the hermit, the ferryman's wife arrived bringing food. Seeing that wicked man, she said, "Lord, this hermit is the king's teacher; do not strike him." The ferryman, becoming angry again, said, "You do not allow me to strike this rogue hermit," and getting up, he struck that woman and made her fall.

At that time, the food pot fell and broke. Because the woman was heavily pregnant, the fetus fell upon the ground. Then, people surrounded that man and, saying, "He is a murderer and a thief," they seized and bound him and showed him to the king. The king passed judgment and inflicted the king's punishment upon that ferryman.

The Omniscient Buddha, desiring to reveal that matter after becoming fully enlightened, spoke the concluding verse:

7. The food is broken, the wife is struck,
And the fetus has fallen on the ground.
Like a deer [deceived] by gold,
He did not secure any benefit.
218:
He spoke this verse ending with:

“The rice bowl is broken; the wife is beaten; and the fetus has fallen to the ground. Just as a deer is unable to produce its own benefit with gold and silver, so that fool was unable to produce his own benefit through that advice.”

Conclusion of the Jātaka: The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the revelation of the Truths, the monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the Jātaka? “The ferryman of that time was the same ferryman now. Ānanda was the king then. I myself was the ascetic then,” thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Wicked and Vile, Though Admonished, One Suffers Loss

The Avāriya Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Setaketu Jātaka

## Creating Wonders through False Practice

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Setaketu Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Mā tāta kujjhi, na hi sādhu kodho,” concerning a monk who was a hypocrite.

(The present story will be made clear in the Uddāla Jātaka.)

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Bārāṇasī and taught the Vedas to five hundred young students.

## The Proud Young Man

The eldest of those students, a young man named Setaketu, was born into a high-class (Udicca) Brahmin family and was very proud of his birth. One day, while leaving the city with other students, he saw a Caṇḍāla entering the city and asked, “Who are you?” When the man replied, “I am a Caṇḍāla,” Setaketu, fearing that the wind blowing from the Caṇḍāla's body might touch his own, said, “Be gone, you wretched Caṇḍāla! Do not stay upwind!” and quickly moved to the windward side. The Caṇḍāla moved even faster and stood upwind of Setaketu. Then Setaketu reviled him harshly, saying, “Perish, you outcaste!”

## Fallen Under the Caṇḍāla

The Caṇḍāla asked, “What is your name?”
219:
8. Do not be angry, dear one, for anger is not good;
much is unseen and unheard by you.
Mother and father are called the quarters, Setaketu;
teachers are praised as the quarters by the wise.

9. Householders who give food, drink, and clothing,
and who invite [the virtuous], they too are called a quarter.
This is the supreme quarter, Setaketu,
reaching which the suffering become happy.

He spoke these two verses.

Dear Setaketu, do not be angry. Anger is indeed not good. There is much that you have not seen and much that you have not heard. Parents are called the Eastern quarter. The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Ones (Ariyas) say that the teacher is the Southern quarter.

Householders who give food, drink, and clothing invite righteous recluses and brahmins. They call those righteous recluses and brahmins the Upper quarter. Setaketu, reaching which Nibbāna the suffering become happy, that state of Nibbāna alone is the supreme quarter.

“I am a young Brahmin,” he said. “Be you a Brahmin, can you answer the question I ask?” the Caṇḍāla asked. “I can,” he replied. “If you cannot answer, I will make you pass between my legs,” said the Caṇḍāla. Setaketu, thinking of his own ability, said, “Do so.”

The Caṇḍāla son, making the crowd witness Setaketu's words, asked, “Young Brahmin, what is a quarter (disā)?” “Quarters are the four directions, starting with the East,” he replied. The Caṇḍāla son said, “I am not asking about those quarters. You do not even know this much, yet you loathe the wind that touches my body.” He then grabbed the young Brahmin by the neck and made him pass between his legs.

The students reported this to the teacher. The teacher asked, “Dear Setaketu, is it true that the Caṇḍāla son made you pass between his legs?” “Teacher, it is true. That Caṇḍāla son made me pass between his legs, saying I do not even know the quarters. I will see what I must do now,” he said, and in anger, he reviled the Caṇḍāla son.
220:
## The Quarters

Then the teacher, wishing to admonish Setaketu, said, “Dear Setaketu, do not be angry with that Caṇḍāla son. He is wise. He did not ask about the quarters like the East and so on; he asked about a different kind of quarter. There is much more that is unseen and unheard than what you have seen, heard, and known.”

## Setaketu Becomes an Ascetic

Thus the Bodhisatta spoke to the young man Setaketu about the quarters. Setaketu, however, because he had been made to pass between the legs of a Caṇḍāla, would not stay in that place. He went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts from a world-renowned teacher, and having received permission from the teacher, left Takkasilā and wandered about learning all the arts.
221:
10. With rough skins, matted hair, and dirty teeth,
With a squalid appearance, these who mutter mantras.
Abiding in the practices performed by humans,
Do they, knowing this [world], escape from states of misery?

He spoke this stanza which completes the three.

*Brāhmaṇa*, O Brahmin. *Kharājinā*, those who wear rough antelope skins with hooves. *Jaṭilā*, those with matted hair. *Paṅkadantā*, those with teeth covered in grime. *Dummakkharūpā*, those with a squalid appearance. *Ye ime*, these [ascetics] who *jappanti*, recite *mante*, the Vedas. *Ṭhitā*, abiding *payoge*, in the practices *mānusake*, performed by humans. *Kacci nu*, do *ete isayo*, these ascetics, *vidū*, knowing *idaṃ*, this world, *parimuttā*, escape *apāyā*, from states of misery?

That Setaketu, seeing five hundred ascetics living near a border village, went forth as an ascetic in their presence. He learned the Vedas and the texts of mantras which those ascetics did not know. He became the leader of the group and, surrounded by those ascetics, arrived at Bārāṇasī. On the following day, while wandering for alms, he reached the palace courtyard.

## Practices of the Ascetics
The King, being impressed by the deportment of the ascetics, offered them food in the palace and had them stay in his park. One day, after serving the ascetics with food, the King said, "I will come to the park this evening to pay homage to the venerable ones."

The ascetic Setaketu went to the park, assembled the ascetics, and said, "Friends, the King will come today. If one can please a King once, one can live happily for the rest of one's life. Today, let some of you practice the austerity of sleeping on a bed of thorns; let some practice the effort of squatting; let some perform the act of entering the water; let some recite the Vedas." Having arranged this, he himself sat on a chair with a backrest at the door of the dwelling. He placed a manuscript, one cubit in length and bright with five colors, on a colorful stand, and explained the meanings asked by four well-trained youths.

## The King is Displeased
At that moment, the King arrived and, being displeased with those ascetics who were practicing false austerities, approached the ascetic Setaketu, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Desiring to converse with the Chaplain, he spoke [the verse]:
222:
11. "O King, if a learned man commits evil deeds and does not practice the Dhamma, even if he knows a thousand Vedas, he will not be released from suffering, for he has not attained virtuous conduct (caraṇa)."

He spoke this fourth verse.

O King. Having committed evil deeds. Even a person of great learning. If he does not practice the Dhamma. Depending on those Vedas. Without reaching virtuous conduct and meditative attainment. Even one who knows a thousand Vedas. From suffering. He shall not be released.

12. "Even if one knows a thousand Vedas, if he does not attain virtuous conduct, he cannot be released from suffering. I think the Vedas are fruitless; conduct with restraint alone is the truth."

He spoke this fifth verse.

Even one who knows a thousand Vedas. Depending on those Vedas. Without reaching virtuous conduct and meditative attainment. From suffering. If he cannot be released. Meditative attainment along with virtue. Conduct alone. Is the truth. If it be so. The Vedas. Are fruitless. They become so. Thus. I think.

Hearing those words, the Chaplain said:

## Only the Vedas are Noble

Hearing those words, the King discarded his devotion to the ascetics. Then the ascetic Setaketu thought, "Devotion to the ascetics arose in this King, but this Chaplain has cut it off as if with an adze. It is proper for me to speak with this Brahmin." Desiring to speak with the Brahmin, Setaketu said:

## Only Attainment is Noble

Hearing those words, the Chaplain spoke this sixth verse:

13. "The Vedas are not entirely fruitless, yet conduct with restraint is the truth. One attains fame by studying the Vedas, but the disciplined one reaches peace through conduct."

The Vedas. Are fruitless. They are not so indeed. Meditative attainment along with virtue. Conduct alone. Is the truth. Depending on the Vedas. Fame indeed. One attains. By means of virtuous conduct and meditative attainment. One who is disciplined. To Nibbāna (Peace). Reaches.
223:
## The Ascetics Had to Return to Lay Life

In this way, the Chaplain broke Setaketu's argument and made all the ascetics return to lay life. He made them carry weapons and appointed them as 'Mahantaraka' officials to serve the King. This is said to be the lineage of the Mahantarakas.

In identifying the birth: The Blessed One, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "The monk who now makes a display of wonders was then the ascetic Setaketu. Sāriputta was then the Caṇḍāla. Ānanda was then the King. I myself was then the Chaplain."

## Through Virtue and Conduct, One Reaches Nibbāna

The Setaketu Jātaka ends.

## 3. Darīmukha Jātaka

## Heeding the Advice of the Virtuous

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, spoke this Darīmukha Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with 'Paṅko ca kāmā,' concerning the Great Renunciation.

(The story of the present has already been told.)

In the past, King Magadha reigned in the city of Rājagaha. At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of King Magadha's chief queen. They named him Prince Brahmadatta. On the very day the Bodhisatta was born, a son was also born to the Chaplain. The face of the Chaplain's son was exceedingly beautiful like the color of gold. Therefore, they named the Chaplain's son Darīmukha.

Both the Prince and the Chaplain's son grew up in the royal palace. They became dear friends to each other.

## The Prince Became King

When they reached the age of sixteen, they went to the city of Takkasilā and learned all the arts. Thinking, "We shall learn all the traditional arts and also learn the customs of various regions," they traveled through market towns and villages. Eventually, they reached the city of Bārāṇasī, stayed at a shrine, and on the following day, entered Bārāṇasī for alms.
224:
In that city of Bārāṇasī, a certain family, wishing to perform an offering of food and recite blessings for Brahmins, cooked thick milk-rice and prepared seats. Seeing those two wandering for alms, the people said, "The Brahmins have come; let them enter the house and be seated." They spread a pure white cloth on the Bodhisatta's seat and a red rug on Darīmukha's seat.

Seeing that omen, Darīmukha knew, "Today my friend will become the King of Bārāṇasī, and I shall be the Commander-in-Chief." Having eaten there and received the gift for the blessing, they recited the blessing, departed, and went to the royal park. There, the Bodhisatta lay down on the auspicious stone slab, while Darīmukha sat massaging the Bodhisatta's feet.

At that time, it was the seventh day since the King of Bārāṇasī had died. The Chaplain, having performed the funeral rites for the King, released the ceremonial chariot (phussaratha) on the seventh day in the heirless kingdom. (The matter of the ceremonial chariot will be made clear in the Mahājanaka Jātaka.) The ceremonial chariot left the city, surrounded by the fourfold army and accompanied by the sounds of many musical instruments, and reached the gate of the park.

Hearing the sound of the music, Darīmukha thought, "The ceremonial chariot is coming for my friend. Today he will become King and give me the post of Commander-in-Chief. What is the use of household life to me? I will go forth and become a monk." Without consulting the Bodhisatta, he went to a suitable place and stayed in hiding.

The Chaplain, leaving the chariot at the park gate and entering the park, saw the Bodhisatta lying on the auspicious stone slab. Observing the marks on his feet, he thought, "This is a meritorious being. He is capable of ruling the four great islands with their two thousand surrounding islands. But what is his steadfastness like?" He then ordered all the musical instruments to be played.

The Bodhisatta awoke, removed the cloth from his face, looked at the people, covered his face again with the cloth, slept for a short while, and then, with his fatigue subsided, arose and sat cross-legged on the stone slab. The Chaplain knelt and said, "Sire, the kingship has come to you." He asked, "Friend, is there no son of the King?" "No, Sire," he replied. "In that case, very well," he accepted. They performed the consecration for the Bodhisatta right there in the park.

Due to the greatness of his retinue, the Bodhisatta did not remember Darīmukha. He mounted the chariot, entered the city surrounded by the multitude, made a clockwise circumambulation, and standing at the palace gate, assigned positions to the ministers before ascending the palace.
225:
## Darīmukha Becomes a Paccekabuddha
At that moment, Darīmukha, thinking "The park is now empty," came and sat on the auspicious stone slab. Then, a withered leaf fell before him. Contemplating the nature of decay and dissolution in that withered leaf, he meditated on the three characteristics and, making the earth resound, attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha.

At that very moment, his lay appearance vanished, and a bowl and robes created by psychic power descended from the sky and clad his body. Instantly, he became like an elder of sixty years' standing, endowed with the eight requisites and perfect deportment. By psychic power, he flew into the sky and went to the Nandamūla Cave in the Himālaya region.

## Remembering the Friend
The Bodhisatta ruled the kingdom righteously. However, due to the greatness of his retinue and being delighted by his glory, he did not remember Darīmukha for forty years. After forty years had passed, he remembered Darīmukha and, wishing to see him, thought, "I have a friend named Darīmukha; where could he be?"

From then on, the Bodhisatta would say, whether in the inner palace or in the midst of the assembly, "Where indeed is my friend Darīmukha? To anyone who tells me the dwelling place of Darīmukha, I shall give great wealth." While he was thus repeatedly remembering Darīmukha, another ten years passed for the King.

## Seeing the Friend Paccekabuddha
After fifty years had passed, Darīmukha Paccekabuddha, while reflecting, knew, "My friend is remembering me." Thinking, "Now my friend is old and has attained growth with sons and daughters; I shall go, preach the Dhamma, and make him renounce the world," he descended from the sky by psychic power into the park and sat on the stone slab like a golden statue.

The park keeper saw him, approached, and asked, "Venerable Sir, from where have you come?" "I have come from the Nandamūla Cave," he replied. "What is your name, Venerable Sir?" "Layman, I am called Darīmukha Paccekabuddha." "Venerable Sir, do you know our King?" "Yes, I know him; he was our friend during our time as laymen." "Venerable Sir, the King wishes to see you. I shall inform the King of your arrival." "Go and tell him," he said.

The park keeper went and told the King that Darīmukha Paccekabuddha was sitting on the stone slab. The King, saying "It is said that my friend has arrived; I shall see him," mounted his chariot and went to the park with a large retinue. He paid homage to the Paccekabuddha, exchanged friendly greetings, and sat down in a suitable place.
226:
## Exhortation to Ordain
At that time, the Paccekabuddha, after making a friendly greeting by saying, "King Brahmadatta, do you rule justly? Do you avoid falling into the four biases (agati)? Do you refrain from oppressing the people for the sake of wealth? Do you perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna)?" and so on, said, "King Brahmadatta, you are now old. It is time for you, Great King, to renounce sensual pleasures and ordain." Wishing to preach the Dhamma to the King, he spoke this first verse:

14. "Sensual pleasures are mud, sensual pleasures are a quagmire,
And this is called a fear with three roots.
Dust and smoke have been revealed by me;
Having abandoned them, do you ordain, Brahmadatta."

Brahmadatta: O King Brahmadatta. Kāmā: Sensual pleasures. Panko ca: Are like grass, moss, lilies, and so on [in water]. Kāmā: Sensual pleasures. Palipo ca: Are like a great quagmire. Etaṃ: This sensual pleasure. Timūlaṃ: As if having three roots. Bhayañca: Is also called a fear. Pavuttaṃ: Has been taught. Razo ca: As dust. Dhumo ca: As smoke. Mayā: By me. Pakāsito: Has been revealed. Tuvaṃ: You. Hitvā: Having abandoned sensual pleasures. Pabbaja: Do ordain.
227:
"I am attached, infatuated, and obsessed with sensual pleasures, O Brahmin, which are of a terrible nature.
I am unable to abandon them for the sake of my livelihood;
I shall perform many meritorious deeds."

He spoke this second verse:

Brāhmaṇa: O monk who has put away evil. Ahaṃ: I. Kāmesu: In sensual pleasures. Gadhito ca: Am attached. Homi: I am. Ratto ca: Am infatuated. Homi: I am. Adhimucchito ca: Am greatly obsessed. Homi: I am. Jīvikattho: Desiring such a livelihood. Ahaṃ: I. Bhiṃsarūpaṃ: Which has a terrible and very powerful nature. Taṃ: Those sensual pleasures. Pahātuṃ: To abandon. Anussahé: I am unable. Anappakāni: Many. Puññāni: Meritorious deeds. Kāhāmi: I shall perform.

## Unable to Ordain Yet
Hearing those words, the King, wishing to express how he was bound by defilements, said:
228:
## The Suffering of Taking Conception

Although the Bodhisatta said, "I am unable to ordain," the Darīmukha Paccekabuddha did not relinquish his task and, desiring to advise him further—
229:
17. "He enters a terrible hell,
Which is foul and filled with urine and excrement.
Beings, being greedy, do not abandon their bodies,
Those who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures."

He spoke these two verses.

Yo: Whosoever. Atthakāmassa: One who desires his welfare. Hitānukampino: One who looks after his benefit. Ovazzamāno: When being advised. Sāsanaṃ: The instruction. Na karoti: Does not follow. Idaméva: Only this view of mine. Seyyo: Is noble. Iti: Thus. Maññamāno: He thinks. So mando: That person of little wisdom. Punappunaṃ: Again and again. Gabbhaṃ: To the state of dwelling in a womb. Upeti: He arrives.

So: That person who arrives at the state of dwelling in a womb. Ghorarūpaṃ: Having a terrible nature. Subhāsubhaṃ: Which is regarded as foul (asubha) by the noble practitioners (yogāvacara). Mutta-karīsa-pūraṃ: Filled with urine and excrement. Nirayaṃ: Into the hell that is the mother's womb. Upeti: He enters. Ye sattā: Which beings. Sakāye: In their own bodies. Giddhā: Being greedy. Na jahanti: Cannot abandon. Te sattā: Those beings. Kāmesu: In sensual pleasures. Avītarāgā: Are not free from lust. Honti: They are.

Thus, the Paccekabuddha Darīmukha, having shown the suffering rooted in entering the mother's womb and the suffering rooted in being carried in the mother's womb, now, in order to show the suffering rooted in giving birth to the fetus—
230:
18. "Smeared with excrement, stained with blood, and smeared with phlegm, they emerge. Whatever part of the body they touch at that time, all is unpleasant, nothing but pure suffering."

19. "I speak having seen it myself, not having heard it from another. I remember many past lives."

He taught these two verses along with their word-by-word commentary.

"Great King, these beings, when emerging from the mother's womb, do not emerge anointed with the four types of perfumes or wearing fragrant garlands. Instead, they emerge smeared and obstructed by old excrement. 'Stained with blood' means they do not emerge anointed with red sandalwood paste, but emerge stained with red blood. 'Smeared with phlegm' means they do not emerge anointed with white sandalwood, but emerge smeared with thick, slippery phlegm. Indeed, at the time of birth, women's wombs discharge these impurities. 'At that time' means at that moment. This is what is meant: Great King, at the time of emerging from the mother's womb, these beings, smeared with excrement and such, whatever part of the birth canal, or whatever hand or foot they touch, they touch only that which is unpleasant, disagreeable, and unmixed suffering. At that time, there is no such thing as happiness for them."

"'I speak having seen it myself, not having heard it from another' means: Great King, in saying this much, I do not speak from hearing it from another, nor from hearing it from another recluse or brahmin. I speak having seen it, realized it, and witnessed it through my own knowledge of Paccekabodhi. 'I remember many past lives'—he said this to demonstrate his own power. This is what is meant: Great King, I remember many past lives consisting of the succession of aggregates lived in the past; I remember two incalculables and a hundred thousand eons."

Now, the Teacher, having become fully enlightened, said, "In this way, that Paccekabuddha favored the king with well-spoken words," and at the conclusion, he spoke this half-verse:

## The Friend Paccekabuddha Returns

20. "With varied and well-spoken verses, Darīmukha enlightened the wise one."

Darīmukha, the Darīmukha Paccekabuddha, by means of varied and well-spoken verses, enlightened the wise king, who was capable of knowing right from wrong.
231:
"With varied and well-spoken verses, Darīmukha enlightened the wise one."

In that verse, 'varied' means based on many meanings. 'Well-spoken' means well-said. 'Darīmukha enlightened the wise one' means: O monks, that Darīmukha Paccekabuddha enlightened, convinced, and made the king—who was of excellent wisdom and capable of knowing right from wrong—accept his words.

Thus, the Paccekabuddha, having shown the faults in sensual pleasures and having made the king accept his words, said, "Great King, whether you renounce now or not, I have told you the dangers of sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation. May you be diligent." Having said this, he rose into the air like a golden king swan and, treading upon the clouds, went to the Nandamūla Cave.

## The King's Renunciation

The Bodhisatta, placing his hands—shining with the light of his ten fingernails—together upon his head in worship, watched until the Paccekabuddha passed out of sight. Then, he summoned his eldest son, handed over the kingdom, and while the people were weeping and lamenting, he renounced sensual pleasures and entered the Himalayas. There, he built a leaf hut, became an ascetic, and before long, attained the higher knowledges and meditative attainments. At the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, linked the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many monks became Stream-enterers and so forth. As for how the Jātaka was linked: "At that time, I myself was the king." Thus he linked the Jātaka.

## Having heard the Dhamma and practiced well, they attained happiness.

The Darīmukha Jātaka ends.

## 4. Neru Jātaka
## On not staying in a place where virtue is not recognized

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Neru Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kākolā kākasaṅghā ca," concerning an obscure monk.

That monk, having taken a meditation subject from the Fully Enlightened One, went to a certain border village. The people, being pleased with his deportment, offered him alms-food, received his consent to stay, built a leaf hut in the forest, and settled him there. They paid him great honor and respect.

Then, some who held the view of Eternalism arrived. Having heard their words, the people abandoned the Elder, accepted the view of Eternalism, and paid honor and respect only to those Eternalists.
232:
After that, those who held the view of Annihilationism arrived. Those people abandoned Eternalism and accepted Annihilationism. Then, other Naked Ascetics arrived. Those people abandoned Annihilationism and accepted the doctrine of the Naked Ascetics.

That monk, having lived in hardship near those people who did not know the difference between virtue and vice, finished the rainy season retreat. After performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he went to the Fully Enlightened One. After the customary greetings, when asked, "Monk, where did you spend the rainy season?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, I stayed near a border village." When asked, "Did you live comfortably?" he said, "Venerable Sir, I lived in hardship near people who do not know the difference between virtue and vice."

"Monk," the Teacher said, "wise men of old, even when born in the animal kingdom, would not stay even for a single day with those who do not know the difference between virtue and vice. Why did you stay in a place where your own virtue and vice were not recognized?" Having been requested by the monk, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a golden swan. He also had a younger brother. While living on Mount Cittakūṭa, they ate self-sown paddy in the Himalayan region. One day, after foraging there, while returning to Mount Cittakūṭa, they saw a golden mountain named Neru on the way and perched on its summit.

## Golden Birds Near the Golden Mountain

The flocks of birds and the four-footed beasts living near that mountain appeared in various colors in their feeding grounds. However, from the moment they entered the mountain, all those creatures became golden-hued due to the mountain's radiance. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta's younger brother, not knowing the reason, wished to discuss it with his elder brother and spoke these two verses:

20. "Ravens and flocks of crows, and we, the best of flyers—all become alike upon reaching this mountain."

21. "Here, lions, tigers, jackals, and the lowest of deer—all become alike. What is the name of this mountain?"

"Brother, O King of Swans, having reached this mountain, the forest crows, the common flocks of crows, and we, who are the best among birds—all of us birds become identical in color."
233:
22. "People know this as Neru, the best of mountains. Here, all living beings dwell endowed with [golden] color."

He spoke this third verse. 

*Idha*: on this mountain. *Sabbapāṇino*: all living beings. *Vaṇṇena sampannā*: being endowed with a golden hue. *Vasanti*: they dwell. *Uttamaṃ*: the noble. *Imaṃ pabbataṃ*: this mountain. *Nerūti*: as Mount Neru. *Manussā*: people. *Jānanti*: they know.

*Idha*: on this mountain. *Sīhā ca*: lions. *Byagghā ca*: tigers. *Migādhamā siṅgālā ca*: and jackals, the lowest of beasts. *Sabbeva*: all these animals. *Sadisā*: are similar in color. *Honti*: they are. *Ayaṃ pabbato*: this mountain. *Ko nāma*: what is its name?

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta said:

## Places Where One Should Not Dwell

Hearing those words, the younger swan spoke the remaining verses:

23. "Where there is no honor for the virtuous, or where they are despised, or where the base are honored—one should not dwell there.

24. "Where the lazy and the diligent, the brave and the cowardly are honored equally, the virtuous do not stay among men who make no distinction.

25. "This Neru does not distinguish between the low, the high, and the middle. Neru makes no distinction; come, let us leave Neru."

*Yattha*: in which place. *Santānaṃ vā*: to the virtuous. *Amānanā*: there is no respect or worshipful honor. *Siyā*: there may be. *Vimānanā*: there is contempt. *Siyā*: there may be. *Hīnasammānanā vāpi*: or there is honor and worship for the base. *Siyā*: there may be. *Tattha vasatiṃ—asmiṃ nivāse*: in that dwelling place. *Na vase*: one should not stay.

*Yattha*: in which place. *Alaso ca*: the lazy one who lacks knowledge. *Dakkho ca*: the skillful one. *Sūro ca*: the brave one. *Bhīru ca*: the cowardly one. *Pūjiyā*: they receive equal honor. *Nare*: among men. *Avisesakare*: who make no distinction. *Tattha*: in that place. *Santo*: the virtuous. *Na vasanti*: they do not stay.

*Ayaṃ neru*: this Mount Neru. *Hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime*: those who are low, noble, or middle. *Na vibhajati*: it does not distinguish. *Neru*: the mountain named Neru. *Avisesakaro*: is devoid of making distinctions. *Nerūṃ*: Mount Neru. *Handa*: [an exclamation of resolve]. *Jahāmase*: let us abandon it.

Having spoken thus, both swans flew up and went to Mount Cittakūṭa.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How was the Jātaka identified? At that time, Ānanda was the younger swan, and I myself was the elder swan. Thus did he identify the Jātaka.

## Where distinctions are not seen, one should not stay.

The Neru Jātaka is finished.
234:
## 5. Āsaṅka Jātaka

## The Cause of Suffering Due to Sensual Pleasures

While the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he spoke this Āsaṅka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Āsāvatī nāma latā," concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

(The present story will become clear in the Indriya Jātaka.)

In this Āsaṅka Jātaka, the Buddha called that monk and asked, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha asked, "Who has caused you to be dissatisfied?" The monk replied, "My former wife, Bhante." The Buddha then said, "Monk, this woman is one who habitually works for your disadvantage. In the past, because of this woman, you abandoned your fourfold army and lived in the Himalayan region for three years, experiencing great suffering." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a village of Kāsi. When he reached maturity, he completed his education at Takkasilā, became an ascetic, and lived in the Himalayan region, subsisting on forest roots and fruits, and attaining the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti).

## The Lotus-born Maiden

At that time, a certain merit-filled being passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and was reborn as a young girl inside a lotus bud in a lotus pond in that Himalayan region. While the other lotuses reached old age and withered, this lotus remained as a large bud.

The ascetic thought, "What could be the reason for this?" He put on his bathing cloth, waded into the water, opened the lotus, and seeing the young girl, he developed the perception of her as his daughter, took her to his leaf-hut, and raised her. Later, when she reached sixteen years of age, she was exceedingly beautiful. She possessed a noble appearance, surpassing human beauty, though not quite reaching divine beauty.

## Living in a Crystal Palace

At that time, Sakka, the King of Devas, came to attend upon the Bodhisatta. Sakka saw the maiden and asked, "From where did you get this maiden?" He heard the reply, "I got her from the lotus pond." Sakka then asked, "What is suitable for this woman to have?" The ascetic replied, "She should have a dwelling place, clothing, ornaments, and food."

Sakka said, "Very well, Bhante," and created a crystal palace near the ascetic's leaf-hut, along with divine clothing, ornaments, and divine food and drink. That palace would descend and rest on the ground when the maiden needed to attend to her personal needs, and when she entered it, it would rise and stay in the sky.
235:
## When the hunter saw her and informed the King

That maiden lived in the palace, performing great and small duties for the Bodhisatta. A certain forest hunter saw that maiden and asked, "Venerable sir, how is this maiden related to you?" Hearing the words, "She is my daughter," he went to the city of Bārāṇasī and informed the King, "Great King, I have seen such a daughter of an ascetic in the Himavanta region."

## The King coming and asking

The King of Bārāṇasī, being bound by the attachment of what he had heard, made the hunter his guide and went to that place with a four-fold army. Having established a stockade and calling the hunter, he entered the hermitage surrounded by a group of ministers. Having paid respects to the monks, he said, "Venerable sir, women are indeed a stain to the holy life of ascetics who practice the noble practice. I shall look after your daughter."

The Bodhisatta, however, had wondered, "What is in this lotus?" and because she was brought forth from the water, he gave the maiden the name "Āsaṅkā."

## If you can say the name, take her

The Bodhisatta did not speak directly, saying, "Great King, take this maiden and go." Instead, he said, "Great King, this maiden has a hidden and subtle name. If you know the name, take her and go." The King said, "Venerable sir, if you tell me, I shall know it." The Bodhisatta replied, "I will not tell you, O King. If you yourself know the name through the power of your wisdom, then take her and go."

The King of Bārāṇasī accepted, saying, "Very well," and from that day on, together with his ministers, he pondered the name, wondering, "What is this maiden's name?" That King Brahmadatta mentioned various names that are difficult to know, saying, "It might be such and such a name," but the Bodhisatta rejected them, saying, "It is not this name."

While the King was pondering the name, a year passed. Wild animals such as lions caught the elephants, horses, and men. They were oppressed by snakes. They were troubled by flies. Many people suffered and died. The King said to the Bodhisatta, "What is the use of this woman to me?" and prepared to leave. The maiden Āsaṅkā opened the crystal window and stood there.
236:
26. There is a creeper named Āsāvatī, born in the Cittalatā Grove.
In a thousand years, it brings forth a single fruit.

27. The devas attend to it, even though the fruit is so far off.
O King, do you also hope; hope is fruitful and pleasant.

28. That bird hoped, that twice-born one hoped.
And its hope was fulfilled, even though it was far away.
O King, do you also hope; hope is fruitful and pleasant.

She spoke these verses.

"Great King, at first, although the state of being far away existed, that crane bird only hoped. That twice-born bird only hoped. And for that crane, the benefit of hope was fulfilled. O King, you should only hope. To obtain the fruit of hope is pleasant."

## The Maiden's Words

The King saw the maiden Āsaṅkā and said, "We are unable to know your name. You remain here in the Himavanta region; we shall go."

"Great King, if you go, where will you find a woman like me? In the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in the Cittalatā Grove, there is a creeper named Āsāvatī. Inside the fruit of that Āsāvatī creeper, a divine drink is produced. If one drinks that divine drink once, they remain intoxicated for four months and sleep on a divine bed. The fruit of that Āsāvatī creeper, however, fruits only after a thousand years. The sons of devas who are fond of liquor, thinking 'We shall obtain the fruit from this Āsāvatī creeper,' endure their longing and go constantly for a thousand years to see if that Āsāvatī creeper is free from disease. You, O King, are weary after only one year. To obtain the fruit of hope is indeed pleasant; do not be weary."

Saying this, she spoke these two verses:

"Great King, in the Cittalatā Grove, a creeper named Āsāvatī is born. To that Āsāvatī creeper, in a thousand years, a single fruit is produced."

"Great King, at first, although the fruit is far off, the devas attend to that Āsāvatī creeper many times repeatedly. O King, you should only hope. To obtain the fruit of hope is pleasant."

## The King discouraged again

The King, being attached by the words of the princess Āsaṅkā, again assembled his ministers, made arrangements, and stayed for another year searching for the name. When he asked what the maiden's name was and suggested a name, the Bodhisatta simply rejected it.

Again the King said, "What is the use of this woman to me?" and prepared to leave. That maiden also stood at the window and showed herself. The King of Bārāṇasī said, "You remain here; we shall go."

## The Maiden's Words

"Great King, why will you go?" she asked. "I am unable to know your name," he replied. "Great King, why will you not know the name? There is no such thing as hope not being fulfilled. It is said that a certain crane, staying on a mountain top, obtained what it desired. Why should you, O King, not obtain it? Great King, please endure a while longer."

"Great King, a certain crane took food in a lotus pond and perched on a mountain top. That crane stayed there on that mountain top one day, and the next day it thought: 'If I could stay here on this mountain top comfortably, without descending from this mountain top, and while staying in this place, take food and drink water and spend this whole day, it would be good.'"
237:
At that time, on that very day, Sakka, the king of devas, having subdued the Asuras and enjoying divine sovereignty in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, thought: "My heart's desire has reached its fulfillment. Is there anyone else whose heart's desire is not yet fulfilled?" Upon reflecting, Sakka saw that crane and thought, "I shall bring this crane's heart's desire to fulfillment." Not far from where the crane sat, there was a river. Sakka caused that river to be filled with a torrent of water and made it flow to the mountain top.

The crane, staying right there by the river flowing to the mountain top, ate fish and drank water, and remained there for the whole day. Then the water receded and was gone.

"Great King, in this way, even a crane obtained the fruit of its longing. Why should you not obtain yours?" having said this—

## The King’s Despair Again

The King, hearing the maiden's words, was bound by her beauty and entangled by her speech. Unable to leave, he gathered his ministers and had them devise a hundred names. While searching for her name by means of these hundred names, another year passed for the King.

After three years had passed, the King approached the Bodhisatta and asked, using the hundred names, "Could her name be such-and-such?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, you do not know."

The King said, "Now we shall go," and having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, he departed.

The maiden Āsaṅkā stood leaning against a crystal window. Seeing her, the King said, "You stay here; we shall go."

She asked, "Great King, why are you going?"

He replied, "You satisfy me only with words, but not with the pleasure of sensual desire. While I have lived here entangled by your sweet words, three years have passed. Now I shall go," and he spoke these verses:

29. You satisfy me indeed with words, but you do not satisfy me with deeds. Like the flower of the Sereyyaka, you are beautiful in color but without scent.

30. Whoever speaks sweet but fruitless words to friends, without giving or relinquishing wealth, the bond of friendship with that person perishes.

31. One should speak only of what one would do; one should not speak of what one would not do. The wise recognize the one who speaks but does not act.

32. Indeed, my strength is exhausted, and provisions are no longer found. I fear for the destruction of my life. Behold, now I depart.
238:
30. Whoever speaks sweet but fruitless words to friends, without giving or relinquishing wealth, the bond of friendship with that person perishes.

31. One should speak only of what one would do; one should not speak of what one would not do. The wise recognize the one who speaks but does not act.

32. Indeed, my strength is exhausted, and provisions are no longer found. I fear for the destruction of my life. Behold, now I depart.

Dear lady, like the flower of the Sereyyaka (yellow amaranth), which has color but no scent, you satisfy me indeed with words, but you do not satisfy me with deeds.

Dear lady, whoever speaks sweet but fruitless words to friends, without giving or relinquishing wealth, the bond of friendship with that person perishes.

Dear lady, one should speak only of what one would do; one should not speak of what one would not do. The wise recognize the one who speaks but does not act.

Dear lady, indeed, my strength (the army) is exhausted, and provisions (rations) are no longer found. I fear for the destruction of my life. Behold, now I depart.

## The Maiden Reveals Her Name

The maiden Āsaṅkā, hearing the King's words, said, "Great King, you say you do not know my name, but you have just uttered my very name. This is indeed my name. Speak to my father and take me with you." Wishing to converse with the King, she spoke this verse:

33. That is indeed my name, which I have, O best of charioteers. Wait, Great King, I shall consult my father.

O best of charioteers, most noble among kings! Great King, that name of mine, which is Āsaṅkā, is indeed the name you have just spoken. Great King, wait a moment. I shall consult with my father.
239:
## Āsaṅka has been Obtained
The King went to the Bodhisatta and said, "Venerable Sir, your daughter is named Āsaṅka." The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, since the time you have known her name, take her and go."

The King paid homage to the Bodhisatta, went to the door of the crystal palace, and said, "Lady, your father has given you to me. Come now, let us go." She replied, "Wait, Great King, I shall first consult with my father." She descended from the palace, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, wept, asked for forgiveness, and then returned to the King.

The King took the maiden Āsaṅka and went to the city of Bārāṇasī. There, he lived in pleasant companionship, his family increasing with sons and daughters. The Bodhisatta, with his meditative absorptions (jhāna) intact, was reborn in the Brahma realm.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, the Teacher (the Buddha) identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). To identify the Jātaka: "The former wife of that time was the maiden Āsaṅka. The dissatisfied monk was the King. I myself was the ascetic."

## Women, when in love, give what is desired
The Āsaṅka Jātaka ends.

## 6. Migālopa Jātaka
## Destruction through not following the words of the wise

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, who is the instructor of the world including the devas, told this Migālopa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na me rucci," concerning a certain monk who was difficult to admonish.

The Teacher summoned that monk and asked, "Monk, is it true that you are difficult to admonish?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, not only now are you difficult to admonish; in the past also you were difficult to admonish. Because of your stubbornness, you did not listen to the words of the wise and met with destruction in the mouth of the Veramba winds." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the species of vultures and was named Apananda. This vulture king Apananda lived on Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, surrounded by a flock of vultures.

## If one flies too high
The son of that vulture king Apananda was named Migālopa. He was endowed with great strength and power. This vulture Migālopa would fly extremely high, exceeding the limits of other vultures. The vultures reported to the vulture king, "Your son is flying too high."
240:
34. "I do not like it, Migālopa, that you have such a flight. You fly too high, dear son; you frequent a region that is not your proper range."
35. "When the earth appears to you like a four-cornered field, then, dear son, turn back; do not go further than that."
36. "There are other birds, wing-borne sky-goers, who, tossed by the force of the wind, perished, though they thought themselves eternal."

He spoke these three verses.

"Dear Migālopa, you fly too high. Dear Migālopa, you frequent what is not your proper range. I do not like such a flight of yours, flying so high."

"Dear Migālopa, when the earth appears to you like a four-cornered field, turn back from that place. Do not fly further than this."

"There are other vultures besides you, sky-goers with wings as their vehicles. These vultures, thinking themselves eternal like the earth and mountains, were tossed by the force of the wind and perished, unable to complete their natural lifespan of a thousand years."

37. "Not having followed the instruction of Apananda, his aged father, and having exceeded the Kāla winds, he fell under the power of the Veramba winds."
38. "His sons, his wife, and all others who depended on him, all came to ruin because of the bird who would not take advice."
39. "Even so in this world, whoever does not understand the words of the elders, exceeding the limits and being arrogant, like the vulture who ignored the instruction, all come to ruin by not following the advice of the elders."

## Prone to destruction
The vulture king called his son and meant to say, "Dear boy, you fly too high; a vulture that flies too high will reach the end of its life."

## Moderation is safe, excess is perilous
Because the vulture Migālopa was difficult to admonish, he did not listen to his father's words. As he flew, he saw the limit described by his father, but he exceeded that limit and reached the Kāla winds. Having flown beyond the Kāla winds, he reached the Veramba winds. Then, the Veramba winds struck that vulture Migālopa. As soon as he was struck by the Veramba winds, he was torn into pieces and vanished in the sky.

The Teacher, having become the Buddha, taught these verses:

"Monks, the vulture Migālopa, not listening to the instruction of his elder father Apananda, exceeded the Kāla winds and came under the power of the Veramba winds."

"His sons, his wife, and all other vultures who lived depending on Migālopa, all reached destruction because the vulture Migālopa did not listen to the advice."
241:
“Likewise, in this world, if one does not understand the words of the elders (vuddhānaṃ), one wanders beyond limits, is fierce, and oversteps the instruction. All such people, by not following the advice of the elders, reach destruction like the vulture Migālopa.”

The All-Knowing Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: “At that time, the vulture Migālopa was the difficult-to-admonish monk, but I myself was the vulture king named Apananda.”

## If one oversteps the advice of elders, destruction is certain
The Migālopa Jātaka ends.

## 7. Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka
## Good conduct and virtue are called glory
While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Kā nu kāḷena vaṇṇena,” concerning the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.

From the time he was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala), that merchant Anāthapiṇḍika kept the five precepts (pañcasīla) without breaking or tarnishing them. His wife, his sons and daughters, and all those who worked for wages also kept them.

Then one day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika is pure and lives with a pure retinue.” The All-Knowing Buddha came and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they replied, “Venerable Sir, we are gathered for such a discussion,” he said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past also, the wise were pure and had pure retinues,” and he told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta became a merchant and gave alms, observed virtue, and kept the Uposatha. His wife, his sons and daughters, and his male servants and laborers also kept the five precepts. That merchant was well-known as the merchant Suciparivāra.
242:
## One should worship the virtuous
That merchant thought, “If someone who is purer in virtue than I should come, it is not proper to give him my own couch or bed. I should provide an unused seat.” Thus, in his own living quarters, he had an unused couch and an unused bed prepared on one side.

## Lake Anavatatta
At that time, two goddesses, one named Kāḷakaṇṇi, the daughter of the Great King Virūpakkha from the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika), and the other named Sirī, the daughter of the Great King Dhataraṭṭha, took many flowers and went to Lake Anavatatta, saying, “We shall play in Lake Anavatatta.”

In that Lake Anavatatta, there are many bathing places. Among those places, only the All-Knowing Buddhas bathe at the Buddhas' bathing place. Only Paccekabuddhas bathe at the Paccekabuddhas' bathing place. Only monks bathe at the monks' bathing place. Only ascetics bathe at the ascetics' bathing place. Only the sons of devas living in the six sensual heavens, such as the Realm of the Four Great Kings, bathe at the devas' bathing place. Only the daughters of devas bathe at the goddesses' bathing place.

## The Dispute between the Two Goddesses
Arriving at that bathing place, the two goddesses quarreled over the spot, saying, “I shall bathe first! I shall bathe first!”

The goddess Kāḷakaṇṇi said, “I govern the world. Therefore, it is proper that I bathe first.” The goddess Sirī said, “I am established in the practice that bestows sovereignty upon many people. Therefore, it is proper that I bathe first.”

The goddesses thought, “The Four Great Kings will know who among us is worthy to bathe first.” They went to those Great Kings and asked, “Who among us is worthy to bathe first in Lake Anavatatta?”

The Great Kings Dhataraṭṭha and Virūpakkha said, “We are not able to decide,” and passed the burden to the Great Kings Virūḷhaka and Kuvera. Virūḷhaka and Kuvera were also unable. Thinking, “We shall send them to the feet of Sakka,” they sent the goddesses to Sakka. Sakka heard the words of the goddesses and thought, “I should not decide the case of these two goddesses.”

## Sakka's Instruction
Then Sakka said, “In the city of Bārāṇasī, there is a merchant named Suciparivāra. In his house, an unused seat is prepared. Whichever goddess obtains the right to sit or lie in that house, she is the one worthy to bathe first.”
243:
41. "I am the daughter of the Great King Virūpakkha, the fierce one. I am Kāḷī, the unlucky one; they know me as Kāḷakaṇṇī. Being entreated, give me space; let us dwell in your presence."

O Great Merchant (Mahāseṭṭhi). I am the fierce daughter of the Great King named Virūpakkha. I am the goddess named Kāḷī, who lacks virtue and wisdom. They know me as Kāḷakaṇṇī. I wish to dwell in your presence. You, being entreated, give me permission to stay.

42. "In a man of what virtue, of what conduct, do you take up residence? Being asked by me, O Kāḷī, tell me; how may we know you?"

O Goddess Kāḷī. In a man of what virtue and of what conduct do you enter and dwell with your mind? Being asked, O Goddess, tell me. How shall we know you?

## Kāḷakaṇṇī Goes to the Merchant's House
Upon hearing those words, that goddess Kāḷakaṇṇī immediately dressed in blue garments, anointed herself with blue ointment, and adorned herself with blue sapphire ornaments. Like a stone set in a machine, she descended from the celestial realm and, during the middle watch of the night, stood in the air at the entrance of the merchant's mansion, near the bed, emitting a blue radiance.

## Who Are You?
When the merchant looked, he saw the goddess. As soon as he saw her, he felt a sense of dislike and displeasure toward her. Wishing to speak with the goddess, the merchant spoke this first verse:

40. "Who is this with a dark complexion, and not of pleasant appearance? Who are you, or whose daughter? How may we know you?"

O lady (bhadde). You, with your dark complexion, are certainly not of pleasant appearance. What is your name? Who are you? Whose daughter are you? How shall we know you?

## I am the Goddess Kāḷakaṇṇī
Hearing these words, the goddess Kāḷakaṇṇī—

## What Kind of Man Do You Like?
After that, the Bodhisatta—
244:
43. "The ungrateful, the malicious, the quarrelsome, the envious, the stingy, and the deceitful; that man is dear to me, whose gains perish."

## She Likes the Fool
After that, the goddess Kāḷī, wishing to speak of her own attributes, spoke these verses:

44. "One who is angry and holds grudges, a slanderer and a divider of friends, harsh-spoken and rough; he is even dearer to me than the former."

45. "The man who says 'today' or 'tomorrow' and does not understand his own benefit, who gets angry when being exhorted, and who disregards his superiors."

46. "The man obsessed with idle play, who falls away from all friends; that man is dear to me; in him, I am free from illness (at ease)."

Whosoever is ungrateful (makkhī), malicious (paḷāsī), quarrelsome (sārambhī), envious (issukī), stingy (maccharī), and deceitful (saṭho); and whosoever destroys the wealth and possessions he has obtained—that man, I like.

Whosoever is angry (kodhano), holds grudges (upanāhī), speaks slanderous words (pisuṇo), divides friends (vibhedako), speaks malicious words (kaṇḍakavāco), and is rough (pharuṣo)—that man, I love even more than the one mentioned before.
245:
47. "Depart from here, O Kāḷī! This [nature] is not found in us. Go to another district, to market towns and royal capitals."

O goddess named Kāḷī. You, depart from this place. This ungratefulness and such matters do not exist in us. You, go to another district, to market towns and royal capitals.

48. "I also know that this is not found in you. There are unlucky ones in the world who amass much wealth; I and my brother, the god (Deva), both of us destroy it."

O Great Merchant. I also know that this ungratefulness and such matters do not exist in you. In the world, there are those who lack virtue and wisdom. They, too, amass much wealth. That wealth, I and my brother, the deity named Deva—both of us siblings—destroy.

Whosoever does not know his own business, thinking, "This task is for today, that task is for tomorrow"; who gets angry when being exhorted; that man disregards those who are superior.

One who is constantly obsessed with sensual pleasures and falls away from all friends; that man, I love. In that man, I exist free from suffering and anxiety.

## Go Back!
Then, wishing to rebuke the goddess, the Bodhisatta—

Hearing those words, the goddess Kāḷakaṇṇī, being ashamed—
246:
## The Arrival of Goddess Siri at the Merchant's House
Having said this, she departed. When the goddess Kaḷakaṇṇī had left, the goddess Siri arrived, adorned with golden-colored garments, ointments, and golden ornaments. Emitting a golden radiance at the entrance, she stood with reverence, her feet planted firmly and evenly on the ground. 

## Who Are You?
Seeing the goddess Siri, the Great Being spoke the first verse:

49. "Who is this, standing firmly on the earth with divine radiance? Who are you, and whose daughter? How may we know you?"

[Word-by-word meaning:] Dear lady, you stand well upon the earth with a divine complexion. What is your name? Who are you? Whose daughter are you? How shall we know you?

## I am Goddess Siri
Hearing the words of the Great Being, the goddess Siri spoke the second verse:

50. "I am the daughter of the glorious Great King Dhataraṭṭha. I am Siri and Lakkhi; the wise know me as one of vast wisdom. Being requested, give me a place; let us dwell in your presence."

[Word-by-word meaning:] Great Merchant, I am the daughter of the glorious and wise Great King named Dhataraṭṭha. I am called Siri and I am called Lakkhi. They know me in the realm of the Four Great Kings as a goddess endowed with wisdom as vast as the earth. I wish to dwell in your presence. You, being requested, please give me the opportunity to stay in a seat or bed that has not been used by others for one night.

## What Kind of Man Do You Like?
Hearing the words of the goddess, the Great Being spoke this verse:

51. "In a man of what virtue and what conduct do you dwell? O Lakkhi, being asked, tell me; how may we know you?"

[Word-by-word meaning:] Goddess named Lakkhi, in a man of what kind of virtue and what kind of conduct does your heart find delight and dwell? Being asked, O goddess, tell me. How shall we know you?

## I Like the Virtuous
Hearing the words of the Great Being, the goddess Siri spoke:

52. "He who, whether in cold or heat, wind or sun, gadflies or reptiles..."
247:
