...wind or sun, gadflies or reptiles, overcomes all hunger and thirst, and is constantly diligent day and night.

53. "He who does not let the timely benefit pass away—he is pleasing to me, and in him I dwell. He who is free from anger, has friends, is generous, endowed with virtue, not deceitful, and upright."

54. "He who is helpful, friendly, gentle in speech, and humble even when attaining greatness—in that man I become abundant, like the appearance of waves in the ocean."

55. "He who, towards friends or enemies, superiors, equals, or inferiors, whether they act for his benefit or harm, practices kindness both openly and in secret."

56. "He who would never speak harsh words—I am his friend in death and in life. But if a person of little wisdom, having obtained the beloved Siri, becomes intoxicated, I avoid that one of fierce nature and uneven conduct, like a place of excrement."

57. "One creates fortune for oneself, and misfortune for oneself. Indeed, no one else is the maker of another's fortune or misfortune."

[Word-by-word meaning:] Whichever man is diligent, whether it be cold or hot, or when there is wind and sun, or when there are gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, scorpions, and lice. And whichever man, having overcome all hunger and thirst, is constantly diligent day and night.

Whichever man does not let the benefit that has arrived at the right time diminish. I delight in that man; I enter and dwell in him with my heart. Whichever man is not prone to anger, has good friends, is generous, is endowed with virtue, is not deceitful, and is upright.

He who practices the bases of sympathy (saṅgaha), is friendly, and has gentle speech. Even when he has attained greatness, he remains humble in conduct. Just as the successive waves appear when looking at the beauty of the ocean, so do I become abundant with a great surge of joy in that man.

And whichever man practices kindness (saṅgaha) both openly and in secret towards friends, or even towards non-friends, towards superiors, equals, or inferiors, and towards those who act for his benefit or harm.

Whichever man never speaks harsh words. I am the friend of that person, whether he is dead or alive. Among such men mentioned, whoever, having obtained the lovely Siri, fulfills any of these virtues, I am his friend. But whichever man is of little wisdom, and practices uneven conduct with a fierce nature, I avoid that man as one avoids a place of excrement.

One creates fortune (Lakkhi) for oneself through virtue and wisdom; one creates misfortune (Alakkhi) for oneself through the lack thereof. Truly, one person cannot create fortune or misfortune for another.

## Please Sit Here
When she had spoken thus, the Great Being, delighted by the words of the goddess Siri, said: "This unused seat is suitable only for you."
248: "Sit on the seat," he said. The goddess Sirī stayed on that bed, and at dawn, she departed and went to the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika), where she was the first to receive a bath in Lake Anavatatta.
249:
The bed is called the Siri-bed (Siri-sayana) because it was used by the goddess Siri. This lineage is the lineage of the Siri-sayana. For this reason, even to this day, it is called the Siri-sayana.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the birth: "At that time, Uppalavaṇṇā was the goddess Siri, and I myself was the merchant Suciparivāra."

## Only the Virtuous Deserve the Noble Place
The Siri-Kāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka is concluded.

## 8. Kukkuṭa Jātaka
## One Should Not Follow the Seduction of Women
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kukkuṭa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sucittapattacchadana," concerning a dissatisfied monk.

The All-Knowing Buddha asked that monk, "Monk, why are you dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "Venerable Sir, I am dissatisfied due to the power of defilement after seeing an adorned woman," the Buddha said, "Monk, women deceive and entice men, and when men fall under their power, they bring them to ruin, just like a fickle she-cat," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the species of a rooster and lived in the forest surrounded by a large flock of roosters. Nearby, a certain she-cat also lived. That she-cat, except for the Bodhisatta, deceived and ate the remaining roosters by various means. The Bodhisatta did not desire the approach of that she-cat.
250:
59. You are four-footed, O fair one; I am two-footed, O pleasant one.
A beast and a bird are unmatched; seek another husband.

He spoke this verse to complete the two.

Kalyāṇi: O fair one. Manorame: O one who delights the heart. Migī: O she-cat. Tvaṃ: You. Catuppadī: Have four feet. Ahaṃ: I. Dvipado: Have two feet. Tvaṃ: You. Migī: Are a beast (she-cat). Ahaṃ: I. Pakkhī: Am a bird (rooster). Tesaṃ: For them (the cat and rooster). Asaññuttā: It is not suitable to be husband and wife. Aññaṃ: Another. Sāmikaṃ: Husband. Pariyesa: Seek.

60. I will be your young maiden wife, sweet and pleasant-spoken.
Take me with noble gain; let me be known as you wish.

He spoke this verse to complete the three.

Kukkuṭa: O rooster. Ahaṃ: I. Te: Your. Komārikā: Young maiden, a pure virgin. Mañjukā: Having a sweet voice. Piyabhāṇinī: A wife who speaks pleasant words. Homi: Shall be. Tvaṃ: You. Ariyena: With blameless. Vedena: Gain. Maṃ: Me. Vinda: Obtain. Maṃ: Me. Yadicchasi: If you wish to be known as a slave. Sāvaya: Make it known in the city of Bārāṇasī, which is twelve leagues in extent, that I am your slave.

"She is like a fickle she-cat," he said, and brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the species of a rooster and lived in the forest surrounded by a large flock of roosters. Nearby, a certain she-cat also lived. That she-cat, except for the Bodhisatta, deceived and ate the remaining roosters by various means. The Bodhisatta did not desire the approach of that she-cat.

## How the She-cat Enticed
That she-cat thought, "This rooster is very clever. He does not know my cunning and skill in means. I should entice this rooster by saying 'I will be your wife,' and eat him when he falls under my power." She went to the foot of the tree where the Bodhisatta was perched and, wishing to entreat the Bodhisatta with words preceded by praise, spoke this first verse:

58. O bird with beautiful variegated wings and a red crest,
Come down from the tree branch; I will be your wife for free.

Sucittapattacchadana: Covered with very beautiful wings. Tambacūḷavihangama: A bird with a red crest. Dumassākhāya: From the tree branch. Oroha: Come down. Mudhā: For free. Te: Your. Bhariyā: Wife. Bhavāmi: I shall be.

## Seek a Husband of Your Own Kind
Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta thought, "This she-cat has eaten all my relatives. Now she wants to entice and eat me. I will send her away." Thinking thus, he said:
251:
61. O eater of carcasses, blood-drinker, thief, rooster-slayer,
You do not desire me as a husband with noble gain.

He spoke this verse to complete the four.

Kuṇapādini: One who habitually eats rotting carcasses and such. Lohitape: One who drinks blood. Kukkuṭapothini: One who kills roosters. Cori: O thief. Tvaṃ: You. Ariyena: With blameless. Vedena: Gain. Maṃ: Me. Bhattāraṃ: As your husband. Kātuṃ: To make. Na icchasi: Do not desire.

62. Even so, clever women, seeing a wealthy man,
Lead him away with smooth words, like the she-cat the rooster.

## I Will Be Your Slave
Hearing those words, the she-cat thought, "This rooster is very clever. I will deceive and eat him by some other means."

## Hey, Rooster-Thief!
Then the Bodhisatta thought, "It is proper to threaten her so that she flees."

## Beware of the Sweet-Spoken
That she-cat fled away. She did not dare to look back again. Having brought forth this past story, the All-Knowing Buddha spoke these verses:

63. He who does not quickly understand a matter that has arisen,
Falls under the power of his enemy and later regrets it.

64. He who quickly understands a matter that has arisen,
Is released from the oppression of the enemy, like the rooster from the she-cat.

Kukkuṭaṃ: The rooster. Nentī: Leading. Biḷārī viya: Like the she-cat. Evampi: In this same way. Cāturā: Women who are endowed with beauty. Nārī: Women. Sadhanaṃ: A wealthy. Naraṃ: Man. Disvāna: Having seen. Saṇhāhi: With smooth and gentle. Vācāhi: Words. Nenti: Lead away.

Yo ca: And whoever. Uppatitaṃ: That has arisen. Atthaṃ: Matter. Khippaṃ: Quickly. Na anubujjhati: Does not understand. So: That person. Amittavasaṃ: Under the power of the enemy. Anveti: Follows. Pacchā ca: And later. Anutappati: Regrets.

Yo ca: And whoever. Uppatitaṃ: That has arisen. Atthaṃ: Matter. Khippameva: Very quickly. Nibodhati: Understands. Biḷāriyā: From the she-cat. Mutto: Released. Kukkuṭova: Like the king of roosters. Sattusambādhā: From the oppression caused by enemies. Muccate: Is released.
252:
Having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, the Omniscient Buddha identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the weary monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the birth? He said, "At that time, I, the Buddha, was the Rooster King."

## Be careful of those with sweet words; consider before acting

The Kukkuṭa Jātaka ends.

65. Practice the Dhamma, O kinsmen; practice the Dhamma, may it be a blessing to you.
The practitioner of Dhamma dwells in happiness, in this world and in the next.

He spoke this first verse. 

O kinsmen, you birds who are my relatives. Practice the Dhamma, the practice of good conduct in body and so forth. Practice the Dhamma, practice it repeatedly. May it be a blessing to you; it will be for your benefit. The practitioner of Dhamma dwells in happiness; he sleeps in happiness. This is the head of the teaching: the practitioner of Dhamma stands, walks, sits, and sleeps in happiness; he is happy in all four postures.

## 9. Dhamma-dhaja Jātaka

## About the foolish crow who pretended to be a holy person

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Dhamma-dhaja Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Dhammaṃ caratha ñātayo," regarding a hypocritical monk.

At that time, the Omniscient Buddha said, "Monks, not only now is this monk a hypocrite; in the past, he was also a hypocrite," and he brought the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the family of birds. When he reached maturity, he lived on a small island in the middle of the ocean, surrounded by a flock of birds. At that time, some merchants living in the kingdom of Kāsi took a direction-finding crow (disākāka) and set out to sea by ship.

## The crow pretending to be a holy bird

When the ship was wrecked in the middle of the ocean, the direction-finding crow reached that small island and thought, "This flock of birds is large. I should perform an act of hypocrisy and eat their eggs and young ones one by one."

Having thought so, the crow descended into the midst of the birds, opened his mouth, and stood on the ground on only one leg. When asked by the birds, "Sir, what is your name?", he replied, "I am named Dhammika (The Righteous One)." They asked, "Why do you stand on only one leg?" He replied, "If I were to put down my second leg, the earth would not be able to support it." They asked, "Why do you stand with your mouth open?" He replied, "I eat no other food; I eat only the wind."
253:
66. How good indeed is this bird, a bird of supreme righteousness.
Standing on one leg, he speaks only of the Dhamma.

He spoke this verse which completes the two.

O birds, this bird is indeed good. He is of supreme righteous character. Standing on one leg, he speaks and admonishes only the Dhamma.

67. You do not know his character, yet you praise him without knowing.
Having eaten both the eggs and the young, he speaks, "Dhamma, Dhamma."

68. He says one thing with his speech, but does another with his body.
He is not established in the Dhamma by speech alone, but not by body.

69. His speech is kind, but his mind is a pit of misery (corrupt),
Hidden like a black snake in its hole.
He carries the flag of Dhamma (as a pretense) in villages and towns,
But he is difficult to be known by a foolish person.

70. Strike him with your beaks and wings, and harm him with your feet.
Destroy this corpse-like creature; he is not worthy of living together.

After saying this, he called the birds and said, "I will give you an admonition. Listen to that admonition," and by way of giving advice:

## The birds believed him

The birds, not knowing that "this crow speaks thus to eat the eggs by practicing hypocrisy," praised that crow.

## The wicked crow eating the bird eggs

The birds, trusting that immoral crow, said, "Sir, it is said you take no other food and eat only the wind. Therefore, please look after our eggs and our young ones," and they went to search for food.

When the birds were gone, the wicked crow ate the eggs and the young ones until his belly was full. When the birds returned, he became very calm, opened his mouth, and stood on one leg. When the birds returned and did not see their young ones, they cried out with a loud sound, "Who has eaten them?" They did not have even a slight suspicion, thinking, "This crow is righteous."

## The Bird King thought

Then one day, the Bodhisatta thought, "In this place, there was no danger before. It has arisen since the time this crow arrived. It is proper to investigate him." Having thought so, the Bodhisatta acted as if he were going to search for food with the birds, but turned back and stayed in a hidden place.

The crow, being free from suspicion that the birds had gone, got up, went and ate the eggs and the young ones, then returned, opened his mouth, and stood on one leg.

## Kill the wicked crow

When the birds returned, the Bird King gathered all the birds and addressed the flock, "While I was investigating the enemy of your young ones today, I saw this wicked crow eating them. Come, let us catch him!" He surrounded the crow and said, "If he flees, catch him!" and spoke these verses.
254:
O birds! You do not know the virtue of this crow. Without knowing, you praise him. Having eaten eggs and young ones, he says, 'Dhamma, Dhamma.'

With his speech, he says one thing; with his body, he does another. With his speech, he practices the Dhamma; but with his body, he does not. He is not established in that Dhamma.

In speech, he is pleasant; in mind, he is impenetrable. He is like a cobra lying in a hidden hole. He is a 'Dhamma-banner' (hypocrite). In villages and market towns, he is renowned as a good man. This wicked bird is difficult for a foolish man to recognize.

Attack this crow with your beaks, wings, and feet! Destroy this wretched crow! Indeed, he is not worthy of living with us.

## The Wicked Crow Dies

Having said this, the king of birds himself leaped up and struck the crow's head with his beak. The remaining birds struck him with their beaks, feet, and wings. The crow died right there.

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the monk who makes a false show was the crow; I myself was the king of the birds."

## Speech is Dhamma, Action is Wrong; One Falls into Ruin

The Dhammadhaja Jātaka is concluded.
255:
## 10. Nandiyamigarāja Jātaka
## On Supporting Parents at the Cost of One's Life

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Nandiyamigarāja Jātaka, starting with the verse "Sace brāhmaṇa gacchesi," concerning a monk who supported his mother.

The Teacher asked, "Monk, is it true that you support laypeople?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher asked, "Whom do you support?" The monk answered, "Exalted One, I support my mother and father." The Teacher said, "Excellent, excellent, monk! You are maintaining the lineage of the wise of old. Even when born in the animal kingdom, the wise of old gave their lives for their parents." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when the King of Kosala was reigning in Sāketa in the kingdom of Kosala, the Bodhisatta was born in the womb of a deer. When he reached maturity, he was named Nandiya. Being endowed with virtue and good conduct, he supported his parents.

At that time, the King of Kosala was very fond of hunting deer. He did not allow the people to do their farming and other work, but went hunting every day with a large retinue.

## Driving the Deer into the Enclosure

The people gathered and consulted: "Sirs, this king is causing our work to cease. Our household affairs are being ruined. What if we were to fence the Añjanavana park, fix a gate, dig a pond, and plant grass? Then, holding sticks, clubs, and other weapons, we could enter the forest, beat the bushes, drive out the deer, and herd them into the park like cattle into a pen. After closing the gate, we could inform the king and then attend to our own work."

Knowing this plan, all the people agreed. They prepared the park, entered the forest, and surrounded an area of one league. At that moment, the deer Nandiya was lying on the ground in a small bush, having taken his parents there. The people, holding various shields and weapons, pressed close together and struck the bushes. Then, some people, looking for deer, entered that bush.
256:
71. If, O Brahmin, you go to Sāketa, to the Arjuna forest,
Tell Nandiya, our own dear son,
That your mother and father are old, and they wish to see you.

This was the first verse spoken.

Brahmin, O Brahmin. Tvaṃ, you. Sāketaṃ, to the city of Sāketa. Sace gacchesi, if you should go. Sākete, in the city of Sāketa. Arjunaṃ vanaṃ, the Arjuna forest park. Atthi, there is. Tattha, in that park. Asmākaṃ, our. Orasaṃ, born of our breast. Nandiyaṃ nāma, named Nandiya. Puttaṃ, to our son. Te, your. Mātāpitā ca, parents also. Vuddhā, have grown old. Te, those parents. Taṃ, you. Passituṃ, to see. Icchanti, they desire. Iti, thus. Vajjāsi, please tell him.

Nandiya the deer king, seeing the humans, thought, "Today it is proper that I should sacrifice my life to give life to my parents." He rose, paid respects to his mother and father, and said, "Mother and Father, these people will enter this thicket and kill the three of us. It is better for you to live through this one means. I will offer my life for you. When the people stand at the edge of the thicket and beat the bushes, I will emerge. At that time, the people will think there is only one deer in this small thicket and will not enter. May you both be heedful." Having paid homage to his parents, he stood ready to depart.

That Nandiya deer emerged from the thicket just as the people stood at the edge, making echoes and beating the bushes. The people, thinking there was only one deer in the thicket, did not enter. Then Nandiya went and joined the other deer. The people surrounded all the deer, drove them into the park, closed the gate, informed the King, and returned to their respective places.

## The Parents' Desire to See Their Son

From then on, the King himself would go, shoot one deer, and take it. Or he would send someone to fetch one. The deer established a turn. The deer whose turn it was would stand in a suitable place. The King would shoot and take that deer.

Nandiya the deer drank water from the pond and ate grass. His turn had not yet arrived.

Then, after many days had passed, the parents of that Nandiya deer king, wishing to see him, thought, "Our son Nandiya the deer king is as strong as a noble elephant and full of power. If he is alive, he will surely jump the fence and come to see us. Let us send a message to him." Standing near the road, they saw a Brahmin and asked in human speech, "Sir, where are you going?" When he replied, "To Sāketa," they wished to send a message to their son—
257:
72. I have eaten the rations, the King's food and drink.
I do not dare, O Brahmin, to consume that royal morsel ungratefully.

73. I will offer my side to the King's barbed arrows.
Then, being happy and free, I might see my mother.

These two verses were spoken.

Brahmin, O Brahmin. Mayā, by me. Rājino, the King's. Nivāpāni, rations. Bhuttā, have been eaten. Pānabhojanaṃ, the water and grass fodder. Bhuttaṃ, has been consumed. Rājapiṇḍaṃ, that food gathered by the King. Taṃ, that. Avabhottaṃ, to consume ungratefully (badly). Na ussahe, I do not dare.

Brahmin, O Brahmin. Assa rājino, of that King. Khurappāni, the barbed arrows. Ahaṃ, I. Passaṃ-passena, with my right side. Odahissāmi, will receive. Tadā, at that time. Ahaṃ, I. Sukhito, being happy. Mutto, being free from the fear of death. Mātaraṃ, my mother. Api passeyyaṃ, might see.

## Will Come Only When All Are Safe

That Brahmin agreed, saying "Very well," and upon reaching Sāketa, he entered the park the next day and asked, "Which deer is named Nandiya?" Nandiya the deer stood near the Brahmin and said, "It is I." The Brahmin informed him of the matter.

Hearing those words, Nandiya said, "Brahmin, it is not that I cannot jump the fence and go; I certainly can. However, I have eaten the rations and food that belong to the King, and thus I stand in the position of a debtor. I have also lived for a long time among this herd of deer. It is not proper for me to go by showing my own strength without ensuring the welfare of the King and these deer. When my own turn arrives, I shall ensure the safety of these deer and then come back happily." Desiring to explain this matter, he spoke the verses.

## The Deer King is Not Hit by the Arrow

After hearing those words, the Brahmin departed. Later, on the day of Nandiya the deer king's turn, the King came to the park with a large retinue. The Bodhisatta stood in a suitable place.

The King prepared his arrow, thinking, "I shall shoot the deer." The Bodhisatta, unlike other deer who flee being terrified by the fear of death, did not flee. Being fearless and placing loving-kindness (mettā) at the forefront, he stood perfectly still, offering his right side. Due to the power of the deer king's loving-kindness, the King was unable to release the arrow.

The Bodhisatta said, "Great King, why do you not release the arrow? Release it!" "Deer king, I am unable to release the arrow," the King replied. "If that is so, Great King, recognize the virtue of the virtuous," said the Bodhisatta.

## Granting Immunity

Then the King, being inspired by the Bodhisatta, discarded his bow and said, "Even this mindless arrow already knows your virtue. Although I am a mindful human, I did not know your virtue. Deer king, forgive me. I grant you immunity (freedom from fear)."
258:
74. I was formerly a deer king in the residence of the Kosalan king, named Nandiya, a handsome four-footed creature.
75. The Kosalan king came to kill me in the Ajjuna forest grove, having strung his bow and prepared his arrow.
76. I offered my side to the king's arrow; then I was happy and released, and have come to see my mother.

The Teacher preached these three verses.

O monks, in the past, in the capital of the Kosalan king, there was a deer king named Nandiya, who was very beautiful and four-footed.

O monks, the Kosalan king came to the Ajjuna forest grove, which was filled with Ajjuna trees, to kill me. He came having strung his bow and prepared his arrow.

I offered my right side to him. I offered myself to the king's arrows. At that time, I was happy, being released from the fear of death, and I have come to see my mother.

"Great King, you have first granted me safety; but what will you do for the multitude of deer in the park?" he asked. "I grant safety to those deer as well," the king replied.

## Preaching the Dhamma
In this way, the Great Being, following the method described in the Nigrodha Jātaka, secured safety for all forest animals, for the birds that fly in the sky, and for the fish that live in the water. He established the king in the Five Precepts and said, "Great King, a king should abandon bias and rule with righteousness and justice, in accordance with the Ten Royal Virtues."

Generosity, virtue, self-sacrifice, integrity, gentleness, austerity,
Non-anger, non-violence, patience, and non-opposition.
When I see these wholesome qualities established in myself,
Then there arises in me joy and no small amount of happiness.

## Visiting the Parents
Having thus shown the Ten Royal Virtues in the form of verses, the deer king stayed with the king for a few days. To announce the granting of safety to all beings in the city, he had the golden drum beaten. He said, "Great King, be diligent," and then departed to see his parents.

Bringing forth this past story, the All-Enlightened One...
259:
The All-Enlightened One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. As for the identification of the Jātaka: "The royal family of that time are now the Great Royal Family; the Brahmin of that time was Sāriputta; the king of that time was Ānanda; and the deer king Nandiya was I myself."

## Even as an Animal, He Sacrificed His Life for His Parents
The Nandiyamigarāja Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Kharaputta Vagga
## 1. Kharaputta Jātaka
## Why One Should Not Follow a Woman's Desires
The Story of the Present: While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kharaputta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Saccaṃ kira evamāhaṃsu," concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

The All-Enlightened One asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you are discontented?" When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha asked, "Who caused your discontent?" He replied, "Exalted One, my former wife caused my discontent." The Buddha said, "Monk, this woman causes you harm. In the past, because of this woman, you were about to die by entering a fire, but you regained your life because of the wise," and he brought forth the past story.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Senaka was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as Sakka. At that time, King Senaka was friends with a certain Nāga king.

## Saving the Nāga King
That Nāga king would leave the Nāga realm and wander on land in search of food. Then, village boys saw him and, thinking "This is a snake," attacked him with clods of earth, sticks, and so on.

At that time, the king, while going to play in the park, saw this and asked, "What are these boys doing?" Hearing that they were attacking a snake, he said, "Do not let them attack it; drive those boys away," and he had the boys driven away.

## Gratitude Repaid
The Nāga king, having regained his life, went to the Nāga realm, took many jewels, and entered the king's bedchamber at midnight. Showing those jewels, he said, "Great King, I have regained my life because of you." He formed a friendship with the king and visited him repeatedly.

That Nāga king left one of his young Nāga maidens, who was insatiable in sensual pleasures, with King Senaka to be protected. He gave the king a mantra, saying, "Whenever you do not see that Nāga maiden, recite this mantra."
260:
## The Misconduct of the Naga Maiden
One day, King Senaka went to the park and played in the water with a young Naga maiden. The Naga maiden saw a water snake, abandoned her [Naga] form, and committed misconduct with that water snake. The King, not seeing the Naga maiden, recited the mantra [to see her], and upon seeing her committing misconduct, struck her with a bamboo split.

## The Naga Maiden Slanders
The young Naga maiden became angry and went from that park to the Naga realm. When asked, "Why have you come?" she showed the marks of the strike and said, "The King, who is your friend, struck me on the back, saying I did not follow his words."

## The Naga King's Anger
The Naga King, not knowing the truth, summoned four young Nagas and said, "Go, enter King Senaka's bedchamber and destroy him with your poisonous breath like chaff." Those young Nagas went and entered the chamber while the King was lying in his royal bed.

## Receiving the Mantra
At the moment the young Nagas entered, the King said to the Queen, "My Queen, do you know where the young Naga maiden has gone?" "I do not know, O King," she replied. "Today, while we were playing in the water in our pond, that Naga maiden abandoned her form and committed misconduct with a water snake. Therefore, to teach her a lesson so she would not do so again, I struck her with a bamboo split. I fear that she might go to the Naga realm and say something else to my friend to break our friendship. If our friendship is broken, some danger will come to me."

Hearing these words, the young Nagas returned from King Senaka's chamber to the Naga realm and reported the matter to the Naga King. The Naga King was struck with remorse and immediately went to the King's bedchamber. He explained the matter, asked for forgiveness, and saying, "This is my compensation for the wrong done," gave him the mantra called Sabba-ruta-jānana (Knowledge of all sounds). He said, "Great King, this mantra is priceless. If you give this mantra to another person, you must enter the fire and die immediately after giving it." The King accepted, saying, "Very well." From that time on, King Senaka understood even the sounds of ants.
261:
One day, while King Senaka was sitting on the upper terrace eating sweets made with honey and syrup, a drop of honey, a drop of syrup, and a piece of cake fell to the ground. An ant saw them and wandered about crying out, "A honey jar has broken on the King's upper terrace! A syrup cart and a cake cart have overturned! Come and eat the honey, syrup, and cake!"

## Understanding the Speech of Animals
Then the King, hearing the sound of that ant, laughed. The Queen, standing near the King, thought, "What did the King see that made him laugh?"

While the King was sitting on his throne after eating and bathing, a male fly said to a female fly, "Come, my dear, let us enjoy ourselves in sensual pleasure." Then the female fly said to the male fly, "Wait a moment, master. Now they will bring perfumes for the King. When the King is being anointed, perfume powder will fall at his feet. I will roll in that perfume powder and become fragrant. After that, we shall enjoy ourselves on the King's back."

The King, hearing that sound as well, laughed. The Queen again thought, "What did he see that made him laugh?" Again, while the King was eating his evening meal, a grain of rice fell to the ground. An ant cried out, "A rice cart has broken in the royal palace! Come and eat the rice!" Hearing those words, the King laughed once more.

## Promising the Queen
The Queen, holding a golden ladle and serving him, thought, "Is the King laughing at me?" Having thought so, when she went up to bed with the King, she asked, "Great King, why did you laugh?" When the King said, "What use is the reason for my laughter to you?" the Queen pressed him repeatedly. The King then told her.

Then the Queen said to the King, "Give me the mantra that you know." Even though he refused, saying, "It cannot be given," she continued to press and beg. The King said, "If I give this mantra to you, I shall die." She replied, "O King, give it to me even if you die." The King, falling under the influence of the woman, accepted, saying, "Very well." He decided to give the mantra to the Queen and then enter the fire, so he set out for the park by chariot.

## Sakka's Admonition
At that moment, Sakka, looking down upon the world, saw this matter and thought, "This foolish King is going to enter the fire because of a woman. I will give him the gift of life." He took Sujātā, the daughter of the Asura King, went to Bārāṇasī, turned her into a she-goat, and he himself became a he-goat. He resolved, "Let the common people not see me," and stood before the King.

The King and the Sindh horses yoked to the chariot saw the goat, but no one else saw him.

That [he-]goat, in order to start a conversation, acted as if he were committing misconduct with the she-goat in front of the chariot.

Hearing those words, the King of Goats, wishing to explain, spoke this fifth verse:

5. "Having obtained the supreme goal, he who gives it to his wife, by that he will lose himself, and she will not be his."

## One should love only oneself

Then, the King, hearing the goat's words, said, "King of Goats... if you are to act for our welfare, you shall do so; first, tell us the proper course of action."

At that time, the King of Goats said to King Senaka, "Great King... for these beings, there is no one dearer than oneself. It is not fit to destroy oneself or give up attained glory for the sake of one dear object." Having said this, he spoke:

## Teach her only after she receives the lash

In this way, the Bodhisatta gave advice to the King. The King was pleased and asked, "King of Goats... where have you come from?" "Great King... I am Sakka; out of compassion for you, I have come to save you from the danger of death," he replied. "King of the Devas... I have already said to that woman, 'I will give you the mantra.' What should I do now?" the King asked.

"Great King... there is no need for the destruction of both of you. Say that you will perform the ritual for the craft, and then have that Queen struck two or three times. By this means, she will not take it," Sakka said. The King agreed, saying, "Very well." The Bodhisatta, having advised the King, went to his own place, the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
264:
King Senaka went to the garden, summoned the Queen, and asked, "Queen, will you take the mantra?" "Great King, I will," she said. "If so, then perform the ritual," he said. "What is the ritual?" she asked. "Even when a hundred lashes are dealt upon your back, it is not proper to make a sound," he said.

The Queen, being greedy for the mantra, agreed, saying, "Very well." The King summoned the executioners and had them take canes and strike her on both sides. The Queen endured two or three lashes, but when struck further, she cried out, "I have no need for the mantra!"

Then the King said to the Queen, "You wished to kill me to take the mantra," and after having her back lashed until the skin was gone, he released her. From that time on, she was unable to speak of it again.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and illustrated the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). To identify the Jātaka: The discontented monk of now was then King Senaka. The former wife was then the Queen. Sāriputta was then the horse. I, the Buddha, was then Sakka. Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Keep your promise firmly, never break it at any time

The Kharaputta Jātaka ends.

7. Smooth, not rough, polished with stone, well-eyed.
Fine and sharp-pointed; who wishes to buy this needle?
He spoke this first verse.
*Akakkasaṃ*, without dross. *Apharusaṃ*, not coarse. *Kharadhotaṃ*, polished with a whetstone. *Supāsiyaṃ*, with a well-pierced eye. *Sukhuman*, delicate. *Tikhinaggañca*, having a sharp point. *Sūciṃ*, the needle. *Ko*, who. *Ketum*, to buy. *Icchati*, desires?

## 2. Sūci Jātaka
## Fulfillment of Desire through the Power of Wisdom
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sūci Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Akakkasaṃ apharusaṃ," concerning the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññāpāramī).

The story of the present will be clearly manifested in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka. At that time, the All-Enlightened Buddha addressed the monks, saying, "Monks, not only now is the Tathāgata wise and skillful in means; in the past also, the Tathāgata was wise and skillful in means," and he related the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a smith's family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he came of age, he became fully proficient in his craft. His parents were poor. Near their village, there was another smiths' village of a thousand houses.

## The Beautiful Daughter of the Head Smith
In that village, the head smith of the thousand smiths was a favorite of the king. He was wealthy and possessed great riches. The head smith had a daughter who possessed supreme beauty. She was like a celestial nymph and was endowed with the marks of a Janapadakalyāṇī (the Belle of the Country).

People from the surrounding villages would go to that village to have adzes, axes, plowshares, goads, and so on made, and they mostly saw the young maiden. When those people returned to their own villages, they would praise her beauty in their meeting places and elsewhere.

## The Young Smith Sells a Needle
The Bodhisatta, upon hearing those words, became bound by the mere hearing of her. Thinking, "I will make her my wife," he took some high-quality iron and made a single delicate needle. He pierced the eye and made it so it would float on water. Then he made another needle-case of the same kind and pierced its eye.
266:
8. Well-polished, well-eyed, gradually tapered and well-rounded.
Solid-struck and firm; who wishes to buy this needle?
He spoke this second verse.
*Sumajjañca*, well-polished with Kuruviṇḍaka stone powder. *Supāsiyaṃ*, with a well-pierced eye. *Anupubbaṃ*, gradually. *Suvaṭṭitaṃ*, well-rounded. *Ghanaghātimaṃ*, which, when struck with a hammer, penetrates the anvil; such is the meaning. *Paṭithaddaṃ*, very hard, not soft. *Sūciṃ*, the needle. *Ko*, who. *Ketum*, to buy. *Icchati*, desires?

In this manner, he made seven cases for that needle.
★ It should not be said, "How could he be able to do this?" For the Bodhisattas, because of the greatness of their wisdom, the task is indeed accomplished. ★

The Bodhisatta placed the needle in a needle-tube, put it in his waist-pocket, and went to that village. Having asked for the street where the head smith lived, he went to that house, stood at the door, and praising the needle, said, "Who from my hand wishes to buy such a needle for a price?" Standing at the door of the head smith's house—
Having said this, wishing to praise the needle again—

## Do Not Come to Sell Needles in a Smiths' Village
At that moment, the maiden, having finished her morning meal, was fanning her father with a palmyra fan as he lay on a small couch to relieve his fatigue. Hearing the sweet voice of the Bodhisatta, it was as if her heart was struck by a moist lump of meat, or as if her fatigue was quenched by a thousand jars of water poured over her. Thinking, "Who is this selling a needle in the smiths' village with such a sweet voice? Who is he, and for what purpose has he come? I shall find out," she put down the palmyra fan, left the house, stood on the outer veranda, and spoke with him.

For Bodhisattas, what is desired is fulfilled. Indeed, he had come to that village for the sake of that maiden. She, speaking with the Bodhisatta, said, "Young man, people living in the whole country come to this village for the sake of needles and such. You, out of foolishness, wish to sell a needle in the smiths' village. Even if you speak of the needle's virtues all day long, no one will buy a needle from your hand. If you wish to get a price, go to another village." Saying this, she spoke these two verses:

9. From here now are sent out needles and fishhooks.
Who is this that wishes to sell a needle in a smiths' village?
10. From here go out weapons and various extensive works.
Who is this that wishes to sell a needle in a smiths' village?

*Māṇava*, young man. *Idāni*, now. *Ito*, from this village. *Sūciyo ca*, needles. *Baḷisāni ca*, fishhooks. *Patāyanti*, go out. *Kammāragāmasmiṃ*, in such a smiths' village. *Yo*, he who. *Sūciṃ*, a needle. *Vikketuṃ*, to sell. *Icchati*, desires. *Ayaṃ*, this person. *Ko*, who is he?

*Māṇava*, young man. *Ito*, from this village. *Satthāni ca*, merchants who trade in collections of goods such as knives, drills, and chisels. *Vividhā*, of various kinds. *Kammantā*, workers. *Puthū*, many. *Gacchanti*, go out. *Kammāragāmasmiṃ*, in such a smiths' village. *Yo*, he who. *Sūciṃ*, a needle. *Vikketuṃ*, to sell. *Icchati*, desires. *Ayaṃ*, this person. *Ko*, what kind of person is he?

## The Smiths Will Know Better
The Bodhisatta, hearing the maiden's words, said, "Sister, you do not know; you speak thus because of your ignorance."

## The Smiths Must Snap Their Fingers in Admiration
Thus, the Bodhisatta praised his own merit with this verse. The head smith, hearing all their conversation, called his daughter, "Dear," and asked, "With whom are you speaking?" "Father, someone has come to sell a needle; I am speaking with him," she said. "Call that man who sells needles," he said.
267:
11. "A needle should be sold in a blacksmith village by one who knows. Only masters know the work well-done or poorly-done."

12. "If your father, dear girl, knew this needle made by me, he would invite me with you and whatever other wealth is in the house."

He spoke these two verses.

Dear girl, a wise man should sell a needle only in a blacksmith village. Only blacksmith masters know whether a work is well-done or poorly-done.

Dear girl, if your father knew this needle of special quality made by me, he would invite me with you. He would also invite me with whatever other wealth exists in this house besides you.

The young woman went and called him. The Bodhisatta entered the house, paid respects to the head blacksmith, and sat in a suitable place. Then he was asked, "From which village are you?" He replied, "From such-and-such a village." "Whose son are you?" "The son of such-and-such." "Why have you come here?" "I have come to sell a needle."

When told, "Let us see your needle," the Bodhisatta, wishing to display his merit in the midst of all the people, said, "It should not be seen by one person alone. Seeing it in the midst of all the people is far better than seeing it alone."

The head blacksmith said, "Very well, young man," and gathered all the blacksmiths. Surrounded by them, he said, "We shall see; produce your needle." The Bodhisatta said, "Teacher, please have an anvil and a bronze bowl filled with water brought here." The head blacksmith had them brought.

The Bodhisatta took a needle case from his waist-pocket and gave it. The head blacksmith took a needle from the case and asked, "Young man, is this the needle?" "This is not the needle; it is the needle case," he replied. When the head blacksmith examined it, he could see neither the end nor the edge.

The Bodhisatta took it, gradually removed the needle sheath with his fingernail, and showing it to the people, said, "This is the needle sheath," and placed it at the teacher's feet. Again, when the head blacksmith said, "This, I think, is the needle," he said, "This too is just a needle sheath," and peeling it with his fingernail, he placed six needle sheaths in succession at the head blacksmith's feet, then placed the actual needle in the head blacksmith's hand. A thousand blacksmiths snapped their fingers and tossed their upper garments in the air.
268:
## The Great Power of the Needle
Then the head blacksmith asked the Bodhisatta, "Young man, what power does this needle have?" He replied, "Teacher, have a strong man lift the anvil, place a bronze bowl filled with water under the anvil, and strike this needle into the middle of the anvil." The head blacksmith did as the Bodhisatta said and struck the needle's point into the middle of the anvil.

That needle pierced the anvil and remained floating on the surface of the water, neither rising even a hair's breadth above nor sinking below, but staying level.

All the blacksmiths snapped their fingers and tossed a thousand upper garments, saying, "In all this time, we have never even heard it said that blacksmiths could be like this."

## Winning the Maiden
The head blacksmith called his daughter and, in the midst of that assembly, poured water [on their hands] and gave her, saying, "This maiden is worthy of you alone." Later, upon the death of the head blacksmith, the Bodhisatta became the head blacksmith in that very village.
269:
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the daughter of the head blacksmith was the mother of Rāhula, and I myself was the wise blacksmith."

## Only by showing wisdom to the wise will one surely become famous.
The Sūci Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Tuṇḍila Jātaka
## Escaping the Fear of Death through Courage
The Story of the Present: While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who is the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Tuṇḍila Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Navachannake," concerning a monk who was afraid of death.

That monk was a son of a good family living in Sāvatthī. Having ordained in the Buddha's Dispensation, he was fearful of death. Hearing even the slight rustling of a branch, the falling of a stick, the sound of a bird or a four-footed animal, or any other such sound, he would be terrified by the fear of death and go about trembling in his vitals.

The monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, they say such-and-such a monk is afraid of death; hearing even a slight sound, he trembles and flees. For these beings, death alone is certain, life is uncertain. Should one not reflect on this with wise attention?"

The All-Knowing Buddha came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered now?" When they replied, "For such-and-such a discussion," he had that monk summoned and asked, "Monk, is it true that you are afraid of death?" When the monk admitted, "It is true, Blessed One," the Buddha said, "Monks, not only now is he afraid of death; in the past too, he was fearful of death," and he brought the story of the past.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of a sow. When the sow's pregnancy was mature, she gave birth to two young pigs. One day, she took her young and lay down in a pit.
270:
13. Now a new meal is given,
The trough is full, the mistress stands by.
Many people with snares in hand are here,
It does not please me to eat.

He spoke this first verse:

Brother. Now, at this time. Navachannake: the pig trough filled with new food. Diyyati: is given. Ayaṃ doṇi: this trough. Puṇṇā: is full of clean food. Suvāminī: our mother also. Ṭhitā: stands near the trough. Pāsapāṇike: having snares in their hands. Bahuke jane: many people also. Ṭhito: stand near the trough. Idaṃ bhattaṃ: this food. Or, this food. Bhuñjituṃ: to eat. Me: to me. No ca kho paṭibhāti: does not bring delight.

## Two Young Pigs
At that time, an old woman living at the gate of the city of Bārāṇasī was coming from a cotton field with a basket full of cotton, leaning on a staff. A wild sow, hearing that sound and fearing death, fled, abandoning her two young piglets. The old woman saw the piglets, treated them as her own sons, put them in her basket, and brought them home. She named the elder "Mahātuṇḍila" and the younger "Cūḷatuṇḍila," and raised them like her own children. Later, those piglets grew up and had well-filled bodies.

## The Pig is Sold
When people said, "Give these pigs to us for a price," the old woman replied, "These pigs are my sons," and would not give them to anyone.

Then, during a festival, some drunkards were drinking liquor. When their meat ran out, they wondered where they could find meat. Learning that there were pigs at the old woman's house, they took money, went to the house, and said, "Mother... take this money and give us one pig." The old woman refused, saying, "Dear ones... these pigs are my sons. I do not want your money."
271:
14. You tremble, you wander, you seek a shelter,
You are without protection, where will you go?
Eat without anxiety, Tuṇḍila,
For we have been reared for the sake of our meat.

15. Plunge into the mudless lake,
Wash away all the sweat and impurity.
Take the new ointment,
Whose fragrance never fades.

He spoke these two verses:

Dear Tuṇḍila, younger brother Cūḷatuṇḍila. Tvaṃ: you. Tasasi: tremble. Bhamasi: wander. Leṇaṃ: a hiding place. Icchasi: desire. Attāṇo: without protection. Asi: you are. Kuhiṃ: where. Gamissasi: will you go? Appossukko: without anxiety. Bhuñja: eat. Maṃsatthāya hi: only for the sake of meat. Positāmhase: we have been reared.

Akaddamaṃ: without mud. Rahadaṃ: into the lake. Ogaha: plunge. Sabbaṃ: all. Sedamalaṃ: sweat and impurity. Pavāhaya: wash away. Yassa: of which ointment. Gandho: the scent. Kadāci: at any time. Na chijjati: does not fade. Navaṃ: new. Taṃ vilepanaṃ: that ointment. Gaṇhāhi: take.

The drunkards said, "Mother... pigs are not the sons of humans; give us those pigs." Even though they pleaded repeatedly, they did not get them. So they made the old woman drink liquor, and when she was drunk, they said, "Mother... what will you do with the pigs? Take the money and use it for your provisions," and they placed the coins in her hand. The old woman took the coins and said, "Dear ones... I cannot give Mahātuṇḍila. Take Cūḷatuṇḍila."

## Fearing and Refusing Capture
They asked, "Where is that Cūḷatuṇḍila?" She said, "He is in a certain bush," and the drunkards had a bowl of rice brought with the money. The old woman took the rice and filled the pig trough at the gate and stood near it. About thirty drunkards also stood there, holding snares in their hands.

The old woman called out to Cūḷatuṇḍila, "Dear son Cūḷatuṇḍila... come!" Mahātuṇḍila heard that sound and thought, "For all this time, my mother has never called Cūḷatuṇḍila first; she always calls me first. Today, surely, the danger of death has come to us." Realizing this, Mahātuṇḍila called his brother and said, "Younger brother Cūḷatuṇḍila... mother is calling you; go and find out first."

Cūḷatuṇḍila came out of the bush and, seeing the men standing near the rice trough, thought, "Today the danger of death has reached me." Terrified by the fear of death, he returned trembling to his brother, unable to stand firm, and collapsed while shaking.

Mahātuṇḍila saw Cūḷatuṇḍila and asked, "Younger brother Cūḷatuṇḍila... you are collapsing now. You look for a place to flee. For what reason do you do this?" Cūḷatuṇḍila, wishing to tell what he had seen, said:

## Undertake the Precepts
Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta said, "Younger brother Cūḷatuṇḍila... our mother who reared the pigs in this place did so for a certain purpose; that purpose has reached its end today. Do not worry." Wishing to preach the Dhamma with a sweet voice and the grace of a Buddha:

Reflecting on the ten perfections (pāramīs) and placing the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī) at the forefront, as soon as the Bodhisatta began chanting the verse, his voice spread and covered the entire city of Bārāṇasī, which was twelve leagues in extent.

At the very moment they heard it, the people living in Bārāṇasī, starting with the sub-king and others, came. Those who did not come listened while staying in their houses.
272:
16. What is the lake that is free from mud?
What is called the impurity of sweat?
What is the new ointment
Whose fragrance never fades?

He spoke this fourth verse. 

'Free from mud' means without mire. 'Lake' refers to a body of water. 'What is it?' 'What indeed' is called 'the impurity of sweat'? 'Whose fragrance' of that ointment 'never fades' at any time? 'What is' that 'new ointment'?

17. Dhamma is the lake free from mud,
Evil is called the impurity of sweat.
Virtue is the new ointment,
Whose fragrance never fades.

18. Slayers of bodies rejoice,

The king's attendants cleared the bushes, leveled the ground, and scattered sand. The intoxication of the drunkards vanished. They cast away their snares and stood there merely listening to the Dhamma. The old woman's intoxication also vanished. The Great Being began the Dhamma teaching to Cūḷatundila in the midst of the crowd.

Hearing those words, Cūḷatundila thought: "My brother speaks thus. In our lineage, there is no time for descending into a lake to wash the impurity of sweat from the body, nor for taking new ointment. To what is my brother referring when he speaks to me thus?" Wishing to ask, he spoke the verse.

Hearing that, the Great Being said, "Younger brother Cūḷatundila, if that is so, listen with attentive ears." Wishing to preach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, he spoke these verses:

But those who bear bodies do not rejoice.
On the full moon day,
They give up life while delighting.

Dear Cūḷatundila, the Dhamma of Nibbāna is called the lake free from the mud of defilements. Evil is...
273:
...called the impurity of sweat. Virtue is called the new ointment. Its fragrance never fades.

Those who slay beings rejoice. Those who bear bodies do not rejoice. On the full moon day, those endowed with virtue and conduct give up their lives while delighting.
274:
Thus, the Great Being preached the Dhamma with a sweet voice and the grace of a Buddha. The great crowd of people snapped their fingers and waved their garments. The sky was filled with the sound of "Sādhu."

## The King Rescues

The King of Vārāṇasī honored the Great Being with the kingship, gave wealth to the old woman, took the two pigs, bathed them in scented water, anointed them with perfumes and such, adorned their necks with jewels, brought them to the city, treated them as sons, and looked after them with a great retinue.

The Great Being, the King of Pigs, gave the five precepts. All the inhabitants of Vārāṇasī also observed the five precepts. The Great Being preached the Dhamma to them on the Uposatha days. He sat in the place of judgment and decided cases. While the Great Being was present, there were no people who practiced crooked or deceitful ways.

Later, the King died. The Great Being had the King's body honored and cremated. He had the judgments written on palm leaves and said, "Judge cases by looking at this book." He exhorted the people to be heedful and, while everyone wept, he entered the forest with Cūḷatundila. At that time, the Great Being's admonition lasted for sixty thousand years.
275:
The Teacher, the Omniscient One, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was afraid of death was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. As for the identification of the Jātaka: 'At that time, Ānanda was the King, the monk afraid of death was Cūḷatuṇḍila, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and I myself was Mahātuṇḍila.'

## Truly without mud, that pond is named Nibbāna.

The Tuṇḍila Jātaka is concluded.

## 4. Suvaṇṇakakkaṭaka Jātaka
## About the Grateful Golden Crab

The Teacher, the Omniscient One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Suvaṇṇakakkaṭaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Siṅgīmigo,' concerning the Elder Ānanda's sacrifice of his life for the sake of the Teacher.

The present story up to the point of sending the archers is told in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka. The release of the elephant Dhanapāla is told in the Cūḷahaṃsa and Mahāhaṃsa Jātakas.

At that time, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: 'Friends, the Elder Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, being a trainee (sekha) who has attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), sacrificed his life for the Perfectly Enlightened One when the elephant Dhanapāla approached.'

The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you gathered now?' When they replied, 'For such a discussion,' he said, 'Monks, not only now has Ānanda sacrificed his life for me; in the past also, he sacrificed his life for me,' and he brought forth the past.
276:
In the past, when King Senaka was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a Brahmin village named Sālindiya to the east of Bārāṇasī. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a farming Brahmin family in that village. When he came of age, he established his wealth and had a field of about a thousand karīsas cultivated in a village field to the northeast of that village.

One day, the Bodhisatta went to the field with his men, ordered the workers, 'Plough!' and approached a large pond at the edge of the field to wash his face.

## Becoming Friends with the Crab

In that pond lived a crab of golden hue. It was very beautiful and pleasing to the sight. The Bodhisatta, having used a tooth-stick, went down into the pond. While the Bodhisatta was washing his face, the crab came near him. Then the Bodhisatta picked up the crab, placed it in the fold of his upper garment, and after finishing his work in the field, he placed the crab back in the pond and went home.

From then on, whenever he came to the field, he first went to the pond, placed the crab in his upper garment, and only then managed the work. Thus, their mutual intimacy became firm. The Bodhisatta came to the field regularly. His eyes were clear with the fivefold clarity and had three circles, appearing pure.

## Wanting to Eat the Brahmin's Eyes

At that time, a female crow living in a nest at the top of a palm tree at the edge of the field saw the Brahmin's eyes and, desiring to eat them, said to the male crow, 'Lord, a pregnancy craving has arisen in me.' He asked, 'What kind of craving?' She said, 'I want to eat the eyes of that Brahmin.'

'Your craving is a difficult one; who will be able to bring those eyes?' he said. She asked, 'Can you not do it?' He replied, 'I cannot.' She said, 'I know the way. In this termite mound near the palm tree, a cobra lives. Serve that cobra. That cobra will bite and kill the Brahmin. Then you can pluck out the Brahmin's eyes and bring them.'
277:
19. Siṅgīmigo āyatacakkhunetto,
Aṭṭhitaco vārisayo alomo.
Tenābhibhūto kapaṇaṃ rudāmi,
Hare sakhā kissa nu maṃ jahāsi.

He uttered this first verse:

'O friend' (hare sakhā). 'With protruding long eyes' (āyatacakkhunetto) means having eyes that are prominent and long. 'Bone-skinned' (aṭṭhitaco) means having a skin made of bone. 'Water-dweller' (vārisayo) means sleeping in water. 'Hairless' (alomo) means having no hair. 'A horned beast' (siṅgīmigo) refers to the crab, which has a golden hue. 'Overcome by him' (tenābhibhūto) means being oppressed by that crab. 'I' (ahaṃ) 'cry out piteously' (kapaṇaṃ rudāmi). 'You' (tvaṃ) 'why' (kissa nu) 'abandon me' (maṃ jahāsi)?

The male crow agreed, saying 'Very well,' and from then on served the cobra.

## Making the Snake Bite

While the Bodhisatta's sown crops were swelling, the crab grew large. Then one day, the snake said to the crow, 'Friend crow, for what reason do you serve me constantly? What task shall I perform for you?' 'Lord, your servant-maid has a craving for the eyes of a certain landowner. Therefore, I wish to obtain that Brahmin's eyes through your power,' he said.

The snake said, 'Let it be so; this task is not heavy. You shall have them.' Comforting the crow, the next day the snake lay waiting for the Brahmin's arrival, hidden by grass near the field embankment on the path he would take.

The Bodhisatta arrived, first went down to the pond, washed his face, showed his affection, called the golden crab, placed it in the fold of his upper garment, and entered the field. The snake, seeing the Bodhisatta coming, rushed forward quickly, bit him on the calf, made him fall right there, and fled toward the termite mound.

## The Crow Comes to Peck the Eyes

The falling of the Bodhisatta, the crab jumping out from the fold of the garment, and the crow coming to perch on the Bodhisatta's chest happened almost simultaneously. The crow perched and began pecking at the eyes with its beak.

The snake reached the crab.
Protecting his friend,
The crab seized the snake.

He spoke this second verse:
That snake, hissing with a great hood, reached the crab. The crab, being a friend, wishing to protect his friend the Bodhisatta, seized the snake.

Would a crab, seeking food, take.
I ask you, O long-eyed one,
For what reason are we both caught?

O crab with eyes called long eyes. A crab would not take a crow for the sake of wanting to eat. Nor would it take a black snake. However, for what reason are both of us caught? I ask you.

Who took me and leads me to the water.
If he dies, great will be my suffering,

23. Seeing my well-grown body,
Everyone would wish to harm me.
Sweet, fat, and tender meat,

## The Crab Pinches the Crow's Neck
Thinking, "Because of this crow, danger has come to my friend; if I catch this crow, the snake will come," the crab pinched the crow's neck firmly with its claw as if with a pair of tongs, causing it distress, and then loosened it slightly.

## Calling the Snake
The crow, wishing to call the snake, said, "Friend snake... why do you leave me and flee? A single crab is tormenting me greatly. As long as I am not yet dead, come quickly!"

## Catching the Snake Too
Hearing those words, the snake made a great hood and came to relieve the crow. The All-Enlightened Buddha, having attained Buddhahood, wishing to show that matter, said:

## Why Catch Us?
Then the snake thought, "Crabs do not eat crow's meat, nor do they eat snake's meat. That being so, why does this crab catch us?" Having thought so, wishing to ask the crab:

Hearing those words, the crab, wishing to state the reason for catching them:

I and he, both of us shall not be.

Let the man rise; I shall vomit the venom.
Release me and the crow quickly,
Before the venom reaches the mortal intensely.

He spoke this sixth verse:
If both of us are caught because of that man, let the man rise. I shall vomit (withdraw) the venom. Before the venom reaches the mortal (man) intensely, release me and the crow quickly.

He spoke these verses.

## Treat the Brahmin
O black snake (kaṇhasappa). The man who took me and leads me to the pond, this man is my well-wisher. If that man dies, great suffering will come to me. I and this man, both of us shall not be.

Seeing me with a well-grown body, all people would wish only to harm me. Seeing me who has good meat, fat meat, and tender meat, even crows would harass me.

## Release Both of Us
Hearing those words, the snake thought, "I will deceive this crab by some means and have both the crow and myself released." Having thought so, in order to deceive the crab:

## The Venom is Sucked Out
Hearing those words, the crab thought, "This snake wants to flee by having both creatures released through some means. He does not know my skill in means. Now, I will loosen my claw in such a way that this snake is able to move and withdraw the venom, but I will not yet release the crow." Having thought so:

## The Crab Kills the Snake and the Crow
Having said this, he loosened the claw that held the snake so that it could withdraw the venom. The snake withdrew the venom and made the Bodhisatta's body free of poison. When the Bodhisatta was free from suffering, he stood up in his natural appearance.

The crab thought, "If these two creatures recover, it will not be for the benefit of my friend. I will destroy them." Thinking thus, he cut off the heads of both creatures with his claws, as if cutting a lotus bud with a pair of scissors, and brought them to their end. The female crow fled from that place.

The Bodhisatta wrapped the snake's body around a stick and threw it onto a thicket. He released the golden crab into the pool, bathed, and went back to the village of Sālindiya. From that time on, there was even greater intimacy with the golden crab.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka by reciting the concluding verse:

26. The crow then was Devadatta.
The black snake was Māra.
The noble Ānanda was the crab.
I was then the Brahmin, the Teacher.

"Monks, at that time, Devadatta was the crow. Māra was the black snake. The venerable Ānanda was the crab. I, the Teacher who disciplines the world including the devas, was the Brahmin."

At the conclusion of the Truths, many monks became Stream-enterers and so forth. The female crow was not mentioned in the verse; she was Ciñcamāṇavikā. This should be noted.

## Dear friend, help me; a parasitic friend is useless

The Suvaṇṇakakkaṭaka Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Mayhaka Jātaka

## The Three Intentions Should Be Harmonious When Giving

The Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Mayhaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sakuṇo mayhako nāma," concerning a foreign merchant.

In Sāvatthī, there was a merchant named Āgantuka who was wealthy and possessed great riches. That merchant neither enjoyed those riches himself nor gave them to others. When various excellent and delicious foods were brought to him, he would not eat them; he ate only broken rice porridge with sour gruel. 

When clothes from the Kāsī country, scented with perfumes, were brought to him, he rejected them and wore only coarse garments. When a chariot adorned with jewels and gold and yoked with thoroughbred horses was brought to him, he rejected it and traveled in a wooden cart. When golden umbrellas were held over him, he rejected them and traveled with a leaf umbrella held over him.
281:
That merchant Āgantuka, without performing even a single meritorious deed such as giving throughout his life, died and was reborn in the Roruva hell. His wealth, being heirless, was moved to the royal palace over seven days and nights.

After the wealth had been moved, the King, having finished his morning meal, went to the Jetavana Monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat down. When asked, "Great King, why have you not come to attend upon the Buddha?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, a merchant named Āgantuka in Sāvatthī has died, and seven days and nights have passed while I was bringing his ownerless wealth to our palace.

Even though he obtained this wealth, he neither enjoyed it himself nor gave it to others. His wealth was like a lotus pond guarded by a demon. Without enjoying the taste of excellent food and such even for a single day, he entered the jaws of death. What did such a stingy person of little merit do to obtain so much wealth? And why did his mind not take delight in his possessions?" Thus he asked the Teacher.

The Teacher said, "Great King, both the acquisition of wealth and the reason for not being able to enjoy it after acquiring it were done by himself," and being requested by King Kosala, he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: (1) Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there was a merchant in Benares who was faithless and stingy. He gave nothing to anyone and did not fulfill anyone's wishes.

## Preliminary and Relinquishing Intentions

One day, while going to attend upon the King, he saw a Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī walking for alms. He paid homage and asked, "Venerable Sir, have you received alms?" When told, "Great merchant, we are wandering [for it]," he ordered a man, saying, "Go, invite this Paccekabuddha to our house, seat him on my couch, fill his bowl with the rice prepared for me, and give it to him."
282:
That man invited the Paccekabuddha to his house and informed the merchant's wife. The merchant's wife filled the bowl with various kinds of excellent, delicious food and offered it to Tagarasikhī Paccekabuddha.

## Subsequent Volition (Apara-cetanā)
The Paccekabuddha took the food, left the merchant's house, and was walking along the road. When the merchant returned from the palace, he saw the Paccekabuddha, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, did you receive food?" "Great merchant, I did," he replied. Looking at the food, the merchant was unable to gladden his mind.

"If I had given this rice to my slaves or workers, they would have performed even difficult tasks. Alas, it is a loss for me!" Thus, he was unable to fulfill the subsequent volition (apara-cetanā).

## Fulfillment of the Three Volitions
This statement is true: what is called a gift is of great fruit only for one who is able to fulfill the three volitions. Before giving, one should have a good mind. While giving, one should make the mind clear and confident. After giving, one should be delighted. This is the fulfillment of merit.

## Incomplete Volition, Incomplete Result
"Great King, the merchant Agaññuka obtained great wealth because of the gift he gave to Tagarasikhī Paccekabuddha. However, because he was unable to exercise subsequent volition, he was unable to enjoy his riches," the Teacher preached.

"Venerable Sir, why did he not have a son?" the King asked. The Blessed One said, "Great King, the cause for not having a son was also created by that same man." Being requested by King Kosala, He brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past (2): Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family worth eighty crores. When he came of age, after his parents passed away, he supported his younger brother, managed the estate, built an alms-hall at the gate of his house, and lived as a householder, providing great alms.

## The Elder Brother Renounces
At that time, a son was born to the Bodhisatta. When the son was able to walk, the Bodhisatta saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation. He handed over his wife, son, and all the household wealth to his younger brother, gave him the advice, "Provide alms diligently," and went forth as an ascetic. Having attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), he lived in the Himavanta region.
283:
27. There is a bird called Mayhaka, which wanders in the mountain caves. It perches on a ripe Pipphali tree and cries, "Mine! Mine!"

28. While it is thus lamenting, a flock of birds gathers, eats the Pipphali fruits, and flies away, while that bird continues to lament.

29. Even so, a certain person in this world, having accumulated much wealth, provides neither for himself nor for his relatives according to their needs.

## The Brother Kills the Nephew
The Bodhisatta's younger brother also had a son. Seeing the boy growing up, the merchant thought, "If my brother's son lives, the estate will be split into two. I will kill my brother's son." Having so planned, one day he drowned the brother's son in the river and killed him. When the merchant returned from bathing, the brother's wife asked, "Where is my son?" "He was playing in the river, and when I searched for the boy, I did not see him," he said. The brother's wife wept and lamented, then became silent.

## The Great Ascetic Brother Teaches
The Bodhisatta, knowing this matter, thought, "I will make this deed known." He came through the air, descended in Bārāṇasī, and properly robed, stood at the merchant's door. Seeing no alms-hall, he thought, "This base man has destroyed the alms-hall as well." The younger brother, knowing the Bodhisatta had arrived, came and paid homage to the Great Being, invited him up to the palace, and fed him excellent food.

At the end of the meal, while sitting in pleasant conversation, the Bodhisatta asked, "The boy is not seen; where has he gone?" "Venerable Sir, he is dead," he replied. "For what reason did he die?" he asked. "I do not know; he died for such-and-such a reason while playing in the water," he said.

"You base man, how could you not know? Is not the deed you committed clear to me? Did you not kill the boy for such-and-such a reason? Will you be able to protect the wealth that is destroyed by the power of kings and others? What is the difference between the Mayhaka bird and you?" Having said this, the Bodhisatta, wishing to preach the Dhamma to the merchant with the grace of a Buddha, spoke these verses:

30. He does not enjoy clothing, food, garlands, or ointments even once, nor does he support his relatives.

31. While he is thus lamenting and guarding it, crying "Mine! Mine!", kings or thieves or unloved heirs take the wealth and go, while that man continues to lament.

32. The wise man, having acquired wealth, supports his relatives. Thereby he attains fame and rejoices in heaven after death.
284:
“Dwelling in the mountain clefts and valleys, the bird named Mayhaka perches upon the fruiting Pipphali tree and cries, ‘Mine! Mine!’

While that bird is thus lamenting, flocks of other birds gather, eat the fruit of the Pipphali tree, and fly away. But that bird continues only to lament.

Even so, in this world, some people gather much wealth, but it does not serve their own benefit. They do not provide for their relatives according to their respective portions.

Such a person does not enjoy clothing, nor food, nor flowers, nor perfumes. Not even once do they enjoy anything, nor do they support their kinsmen.

While that person is thus lamenting and guarding the wealth, crying ‘Mine! Mine!’, unloved heirs, or kings, or thieves take that wealth and go away. That person is left only with lamentation.

A wise person, having acquired wealth, supports their kinsmen. Because of that support, that wise person attains fame and praise in this life, and after death, rejoices in the celestial city of heaven.”

Thus the Bodhisatta, having preached the Dhamma to the treasurer and established him in his former practice of charity, returned to the Himālaya regions. Having maintained his meditative absorptions (jhāna) without decline, he was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, “Thus, O Great King, because the visiting treasurer killed his brother’s son, he remained without a son or daughter for all this time.” Having said this, He identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the younger brother was the visiting treasurer, and I myself was the elder brother.”

## The Mayhaka bird, unwilling to give, finds no benefit for himself.

End of the Mayhaka Jātaka.
285:
## 6. Vijjādhara Jātaka
## On Dispelling Wrong Views

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Vijjādhara Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with “Dubbaṇṇarūpaṃ,” concerning His conduct for the benefit of the world.

The introductory story will become clear in the Mahākaṇha Jātaka. At that time, the Fully Enlightened Buddha said, “Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has practiced for the benefit of the world; in the past, I have also practiced for the benefit of the world.” Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka.

## The Vijjādhara’s Misconduct

At that time, a certain Vijjādhara (a sorcerer), having recited a mantra, came at midnight and committed misconduct with the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. The Queen’s attendants became aware of this.

The Queen herself approached the King and said, “My Lord, a man enters the royal bedchamber at midnight and violates me.” The King asked, “Are you able to make some kind of mark on him?” “I can, My Lord,” she replied. The Queen then had a bowl of pure red-lead (vermilion) brought, and when the man came at night and was leaving after his pleasure, she placed a five-finger mark on his back. Early the next morning, she informed the King. The King commanded his men, “Go, search in all directions and seize the man who has a five-finger mark of red-lead on his back.”

## Disguised as an Ascetic

The Vijjādhara, having committed the misconduct at night, stood on one leg in a cemetery during the day, worshipping the sun. The King’s men saw him and surrounded him. The Vijjādhara, thinking, “My deed has become known,” recited his mantra and flew away into the sky.

The King, seeing his men, asked those who returned, “Did you see him?” “Yes, we saw him,” they replied. “What is that man’s name?” the King asked. “My Lord, he is an ascetic (pabbajita). That ascetic commits misconduct at night and lives in the guise of an ascetic during the day.”

## Banishing the Ascetics from the Kingdom

The King, becoming angry at the ascetics, thought, “These ascetics practice in the guise of monks during the day and commit misconduct at night.” Taking up a wrong view, he had the drum beaten to proclaim: “Let all these ascetics flee from my kingdom; wherever they are seen, the royal punishment shall be inflicted.”

All the ascetics fled from the kingdom of Kāsī, which was three hundred leagues in extent, and went to other royal cities. In the entire kingdom of Kāsī, there was not a single righteous ascetic or brahmin left to give counsel to the people. The people, being without guidance, became harsh. They turned away from charity and virtue. As they died, most of them were reborn in the four woeful states (apāya).

33. "You of noble complexion, why do you honor this one of ugly appearance, placing him in front and standing with palms joined? Is he superior to you, or is he your equal? Tell me the name of this other person and your own as well."

Māṇava, O youth. Tvaṃ, you. Ariyavaṇṇī, being of noble complexion. Dubbaṇṇarūpaṃ, the monk of unattractive appearance. Purakkhatvā, placing him in front. Pañjaliko, with palms joined. Tidasānaṃ, of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Indo, the lord. Sakka, Sakka. Asmi, am.

## Sakka Comes with a Monk

Those born in the celestial realm did not exist [newly]. Sakka, not seeing any new devas, reflected, "What is the reason?" and realized that the King of Bārāṇasī, influenced by a wizard, had become angry, adopted a wrong view, and expelled the monks from the kingdom.

Thinking, "Except for me, there is no one else capable of breaking this king's wrong view; I shall be the refuge for the king and the citizens," he went to the Paccekabuddhas at the Nandamūla cave. After paying homage, he said, "Venerable sirs, please give me one elderly Paccekabuddha who is the Saṅghatthera; I will inspire faith in the kingdom of Kāsi." Sakka obtained the Saṅghatthera and departed.
