## What is the Benefit of Homage?

35. "Seeing a monk endowed with conduct, one honors him, placing him in front with palms joined. I ask you this matter, O King of Devas: having passed away from here, what happiness does he obtain?"

Devarāja, O Sakka, King of Devas. Yo, whoever. Caraṇūpapannaṃ, endowed with virtuous conduct. Bhikkhuṃ, a monk. Disvā, seeing. Purakkhatvā, placing him in front. Pañjaliko, with palms joined. Namassasi, honors him. So, that person. Ito, from this life. Cuto, having passed away. Kiṃ sukhaṃ, what happiness. Labhate, does he obtain? Ahaṃ, I. Etamatthaṃ, this matter. Taṃ, you. Pucchāmi, I ask.

36. "Seeing a monk endowed with conduct, one honors him, placing him in front with palms joined. In this very life, he receives praise, and after the breaking up of the body, he goes to heaven."

Rāja, O King. Yo, whoever. Caraṇūpapannaṃ, endowed with virtuous conduct. Bhikkhuṃ, a monk. Purakkhatvā, placing him in front. Pañjaliko, with palms joined. Namassasi, honors him. So, that person. Diṭṭheva dhamme, in this very life. Pasaṃsaṃ, praise. Labhate, receives. Sarīrabhedā, after the breaking up of the body. Paraṃ, thereafter. Saggañca, to heaven. Yāti, he goes.

37. "Indeed, today good fortune has arisen for me, as I have seen Vāsava, the Lord of Beings. Having seen both the monk and you, Sakka, I shall perform many meritorious deeds."

Sakka, O Sakka. Ajja, now. Vata, indeed. Me, for me. Lakkhī, glory and fortune. Udapādi, has clearly arisen. Bhūtapatiṃ, the lord of devas. Yaṃ vāsavañca, that Vāsava. Addassāma, we have seen. Bhikkhuñca, the monk. Tuvañca, and you, Sakka. Disvāna, having seen. Ahaṃ, I. Anappakāni, many. Puññāni, meritorious deeds. Kāhāmi, shall perform.

At that time, taking the bowl and robes of that Paccekabuddha, letting the Paccekabuddha proceed in front while he followed behind, Sakka, in the form of a youth of supreme beauty, stood with palms joined above his head, honoring the Paccekabuddha. He circled the city three times through the air and arrived at the palace gate, standing in the sky.

## Who Are You?

The ministers informed the king, "Great King, a very beautiful youth has brought a monk and is standing in the air at the palace gate." The king rose from his seat, stood at the lion-window, and spoke with Sakka, saying, "Youth, why do you, being so beautiful, stand honoring this ugly monk and holding his bowl and robes?"

## I am Sakka

Then Sakka said to the king, "Great King, monks are in a position of respect. Therefore, I may not address him by name. As for me, I have a name; I shall tell it to you."

## Praised in This Life, Reaching Heaven After Death

Sakka said—

38. "Indeed, one should associate with the wise and the learned, who are capable of contemplating many matters. O King, having seen the monk and me, perform merits of no small measure."

He spoke this sixth verse. 

O King! Indeed, truly, one should associate with those who are wise, who possess great learning, and who are capable of contemplating many causes. Having seen both the monk and me, perform merits of no small measure.

## I Shall Perform Merits
Having heard the words of Sakka, the King abandoned his wrong views and, with a delighted mind—

## The King is Praised
Hearing those words, Sakka, wishing to praise the wise King—

## I Shall Worship
Hearing those words, the King spoke this final verse:

39. "Free from anger, with a mind always serene, being devoted to welcoming all guests, I shall pay homage, having abandoned pride, after hearing your well-spoken words, O Lord of Devas."

O Lord of Devas! Having heard your well-spoken words, I shall be free from anger and possess a mind that is always serene. Being devoted to the practice of welcoming all guests and visitors with whatever they request, and giving them everything they ask for, I shall pay homage, having lowered my pride (or, having a mind that does not offend).

## Exhortation of the Paccekabuddha
Having said this, he descended from the palace, paid homage to the Paccekabuddha, and stood in a suitable place. The Paccekabuddha, sitting cross-legged in the air, exhorted the King: "Great King, the one who appeared in your palace at night was a Vijjādhara (sorcerer), not a monk. From this day forward, knowing that the world is not empty and that there are righteous monks and brahmins, give alms, observe the precepts, and perform the Uposatha duties."

## All is Well
Sakka also, standing in the air by his celestial power, gave an exhortation to the citizens, saying, "From this day forward, be heedful," and had the drum beaten to announce, "Let the monks and brahmins who fled return." Then both the Paccekabuddha and Sakka returned to their respective abodes. The King, established in the exhortation of the Paccekabuddha, performed merits such as almsgiving.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained Parinibbāna. The King was Ānanda, and I myself was Sakka, the King of Devas."

## Monks and the Sangha should be carefully scrutinized and properly worshipped
The Vijjādhara Jātaka ends.
289:
40. "This water-born flower which you smell, though it was not given; this is one part of theft. You are a scent-thief, O monk."

41. "I do not carry it away, nor do I break it; I smell the water-born flower from afar. Then on what grounds am I called a scent-thief?"

He spoke these two verses.

O Goddess! I do not carry away your lotus, nor do I break it. I smell it from afar. That being so, for what reason am I called a scent-thief?

## 7. Siṅghapuppha Jātaka

## Only those easy to admonish should be admonished
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Teacher, who admonishes the world including the devas, told this Siṅghapuppha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yametaṃ," concerning a certain obscure monk.

That monk, having left Jetavana, was living in a forest in the Kosala country. One day, he went down to a lotus pond, and seeing the lotuses in full bloom, he stood downwind and inhaled the scent. Then, a goddess residing in that forest startled him, saying, "O monk free from suffering, such a practice is the practice of stealing scent."

When that monk was thus startled by the goddess, he returned to Jetavana, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat down. When asked, "Monk, where have you been living?" he replied, "I lived in such-and-such a forest grove. There, a goddess startled me in this manner."

Then the Teacher said, "Monk, it is not only you, smelling a flower, who has been startled by a goddess; the wise of old were also startled before," and at the monk's request, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a village of Kāsi. When he came of age, he completed his education at Takkasilā. Later, he became an ascetic and lived near a lotus pond. One day, he went down to the pond and stood smelling a lotus in full bloom.

## The Scent-thief Monk
At that time, a goddess, standing inside the hollow of a tree trunk and wishing to startle the Bodhisatta, spoke this first verse:

"O monk, this water-born lotus which you smell without it being given; this is one part of theft. You are a scent-thief."
290:
42. "He who digs up lotus stalks and breaks the white lotuses,
With such cluttered actions, why is he not spoken to?"

He spoke this third verse:

"O Goddess, this man digs up lotus stalks and breaks the white lotuses. Why do you not speak to this man who performs such harsh deeds?"

43. "A man cluttered with cruelty, like a nurse’s cloth stained [with filth],
In him, I have no words to say; but you, I am fit to speak to."

44. "To a person without blemish, who is always seeking purity,
Even a sin the size of a hair-tip appears as large as a cloud."

45. "Surely, O Yakkha, you know me, and you have compassion for me.
Speak to me again, O Yakkha, whenever you see such [a fault]."

He spoke this sixth verse:

"O Yakkha (Goddess), you certainly know me. Moreover, you protect me with compassion as if I were your own child. O Yakkha, whenever you see such a fault in me, please speak to me again."

## I did not break or steal either

Then the Bodhisatta—

## Do you not speak to that man?

At that moment, a certain man was digging up lotus stalks and breaking white lotuses in that pond. 

The Bodhisatta, seeing that man, wishing to converse with the goddess, said: "You call me a thief for standing at a distance and smelling without taking anything; why do you not speak to that man?"

## There is no need to speak, Venerable Sir

The goddess, wishing to explain why she did not speak to that man, spoke the fourth and fifth verses:

"Venerable Sir, a man cluttered with cruel deeds is like the cloth worn by a nurse-maid, stained with saliva, phlegm, urine, and excrement; he is simply stained with evil. For that reason, I have no words for him. But you, I am fit to speak to."

"To a person without blemish, like yourself, who always seeks purity, a sin even the size of a hair-tip appears as large as a great rain cloud."

## Please speak again

When the goddess thus stirred him, the Bodhisatta, having reached a state of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), spoke the verse:
291:
46. "I do not live off you, nor am I your servant.
You yourself, Bhikkhu, should know that by which you may go to a happy destination."

She spoke this seventh verse:

"Venerable Sir, I do not live depending on you, nor am I your hired laborer. O Monk, you yourself should know the good deeds by which one should go to a happy destination."

## Mind your own business

Then, the goddess gave this advice to the Bodhisatta and remained in her own mansion. The Bodhisatta, having attained jhāna, was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and declared the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. How was the Jātaka identified? At that time, Uppalavaṇṇā was the goddess, and I myself was the ascetic. Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Mind yourself, rely on yourself, do not seek a teacher

The Siṅghapuppha Jātaka is finished.

## 8. Vighāsāda Jātaka

## Eating after giving leads to the happy destination of heaven

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at the Pubbārāma monastery, told this Vighāsāda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Susukhaṃ vata jīvanti," concerning some playful monks.

When those monks were stirred by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, who shook the palace, they sat in the Dhamma Hall talking about the lack of virtue of those monks. The All-Knowing Buddha came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now are these monks playful; in the past also they were playful," and he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. Then, in a certain village of Kāsi, seven brothers, seeing the faults in sensual pleasures, went forth and became ascetics. While living in the middle of a forest, they did not practice meditation but became preoccupied with strengthening their bodies and engaged in various kinds of play...
292:
47. Happy indeed live those people who are eaters of remains (vighāsādino). They are praiseworthy in this very life, and their destination in the next world is a happy one.
(He spoke this first verse.)
Those people who live happily as eaters of remains, they are praiseworthy in this present state of existence, and in the future life, they are reborn in a happy destination (sugati).

(He spoke this third verse.)
I do not praise you. O ascetics who eat the carcasses of animals, listen to my words. You eat the leftovers of other creatures. You are not true eaters of remains.

(He spoke this fourth verse.)

In an obscure village of Kāsi, seven brothers, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, left for the forest to become ascetics. Living in the middle of the forest, they did not strive in meditation but focused on fattening their bodies, spending their time playing in various ways.

## Eating remains is noble
Sakka, the King of Devas, thinking, "I will stir these ascetics with spiritual urgency," took the form of a parrot, went to their dwelling place, perched on a tree, and wishing to stir them, said:

## He is praising us
Then, one of the ascetics, hearing the parrot's words, called the other ascetics and said:

## Refuse leftovers
Then, wishing to refute the ascetics, the parrot said:

## Those who are eating
All those ascetics, hearing the parrot's words, said:

## Not noble

Wishing to make those ascetics feel ashamed, the Bodhisatta said:

## Noble is eating after giving

Hearing those words, the ascetics asked, "If we are not eaters of remains, then who are the eaters of remains?"
293:
51. You live on the leftovers of lions, tigers, and other beasts of prey. Subsisting only on refuse, do you think of yourselves as eaters of remains (vighāsādino)?
(He spoke this fifth verse.)
Do you consider yourselves eaters of remains while you subsist on the refuse and leftovers of lions, tigers, and other beasts of prey?

Thereafter, wishing to inform the ascetics of the matter, the Bodhisatta spoke this sixth verse:

52. Those people who, having first given to a Brahmin, an ascetic, or any other beggar, eat the remainder—they are the ones called eaters of remains (vighāsādino).
(He spoke this sixth verse.)
Those people who give to a Brahmin, an ascetic, or any other beggar, and then eat what remains, they are truly called eaters of remains.

Having thus shamed the ascetics, the Bodhisatta returned to his own place in Tāvatiṃsa.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the seven brothers who were fond of playing were these monks, and Sakka was I myself."

## Noble is the food eaten after giving
The Vighāsāda Jātaka ends.

## 9. Waṭṭaka Jātaka
## Contentment with what is received is the cause of happiness
The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who admonishes the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Waṭṭaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Paṇītaṃ," concerning a greedy monk.

The Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are greedy?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Monk, you are not greedy only now; in the past too, you were greedy. Because of your greed, you were not satisfied with the carcasses of elephants, oxen, and humans in Bārāṇasī, and thinking 'I will get something better than this,' you entered the forest." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a quail and lived in the forest, subsisting on dry grass seeds.
294:
## Why Are You Thin?

53. "You eat choice food, rice with ghee and oil, Uncle.
Then for what reason, O Crow, are you thin?"

He spoke this first verse. 
Uncle, O Crow, you eat choice food, rice which is the food of humans, as well as ghee and oil, do you not? That being so, for what reason are you thin?

54. "Living in the midst of enemies, seeking food among them,
For a crow whose heart is always trembling, where is there any robustness?

55. Crows are always anxious, greedy due to their evil deeds.
The morsel obtained does not satisfy; therefore, O Quail, I am thin.

56. You eat dry grass seeds with little essence.
Then for what reason, O Quail, are you fat?"

He spoke these three verses.
O Quail, for me, a crow who must live in the midst of enemies and seek food among those enemies, always having a trembling heart, where can there be robustness or fatness?
O Quail, crows, known as greedy ones, always have anxious minds. The morsel of food obtained through the evil deed of snatching the food of humans does not bring satisfaction or contentment. Therefore, I am thin.

At that time in the city of Bārāṇasī, a certain greedy crow, not being satisfied with elephant carcasses and such, thinking he would get more than this, entered the forest. Seeing the Bodhisatta who was eating various fruits, he thought, "This quail has an extremely fat body. I suppose he eats delicious food. I will ask about his food, and by eating that, I too shall become fat." He perched on a branch above the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, wishing to exchange friendly greetings with that crow, said:

## Always Living in Fear

Hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the crow said:

## Why Are You Fat?

"Quail, you eat dry grass seeds that are parched and have little essence. That being so, for what reason are you fat?"

## Content with Whatever is Received

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta, wishing to explain the reason for his robustness, said:
295:
57. "Through fewness of desires, through little worry, and by not traveling far,
Living on whatever is obtained—therefore, O Crow, I am fat.

58. For a person of few desires, who has the happiness of little worry,
And whose mind is well-restrained, livelihood is easily maintained."

He spoke these two verses.
O Crow, through having few desires, through having little worry regarding food, and by not traveling far, I sustain myself with whatever food is obtained, whether it be coarse or choice. Therefore, I am fat.
Truly, for a person of few desires, who possesses the happiness of having little worry, and who has a well-restrained measure of food, thinking 'I will be able to digest this much after eating,' livelihood is easily maintained with happiness.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. As for the identification of the Jātaka: "The crow of that time was the greedy monk, and the quail was I myself."

## Happiness Increases Only Through Contentment with What is Received

The Vaṭṭaka Jātaka is finished.

## Destruction Through Discontent with What is Received

The Perfectly Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Pārāvata Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Cirassaṃ vata passāmi," concerning a certain greedy monk.

The present story is the same as the one mentioned below.

The story of the past: In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a pigeon.

## 1. Kukku Vagga

## 1. Kukku Jātaka

## Kings Should Rule Righteously

The Teacher, who guides the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana, spoke this Kukku Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Diyaddha-kukkū', concerning advice to a king.

The story of the present will become clear in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a minister who advised him on matters of welfare and Dhamma.

## The King's Error

King Brahmadatta, established in prejudice, ruled unrighteously. He oppressed the country and only collected wealth.

## Why Does the Pinnacle Stay Firm?

Then the Bodhisatta, wishing to advise the king, went about looking for a metaphor. In the king's garden, a summer house was unfinished. The roof was not yet completed. The pinnacle had been set, and the rafters had just been inserted.
299:
2. Those thirty rafters, made of heartwood, not straight, standing evenly all around; well-held together and pressed by force, the pinnacle standing evenly above does not fall.

3. Even so, a wise king, well-supported by firm friends of unbreakable nature, pure and wise in counsel, does not fall from his glory, like the pinnacle bearing the weight of the rafters.

He spoke these verses.

Mahārāja, Great King. Tiṃsati, thirty. Sāramayā, made of heartwood. Anujjukā, without sapwood. Yā gopānasiyo, those rafters. Parikiriya, surrounding all around. Samaṃ ṭhitā, they stand in equal parts. Balasā, by the power of strength. Pīḷitā, being pressed together. Susaṅgahitā, being well-supported. Sā kaṇṇikā, that pinnacle. Samaṃ ṭhitā, standing in equal parts. Upparito, from above. Na dhaṃsati, does not fall.

Mahārāja, Great King. Evampi, in this same way. Paṇḍito, a wise king. Daḷhehi, by those who are firm. Abhejjarūpehi, by those of unbreakable nature. Sucīhi, by those who are pure. Mantibhi, by those skilled in counsel. Mittehi, by friends. Susaṅgahito, being well-supported. Gopānasībhāravahā, bearing the weight of the rafters. Kaṇṇikāva, like the pinnacle. Siriyā, from his glory. Na dhaṃsati, does not fall.

The King also went to the garden for sport, and while wandering in that garden, he entered that house. Looking up, he saw the roof-pinnacle and, fearing it might fall upon him, he went out and stood outside. Looking again, he thought, "Upon what does the pinnacle depend to stand? Upon what do the rafters depend to stand?" and wishing to ask the Bodhisatta—

## Because of the Circle of Friends

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta thought, "Now I have found a simile to advise the King," and said—

The King, following exactly what the Bodhisatta said, noted his own conduct and thought: "Without the pinnacle, the rafters do not stand; if the rafters do not support it, the pinnacle does not stand. If the rafters break, the pinnacle falls. In the same way, an unrighteous king who does not support his friends, ministers, army, brahmins, and householders—when those people perish and he is no longer supported by them—will fall from his sovereignty."

4. Just as a man with a knife, not knowing how to handle a citron with a rough skin, makes it bitter; but one who collects it well makes it sweet, O King; if he removes the skin too thinly, he makes it unpleasant.

He spoke these verses.

Karoti, he makes it. Bandhaṃ, the skin. Tanu, thinly. Uddharaṃ-uddharanto, he who peels it. Asāduṃ, unpleasant. Kayirā, he would make it. Samāharaṃ, he who peels the skin well. Sāduṃ, sweet. Karoti yathāpi, just as he makes it.

Evampi, in this same way. Rāja, O King. Paṇḍito, a wise king. Gāmanigamesu, in villages and market towns. Asāhasaṃ, not following the power of craving. Dhammānuvattī paṭipajjamāno, practicing in accordance with the Ten Royal Virtues. Dhanāni, wealth. Saṅgharaṃ-saṅgharanto, collecting. Sa- so rājā, that king. Paraṃ, others. Aviheṭhayaṃ-aviheṭhayanto, without oppressing. Phātiṃ, prosperity. Kayirā, he should bring about.

"A king should be one who observes the Dhamma," he thought.

## Do Not Make the Citron Bitter

At that moment, they presented a citron to the King as a gift. The King gave it to the Bodhisatta, saying, "Friend, eat this citron."

The Bodhisatta took the citron and said, "Great King, those who do not know how to eat this citron make it bitter or sour. But the wise who know, removing the bitterness without taking out the sourness and without destroying the flavor of the citron, eat it." Wishing to show the King the method of collecting wealth through a simile—

6. Like a lotus born in a pond, with white roots, produced in pure water, blossomed by the sun's rays, which neither mud, nor dust, nor water smears.

7. Even so, one who is pure in legal dealings, non-violent, pure in action, and free from evil—such a one is not smeared by the defilements of action, like the lotus born in the pond.

He spoke these verses.

Padumaṃ, the lotus. Kaddamo-kaddame, in mud. Na limpati yathā, just as it is not smeared. Rajo-raje, in dust. Na limpati yathā, just as it is not smeared. Vāri-vārimhi, in water. Na limpati yathā, just as it is not smeared.

## No Mud on the Lotus

The King, while consulting with the Bodhisatta, went to the edge of a pond. Seeing a lotus that was well-blossomed, having the color of the young sun and unsmeared by water, he said, "Friend, this lotus, though born in the water, stands unsmeared by the water."

## Avoid Evil Actions

Then, the Bodhisatta, wishing to advise the King, saying, "Great King, a king should be of such a nature," said:

Neither mud, nor dust, nor water smears it.

The King, hearing the Bodhisatta's words, from that time forward ruled with the Ten Royal Virtues, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and was destined for heaven.

## 2. Manoja Jātaka

## Ruin through Associating with a Wicked Friend

While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Manoja Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Yathā cāpo ninnamati," concerning a monk who associated with enemies.

The present story is detailed in the Mahilāmukha Jātaka below. At that time, the All-Knowing Buddha said, "Monks, not only now has this monk associated with enemies; in the past also, he associated with enemies," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a lion. Living with a lioness, he had two offspring: a son and a daughter. He named the son Manoja.

When Manoja reached maturity, he took a young lioness as his mate. Thus, there were five lions. Manoja hunted wild buffaloes and such, bringing the meat to support his parents, his sister, and his wife.

## Adopting a Jackal

One day, in his hunting grounds, Manoja saw a jackal named Giriya who was unable to flee and lay prostrate on his chest. Manoja asked, "Friend, what is the matter?" When the jackal replied, "Lord, I wish to serve you," Manoja said, "Very well, then serve me," and took the jackal to his cave.

## Do Not Associate with the Jackal

The Bodhisatta, seeing the jackal, warned him, "Dear Manoja, jackals are immoral and of wicked character; they lead one into improper actions. Do not keep this jackal near you." However, he was unable to stop him.

Then one day, the jackal, desiring to eat horse meat, said to Manoja, "Lord, except for horse meat, there is no meat we have not eaten. Let us catch a horse." Manoja asked, "Friend, if that is so, where are the horses?" The jackal replied, "By the river in Vārāṇasī."
303:
Manoja took the jackal's word and went with him to the river when the horses were being bathed. He caught a horse, placed it on his back, and swiftly returned to his cave.

## Do Not Catch Horses

Then Manoja's father, having eaten the horse meat, said, "Dear Manoja, horses are the King's mounts. Kings employ archers skilled in many ruses to shoot. Lions that eat horse meat do not live long. From this day forth, do not catch horses." Manoja, however, did not heed his father's words and continued to catch them.

Hearing that "a lion is catching horses," the King had a pond dug within the city. Even from that pond, the lion came and took them. The King then had a stable built and provided grass and water inside it. The lion, leaping over the top of the wall, took them from inside the stable as well.

## Shot by an Arrow

The King summoned an archer who could shoot as fast as a flash of lightning (akkhaṇavedhī) and asked, "Will you be able to shoot the lion?" The archer replied, "I can." He leaned against the wall and built a platform on the path where the lion came.

The lion came, left the jackal at the outer cemetery, and leaped into the city to take a horse. The archer thought, "His speed is too great while coming," and did not shoot. But when the lion was returning with the horse, slowed down by the heavy burden, the archer shot him in the hindquarters with a sharp arrow. The arrow passed through the front of his body and flew into the air. The lion roared, "I am hit!" After shooting the lion, the archer twanged his bowstring like a clap of thunder.

## The Jackal Flees

The jackal, hearing the sound of the lion and the bowstring, thought, "My friend must have been shot and killed by the archer. There is no such thing as friendship with a corpse. Now I will go back to my original forest dwelling." Desiring to speak to himself, he uttered these verses:

8. As the bow bends, and the string also twangs,
Surely Manoja, the king of beasts, my friend, is slain.

9. Come now, I shall depart to the depths of the forest as I please;
Such as he are no longer friends; a living man may find a friend.

[Word-for-word explanation:] Yathā, in such a manner; cāpo, the bow; ninnamati, bends. Jiyā cāpi, and the bowstring; nikūjati, twangs. Manojo, the one named Manoja; migarājā, the king of beasts; mama sakhā, who is my friend; haññate nūna, is surely slain.

Handa dāni, now; ahaṃ, I; yathāsukhaṃ, as I please; vanantāni, to the forests; pakkamāmi, shall depart. Etādiso, such as these who are dead; sakhā, friends; na honti, are not. Jīvato, being alive; me, I; sakhā, friends; labbhā, may find.

## The Relatives Weep

The lion, with a single burst of speed, went and dropped the horse at the mouth of the cave and fell dead himself. Then Manoja's relatives came out and saw Manoja covered in blood, which was flowing from the arrow wound. They saw that Manoja had reached the end of his life because of associating with a wicked friend. Seeing this, Manoja's mother, father, sister, and wife [said]:

13. Thus it shall be for him, and even worse than that,
304:
They spoke these verses in succession:

10. "One who associates with wicked people does not attain lasting happiness. Look at Manoja lying there, having followed the advice of Giriya."

11. "A mother does not rejoice in a son who keeps bad company. Look at Manoja lying there, submerged in his own blood."

12. "Thus a man falls into ruin and meets with evil, who does not follow the words of those who wish him well and see his benefit."

13. "He becomes like this, and even worse—the noble one who associates with the base. Look at the noble king of beasts, who associated with the base, now pierced by the swift force of an excellent arrow."

One who associates with wicked people (*pāpajanasamsevī*) does not attain (*na edhati*) lasting happiness (*accantaṃ sukhaṃ*). Look at (*passa*) Manoja who lies (*semānaṃ*) having taken the advice (*anusāsanī*) of the jackal named Giriya.

## The Consequences of Bad Friendship
Because of associating with wicked companions (*pāpasampavaṅkena*), a mother (*mātā*) does not rejoice (*na nandati*) in her son (*puttena*). Look at Manoja who lies submerged in his own blood.

## For Not Listening to Parents' Words
Whatever man (*yo poso*) does not listen (*na karoti*) to the words (*vacanaṃ*) of those who desire his welfare (*hitānaṃ*) and see his benefit (*atthadassīnaṃ*), that man falls into such misery. He also meets with (*nigacchati*) evil (*pāpiyo*), such as the act of killing.

Whatever noble man (*yo puriso*) associates with one of base conduct (*adhamajanuupasevī*), that man meets with such misery and becomes even worse (*pāpiyo*). Look at that Manoja, the king of beasts (*migādhipaṃ*), who possessed great strength but associated with one of base conduct, now pierced by the swift force of an excellent arrow.

## Associate with Those Better Than Oneself
The Buddha, wishing to teach that association with the wicked leads to ruin and that one should associate with the wise, spoke this final verse:

14. "A man declines by associating with the low; he never declines by associating with equals. By approaching the superior, one quickly rises; therefore, one should associate with those better than oneself."

Monks (*bhikkhave*), a man who associates with the low (*nihīnasevī*) declines (*nihīyati*). A man who associates with equals (*tulyasevī*)...
305:
...a man [who associates with equals] never declines at any time. By approaching the superior (*seṭṭhaṃ*), one who seeks those higher in virtue and so on, one quickly rises (*udeti*) and grows in qualities such as virtue. Therefore, one should associate with (*bhajetha*) those who are more excellent (*uttaritaram*) than oneself in virtue and the like.

The Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the monk who associated with the enemy was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).

To identify the Jātaka: At that time, Devadatta was the jackal. The monk who associated with the enemy was the lion Manoja. Uppalavaṇṇā was the sister. The bhikkhunī Khemā was the wife. Rāhula's mother was the mother. And I, the Buddha, was the lion king, the father.

## Associating with the wicked leads to ruin
The Manoja Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Sutanu Jātaka
## On Supporting One's Parents
The Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sutanu Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Rājā te bhattaṃ," concerning a certain monk who supported his mother.

The present story will become clear in the Sāma Jātaka.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family. They named him Sutanu. When he reached maturity, he worked as a laborer to support his parents. After his father died, he supported his mother.

## The King Goes Hunting
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was fond of hunting deer. One day, with a large retinue, he entered a forest a hundred yojanas in extent and announced to everyone: "If a deer escapes from the place where someone is standing, that person shall receive such-and-such punishment."

The ministers assigned posts along the path as the King had ordered. People surrounded the deer's habitats and raised a clamor to drive them out. Among the deer, one Eṇi deer ran toward the King's post. The King, thinking "I will shoot it," released an arrow. The deer, being skilled in trickery, realized the arrow was coming toward its right flank, turned, and fell as if pierced by the arrow. The King, thinking "I have hit the deer," ran to catch it. The deer stood up and fled with the speed of the wind. The ministers and others mocked the King.
306:
## Captured by the Yakkha
When the King, exhausted from chasing a deer, had cut it with his sword, slung it on a carrying pole, and was returning, he thought, "I will rest for a while." He approached a banyan tree standing near the road, lay down, and fell into a deep sleep.
A yakkha named Maghadeva, who lived in that banyan tree, had received permission from King Vessavaṇa to eat anyone who entered the shade of that tree. Seeing the King getting up to leave, the yakkha seized his hand and said, "Stop! You are my food." The King asked, "What is your name?" The yakkha replied, "I am the yakkha born in this banyan tree. I am allowed to eat those who enter this place."

## A Daily Offering of Rice
The King, regaining his composure, asked, "Will you eat me today, or will you eat regularly?" The yakkha replied, "If I can get it, I will eat regularly." The King said, "Eat this deer today and let me go. From tomorrow onwards, I will send you one person along with a bowl of rice." The yakkha said, "If that is so, do not be negligent. On the day you fail to send someone, I will come and eat you." The King replied, "I am the King of Bārāṇasī; there is nothing I do not have." Having received the promise, the yakkha released him.

## The Poor Man Who Carried the Rice
The King entered the city and informed a minister of the matter, asking, "What should be done now?" The minister asked, "Great King, did you set a time limit?" "I did not," the King replied. The minister said, "Though you have done something improper, do not worry. There are many people in the prisons." The King said, "Then you perform this task; give me my life."
The minister agreed, saying, "Very well." Every day, he took a man from the prison, gave him a bowl of rice, and sent him to the yakkha without letting anyone else know. After eating the rice, the yakkha would eat the man. Later, the prisons became empty of people. The King, unable to find anyone to carry the rice, trembled with the fear of death.
Then the minister consoled the King, saying, "Great King, the desire for wealth is stronger than the desire for life. Let us place a bundle of a thousand pieces of money on an elephant's back and have a drum beaten, announcing, 'Who will take this wealth and carry the rice to the yakkha?'" The King did as the minister suggested.
At that time, hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought, "I support my mother with great difficulty by working for wages and collecting small coins. I will take this money, give it to my mother, and go to the yakkha. If I am able to tame the yakkha, that will be good. If I am not able, my mother will live comfortably."
Having thought this, he informed his mother. She refused twice, saying, "No, my son, I have no need for the money." On the third time, without asking her permission, he said, "Sirs, bring the thousand pieces; I will carry the rice." He took the thousand pieces, gave them to his mother, and said, "Mother, do not worry. I will tame the yakkha and bring happiness to the people. Today, I will return and make your tear-stained face joyful." He paid respects to his mother and, accompanied by the king's men, went to the King and stood there after paying respects.
307:
15. "The King has sent this rice to you, pure and seasoned with meat;
O Maghadeva, who dwells herein, come forth and eat!"

He recited this first verse. 
(The meaning is:) Maghadevasmiṃ, in the banyan tree. Adhivatthe, the deity who dwells there. Te, for you. Rājā, the King. Suciṃ, pure. Maṃsūpasecanaṃ, mixed with meat. Bhattaṃ, rice. Pāhesi, has sent. Ehi, come. Nikkhamma, coming out. Bhuñjassu, eat.

Then the King asked, "My son, will you carry the rice?" "Yes, Great King," he replied. "What do you need to receive?" the King asked. "Your golden slippers, Great King," he said. "For what reason?" "Great King, that yakkha is allowed to eat those who stand on the ground at the foot of his tree. I will not stand on the ground belonging to him, but will stand on the slippers."
"What else do you need to receive?" "Your parasol, Great King." "For what purpose is this parasol?" "Great King, the yakkha is allowed to eat those who stand in the shade of his tree. I will not stand in the shade of his tree, but will stand in the shade of the parasol."
"What else do you need to receive?" "Your sword, Great King." "What is the use of this sword?" "Great King, even non-humans are afraid of those who hold weapons in their hands."
"What else do you want?" "Great King, fill your golden bowl with the rice you eat and give it to me." "My son, why?" "Great King, it is not fitting for a wise man like me to carry coarse food in a clay bowl." "Very well, my son," the King said, and gave him everything, and ordered attendants to serve the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta said, "Great King, do not be afraid. Today I will tame the yakkha, bring you peace, and return." He paid respects to the King, had the equipment carried, and went to that place. He left the people not far from the tree, put on the golden slippers, girded on the sword, held the white parasol over his head, took the rice in the golden bowl, and approached the yakkha.
As the yakkha was watching the road, he saw the Bodhisatta and thought, "This man does not come in the same manner as others have come on other days. What could be the reason?"
The Bodhisatta also went near the tree, and using the tip of his sword, he placed the bowl of rice inside the shade, while he himself stood at the edge of the shade—

## Calling the Yakkha
Hearing these words, the yakkha thought, "I will eat this man who is trying to deceive me and enter the shade," and—
308:
16. "Come, young man, to this side, taking the alms well-prepared with soup. Both you, young man, and the alms will become my food."

He spoke this second verse. Māṇava, young man. Sūpitaṃ, well-prepared with soup. Bhikkhaṃ, the regular alms food for me. Ādāya, taking. Orena, to this side. Ehi, come. Māṇava, young man. Tvañca, you too. Bhikkhā ca, are you not my food? Ubho, both the rice and you. Bhakkhā, my food. Bhavissatha, will become.

17. "For a small matter, O Yakkha, you will lose a great benefit. People, perceiving death, will not bring you alms."

18. "Having obtained your regular alms, O Yakkha, pure, excellent, and endowed with flavor, if I am eaten, a man who dares to bring you alms here will be very hard to find."

He spoke these verses. Yakkha, ogre. Tvaṃ, you. Appakena, for a small reason. Thullaṃ, great. Atthaṃ, benefit. Jahissasi, will lose. Janā, people. Maraṇasaññino, perceiving that they will die. Te, to you. Bhikkhaṃ, alms. Nāharissanti, will not bring.

Yakkha, ogre. Tava, for you. Suciṃ, pure. Paṇītaṃ, excellent. Rasasā upetaṃ, endowed with flavor. Niccabhikkhaṃ, regular alms. Laddhā, having obtained. Ayaṃ, this coming of mine. Hoti, is. Mayi, if I am eaten. Bhakkhite, being eaten. Te, your. Bhikkhañca, alms too. Āhariyo, one who dares to bring. Naro, a man. Idha, here in the city of Bārāṇasī. Sudullabho, very hard to find. Hehiti, will be.

## Explaining the Cause and Effect

Then the Bodhisatta said:

## I Have a Sword

Why will it be so? "In the city of Bārāṇasī, there is no other wise man like me. If I am eaten, people will think, 'Even Sutanu was eaten by the ogre; why would he feel any shame toward anyone else?' Thus, you will not find anyone to deliver food. If that happens, from this day forward, it will be difficult for you to obtain food. You will also not be able to catch our King. Why? Because he stays outside the range of the tree."

"If you eat this food and let me go, I will speak to the King and have regular food sent to you. I will not give myself to you to be eaten. I do not stand on your ground; I stand on my sandals. I do not stand in the shade of your tree; I stand only under the shade of my parasol. If you fight with me, I will cut you into two pieces with my sword. I have come prepared for that very purpose." Thus the Bodhisatta threatened the ogre.

## You are Wise, You May Go

The ogre, realizing "This young man speaks what is right," felt a sense of devotion and said:

## Making the Ogre Receive Offerings

Hearing the ogre's words, the Bodhisatta felt joyful, thinking, "My task is complete. I have tamed the ogre, I have obtained great wealth, and I have fulfilled the King's command." Wishing to express appreciation (anumodanā) to the ogre, he spoke thus.

Calling the ogre, he said, "Friend, in the past, you committed unwholesome deeds and became harsh and cruel, eating the flesh and blood of others. From this day forward, do not commit such acts as killing (pāṇātipāta)." He spoke of the benefits of virtue and the faults of lacking virtue, established him in the Five Precepts (Pañcasīla), and said, "What benefit is there in just preaching to you? Come, I will settle you at the city gate and ensure you receive the first portion of food." He went out with the ogre, making the ogre carry the sword and other items, and arrived at the city of Bārāṇasī.

## Becoming the Commander-in-Chief

It was reported to the King, "The young man Sutanu has returned with the ogre." Surrounded by his ministers, the King went out to welcome the Bodhisatta. He settled the ogre at the city gate, arranged for him to receive the first portion of food, and entered the city. He had the drum beaten to assemble the citizens, proclaimed the virtues of the Bodhisatta, and appointed him to the position of Commander-in-Chief. The King himself followed the Bodhisatta's advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and went to the heavenly realm.

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the Jātaka? At that time, Angulimāla was the Maghadeva Yakkha, Ānanda was the King, and I, the Buddha, was the youth Sutanu. Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Caring for Parents, Giving Life, and Supporting Them

The Sutanu Jātaka ends.

## 4. Gijjha Jātaka

## Escaping Death through the Virtue of Parents

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the Teacher of the world including the devas, told this Gijjha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Te kathaṃ nu karissanti," concerning a monk who supported his mother.

The story of the present will become clear in the Sāma Jātaka.
309:
19. "O Sutanu, my purpose is served just as you say, young man. I permit you; go in safety and see your mother."
20. "Take the sword, the parasol, and the bowl, young man. May your mother see you in safety, and may you see your mother."
He spoke these verses.

"Sutano" means the one named Sutanu. "Māṇava" means young man. "Just as you say" means in the manner you speak. "The purpose spoken by you" means my own benefit, my own growth. "I permit you" means I give you leave. "See your mother in safety" means look upon her in well-being.

"Young man, take the sword, the parasol, and the golden bowl and go. May your mother see you in safety, and may you also see your mother in safety."

21. "Thus, O Yakkha, may you be happy with all your kinsmen. I have obtained wealth and fulfilled the King's word."
He spoke this final verse.

"O Yakkha, I have obtained wealth and I have fulfilled the King's word. Likewise, may you be happy together with all your kinsmen."

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the species of vultures. When he reached maturity, he kept his aged and blind parents in a vulture cave and nourished them by bringing cow's flesh and such.

## The Vulture who nourished his parents

At that time, a hunter at a cemetery near Bārāṇasī, without marking it, set a snare in the place where vultures alight.

## Lamenting upon being caught in the snare

Then one day, while the Bodhisatta was searching for cow's flesh and such and entered the cemetery, he was caught in the snare. He did not think of his own benefit. He thought only of his aged and blind parents, lamenting: "How will my parents survive? They do not know that I am caught in a snare. Having no refuge or support, they will surely wither and die in the mountain cave." Thus he spoke this first verse:

22. "How will they manage, the aged ones dwelling in the mountain cave? I am bound by a snare, fallen into the power of Niliya."

"I am caught by the snare. I have fallen into the power of the hunter named Niliya. How will those aged parents of mine, dwelling in the mountain cave, manage?"

## Never seen a bird cry

Then the hunter, hearing the cry of the vulture king, spoke this second verse:

23. "Why do you lament, O vulture? What is this wailing of yours? I have never heard or seen a bird speaking the language of humans."

"O vulture, why do you cry? What is this wailing of yours? I have never seen nor heard of a bird speaking the language of humans."

## I worry for my parents

Thereupon the vulture king spoke this verse:

24. "I support my parents, aged and dwelling in the mountain cave. How will they manage, now that I have fallen into your power?"

"O hunter, I support my parents who are aged and dwell in a mountain cave. Now that I have fallen into your power, how will those parents manage?"

## Did you not see the snare?

Thereupon the hunter spoke this verse:

25. "It is said that a vulture can see carcasses from a hundred leagues. Why then, even upon reaching it, did you not notice the net and the snare?"

"It is said in the world that a vulture sees carcasses that lie beyond a hundred leagues. If so, why did you not notice the net and the snare even when you reached them?"

## When ruin is destined, one sees nothing

Thereupon the vulture king spoke this verse:

26. "When ruin comes to a person at the end of life, then even upon reaching it, one does not notice the net and the snare."

"O hunter, when a being desires ruin because of the exhaustion of life, then even upon reaching the net and the snare, one does not notice them."

## I release you

The hunter, having heard the Dhamma discourse of the Bodhisatta, thought: "This wise vulture king, though he laments, does not lament for his own sake, but only for the sake of his parents. It is not proper to kill this vulture king." Delighted with the vulture king, he spoke this sixth verse:

27. "Support your parents, aged and dwelling in the mountain cave. I permit you; go in safety and see your kinsmen."
310:
"O King of Vultures, support your parents, aged and dwelling in the mountain cave. I permit you; go in safety and see your kinsmen."

## May the hunter be happy

Having said this, he released the snare with a loving and tender heart. The Bodhisatta, being free from the jaws of death and being at ease, wishing to express his appreciation to the hunter, spoke this final verse:

28. "Thus, O hunter, may you rejoice with all your kinsmen. I shall support my parents, aged and dwelling in the mountain cave."

"O hunter, likewise, may you rejoice together with all your kinsmen. I shall support my parents who are aged and dwell in the mountain cave."

Having said this, he took enough meat to fill his beak and gave it to his parents.

Identification of the Jataka: The Blessed One, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jataka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). As for the identification of the Jataka: Channa was the hunter at that time, the members of the noble royal family were the parents, and I, the Buddha, was the vulture king. Thus he identified the Jataka.

## When ruin is destined, when the time to die arrives, one sees no danger

The Gijjha Jataka ends.
312:
Being pleased, thinking, "It is not right to kill this one who laments for his parents," he spoke thus. Having spoken with a loving and gentle heart, he released him from the snare.

Then the Bodhisatta, freed from the jaws of death and being happy, expressed his appreciation by reciting the concluding verse, and taking a mouthful of meat, he gave it to his parents.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: At the end of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.

At that time, the hunter's son was Channa, the parents were the Great Royal Family, and the Vulture King was I myself.

Exposition of the Mātuposaka Gijjha Jātaka, the fourth.

## 5. Dabbhapuppha Jātaka
## The Cause of Loss through Quarreling

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the Teacher of the world including the devas, told this Dabbhapuppha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Anutīracārī bhaddante," concerning the Elder Upananda of the Sakyan clan.

## The Great Greed of Venerable Upananda

That Elder Upananda, having ordained in the Dispensation, abandoned virtues such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and became one of great desire. During the rains retreat, he would take possession of two or three monasteries. In one monastery, he would place an umbrella; in another, sandals; in another, an alms-bowl; in another, a walking staff; and in another, a water pot, while he himself resided in one.

That Elder Upananda, having entered the rains retreat in a certain country monastery, preached the Ariyavaṃsa practice—which leads to contentment with requisites—to the monks, as if making the moon appear in the sky, saying, "Monks should be of few wishes." Hearing that teaching, the monks discarded their attractive alms-bowls and robes, and took up clay bowls and rag-robes (paṃsukūla).
313:
One should first establish oneself in what is proper;
Then only should one instruct others. Thus the wise man will not be stained.

## The Vinaya Expert Takes the Best

Venerable Upananda placed the other items in his own residence. When the rains retreat was over, he performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, filled a small cart, and while traveling to the Jetavana Monastery, his foot got caught in a vine behind a certain monastery along the way. Thinking, "Surely, something is to be gained in this monastery," he entered it.

In that monastery, two elderly monks had spent the rains retreat. Those two elderly monks had received two coarse robes and one fine blanket (kambala), but being unable to divide them, they saw Venerable Upananda and, with joyful hearts, thought, "The Elder will divide them for us." They said, "Venerable sir, we are unable to divide this rains-residence cloth; a dispute has arisen between us regarding this cloth. Please divide this cloth for us."

Venerable Upananda said, "Very well, I shall divide it." He gave the two coarse robes to the two elderly monks and took the blanket, saying, "This blanket is suitable for me, an expert in the Discipline (Vinayadhara)," and then he departed.

## The Monks' Criticism

Those elderly monks, still being attached to the blanket, went to the Jetavana Monastery along with Venerable Upananda. They reported the matter to the monks, asking, "Venerable sirs, is it proper for monks who carry the Discipline to plunder and consume in this manner?"

The monks, seeing the pile of alms-bowls and robes brought by the Elder Upananda, said to him, "Friend, you are of great merit. You have obtained many alms-bowls and robes." He replied, "Friends, where is the merit? I obtained these through such a means," and he told them the whole story.

In the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, the Sakyan son, Venerable Upananda, is of great desire and great greed."

The All-Knowing Buddha came and asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a conversation," He said, "Monks, Upananda has not acted in a way suitable to the practice. A monk who teaches the practice to others should first practice suitably himself, and only then should he admonish others."
314:
29. "O bank-walker, may you be well! O friend, run to me. A great fish has been caught by me; it is dragging me away with speed."

He spoke this first verse. 
Anutīracārī: O otter who walks along the bank. Te: To you. Bhaddaṃ: May goodness. Hotu: Be. Me: By me. Gahito: Caught. Yo maccho: Which Rohita fish. Mahā: Is great. So: That fish. Maṃ: Me. Vegasā: With speed. Harati: Drags away. Sahāyaṃ: As a friend. Maṃ: To me. Anudhāva: Run and hold it by the tail.

30. "O deep-swimmer, may you be well! Hold on firmly with strength. I will lift it up for you, as a Garuḍa lifts a snake."

He spoke this second verse.
Gambhīracārī: O otter who goes into the deep water. Te: To you. Bhaddaṃ: May goodness. Hotu: Be. Thāmasā: With strength. Daḷhaṃ: Firmly. Gaṇhāhi: Hold on. Suppaṇṇo: As a Garuḍa. Uragaṃ: A snake. Uddharati iva: Just as it lifts up. Ahaṃ: I. Taṃ: You. Uddharissāmi: Shall lift up.

31. "A dispute has arisen between us; O Dabbapuppha, listen to me. Settle our quarrel, friend, so that the dispute may be calmed."

He spoke this third verse.
Samma Dabbapuppha: O friend jackal, who has the color of the Dabbu flower. Me: My. Vacanaṃ: Words. Suṇohi: Listen. No: To us. Vivādo: A dispute. Samuppanno: Has arisen. Medhagaṃ: The quarrel. Samehi: Settle. Vivādo: The dispute. Vūpasammatu: May it be calmed.

32. "I was formerly a judge; many cases have been decided by me. I shall settle your quarrel, friend, so that the dispute may be calmed."

He spoke this verse.
Samma: Friend otter. Ahaṃ: I. Pure: Formerly. Dhammaṭṭho: Was a great minister who decided cases. Āsiṃ: Have been. Me: By me. Bahū: Many. Aḍḍā: Cases. Tīritā: Have been decided. Vo: Your. Sabbaṃ: All. Medhagaṃ: Quarrel. Samemi: I shall settle. Vivādo: The dispute. Vūpasammatu: May it be calmed.

Preaching with these verses found in the Dhammapada, the Teacher said, "Monks, Upananda is not only now possessed of great desire and great greed; in the past also he was possessed of great desire and great greed. He has not only now plundered the property of these monks; in the past also he plundered it." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree-deity by the river.

## The Otter Cannot Pull the Fish

At that time, a jackal lived in a certain place by the river with his wife named Māyāvī. One day, the female jackal said to the male jackal, "Lord, I have a pregnancy craving. I wish to eat the fresh meat of a Rohita fish." The male jackal said, "Be at ease; I shall bring it for you." While wandering along the riverbank, he walked along the shore with a vine entangled in his feet.

At that moment, two otters—one who swam in the deep and one who walked along the bank—were searching for fish and stood by the shore. Among the two, the deep-swimming otter saw a large Rohita fish, dived quickly into the water, and bit its tail. The powerful fish dragged him along.
315:
33. "The tail for the bank-walker, the head for the deep-swimmer. This middle part shall belong to the judge."

He spoke this verse.
Anutīracārī: O otter who walks along the bank. Tvaṃ: You. Naṅguṭṭhaṃ: The tail part. Gaṇha: Take. Sīsaṃ: The head part. Gambhīracārino: To the otter who goes into the deep. Hotu: Let it be. Acca: Beyond the two parts of head and tail. Ayaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍo: This middle part. Dhammaṭṭhassa: To me, the judge. Bhavissati: Shall be the fee for my wisdom.

34. "It would have been food for a long time, if we had not quarreled. The jackal carries away the Rohita fish, without the head and without the tail."

He spoke this verse.
Mayaṃ: We. Sace na vivademase: If we had not quarreled. Cirampi: For two or three days. Bhakkho: Food to eat. Abhavissa: It would have been. Asīsakaṃ: Which is not the head. Anaṅguṭṭhaṃ: Which is not the tail. Rohitaṃ: The Rohita fish meat including the middle belly. Siṅgālo: The jackal. Harati: Carries away.

35. "Just as a Khattiya king would rejoice upon gaining a kingdom, so do I rejoice today, seeing my husband with a full mouth."

He spoke this verse.
Khattiyo rājā: The Khattiya king. Rajjaṃ: The kingship. Laddhāna: Having obtained. Nandeyya yathā: Just as he would rejoice. Evaṃ tathā: Likewise. Ahampi: I also. Ajja: Today. Puṇṇamukhaṃ: Whose mouth is full. Patiṃ: My husband. Disvā: Having seen. Nandāmi: I rejoice.

36. "How is it that you, being a land-dweller, have caught a fish in the water? Tell me, friend, when asked; how was it obtained by you?"

He spoke this verse.
Samma: Lord jackal. Thalajo santo: Being a land-dweller. Udake: In the water. Macchaṃ: A fish. Kathaṃ nu: How. Parāmasi: Did you take? Puṭṭho: Being asked. Tvaṃ: You. Me: To me. Akkhāhi: Tell. Tayā: By you. Kathaṃ: How. Adhigataṃ: Was it obtained?

## Call the Otter for Help

The deep-swimming otter, wishing to speak with the bank-walking otter, said: "Friend otter, the fish is large. It will be enough for both of us; come, be my companion."

## I will help pull it up

Hearing those words, the bank-walking otter [responded with the second verse].

## They cannot agree on the division

Then those two otters together pulled out the Rohita fish, placed it on the bank, and killed it. They said to each other, "You divide it," "No, you divide it," and being unable to divide it, they sat there leaving it.

## Appointing the Jackal as Judge

At that time, when the jackal arrived at that place, the otters saw him and went to meet him, saying: "Friend jackal, we have together pulled out this Rohita fish. Being unable to divide it, a dispute has arisen between us. Please divide it into equal shares for us."

## I will divide it

Hearing those words, the jackal, wishing to show his power [spoke the verse].

## The middle part is my share

Wishing to divide the fish, he spoke this verse. Having said this, he divided the fish and said, "Do not quarrel; you eat the tail and the head," and while the otters were watching, he bit the middle part and ran away.
316:
37. "Through dispute they become lean; through dispute wealth is destroyed. The otters were defeated through dispute; eat the Rohita fish, O wily one."

He spoke this verse. Māyāvi: O wily one. Through dispute: because of quarreling. They become lean: they become thin. Through dispute: because of quarreling. Wealth is destroyed: property is exhausted. The otters: the two otters. Through dispute: because of quarreling. Were defeated: they lost the middle part of the Rohita fish. O wily one: O clever one. Eat the Rohita: eat this Rohita fish meat.

## Because we were quarreling
The two otters, like men who had lost a thousand pieces of wealth, sat with unhappy faces.

## The jackal's wife rejoices
The jackal, with a joyful heart thinking, "Today I shall let my wife eat Rohita fish meat," went to the presence of the female jackal. The female jackal, seeing the male jackal coming, was delighted.

## How did you get the big fish?
Wishing to ask about the cause of obtaining it, she spoke this verse.

## Obtained by dividing
The male jackal, wishing to inform the female jackal of the cause of obtaining it, spoke thus.

Having brought this past story, the All-Enlightened Buddha, after attaining Buddhahood, preached this verse:

38. "Even so among humans, wherever dispute arises, they run to the one who stands in Dhamma; for he is their leader. Wealth is also lost there, and the royal treasury increases."

Monks: O bhikkhus. Even so: in this very manner. Among humans: among people. Wherever: in whatever place. Dispute: quarreling. Arises: occurs. There: in that place. To the one who stands in Dhamma: they approach the judge. Indeed: it is true. He: that judge. Their: of those who are in dispute. Leader: he is the refuge who settles the dispute. There: in the presence of that judge. Wealth: even property. Is lost: they are defeated. The royal treasury: the King's treasury. Increases: it grows.

Concluding the Jātaka, the Teacher identified the birth: "At that time, the jackal was Upananda, the two otters were the two old monks, and I myself was the tree deity who witnessed the event."

## When among ourselves, we don't want to lose; but an outsider benefits
The Dabbhapuppha Jātaka is finished.
317:
## 6. Paṇṇaka Jātaka
## Curing a great illness with wisdom

Present Story: The All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, preached this Paṇṇaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Paṇṇakaṃ tikhiṇadhāraṃ," concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

The All-Enlightened Buddha asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha asked, "Who caused you to be dissatisfied?" When he replied, "My former wife caused it," the Buddha said, "Monk, this woman is one who works for your harm. In the past also, because of this woman, you were afflicted by a mental illness and were on the verge of death, but you regained your life by relying on the wise," and he brought the past story.

Past Story: Long ago, when King Maddava was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. They named him Senaka-kumāra. When he reached the age of maturity, he learned all the arts in Takkasilā and returned to Bārāṇasī to become a minister who advised King Maddava on matters of welfare and Dhamma. Known as Senaka the Wise, he was as famous throughout the city as the moon and the sun because of his wisdom.

## Giving away the Queen
At that time, the son of King Maddava's royal chaplain came to serve the King. Seeing the King's Chief Queen, who was adorned with all ornaments and possessed supreme beauty, he became infatuated. He went home, stopped eating, and lay down. When his friends asked him, he told them the reason.
318:
39. "A man swallows a sharp-edged sword, a Paṇṇaka blade that drinks [blood] well, in the midst of the assembly. What is more difficult than that? Tell me, being asked, what other difficult thing there is."

He spoke this first verse. Wise one: O sage. Paṇṇaka: made in the Paṇṇaka country. Sharp-edged: having a keen blade. That drinks well: that drinks the blood of others. Sword: the blade. A man: a person. In the midst of the assembly: in the middle of the crowd. Swallows: he gulps it down. Than that: than swallowing that sword. More difficult: is there any cause more difficult? Other: another. Difficult: hard to do. Whatever cause: if there is any such cause. That cause: that matter. Being asked: you who are questioned. Tell me: please inform me.

The King also asked, "The chaplain's son is not seen; where is he?" Hearing the reason, he summoned the chaplain's son and said, "I give this Queen to you for seven days. Keep her in your house for seven days and bring her back on the eighth day."

The chaplain's son agreed, saying, "Very well," and took the Queen to his house. Delighting with her and being mutually infatuated, they fled through the main gate without letting anyone know and went to the territory of another king. No one knew where they went; it was like the path of a boat [leaving no trace].

## The King falls ill
Although the King had the drum beaten throughout the city and searched in various ways, he did not find the Queen's whereabouts. Then, because of the Queen, great grief arose in the King. His heart became hot and blood flowed. From that time on, blood came out from the King's bowels. A great illness occurred. Even the great royal physicians were unable to cure him.
319:
40. A man might swallow a sword, well-honed and blood-drinking, out of greed;
But he who says "I give," that is harder than that.
Know thus, O Maddava, that everything else is easy.

He spoke this second verse. 
O Maddava, King of the Maddava lineage. A man, out of greed, might swallow a sword that drinks the blood of others. But he who says "I give," that word of promising to give is more difficult than swallowing that sword. Every other matter is easy. Know this to be so.

41. Ayura has answered the question, he who is skilled in the meaning of the Dhamma.
Now I ask Pukkusa: what is harder than that?
Whatever other difficult thing there is, tell me when asked.

He spoke this third verse.
Ayura, who is skilled in the Dhamma, has explained the meaning of the question. Now I shall ask Pukkusa. Is there any matter more difficult than the word of promising to give? If there is any other difficult matter, you who are asked, please tell me.

42. They do not live by words alone, an empty speech uttered;
But he who, having given, does not turn back, that is harder than that.
Know thus, O Maddava, that everything else is easy.

He spoke this fourth verse.
O Maddava, King of the Maddava lineage. Those who are wise do not live by depending on empty, fruitless words that are uttered. But he who, having given, does not remain attached [to the gift]. That act of giving is more difficult than the word of promising to give that object. Every other matter is easy. Know this to be so.

## Healing through a Story
The Bodhisatta thought, "This king has no physical illness; he has a mental illness because he does not see his queen. I will treat him with a stratagem." He called the wise ministers named Ayura and Pukkusa and said, "The king has no illness other than the mental distress caused by not seeing the queen. Indeed, he has been very kind to us; therefore, let us treat him.

We shall hold a festival in the palace courtyard and have those skilled in sword-swallowing perform. We will place the king at the lion-cage window to watch the performance. When the king sees the sword-swallower, he will ask the question, 'Is there any other task more difficult than swallowing a sword?' Friend Ayura... you shall answer, 'Saying "I give this much wealth" is more difficult than swallowing this sword.'

After that, friend Pukkusa... he will ask you. Then you shall answer the king, 'Great King... the words of one who says "I give" but does not give are fruitless. Some do not live by such words. Those who act in accordance with their words and give the wealth as promised—such giving is more difficult than the word "I give".' I shall know what to do beyond that," he said, and had the festival prepared.

## The King Watches the Performance
Then those three wise men went to the king and said, "Great King... there is a festival in the palace courtyard. For those who watch the festival, even suffering becomes happiness. Please come, let us go." They escorted the king, opened the lion-cage window, and let him watch the festival.
320:
After hearing those words, the king reflected, "I first said 'I give the queen to the chaplain's son,' and acting in accordance with my word, I gave her. Truly, I have done a very difficult thing." As he contemplated this, the sorrow in his heart lessened slightly. Then he thought, "There is no one wiser than the wise Senaka; I will ask him this question." Then, wishing to ask him, he spoke the fifth verse:

43. Pukkusa has answered the question, he who is skilled in the meaning of the Dhamma.
Now I ask Senaka: what is harder than that?
Whatever other difficult thing there is, tell me when asked.

He spoke this fifth verse.
Pukkusa, who is skilled in the Dhamma, has explained the meaning of the question. Now I shall ask Senaka. Is there any matter more difficult than swallowing a sword, promising to give, or the act of giving? If there is any other difficult matter, you who are asked, please tell me.

44. A man may give a gift, whether it be little or much;
But he who, having given, does not regret it, that is harder than that.
Know thus, O Maddava, that everything else is easy.

He spoke this sixth verse.
O Maddava, King of the Maddava lineage. A man may give a gift, whether it be small or great. But he who, having given, does not later feel regret or remorse. That state of not regretting is more difficult than the act of giving itself. Every other matter is easy. Know this to be so.

Many people displayed the arts they were skilled in. One man swallowed a sharp-edged sword thirty-three finger-breadths long.

## Swallowing a Sword is Difficult
The king, seeing that man, thought, "This man swallows a sword. I will ask the wise men if there is any task more difficult than swallowing this sword." Wishing to ask Ayura—

## Saying "I Give" is Harder
At that time, the minister Ayura, wishing to answer that matter—

Hearing the words of the wise Ayura, the king thought, "Saying 'I give this much wealth' is more difficult than swallowing a sword. I also said 'I give the queen to the chaplain's son.' Truly, I have done what is very difficult." As he investigated and reflected, the sorrow in the king's heart became somewhat lighter.

Then the king thought, "Is there any other matter more difficult than the word of promising to give to another?" Wishing to speak with the wise Pukkusa—

## Giving is Even Harder
At that time, the wise Pukkusa, wishing to answer—

Hearing those words, the king thought, "I first said 'I give the queen to the chaplain's son,' and in accordance with that, I gave her. Truly, I have done what is very difficult." For the king who thought thus, his sorrow became very light.

## What is Most Difficult?
Then the king had the thought, "There is no one truly wise except the counselor Senaka. I will ask this question to the counselor Senaka." Then, wishing to ask the counselor Senaka—

## Do Not Regret After Giving
At that time, the minister Senaka, wishing to answer—

## The King's Illness is Cured
The king, hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, thought, "I gave the queen to the chaplain's son by my own will, yet I am unable to keep my mind firm; I grieve and suffer. This is not appropriate for me. If she still had affection for me—"
321:
45. Āyura explained the problem, and then the man Pukkusa.
Senaka’s words surpass all, just as he speaks.

He uttered this concluding verse. 
Āyura, the minister Āyura. Pañhaṃ, the problem. Vyākāsi, explained. Atho, thereafter. Pukkusaporiso, the man Pukkusa. Pañhaṃ, the problem. Vyākāsi, explained. Bhāsito, the words spoken by the wise Senaka. Sabbe, all. Pañhe, problems. Atibhoti, stands surpassing. Yathā, in which manner. Senako, the wise Senaka. Bhāsati, speaks. Tatheva, in that very manner. Hoti, it is.

“I am distressed and weary. Such distress is not fitting for me. If that queen had affection for me, she would not have fled, abandoning this sovereignty. What use is a wife to me who fled without having affection for me?” As the king thought thus, all his sorrow fell away and vanished like a water drop from a lotus leaf. At that very moment, the king’s diarrhea ceased. The king became healthy and happy, and wishing to praise the Bodhisatta—

Being pleased, he praised the Bodhisatta with this verse and gave him much wealth.

Conclusion of the Jātaka: The Perfectly Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). How was the Jātaka identified? At that time, the former wife was the Chief Queen. The weary monk was the King. Moggallāna was the wise Āyura. Sāriputta was the wise Pukkusa. I, the Buddha, was the wise Senaka. Thus, He identified the Jātaka.

## The Disease Caused by the Mind, Cure it with the Mind
The Paṇṇaka Jātaka ends.

## 7. Sattubhasta Jātaka
## Saving the Life of Another through Wisdom
The Present Story: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sattubhasta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Vibbhantacitto,” concerning His own Perfection of Wisdom.

The Present Story will become clear in the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Janaka was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. They named the Bodhisatta “Young Senaka.”

## Minister Senaka
When young Senaka reached maturity, he studied all the arts at Takkasilā and returned to Bārāṇasī to have an audience with the king. The king appointed young Senaka to the position of minister and granted him great wealth.

That minister Senaka advised the king on matters of benefit and Dhamma. He was a sweet-spoken preacher of the Dhamma, establishing the king in the five precepts, and leading him to stay in good practices such as giving alms, observing the Uposatha, and the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakamma-patha). Throughout the whole country, it was as if a Buddha had appeared.
322:
On Uposatha days, the king, the viceroy, and all other royals would gather and prepare a hall for the Dhamma. The Great Being, seated upon a magnificent jeweled throne in the prepared Dhamma hall, would preach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha; his Dhamma talk was like the Dhamma talk of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas.

## The Wife with a Paramour
At that time, a certain old Brahmin went to beg for money and, having obtained a thousand coins, he entrusted them to a certain Brahmin family and went away saying, “I shall go begging again.” During the time the old Brahmin was away, that family spent the coins. When the old Brahmin returned, he asked for the coins to be brought to him.

The Brahmin, being unable to return the coins, gave his own daughter to the old Brahmin to serve as his handmaid. The old Brahmin took their daughter and lived in a certain Brahmin village near the city of Bārāṇasī. Then, the old Brahmin’s wife, because of her youth, was not satisfied with sensual pleasures and committed misconduct with another young Brahmin.

## The 16 Types of Persons Who Are Not Satisfied
There are sixteen things that are called “unsatisfied.” What are the sixteen?
1. The ocean is not satisfied with all the river waters.
2. Fire is not satisfied with fuel.
323:
3. A king is not satisfied with his kingdom.
4. A fool is not satisfied with evil conduct.
5. A woman is not satisfied with three things: sexual intercourse, adornment, and giving birth.
6. A Brahmin is not satisfied with the Vedas.
7. One who has attained Jhāna is not satisfied with meditative attainments (samāpatti).
8. A trainee (sekha) is not satisfied with Nibbāna.
9. One of few desires is not satisfied with the dhutaṅga practices.
10. One who has initiated effort is not satisfied with making effort.
11. A Dhamma preacher is not satisfied with discussion.
12. A confident person is not satisfied with an assembly.
13. A person of faith is not satisfied with serving the Saṅgha.
14. A donor is not satisfied with generosity.
15. A wise person is not satisfied with hearing the Dhamma.
16. The four assemblies are not satisfied with seeing the Exalted Buddha.
These are the sixteen.

## The Old Brahmin Goes to Find a Servant
That young Brahmin wife, also being unsatisfied with sexual intercourse, wished to send the old Brahmin away so she could practice evil conduct freely. One day, she lay down with a displeased face. When asked, “My dear, what is it?”, she said, “Brahmin, I am unable to do the work in your house. Go and bring a female slave and a male slave.” “My dear, I have no wealth. What shall I give to bring them?” he asked. “Go wandering for alms, seek wealth, and bring them,” she said. “If that is so, my dear, prepare travel provisions for me,” he replied.
324:
46. Your mind is wandering, your senses are disturbed,
Tears are flowing from your eyes.
What have you lost, or what do you desire,
That you have come here, O Brahmin? Tell me that.

He spoke this first verse. 
Brahma, Brahmin. I urge you. You have an agitated and trembling mind. You have impaired visual senses. Tears flow from your eyes. What property of yours is lost? What do you seek that you have come to this place? Speak.

47. My wife would die today if I go,
The Yakkha said I would die if I do not go.
I am shaken by this suffering.
Tell me this matter, O Senaka.

He spoke this second verse. 
Brahmin, today both of you would die. If you go home, your wife will die. If you do not go, I (you) will die. Thus said the Yakkha (tree deity). I am shaken by this suffering. Senaka the Wise, tell me this matter.

The Brahmin's wife filled a leather bag with both bound and unbound cakes for the old Brahmin. While wandering through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, the Brahmin obtained seven hundred coins. Thinking, "This much wealth is enough for a maidservant and a manservant," he returned toward his village. On the way, at a pleasant place with water, he untied the bag, ate some cakes, and then went down to drink water without tying the bag.

## You and Your Wife Will Die
At that time, a cobra in a hollow tree smelled the scent of the cakes, entered the bag, coiled up, and slept while eating the cakes. The Brahmin returned and, without looking inside, tied the bag, placed it on his shoulder, and went on.

A tree deity residing in a fork of a tree said, "Brahmin, if you stay on the way, you will die; if you reach home today, your wife will die," and then vanished.

## The Old Brahmin Follows to Hear the Dhamma
The Brahmin looked but did not see the deity. Being afraid and terrified by the fear of death, he reached the gate of Bārāṇasī weeping.

It was the fifteenth-day Uposatha. Seeing people going to hear the Dhamma from the wise Senaka, who was seated on a decorated Dhamma-throne, he asked, "Where are you going?" When they said, "Brahmin, today the wise Senaka is preaching the Dhamma with a sweet voice and the splendor of a Buddha; do you not know?", the Brahmin thought, "The wise one is preaching. I am terrified by the fear of death. Wise men are able to dispel great sorrow. It is proper for me to go to that wise one and hear the Dhamma."
