Having thought so, the Brahmin went with them and stood weeping near the Dhamma-throne at the edge of the assembly, which included the King surrounding the Bodhisatta, with the bag slung over his shoulder, terrified by the fear of death. The Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma like a falling waterfall. The multitude, being joyful and delighted, gave shouts of applause and listened to the Dhamma.
325:
## Why?
Wise men usually open the four directions and look around at the assembly. Looking thus, he saw the Brahmin and thought, "This vast assembly is joyful, giving applause and listening to the Dhamma. But this one Brahmin has reached a state of unhappiness and is weeping. There must be a sorrow within this Brahmin capable of producing tears. Just as one removes the tarnish of copper with acid, or as a drop of water is made to fall from a lotus leaf, I will submerge his sorrow and make him free of grief and joyful in mind, and then I will preach the Dhamma." He called the Brahmin and said, "Brahmin, I am the one called Senaka the Wise. Now I will make you free of sorrow. Speak without hesitation." Desiring to converse with the Brahmin—

## Because the Deity Said He Would Die
Then, desiring to tell the Bodhisatta the cause of his sorrow, the Brahmin said—

## How Senaka the Minister Thought
The Bodhisatta, hearing the Brahmin's words, spread the net of his knowledge like one spreading a net over the surface of the ocean, thinking: "There are many causes of death for beings. Those submerged in the ocean die; those caught by fierce fish in the ocean die; those crossing the Ganges die; those caught by crocodiles in the Ganges die; those falling from trees die; those pierced by thorns, or struck by various weapons, or eating poison, or hanging themselves, or falling from cliffs, or oppressed by various diseases such as cold, also die. Among these many causes of death, for what reason would this Brahmin die today if he stays on the way, and why would his wife die if he goes home?"

As he was thinking, he saw the bag on the Brahmin's shoulder and thought, "There must be a snake that has entered this bag. When the Brahmin went to drink water and returned, he must have tied the bag and carried it away without knowing the snake had entered. If he stays on the way and unties the bag to eat the cakes, he will put his hand in. Then the snake will bite his hand and cause his death. This is the cause of death for the Brahmin staying on the way.

If he goes home, the bag will reach his wife's hands. Thinking, 'I will look at the goods inside,' she will untie the bag and put her hand in. Then the snake will cause that Brahmin woman's death. This is the cause of death for the wife when the Brahmin reaches home today." Thus he knew by his knowledge of skillful means (upāyakosalla-ñāṇa).
326:
48. Having reflected on many grounds,
What I shall say here is the truth.
I think, O Brahmin, into your flour bag,
A black snake has entered without your knowledge.

He spoke this third verse. 
Brahmin, O Brahmin. Bahūni, many. Ṭhānāni, grounds or reasons. Vicintayitvā, having reflected. Ettha, among these grounds. Yaṃ, which ground. Ahaṃ, I. Vakkhāmi, shall say. Tadeva, that very ground I say. Saccaṃ, is true; thus I think (maññāmi). Ajānato, while you were unaware. Te, your. Sattubhastaṃ, into the flour bag. Kaṇhasappo, a black snake (cobra). Paviṭṭho, has entered; thus I think (maññāmi).

49. Taking a stick, strike the bag; see the slavering, double-tongued reptile.
Cut off your doubts and uncertainties today; see the serpent and loosen the bag.

He spoke this fourth verse. 
Brahmin, O Brahmin. Daṇḍaṃ, a stick. Ādāya, taking hold of. Bhastaṃ, the bag. Parisumbha, strike it. Eḷamūgaṃ, having a mouth that drivels saliva. Dujivhaṃ, double-tongued. Uragaṃ, the snake. Passa, behold. Ajja, today. Kaṅkhaṃ, doubt. Vicikicchitāni, repeated uncertainties. Chinda, cut off. Bhastaṃ, the bag. Pamuñca, loosen. Bhujangamaṃ, the serpent. Passa, behold.

At that time, the Bodhisatta thought: “This cobra must be brave and fearless. Even though it is struck against the side, it does not make even a slight movement in the bag, nor does it reveal its presence in the midst of such an assembly. Therefore, this snake must be brave and fearless.”

## A Snake is in Your Bag

Having so reflected, the Bodhisatta, knowing this snake through his wisdom skilled in means as if seeing it with divine vision, and wishing to solve the Brahmin’s problem by discerning it with his wisdom skilled in means—like a man standing in the midst of an assembly including the King who sees a snake entering a bag—said:

After saying this, he asked, “Brahmin, is there flour in your bag?” “Wise One, there is,” he replied. “Did you eat flour at the time of your morning meal today?” he asked. “Yes, Wise One, I did,” he replied. “Where were you sitting when you ate?” he asked. “Wise One, I sat at the foot of a tree in the forest and ate,” he replied.

“Brahmin, when you went to drink water after eating the flour, did you tie the mouth of the bag or not?” he asked. “Wise One, I did not tie it,” he replied. “When you returned from drinking water, did you look into the bag before tying it?” he asked. “Wise One, I tied it without looking,” he replied. “Brahmin, while you were away drinking water, I think a snake entered the bag without your knowledge, drawn by the scent of the flour.

## Open the Bag and Look for the Snake

In this matter, that thought is indeed true. Therefore, set the bag down, place it in the midst of the assembly, untie the mouth of the bag, and after stepping back, take a stick and strike the bag. Then, seeing the cobra emerge with its hood raised and making a hissing sound, you will be free from doubt.”
327:
50. Trembling with fear in the midst of the assembly,
That Brahmin untied the flour bag.
Then out came the snake of fierce power,
A venomous serpent with its hood raised.

He preached this fifth verse.
Bhikkhave, O monks. Saṃviggarūpo, having a trembling nature. So brāhmaṇo, that Brahmin. Parisāya majjhe, in the midst of the assembly. Sattubhastaṃ, the flour bag. Pamuñci, untied. Atha, then. Urago, the breast-goer (snake). Uggatejo, of fierce power. Āsīviso, having swift venom. Sappo, the snake. Phaṇaṃ, its hood. Karitvā, having raised. Nikkhami, emerged.

## The Cobra Has Emerged

Upon hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, the Brahmin was struck with terror and did exactly as the Bodhisatta had said. When the bag was struck with the stick, the snake emerged from the mouth of the bag and stood looking at the great crowd.

Wishing to illustrate this matter, the Fully Enlightened Buddha said:

## The Power of Wisdom

When the snake emerged with its hood raised, the people, thinking, “The Bodhisatta’s explanation is like that of a Fully Enlightened Buddha,” caused thousands of head-cloths to be tossed in the air. They also snapped their fingers by the thousands. A rain of the seven kinds of jewels fell like a heavy downpour of rain. Thousands of cheers arose. It was like the sound of the great earth cracking.

This explaining of such a problem with Buddha-like grace is not the power of birth, nor the power of lineage or family. Whose power is it? It is the power of wisdom.

This is true. A wise person, having developed insight (vipassanā) and opened the door of the Noble Path (ariya-magga), enters the Great Deathless Nibbāna. He penetrates and knows the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī), the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of a Fully Enlightened Buddha (sammā-sambodhi). Among the qualities that lead to the Great Deathless Nibbāna, wisdom is supreme; the remaining qualities are merely its retinue. Therefore, it is said:

“Wisdom is indeed supreme, say the skilled,
Like the moon, the king of stars, among the stars.
Virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the righteous,
Follow in the wake of the wise.”

When the Bodhisatta had thus solved the problem, a snake charmer performed a mouth-binding on the snake, took it, and released it in the forest. The Brahmin approached the King, wished him victory, and with hands raised in salutation, wishing to praise the King, spoke this half-verse:

51. Great is the gain for King Janaka,
Who beholds Senaka of excellent wisdom.

Yo, which King Janaka. Sādhupaññaṃ, who has excellent wisdom. Senakaṃ, the minister Senaka. Passati, beholds. Janakassa, of that King Janaka. Tassa rañño, of that King. Lābhā, the gain of beholding the wise one. Suladdhalābhā, is a gain well-attained.
328:
## The Brahmin’s Homage

After praising the King, the Brahmin took the seven hundred coins from his bag and, wishing to give a gift of appreciation to the Bodhisatta, praised him and spoke this verse along with its word-for-word explanation:

“Are you the one who has removed the veil, the All-Seer?
Is your wisdom, O Brahmin, of such a formidable nature?

52. I have these seven hundred coins;
I give them all to you.
For through you, my life was saved today,
And you have also brought safety to my wife.”

O Brahmin, are you the Omniscient Buddha, who has removed the veil of defilements and sees all things? Is your wisdom, though you are not omniscient, extremely formidable and powerful like the knowledge of omniscience?

I have these seven hundred coins. Take them. I give all these riches to you. It is true; because of what you have given, I have received my life today. Furthermore, you alone have brought about the welfare of my wife.

The Brahmin spoke thus and repeatedly entreated the Bodhisatta, saying, “Even if I had a hundred thousand, I would give it. This is all the wealth I have; please take these seven hundred coins of mine.”

## The Gift of Three Hundred Coins

53. “Wise men do not take payment
For beautifully spoken, diverse verses.
O Brahmin, let them give you wealth even from here;
Take it and go to your own home.”

He spoke this sixth verse. O Brahmin, wise men do not take a fee for diverse and well-spoken words. O Brahmin, let them give you three hundred coins even from here, at my feet. Take them and go to your own home.

## Instructions for Going Home

Having said this, the Bodhisatta made the amount up to a thousand for the Brahmin, gave him the coins, and asked, “Brahmin, who sent you to beg for wealth?” “O Wise One, my wife sent me,” he replied. “Is your wife old or young?” he asked. “O Wise One, she is young,” he said.
329:
“Since it is so, that young woman, while committing misconduct with another, sent you away so that she could do so without fear. If you bring these coins home, she will give the coins you earned with such difficulty to her lover. Therefore, do not take that wealth directly to the house; hide the coins under a tree or in some unmarked place outside the village before entering.” Having said this, he sent the Brahmin away.

## The Thousand Coins are Lost

The Brahmin reached the vicinity of the village, hid the coins at the foot of a tree, and went home at night. At that moment, the Brahmin’s wife was with her lover. The Brahmin stood at the door and called out, “My lady!”

The young woman recognized the Brahmin’s voice, extinguished the lamp, and opened the door. As the Brahmin entered the house, she let her lover out, kept him by the door, and then went back inside. Seeing nothing in the bag, she asked, “Brahmin, how much wealth did you receive from begging?” “My lady, I received a thousand coins,” he said. When she asked, “Where is that wealth?” he replied, “I left it in such-and-such a place. I will bring it tomorrow morning; do not worry.” The young woman went and told her lover, and the lover went out and took the wealth as if it were his own.

## Reporting the Loss

The next day, the Brahmin went and did not see the coins. He went to the Bodhisatta, and when asked, “Brahmin, what is it?” he said, “O Wise One, I do not see the coins.” “Did you tell your wife?” the Bodhisatta asked. “O Wise One, I told her,” he replied. The Bodhisatta, knowing that the wife had told her lover, asked, “Brahmin, does your wife have a family priest (teacher-brahmin)?” “O Wise One, she has,” he said.

## The Method of Investigation

Then the Bodhisatta gave the Brahmin provisions for seven days and said, “Go. On the first day, invite and feed fourteen Brahmins: seven who are your teachers and seven who are your wife’s teachers. From the next day onwards, reduce the number by one each day. On the seventh day, invite two Brahmins: one who is your teacher and one who is your wife’s teacher. Observe which Brahmin among those invited by your wife comes consistently for all seven days, and then report back to me.”
330:
That Brahmin did as the Bodhisatta said and informed the Great Being, "Wise one, I have identified the Brahmin who constantly comes to eat."

The Bodhisatta sent men along with that Brahmin to fetch the other Brahmin. He then asked, "Did you take a thousand kahāpaṇas belonging to this Brahmin from the foot of such-and-such a tree?" "I did not take them, wise one," he replied. The Bodhisatta said, "Brahmin, do you not know that I am Senaka the Wise? I shall have those kahāpaṇas brought forth."

Being afraid, that Brahmin confessed, "I have taken them." "Where have you kept them?" he was asked. "Wise one, they are kept in that very place," he replied. The Bodhisatta then asked the old Brahmin, "Brahmin, do you wish to have that same woman as your wife, or would you like to take another?" "Wise one, I wish for that very young Brahmin woman to be my wife," he replied.

## The Paramour is Apprehended

The Bodhisatta sent men to fetch both the Brahmin's kahāpaṇas and the young Brahmin woman. He had the kahāpaṇas returned to the old Brahmin from the hands of the thief Brahmin. He then inflicted royal punishment upon the thief Brahmin and had him paraded through the city. He also exercised royal authority over the Brahmin woman. He gave the old Brahmin great attendants and let him reside in his own presence.

To conclude the Jātaka, the All-Enlightened Buddha delivered this Dhamma teaching, revealed the Truths, and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, many attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. As for the identification of the birth: "At that time, the old Brahmin was Ānanda, the tree deity was Sāriputta, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Senaka the Wise was I myself."

## Associating with the Wise Brings Happiness to All

Here ends the Sattubhasta Jātaka.

## 8. Aṭṭhisena Jātaka

## Why the Virtuous Do Not Beg

While residing at the Aggāḷava Shrine near the city of Āḷavī, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Aṭṭhisena Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yeme ahaṃ na jānāmi," concerning the Kuṭikāra training rule.

The present story has already been told below in the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka. In particular, the All-Enlightened Buddha called those monks and said, "Monks, in the past, before the Buddha appeared, those who went forth in external ordinations did not beg, even when invited by kings, thinking, 'Begging is unloved and unpleasant to others.'" Having said this, he brought forth the past story.
331:
54. "Yeme ahaṃ na jānāmi, aṭṭhisena vanibbake.
Te maṃ saṅgamma yācanti, kasmā maṃ tvaṃ na yācasi."

He spoke this first verse:
"Aṭṭhisena, O Venerable Aṭṭhisena. These beggars whom I do not know, they come to me in a group and beg. Why do you not beg of me?"

55. "Yācako appiyo hoti, yācaṃ adadamappiyo.
Tasmāhaṃ taṃ na yācāmi, mā me videssanā ahu."

He spoke this second verse:
"Great King, a person who begs becomes unloved by the giver. A person who does not give the requested object becomes unloved by the beggar. Therefore, I do not beg of you, O King, lest there be mutual dislike between us."

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a certain market town. They named him Young Aṭṭhisena.

## Becoming an Ascetic

When he reached the age of maturity, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā. Later, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he left the household life and became an ascetic. He attained the Jhanas, the Higher Knowledges (Abhiññā), and the Attainments (Samāpatti). After living for a long time in the Himalayan region, he descended to the human realm to seek salt and acidic foods. In due course, he reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in the royal park. The next day, while going for alms, he arrived at the palace courtyard.

## The King's Devotion

The King, being impressed by the Bodhisatta's conduct and deportment, invited him and had him sit on a prepared couch on the palace terrace. He fed him excellent food. At the end of the meal, having heard the words of appreciation (Anumodanā), the King was pleased. He requested the Great Being to stay permanently in the royal park and, having received his consent, settled him there. Every day, the King went to attend on him two or three times. One day, being pleased with a Dhamma talk, the King invited him, saying, "Starting from my kingship, whatever object you desire, Venerable Sir, please ask for it."

The Bodhisatta, however, did not say, "Give me this object."
332:
Other beggars ask for whatever they desire, saying, "Give me this, give me that." The King, being unattached, gives to them.

## Why Do You Not Ask?

One day, the King thought: "Other beggars ask us for such and such things, saying, 'Give this to us.' However, the Venerable Atthisena has not asked for anything since the time of his invitation. This monk is truly wise and skilled in means. I shall ask him about this matter."

Having thought so, one day after his morning meal, the King went to the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Desiring to ask why others beg and why the hermit does not, he said—

## Asking Leads to Dislike

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta—

## Ask for Whatever You Desire

Then, hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, the King spoke these three verses:

56. "Indeed, one who lives by begging but does not ask when it is time to ask, deprives others of merit and does not live [well] himself.

57. "But one who lives by begging and asks when it is time to ask, enables others to gain merit and lives [well] himself.

58. "The wise do not feel resentment upon seeing a beggar arrive. O practitioner of the holy life, you are dear to me; speak, what do you wish to say?"

Ayya Atthisena: Venerable Atthisena. Yācanajīvāno: one who lives by begging. Yo ca: whichever monk or brahmin. Ve: indeed. Kāle: at the proper time for begging. Yācaṃ: the object to be requested. Na yācati: does not ask. That monk or brahmin parañca: others also; puññaṃ: merit; dhamsati: causes to diminish. Attanāpi: he himself also; na jīvati: does not live happily.

Ayya Atthisena: Venerable Atthisena. Yācanajīvāno: one who lives by begging. Yo ca: whichever monk or brahmin. Kāle: at the proper time for begging. Yācanaṃ: the object to be requested. Yācati: asks. That monk or brahmin parañca: others also; puññaṃ: merit; labbheti: enables them to obtain. Attanāpi ca: he himself also; jīvati: lives happily.

Ayya Atthisena: Venerable Atthisena. Sappaññā: the wise who know about giving and the fruits of giving. Yācakamāgate: beggars who have arrived. Disvā: having seen. Na vedessanti: do not get angry. Me: to me. Brahmacārī: the practitioner of the holy life. Piyo: is dear. Asi: you are. Tasmā: therefore. Tvaṃ: you. Bhaññaṃ—bhaṇitabbavacanaṃ—yaṃ kiñci vattabbaṃ: whatever should be said. Icchasi: if you desire. Vada: just speak. Sabbañca rajjampi: even the entire kingdom. Te: to you. Taṃ: that prize. Dassāmiyeva: I shall certainly give.

In this way, even though the King invited him by offering his kingship, the Bodhisatta did not ask for anything.
333:
59. "The wise indeed do not beg; the wise [donor] should know for himself. The Noble Ones stand [for alms] with a purpose; that is the begging of the Noble Ones."

Mahārāja: O Great King. Ve: indeed. Sappaññā: the wise, such as the Buddhas and others. Na yācanti: do not beg. Ca: even though they do not beg. Dhīro: the wise donor. Vedituṃ: to know [the need] on his own. Arahati: is worthy. Ariyā: the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others. Uddissa: with a purpose. Tiṭṭhanti: they stand. Esā: this standing with a purpose. Ariyānaṃ: of the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others. Yācanā: is called begging.

## The Noble Way of Begging

When the King expressed his wish in this way, the Bodhisatta, intending to show the practice of monks, said: "Great King, this act of begging is the habit of laypeople who enjoy sensual pleasures, not of those who have gone forth. From the time of ordination, a monk should have a pure livelihood that is unlike that of laypeople." Thus, desiring to show the practice of a monk, he spoke the sixth verse:

## Offering a Thousand Cows

Hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the King said: "Venerable Sir, if a wise attendant, knowing for himself, should offer what is suitable to his teacher, I too shall offer such and such objects to you."

## The Hermit Does Not Accept

When this was said, the Bodhisatta declined, saying: "Great King, I am a monk without encumbrances; I have no need for cows." The King, established in the Bodhisatta's teaching, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and passed away to the heavenly realm. The Bodhisatta, having attained unwavering meditative absorption, was reborn in the Brahma realm.
334:
60. “O Brahmin, I give you a thousand cows along with a bull; for how could a noble person not give to another noble person, having heard your verses endowed with the Dhamma?”

[The King said:] “O Brahmin, O Monk. To you, I give a thousand cows, including a bull, which are of red color and provide the sweet taste of milk and curd. Please accept them from me. I, being noble in conduct, how could I not give to you, who are also noble in conduct? For what reason would I not give?”

When this was said, the Bodhisatta declined, saying, “O Great King, I am a penniless ascetic; I have no need for cows.” The King, established in his advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and became destined for heaven. The Bodhisatta, with his meditative absorptions (jhāna) unimpaired, was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. To identify the Jātaka: “At that time, Ānanda was the King, and I myself was the ascetic Aṭṭhisena.”

## Even if one asks, they are hated; if one does not give, they are hated; finally, friendship is destroyed.
The Aṭṭhisena Jātaka is concluded.

## 9. Kapi Jātaka
## Destruction due to not listening to the words of the wise

While the All-Enlightened Teacher, the instructor of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he spoke this Kapi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Yattha verī nivasati,” concerning Devadatta being swallowed by the earth. When Devadatta was swallowed by the earth, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, Devadatta has perished along with his followers.”

The All-Enlightened Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they replied, “For such a discussion,” he said, “Monks, not only now has Devadatta perished along with his followers; in the past also, he perished indeed.” Having said this, being requested by the monks, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the monkey tribe and lived in the royal garden surrounded by five hundred monkeys. The future Devadatta was also reborn in the monkey tribe and lived in that same garden surrounded by five hundred monkeys.

## The Foolishness of a Monkey
Then one day, as the royal chaplain went to the garden, bathed, adorned himself, and was leaving, a mischievous monkey went ahead and sat on top of the ornamental archway of the garden gate. He dropped excrement on the Brahmin’s head, and when the Brahmin looked up, he dropped it again on his face.

## The Brahmin Harbors a Grudge
The Brahmin turned back and threatened the monkeys, harboring a grudge, saying, “Let it be so; I shall know what must be done to you.” He then bathed again and departed.
335:
## The Wise Monkeys Relocate
The monkeys informed the Bodhisatta about the Brahmin harboring a grudge and his threats. The Bodhisatta said, “It is not proper to dwell in a place where enemies reside. Let the entire troop of monkeys go elsewhere.” He informed the thousand monkeys. However, a stubborn monkey, taking his own followers, said, “I will see about it later,” and remained in that very garden. The Bodhisatta took his own followers and entered the forest.

## The Elephants Develop Sores
Then one day, a goat was eating grain that had been spread out in the sun by a servant girl who was pounding rice. The goat was struck with a torch and, with its body on fire, ran and rubbed itself against the wall of a grass hut located near the elephant stable. The fire caught the grass hut. From that grass hut, it spread to the elephant stable. When the stable caught fire, the backs of the elephants were burned. The elephant doctors were unable to treat them. The chaplain, meanwhile, was wandering about looking for a way to catch the monkeys.

## The Foolish Monkeys Die
At that time, the King saw the Brahmin who had come to attend on him and asked, “Teacher, many of our elephants have developed sores. The elephant doctors are unable to cure them. Do you know of any medicine?” The chaplain replied, “O Great King, there are medicines derived from monkeys.”

“Teacher, what is this medicine derived from monkeys?” the King asked. “O Great King, it is monkey fat,” he replied. “Teacher, where shall we get it?” When asked, he said, “Are there not many monkeys in your Majesty’s garden?” The King said, “Go and kill the monkeys in the garden and bring the fat.” Archers went and shot and killed the five hundred monkeys.

## The Dhamma Words of the Wise Monkey
One monkey leader, though he received a fatal wound while fleeing, did not fall there but reached the place where the Bodhisatta resided and then fell. The monkeys informed the Bodhisatta that he had reached their place and died, and about his being wounded and his death.

The Bodhisatta went and sat in the midst of the monkey troop. Desiring to admonish the monkeys, he spoke these verses, saying, “Those who dwell in an enemy’s place without listening to the advice of the wise perish in this way”:

61. “Where an enemy dwells, a wise man should not stay. Even for one or two nights, dwelling among enemies is painful.”
62. “A person of fickle mind who follows such a one is an enemy to himself. Because of a single monkey, the whole troop was brought to ruin.”
63. “A fool who thinks himself wise, when he is the leader of a troop, falls under the power of his own mind and lies down like this monkey.”
64. “A powerful fool who is the leader of a troop is not good. He brings harm to his kinsmen, like a fowler to the birds.”
65. “A powerful wise man is good as a leader of a troop. He brings welfare to his kinsmen, like Vāsava to the Thirty-three Gods.”
66. “He who sees in himself virtue, wisdom, and learning...”
336:
67. "Therefore, one should weigh oneself, as if with virtue, wisdom, and learning. A wise person should either lead a group or wander alone."
He spoke these verses.
"He acts for the benefit of both, for himself and for others."

## One Should Not Dwell Where There Is an Enemy
In whatever place an enemy dwells, a wise person should not stay there even for one or two nights. One lives in suffering among enemies.

Truly, for a man who follows one of fickle mind, that fickle-minded person becomes an enemy. Because of a single monkey, ruin was brought upon the whole troop.

Though being a fool, one who considers himself wise and leads a troop, following the whims of his own mind, lies down as if lying in death; this monkey, being dead, lies down.

## If a Fool Leads, There Will Be Ruin
A fool who is powerful and leads a troop is not good. Like a decoy bird to other birds, he brings no benefit to his kinsmen.
337:
A wise person who is powerful and leads a troop is good. Like Vāsava among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, he brings benefit to his kinsmen.

## Virtue, Wisdom, and Knowledge
And whoever sees virtue, wisdom, and learning in himself, that person can act for the benefit of both himself and others.

Therefore, like virtue, wisdom, and learning, one should weigh oneself in virtue, in wisdom, and in learning. Having weighed them, a wise person should either lead a group or wander alone.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, even as a monkey king, taught through the method of the Vinaya.

The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the difficult monkey was Devadatta, his followers were the followers of Devadatta, the followers of the Buddha were then the followers of the wise monkey king, and I myself was the wise monkey king."

## A Foolish Leader in This World Will Cause Much Destruction
The Kapi Jātaka ends.

## 10. Baka Jātaka

## Long Life Due to Saving Others' Lives
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Baka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Dvāsattati," concerning Baka Brahma.

To that Baka Brahma, such a view arose: "This state is permanent, it is not subject to falling away; apart from this, there is no other Nibbāna that is an escape from the suffering of the round (saṃsāra)."

That Baka Brahma was associated with birth through lower jhāna. Formerly, having developed jhāna, he was reborn in the Vehapphala realm. Having exhausted a lifespan of five hundred great aeons there, he was reborn in the Subhakiṇṇa realm. Having exhausted sixty-four aeons, he passed away from the Subhakiṇṇa realm and was reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma realm, where the lifespan is eight great aeons.
338:
68. "Seventy-two, O Gotama, of meritorious deeds, exercising authority, have transcended birth and old age. This is the final attainment of Brahma, reached through knowledge, which many people long for."
He spoke this first verse.

O Gotama. We seventy-two, who possess meritorious deeds, exercise our own will. We have transcended birth and old age. This birth in the Brahma realm, reached by the wise, is the final birth. Many people long for us.

## How the View Cannot Be Right
In that Ābhassara realm, such a view arose in that Brahma. That Baka Brahma could not remember his passing away from the higher Brahma realm. He could not remember his rebirth in that Brahma realm. Not seeing both passing away and rebirth, he held such a view.

## The Buddha Went to the Brahma Realm
The All-Knowing Buddha, knowing the thought in Baka Brahma's mind, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, vanished from Jetavana Monastery and appeared in the Brahma realm.

## Welcoming and Stating the View
Baka Brahma, seeing the All-Knowing Buddha, said: "Come, Venerable Sir; welcome, Venerable Sir. It has been a long time, Venerable Sir, since you made this turn to come here."

"Venerable Sir, this state is permanent, this state is certain, this state is eternal, this state is firm, this state does not age, this state does not pass away, this state is not reborn; apart from this state, there is no other superior Dhamma that is an escape from the suffering of the round."

## How Great Is the Foolishness
When he had spoken thus, the All-Knowing Buddha said to Baka Brahma: "Friends, Baka Brahma is indeed full of ignorance. Friends, Baka Brahma is indeed full of ignorance, in that he says what is impermanent is permanent. And says there is no other superior escape when there is indeed another superior escape from the suffering of the round."
339:
69. Short indeed is this life, not long,
Which you, Baka, think is long.
A hundred thousand nirabbudas,
I know your lifespan to be, O Brahmā.

Regarding this second verse:
Baka, the Baka Brahmā. You (tvaṃ). That lifespan (yaṃ āyuṃ). Which you think (maññasi) is long (dīghaṃ). That lifespan (etaṃ āyu) is short (appaṃ). It is certainly not long (na hi dīghaṃ). O Brahmā (brahme). I (ahaṃ) know (pajānāmi) your (tava) lifespan (āyuṃ) to be of such an extent, namely the number called ahaha, which is a hundred thousand of the numbers known as nirabbuda.

## I am long-lived

Hearing these words, Baka Brahmā thought, "He says this, he says that. This ascetic Gotama will pursue me with scrutiny." Just as a weak thief, after receiving two or three blows, might cry out, "Am I the only thief? This person is also a thief, and that person is also a thief," naming all his accomplices; so too, out of fear of the Blessed One's scrutiny, Baka Brahmā wished to mention his other companions.

## This is insignificant

Hearing the words of the Brahmā king, the All-Knowing Blessed One—

## Tell me of my past life

Hearing those words, Baka Brahmā spoke this third verse:

70. The Blessed One is the seer of the infinite,
Having transcended birth, aging, and sorrow.
What was my ancient vow and virtuous practice?
Tell me that, so that I may know it.

O Gotama, you say, "I am the seer of the infinite, having transcended birth, aging, and sorrow." If this is so, what was my ancient (purāṇaṃ) vow and virtuous practice (vatasīlavattaṃ)? Tell me that (taṃ me ācikkha), so that I may understand it truly as you describe it.
340:
71. When you gave many people drink,
Who were thirsty and overcome by heat.
That was your ancient vow and virtuous practice,
I remember it like one awakened from sleep.

O Brahmā. You (tvaṃ). Many (bahū) people (manusse) who were thirsty (pipāsite) and exhausted by the intense heat of the sun (ghammani samparete). That you gave them water to drink (yaṃ apāyesi). That ancient (purāṇaṃ) vow and virtuous practice (vatasīlavattaṃ) of yours (te). I (ahaṃ) can remember (anussarāmi) like a man who, having seen a dream in the morning, awakens from his bed (suttappabuddho va).

73. When a boat was seized in the stream of the Ganges,
By a fierce Naga wishing to destroy humans.
You released it by force and power,
That was your ancient vow and virtuous practice.
I remember it like one awakened from sleep.

O Brahmā. In the stream (sotasmiṃ) of the Ganges (gaṅgāya). A fierce (luddena) Naga (nāgena) who, out of a desire to destroy humans (manussakappā), seized a boat (gahītanāvaṃ) by force (balasā) and oppression (pasayha). You released it (amocayi). That ancient (purāṇaṃ) vow and virtuous practice (vatasīlavattaṃ) of yours (te). I (ahaṃ) can remember (anussarāmi) like a man who awakens after seeing a dream in the morning.

74. And I was your disciple named Kappa,
Who thought of you as a wise and virtuous ascetic.
That was your ancient vow and virtuous practice,
I remember it like one awakened from sleep.

O Brahmā. I (ahaṃ) was (ahosiṃ) your (te) disciple (baddhacaro) named Kappa. I thought (amaññaṃ) of you as an ascetic (tāpaso) who was endowed with wisdom (sambuddhimantaṃ) and endowed with practice (vatinaṃ). I (ahaṃ) can remember (anussarāmi) that ancient (purāṇaṃ) vow and virtuous practice (vatasīlavattaṃ) of yours (te) like a man who awakens from sleep after seeing a dream.

## Past Story

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to recount the past stories to Baka Brahmā—

## Giving Water

In a certain eon, that Baka Brahmā was an ascetic living in a sandy desert, and he brought water to many people traveling through the desert.

At one time, a caravan leader with five hundred wagons entered the sandy desert. The people, unable to determine the directions, wandered for seven days until their food and water were exhausted. Overcome by the heat, they thought, "Now there is no life for us," and they turned their wagons, unyoked the oxen, and lay down under the wagons.

Then the ascetic, reflecting, saw those caravan travelers and thought, "Let them not perish while I am watching." By his psychic power, he caused the waters of the Ganges to flow back and directed them toward the caravan travelers. He also created a forest nearby.

The people drank and bathed in the water, satisfied the oxen, reaped grass from the forest, took firewood, determined their direction, and being free from illness, crossed the desert.
341:
## Saving from Robbers

Then, referring to another past story:

72. When you released the people captured,
On the bank of the Eṇī, being led away as prisoners.
That was your ancient vow and virtuous practice,
I remember it like one awakened from sleep.

O Brahmā. The people (janaṃ) who were captured (gahitaṃ) on the bank of the Eṇī river (eṇīkūlasmiṃ) and were being led away as prisoners (gayhaka niyyamānaṃ). That you released them (yaṃ amocayi). That ancient (purāṇaṃ) vow and virtuous practice (vatasīlavattaṃ) of yours (te). I (ahaṃ) remember (anussarāmi) like a man who awakens from his bed after seeing a dream.

In a later time, that ascetic lived in a forest near a river, depending on a frontier village. One day, robbers came down from the mountain, raided that village, captured the people, and made them climb the mountain. They stationed spies along the way and entered a mountain cave to cook their meal.

The ascetic heard the great cries of distress from the cattle, buffaloes, and the young boys and girls. Thinking, "Let them not perish while I am watching," he gave up his ascetic form through psychic power and became a king surrounded by a fourfold army. Beating the war drums, he went to that place.

The spies saw him and informed the robbers. The robbers thought, "It is not proper to wage war with a king," and abandoning all the goods they had taken, they fled without even eating their meal. The ascetic brought all those people back and established them in their own village.

## Protecting from the Naga

Then, referring to another past story:

At that time, this ascetic lived on the bank of the Ganges. People had lashed together two or three boats to form rafts, built flower pavilions on top, and were traveling to the other side while eating and drinking liquor, rice, fish, and meat. Those people threw the dregs of the liquor and the leftovers of the rice, fish, meat, and betel into the Ganges.

The Naga king of the Ganges became angry, thinking, "These people are throwing their refuse on top of me." He thought, "I will seize all these people and sink them in the Ganges." He then created a massive body the size of a single-hulled boat and [disturbed] the water...
342:
“Having abandoned the lord of men, who is endowed with all that is desirable,
How, O Blessed One, Kesī, do you delight in the hermitage of Kappa?”

He spoke this verse:
Bhagavā: the Blessed One. Kesī: the hermit Kesī. Sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ: endowed with all desirable things. Manussindaṃ: the lord of men. Jahitvāna: having abandoned. Kathaṃ nu: for what reason? Kappassa: of the hermit Kappa. Assame: in the hermitage. Ramati: do you delight?

“There are sweet and delightful things; there are pleasant words.
The well-spoken words of Kappa, O Nārada, delight me.”

He spoke this verse:
Nārada: the minister Nārada. Kappassa assame: in the hermitage of the hermit Kappa. Sādūni: good things. Ramaṇီyāni: delightful things. Santi: there are. Manoramā: pleasant. Vakkhā: words. Santi: there are. Kappassa subhāsitāni: the well-spoken words of Kappa. Maṃ: me. Ramayanti: they cause to delight.

75. “Indeed, you know this life-span of mine,
You know others as well, for you are the Buddha.
For thus your blazing majesty
Stands illuminating the Brahma world.”

He spoke this final verse:
Bho Gotama: O Venerable Gautama. Tvaṃ: you. Mama etaṃ āyuṃ: this life-span of mine. Addhā: certainly. Pajānāsi: you know. Aññampi: other things (Dhamma) as well. Jānāsi: you know. Tathā hi: because you know thus. Buddho: you are the Buddha. Tathā hi: because you are thus the Buddha. Te ayaṃ jalitānubhāvo: this blazing majesty of yours. Brahmalokaṃ: the Brahma world. Obhāsayaṃ: illuminating. Tiṭṭhati: stands.

The Naga king living in the Ganges, becoming angry thinking, “These people throw their leftovers on top of me,” intended to seize all the people and drown them in the Ganges. He created a physical form as large as a great boat, and parting the water, he approached those people with his hood raised. Seeing the Naga king and being terrified by the fear of death, the people cried out with a great shout all at once. 

The hermit, hearing their sound of lamentation and knowing the Naga king's state of anger, thought, “May they not perish while I am watching.” By quickly entering into meditative absorption (jhāna) and through his own psychic power, he instantly transformed himself into the form of a Garuḍa and went there. Seeing the Garuḍa and being terrified by the fear of death, the Naga dived into the water. The people reached safety and went their way.

## What the Hermit Did
Then, referring to a past story—
What is shown by these words? “Great Brahma, in the past when you were the hermit Kesava, I was the disciple named Kappa who performed various duties for you. The minister named Nārada brought you from the city of Bārāṇasī to the Himālaya and I cured your illness. At that time, the minister Nārada came for a second time and, seeing that the hermit Kesava was free from illness, spoke [the verse].

Then the hermit Kesava spoke to the minister Nārada—
In this way, the Omniscient Buddha showed the fact that he himself had been the disciple of the hermit Kesava and had cured the illness. Thus showing this, the Omniscient Buddha preached to Baka Brahma, making him mindful of all the meritorious deeds he had performed in the human world.

## Realization Gained
Baka Brahma, remembering the deeds he had performed through the words of the Buddha, wished to praise the Buddha and spoke—
343:
In that verse, 'Tathā hi Buddho' means: for you are the Buddha. It shows that there is nothing unknown to the Buddhas; indeed, they are called 'Buddhas' because of their enlightenment regarding all phenomena. 'Tathā hi tāyaṃ' means: because of being the Buddha, this blazing majesty of your body's radiance stands. 'Obhāsayaṃ tiṭṭhati' means: it stands illuminating this entire Brahma world.

Thus the Teacher, making his own Buddha-virtues known, taught the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the minds of ten thousand Brahmas who had gathered were liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging. 

Identification of the Jātaka: Thus the Blessed One, having become the refuge for many Brahmas, returned from the Brahma world to Jetavana. He preached that Dhamma teaching to the monks in the same manner as it was preached there and identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the hermit Kesava was Baka Brahma, and I myself was the youth Kappa.”

## Baka Brahma’s Wrong View Dispelled by the Buddha
The Baka Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Gandhāra Vagga
## 1. Gandhāra Jātaka
## Hermits and Monks Should Not Store Requisites

The Story of the Present: The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Gandhāra Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Hitvā gāma-sahassāni', concerning the training rule on the storage of medicines (bhesajja-sannidhikāra).

The story originated in the city of Rājagaha. When the Venerable Pilindavaccha went to the King's palace to free a family of park-keepers, he turned King Bimbisāra's palace into gold by his psychic power. The people, being inspired with faith, offered the five kinds of medicine to the Elder Pilindavaccha. The Elder Pilindavaccha gave those medicines to his followers.

That assembly of followers of the Elder Pilindavaccha came to possess many requisites. They stored the medicines they received, filling jars, pots, and alms-bowl bags. Seeing this, the people criticized them, saying, “These monks, sons of the Sakyans, are very greedy. They have granaries inside.”

The Omniscient Buddha, hearing of this matter, prescribed the training rule beginning with 'Yāni kho pana tāni bhesajjāni gilānānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ' and said: “Monks, in the past, wise men who went forth in external ordinations before a Buddha appeared, even while observing only the five precepts, criticized the storing of even a bit of salt for the sake of the next day. You, having gone forth in such a Buddha's dispensation that leads out of the suffering of the round of rebirths, do what is improper by storing for the sake of tomorrow, the day after, and so on.” Having said this, he brought forth the past story.
344:
In the past, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, the Bodhisatta was born as the prince of Gandhāra. Upon his father's passing, he was established in the kingship and ruled righteously. In the Middle Country, in the kingdom of Videha, a king named Videha also reigned.

Those two kings became friends without having ever met, and they shared a firm mutual trust. At that time, humans were long-lived, living for thirty thousand years.

## The Lunar Eclipse

Once, on a full-moon Uposatha day, King Gandhāra, having observed the precepts, sat in the middle of a noble couch prepared on the upper terrace of his palace. Looking out through an open casement window toward the eastern world-sphere, he sat speaking words of Dhamma to his ministers.

At that moment, Rāhu seized the full moon as if it were leaping across the sky. The moonlight vanished. When the ministers could no longer see the moonlight, they informed the king that Rāhu had seized the moon.

## King Gandhāra Becomes an Ascetic

While the king was looking at the moon, he thought: “This moon has become stained and lusterless due to an adventitious impurity. To me, this royal retinue is also an impurity. It is not proper for me to become lusterless like the moon seized by Rāhu. Like the moon-disk shining in the pure sky, I shall renounce the kingship and become an ascetic. What benefit is there for me in admonishing others? I shall wander about admonishing only myself, being unattached to family or followers. This practice is suitable for me.”

Thinking thus, he handed over the kingdom to his ministers, saying, “Appoint as king whomever you desire.” Having surrendered the kingship, he renounced the great sovereignty over the two kingdoms of Kashmīra and Gandhāra and became a hermit. Having attained the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher powers (abhiññā), he dwelt in the Himalayan region, devoted to the bliss of meditation.

## King Videha Becomes an Ascetic

King Videha also asked merchants, “Is my friend well?” and upon hearing of King Gandhāra's renunciation, he thought, “Since my friend has renounced, what shall I do with the kingship?” He then abandoned the city of Mithilā, which was seven leagues in extent, the kingdom of Videha, which was three hundred leagues in extent with sixteen thousand villages, and his filled granaries, as well as sixteen thousand dancing women. Without a thought for his sons or daughters, he entered the Himalayas and became a hermit. Subsisting on wild fruits, he lived a life of well-conducted practice.

## They Did Not Recognize Each Other

Those two hermits, practicing the well-conducted life, met each other at a later time. However, they did not recognize one another. Rejoicing together, they lived the well-conducted life in the same place.

At that time, the hermit Videha attended to the hermit Gandhāra. On a certain full-moon day, while they were sitting at the foot of an obscure tree and speaking words connected with the Dhamma, Rāhu seized the moon-disk shining in the sky.
345:
When the hermit Videha looked up, wondering, “Why has the moonlight vanished?” he saw the moon seized by Rāhu and asked, “Teacher, who is this that has seized the moon and made it lusterless?”

“Disciple, this is one named Rāhu, an impurity of the moon; he does not allow it to shine. I too, seeing the moon-disk seized by Rāhu, thought: ‘This pure moon-disk has become lusterless due to an adventitious impurity. To me, this kingship is also an impurity. As long as this impurity does not make me lusterless like Rāhu does to the moon, I shall renounce.’ At that very moment, thinking ‘This kingship causes one to be without luster,’ I took the moon-disk seized by Rāhu as my object of meditation, renounced the great kingship, and became a monk.”

## They Became Friends

“Teacher, are you the King of Gandhāra?” he asked. When he replied, “Yes, I am,” Videha said, “Teacher, I was the King named Videha in the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha. Are we not friends who have never met before?” Gandhāra asked, “What was your object of meditation?” He replied, “I heard that you had renounced, and seeing that there is surely great merit in the life of a monk, I took you alone as my object, renounced the kingship, and became a monk.”

From then on, those two hermits were exceedingly harmonious and lived rejoicing together, subsisting on wild fruits.

## Ascetic Videha Stores Salt

After living in the Himalayas for a long time, they descended from the mountains to seek salt and sour foods and reached a certain border village. The people, being pleased with the deportment of the hermits, received their promise to accept alms and created night-quarters and day-quarters in the forest for them to dwell in.

Between the paths, they also built a rest house in a pleasant place for the hermits to perform their meal-time duties. Those hermits, having collected alms in the border village, would sit in that rest house to eat their meal and then return to their own dwelling place.
346:
1. "Having left sixteen thousand villages, all full and prosperous,
And wealthy granaries, do you now make a hoard?"
He spoke this first verse.
Videha, O Videha ascetic. You. Full. Sixteen thousand main villages. Full. Granaries of jewels, granaries of clothes, and granaries of grain. Having left. Now. Just a bit of salt. Hoarding. You do.

2. "Having left the Gāndhāra realm, which bears great wealth,
Having departed from ruling, do you now rule here?"
He spoke this second verse.
Teacher. Bearing great wealth. The Gāndhāra realm. Having left. From admonishing and instructing others. Having departed. Now. Here in this forest. Why. Me. Do you admonish?

When those people gave food to the ascetics, sometimes they gave salt in a bowl. Sometimes they gave salt wrapped in a leaf. Sometimes they gave food without salt.
One day, people took much salt in a leaf-wrap and gave it. The Videha ascetic took the salt and came, gave the Bodhisatta salt suitable for the meal, took a measured amount for himself, and wrapped the remaining salt in a leaf, placing it in the thatch of the roof, thinking, "It will be for days without salt."
Then one day, when they received food without salt, the Videha ascetic gave a bowl to the Gāndhāra ascetic, brought the salt from the thatch, and said, "Teacher, take some salt." "Today people did not give salt; where did you get it?" he asked. "Teacher, yesterday people gave much salt; then I kept the remaining salt, thinking it would be for days without salt," he said.

## Do you crave salt?
Then the Bodhisatta, wishing to admonish the Videha ascetic, rebuked him: "O hollow man, having left the great Videha realm of three hundred leagues, having become a monk and reached the state of having no possessions, do you now give rise to craving for a grain of salt?"

## No need to admonish
When the Videha ascetic was thus blamed, being unable to endure the blame and becoming antagonistic, he said: "Teacher, you do not see your own fault but see only mine. Did you not leave the kingship and become a monk, thinking, 'What use is there in my admonishing others? I will admonish only myself'? Why do you admonish me now?" Thus he wished to challenge him.

## Just speaking the Dhamma
Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta spoke this third verse:
3. "I speak the Dhamma, O Videha; unrighteousness is not pleasing to me.
As I speak the Dhamma, no evil clings to me."
Videha, O Videha ascetic. I. The Dhamma.
347:
4. "By whatever means another person is pained,
Even if the speech is of great benefit, a wise man should not speak it."
He spoke this fourth verse.
Teacher. By whatever means. Another. Anger. Receives. If. Even if of great benefit. That speech. A wise man. Should not speak.

5. "Let him be pained or not; let him be scattered like chaff.
As I speak the Dhamma, no evil clings to me."
He spoke this fifth verse.
Videha, O Videha ascetic. One being admonished. Certainly. Whether he is pained. Or not pained. Like chaff. Whether he is scattered. The Dhamma. Speaking. To me. Evil. Does not cling.
Only the Dhamma. I speak. By me. Unrighteousness. Is not pleasing. The Dhamma. Speaking. To me. Evil. Does not cling.

It does not smear or cling to the heart. Giving admonition is the tradition of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Disciples, and Bodhisattas. Fools do not accept the admonition given by them, but for the giver of admonition, there is no such thing as evil.
"One should follow the wise man who shows one's faults, like one who points out hidden treasure. One should follow such a sage who speaks rebuking words. For one who follows such a person, it is better, not worse."
"Let him admonish, let him instruct, and let him restrain one from the unseemly. He is pleasing to the good, but displeasing to the bad." (Dhp. 76-77).

## Harsh speech is unbearable
The Videha ascetic, hearing the Bodhisatta's words, meant to say: "Teacher, even one who speaks words based on benefit should not speak by hurting or restricting another. You speak very harsh words to me, as if cutting me with a sharp small knife."

## Listen to what is beneficial
Then the Bodhisatta, to the Videha ascetic:
And having said this:
"Ānanda, just as a potter makes an effort by pressing the damp clay, so will I make an effort. Ānanda, I, the Buddha, will speak. That which is the core (essence) will remain."
348:
6. "If one had no wisdom of one's own, nor well-learned discipline,
Many people would wander like a blind buffalo in the forest."
7. "But because some here are well-trained by a teacher,
Therefore, with discipline mastered, they wander well-composed."
He spoke these two verses.
Videha, O Videha ascetic. For these beings. If their own wisdom, or the discipline of conduct and rules learned by relying on a wise admonisher, were not well-learned. If it were so, just as a blind buffalo in a forest thick with grass and creepers wanders without knowing the proper or improper grazing ground, or places of safety or danger, so would many people like you wander. But because some beings here, though lacking their own wisdom, are well-trained in conduct and rules in the presence of a teacher, therefore, being disciplined by the teachers with discipline suitable for each, they wander with mastered discipline and well-composed, one-pointed minds.

Standing in the practice suitable for this advice of the Sugata: "Just as a potter, repeatedly striking the vessels, does not take the raw ones but takes only the well-baked vessel, so by repeatedly admonishing and rebuking, the person who is like a baked vessel should be taken." To show this, admonishing the Videha ascetic again:

This shows: A being, as a layperson, should learn the training suitable for his family; as a monk, the training suitable for a monk. Even laypeople, being trained in agriculture, cattle-rearing, etc., suitable for their families, wander with well-composed lives. Monks too, being trained in the trainings of higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom, such as the graceful manner of approaching and departing, wander without distraction and well-composed. In the world:
"Great learning, craft, well-learned discipline,
And well-spoken speech; this is the highest blessing." (Khp. 5.5, Sn. 264).

## I was wrong
Hearing this, the Videha ascetic said: "Teacher, from this day forward, please admonish and instruct me. Admonish me repeatedly. I spoke with you because of my nature of being unable to endure. Please forgive that fault of mine." He bowed and paid homage to the Bodhisatta.
Those two ascetics lived in harmony and went back to the Himalayas. In that Himalaya, the Bodhisatta taught the preliminary meditation to the Videha ascetic.
349:
That ascetic Videha performed the preliminary tasks and produced the higher knowledges and meditative attainments. Thus, both ascetics, with their dhyānas unimpaired, were destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching to a close, identified the Birth: "At that time, Videha was Ānanda, and the King of Gandhāra was I myself."

## Possessions, keep them, only causes of sorrow
The Gandhāra Jātaka is concluded.

## 2. Mahākapi Jātaka

## Not sparing one's life for one's kinsmen
The Present Story: The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Mahākapi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Attānaṃ saṅkamaṃ katvā," concerning his conduct for the benefit of his kinsmen.

The Present Story will become clear in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka. At that time, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, the All-Knowing Buddha acts for the benefit of his kinsmen." The All-Knowing Teacher came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata acts for the benefit of his kinsmen; in the past also, the Tathāgata acted for the benefit of his kinsmen," and he brought up the past.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey. When he reached maturity, he was perfect in stature and girth, endowed with strength and power, possessing the strength of five elephants. He lived in the Himalayan region surrounded by a troop of eighty thousand monkeys.

## The Abbhantara Mango
In that Himalayan region, near the bank of the Ganges, there was a mango tree with many branches and twigs, providing cool shade with thick leaves, rising up like a mountain peak. (Some also call it a banyan tree.) That mango tree had sweet fruits with divine fragrance and flavor, large in size like a water jar.

The fruits from one branch of that mango tree fell on the land. The fruits from another branch fell into the waters of the Ganges. The fruits from the two branches in the middle fell at the foot of the tree.
350:
The Bodhisatta, taking the troop of monkeys and eating the fruits of that mango tree, thought at one time, "Because of a fruit of this mango tree falling into the water, danger will arise for us." Thus, from the time the flowers turned into fruit the size of a kidney bean, he made them eat or drop every single fruit from the branch over the water, leaving none behind.

## The King Learns
Even though this was done, one ripe fruit, unseen by the eighty thousand monkeys and covered by a leaf-nest made by ants, fell into the river. As it floated down the Ganges, it got caught in the upper net of the King of Vārāṇasī, who had nets spread above and below while playing in the water.

The King played all day, and in the evening, when the fishermen hauled in the net, they saw that mango. Not knowing what kind of fruit it was, they showed it to the King. The King asked, "What fruit is this?" "Your Majesty, we do not know," they replied. "Who will know?" he asked. "Your Majesty, the hunters will know," they said.

The King had the hunters summoned and questioned them. Hearing from the hunters that it was a "ripe mango," he cut it with a small knife, had the hunters eat it first, and then ate it himself. He also gave some to his harem and his ministers. The flavor of the ripe mango pervaded the King's entire body. Bound by the craving for that flavor, he asked the hunters where that mango tree stood.

When the hunters said, "It is on the riverbank in the Himalayan region," he had many boats and rafts joined together and traveled upstream by the route pointed out by the hunters. It is not mentioned how many days he traveled. Gradually, however, he reached that place, and the hunters informed the King, "Your Majesty, this is the tree."

The King left the boats in the river and, surrounded by a great multitude, went to that spot on foot. He had a bed prepared at the foot of the mango tree, ate the ripe mangoes and various delicious foods, and then lay down to sleep.

## Ordering the Monkeys to be Killed
Guards were placed in all directions and fires were lit. When the people had fallen asleep, at midnight, the Bodhisatta came with his followers. The eighty thousand monkeys, moving from branch to branch, ate the mangoes.
351:
8. "Having made myself a bridge, he who crossed them over to safety. Who are you to them, and what are these to you, O Great Monkey?"

He spoke this first verse.

"O Great Monkey, you who made yourself a bridge and caused these monkeys to cross over to safety. What are you to them? And what are they to you?"

The King woke up and saw the troop of monkeys. He made the men rise and called the archers, saying, "If we surround them in this way, these monkeys who eat the mangoes will not escape. Surround that place in this manner; tomorrow we shall eat both the mangoes and the monkey flesh." The archers agreed, saying, "Very well," and they surrounded the mango tree, standing with their arrows ready.

Seeing them, the monkeys became terrified of the threat of death. Unable to flee, they approached the Bodhisatta and asked, "O Lord, the archers stand surrounding the mango tree to shoot the fleeing monkeys. What shall we do?" They stood there trembling.

## How the Monkey King Rescued Them

Then the Bodhisatta comforted the troop of monkeys, saying, "Do not be afraid; I will give you your lives." He climbed a straight-growing branch, went towards the Gaṅgā, and leaped from the tip of that branch. Crossing a distance of a hundred bow-lengths, he landed on top of a thicket near the Gaṅgā. Descending from that thicket, he thought, "This is the distance I have come," and measuring the space in the air, he cut a rattan vine, thinking, "This much will be tied to the tree, and this much will be in the air."
352:
9. "I am their king and lord, the leader of the troop. For them, overcome with sorrow and afraid of you, O subduer of enemies."
10. "Having leaped a hundred bow-lengths, I tied a firm bond of vine to my hind legs."
11. "Like a cloud torn by the wind, I reached the tree, driven by the force. There, failing to reach, I grasped the branch with my hands."
12. "While I was stretched out like a string, held by the branch and the vine, the monkeys went to safety, treading upon me with their feet."
13. "That bond does not distress me, nor will my death distress me. Happiness has been brought to those over whom I exercised sovereignty."
14. "This is an example for you, O King; listen to it, O subduer of enemies. By a king who understands, the happiness of the kingdom, the charioteers, the army, and the villagers—the happiness of all—should be sought by a Khattiya."

He spoke these verses.

"O subduer of enemies, O King. I am the leader and lord who guides the troop of monkeys. I am the king of those eighty thousand monkeys. For the sake of those monkeys who were afraid of you and oppressed by sorrow.

Having leaped a distance of a hundred bow-lengths, like an arrow released from a bowstring. From there, I tied a vine firmly to my hind legs.

Like a cloud severed by the wind, I was propelled by the wind of my own momentum and reached the mango tree. I, being unable to fully reach the mango tree in that mid-air, grasped the mango branch with both hands.

Like a lute string stretched on a lute, both the mango branch and the vine were stretched. While I was thus stretched, the monkeys went to safety, treading respectfully upon me with their feet.

Because I have brought happiness to those monkeys over whom I ruled as king, therefore, this binding with the rattan vine does not distress me. Death will not distress me.

O subduer of enemies, O Great King. This example has been told to you. Listen to the words spoken in connection with this example. A king should seek the happiness of the country's people, the chariot-warriors and such, the army, and the inhabitants of the market towns—of all people. A Khattiya must be endowed with wisdom."

"This much will be in the air." Having marked these two points, he failed to account for the portion to be tied around his own waist.

The Bodhisatta took that vine, tied one end to a tree standing on the bank of the Gaṅgā, and tied the other end to his own waist. With the speed of a cloud severed by the wind, he leaped across the distance of a hundred bow-lengths. Because he had not accounted for the length tied to his waist, he was unable to reach the tree. He firmly grasped a mango branch with both hands and gave a signal to the monkey troop: "Quickly, treading upon my back, go to safety by way of the rattan vine!" The eighty thousand monkeys paid homage to the Bodhisatta, asked for his forgiveness, and went as he had said.

## The Wicked Monkey

At that time, Devadatta was also a monkey among them. He thought, "This is the time to see the back of my enemy." He climbed a high branch, gained momentum, and leaped onto the Bodhisatta's back. The Bodhisatta's heart broke, and intense pain arose. Having caused him such pain, Devadatta departed. The Bodhisatta remained all alone.

## The King's Inquiry

The King of Benares, staying awake, saw all the actions performed by the monkeys and the Bodhisatta. He lay there thinking, "This monkey, though an animal, disregarded his own life and acted only for the safety of his followers."

When the night had turned to dawn, the King, being pleased with the Bodhisatta, thought, "It is not right to let this monkey king perish."
353:
By means of a stratagem, I will save this monkey and care for him." So thinking, the King placed a boat-raft in the Gaṅgā, built a scaffold on that raft, and gently lowered the Bodhisatta. He spread a cloth dyed with saffron on a rock, bathed him with Gaṅgā water, gave him syrup to drink, massaged his dry body with oil refined a thousand times, spread a sheepskin on a bed, and laid him gently on the sheepskin. He himself sat in a lower place.

## The Monkey King's Answer
Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta, wishing to admonish the King, spoke.

## Cremation and Honor
Thus, while admonishing the King, the Bodhisatta died. The King summoned his ministers and said, "Perform the cremation ceremony for this monkey king's body just as you would for a king." He then ordered the assembly of royal concubines, "Wear red garments, let your hair hang loose, carry torches in your hands, and follow the monkey king to the cemetery in a procession."

The ministers made a pyre with a hundred bundles of wood. They performed the cremation ceremony for the Bodhisatta's body in the same manner as for kings, took the skull, and went to the King's presence.
354:
The King built a stupa at the burial site of the Bodhisatta, lit lamps, and made offerings of perfumes, flowers, and other requisites. He had the skull gilded with gold, placed it on the tip of a spear, and had it carried in front. Making offerings with perfumes and flowers, he reached Bārāṇasī. He placed the spear at the palace gate, had the entire city decorated, and performed a worship of the bone relics for seven days. Then, taking the relics, he built a stupa and honored them with flowers and perfumes for the rest of his life. Abiding by the Bodhisatta's admonition, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna), ruled righteously, and was destined for heaven.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, the Teacher, the All-Knowing One, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the King, Devadatta was the wicked monkey, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and the Monkey King was I myself."

## A king is one who works for the welfare of the many

The Mahākapi Jātaka ends.

## 3. Kumbhakāra Jātaka

## On not following the dictates of defilements

The Present Story: The Teacher, the All-Knowing One, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kumbhakāra Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ambāhamaddaṃ vanamantarasmim," concerning the suppression of defilements.

The present story will become clear in the Pānīya Jātaka. At that time, five hundred friends in Sāvatthī became monks and, while living within the Jetavana Monastery, had sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) at midnight.

The All-Knowing Buddha watches over his disciples six times a day and night—three times at night and three times during the day—just as a hen guards her eggs, a yak guards its tail, a mother guards her beloved son, or a one-eyed man guards his single eye. He suppresses the defilements that arise at those very moments.
355:
At midnight, the Blessed One, while surveying the Jetavana Monastery, thought: 'If these defilements grow within these monks, they will destroy the basis for the Fruit of Arahantship. Right now, I shall suppress their defilements and grant them the Fruit of Arahantship.' He then emerged from the Gandhakuṭi and called the Elder Ānanda, saying, 'Ānanda, assemble all the monks residing within the Jetavana Monastery.' Having had them assembled, he sat upon the prepared noble Buddha-seat and said:

'Monks, it is not proper to follow the will of the defilements that arise within. When defilements grow, they lead to great destruction like an enemy. A monk should suppress even the slightest defilement. Wise men of old, upon seeing even a small object of the senses, suppressed the defilements within and attained the Knowledge of Private Enlightenment.' Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a potter’s family in a village at the gate of Bārāṇasī. When he came of age, he established a household, had a son and a daughter, and supported his wife and children by working as a potter.

## King Kaliṅga’s Sense of Urgency regarding the Mango Tree
At that time, in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, a king named Karaṇḍaka was going to the park with a large retinue. At the gate of the park, he saw a mango tree laden with sweet fruit. While still mounted on his noble elephant, he stretched out his hand, plucked a cluster of mangoes, and entered the park. Sitting on the auspicious stone slab, he gave some to those worthy of receiving them and ate the mangoes himself.

From the moment the king took some, it was as if the remaining fruit were free for others to take. Therefore, the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others knocked down the mangoes and ate them. Those who came later climbed the tree, beat it with clubs, and left the branches broken and mangled, eating even the unripe fruit until nothing remained.

The king played in the park all day. In the evening, while departing on his decorated noble elephant, he saw that mango tree. He dismounted, went to the foot of the tree, and looking at it, thought: 'In the morning, this tree filled those who looked at it with insatiable delight. It was laden with fruit and stood beautifully. Now, its fruit having been taken, its branches are broken and mangled, and it stands devoid of beauty.'

Looking elsewhere, he saw another mango tree that was barren. He thought: 'This tree, because of its fruitlessness, stands as beautiful as a jewel mountain. This [other] tree has come to such destruction because of its fruitfulness.

Living in the midst of this household is like the fruitful mango tree. The state of a monk is like the barren mango tree. Only for the one with wealth is there danger; for the one without wealth, there is no danger. I, too, should become like the barren mango tree.' Taking the fruitful mango tree as his object of meditation, while standing at the foot of the tree, he contemplated the Three Characteristics, developed insight, and attained the Knowledge of Private Enlightenment.
356:
'Now I have destroyed the hut of the mother's womb; I have destroyed rebirth in the three realms of existence; I have cleansed the filth-ground of Saṃsāra; I have dried up the ocean of tears; I have broken the wall of bones; for me, there is no further rebirth,' he stood there adorned in all his finery, reflecting thus.

Then the ministers said to him, 'Great King, you have been standing for a very long time.' He replied, 'Ministers, I am no longer a king. I am called a Paccekabuddha.' They said, 'Great King, Paccekabuddhas are not like you.' He asked, 'If they are not like this, what are they like?'

'Great King, Paccekabuddhas have their hair and beards shaven; they wear saffron-dyed robes; they have no attachment to family or followers; they are like clouds scattered by the wind, or like the moon's orb released from the mouth of Rāhu; they dwell in the Nandamūla Cave in the Himālaya. Such, O King, is the nature of Paccekabuddhas.'

At that moment, the king raised his hand and touched his head. Instantly, his lay appearance vanished, and the appearance of a monk became manifest. The eight requisites—the three robes, the bowl, the razor, the needle, the girdle, and the water-filter—which are suitable for a monk devoted to meditation, appeared upon his body. That Paccekabuddha, standing in the air, gave an exhortation to the multitude and then traveled through the sky to the Nandamūla Cave in the Himālaya.

## King Gandhara’s Sense of Urgency regarding the Sound of Bangles
In the city of Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhara, a king named Naggaji was sitting on a noble throne in the upper palace. He saw a woman sitting nearby grinding perfume, wearing a single jeweled bangle on each arm. He sat watching, thinking, 'These bangles, being single, do not strike each other and do not make a sound.'

Later, that woman took the bangle from her right arm and put it on her left arm, and began to grind the perfume with her right hand. The jeweled bangle on her left arm, having a companion, struck against it and made a sound.

The king, seeing those two bangles striking each other and making a sound, thought: 'This bangle did not strike when it was alone; having a companion, it strikes and makes a sound. In the same way, when beings live alone, they do not clash and do not quarrel. When there are two or three, they strike against each other.'
357:
“I rule over the inhabitants of these two kingdoms, Kasmīra and Gandhāra. I too should live like a single bracelet, not ruling over others but only over myself.” Thus, taking the clashing bracelets as his object of meditation, while sitting in that very place, he noted the three characteristics, developed insight, and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. (The rest of the story is just as before.)

## The King of Videha’s Sense of Urgency Regarding a Piece of Meat

In the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, a king named Nimi, having finished his morning meal, stood looking out at the street through an open lion-window, surrounded by his ministers.

At that time, a hawk took a piece of meat from a meat market and flew into the sky. Other birds, such as vultures, surrounded that hawk from all sides and, for the sake of food, pecked it with their beaks, struck it with their wings, and trampled it with their feet. That hawk, unable to bear the harassment, dropped the piece of meat. Another bird seized it.

Those birds then left the bird that had dropped the meat and pursued the bird that had seized it. When that bird dropped it, another bird seized it. Those birds harassed that one in the same way.

The king, seeing those birds, thought: “Whoever seizes the piece of meat, only that one suffers. Whoever lets it go, only that one is happy. Regarding these five cords of sensual pleasure, whoever seizes them, only that person suffers. Only the one who does not seize them is happy. These sensual pleasures are common to many.

I have sixteen thousand court ladies. Like the hawk releasing the piece of meat from its beak, I should abandon the five cords of sensual pleasure and live happily.” Having reflected thus, the king, applying his mind systematically while standing in that very place, noted the three characteristics, developed insight, and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. (The rest of the story is just as the previous one.)

## The King of Pañcāla’s Sense of Urgency Regarding Defilements

In the city of Kapila in the kingdom of Uttara-Pañcāla, a king named Dummukha, having finished his morning meal and being adorned with all ornaments, stood looking at the royal courtyard through an open lion-window, surrounded by his ministers. At that moment, cowherds opened the gate of the cattle pen. The bulls, emerging from the pen, pursued a cow out of lust. Among them, a great bull with sharp horns, seeing another bull approaching and being overcome by lust and jealousy, struck the other bull between the thighs with its sharp horns. Through that wound, the intestines came out, and it died right there. The king—
358:
Seeing that, he thought: “These beings, starting from animals, reach suffering through the power of defilements. This bull has reached the end of its life because of defilement. Other beings also tremble through the power of defilements. I should abandon these defilements that cause beings to tremble.” While standing there, he noted the three characteristics, developed insight, and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. (The rest of the story is just as before.)

Then one day, the four Paccekabuddhas, noting the time for alms-round, emerged from the Nandamūla Cave, chewed nagalatā tooth-sticks at Lake Anotatta, performed their bodily ablutions, and stood on the Manosilā plateau. They adjusted their lower robes, took their bowls and robes, and flew into the sky by psychic power. Passing through clouds of five colors, they descended near the gate-village of the city of Vārāṇasī. At a pleasant spot, they donned their robes, took their bowls, entered the gate-village, and while wandering for alms, reached the door of the Bodhisatta’s house.

The Bodhisatta, seeing them, was filled with joy. He invited them into his house, seated them on prepared seats, offered water of donation, and served them with excellent hard and soft food. Sitting to one side, he paid homage to the Elder of the Saṅgha and asked: “Venerable sirs, your renunciation is exceedingly beautiful. Your faculties are serene, and your complexion is pure. What object did you see that led you to this life of wandering for alms?” Just as he asked the Elder of the Saṅgha, he approached and asked the others as well. Then those four persons related their own stories of renunciation, saying, “I was a king named so-and-so in such-and-such a city and kingdom,” and they recited one verse each in succession:

15. “I saw a mango tree in the midst of the forest,
Lush and green, laden with fruit.
I saw it again, broken down because of its fruit;
Seeing that, I wander for alms.”

16. “A woman wore a pair of smooth, well-crafted bracelets,
Fashioned by a master craftsman, which made no sound.
But when a second one was added, there was sound;
Seeing that, I wander for alms.”

17. “A bird carrying a piece of meat,
Though alone, was met by many birds.
They attacked it for the sake of food;
Seeing that, I wander for alms.”

18. “I saw a bull in the midst of the herd,
With a swaying hump, possessed of beauty and strength.
I saw it again, pierced because of desire;
Seeing that, I wander for alms.”

Thus they recited these verses one by one.
