(The commentary explains:) “I” refers to the speaker. “In the midst of the forest” means in the middle of the mango grove. “Lush and green” means having a dark green color. “Laden with fruit” means full of fruit. “Thriving” means flourishing. “Mango tree” (ambaṃ) is what I saw first upon entering the garden. “Because of its fruit” means due to the fruit as the cause. “Broken down” means destroyed. “That very mango tree” I saw again upon leaving. “Seeing that” mango tree, “I practice the habit of wandering for alms.”

“A woman” wore “bracelets” made of gems, “very smooth,” “fashioned by wise men,” “making no sound,” “a pair” meaning one on each side. Furthermore, “a second” bracelet, which was the companion added from the right side to the left, “due to” that, “sound” “occurred.” “Seeing that” bracelet, “I practice the habit of wandering for alms.”

“A bird” that was “carrying” “a piece of meat,” “a single bird,” “many” “birds” “gathering together,” “for the sake of food,” “pecked and pursued.” “Seeing that” bird, “I practice the habit of wandering for alms.”

“In the midst” of the “herd” of cattle, “with a swaying hump,” “possessed of beauty and strength,” “a bull,” “I” “saw.” “Because of desire” (kāma), “pierced” or oppressed, “that” bull “I saw again.” “Seeing that” bull, “I practice the habit of wandering for alms.”

At that moment, they opened the gate of the cattle pen. The bulls emerged from the pen and pursued a cow through the power of defilement. Among those bulls, a great bull with sharp horns, as it was coming, saw another bull and, being oppressed by jealousy in defilement, gored the other bull between the thighs with its sharp horns. From the place where that bull was gored, the intestines came out. That bull reached the end of its life right there.

The king, seeing that bull, thought: “These beings, starting from animals, reach suffering through the power of defilements. This bull has reached the end of its life depending on defilement. Other beings also tremble by the power of defilements. I should abandon these defilements that cause these beings to tremble.” Having reflected thus, the king, while standing, noted the three characteristics, developed insight, and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. (The rest of the story is just as before.)

Then one day, the four Paccekabuddhas, noting the time for alms-round, emerged from the Nandamūla Cave... (as described above). When they arrived at the Bodhisatta’s house door:

## How the Potter Heard the Dhamma

The Bodhisatta, seeing those Paccekabuddhas, was filled with joy, went to the house, seated them on prepared seats, offered the water of donation, served them with noble food, and sitting in a suitable place, paid homage to the Elder of the Saṅgha—
359:
“Venerable sirs, your state as monks is exceedingly beautiful; your faculties are especially serene, and your complexion is pure. Having seen what object, venerable sirs, have you entered into this state of a monk who practices alms-gathering?” thus he asked. Just as he approached the Elder of the Saṅgha, he likewise approached and questioned the remaining Paccekabuddhas.

Then, to the Bodhisatta, those four Paccekabuddhas, intending to relate the stories of their own renunciation, such as, “In such a city, in such a country, there was such a king,” spoke in due order—

## Desiring to Ordain, He Instructs His Wife

Having heard each verse, the Bodhisatta praised each Paccekabuddha, saying, “Excellent, venerable sirs, excellent! That object is indeed suitable only for you.” Having heard that Dhamma teaching preached by the four Paccekabuddhas, he became without desire for household life. When the Paccekabuddhas had departed—

Having finished his morning meal and sitting comfortably, he called his wife and said, “Dear lady, these four Paccekabuddhas have abandoned their kingship, ordained, and being free from impediments, they pass their time in the bliss of renunciation. As for me, I make my living through wage-labor. What is the use of me living in a house? You stay behind in the house and care for the young children,” intending to say this—
360:
19. Karaṇḍaka of the Kaliṅgas, and Naggaji of the Gandhāras;
King Nimi of the Videhas, and Dummukha of the Pañcālas.
These, having abandoned their kingdoms, ordained, possessing nothing.

20. All these have come together, equal to the gods;
Just as a fire blazes, so do these shine.
I too will wander alone, Bhaggavī,
Having abandoned sense pleasures according to their limits.

He spoke these two verses.

Bhaggavī, O potteress. Karaṇḍaka, the king of the Kaliṅga people. And Naggaji, the king of the Gandhāra people. And King Nimi, the king of the Videha people. And Dummukha, the king of the Pañcāla people. These four kings, having abandoned their kingdoms, and being free from impediments, have ordained.

Bhaggavī, O potteress. All these Paccekabuddhas are equal to the previous Paccekabuddhas who are gods of purity (visuddhideva). They have come together with the previous Paccekabuddhas. Just as a fire blazes and shines, so too do these Paccekabuddhas shine with the five virtues such as morality. Just as they do, I too, having ordained, will wander alone. Bhaggavī, he addresses his wife. Having abandoned sense pleasures, having abandoned the physical objects of sense pleasure such as forms. According to their limits, as they stand according to the limits of forms and so on. This is what is said: Having abandoned sense pleasures as they stand according to the limits of forms and so on, I too, having ordained, will wander alone.

## The Wife Ordains as a Female Ascetic

The wife, hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, said, “My lord, for me too, from the time I heard the Dhamma teaching of the Paccekabuddhas, my mind does not settle in the home,” intending to say—
361:
21. This is the very time, for there is no other;
I might not have a teacher for me later.
I too will wander alone, Bhaggava,
Like a bird escaped from the hand of a man.

She spoke this verse.

Bhaggava, O potter. Because there might not be a teacher to instruct me in the future, therefore, this is the very time to ordain. There is indeed no other time to ordain. Like a female bird escaped from the hand of a man who catches birds, I too will wander alone.

## The Potter Ordains as an Ascetic

The Bodhisatta, hearing his wife’s words, remained silent. That wife, however, wishing to ordain before the Bodhisatta by deceiving him, said, “My lord, I will go to the water-landing; look after the children,” and acting as if she were going to fetch water by taking a pot, she fled and went to the presence of female ascetics near the city and ordained.

The Bodhisatta, knowing his wife’s non-return, raised the children himself. Later, when those children had grown somewhat and reached an age capable of knowing their own welfare and illfare, he cooked rice one day to test them, making it slightly undercooked. One day he cooked it slightly soft. One day he cooked it well-cooked. One day he cooked it very soft. One day he cooked it with little salt. One day he cooked it very salty.

The children said, “Father, today the rice is undercooked; today the rice is soft; today it is well-cooked; today the rice is very soft; today it is low in salt; today it is very salty.” Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta said, “Yes, dear sons,” and thought, “The children now know what is raw, cooked, salty, and low in salt. They will be able to live by their own nature. It is proper for me to ordain.”

Having thought thus, he gave and entrusted those children to his relatives, saying, “O mothers and fathers, please raise these children well.” While the relatives were weeping, the Bodhisatta departed from the city, ordained as an ascetic, and lived near the city.
362:
22. They know what is raw and what is cooked, also what is salted and what is unsalted. Having seen that [behavior of the children], I have gone forth. You practice [the alms-round], and I shall practice too.

This final verse was spoken.

Sister (bhagini). Raw and cooked. Also that city. Salted and unsalted. The children (dārakā) know. I, having seen the behavior of those children, have gone forth. You, practice only the practice of collecting alms. I, too, shall practice.

## Admonishing the Female Ascetic

One day, the female ascetic saw the Bodhisatta going for alms in Bārāṇasī, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, it seems you have ruined the children." The Bodhisatta replied, "I did not ruin these children; they went forth when they knew their own happiness and suffering. Do not think of those children, but delight in the state of a monk."

Thus, the Bodhisatta admonished the female ascetic and sent her away. She took the advice, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and went to her desired place. From that day on, the monk and the nun did not see each other again. The Bodhisatta developed meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledge (abhiññā) and was reborn in the Brahma realm.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, the Teacher, the All-Knowing One, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, those five hundred monks were established in the Fruit of Arahantship. As for the identification of the Jātaka: "At that time, Uppalavaṇṇā was the daughter, Rāhula was the son, Rāhula's mother was the female ascetic, and I myself was the male ascetic."

## One who takes spiritual urgency and goes forth finds happiness

The Kumbhakāra Jātaka ends.

## 4. Daḷhadhamma Jātaka

## On the need to recognize past favors

The Present Story: The Teacher, the All-Knowing One, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Ghositārāma Monastery near Kosambī, told this Daḷhadhamma Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ahaṃ ce Daḷhadhammassa," concerning King Udena's elephant Bhaddavatikā.

The treatment received by that elephant and the lineage of King Udena will become clear in the Mātaṅga Jātaka.

## Bhaddavatikā the Elephant's Appeal

One day, in the morning, that elephant saw the All-Knowing Buddha entering the city for alms, surrounded by a host of Noble Ones and endowed with incomparable Buddha-glory. She prostrated at the feet of the All-Knowing Buddha.
363:
"O Blessed One, Knower of all things, Deliverer of the whole world from the suffering of Saṃsāra... King Udena, when I was young and capable of performing work, loved me and gave me great honor, thinking, 'Depending on this elephant, I have gained my life, my kingdom, and my queen.' He decorated me with all kinds of ornaments, anointed my standing place with perfumes, had a golden star canopy fastened above, surrounded me with colorful curtains, lit oil lamps, placed incense burners, and even had a golden vessel placed where I passed excrement. He placed me on a platform with colorful rugs and gave me various flavors of food fit for a king.

Now, in my old age, when I am unable to perform work, he has cut off all those honors. Being helpless and without support, I live in the forest eating Ketaka plants. I have no other refuge. O Blessed One, please make King Udena recognize my service and restore my former honors to their original state," she pleaded, weeping before the Tathāgata.

## The Buddha's Admonition
The All-Knowing Buddha said, "Go, I will speak to the King and restore your wealth and retinue to their original state." He then went to the gate of the King's palace. The King invited the All-Knowing Buddha into the palace and offered a great gift of alms to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

At the end of the meal, while performing the Anumodanā (thanksgiving), the All-Knowing Buddha asked, "Great King, where is Bhaddavatikā?" When the King replied, "Venerable, I do not know," the Buddha said, "Great King, it is not right to take away the honors of those who have been helpful when they reach old age. One should be grateful and appreciative. Bhaddavatikā is now old and infirm; being helpless, she lives in the forest eating Ketaka plants. It is improper for you to leave her helpless in her old age." Having spoken of Bhaddavatikā's virtues, he said, "Restore all her former honors to their original state," and then he departed.

King Udena did exactly as the Buddha had commanded. The news spread throughout the city: "The All-Knowing Buddha spoke of Bhaddavatikā's virtues and had her former wealth and honors restored." This matter also became well-known among the community of monks.

Then, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the All-Knowing Buddha spoke of Bhaddavatikā's virtues and caused her former wealth and honors to be restored."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past also, the Tathāgata spoke of her virtues and restored her lost honors." Having said this, he brought the past story.

In the past, a king named Daḷhadhamma reigned in Vārāṇasī. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a minister's family and, upon reaching maturity, served that king.
364:
23. If I, who served Daḷhadhamma, carrying out his tasks, bearing a sword in my breast, and acting with valor in battle, could not please him [who else could]?

24. Surely the King does not know my valor and manly strength, my well-performed deeds in battle, and my missions as a messenger.

25. Thus, I shall surely die, friendless and without refuge; for now I have been given to a potter to carry cow dung.

She spoke these three verses.

Sāmi, my lord. Ahaṃ, I. Vahantī, while carrying out various tasks. Urasi, in the breast. Sallaṃ, a fixed sword. Dharantī, while bearing it forward. Yuddhe, in battle. Vikkantacārinī, while exerting effort with victorious combat. Daḷhadhammassa, of King Daḷhadhamma. Cittaṃ, the mind. Ce nābhirādhayiṃ, if I could not please. Ko, who. Tassa, of that King. Cittaṃ, the mind. Ārādhayissati, will be able to please?

Mama, my. Vikkamaporisaṃ, manly strength and exertion. Saṅgāme, in battle. Sukatantāni, well-performed deeds. Dūtavippahitāni ca, and when sent with a scroll tied to my neck to be given to such-and-such a king, I would travel a hundred leagues in a single day to carry out the messenger's task. Rājā, King Daḷhadhamma. Na jānāti nūna, surely does not know.

Sā ahaṃ, that I. Abandhu, being without friends. Aparāyinī, being without refuge. Marissāmi nūna, shall surely die. Tadā hi, for that reason. Chakaṇahārikā, the task of carrying cow dung. Katvā, having performed. Rājā, the King. Kumbhakārassa, to the potter. Dinnā, has given me.

The Omniscient Buddha, having arrived, asked: "Monks, for what purpose are you now gathered?" When they replied, "We are gathered for such-and-such a discussion," He said, "Monks, not only now have I made known the virtues of this elephant and restored her honors; I have done so in the past as well." He then brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Daḷhadhamma was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having received great wealth from the King, held the position of a minister.

## The Royal Elephant
King Daḷhadhamma had an elephant named Oṭṭhibyādhi, who was endowed with great power and strength. She could travel a hundred leagues in a single day. She performed the tasks of a messenger. In battle, she engaged in combat and crushed the enemies.

The King, thinking, "This Oṭṭhibyādhi is of great service to me," gave her all kinds of ornaments and provided her with all honors, similar to those given by King Udena to the elephant Bhaddavatikā.

## Stripped of Rank
Later, when Oṭṭhibyādhi became old and weak, the King took away all her honors. From then on, being without refuge, she lived in the forest eating grass and leaves.
365:
26. As long as a man has hope [of gain], so long does he associate [with another]. When benefit ceases, they abandon him, just as the King abandoned Oṭṭhibyādhi.

27. He who, having received a favor in the past and having his purpose fulfilled, does not recognize it—his desired goals will perish.

28. He who, having received a favor in the past and having his purpose fulfilled, recognizes it—his desired goals will flourish.

29. I say this to you, O sirs, as many as are gathered here: be grateful, all of you, and you shall long remain in heaven.

He spoke these four verses.

Poso, a man. Yaṃ purisaṃ, that person. Yāvatā, for as long as. Āsīsati, he hopes for [gain]. Tāvadeva, for that long only. Taṃ purisaṃ, that person. Pavīṇati, he associates with. Khattiyo, the King. Oṭṭhibyādhiṃ, the elephant named Oṭṭhibyādhi. Jahati iva, just as he abandons. Atthāpāye, when benefit is gone. Naṃ, that person. Jahanti, they abandon.

Then one day, when there were not enough pots in the palace, the King summoned the potter and said, "It is said there are not enough pots."
"Great King, I cannot find oxen to harness to the cart for carrying cow dung," the potter replied.

The King, hearing the potter's words, asked, "Where is my Oṭṭhibyādhi?"
"Great King, she wanders about according to her nature," he said.
The King said, "From this day forth, harness Oṭṭhibyādhi and carry cow dung," and he gave Oṭṭhibyādhi to the potter. The potter said, "Very well, Great King," and did as the King commanded.

## Reporting to the Wise Minister
One day, Oṭṭhibyādhi, leaving the city, saw the Bodhisatta entering the city at night. She paid homage, prostrated at the Bodhisatta's feet, and weeping, said: "My lord, the King recognized my service when I was young and gave me great honors. Now that I am old, he has cut off all my honors and does not even think of me. Being without refuge, I must live in the forest eating grass and leaves. Now that I have reached such misery, he has given me to a potter to be harnessed to a cart. Apart from you, I have no other refuge. May you know the service I have rendered to the King; I beg of you. Now, please restore my lost honors to their original state."

## Addressing the King
The Bodhisatta, having heard the words of Oṭṭhibyādhi, said: "Do not worry. I will speak to the King and restore your honors to their original state." Having comforted Oṭṭhibyādhi, he entered the city, and after eating his morning meal, he went to the King. Initiating a conversation, he asked: "Great King, did not your elephant named Oṭṭhibyādhi carry out the work of battle with a sword and spear fixed to her breast in such-and-such a place? On such-and-such a day, she was sent with a letter tied to her neck and traveled a hundred leagues. You also gave great honors to that Oṭṭhibyādhi. Where is she now?"

"I have given that Oṭṭhibyādhi to a potter to carry cow dung," the King replied. Then the Bodhisatta said to the King: "Great King, what you have done is not proper. Giving her to a potter to be harnessed to a cart is indeed improper." Thus, by way of admonishing the King, he said:

## Ruin through Ingratitude
Yo, he who. Pubbe, in the past. Katakalyāṇo, having had a favor done for him. Katattho, having had his purpose fulfilled by another.
366:
He does not recognize [the favor]. For him, whatever benefits are desired, those benefits perish.

He who, having had a favor done for him in the past and having had his purpose fulfilled, recognizes the favor; for him, whatever benefits are desired, those benefits increase.

Sirs, for that reason, I say to you: as many as are gathered here, may you all be grateful. You shall stay in heaven for a long time.

## Reinstatement of Position
In this way, the Great Being gave advice to all those assembled, starting with the king. Having heard those words, the king restored the wealth and retinue of Oṭṭhibyādhi to their original state. Abiding by the advice of the Bodhisatta, the king performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms for a long time and passed away to heaven.

The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Bhaddavatikā was Oṭṭhibyādhi, Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the minister."

## For the Grateful, Many Benefits Flourish
The Daḷhadhamma Jātaka ends.

## 5. Somadatta Jātaka
## Weeping for the Dead is Useless
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who teaches the world including the devas, told this Somadatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yo maṃ pure paccuḍḍeti," concerning a certain elderly monk.

That elderly monk, it is said, had ordained a certain novice. That novice, having been of great service to the elderly monk, died of a certain disease. When that novice died, the elderly monk wandered about weeping and lamenting.

Seeing that elderly monk, the monks in the Dhamma Hall started a conversation: "This elderly monk of such-and-such name wanders about weeping and lamenting because of the death of the novice. He seems to be devoid of the meditation on the mindfulness of death (maraṇassati-kammaṭṭhāna)."

The All-Knowing Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what subject are you gathered here discussing now?" When they replied, "We are gathered to discuss this matter," He said, "Monks, not only now has this monk wept when this novice died; in the past, he also wept," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

## The Brahmin Becomes an Ascetic
At that time, a certain brahmin living in a Kāsī village possessed great wealth. Renouncing sensual pleasures, he entered the Himalayas and became an ascetic. He spent his life subsisting on alms-gathering and on forest roots and fruits.

## Adopting the Young Elephant
One day, while going for the sake of fruits, he saw a young elephant. He brought it to his hermitage, placed it in the position of a son, named the elephant Somadatta, and raised it by feeding it grass and leaves. When that elephant reached maturity, it had a large body. One day, after consuming a large amount of food, it became weak due to indigestion. The ascetic left the elephant at the hermitage and went for the sake of fruits. Before the ascetic returned, the young elephant died.

## Lamentation at the Time of Death
When the ascetic returned with the fruits, he thought, "On other days, my son comes out to meet me. Today he is not seen; where has he gone?" and wishing to weep, he spoke this first verse:

30. He who used to come out to meet me from afar in the forest in the past, that elephant is not seen; where has Somadatta gone?

[Word-for-word meaning:] Āyato: endowed with a complete form. Somadatto: named Somadatta. Yo mātaṅgo: which elephant. Maṃ: me. Pure: in the past. Araññe: in the forest. Dūraṃ: from afar. Paccuḍḍeti: comes out to meet. So mātaṅgo: that elephant. Na dissati: is not seen now. Kuhiṃ: where. Gato: has he gone?
368:
31. "This one lies dead, like a green sprout cut off. Fallen on the ground he lies; alas, the tusker is dead."

He spoke this second verse. 

"This elephant (kuñjaro) lies dead. This very elephant is Somadatta, and no other. Just as a large sprout of a māluva creeper (allasiṅgaṃ), having been cut (vacchito) with a fingernail and dropped on the ground (bhūmyā) in the midday heat of the summer, so too does the elephant Somadatta lie on the ground. Alas (vata), he is dead (amarā)."

33. "Indeed, Sakka, through living together, whether with a human or a beast, love arises in the heart; it is not possible not to grieve for that."

He spoke this fourth verse.

"O Sakka, indeed (have), through living together (saṃvāsena), love (pemaṃ) arises in the heart (hadaye) of a human (manussassa) or a beast (migassa). It is not possible (na sakkā) not to grieve (asocituṃ) for that beloved being (taṃ piyaṃ)."

34. "They weep for the dead and for those who will die, those who weep and lament. Therefore, O Sage, do not weep; the virtuous say weeping is in vain."

35. "If by lamenting, O Brahmin, the dead who have passed away could rise again, we would all gather and weep for one another's kinsmen."

He spoke these two verses.

"O Sage (isi), those (ye) who weep for the dead (mataṃ) and for those who are about to die (marissaṃ), who shed tears (rudanti) and lament (lapanti)—for them, there is no day when tears cease. The virtuous (santo) say (āhu) that weeping (roditaṃ) is in vain (moghaṃ). Therefore, do not weep."

"O Brahmin (brahme), indeed (ve), if by weeping (kanditena) the dead (mato) who has passed from this life (peto) could rise again (samuṭṭhahe), then all of us (sabbe) would gather (saṅgamma) and weep (rodāma) for one another's kinsmen (ñātake)."

While coming along lamenting in this way, he saw the elephant fallen at the end of the cloister walk, and embracing its neck, he wept.

## Sakka's Warning
At that moment, Sakka, surveying the world, saw the hermit and thought: "This hermit left his wife and children to ordain. Now, he grieves for a young elephant, perceiving it as a son. I shall stir him with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and cause him to regain his mindfulness." He went to the hermit's hermitage and, standing in the air, spoke the third verse:

32. "For you, who have entered the homeless life and are liberated, being a recluse, it is not good that you mourn for the dead."

"That you mourn (yaṃ anusocasi) for the dead being (petaṃ) is not good (na sādhu) for you (te), who are a recluse (samaṇassa) endowed with the homeless life (anagāriyupetassa) and liberated from the state of a layman (vippamuttassa)."

## Grieving out of Love
Then, having heard Sakka's words, the hermit said:

## You will always be weeping
Thereafter, wishing to admonish the hermit, Sakka said:

## Thank you, Lord
Having heard Sakka's words, the hermit regained his mindfulness, became free from sorrow, wiped away his tears, and wishing to praise Sakka, spoke the remaining verses:
369:
36. "Indeed, I was burning like a fire sprinkled with ghee; just as one pours water, you have extinguished all my distress."

37. "Indeed, you have pulled out the arrow that was lodged in my heart; you have removed the grief for my son from me who was overwhelmed by sorrow."

38. "I, with the arrow pulled out, am free from sorrow and undisturbed. I do not mourn, nor do I weep, having heard your words, O Vāsava."

He spoke these remaining verses.

"Just as one pours (osiñcaṃ) water (vārinā) upon a fire (pāvakaṃ) sprinkled with ghee (ghatasittaṃ), so indeed (vata) have you extinguished (nibbāpaye) me, who was burning (ādittaṃ) with the fire of grief. You have extinguished all my distress (daraṃ)."

"You (yo tvaṃ) have removed (apānudi) the grief for my son (puttasokaṃ) from me (me) who was overwhelmed by sorrow (sokapare tassa). The arrow (yaṃ sallaṃ) of grief that was lodged in my heart (hadayassitaṃ)—that arrow you (te/tayā) have indeed pulled out (abbahī vata)."

"O Vāsava (Sakka), having heard (sutvāna) your (tava) words, I (so ahaṃ) am one whose arrow has been pulled out (abbūḷhasallo). I am free from sorrow (vītasoko) and undisturbed (anāvilo). I do not mourn (na socāmi), nor do I weep (na rodāmi)."

In this way, Sakka admonished the hermit and returned to his own abode.

To conclude the Jātaka, the Blessed One, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, the elephant calf was the novice, the hermit was the old monk, and I myself was Sakka."

## Grieving for the dead only brings sorrow
The Somadatta Jātaka ends.

## 6. Susīma Jātaka
## On Renouncing the Kingdom to Enter the Forest
The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who admonishes the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Susīma Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kāḷāni kesāni pure ahesuṃ," concerning the Great Renunciation.
370:
At that time, while the monks were seated in the Dhamma hall, the Exalted One arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?” When they replied, “We are gathered here to discuss such and such a matter,” the Buddha said, “Monks, it is not surprising that I, having fulfilled the perfections for many hundreds of thousands of crores of aeons, have now made the Great Renunciation. In the past, I also renounced the kingship in the Kingdom of Kāsi, which was three hundred leagues in extent, and went forth into the forest.” Having said this, he brought forth the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen of that King’s chaplain. On the very day the Bodhisatta was born, a son was also born to the King of Bārāṇasī. On the day of the naming ceremony, they named the Bodhisatta “Prince Susīma” and the King’s son “Prince Brahmadatta.” The King of Bārāṇasī, thinking, “He was born on the same day as my son,” ordered the Bodhisatta to be brought, provided him with nurses, and had him raised together with his own son.

## Two Friends

When those two youths reached the age of maturity, they were exceedingly handsome, possessing an appearance like that of celestial beings. Having learned all the arts in the city of Takkasilā, they returned. The Prince became the Viceroy and lived, ate, and slept together with the Bodhisatta. Upon the death of his father, the Prince ascended to the throne; he granted great wealth and status to the Bodhisatta and appointed him to the position of royal chaplain.

One day, the King had the city decorated and, adorned like Sakka, the King of Devas, he mounted the back of a noble, rutting elephant that resembled the elephant Erāvaṇa. He had the Bodhisatta sit behind him on the elephant’s back and made a ceremonial procession around the city, turning to the right.

## The Queen Mother Falls in Love

His mother, thinking, “I shall look upon my dear son,” stood at the lion-window. As the King returned from his procession around the city, she saw the chaplain’s son sitting behind him and her heart became filled with passion. She entered her bedchamber and lay down, refusing food, thinking, “If I do not get this chaplain’s son, I shall die right here on this bed.”
371:
39. Black were the hairs before,
Grown on the head in their proper places.
Today, seeing them white, O Susīma,
Practice the Dhamma; it is time for the holy life.

He spoke this first verse:

Susīma, Susīma. Pure, in the past. Sīsamhi, on the head. Yathāpadese, in their proper places. Jātāni, which were. Kāḷāni, black in color. Kesāni, the hairs. Ahesuṃ, they were. Ajja, now. Setāni, those that are pure white. Tāni, those hairs. Disvā, having seen. Dhammaṃ, the ten courses of wholesome action. Cara, practice. Brahmacariyassa, for practicing the holy life. Kālo, the time has come.

When the King did not see his mother, he asked, “Where is my mother?” Hearing that she was ill, he went to her, paid his respects, and asked, “Mother, what kind of illness do you have?” Due to her shame, she did not speak.

The King went and sat upon his royal throne, summoned his Chief Queen, and sent her, saying, “Go and find out the cause of my mother’s discomfort.” The Queen went and, while massaging her back, questioned her. Women do not hide secrets from other women. The Queen Mother informed the Queen of the matter. The Queen, having heard this, went and informed the King. The King said, “Let it be so. Go and comfort her. I shall make the chaplain the King and make my mother his Chief Queen.” The Queen then went and comforted the Queen Mother.

## Handing Over the Kingdom and Marriage to the Mother

The King then summoned the chaplain, informed him of the matter, and said, “Friend chaplain, give life to my mother. You shall be the King, she shall be the Chief Queen, and I shall be the Viceroy.” The chaplain refused, saying, “It is not possible to do such a thing,” but after being repeatedly entreated, he accepted. The King made the chaplain the King and he himself became the Viceroy.

Later, while they were living together in harmony, the Bodhisatta became weary in the midst of the household life. Renouncing sensual pleasures, his mind inclined toward going forth as an ascetic. Not delighting in the pleasures of the defilements, he would stand alone, sit alone, and sleep alone.
372:
40. "O King, this grey hair is mine, not yours; it is from my head, my very own head. I spoke a lie, saying 'I will do what is beneficial'; O Excellent King, forgive this one fault of mine."
41. "O King, you are young and beautiful, like a newly sprouted bamboo shoot. Rule the kingdom and look upon me; do not run after that which is delayed (kālika), O Lord of Men."
She spoke these two verses.
'Deva', O King. 'Mameva', mine alone. 'Palitaṃ', grey hair. 'Tuyhaṃ', your. 'Na', not. 'Mameva', mine alone. 'Sīsaṃ', the grey hair on the head. 'Mama', my. 'Uttamaṅgaṃ', the grey hair on the head. 'Ahaṃ', I. 'Atthaṃ', benefit. 'Karissaṃ', I will do. 'Musā', a lie. 'Abhāṇiṃ', I spoke wrongly. 'Rājaseṭṭha', O Excellent King. 'Ekāparādhaṃ', my one fault. 'Khama', please forgive.
'Rāja', O Excellent King. 'Paṭhamuggato', newly sprouted. 'Kaḷīro', a bamboo shoot. 'Dassaniyo', beautiful to look at. 'Hoti yathā', just as it is. 'Evaṃ', in the same way. 'Tuvaṃ', you, O King. 'Daharo', being young. 'Dassaniyo', are beautiful to look at. 'Asi', you are. 'Rajjañca', the kingship also. 'Kārehi', exercise/rule. 'Mamañca', and me. 'Passa', look upon. 'Janinda', O King. 'Kālikaṃ', the state of a monk which gives fruit only later. 'Mā anudhāvi', do not pursue.
He sits; he sleeps. He is like one bound in a prison, or like a cock kept in a cage.
## The King's Sense of Urgency
At that time, the Chief Queen of the King thought: "This King does not delight with me; he stands, sits, and sleeps alone. This King is young and tender, while I am old; grey hairs have appeared on my head. If I were to tell a lie, saying 'A grey hair has appeared on your head, O King,' and by some means make the King aware so that he might delight with me, it would be good."
One day, while pretending to look for lice on the King's head, she said, "O King, you are old; a grey hair has appeared on your head." He said, "If that is so, pluck that grey hair and place it in my hand." The Queen plucked a single black hair from the King's head. Discarding that hair, she took a grey hair from her own head and placed it in the King's hand, saying, "O King, this is your hair." Seeing that grey hair, the Bodhisatta was struck with terror (saṃvega), and sweat poured from his forehead, which was like a golden plate.
Admonishing himself, the Bodhisatta thought: "Susīma, you are old! Having been submerged in the mire of sensual pleasures for so long like a pig submerged in filth, you are unable to abandon that mire of sensuality..."

42. "I see a young maiden, with smooth limbs, a beautiful body, and a slender waist. Like a dark creeper with leaves like black coral swaying in a gentle breeze, she moves among men as if enticing them."
43. "Later, I see that same woman, eighty or ninety years of age by birth. Holding a staff, trembling, she moves about bent like a roof-rafter."
He spoke this pair of verses.
'Bhadde', my dear. 'Ahaṃ', I. 'Sāmaṭṭhapassaṃ', having smooth complexion on all sides. 'Sutanuṃ', having a beautiful body. 'Sumajjhaṃ', having a beautiful waist. 'Dahariṃ', young. 'Kumāriṃ', a maiden. 'Passāmi', I see. 'Pavellamānā', swaying here and there when struck by a gentle wind. 'Kāḷappavāḷāva', like a black creeper with dark shoots. 'Sā itthī', that woman. 'Naresu', near men. 'Palobhayantīva', as if enticing them by the power of defilements. 'Gacchati', she goes.
'Aparena samayena', at a later time. 'Jaccā', from birth. 'Asītikñca', being eighty years old. 'Nāvutikañca', being ninety years old. 'Tamenaṃ nāriṃ', that woman. 'Daṇḍaṃ', a staff. 'Gahetvāna', having taken. 'Pavedhamānaṃ', trembling. 'Gopānasībhoggasamaṃ', having a body bent like a rafter. 'Carantiṃ', walking. 'Passāmi', I see.
He thought: "It is time to abandon sensual pleasures, enter the Himalayas, and become a monk to live the holy life."
## Not Old Yet, Lord
When the Bodhisatta thus praised the virtues of living the holy life, the Queen was terrified, thinking: "I intended to make this King attached to me, but I have only caused his detachment." Thinking she would now praise her own beauty so that the King would not become a monk, she said:
[Forgive this one fault, O Excellent King.]
## Later, We Must All Grow Old
Hearing the Queen's words, the Bodhisatta said: "My dear, it must be as you say. As my age matures, these dark hairs will change and become white like hemp. When they reach old age, I see the change of appearance and the breaking of the body of maidens who are like garlands of blue lotuses, who resemble golden statues, and who are endowed with the grace of supreme youth. My dear, this world of living beings thus ends in ruin." Desiring to preach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, he said:
374:
## My Lord is Going to the Forest
Having spoken of the gratification (assāda) in the body with the first verse and the danger (ādīnava) of the body with the second verse, the Bodhisatta now desired to express his lack of delight in the midst of the household life:
44. "Thinking of that very thing, I see [myself] alone in the midst of my bed. Reflecting, 'I too will be like this,' I find no delight in the house; it is time for the holy life."
45. "The delight of one living at home is like a support-rope. The wise cut even this, and having abandoned the pleasure of the senses, they go forth without longing."
He spoke this pair of verses.
'So ahaṃ', that I. 'Tameva anuvicintayanto', repeatedly thinking of the gratification and danger of those forms. 'Sayanassa majjhe', in the middle of the bed. 'Eko', alone. 'Passāmi', I see. 'Ahaṃ', I too. 'Evaṃ tathā', in that same way. 'Bhavissāmi', will become. 'Iti', thus. 'Pekkhamāno', reflecting. 'Gehe', in the house. 'Na rame', I do not delight. 'Brahmacariyassa', of practicing the holy life. 'Kālo', it is the time.
'Geha', in the house. 'Vasato', of one living. 'Yā rati', whatever delight there is. 'Atthi', there is. 'Esā rati', that delight. 'Ālambanī', a thing to be grasped. 'Rajjuva', is like a rope. 'Hoti', it is. 'Dhīrā', the wise. 'Etampi', even this delight in sensual pleasures. 'Chetvāna', having cut. 'Kāmasukhaṃ', sensual pleasure. 'Pahāya', having abandoned. 'Anapekkhino', being without longing. 'Vajanti', they go.
Thus the Bodhisatta, showing the gratification and danger in sensual pleasures, preached the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha. He summoned his friend, King Brahmadatta, handed over the kingship to him, and while his relatives and friends were weeping, he abandoned his glory and wealth, entered the Himalayas, became a hermit, developed meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and was reborn in the Brahma realm.
375:
The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, many people drank the nectar of immortality. He then identified the birth: "At that time, the mother of Rāhula was the Chief Queen, Ānanda was the friend king, and I myself was King Susīma."
## Seeing the grey hair, being moved by spiritual urgency, I shall delight in the forest
The Susīma Jātaka ends.
## 7. Koṭasimbali Jātaka
## On why one should not tolerate everything
The story of the present: While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Koṭasimbali Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ahaṃ dasasataṃbyāmaṃ", concerning the suppression of defilements.
The story of the present will become clear in the Pānīya Jātaka. In this Koṭasimbali Jātaka, the All-Enlightened Buddha saw five hundred monks within Jetavana Monastery who were overcome by sensual thoughts. He gathered the Sangha of monks and said, "Monks, it is proper to be suspicious of what is worthy of suspicion. When defilements grow, they overwhelm a person just as banyan trees and the like overwhelm a tree. Therefore, in the past, a deity born in a great silk-cotton tree saw a bird that had eaten banyan seeds and was dropping its excrement in the fork of his tree. Realizing that 'from this excrement, the destruction of my mansion will occur,' he became terrified." Having said this, he brought forth the past.
The story of the past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a tree deity in a great silk-cotton tree.
376:
45. "I come carrying a dragon of a thousand spans. Though I carry both him and my own great body, you do not tremble."
46. "But seeing this tiny bird, which has far less flesh than I, you tremble in fear. For what reason, O Koṭasimbali?"
These were the two verses he spoke.
O Koṭasimbali, deity of the great silk-cotton tree. I, the Garuda, come having seized a dragon (naga) of a thousand spans. Seeing me, who carries that large-bodied dragon and my own great self, you do not tremble.
Yet, seeing this tiny female bird with very little flesh, which I have brought along, for what reason do you tremble in fear?
## The Garuda seizes the dragon
At that time, a certain Garuda king manifested a body one hundred and fifty leagues in size. With the wind from his wings, he split the waters of the great ocean into two. He seized a dragon king, a thousand spans in length, by the tail, made it drop the food it held in its mouth, and flew over the forest toward the great silk-cotton tree.
The dragon king, hanging down, thought, "I will free myself," and wrapped its coils around a banyan tree, gripping it tightly. Due to the great strength of the Garuda king and the large body of the dragon king, the banyan tree was uprooted. The dragon king did not let go of the tree. The Garuda king, taking the dragon king along with the banyan tree, reached the great silk-cotton tree. He laid the dragon king on the trunk, split its belly, ate the dragon's fat, and discarded the remaining carcass into the ocean.
## The deity trembles
Now, in that banyan tree, there was a small female bird. When the banyan tree was dropped, she flew up and perched in the fork of the silk-cotton tree.
The tree deity, seeing her, thought, "This bird will drop her excrement in the fork of my tree. From that excrement, a banyan or a pilakkha sapling will grow, spread over the entire silk-cotton tree, and destroy it. Then my mansion will be ruined." Terrified and shaken, the deity trembled.
377:
Then, explaining the reason, the deity spoke these four verses:
47. "O King, you are a meat-eater; this bird is a fruit-eater. Having eaten the seeds of banyan, pilakkha, udumbara, and assattha trees, she will drop her excrement on my trunk."
48. "Those trees, born in the windless shade near me, will grow. They will entwine me and make me a 'non-tree'."
49. "There are other trees, well-rooted and with strong trunks, that have been killed by such trees originating from seeds brought by this bird."
50. "Parasitic trees grow even over the great lords of the forest. Therefore, O King, I tremble, seeing the danger yet to come."
O King Garuda, you eat meat. This bird eats fruit. This bird, having eaten the seeds of banyan, pilakkha, udumbara, and assattha trees, will drop its excrement on my trunk. In the windless shade near me, those trees will grow. Those trees, such as the banyan, will entwine me and destroy me. There are other trees, well-rooted and with strong trunks, that have been killed by such trees originating from seeds brought by this bird. Parasitic trees grow even over the great lords of the forest. Therefore, O King, I tremble, seeing the danger yet to come.
51. "One should suspect what is to be suspected; one should guard against future danger. Through fear of future danger, the wise man looks to both worlds."
This was the final verse he spoke.
One should be wary of what is worthy of wariness. One should guard against future danger. A wise person, through fear of future danger, considers both the present world and the world beyond.
Because of the deity's trembling, the great silk-cotton tree shook down to its roots.
## Why do you tremble?
The Garuda king, seeing the trembling deity and wishing to ask the reason—
## She will destroy my mansion
Then, wishing to tell the reason to the Garuda king, the tree deity—
## Drove the bird away
Having heard the words of the tree deity, the Garuda king—
378:
Having said this, the Garuda king, by his own power, drove that female bird away from that silk-cotton tree.

The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching to a close, said, "One should fear that which is worthy of fear," and after proclaiming the Truths, he identified the Birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, five hundred monks were established in the fruit of Arahantship. As for the identification of the Birth: At that time, Sāriputta was the Garuda king, and I myself was the tree deity.

## One should contemplate and fear future dangers

The Koṭasimbali Jātaka is concluded.

## 8. Dhūmakāri Jātaka

## One should not favor new friends while abandoning old ones

The Present Story: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Dhūmakāri Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Rājā apucchi Vidhuraṃ," concerning the hospitality shown by the King of Kosala to newcomers.

On one occasion, that King of Kosala neglected the veteran soldiers who had served for generations and instead showed honor and respect only to newly arrived newcomers.

Then, when robbers were plundering the frontier of the King of Kosala, the king went out to do battle. The veteran soldiers thought, "The newcomers who have received honor and gifts will fight," and so they did not fight. The newcomers also thought, "The veteran soldiers will fight," and they too did not fight. The robbers defeated the king.

Realizing that he had been defeated because of his fault in favoring the newcomers, the king returned to Sāvatthī. Thinking, "Am I the only one who has been defeated by acting in this way, or have other kings also been defeated before? I will ask the Possessor of Ten Powers," after his morning meal, he went to Jetavana Monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and asked about the matter.

"Great King, it is not only you; ancient kings also suffered defeat by favoring newcomers," the Buddha said. Being requested by the king, he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: In the past, in the city of Indapatta in the kingdom of Kuru, a king named Dhanañjaya of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan reigned.
379:
## Vidhura the Wise

At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of the court chaplain. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā. Upon returning to Indapatta, he received the position of chaplain after his father's passing and became the minister who advised the king on matters of welfare and Dhamma. They gave him the name "Vidhura the Wise."

## Defeat in War by Favoring Outsiders

At that time, King Dhanañjaya disregarded his veteran soldiers and showed hospitality only to newly arrived soldiers. When robbers plundered the frontier of that Kuru king, the king went out to do battle. The veteran soldiers thought, "The new soldiers will know what to do," and did not fight. The new soldiers thought, "The veteran soldiers will know what to do," and they too did not fight.

The king was defeated and returned to Indapatta, reflecting, "I have been defeated because I showed hospitality only to newcomers." One day, he thought, "Am I the only one who has been defeated by favoring newcomers, or have there been other kings who were defeated in the past? I will ask Vidhura the Wise." Having so thought, he asked Vidhura the Wise, who had come to wait upon the king, about the matter.

## The Buddha's Proclamation of Vidhura's Answer

Then, the Omniscient Buddha, wishing to make clear the manner of King Dhanañjaya's questioning, spoke this verse:

52. The king, Yudhiṭṭhila, a lover of Dhamma, asked Vidhura:
"O Brahmin, do you know who is the one person who grieves much?"

(Brahmin, O Brahmin. Eko, one. Ko, who. Bahu, much. Socati, grieves? Tvaṃ, you. Jānāsi api, do you know? Iti, thus. Yudhiṭṭhilo, of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan. Dhammakāmo, lover of virtuous Dhamma. Rājā, the Kuru king. Vidhuraṃ, Vidhura the Wise. Apucchi, asked.)

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, what kind of grief is your grief? In the past, a goat-herd Brahmin named Dhūmakāri took a flock of goats, built a pen in the forest, kept the goats there, and lived there tending the flock by making fire and smoke, and consuming their milk and other products.

That Dhūmakāri Brahmin saw some golden-colored animals called sarabha deer that had come to that place. He fell in love with them and, disregarding his goats, he showed favor to the sarabha deer instead of the goats. When the sarabha deer fled to the Himalayas during the autumn season (Sarat-kāla), and the goats had also perished, he could no longer see the sarabha deer. Because of his grief, he suffered from jaundice and reached the end of his life."
380:
53. A Brahmin of the Vāseṭṭha clan, living in the forest with a herd of goats, kept a fire and smoke going day and night, being unwearied.
54. Attracted by the smell of that smoke, serabha deer, who were tormented by mosquitoes, came to stay for the rainy season near the smoke-maker.
55. Having set his heart on the serabha deer, he did not notice his goats. Whether they were coming or going, those goats of his perished.
56. When the autumn season arrived and the forest was free of mosquitoes, the serabha deer entered the mountain fastnesses and the sources of the rivers.
57. Seeing the serabha deer gone and his goats destroyed, the Brahmin became thin, discolored, and afflicted with jaundice.
58. Thus, whoever neglects his own and cherishes a newcomer, he grieves much alone, like the smoke-making Brahmin.
He spoke these verses.
Great King, the Brahmin named Dhūmakārī, of the Vāseṭṭha clan, lived in the forest with a herd of goats. Having plenty of fuel, he kept a smoke going day and night without laziness.
Because of the smell of that smoke, the serabha deer, being oppressed by mosquitoes, came to stay near the smoke-making Brahmin for the duration of the rainy season.
That smoke-making Brahmin, having developed affection for the serabha deer, did not know whether the goats were coming to the fold or leaving the fold. Those goats of his were destroyed.
When the autumn season came and the forest was free of mosquitoes and flies, the serabha deer entered the difficult mountain regions and the sources of the rivers.
The Brahmin Dhūmakārī, seeing that the serabha deer had gone and the goats had reached destruction, became thin, lost his complexion, and suffered from jaundice.
In this way, whoever treats his own internal people as outsiders and cherishes newcomers, he, like this smoke-making Brahmin, must grieve much alone.
Intending to show this example, "This smoke-making Brahmin, by showing hospitality to newcomers, suffered and reached destruction a hundredfold and a thousandfold more than you," he said:
## Honoring the Internal People
Thus the Bodhisatta made the King understand. The King, having reached a state of full understanding, gave much wealth to the wise Vidhura. From then on, he showed hospitality only to his own people, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and was destined for heaven.
381:
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the King of the Kurus, Pasenadi of Kosala was the Brahmin Dhūmakārī, and I myself was the wise Vidhura."
## Honoring the internal people will bring many benefits
The Dhūmakāri Jātaka ends.
## 9. Jāgara Jātaka
## The Present Story
That lay follower, who was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and a disciple of the Buddha, set out from Sāvatthī on a journey through the wilderness with five hundred wagons. The caravan leader, at a certain place in the wilderness where water was convenient, unyoked the five hundred wagons, prepared food and drink, and stayed there. The people lay down and slept in various places, but the lay follower undertook walking meditation at the foot of a tree near the caravan.
## The Benefit of Wakefulness
At that time, five hundred robbers, desiring to plunder the wagons, took various weapons and surrounded the caravan. Seeing the lay follower performing walking meditation, they waited there, thinking, "We will plunder when this man falls asleep." However, that lay follower continued his walking meditation throughout the three watches of the night.
At dawn, the robbers threw away the stones, clubs, and other weapons they had held and said, "O caravan leader... because of this man who watched without negligence, you have kept your life and remain the owner of your property. You should pay honor to him," and then they departed.
382:
59. Who here is asleep among those awake? Who here is awake among those asleep?
Who understands this of mine? Who can answer this for me?
She spoke this first verse.
O ascetic. In this world. Who is called one who sleeps among those who are awake? O ascetic. In this world. Who is called one who is awake among those who sleep? Who is able to answer this problem of mine?

60. I am asleep among those awake. I am awake among those asleep.
I understand this. I can answer this for you.
He spoke this second verse.
O daughter of the devas, tree deity. I am called one who sleeps among the great Arahants who are awake. I am called one who is awake among those who sleep. I understand this problem. I am able to answer your problem.

61. How are you asleep among those awake? How are you awake among those asleep?
How do you understand this? How can you answer this for me?
She spoke this third verse.
O ascetic. How are you called one who sleeps among those who are awake? How are you called one who is awake among those who sleep? O ascetic. How do you understand this problem of mine? How are you able to answer my problem.

62. Those who do not know the Dhamma, called restraint and self-control.
Among those who are heedless and sleeping, I am awake, O deity.

People, having risen early and seeing the stones, clubs, and so forth discarded by the thieves, honored the lay devotee, saying, "Because of this man, we have gained our lives."

The lay devotee also went to his desired place, and having completed his business, returned to Sāvatthī. He went to the Jetavana monastery, worshipped and honored the Blessed One, and sat down. When asked, "Lay devotee, why have you not been seen?" he reported the matter.

The Omniscient Buddha said, "Lay devotee, it is not only you who, staying awake without sleeping, gained a special benefit; wise men of old also, being awake, gained special virtues." Being requested by the lay devotee, He brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. When he came of age, he learned all the arts in Takkasilā. Returning, he lived in the midst of his house, but later went forth and became an ascetic. Before long, he attained the Jhanas and Abhiññās. Living in the Himavanta region, he remained in the postures of standing and walking, and without going to sleep, he practiced walking meditation throughout the entire night.

## The One Awake and the One Asleep

Then, the tree deity born at the end of the Bodhisatta's walking path, being pleased and standing in the fork of a tree, wishing to ask a question—

The Bodhisatta, hearing the words of the tree deity—

When he spoke this verse, the deity, wishing to ask again—

The Bodhisatta, wishing to explain the meaning—
383:
65. Excellent! Asleep among those awake. Excellent! Awake among those asleep.
Excellent! You understand this. Excellent! You can answer this for me.
She spoke this final verse.
O ascetic. Excellent. You have spoken this problem well. O ascetic. Excellent. You are called one who sleeps among the great Arahants who are awake. O ascetic. Excellent. You are called one who is awake among those who sleep. O ascetic. Excellent. You understand this problem of mine. O ascetic. Excellent. You are able to answer my problem.

63. Those whose lust, hatred, and ignorance are faded away.
Among those who are awake, I am asleep, O deity.

64. Thus, I am asleep among those awake. Thus, I am awake among those asleep.
Thus, I understand this. Thus, I can answer this for you.
He spoke these three verses.

O daughter of the devas, deity. Those who do not know the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, namely virtue (Sīla) attained through the Path as restraint (Saṃyama), and the restraint of the senses (Indriya-saṃvara) as self-control (Dama). Among those who are heedless through the power of the sleep of defilements, I am awake.

Those Arahants whose lust (Rāga), hatred (Dosa), and ignorance (Avijjā) are faded away and abandoned. Among those noble ones (Ariyas) who are awake in every way, compared to them, I am called one who sleeps, O deity.

Thus, O deity, for this reason, I am called one who sleeps among those who are awake. Thus, I am awake among those who sleep. Thus, I understand this problem. Thus, I am able to answer your problem.

When the Bodhisatta thus answered the problem, the tree deity was pleased and, wishing to praise the Bodhisatta—

Thus the deity, having praised the Bodhisatta, entered her own celestial mansion.
384:
Having brought this Dhamma teaching to a close, the Omniscient Buddha identified the birth: "At that time, Uppalavaṇṇā was the deity, and I myself was the ascetic."

## One who is awake and energetic shall prosper.
The Zagara Jātaka ends.

## 10. Kummasapiṇḍi Jātaka
## Obtaining royal wealth by giving a small gift
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kummasapiṇḍi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na kiratthi," concerning Queen Mallikā.

This Queen Mallikā was the daughter of a chief florist in Sāvatthī. She possessed great beauty and wisdom. One day, when she was sixteen years old, while going to the flower garden with other young girls, she took three balls of barley gruel, placed them in a flower basket, and set out.

As she was leaving the city, she saw the Blessed One, radiating light and surrounded by a company of monks, entering the city. She offered the three balls of barley gruel. The Omniscient Buddha lowered the bowl offered by the Four Great Kings and accepted them. Mallikā then paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One with her head, and stood at a suitable place, filled with joy directed towards the Buddha.

## Offering cakes to the Buddha
The Omniscient Buddha looked at Mallikā and smiled. Venerable Ānanda, wondering, "What is the cause and what is the reason for the Blessed One's smile?" asked the Omniscient Buddha.

Then, the Omniscient Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, as a result of offering these balls of barley gruel, this young girl will become the chief queen of the King of Kosala this very day," thus explaining the reason for his smile. The young girl then proceeded to the flower garden.

## Becoming the Chief Queen
On that very day, the King of Kosala, having fought a battle with King Ajātasattu and being defeated, was fleeing on horseback. Hearing the sound of Mallikā's singing, his heart became captivated, and he turned his horse toward the garden. The meritorious young girl, seeing the King, did not flee but came forward and held the horse by its nose. The King, still sitting on the horse's back, asked, "Do you have a master (husband)?"
385:
Knowing that she was unmarried, he dismounted from the horse. Exhausted by the wind and heat, he rested for a moment with his head in Mallikā's lap. Then, he had Mallikā sit on the horse's back and, surrounded by his army, entered the city. He sent Mallikā to her parents' home first, then in the evening, he had a carriage prepared and brought her from her parents' home with great honor and respect. Placing her upon a heap of treasures, he consecrated her and made her his chief queen.

From then on, the King loved and cherished her. She was endowed with the five good qualities, such as rising before him, and she served her husband like a deity. She was also beloved by the Buddhas. The fact that Mallikā attained such prosperity by giving three balls of gruel to the Blessed One spread throughout the entire city.

One day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, Queen Mallikā gave three balls of barley gruel to the Buddha, and as a result of that merit, she received her consecration on that very day. How wonderful is the great virtue of the Buddhas!"

The Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such a subject," he said, "Monks, it is not surprising that Mallikā attained the status of chief queen of the King of Kosala by giving three balls of barley gruel to a single Omniscient Buddha.

Why is that? It is because of the greatness of the virtues of the Omniscient Buddhas. In the past, wise men gave unsalted, unseasoned, and plain barley gruel to Paccekabuddhas, and as a result of that gift, in their second existence, they attained the royal splendor of the Kingdom of Kāsi, which was three hundred leagues in extent." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasီ, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family. When he came of age, he lived by working for hire under a certain merchant.

## The Gift of Barley Gruel
One day, thinking, "This will be for my breakfast," he took four balls of barley gruel from the market. While going to his work, he saw four Paccekabuddhas coming toward Bārāṇasī for alms. He thought, "These Paccekabuddhas are going to Bārāṇasī for alms. I have these four balls of barley gruel. What if I were to give these to them?"

He approached the Paccekabuddhas, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sirs, I have these four balls of barley gruel in my hands. I wish to offer these to you. Please, venerable sirs, accept them from me. By this acceptance, may this merit lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time."
386:
Knowing the patience of those Paccekabuddhas, he heaped up sand to prepare four seats, and upon those heaps of sand, he spread plucked leaves. Having invited the Paccekabuddhas to sit, he brought water in a leaf-cup and performed the ritual of pouring water to consecrate the gift. He then placed the four handfuls of barley cakes into their empty bowls, paid homage, and made an aspiration:

“Venerable sirs, by the merit of these barley cakes, may I never be born in a poor household; may this be a cause for the attainment of Omniscience.”

The Paccekabuddhas partook of the meal, and after finishing, they gave a blessing of appreciation (anumodanā) and flew through the air back to the Nandamūla cave.

## Becoming King

The Bodhisatta, with hands joined in reverence, cherished the joy he felt toward the Paccekabuddhas. When they had passed beyond his sight, he returned to his work. Remembering that act of generosity for the rest of his life, he passed away and, by the fruit of that merit, was reborn in the womb of the Chief Queen of the King of Vārāṇasī. They named the prince Brahmadatta.

From the time he could walk on his own, Prince Brahmadatta, through the knowledge of past lives (jātissara-ñāṇa), saw all his past actions as clearly as a reflection in a polished mirror, thinking: “In this very city of Vārāṇasī, while going to work as a laborer, I gave four handfuls of barley cakes to Paccekabuddhas, and by the fruit of that gift, I have been reborn in this royal family.”

When Prince Brahmadatta reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā, mastered all the arts, and upon his return, demonstrated his skills to his father. The father, being pleased, appointed him as the viceroy, and later, after his father’s passing, he ascended to the throne. At that time, a daughter of the King of Kosala, who possessed supreme beauty, was brought and made his Chief Queen. On the day of his coronation ceremony, the entire city was decorated like a city of the gods.

## The Song of the Source of Wealth

King Brahmadatta made a ceremonial procession around the city and ascended his decorated palace. Sitting upon the throne under the white parasol in the center of the palace hall, he looked upon the ministers on one side, the brahmins and householders on the other side—all shining with various riches and splendor—the citizens with various gifts in their hands on another side, and the sixteen thousand dancing women, like a host of celestial nymphs, on yet another side. Beholding this most delightful splendor and wealth, he remembered his past merit and thought:

“This white parasol with golden fittings and golden garlands, these many thousands of elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and chariots, these treasuries filled with rubies, pearls, and other gems, this great earth filled with various grains, and these women like celestial nymphs—all this splendor and wealth of mine belongs to no one else; it belongs only to the gift of four handfuls of barley cakes given to the four Paccekabuddhas. It is because of that barley-cake gift that I have obtained this.”
387:
Reflecting on the virtues of the Paccekabuddhas and making his own wholesome kamma manifest, King Brahmadatta, his entire body drenched in joy, desired to sing a song of exultation in the midst of the great crowd and spoke these two verses:

66. “Indeed, there is no such thing as a small service
Rendered to the Buddhas of noble vision.
See the fruit of a lump of barley cake,
Though it was dry and without syrup.

67. These many elephants, cattle, and horses,
Wealth, grain, and the entire earth,
And these women like celestial nymphs—
See the fruit of a lump of barley cake.”

(Commentary:) *Anomadassīsu*: Because they have seen the noble (anoma), the non-inferior knowledge of Paccekabodhi, the Paccekabuddhas are called 'those of noble vision'. *Pāricariyā*: This refers to acts of respect such as bowing, rising to greet, and joining hands, as well as the act of renouncing a gift—whether small or large, coarse or refined—after seeing a worthy recipient, gladdening the mind, recognizing their virtue, purifying the three intentions (before, during, and after), and having faith in the result. *Buddhesu*: Among the Paccekabuddhas. *Appikā*: It is said that there is no such thing as a small or insignificant result. *Sukkhāya*: Without oil or moisture. *Aloṇikāya*: Without molasses or syrup (though the word literally means 'without salt', here it refers to the lack of sweetener). *Kummāsapiṇḍiyā*: Referring to the barley meal taken together as four lumps. The meaning is that for those who recognize the virtue of virtuous recluses and brahmins, gladden their minds, expect the arising of results, and purify their three intentions, a gift given is never 'small'; it gives great fortune in every place of rebirth. As it is said:

“When the mind is clear, there is no such thing as a small gift,
Whether given to the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One,
Or to his disciples.

Whether he is present or has attained Parinibbāna,
If the mind is the same, the fruit is the same;
For because of the aspiration of the mind, beings go to a happy destination.”

To further illustrate this point:

“I gave milk-rice to a monk wandering for alms;
See my celestial mansion, I have become a nymph who can change form at will.”

## The Palace Women Sing

The Bodhisatta, filled with joy and delight on the day of his coronation, sang this song of exultation through these verses. From that day forward, saying “This is the King’s favorite song,” the Bodhisatta’s harem, the dancers, the musicians, the people inside and outside the city, and those in the festival pavilions all sang that very song, saying, “This is the song beloved by our Great King.”
388:
“I am the foremost among a thousand nymphs; see the result of merits. Because of that, I have such a complexion, and because of that, my wishes are fulfilled here.

Whatever pleasures are dear to my heart arise for me. Because of that, I have such blazing majesty, and my complexion illuminates all directions.”

Such stories from the Vimānavatthu should be brought in as examples.

*Dhanadhañña*: Wealth such as pearls and the seven types of grain. *Pathavī ca kevalā*: The entire great earth; he speaks as if the whole earth has come into his hands. *Passa phalaṃ kummāsapiṇḍiyā*: He says this while showing the fruit of his own gift himself. It is said that only Bodhisattas and Fully Enlightened Buddhas truly know the fruit of giving. Therefore, the Teacher, while teaching the discourse in the Itivuttaka, said:

“Bhikkhus, if beings knew the result of giving and sharing as I know it, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of stinginess obsess their hearts and stay there. Even if it were their last morsel, their last mouthful, they would not eat without having shared it, if there were someone to receive it. But because, bhikkhus, beings do not know the result of giving and sharing as I know it, they eat without giving, and the stain of stinginess obsesses their hearts and stays there.”

The Bodhisatta also sang this song of exultation with these two verses out of the joy and delight that arose on his coronation day. From then on, thinking “This is the King’s favorite song,” the Bodhisatta’s dancers, other musicians, the palace folk, the city dwellers, the country folk, those in taverns, and the circles of ministers all sang that same song, saying, “This is our King’s favorite song.”

## Asking the Meaning of the Song

After a long time had passed, the Chief Queen became desirous of knowing the meaning of that song. However, she did not dare to ask the Great Being. Then, one day, the King, being pleased with one of her virtues, said, “My dear, I grant you a boon; choose a boon.” “Very well, Deva, I accept the boon,” she replied. “What shall I give you? Elephants, horses, or something else?” he asked.

“O King, depending on you, there is nothing I lack. I have no need for those elephants and horses. If you truly wish to give, please tell me the meaning of the song you sing.” “My dear, what use is this boon to you? Choose another boon,” he said. “O King, I have no need for any other boon; I will take only that one,” she insisted.

“My dear, very well, I shall tell you. But I will not tell you alone in a private place. I shall have a drum beaten throughout the twelve-yojana city of Vārāṇasī, have a jeweled pavilion erected at the palace gate, have a jeweled throne prepared, and in the presence of the ministers, brahmins, and citizens...”
389:
68. "O elephant among kings, you constantly speak in verses, O lord of Kosala.
I ask you, O increaser of the realm, you speak with a heart full of great joy."
She spoke this third verse.

Having said this, the King looked at the Queen's splendor and, wishing to ask, "Lady, I have explained my own wholesome deeds in a previous life. Among these women, there is no one equal to you in beauty or grace. What good deed did you perform to obtain this splendor?"

## They Performed Meritorious Deeds
Thus, these two, the King and the Queen, having related their past deeds in detail, from that time onwards, built six alms-halls—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the palace gate. Having made the whole of Jambudīpa ‘ploughed’ [with merit], they performed great acts of charity, kept the precepts, observed the Uposatha, and at the end of their lives, they were destined for heaven.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the Queen was the mother of Rāhula, and I myself was the King.”

## 11. Parantapa Jātaka
## Evil Deeds Bring Evil Results
The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Parantapa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with ‘Āgamiṣṣati me pāpaṃ,’ concerning Devadatta’s attempt to kill the Buddha.

At that time, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised a discussion: “Friends, Devadatta strives only to kill the Tathāgata. He employed archers, rolled a rock, and released the elephant Nāḷāgiri; he acts only for the destruction of the Buddha.”
394:
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," He said, "Monks, not only now has Devadatta striven to kill me; in the past also he strove to kill me. However, being unable to cause even a mere fright, he himself suffered misery." Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen. When he came of age, he studied all the arts in Takkasilā. He also learned the mantra for understanding the cries of all animals.

## Wishing the Death of the Viceroy
The Bodhisatta, having given the teacher's fee, returned to Bārāṇasī, and his father appointed him to the position of Viceroy. Although he appointed him as Viceroy, the King wished to have the Bodhisatta killed and did not even want to see him.

## The Words of the Vixen
At that time, a certain vixen, taking her two cubs, entered the city through a sewer at night when people were asleep. Near the Bodhisatta's palace bedchamber, there was a rest house. In that rest house, a traveler took off his sandals, placed them on the ground at his feet, and lay down on a wooden plank; he was not yet asleep. At that time, the vixen's cubs, being hungry, cried out.

Then their mother, the vixen, said in her own language, "My dears, do not make a sound. In that rest house, a man has taken off his sandals, placed them on the ground, and is lying on a plank. He is not yet asleep. When he is asleep, I will bring those sandals and let you eat them."

The Bodhisatta, through the power of the mantra, understood her language. He came out of his bedchamber, opened the window, and asked, "Who is there?" The traveler replied, "O Lord, I am a traveler." "Where are your sandals?" the Bodhisatta asked. "O Lord, they are on the ground," he replied. "Pick them up and hang them high," said the Bodhisatta.

Hearing these words, the vixen became angry with the Bodhisatta.
395:
Once again, one day, that she-jackal entered the city in the same manner. At that time, a certain drunken man, while descending into a pond to drink water, fell in, drowned, and died. That man had two robes, a thousand kahāpaṇas within the robes, and a ring on his finger.

Then, the she-jackal said to her young cubs, who were crying out from hunger, "My dears, do not make a sound. A man has died in that pond, and there is such and such wealth. Having died, he lies on the steps. I will let you eat that man."

The Bodhisatta, hearing those words, opened the casement window and asked, "Who is in the hall?" When a man stood up and said, "My lord, it is I," the Bodhisatta said, "Go, take the robes, the thousand kahāpaṇas, and the ring from the dead man in that pond. Then, dispose of the body in the water in such a way that it does not rise to the surface." That man did as the Bodhisatta commanded.

The she-jackal became angry once more. "On the previous day, he did not let my cubs eat the sandals; today, he does not let them eat the dead man. So be it! On the third day from now, a rival king will come and besiege the city. Then your father will send you to battle. In that battle, they will cut off your head. Then, I shall drink the blood from your throat and satisfy my grudge. You have held a grudge against me; you shall see!" Thus she howled, threatening the Bodhisatta, and left taking her cubs with her.

## Being Sent to War

On the third day, a rival king came and besieged the city. The King said to the Bodhisatta, "My dear, go and fight against that king." The Bodhisatta replied, "My lord, I have seen an omen; I do not venture to go, for I fear for my life." The King said, "Whether you die or not, what is that to me? You must go!"

"Very well, my lord," said the Bodhisatta. Taking his retinue, he did not exit through the gate where the rival king was stationed, but opened another gate and departed. As the Bodhisatta left, the entire city became as if empty. Everyone followed him. The Bodhisatta established an encampment in a suitable place and stayed there.
396:
## The King's Flight

The King thought, "The Viceroy has emptied the city, taken the army, and fled. The rival king has also besieged the city. Now I must save my own life." Having so thought, he took the Queen, the Chaplain, and a servant named Parantapa who was a close attendant, and fled in disguise during the night into the forest.

## Seizing the Kingdom

The Bodhisatta, knowing that the King had fled, entered the city, drove away the enemy, and took over the kingdom.

## The Queen's Infidelity

The Bodhisatta's father built a leaf-hut by a river and lived there, subsisting on wild fruits. While the King and the Chaplain went out to gather fruits, the servant Parantapa remained in the leaf-hut with the Queen. There, in that forest, the Queen conceived a child by the King.

Through constant association, the Queen became very intimate with the servant Parantapa. One day, the Queen said, "If the King should find out, neither your life nor mine would remain. Therefore, kill that King."

When he asked, "How shall I kill him?", she replied, "This King gives you his sword and makes you carry his bathing robe when he goes to bathe. At that bathing place, knowing him to be off guard, cut off his head with the sword, chop his body into pieces, and bury it in the ground." Parantapa agreed, saying, "Very well."

Then one day, the Chaplain alone went to gather fruits and, climbing a tree near the King's bathing place, was picking fruit. The King, intending to bathe, had Parantapa carry his sword and bathing robe and went to the riverbank. While the King was off guard during his bath, Parantapa, intending to kill him, seized him by the neck and raised the sword.
