79. "Surely my desire for the timid one, dwelling not far away, will make me thin and pale, just as that branch did to Parantapa."

This is the second verse. 

Just as that branch made the slave Parantapa thin and pale, so too will my desire for my brahmin wife—who lives not far away, perhaps two or three leagues from here—surely make me thin and pale.

## The Killing of the King

The king cried out in fear of death. Hearing that sound, the chaplain looked and saw Parantapa killing the king. Terrified, he let go of the branch, climbed down, and hid in a thicket. Parantapa, hearing the sound of the branch dropped by the chaplain, killed the king and buried him. He searched, wondering, "The sound of a branch being released came from here; what is it?" but seeing nothing, he bathed and left.

After Parantapa had gone, the chaplain emerged from his hiding place. Knowing that the king had been cut into pieces and buried in a pit, he bathed. Fearing for his own life, he took on the appearance of a blind man and went to a leaf-roofed rest house.

Seeing the brahmin, Parantapa asked, "Brahmin, what harm has befallen you?" The brahmin, pretending not to know him, said, "O Great King, my eyes have failed. I live near an anthill in a forest full of venomous snakes. A cobra in that anthill must have emitted its venomous breath."

Parantapa thought, "The brahmin does not know me and calls me 'Great King.' I shall comfort him." He said, "Brahmin, do not worry. I will look after you." He comforted him and satisfied him with various fruits.

From then on, the slave Parantapa brought fruits. The Queen also gave birth. When the son grew up, one day at dawn, while resting comfortably, the Queen softly asked the slave Parantapa, "Did anyone see you kill the king?"

"No one saw me. However, I heard the sound of a branch being released. I do not know if a human or an animal released it. Someday, danger will come to me; it will come from the one who released that branch and fled." Wishing to tell the Queen this, he spoke the first verse:

## Discovering the True Father

Later, the prince reached the age of sixteen. The brahmin had the prince hold the end of his staff and went to the bathing ghat. There, he opened his eyes and looked around. The prince asked, "Brahmin, are you not blind?" The brahmin replied, "I am not blind. I preserved my life through this means."

He then asked, "Do you know your father?" When the prince replied, "This Parantapa is my father," the brahmin said, "This Parantapa is not your father. Your father was the King of Bārāṇasī. This man is your slave. He acted wrongly toward your mother, killed your father here, and buried him." He then dug up the bones and showed them. Great sorrow arose in the prince. He asked the brahmin, "What shall I do now?"

## Holding the Sword for Revenge

"Do to this Parantapa exactly what he did to your father at this very ghat," the brahmin said. After explaining everything, he trained the prince for two or three days in how to handle a sword.

One day, taking a sword and a bathing cloth, the prince said, "Father, let us go bathe." Parantapa replied, "Very well, dear son," and went with him.
399:
When that Parantapa went down to bathe, [the prince] seized his sword with his right hand and his topknot with his left, saying: "You killed my father at this very landing while holding his topknot as he cried out; I shall do the same to you."

Parantapa, fearing death, wept and spoke these two verses:

[Verse 159]
"This has come together, the thought of my foolish self;
For then the branch was shaken by a man or a beast."

'That sound' (so saddo) means the sound of the shaking branch. 'Has surely come' (āgamā nūna) means it has reached you. 'That sound' (so saddo) means the sound of the shaking branch. 'Informed you' (asaṃsi nūna) means it seems to have told you. 'The one who' (yo) means the being who 'shook' (akampayi) that branch then. 'By him' (tena) means by that person who shook it. 'Was surely told' (akkhātaṃ nūna) means the reason was surely told as, "Thus was your father killed."

'For' (hi yasmā) because 'when' (yadā) the 'branch' (sākhā) 'moved' (calitā), 'then' (tadā) I did not know whether it moved 'by a man' (manussena vā) 'or by a beast' (migena vā). 'Therefore' (tasmā), the 'thought' (cintitaṃ) occurred to 'my foolish self' (balassa mama) that 'fear' (bhayaṃ) 'will arise' (uppajjissati). 'This very [fear]' (idaṃ kho) 'has come together with you' (taṃsamāgamma-tayāsamāgataṃ).

Then the prince spoke the final verse:

84. Just as you knew, you deceived my father;
Having killed him and covering him with branches, fear will come to you.

Parantapa, Parantapa. 'Just so' (tatheva) you 'knew' (avedesi). You 'killed' (avajjhi) 'my father' (mama pitaraṃ). 'Having killed' (hantvā) him, you 'covered' (chādento) him 'with branches' (sākhāhi). 'Fear' (bhayaṃ) 'will come' (āgamissati) 'to you' (te).

Having said this, he ended his life right there, buried him, and covered him with branches. Then he washed his sword, bathed, and went to the leaf-hut. Having told the chaplain of the killing of Parantapa and rebuked his mother, the three of them returned to Bārāṇasī. The Bodhisatta gave the vice-regency to his younger brother, performed meritorious deeds such as almsgiving, and filled the heavenly realm.

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this legal discourse and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the father king was Devadatta, but the prince was I myself."
401:
## 1. Kaccāni Vagga
## 1. Kaccāni Jātaka
## On the duty of supporting parents

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha who disciplines the world including the devas, while dwelling at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kaccāni Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Odātavatthā suci allakesā", concerning a certain lay follower who supported his mother.

That lay follower was a well-behaved young man of a good family living in Sāvatthī. When his father passed away, he treated his mother like a deity, serving her by providing water for washing the face, tooth-sticks, bath water, water for washing the feet, and other services, as well as providing gruel, rice, and so on.

Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, you have other household duties. Take a maiden of equal birth from a good family. She will support me, and you can do your own work." He replied, "Mother, I do not desire my own welfare and happiness; I wish only to serve you. Who else but I will serve you in this way?" The mother said, "Dear son, it is proper to perform the duty of increasing the family lineage."

"Mother, I have no need for the household life. I will serve you, and when you have passed away, I will ordain," said the son. Then the mother, though she pleaded with him again and again, did not gain his consent. Disregarding his wish, she brought a maiden of equal birth. The young man, not refusing his mother, lived with her.

The young woman also thought, "My husband supports his mother with great effort. I too will support her. By doing so, I will be dear to my husband." Thus thinking, she served her mother-in-law respectfully.
402:
## Misconception

From that time on, the householder, thinking, "This woman serves my mother respectfully," gave his wife whatever fine delicacies and such he obtained. Later, the wife thought, "This man gives me whatever delicacies he gets. He must surely want to drive his mother out. I will create a reason for him to expel her." Thinking wrongly, she said to her husband one day, "Lord, when you are away, your mother abuses me." The householder remained silent.

The woman thought, "I will make the son look down on this old woman and turn him against her." Having planned this, from then on, when she served rice gruel, she made it either too hot, too cold, too salty, or without salt.

When the mother said, "Dear daughter, it is too hot," or "It is too salty," she would fill a bowl with cold water and pour it in. Again, when the mother said, "Dear daughter, it is too cold; there is no salt," she would shout loudly, "Just now you said it was too hot and too salty, and now you say it is too cold and has no salt. Who can satisfy you?"

She also made the bathwater very hot and poured it on the mother's back. When the mother said, "Dear daughter, my back is burning," she would fill it again with very cold water. When the mother said, "Dear daughter, it is too cold," she told the neighbors, "Just now she said it was too hot, and now she says it is too cold. Who can endure the insults of this old woman?"

When the mother said, "Dear daughter, there are many bedbugs on the couch," she took the couch out, shook her own couch over it, and brought it back, saying, "I have shaken the couch," and laid it out. The householder's mother, bitten by bedbugs, spent the whole night sitting up and said, "Dear daughter, the bedbugs bit me all night long."

The daughter-in-law replied, "I shook your couch only yesterday. Who can manage the affairs of an old woman?" Then, thinking, "Now I will make the son despise the old woman," she scattered saliva, mucus, and such in various places. When the householder asked, "Who made this whole house unclean?" she said, "Your mother did this. When told not to do it, she starts a quarrel."

## Loving the Mother, Sending Away the Wife

"I cannot live in the same house with such a wretched woman. Either do not let this old woman stay in the house, or do not let me stay," she said.
403:
Hearing his wife's words, the householder said, "Dear, you are young; you can live and make a living anywhere. But my mother is old and weak, and I am her only refuge. You leave and go to your own parents' house."

Hearing her husband's words, the woman was frightened and thought, "I cannot break the bond between this man and his mother. He truly loves his mother. If I go to my parents' house, I will live miserably as a divorcee. I will serve and please my mother-in-law as before." Having thought so, from then on, she served her mother-in-law just as she had done previously.

Then one day, the householder went to Jetavana Monastery to listen to the Dhamma, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat in a suitable place. When the Buddha asked, "Householder, are you diligent in meritorious deeds? Do you fulfill the duty of serving your mother?" he replied:

"Venerable Sir, I fulfill it as commanded. However, my mother brought a certain young woman for me against my will. That woman committed such and such improper acts." He reported everything to the Buddha and added, "Venerable Sir, that woman was unable to break the bond between me and my mother, and now she serves my mother respectfully again."

The Buddha, hearing the householder's words, said, "Householder, now you do not follow that woman's words. But in the past, you drove your mother out because of her words, and only by relying on me did you bring her back to the house and serve her again." At the householder's request, He related the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the son of a certain family, after his father passed away, treated his mother like a deity and served her in the manner already described. (The whole story should be expanded in the same way as previously told.)

## Driving Out the Mother Based on the Wife's Words

When the wife said, "Lord, I cannot live with such a wretched woman. Either do not let this old woman stay in the house, or do not let me stay," he took her words to heart, blamed his mother, and said, "Mother, you are always quarreling in this house. Leave this house and live wherever you wish."

## The Mother Goes to the Charnel Ground

That mother said, "Very well," and left weeping. She made a living with difficulty by working for a wealthy family.

When the mother-in-law left the house, the daughter-in-law became pregnant. The daughter-in-law went about telling her husband and neighbors, "While that wretched old woman was living in the house, I did not even conceive. Now I have become pregnant." Later, after giving birth to a son, she said to her husband, "Lord, while your mother was in the house, I did not get a son. Now I have one. For this reason, know the wretchedness of that old woman."
404:
1. O woman in white garments, pure, with wet hair,
Kaccāni, why have you set a pot [on the hearth]?
You wash sesame powder and rice;
2. O Brahmin, this well-cooked sesame rice is not for the purpose of eating.
Dhamma is dead; today, for its sake,
I shall perform [an offering] in the middle of the cemetery.

This second verse was spoken.

Brahmin, O Brahmin. Sādhupakko, well-cooked. Ayaṃ kho tilodano, this sesame rice. Bhojanatthāya, for the purpose of eating. Na hehiti, will not be. Dhammo, Dhamma. Mato, is dead. Ajja, today. Ahaṃ, I. Susānamajjhe, in the middle of the cemetery. Tassa, for that Dhamma. Pahuttaṃ, will perform the funeral offering.

3. Kaccāni, do your work after investigating,
Dhamma is dead—who told you this?
The Thousand-eyed One of incomparable power,

The mother-in-law thought, "If she [the daughter-in-law] obtained a son at the very time she drove me out of the house, then surely Dhamma must be dead in this world. If Dhamma were not dead, she would not have obtained a son after striking and driving out her mother-in-law, and she would not live a long and happy life. I will offer a funeral meal for Dhamma."

Having thought thus, one day that mother-in-law took sesame powder, rice, a cooking pot, firewood, and a ladle, and went to the cemetery. She made a tripod out of three human skulls, lit a fire, went down to the water to wash her head, put on [clean] clothes, returned to the place where the tripod was set, loosened her hair, and began to wash the rice.

## Sakka as a Brahmin Inquires

At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. Bodhisattas are never negligent. At that moment, Sakka looked upon the world and saw that woman who had reached such distress that she wished to offer a funeral meal for Dhamma, thinking "Dhamma is dead." Thinking, "Today I will show my power," he took the form of a Brahmin as if traveling on the main road. Seeing the woman, he stepped off the path, stood near her, and wishing to start a conversation, said, "Mother... there is no one who cooks food in a cemetery. What will you do with this sesame rice cooked here in the cemetery?"

He spoke this first verse:

For what reason will there be sesame rice?

Kaccāni, O lady of the Kaccāna lineage. Tvaṃ, you. Odātavatthā, wearing white clothes. Suci, being pure. Allakesā, with wet hair. Kumbhiṃ, the cooking pot. Adhissayitvā, having placed it on a tripod of human skulls. Tilā piṭṭhā, taking sesame powder. Taṇḍulāni, the rice. Kiṃ dhovasi, why do you wash? Kissahétu, for what reason. Tilodano, sesame rice. Hehiti, will there be?

## Performing Funeral Rites for the Death of Dhamma

Then, that woman, wishing Sakka to hear, said:

## I am Not Dead

Thereafter, Sakka spoke this third verse:

The Excellent Dhamma never dies.

Kaccāni, O lady of the Kaccāna lineage. Tvaṃ, you. Anuvicca, having investigated. Kiccaṃ, your work. Karohi, perform. Dhammo, the Dhamma of honoring elders and the Dhamma of good conduct. Mato, is dead. Evaṃ, thus. Tava, to you. Ko nu, who indeed. Saṃsi, told? Atulanubhāvo, of incomparable power. Dhammavaro, the Excellent King of Dhamma. Sahassanetto, the Thousand-eyed Sakka. Kadāci, at any time. Na miyyati, does not die.
405:
4. O Brahmin, my conviction in this is firm;
Dhamma is dead, I have no doubt.
Those who are now wicked
Are the ones who are happy.
5. For my daughter-in-law was barren;
She, having struck and driven me out, gave birth to a son.
She is now the mistress of the whole family,
While I am cast out and live alone.

She spoke these two verses.

Brahme, O great Brahmin. Ettha, regarding this death of Dhamma. Mama, my. Pamāṇaṃ, conviction. Daḷhaṃ, is firm. Dhammo, Dhamma. Mato, is dead. Ettha, in this matter. Mama, to me. Kaṅkhā, doubt. Natthi, there is none. Idāni, now. Ye yeva, those very ones who. Pāpā, are of wicked conduct. Bhavanti, they are. Idāni, now. Te teva, those very ones. Sukhitā, are happy. Bhavanti, they are.

Hi saccaṃ, this is the truth. Mayhaṃ, my. Suṇisā, daughter-in-law. Vañjhā, barren. Ahosi, was. Sā, she. Maṃ, me. Vadhitvāna, having struck and driven out. Puttaṃ, a son. Vijāyi, gave birth to. Idāni, now. Sā, she. Sabbassa, of the entire. Kulassa, family. Issarā, is the mistress. Ahaṃ pana, but as for me. Apaviddhā, being cast out. Ekikā, alone. Amhi, I am.

7. If it pleases you thus, O King of Devas,
You who have come here for my sake.
I, my son, my daughter-in-law, and my grandson,

## The Righteous Suffer

Having heard those words, that woman said:

## I will Kill Your Daughter-in-law and Son

Thereafter, Sakka spoke this sixth verse:

6. I live, I am not dead;
I have come here for your sake.
She who struck you and gave birth to a son—
I will turn her and her son into ashes.

Kaccāni, O lady of the Kaccāna lineage. Ahaṃ, I. Jīvāmi, live. Ahaṃ, I. Mato, dead. Na asmi, am not. Taveva, only for your. Atthāya, sake. Idha, to this place. Āgato, have come. Asmi, I am. Yā, that daughter-in-law who. Taṃ, you. Vadhitvāna, having struck and driven out. Puttaṃ, a son. Vijāyi, gave birth to. Sā, that daughter-in-law. Puttena, with her son. Sahāva, together. Bhasmaṃ, like ashes, scattered and destroyed. Karomi, I shall make.

## Not Wanting the Grandson to Die

Upon hearing those words, the woman thought, "O Thousand-eyed Sakka... what are you saying? I shall act so that my grandson does not die," and spoke this seventh verse:

May we live together happily in the house.

Devarāja, O King of Devas. Te, to you. Evañca, in this way. Ruccati, if it is pleasing. Mameva, only for my. Atthāya, sake. Idha, to this place. Āgato, have come. Asi, you have. Ahañca, I also. Putto ca, and my son. Suṇisā ca, and my daughter-in-law. Nattā ca, and my grandson. Ete mayaṃ, we. Sammodamānā, being joyful. Gharaṃ, in the house. Āvasema, wish to dwell.
406:
8. If this is what you desire, O Kātiyānī,
Even though you have been beaten, you do not abandon the Dhamma.
You, your son, your daughter-in-law, and your grandchild—
9. That Kātiyānī, together with her daughter-in-law,
Lived in the house in harmony.
The son and the grandchild attended to them,
Being favored by the Lord of Devas.

## I Will Reconcile You with Your Daughter-in-law
Then Sakka, the King of Devas, spoke this eighth verse to the woman:

"Live in the house in harmony (sammodamānā gharamāvasetha)."

O Kātiyānī, lady of the Kaccāna lineage. If you so desire. Even though you have been beaten and driven out. You do not abandon the Dhamma, the practice of loving-kindness towards the children. You, your son, your daughter-in-law, and your grandchild. All of you, being joyful and happy, live together in the house.

## The Son and Daughter-in-law Pay Respect
Having said this, Sakka, the King of Devas, adorned in his celestial attire, stood in the air by his psychic power and said, "O lady of the Kaccāna lineage, do not fear. By my power, your son and daughter-in-law will come and apologize to you on the way and take you back. Be diligent." Having said this, he returned to his own abode.

The son and daughter-in-law, remembering their mother's kindness through Sakka's power, asked the people in the village, "Where is our mother?" Hearing that she had gone towards the cemetery, they called out "Mother, Mother!" and followed the path to the cemetery. Seeing their mother, they prostrated at her feet and begged for forgiveness, saying, "Mother, please forgive our faults."

The mother then took the grandchild in her arms. Thus, they returned home in great joy and lived together in harmony from then on.

The All-Enlightened One, having brought forth this past story after attaining Buddhahood, spoke as follows:

Monks, that Kātiyānī, the woman of the Kaccāna lineage, lived in the house in harmony with her daughter-in-law. Favored by Sakka, the King of Devas, both the son and the grandchild attended to them.

The All-Enlightened One, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the lay disciple was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. As for the identification of the Jātaka: The lay disciple who now supports his mother was the one who supported his mother then. The wife of the lay disciple was the wife of the one who supported his mother then. I myself was Sakka, the King of Devas. Thus He identified the Jātaka.
407:
## Prosperity for Children Who Know Gratitude
The Kaccāni Jātaka is concluded.

## 2. Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka
## One Should Reflect on Cause and Effect in All Things
The All-Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Idaṃ pure ninnamāhū," concerning a terrifying and indistinguishable sound heard by King Kosala at midnight.

The story is similar to the Lohakumbhi Jātaka mentioned below.

In this Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka, when King Kosala asked, "Venerable Sir, what will happen to me because of hearing these sounds?", the Buddha replied, "Great King, do not fear. No harm will come to you because of hearing these sounds.

Great King, you are not the only one to have heard such a terrifying and indistinguishable sound. In the past, kings also heard such sounds and, following the words of Brahmins, wished to perform the 'Sacrifice of the Fourfold All' (Sabbacatukka-yañña). Later, hearing the words of the wise, they released the creatures captured for sacrifice and had the drum of non-violence (māghāta-bheri) beaten throughout the city." Having said this, at the King's request, He brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasီ, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family with eighty crores of wealth. Upon reaching maturity, he completed his education in Takkasilā. After his parents passed away, he looked at his treasures, gave away all his wealth in charity, renounced sense-pleasures, and entered the Himalayas. There, he became an ascetic, attained the Jhanas and Higher Knowledges (Abhiññā). Later, while traveling through human habitations to obtain salt and acidic food, he reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in the royal park.

## Hearing Eight Great Sounds
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, while lying on his royal bed, heard eight sounds at midnight.
408:
First, a heron in the park near the King's palace made a sound. Second, while that sound was still continuing, a female crow living on the gate-pillar of the elephant stable made a sound. Third, a woodworm (ghuṇa) living in the roof-peak of the King's house made a sound.

Fourth, a female cuckoo raised in the King's house made a sound. Fifth, a deer raised in the King's house made a sound. Sixth, a monkey raised in the King's house made a sound. Seventh, a kinnara raised in the King's house made a sound. Eighth, while those sounds had not yet ceased, a Paccekabuddha, flying over the King's house towards the park, made a sound while uttering an inspired exclamation (Udāna).

## A Sacrifice Must Be Offered
The King of Bārāṇasī, hearing these eight sounds, was greatly terrified and asked the Brahmins the next day. The Brahmins said, "Great King, danger will come to you. We shall perform the 'Sacrifice of the Fourfold All' (Sabbacatukka-yañña)." The King gave permission, saying, "Do as you please." Being very joyful, they left the palace and began preparing for the sacrifice.

## The Young Disciple Forbids It
At that time, the young disciple of the head Brahmin who was organizing the sacrifice was wise and clever. That youth said to his teacher, "Teacher, do not perform such a cruel, harsh, and unpleasant act that causes the destruction of many living beings."

"My dear, what do you know? Even if nothing else happens, we will at least get to eat plenty of fish and meat."

"Teacher, do not perform an act for the sake of your belly that will lead to rebirth in hell."

Hearing this, the other Brahmins were angry with him, saying, "This fellow is interfering with our gains."

Out of fear of them, the youth said, "In that case, you go ahead with your scheme to eat fish and meat." He then left and, searching for a righteous recluse or Brahmin outside the city who could prevent the King's action, went to the royal park. Seeing the Bodhisatta, he paid homage and said, "Venerable Sir, do you have no compassion for living beings? The King is having many creatures killed to offer a sacrifice. Is it not right for you to free the multitude from their bonds?"

"Young man, the King does not know me, nor do I know the King."

"But Venerable Sir, do you know the outcome of the sounds heard by the King?"

"Yes, I know."

"If you know, why do you not tell the King?"

"Young man, how can I go about with a horn tied to my forehead saying 'I know'? If he comes here and asks me, I will tell him."

The youth went quickly to the palace. When asked, "What is it, dear?", he said, "Great King, an ascetic sitting on the auspicious stone in your park knows the outcome of the sounds you heard. He says, 'If he asks me, I will tell him.' It is proper for you to go and ask him."

The King went there quickly, paid homage to the ascetic, and after exchanging pleasantries, sat down and asked, "Is it true, Venerable Sir, that you know the outcome of the sounds I heard?"

"Yes, Great King."

"Then please tell it to me."

"Great King, no harm will come to you because of hearing those sounds."
409:
10. "This was formerly called a deep place, with many fish and much water.
It was the dwelling of the heron king, my ancestral home.
Today we subsist on frogs; we do not abandon our home."

He spoke this first verse. 

"Idaṃ": this auspicious pond. "Pure": in the past. "Ninnaṃ": was a depression. "Ahu": it was so. "Bahumacchā": it had many fish. "Mahodakaṃ": it had much water, being filled by a conduit. "Bakarājassa": of the heron king. "Āvāso": it was the dwelling. "Mama": my. "Pettikaṃ": ancestral. "Bhavanaṃ": home. "Te mayaṃ": we. "Ajja": now. "Bhekena": with just frogs. "Yāpema": we subsist. "Evaṃ": though oppressed by hunger in this way. "Okaṃ": our home. "Na vijahāmase": we cannot abandon.

11. "Who will pierce the second eye of Bandhara?
Who will bring safety to my children, my nest, and me?"

He spoke this second verse.

"Asīlissa": of the immoral. "Bandharassa": of Bandhara. "Dutiyaṃ": the second. "Akkhi": eye. "Ko": who. "Bheccati": will pierce? "Ko": who. "Me": my. "Putte ca": children. "Kulāvakañca": and nest. "Mañca": and me. "Sotthiṃ": safety. "Karissati": will provide?

The teacher said, "My boy, what do you know? Even if the sacrifice is of no benefit, we shall have much fish and meat to eat." The disciple replied, "Teacher, do not perform an act that leads to hell for the sake of the belly." Hearing this, the Brahmins were angry with the youth, saying, "This young man is an obstacle to our gain."

## Meeting the Bodhisatta

Out of fear of the Brahmins, the youth said, "In that case, you alone shall be the cause of eating fish and meat," and he left. Seeking righteous recluses and Brahmins outside the city who could restrain the King, he went to the King's garden. Seeing the Bodhisatta, he paid homage and said, "Venerable Sir, why do you have no compassion for living beings? The King is having many creatures killed for a sacrifice."

The Bodhisatta said, "Young man, the King does not know us, and we do not know the King." The youth asked, "Venerable Sir, do you know the meaning of the sounds that were heard?" "I know," replied the Bodhisatta. "If you know, why do you not tell the King?" the youth asked. "Young man, how can I go about with a horn on my forehead saying 'I know'? If the King comes to this garden and asks me, I shall answer him," he said.

## Explaining and Preaching

The youth quickly went to the King's palace. When asked, "My boy, what is it?" he replied, "Great King, a hermit who knows the meaning of the sounds you heard is staying on the auspicious stone slab in your garden. He said, 'If the King asks me, I shall answer.' It is proper for you to go and ask that hermit."

The King went quickly to the garden, paid homage to the hermit, and after exchanging pleasantries, sat down and asked, "Venerable Sir, is it true that you know the meaning of the sounds I heard?" "It is true, Great King," he replied. "In that case, Venerable Sir, please tell me," the King said.

## The Sign of the Heron's Cry

Then the Bodhisatta, wishing to explain the sounds the King had heard, said, "Great King, there is no danger to you because of hearing those sounds. In your old garden, there is a single heron. Not finding food and being oppressed by hunger, it made the first sound." Discerning the heron's action with his own wisdom, he said:

"Great King, that heron made such a sound because it was oppressed by hunger. If you wish to free it from hunger, have that garden cleaned and fill the pond with water." The King ordered an official to do as the Bodhisatta said.

## The Sign of the Crow's Cry

"Great King, a female crow lives on the gateway of the elephant stable. Out of anxiety for her children, she made the second sound. There is no danger to you from that sound either," the Bodhisatta said, intending to explain further.
410:
13. "Surely, having gone from here, freed from the King's palace,
I shall enjoy myself, dwelling among the tree branches."

He spoke this fourth verse.

"Sā ahaṃ": that I. "Rañño": of you, the King. "Ito nivesanā": from this palace. "Muttā": being freed. "Gantvā": having gone. "Dumassākhaniketinī": having my dwelling in the nest among the tree branches. "Attānaṃ": myself. "Ramayissāmi nūna": when shall I find delight?

Having said this, he asked, "Great King, what is the name of the elephant trainer in your elephant stable?" "Venerable Sir, his name is Bandhara," the King replied. "Great King, does that Bandhara have only one eye?" the Bodhisatta asked. "Venerable Sir, it is just as you say," the King replied.

"Great King, a female crow has built a nest and laid eggs on the gateway of your elephant stable. The eggs have matured and the young have hatched. Whenever the elephant trainer rides the elephant out of or into the stable, he strikes the crow's young and her nest with his hook.

That crow, distressed by that suffering and wishing for the destruction of the eye of Bandhara the trainer, spoke thus. If you, Great King, have a heart of loving-kindness for the crow, summon that Bandhara and forbid him from destroying the nest." The King summoned Bandhara, rebuked and punished him, and gave the elephant to another person.

## The Sign of the Woodworm's Cry

The Bodhisatta said, "Great King, a woodworm named Ghuṇa lives in the pinnacle of your palace. That worm ate the sapwood in various places, and when the sapwood was exhausted, it was unable to eat the heartwood. Not finding food and being unable to come out, it lamented and made the third sound. There is no danger to you from that sound either." Discerning the worm's action with his own wisdom, he said:

12. "All the sapwood is consumed, as far as its extent went.
With food exhausted, O Great King, the woodworm finds no joy in the heartwood."

He spoke this third verse.

"Mahārāja": Great King. "Tassā": of that sapwood. "Yāva": as much as. "Gati": the extent. "Ahu": was apparent. "Sabbā": all. "Pheggu": the sapwood. "Parikkhayā": has been consumed by eating. "Khīṇabhakkho": having exhausted its food. "Ghuṇo": the woodworm. "Sāre": in the heartwood. "Na ramati": finds no joy.

The Bodhisatta said, "Great King, that worm is lamenting because it cannot see a way to come out from that place. Have that worm removed." The King sent a man to remove the worm by a clever means.

## The Sign of the Cuckoo's Cry

The Bodhisatta asked, "Great King, is there a female cuckoo being raised in your house?" "There is, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Great King, that cuckoo, remembering the forest where she used to live, is weary and thinks, 'When shall I be freed from this cage and go to the delightful forest?' Thus she made the fourth sound. There is no danger to you from that sound either."

Having said this, the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, the cuckoo is weary; release that cuckoo." The King did as the Bodhisatta said.

## The Sign of the Deer's Cry

The Bodhisatta asked, "Great King, is there a deer being raised in your palace?" "There is, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Great King, that deer, remembering his mate, the female deer, is weary through the power of passion and made the fifth sound. There is no danger to you from that sound either."
411:
14. "Now, having gone from here, freed from the king's palace, I shall drink the first waters, walking at the head of the herd."

This is the fifth verse he spoke. 
"I (so ahaṃ), having been freed (mutto) from this palace (ito nivesanā) of the king (rañño), and having gone (gantvā), walking (vajaṃ) at the head (purato) of the herd of deer (yūthassa), when indeed shall I drink (pissāmi nūna) the first waters (aggodakāni)?"

15. "Intoxicated by desires, attached and infatuated with them, I was brought by the hunter Bharata, a foreigner. May you be blessed."

This is the sixth verse he spoke.
"The hunter (luddo) named Bharata (bharato), a foreigner (bāhiko), brought (ānayi) me (taṃ maṃ), who was greatly intoxicated (sammattaṃ) by desires (kāmehi), attached (rattaṃ) to desires (kāmesu), and infatuated (mucchitaṃ) with desires (kāmesu). May blessings (bhaddaṃ) be (atthu) unto you (te)."

16. "In the blinding darkness, upon the high mountain, she spoke to me with smooth and gentle words: 'Do not let your foot slip on the rock.'"

This is the seventh verse he spoke.
"She (sā), that Kinnarī, in the darkness (andhakāratimisāyaṃ) that causes blindness, upon the high (tuṅge) mountain peak (uparipabbate), spoke with smooth (saṇhena) and gentle (mudunā) words (vacanena): 'Lord (sāmi), do not let your foot (pādaṃ) slip (mā khali) on the rock (asmani).' Having said this, and taking me by the hand (hatthena gahetvā), she led me down (otāresi)."

The Great Being then had that deer released.

## The Omen of the Monkey's Sound
The Great Being asked, "Great King, is there a monkey raised in your palace?" "There is, Bhante," the king replied. "Great King, that monkey too, while wandering in the Himalayan region with the troop leaders, became greedy for desires and was brought here by a hunter named Bharata. Now, feeling weary and wishing to go back to that very place, he made the sixth sound. There is no danger to you from that either."

The Great Being then had that monkey released.

## The Omen of the Kinnara's Sound
The Great Being asked, "Great King, is there a Kinnara raised in your palace?" When the king replied, "There is," the Great Being said, "Great King, that Kinnara, remembering the kindness shown by his wife, the Kinnarī, and being pained by defilements, made that sound.

One day, that Kinnara climbed a high mountain peak with that Kinnarī. There, while they were picking, wearing, and enjoying various flowers endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, they did not notice the sun setting. When the sun had set, darkness fell as they were descending. Then the Kinnarī said, 'Lord, it is dark; descend with heedfulness without slipping,' and taking his hand, she led him down. Remembering those words of the Kinnarī, he made that sound. There is no danger to you from that either." Thus, having discerned the cause with the power of his own knowledge, he made it clear.
412:
In this context, "in the blinding darkness" (andhakāratimisāyaṃ) means in the darkness that causes blindness. "High" (tuṅge) means steep. "With smooth and gentle" (saṇhena mudunā) means with polished and soft speech. In the phrase "on the rock" (y-asmani), the letter 'y' is used as a euphonic consonant (vyañjanasandhi). This is what is meant: That Kinnarī, with smooth and soft words, said, "Lord, be heedful, do not let your foot slip on the rock; descend in such a way that you do not stumble and your foot does not slip on the stone," and taking him by the hand, she led him down.

Thus, the Great Being explained the reason for the sound made by the Kinnara and had him released.

## The Omen of the Paccekabuddha's Inspired Utterance
"Great King, the eighth sound was an inspired utterance (udāna). It is said that a certain Paccekabuddha in the Nandamūla cave, knowing the exhaustion of his life-force (āyusaṅkhāra), thought: 'I will go to the world of men and attain Parinibbāna in the park of the King of Bārāṇasī. People will perform the funeral rites for my body, celebrate with festivities, and by honoring the relics, they will fulfill the path to heaven.' Coming through the air by psychic power, when he reached the top of your palace, he laid down the burden of the aggregates (khandhabhāraṃ) and uttered an Udāna signifying his entry into the city of Nibbāna."

Thus, he spoke the eighth verse uttered by the Paccekabuddha:

17. "Without doubt, seeing the end of birth, I shall not enter a womb again. This is my final and last conception; my wandering in rebirth is exhausted."

"I (ahaṃ), seeing the end of birth (jātikhayantadassī), which is Nibbāna, shall without doubt (asaṃsayaṃ) not enter (na āvajissaṃ) a womb (gabbhaseyyaṃ) again (puna). This birth (ayaṃ jāti) is the final (antimā) birth. This conception (ayaṃ) is the last conception (pacchimā gabbhaseyyā). For me (me), the wandering in rebirth (saṃsāro), which is the succession of aggregates, for the sake of renewed existence (punabbhavāya), is exhausted (khīṇo)."

The Great Being said, "Great King, that Paccekabuddha, having uttered this Udāna, came to this park and attained Parinibbāna at the foot of a well-blossomed Sal tree. Come, Great King, let us perform the funeral rites for the Paccekabuddha." He took the king to the place where the Paccekabuddha had attained Parinibbāna and showed him the body.

The king, seeing the body of the Paccekabuddha, honored it along with his army with perfumes, garlands, and so forth. Relying on the words of the Great Being, he abandoned animal sacrifices, granted the gift of life to all beings, and had the drum of non-slaughter (māghāta) beaten throughout the city. After celebrating with festivities for seven days, he cremated the body of the Paccekabuddha on a pyre made of all kinds of incense with great honor, and having enshrined the relics at a crossroads, he had a stupa (cetiya) built.
413:
The Bodhisatta also preached the Dhamma to the King, saying, "Great King, be diligent." Having thus advised him, he entered the Himavanta, practiced the Brahmavihāras, and with undiminished jhāna, was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Great King, there is no danger to you from hearing that sound. Abandon the sacrifice and grant life to many beings." Having thus caused the gift of life to be given, he had the drum of Dhamma beaten in the city, preached the Dhamma, and identified the birth story: "At that time, Ānanda was the King, Sāriputta was the youth, and I myself was the ascetic."

## Worshipping the Lord of Sacrifice, such offerings are fruitless

The Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka ends.

## 3. Sulasa Jātaka

## Not only men but women too are wise

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Sulasa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Idaṃ suvaṇṇakāyūraṃ," concerning a certain servant girl of Anāthapiṇḍika.

It is said that one festival day, that servant girl, wishing to go to the park with a group of other servant girls, asked her mistress, the lady named Puṇṇalakkhaṇadevī, for jewelry to wear. The lady Puṇṇalakkhaṇadevī gave her jewelry worth a hundred thousand. Wearing that jewelry worth a hundred thousand, the servant girl entered the park with the group of servant girls.

## The Thief's Plot

At that time, a certain thief, overcome by greed for her jewelry, thought, "I will kill this girl and take the jewelry." He spoke with her and went to the park, where he gave her fish, meat, liquor, and other things. She thought, "He gives these to me out of lust," and took the fish, meat, and liquor. After playing in the park, she got up and went to the thief in the evening while the other servant girls were sleeping, in order to test him.

The thief said, "Lady, this place is not secluded; let us go a little further ahead."
414:
## The Servant Girl's Wisdom

Hearing those words, the girl thought, "This place is suitable for a secret deed. This man surely wants to kill me and take my jewelry. Be that as it may, I shall teach him a lesson." She then said, "Master, my body is parched from the liquor; let me drink some water." She led him to a well and said, "Draw some drinking water for me from this well," and gave him the rope and the pot.

The thief lowered the rope into the well. Then, as he leaned over to draw the water, the strong servant girl pushed him by the buttocks with both hands, casting him into the well. Saying, "You shall not die by this alone," she threw a large brick onto the thief's head. The thief met his end right there in the well.

The girl then entered the city, returned the jewelry to her mistress, and said, "Today, I almost died because of this jewelry," and related the whole matter.

Anāthapiṇḍika the householder reported this to the Buddha. The Teacher said, "Householder, not only now is she possessed of ready wit; she was possessed of ready wit in the past too. Not only now did she kill that thief; she killed him in the past as well." Being requested by Anāthapiṇḍika, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasီ, there was a courtesan named Sulasa who had five hundred courtesans as attendants. She charged a thousand pieces of money for one night.

## Sattuka the Thief

In that same city of Bārāṇasī, there was a thief named Sattuka who possessed the strength of a noble elephant. During the night, he would enter the houses of the wealthy and plunder as he pleased. The citizens gathered and complained to the King. The King ordered the city guard to station troops here and there, catch the thief, and said, "Cut off his head."
415:
18. "This golden bracelet, many pearls and beryls;
Take them all, dear lord, and proclaim me your slave."

She spoke this first verse.

My lord, may good fortune be with you. Take this golden neck ornament, and these many pearls and beryls—take all these ornaments. And proclaim me as your slave woman in the midst of the multitude, and take me.

## Sulasa's Marriage

The King had the city guarded and said, "Station groups of men in various places, capture the thief, and behead him." The city guard captured the thief, bound his hands behind his back, and led him to the cemetery, whipping him with rods at every crossroads.

The whole city was in an uproar, saying, "The thief has been caught." At that time, Sulasa stood at a lattice window and, looking down at the street, saw the thief. Her heart was filled with passion, and she thought, "If I can free this man called a thief, I will stop this foul practice of courtesans and live in harmony with this thief alone."

By the method mentioned in the Kaṇavera Jātaka below, she sent a thousand pieces of money to the city guard, had the thief released, and lived with him in great joy and harmony.

After three or four days had passed, the thief could not bear to stay there. Yet he could not flee empty-handed. Sulasa's ornaments were worth a hundred thousand.

## The Thief's Deception

The thief, named Sattuka, said to Sulasa, "My lady, when I was being led by the king's men to be executed, I made a vow to the tree-deity on such-and-such a mountain. That deity is now threatening me because he has not received the offering. I must make an offering to that tree-deity."

Sulasa said, "My lord, very well. Prepare the offerings and send them."

"My lady, it is not proper to just send them. Let us both, adorned with all our ornaments and accompanied by a large retinue, go and present the offerings," said the thief named Sattuka. Sulasa replied, "My lord, very well. Do as you say."

## Sulasa is Trapped

Then the thief Sattuka had Sulasa do as he said. When they reached the foot of the mountain, he said, "My lady, if the deity sees many people, he will not accept the offering. Let only the two of us ascend and present the offering."

When Sulasa agreed, he had her carry the vessel of offerings while he himself, armed with five kinds of weapons, ascended to the mountain top. Reaching the foot of a tree near a hundred-fathom precipice, he had her set down the vessel of offerings and said, "My lady, I did not come to make an offering to a deity. I came to kill you, take your ornaments, and leave. Take off your ornaments and wrap them in your upper robe."

## Pleading

When she asked, "My lord, why would you kill me?", he replied, "I kill you for the sake of wealth."

"My lord, remember the kindness I have done. When you were being led away in bonds, I exchanged you for a merchant's son, gave much wealth, and saved your life. Even though I receive a thousand pieces of money every day, I do not look at another man. I have been so kind to you. Do not kill me. I will give you much wealth, and I will be your slave woman," she pleaded.

## Take Off All Clothes

After that, Sattuka spoke this second verse:

19. "Take them off, O fair one, do not lament so much;
I do not know of any wealth brought away without killing [the owner]."

O fair one, endowed with good features, take off the ornaments you are wearing. Do not weep so bitterly. I have never known myself to take wealth without first killing the owner.
416:
22. "Wisdom is not found in all places in men alone;
A woman too is wise, being discerning here and there."

23. "Wisdom is not found in all places in men alone;
A woman too is wise, thinking quickly of her welfare."

24. "Indeed, she reflected on the means of death quickly and soon while standing near;
As one kills a deer with a fully drawn bow, Sulasa killed Sattuka."

25. "He who does not quickly understand the matter that has arisen here,
That dull-witted one is slain, like the thief in the mountain cave."

26. "But he who quickly understands the matter that has arisen,
Is freed from the enemy's oppression, as Sulasa was from Sattuka."

These verses were spoken.

In all matters, it is not only the man who is wise. A woman too is wise and is particularly discerning in various matters.

## Let Me Worship You with Love

Sulasa, having found a way to kill him in an instant, thought, "This thief will not spare my life. I will first make him fall down the precipice and bring him to his end." She then spoke these two verses:

20. "Since I remember myself, since I reached the age of reason,
I have known no other husband dearer than you."

21. "Come, I will embrace you and circumambulate you;
For now, there will never be a union between you and me again."

My lord, from the time I can remember myself, from the time I became wise and sensible, I have known no other husband dearer than you.

My lord, come. I shall embrace and hug you. I shall also perform the right-hand circumambulation. Now, a union between me and you will truly never happen again.

## Pushing the Thief Down

Sattuka, not knowing Sulasa's intention, said, "My lady, very well. Come, embrace me." Sulasa circumambulated Sattuka three times, embraced him, and said, "My lord, now I shall pay homage to you on all four sides." She placed her head on the top of his feet, paid homage to his arms, and then, pretending to go behind him to pay homage, the courtesan, who possessed the strength of an elephant, seized the thief by his two heels from behind, turned him upside down, and threw him into the hundred-fathom abyss. The thief was crushed to pieces in the abyss and died.

## Praise from the Forest Deity

Seeing that action, the deity residing on the mountain top said:

## A Wise Woman

In all matters, it is not only the man who is wise. A woman too is wise; she can think quickly of her welfare.

## Using Quick Wit

Indeed, while standing near death, she could think of the means of the thief's death both quickly and soon. Just as one kills a deer with a fully drawn bow, so did Sulasa kill Sattuka.

## The Foolish will Suffer

In this world, he who does not quickly understand the business that has arisen, that dull-witted person is killed like the thief in the mountain cave.
417:
"In this world, whoever quickly understands a matter that has arisen, that person is freed from the danger of the enemy, just as Sulasa was freed from Sattuka."

Thus, Sulasa, having killed the thief, descended from the mountain and went to her attendants. When asked, "Where is the master?", she replied, "Do not ask about him," and having mounted the carriage, she entered the city.

The Teacher, the Omniscient One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, those two were these very two, and I myself was the mountain deity."

## When the outcome is imminent, if wisdom is small, one will surely face death.

The Sulasa Jātaka ends.

## 4. Sumangala Jātaka

## A ruler should restrain anger

The Teacher, the Omniscient One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Sumangala Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Bhusami kuddho", concerning the Rājovāda Sutta.

At that time, the Teacher, being requested by the King of Kosala, brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen. When he came of age, after his father passed away, he became king. He practiced great generosity. For that King Brahmadatta, there was a gardener named Sumangala.

## Worshipping the Paccekabuddha

At that time, a certain Paccekabuddha, having emerged from the Nandamūla cave, was wandering on a journey and reached Bārāṇasī. He stayed in the royal garden and entered the city for alms.
418:
The King, seeing the Paccekabuddha, was filled with faith. He invited him to the palace, seated him in the royal residence, and served him with various excellent foods of many flavors. After listening to the words of appreciation (anumodanā) and being pleased, he took a promise from him to stay in his garden and sent him there. The King himself, after having his morning meal, went to the garden, arranged the night and day quarters, and appointed the gardener named Sumangala to serve him. Then he entered the city.

## The Gardener shoots with a bow

From then on, the Paccekabuddha regularly took his meals at the palace and stayed in that garden for a long time. Sumangala also served him respectfully.

One day, the Paccekabuddha called Sumangala and said, "I will go and stay near a certain village for two or three days and then return. Inform the King." Having said this, he departed. Sumangala informed the King.

The Paccekabuddha stayed in that village for two or three days and returned to the garden in the evening when the sun had set. Sumangala, not knowing of his arrival, had gone to his own home. The Paccekabuddha, having put away his bowl and robes, walked for a while on the walkway and then sat on a stone slab.
419:
27. Reflecting that 'I am greatly angered,'
A ruler should not yet inflict punishment.
In an improper way, unbefitting himself,
He might cause great suffering to another.

28. And when he knows his own clarity of mind,
He should investigate the other's misdeed and the benefit.
Having personally reflected, 'This is the matter,'
He should then inflict a suitable punishment.

29. He who is not blinded [by passion] and distinguishes right from wrong,
The ruler who is a bearer of punishment here,
Protected by his reputation for virtue, does not fall from glory.

30. Those Khattiyas who act without reflection,
Being blinded and inflicting punishment hastily,
Being associated with ill-repute, they lose their lives;
And even when released from this life, they go to a bad destination.

31. And those who delight in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones,
They are supreme in word, mind, and deed.
Established in peace, restraint, and concentration,
Such ones go to both worlds.

32. I am the King, the lord of men and women;
Even if I am angry, I restrain myself.
Restraining the people in such a way,
I inflict punishment with compassion and wise method.

He spoke these verses.

Dear friend, a king is called a lord. I, indeed, am greatly angry. Knowing this, one should not first inflict punishment. Do not inflict a punishment that is unbefitting to oneself in an improper way. Thus, one might cause great sufferings to another.

And when one knows the clarity of one's own mind, one should investigate the other's misdeed and the benefit. Then, seeing for oneself, 'This is the matter, this is the fault,' one should then inflict a punishment suitable to the fault upon the person who committed it.

In this world, the king who is not overwhelmed by defilements such as favoritism and investigates what is right and wrong, that king burns neither another nor himself. The king who bears punishment suitable to the fault, being protected by his fame and virtues, does not fall from glory.

Those Khattiyas who act without reflection, being overwhelmed by defilements such as favoritism and inflict punishment hastily, those Khattiyas, being associated with ill-repute, must give up their lives. Even when they are released from this present life, they go to a bad destination.

Those Khattiyas who delight in the Dhamma, consisting of the ten-fold royal virtues, known by the ancient kings of good conduct, those Khattiyas are supreme through the door of speech, the door of mind, and the door of the body. Established in peace, virtue, and concentration, such kings of that nature go to both worlds, the human realm and the deva realm.

I am the King, the lord of men and women. If I should happen to be angry even slightly, I will remain restraining myself. Out of compassion for the multitude of people of such nature, I inflict punishment with wise method.

On that day, guests arrived at the park keeper's house. The park keeper, thinking 'I will kill a deer that has been granted sanctuary in the park for the sake of the guests' curry,' took his bow and went to the park. While looking for a deer, he saw the Paccekabuddha and, thinking 'It must be a large deer,' he prepared his arrow and shot.

The Paccekabuddha uncovered his head and called out, 'Sumangala!' Sumangala, becoming terrified, paid homage and said, 'Venerable Sir, I did not know of your arrival and shot you thinking you were a deer. May you, Venerable Sir, forgive me.' When the Paccekabuddha said, 'Sumangala, though you have shot me, what can be done now? Come, pull out the arrow,' Sumangala paid homage and pulled out the arrow. Great pain arose in the Paccekabuddha. Right there, the Paccekabuddha attained Parinibbāna.

## The Park Keeper Flees

The park keeper, thinking 'If the King knows, I will be destroyed,' took his wife and children and fled from that place. At that very moment, by the power of the devas, the news 'The Paccekabuddha has attained Parinibbāna' spread, and the whole city was in an uproar. The next day, people went to the park, saw the Paccekabuddha, and reported to the King, 'The park keeper killed the Paccekabuddha and fled.'
420:
## After Three Years

The King went to the park with a large retinue, performed honors for the body for seven days, and cremated it with great ceremony. Having taken the relics and built a stupa for worship, he ruled righteously.

Sumangala, having let one year pass, came thinking, 'I will find out the King’s mind,' and sent a certain minister. The minister spoke of Sumangala’s virtues in the presence of the King. The King remained as if he had not heard. The minister said nothing further and told Sumangala of the King’s displeasure. Sumangala came and had inquiries made in the second year as well. The King remained silent just as before.

When he came in the third year, he brought his wife and children. The minister, knowing the King’s heart was soft, left Sumangala at the palace gate and informed the King of Sumangala’s arrival. The King had Sumangala summoned, exchanged greetings, and asked, 'Sumangala, why did you kill the Noble Paccekabuddha, who was the field where my merit is sown?'
421:
“O Lord of men, may [they] never leave you. Being free from anger, with a mind ever serene, and free from suffering, may you protect [the kingdom] for a hundred years.”

34. “Endowed with these virtues, O Khattiya, established in noble conduct, easy to speak to, and free from anger; being happy and without oppression, rule the earth. And when released from this life, may you go to a happy destination.”

35. “Thus, with good guidance, well-spoken words, righteousness, justice, and skillful means, may you calm the agitated multitude, just as a great cloud calms the earth with rain.”

He spoke these verses.

Janādhipa: O ruler of men. Khattiya: O noble king. Taveva: only you, the great king. Siri ca: the fulfillment of retinue (glory). Lakkhi ca: fortune and wisdom. Kudācanaṃ mā vijahi: may they never leave you. Tuvaṃ: you, the great king. Akkodhano: being free from anger. Niccapasannacitto: having a mind that is always serene. Anīgho: being free from suffering. Vassasatāni: for a hundred years. Pālaya: may you protect.

Khattiya: O noble king. Tuvaṃ: you, the noble king. Etehi guṇehi upeto: being endowed with those various virtues. Ṭhitamariyavatti: having established noble conduct (the royal virtues). Suvaco: being easy to speak to. Akod hano: being free from anger. Sukhī: being happy. Pasāsamedinīṃ anuppīḷa: rule the earth, which is your property, along with its beings, without oppression. Ito vimuttopi ca: even when released from this life. Suggatiṃ yāhi: go to a happy destination.

Mahāmegho: a great cloud. Salilena mediniṃ nibbāpeti iva: just as it cools the earth with water. Evaṃ tathā: in the same way. Sunītena: by well-led reasons. Subhāsitena: by well-spoken words. Dhammena: by the ten courses of wholesome action. Ñāyena: by justice. Upāyaso: by being skillful in means. Nayaṃ-nayanto: while disciplining. Saṅkhubhitaṃ: the great multitude who are agitated by physical and mental suffering. Nibbāpaye: may you calm them.

Sumangala explained the reason, saying, “Great King, I did not kill the Paccekabuddha; in truth, I did such a deed for such a reason.” Then the King comforted Sumangala, saying, “In that case, do not fear,” and reinstated him as the gardener as before.

## The Royal Virtues

Then the minister asked the King, “Great King, why did you hear the news of Sumangala twice and say nothing, but on the third time of hearing his news, you had him called and showed him mercy?”

To explain this, the King said, “Friend, one who is called a king should not do anything hastily in anger. Therefore, I remained silent at first, and on the third time, knowing that my mind had softened toward Sumangala, I had him called.”

29. He does not burn others, nor himself...
422:
When the King spoke of his own virtues in these six verses, the entire royal assembly was delighted and said, “Endowment with the virtue of morality is fitting only for Your Majesty,” thus praising the King's virtues.

## The Gardener Pays Homage
Sumangala, at the end of the King's words of praise, stood up, paid homage to the King, and with joined palms, wishing to praise the King, said:

33. Glory and fortune are yours alone, O Khattiya,

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching by way of an admonition to the King of Kosala, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained Parinibbāna. Ānanda was then Sumangala, and I myself was the King.”

## If the King Practices the Royal Virtues, He Will Prosper
The Sumangala Jātaka is concluded.

## 5. Gaṅgamāla Jātaka
## One Should Not Follow the Desires of Craving and Greed
The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Gaṅgamāla Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with ‘Aṅgārajātā,’ concerning the practice of Uposatha.

One day, the Teacher addressed the lay followers who were observing Uposatha: “Lay followers, you have done well by observing Uposatha. One should give gifts, keep the precepts, not give way to anger, develop loving-kindness, and observe the Uposatha. Wise men of old, by relying on the Uposatha, attained great glory.” Having said this, at their request, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a treasurer in that city named Suciparivāra, who possessed eighty crores of wealth and delighted in meritorious deeds such as giving.

## The Treasurer's Household Observing Uposatha
The treasurer's wife and children, and even the cowherds in that house, all observed the Uposatha six days a month—on the new moon (Amāvāsī), the eighth (Aṭṭhamī), and the eleventh (Ekadasī) days of the bright fortnight, and likewise three days in the dark fortnight.”
423:
## The Poor Man Gets a Job

At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family and earned his living through difficult manual labor for hire. Thinking, "I will work as a hired laborer," he went to the house of a merchant, paid his respects, and stood in a suitable place. When asked, "For what purpose have you come?", he replied, "Sir, I have come to work for wages in this house."

On the day other hired laborers arrived, the merchant would have them observe the precepts while they worked. He would say, "If you are able to keep the precepts, then do the work." However, for the Bodhisatta, the merchant did not give any instruction regarding the keeping of precepts and simply said, "Very well, son, know your wages and do the work."

From that time on, the Bodhisatta was obedient and, disregarding his own exhaustion as if sacrificing his life, he performed all the merchant's affairs. He went to work early in the morning and returned only at night.

## The Household Observes the Uposatha

Then one day, a festival was proclaimed in the city. The great merchant called his maidservant and said, "Today is the Uposatha day. Cook rice early for the laborers in the house; they will eat early and observe the Uposatha."

The Bodhisatta rose early and went to his place of work. No one informed him, "You should observe the Uposatha today." The other laborers ate early and observed the Uposatha.

The merchant also observed the Uposatha together with his wife, children, and retinue. Thus, all of them, while observing the Uposatha, went to their respective places and sat reflecting on their virtue.

## The Hired Laborer's Death

The Bodhisatta worked the whole day and returned home at sunset. He asked, "Today there is no sound; where has everyone gone?" Upon hearing the words, "Everyone has taken the Uposatha vows and gone to their respective places," the Bodhisatta thought, "I should not live as the only one without virtue among so many virtuous people. If I were to undertake the factors of the Uposatha now, would the act of observing the Uposatha be valid for me or not?"

Having thought thus, the Bodhisatta went and asked the merchant. Then the merchant said to him, "Son, because you did not undertake it early in the morning, the act of observing the Uposatha for the whole day is not possible; however, the act of observing a half-day Uposatha is possible."

The Bodhisatta said, "Let even this much of the Uposatha be mine," and having properly taken the precepts in the presence of the merchant, he undertook the Uposatha observance. He entered his own quarters and lay down reflecting on his virtue.

Then, because he had not consumed food for the entire day, stabbing pains like knives arose within the Bodhisatta during the last watch of the night. Although the merchant brought various medicines and said, "Eat this," the Bodhisatta said, "I will not break my Uposatha; I have undertaken it even at the cost of my life."

Severe pain arose in the Bodhisatta. At the time of dawn, he was unable to maintain consciousness. Then, thinking, "He will die now," they carried the Bodhisatta out from his place and laid him outside the house.
424:
## Becoming King Udaya

At that moment, the King of Bārāṇasī, riding a magnificent chariot and accompanied by a large retinue, was circumambulating the city clockwise and reached that spot. The Bodhisatta, seeing the glory of the King of Bārāṇasī, felt desire for it and longed for kingship. Having passed away, by the merit of the half-day Uposatha he had observed, he was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. The queen, having received pregnancy protection, gave birth to a son after ten months. They named the prince "Udayakumāra."

When Prince Udaya reached the age of maturity, he attained perfection in all arts. Remembering his past good deeds through the knowledge of past lives (jātissara-ñāṇa), he frequently uttered this solemn exclamation: "This is the fruit of my small meritorious deed." After his father passed away, Prince Udaya ascended to the throne, and looking at his own great glory and wealth, he continued to utter that same solemn exclamation.

## The Water-Carrier

Then one day, a festival was held in the city. Many people were devoted to the festivities. At that time, a certain hired man living at the North Gate of Bārāṇasī, who earned his living as a water-carrier, had saved a half-māsaka coin and placed it between the bricks of the city wall. While continuing his work, he reached the South Gate and lived together with a poor woman who also earned her living there as a water-carrier.

## At the Woman's Request

The woman said to the man, "Lord, a festival is being held in the city. If you have any wealth, we too shall enjoy the festival." The husband said, "I have some." The wife asked, "Lord, how much is there?" He replied, "There is a half-māsaka."

"Where is that money?" the wife asked. The husband said, "It is placed between the bricks of the wall at the North Gate. That treasure of a half-māsaka is placed within twelve leagues (yojanas) from here. But is there anything in your hand, lady?" The wife said, "Yes, there is." He asked, "How much is there?" She replied, "There is exactly a half-māsaka."

"Thus, with your half-māsaka and my half-māsaka, there is exactly one māsaka. With one portion of that money, we shall buy flowers; with one portion, perfume; and with one portion, liquor, and then we shall enjoy the festival. Go and fetch that half-māsaka you have placed there," said the wife.

## Going in the Heat

That water-carrier, being exceedingly joyful thinking, "I have received these words from my wife," said, "Lady, do not worry; I shall fetch that money," and he departed.
425:
38. "The heat of the sun does not burn me; it is the heats of desire that burn me. Indeed, O King, there are various purposes; they burn me, not the sun's heat."

He spoke this third verse.

O King, Great King. Me. The heat of the sun and the hot earth. Does not burn. Me. The heats of objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma). They burn. Purposes, the various affairs and matters that arise depending on objective and subjective sensuality. They are various and diverse. They. Me. They burn. The heat of the sun and the hot earth. Me. Does not burn.

A water-carrier, possessing strength like a noble elephant, having traveled six leagues, at the time of midday, treading upon sand as hot as a bed of embers, was exceedingly joyful due to greed for wealth. Wearing dyed robes and palm-leaf earrings in his ears, he went across the royal courtyard singing a song with a single shoulder-wrap.

## The King Asks

King Udaya, standing after opening the lion-window, saw that water-carrier going in such a manner. Thinking, "Why does this man go singing so joyfully, disregarding such wind and heat? I shall ask him," he sent a man to call him.

That man went and said, "The King calls you." The water-carrier replied, "What is the King to me? I do not know the King," and continued on. Being brought by force, he stood in a suitable place near the King.

Then the King, wishing to question the water-carrier, spoke these two verses:

36. "The earth has become like embers; the ground is covered with hot ashes. Yet you sing while wearing your wraps; does the heat not burn you?

37. "Above, the sun burns; below, the sand burns. Yet you sing while wearing your wraps; does the heat not burn you?"

## Are You Not Hot?

O man. The earth. It is hot like embers. The earth. It is accompanied by hot sand which is like hot ashes. Yet. You. The āyogapaṭṭa cloths. Having put them on. You sing. You. The heat. Does it not burn?

Above. The sun. It burns. Below. The sand. It is scorching hot. Yet. You. The āyogapaṭṭa cloths. Having put them on. You sing. You. The heat. Does it not burn?

## I Am Not Hot Because of Internal Heat

That water-carrier, hearing the King's words—

## What Is Your Business?

Then the King asked that water-carrier, "What is your business?" The water-carrier said, "Great King... I live together with a poor woman at the South Gate. That woman asked me, 'Let us enjoy the festival; do you have any wealth in your hand?'"

## To Fetch the Wealth

"Then I said to that woman, 'There is wealth placed between the bricks of the wall at the North Gate.' Then that woman sent me, saying, 'You go and fetch that wealth. We two shall also enjoy the festival.' That word of that woman does not leave my heart; the intense heat of that sensual desire which I remember burns me. My business is that very affair."

## The Reason for Happiness

Then the King asked the water-carrier, "For what reason of joy do you go singing, disregarding such wind and sun? What is the reason for your joy?" The water-carrier replied, "Great King... I shall fetch that stored wealth and enjoy myself with that woman; for this reason, being joyful and glad, I sing."
426:
## How Much Wealth Is There?

"My man... do you have wealth amounting to a hundred thousand placed at the North Gate?" the King asked. "Great King... I do not," he said. The King asked, "In that case, do you have fifty thousand? Forty thousand? Thirty thousand? Twenty thousand? Ten thousand? One thousand? Five hundred? Four hundred? Three hundred? Two hundred? One hundred? Fifty? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Ten? Five kahāpaṇas? Four kahāpaṇas? Three kahāpaṇas? Two kahāpaṇas? One kahāpaṇa? Half a kahāpaṇa? A quarter? Four māsakas? Three māsakas? Two māsakas? One māsaka?"

## Half a Masaka

Rejecting all the questions, when asked, "Do you have half a māsaka?" he replied, "Great King... it is just as you say. I am going to fetch that wealth of mine, which is of this much measure, and enjoy myself with that woman. Because of that rapture and joy, this wind and sun do not burn me," the water-carrier explained.

## Do Not Go, Take Half the Kingdom

Then the King said to that man, "My man... do not go to that place in such heat. I shall give you half a māsaka of wealth." He replied, "Great King... I shall abide by your command and take the wealth you give, but I will not abandon that other wealth. Without failing in my journey, I shall go to that place as well."

"My man... do not go. I shall give you one māsaka. I shall give you two māsakas." Thus increasing it, he said, "I shall give you immeasurable wealth up to a hundred million; do not go." Even then, he said, "Great King... I shall take the wealth you give and also take that other wealth."

After that, though the King tempted him with the position of a Treasurer and so on, up to the position of Viceroy, he spoke in the same way. When the King said, "I shall give you half the kingship; do not go," he then accepted.

The King commanded the ministers, "Go, trim the hair and beard of my friend, bathe him, adorn him, and bring my friend here." The ministers did as the King said. The King divided the kingdom into two and gave half the kingship to that man.

"That man, even after taking half the kingdom, went to the north side and fetched that half-māsaka coin," they say. That king was known as King Addhamāsaka.

## King Addhamāsaka Does Not Want to Rule

Those two kings, being in harmony and full of joy, went to the park one day while ruling. After playing in the park, King Udaya laid his head on King Addhamāsaka's lap and slept. When King Udaya fell into a deep sleep, the attendants went here and there for the sake of enjoying themselves.

King Addhamāsaka thought, "What is the use of half the kingship for me at all times? I shall kill King Udaya and exercise the whole kingship alone." He drew his sword and intended, "I shall kill King Udaya." Then he remembered, "This king made me, who was a very poor person, equal to himself and established me in great prosperity. Greed has arisen in me to kill such a king who gave me this prosperity and to rule. My deed is surely improper." Having remembered this, he put the sword back into its sheath.
427:
Then, for King Aḍḍhamāsaka, for a second and third time, the same thought arose. After that, he thought, "If this thought arises repeatedly, it might lead me to evil deeds." Having thought so, King Aḍḍhamāsaka threw his sword to the ground, made King Udaya stand up, and prostrated at his feet, saying, "Great King, please forgive me."

"Friend, is there no fault between us now?" King Udaya asked. "Great King, there is; I have committed such an act," King Aḍḍhamāsaka replied. "Friend, if that is so, I forgive you. Rule the kingdom if you wish; I will become the viceroy and serve you," said Udaya.

## Uttering an Exclamation
King Aḍḍhamāsaka said, "Great King, I have no desire for kingship. This craving will cause me to be reborn in the lower realms. You alone take your kingship. I shall renounce the world and become an ascetic. I have seen the fault of sensual desire. This desire increases through the thoughts of one who ponders it. From now on, I will not think of that desire." Wishing to utter an exclamation, he spoke this fourth verse:

39. O Lust, I have seen your root; you are born from thought.
I will not think of you; thus, O Lust, you will not exist.

Lust, Lust. Your root, I have seen. Lust, you are born because of thought. Lust, I will no longer think of you. Thus, when I do not think, you will not exist within me.

## Preaching the Dhamma
Having said this, wishing to preach the Dhamma to the people who were still striving for sensual pleasures, he spoke this fifth verse:

40. Small desires are not enough, even with many one is not satisfied.
They are not delightful, the prattle of fools; let the wakeful one avoid them.

Great King. Even small objective and subjective sensualities are not enough for the masses. Even with many, the people are not satisfied. Desires are not delightful. Desires cause fools to say, "This is mine, this is mine." These desires should be abandoned by those of good family who are wakeful and striving to develop the factors of enlightenment.

## Renouncing and Becoming an Ascetic
Thus, King Aḍḍhamāsaka preached the Dhamma to the people, handed over the kingship to King Udaya, and, leaving the weeping people with tear-stained faces, entered the Himalayas, became an ascetic, and lived there having attained the meditative absorptions and higher powers.

## King Udaya's Exclamation
At the time when King Aḍḍhamāsaka became an ascetic, King Udaya, wishing to utter the exclamation in full, spoke this sixth verse:

## Wishing to Reward the Barber
No one knew the meaning of this verse. Then, one day, the Chief Queen asked King Udaya the meaning of the verse. The King did not say anything.
428:
41. This is the fruit of my small deed;
Udaya has attained great majesty.
Truly, it is a well-gained gain for the young man,
Who renounced, having abandoned sensual lust.

My, this fruit. Of a small meritorious deed. The fruit. King Udaya. Attained majesty and prosperity. That young man. Sensual lust. Having abandoned. Renounced. For that young man. Truly. A well-gained gain; obtaining human existence is a good gain.

King Udaya had a royal barber named Gaṅgamāla. When that barber attended to the King's hair and beard, he first performed the act of shaving and then plucked the beard with tweezers. When the shaving was done, the King felt pleasure. When the beard was plucked, he felt pain. King Udaya first wanted to reward the barber, but later he wanted to cut off his head.

## The Queen Wishes to Know the Meaning of the Exclamation
Then one day, the King said to the Queen, "My dear, the barber Gaṅgamāla is a fool." When she asked, "Great King, what should be done?", he said, "He should first pluck the beard with tweezers and then perform the shaving."

The Queen called the barber and said, "Dear man, now on the day you attend to the King's hair and beard, first pluck the beard and then perform the shaving. When the King says, 'Take a boon,' you should say, 'Great King, I have no need for any other boon; please tell me the meaning of your exclamation verse.' I will give you much wealth."

The barber agreed, saying, "Very well," and on the day of attending to the hair and beard, he first took the tweezers. When the King asked, "Friend Gaṅgamāla, why are you doing something new that you have never done before?", he replied, "Great King, those called barbers do even things they have never done before," and he first plucked the beard and then performed the shaving.
429:
“I have no need for other boons; please tell me the meaning of your udāna verse.” The King, being ashamed to speak of what he had done during his time of poverty, said, “Dear friend, what use is this boon to you? Take another.” “O King, please give me only this one,” the barber replied.

Fearing the consequence of a lie, the King agreed, saying, “Very well.” Following the method described in the Kummāsapiṇḍa Jātaka, he arranged everything without omission. Sitting upon a jeweled throne, he revealed his past actions, saying, “Gangamāla, in a previous life, I was in this very city of Bārāṇasī,” and so on. He then explained the meaning of the udāna: “For this reason, I spoke the first half of the verse; but because I became negligent and ruled the kingdom while my friend had gone forth, I spoke the latter half of the verse for that reason.”

## The Barber Becomes a Paccekabuddha

Hearing these words, the barber thought, “It is said that the King obtained this prosperity through the merit of an uposatha observed for only half a day. Merit is indeed something that must be performed. What if I were to go forth and make a refuge for myself?” Having thus reflected, he abandoned his circle of relatives and wealth. After obtaining the King’s permission to go forth, he went to the Himālaya mountains and ordained as a hermit. Developing insight (vipassanā) by applying the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), he attained Paccekabuddhahood. Possessing the bowl and robes created by psychic power, he lived on Mount Gandhamādana for five or six years. Then, thinking, “I shall go to see the King of Bārāṇasī,” he traveled through the air and sat upon the auspicious stone slab in the royal park.

The park keeper, recognizing him, went and informed the King, “O King, Gangamāla has become a Paccekabuddha and, having come through the air, is now seated in the park.” Hearing this, the King set out quickly, saying, “I shall worship the Paccekabuddha.” The Queen Mother also set out together with her son. The King entered the park, worshipped him, and sat down in a suitable place along with his retinue.

## Admonishing the King
