While exchanging friendly greetings with the King, the Paccekabuddha addressed the King by his family name, saying, “Brahmadatta, are you diligent? Do you rule the kingdom righteously? Do you perform meritorious deeds such as giving?” Hearing this, the King’s mother became angry, thinking, “This low-born son of a barber, a cleaner of dirt, does not know his place. He addresses my son, the lord of the earth and a khattiya by birth, by the name ‘Brahmadatta’.” She then spoke this seventh verse:

42. By penance they abandon evil deeds,
By penance the state of barber or potter.
Having overcome [your status] by penance, Gangamāla,
Do you now dare address Brahmadatta by name?

[The commentary explains:] Gangamāla, Gangamāla. Beings (sattā) abandon evil deeds through practice (tapasā). Beings abandon the state of being a barber or a potter through practice. Gangamāla, Gangamāla, having overcome [your status] through practice, is it proper for you to now address my son by the name ‘Brahmadatta’?
430:
43. "Mother, behold the visible result; this is the fruit of patience and gentleness. We, along with the king and ministers, pay homage to him who is worshipped by all people."

Mother. The fruit of patience and virtue has come to pass. That fruit is being worshipped by all people. We, along with the king and ministers, pay homage to that Paccekabuddha. Behold the visible result of patience and gentleness.

44. "Do not say anything [disparaging] to Gaṅgamāla, who is training in the paths of the sages. For he has crossed the ocean, having crossed which the sorrowless ones wander."

Friends. Do not say even a single word against Gaṅgamāla, who is training in the paths of the sages—the practices of the monks known as the three trainings and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—practiced by householders, non-householders, trainees (sekha), non-trainees (asekha), and Paccekamunis. The sorrowless Noble Ones (ariyas) wander after having crossed the ocean of Saṃsāra. This Gaṅgamāla has indeed crossed that ocean of Saṃsāra.

"Perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna)," he said, addressing the King by his name and engaging in friendly conversation.

## The Queen Mother Becomes Angry

Hearing these words, the King's mother became angry, thinking, "This low-born son of a barber, a cleaner of filth, does not know his place and calls my son, the lord of the land, by the name Brahmadatta."

## The Virtues of the Paccekabuddha

The King, restraining his mother and wishing to reveal the virtues of the Paccekabuddha, spoke the eighth verse.

When the King restrained his mother, the rest of the people stood up and said, "Great King, it is not proper for such a low-born person to call you by name."

The King, also restraining the people, spoke the final verse to tell of his virtues.

## Departing for Mount Gandhamādana

Having said this, the King paid homage to the Paccekabuddha and said, "Venerable Sir, please forgive my mother." "I forgive her, Great King," the Paccekabuddha replied. The King also made his retinue ask for forgiveness. The King requested a promise from the Paccekabuddha to reside near him. However, the Paccekabuddha, without giving a promise—
431:
The Paccekabuddha, without accepting anything, stood in the air while the king and the assembly watched, gave advice to the king, and went to Mount Gandhamādana.

Identifying the birth: The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Lay devotees, thus the practice of the Uposatha should indeed be observed," and connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained Parinibbāna. Ānanda was then King Aḍḍhamāsaka. The mother of Rāhula was then the Chief Queen. I myself was then King Udaya."

## Half-day Uposatha, for observing it, the result is becoming a king

The Ganggamāla Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Cetiya Jātaka

## Swallowed by the Earth for Speaking Untruth

The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Cetiya Jātaka, adorned with the verse "Dhammo have hato hanti," while staying at Jetavana Monastery, concerning Devadatta being swallowed by the earth.

One day, the monks in the Dhamma Hall started a conversation: "Friends, Devadatta, having spoken a lie, was swallowed by the earth and went to Avīci." The Omniscient Buddha came and asked, "Monks, what talk are you gathered for now?" When they replied, "For such and such a talk," he said, "Monks, not only now has Devadatta been swallowed by the earth; in the past too, he was swallowed by the earth," and he brought the past story.

In the past, at the beginning of the aeon, there was a king named Mahāsammata who had an incalculable lifespan. His son was named Roja. His son was named Vararoja. His son was named Kalyāṇa. His son was named Varakalyāṇa. His son was named Uposatha. His son was named Varauposatha. His son was named Mandhātu. His son was named Varamandhātu. His son was named Vara. His son was named Upavara. The name Upari-vara was also the name of that King Upavara.

## King Cetiya

That King Upavara ruled in the city of Sotthiya in the kingdom of Cetiya. He was endowed with the four royal powers. He could travel through the air. Four young devas, holding swords in their hands, guarded him on the four sides. The scent of sandalwood wafted from his body, and the scent of blue lotuses from his mouth.

He had a chaplain Brahmin named Kapila. Kapila's younger brother was named Korakalamba. He was a childhood friend who studied under the same teacher along with the king. In his youth, the king had promised Korakalamba, "When I become king, I will give you the position of chaplain."
432:
## The Chaplain Becomes an Ascetic

The king, having become king, was unable to remove the Brahmin Kapila, his father's chaplain, from the position. When the chaplain came to attend on him, the king showed him respect and honor. The Brahmin noticed this and thought, "A king is well-supported when with those of his own age; I will ask the king's permission and go forth as a monk." He said, "Great King, I am old. There is a young son in my house. Make him the chaplain. I will go forth." Having received the king's permission, he installed his son in the chaplain's position, entered the royal garden, became an ascetic, attained jhānas and supernormal powers (abhiññā), and lived there supported by his son.

## To Give the Position

The Brahmin Korakalamba harbored a grudge against his brother, thinking, "Even when going forth, he did not give me the position." One day, while sitting in pleasant conversation, the king asked, "Korakalamba, do you not perform the duties of the chaplain?" He replied, "As you command, I do not; my brother does."

When asked "Why?", he said, "Great King, my brother is the chaplain." "Did your brother not go forth?" "As you command, he went forth, but he gave the position to his son."

"In that case, you be the chaplain," the king said. Korakalamba replied, "Great King, it is not proper for me to take the position that comes by lineage by removing my brother." The king said, "If that is so, I will make you the elder and your brother the younger." Korakalamba asked, "Great King, by what means will you do this?" The king said, "I will do it by telling a lie (musāvāda)."

## Will Tell a Lie

"Great King, do you not know? My brother is endowed with great and wonderful powers. Being a master of magic (vijjādhara), he will deceive you with his wonderful powers. He will make the four young devas seem to disappear. He will make the good scent from your body and mouth seem like a bad scent. He will make you seem as if you have fallen from the sky and are standing on the ground. You will seem to enter the earth. At that time, you will not be able to stand by your word," said Korakalamba.
433:
45. "Dhamma, indeed, when destroyed, destroys; it does not destroy anything when not destroyed. Therefore, one should not destroy Dhamma, lest the destroyed Dhamma destroy you."

He spoke this first verse. 

Great King. Indeed. Destroyed. Dhamma, the practice of honoring elders. Destroys, it kills oneself. Not destroyed, the Dhamma that is not destroyed. Anything, any person. Does not destroy. Therefore. Dhamma, the practice. One should not destroy. Destroyed. Dhamma. You. Lest it destroy.

46. "From one speaking a lie, the deities depart; his mouth smells foul, and he falls from his place, who, knowing the answer to a question, explains it otherwise."

He spoke this second verse. 

Great King. The question. Being asked. Who, whichever king. Knowing, with full knowledge. It, that question. Otherwise, in a different manner. Explains. A lie, an untruthful word. Speaking. To him, to that king. The deities, the four guardian deities. Depart. And the mouth. Foul, like a mass of rot. Smells. And from his own place, from his position in the sky. Falls, he drops to the ground.

"Do not have such a thought; I shall be able to do it," the King said. "Great King, when will you do it?" Korakalamba asked. "On the seventh day from today," the King replied. This word became known throughout the city.

## The Multitude Watching

"The King will speak a lie and make the elder younger and the younger elder; he will give the special position to the younger. What is a lie like? Is it blue in color, or is it of another color such as gold?" Such a thought arose among the people. 

At that time, it was a period when the world spoke only the truth. People did not know, "A lie is of such a nature."

The Chaplain's son also heard that word and went to his father, saying, "Father, they say the King will speak a lie, making you the younger and giving your special position to my uncle." "Son, even by speaking a lie, the King will not be able to take our position. On which day will he speak the lie?" the ascetic Kapila asked. "On the seventh day from today," the son replied. "If that is so, come and inform me at that time," the ascetic Kapila said.

On the seventh day, the people gathered at the palace courtyard, saying, "We will see a lie," and they stood upon tiers of benches they had constructed. The Chaplain's son informed his father.

## Do Not Lie

The King, fully adorned, came out and stood in the air in the palace courtyard in the midst of the people. The ascetic came through the air, spread his sitting-skin before the King, and sat cross-legged in the air, saying, "Great King, is it true that you wish to speak a lie, making the younger the elder to give him the position?" "Teacher, it is true; so I have said," the King replied.
434:
In that context, 'the deities depart' means: Great King, if you speak a lie, the four divine sons will abandon their protection and vanish. 'His mouth smells foul' means: Both your mouth and your body will emit a rotten odor. 'He falls from his place' means: He shows that you will fall from the sky and enter the earth.

Hearing this, the King was afraid and looked at Korakalamba. Then Korakalamba said to him, "Do not fear, Great King; did I not tell you this before?" Although the King heard Kapila's words, he did not heed them, and putting his own words first, he said, "Venerable Sir, you are the younger; Korakalamba is the elder."

Immediately upon speaking that lie, the four divine sons, thinking, "We will not provide protection to such a liar," dropped their swords at his feet and vanished. His mouth smelled like a rotten egg, and his body smelled like an open latrine. He fell from the air and stood on the ground. All four psychic powers vanished. 

Then the Great Chaplain said to him, "Do not fear, Great King; if you speak the truth, I will make everything normal for you," and spoke the third verse:

47. "If you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before. If you speak a lie, O Cetiya, stand upon the ground."

He spoke this third verse. 

Cetiya, the one named Cetiya. Great King. The truth. If indeed you speak. As before. Be. Cetiya. Great King. A lie. If you speak. On the ground. Stand.

Then the ascetic, wishing to admonish the King, said: "Great King, a lie is a heavy fault; it destroys virtues and causes rebirth in the four woeful states. A King who speaks a lie is said to kill the Dhamma. When he kills the Dhamma, he is said to kill himself."

## The Mouth Becomes Foul

Thereafter, wishing to admonish the King further, he said, "Great King, if you speak a lie, your four psychic powers will vanish."

## The First Lie

Hearing this, the King was afraid and looked at Korakalamba. Then Korakalamba said to the King, "Great King, do not fear; did I not tell you this before?" The King, though hearing the words of the ascetic Kapila, did not accept them, and wishing to maintain only what he had said, he said, "Venerable Sir, you are the younger; Korakalamba is the elder."

Because of speaking that lie, the four deities, thinking, "We will not protect a king who speaks such a lie," dropped their swords at the King's feet and vanished. His mouth smelled like a rotten egg, and his body smelled like an open latrine. He fell from the sky and stood on the ground. These four psychic powers also vanished.

Then the Great Chaplain, wishing to say, "Great King, do not fear; if you speak the truth, I will restore all those powers to you," said:

## The Second Lie

That Chaplain said, "Great King, look; first, because of speaking a lie, your four powers have vanished. Take note; even now it is possible to make things normal." But the King did not do as told and said, "You wish to deceive me," and spoke a lie for the second time, sinking into the earth up to his ankles.

## Bad Rain

Then the Great Brahmin, wishing to show, "Great King, take note; even now it is possible to make things normal," spoke the fourth verse:
435:
49. "If indeed you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before. If you speak a lie, O King, enter the earth, O Cetiya."

He spoke this fifth verse. Cetiya, O King named Cetiya. If you speak the truth, be as you were in the past. O King Cetiya, if you speak a lie, enter the earth.

50. "The tongue of him becomes two-fold, like that of a snake, O Lord of the Land, who knowingly, when asked a question, explains it otherwise."

51. "If indeed you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before. If you speak a lie, O King, sink deeper, O Cetiya."

Having spoken these two verses, he said, "It is still possible to restore you to your normal state."

Whosoever, being a king, when asked a question, knowingly explains it in another way; O Lord of the Land, the tongue of that lying king becomes two-fold, like the tongue of a snake.

O King named Cetiya, if you speak the truth, be as you were before. O King Cetiya, if you speak a lie, sink deeper into the earth.

52. "The tongue of him does not exist, like that of a fish, O Lord of the Land, who knowingly, when asked a question, explains it otherwise."

53. "If indeed you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before. If you speak a lie, O King, sink deeper, O Cetiya."

He spoke these two verses.

O Lord of the Land, the king who, when asked a question, knowingly explains it in another way; just as a fish has no tongue, that lying king will have no tongue.

O Noble King named Cetiya, if you speak the truth, be as you were before. O King Cetiya, if you speak a lie, sink deeper into the earth.

48. "It rains for him out of season; in season it does not rain for him, who knowingly, when asked a question, explains it otherwise."

He spoke this fourth verse. Great King, whosoever, when asked a question, knowingly explains it in another way; in the kingdom of that king, it rains out of season, and in the proper season, it does not rain.

At that time, by the power of that lie, the earth swallowed the king up to his ankles. The Great Chaplain said, "Observe, Great King," and spoke—

## The Third Lie

For the third time, the king spoke only a lie, saying, "Venerable Sir, you are the younger; Korakalamba is the elder," and he sank into the earth up to his knees.

## The Tongue Becomes Forked

Then, the Great Chaplain again said to the king, "Observe, Great King," and spoke—

## The Fourth Lie

Though the king heard the Great Chaplain's words, he did not heed them and for the fourth time spoke a lie, saying, "Venerable Sir, you are the younger; Korakalamba is the elder," and he sank into the earth up to his waist.

## The Tongue Disappears

Then, the Great Chaplain said to the king, "Great King, you must observe," and spoke—

## The Fifth Lie

For the fifth time, the king said, "Venerable Sir, you are the younger; Korakalamba is the elder," and he sank into the earth up to his navel.

## No Male Offspring

Then, the Brahmin Chaplain again said to the king, "Observe, Great King," and spoke—
436:
54. "Only daughters are born to him, no males are born in his clan, who knowingly, when asked a question, explains it otherwise."

55. "If indeed you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before. If you speak a lie, O King, sink deeper, O Cetiya."

He spoke these two verses. Great King, whosoever, being a king, when asked a question, knowingly explains it in another way; in the clan of that lying king, only daughters are born, and no sons are born.

O King named Cetiya, if you speak the truth, be as you were before. O King Cetiya, if you speak a lie, sink deeper into the earth.

56. "Sons are not born to him, or they flee in every direction, who knowingly, when asked a question, explains it otherwise."

57. "If indeed you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before. If you speak a lie, O King, sink deeper, O Cetiya."

He spoke these two verses. Great King, whosoever, being a king, when asked a question, knowingly explains it in another way; to that lying king, sons are not born. Even if they are born, they do not help their parents and flee to various directions.

O King named Cetiya, if you speak the truth, be as you were before. O King Cetiya, if you speak a lie, sink deeper into the earth.

## The Sixth Lie

Not heeding the chaplain's words, the king lied for the sixth time as before and sank into the earth up to his breasts. Then, the Great Chaplain again said to the king, "Observe, Great King," and spoke—

## The Seventh Lie

Due to the fault of associating with evil friends, the king did not heed the chaplain's words and for the seventh time lied as before.

## Swallowed by the Earth

Then, the earth opened up for that king. Flames from Avīci rose and seized him. The All-Enlightened Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching after attaining Buddhahood, spoke these two verses:

58. "That king, cursed by the sage, who formerly traveled through the air, entered the earth, the high-born one, having reached his end."

59. "Therefore, the wise do not praise following one's desires (bias); one should speak words associated with truth, with a mind free from corruption."

Monks, that King Cetiya, who formerly traveled through the air, was later cursed by the sage and his nature was ruined. Having reached the end of his time, he entered the earth.

## Bias Should Not Be Followed

Therefore, the wise do not praise following the path of bias (agati). One should speak words connected with truth, with a mind not destroyed by bias such as desire.

## Founding New Cities

The people were struck with terror, saying, "King Cetiya cursed the sage, spoke a lie, and has reached Avīci." The king's five sons came and prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisatta, saying, "Please be our refuge." The Bodhisatta said, "O youths, your father destroyed the Dhamma, spoke lies, cursed the sage, and is now reborn in Avīci."
437:
“This Dhamma kills the one who destroys it. You cannot stay in this place.” Saying thus, among those princes—

To the eldest prince, he said, “Come, dear son. Go out by the East gate and travel straight; you will see an all-white noble elephant. By that sign, establish a city in that place and dwell there. That city shall be named Hatthipura.”

Calling the second prince, he said, “Dear son, go out by the South gate and travel straight; you will see an all-white noble horse. By that sign, establish a city in that place and dwell there. That city shall be named Assapura.”

Calling the third prince, he said, “Dear son, go out by the West gate and travel straight; you will see a maned lion king. By that sign, establish a city in that place and dwell there. That city shall be named Sīhapura.”

Calling the fourth prince, he said, “Dear son, go out by the North gate and travel straight; you will see a chariot frame made of all kinds of jewels. By that sign, establish a city in that place and dwell there. That city shall be named Uttarapañcāla.”

Calling the fifth prince, he said, “Dear son, you cannot stay in this place. Build a great stupa in this city, and after leaving this city, travel straight towards the North-West direction; you will see two mountains clashing against each other repeatedly, making the sound ‘Daddara’. By that sign, establish a city in that place and dwell there. That city shall be named Daddarapura.”

Those five princes went according to those signs and established cities in those respective places and dwelt there.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past also, Devadatta entered the earth because of telling lies,” and he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, King Cetiya was Devadatta, but the Brahmin Kapila was I myself.”

## Foulness of body and breath, and lying are the results of falsehood
The Cetiya Jātaka ends.
438:
## 7. Indriya Jātaka
## One should not follow the desire for sensual pleasures

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Indriya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Yo indriyānaṃ,” concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

It is said that a certain clansman in Sāvatthī, having heard the Dhamma of the All-Knowing Buddha, thought, “It is not possible for one living in the midst of a household to practice the holy life (brahmacariya) which is perfectly complete and perfectly pure. I will ordain in the teaching of the All-Knowing Buddha, which leads out of suffering, and make an end of suffering.” He handed over his household wealth to his wife and children, went forth, and requested ordination from the All-Knowing Buddha. The All-Knowing Buddha then had him ordained.

## Due to not receiving alms-food
Because he was a junior monk (navaka) and because there were many monks, he did not get a seat in the houses of donors or in the refectory. He only reached a stool or a wooden plank at the very end of the Saṅgha’s line.

Regarding food, he only received sour gruel with broken rice grains stirred with the back of a ladle, or foul and dry hard food, or burnt and dry rice. It was not even enough to sustain him.

## Going to the former wife
That monk took the food he received and went to his former wife. Then, the former wife took the monk’s bowl, paid respect, removed the food from the bowl, and gave him well-prepared gruel, rice, and curries. The old monk, being bound by the craving for tastes (rasataṇhā), was unable to abandon his former wife.

That woman thought, “Is this monk bound to me or not? I will test him.” One day, she had a man from the countryside bathe with white clay and fine powder and sit in the house. She called two or three other men to be his attendants and gave them a little drink and food. Those people sat there eating and chewing. At the house door, she had oxen yoked to carts and kept one cart ready. She herself sat in a back room of the house and fried cakes. The old monk arrived and stood at the door.

## Being deceived
Seeing the old monk, an elderly man said, “Lady, a Great Elder is standing at the door.” The woman said, “Pay respect and say, ‘Please go to another house for alms after leaving our house.’” The old man said, “Venerable sir, please receive alms at another house,” but seeing that the old monk did not leave even after being told repeatedly, he said, “Lady, the Elder does not go elsewhere.”

That woman came, lifted the curtain, looked, and said, “Oh, father, he is my husband!” She went out, took the bowl, brought him into the house, and served him food. At the end of the meal, she paid respect and said, “Venerable sir, may you attain Parinibbāna right here in Sāvatthī. We have not taken another family for this long, but a household without a master cannot stand. We shall take another family and go to a distant countryside. Venerable sir, may you be heedful. If there is any fault in me, please forgive it.” It was as if the old monk’s heart was breaking.

## About to disrobe
Then, the old monk said to that woman, “I cannot abandon you. Do not go. I will disrobe. Bring a cloth for me at such-and-such a place. I will go and hand over the bowl and robes to my teachers and preceptors and then come.” The woman agreed, saying, “Very well.”

## Arriving before the Buddha
The old monk went to the monastery and handed over the bowl and robes to his teachers and preceptors. When asked, “Friend, why do you do this?” he replied, “I cannot abandon my former wife. I will disrobe.”
439:
Then, though the elder monk was unwilling, the teachers and preceptors brought him to the presence of the Buddha. When the Buddha asked, "Monks, why have you brought this monk who is unwilling?", they replied, "Venerable Sir, this elder monk is dissatisfied and wishes to return to lay life."

Then the Omniscient Buddha asked the elder monk, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" He replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir." When asked, "Who has caused you to be dissatisfied?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, my former wife has caused me to be dissatisfied."

The Buddha said, "Monk, not only now has this woman caused you harm; in the past also she caused you harm. Because of her, you fell away from the four jhānas and fell into great suffering. But by depending on me, you were freed from that suffering and regained the jhānas you had lost." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the wife of King Brahmadatta's chaplain. On the day the Bodhisatta was born, weapons throughout the whole city glowed. Therefore, they named the Bodhisatta "Jotipāla."

## The Hermit Sarabhaṅga
When the youth Jotipāla reached the age of maturity, he studied all the arts in the city of Takkasilā. After demonstrating his skills to the king, he renounced his wealth and, without letting anyone know, departed through the main gate and entered the forest. He became an ascetic in the hermitage named Kaviṭṭhaka, which was provided by Sakka, and attained jhānas and supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). While the Bodhisatta was residing in that Kaviṭṭhaka hermitage, many hundreds of hermits surrounded him. There was a great gathering. He became the teacher named Sarabhaṅga. He had seven chief disciples.

## The Disciple Hermits
Among those chief disciples, the hermit named Sālissara left his own hermitage and lived by the banks of the river named Sātodikā in the eastern district, surrounded by more than a thousand hermits.
440:
60. He who, through desire, Nārada, goes under the power of the senses,
Having abandoned both worlds, withers even while living.

This was the first verse he spoke.

Nārada, Nārada. Whosoever, that man. Through desire, by the power of sensual defilement. Of the senses, to the will. Goes, follows wrongly. That man. Both worlds, the human world and the deva world. Having abandoned, having given up. In hell and other such places, is reborn. Even while living, he reaches great suffering.

The hermit named Meṇḍissara lived near the market town named Kalabbacūḷaka in the Pañcāla kingdom, surrounded by more than a thousand hermits.

The hermit named Pabbata lived near a certain forest district, surrounded by more than a thousand hermits.

The hermit named Kāḷadevila lived near a solid rock mountain in Avanti-Dakkhiṇāpatha, surrounded by more than a thousand hermits.

The hermit named Kisavaccha lived alone in a park near the city of Kumbhavatī in the kingdom of King Daṇḍakī.

The hermit Anupiya lived in the presence of the Bodhisatta, serving him.

## Nārada's Dissatisfaction
Nārada, the younger brother of the hermit Kāḷadevila, lived alone in a cave within the mountain range named Arañjaragiri in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). Near the Arañjaragiri mountain, there was a populous market town. Between the Arañjaragiri mountain and the market town, there was a large river. Many people crossed that river. Courtesans of supreme beauty also sat on the riverbank, enticing men.

The hermit Nārada saw one of those courtesans and, with a mind full of attachment, his jhāna vanished. Without taking food, his body becoming withered, he followed the power of defilement and lay down for seven days.

When his elder brother, the hermit Kāḷadevila, reflected, he came to know the reason. He came through the air and entered the cave. Seeing Kāḷadevila, Nārada asked, "Why have you come, sir?" He replied, "You are unwell, sir; I have come to treat you." Then Nārada rebuked Kāḷadevila with accusations of lying, saying, "You are speaking what is not true."

Kāḷadevila thought, "It is not proper to abandon Nārada," and he brought the hermit Sālissara. He also brought the hermit Meṇḍissara. He also brought the hermit Pabbata. Nārada rebuked all three hermits with accusations of lying. Kāḷadevila then thought, "I will bring the teacher Sarabhaṅga," and traveling through the air, he brought the teacher Sarabhaṅga.
441:
61. Suffering follows happiness, and happiness follows suffering.
You have fallen from happiness into suffering; look forward to the excellent happiness.

He spoke this second verse.

Narada, Narada. Beings reach the suffering of hell and such immediately after sensual pleasure. They reach the happiness of the human and celestial realms, and the happiness of Nibbāna, immediately after the suffering of guarding virtue. This is what is meant: Narada, these beings, having passed away at the time of indulging in sensual pleasures, are reborn in hell, which is absolute suffering. However, those who guard virtue and practice insight meditation undergo hardship; having guarded virtue through such hardship, they obtain the aforementioned types of happiness by the power of their virtue. It is with reference to this hardship that I speak thus. "You have fallen" means: You, Narada, having now destroyed the happiness of Jhana, have fallen from that happiness into great mental suffering based on sensuality. "Look forward" means: Discard this suffering of defilements and once again desire and long for that same excellent and supreme happiness of Jhana.

62. In times of hardship, one who endures hardship and does not succumb to it,
That wise one attains the happiness that is the end of hardship, the union.

He spoke this third verse.

Narada, Narada. That wise one who, when hardship consisting of physical and mental suffering arises, is diligent and, while employing the means to remove that hardship, endures it and does not succumb to it—not falling under its power but overcoming and destroying it through various means—that wise person attains the happiness of Jhana, which is called the end of hardship and the happiness of detachment. Or, he attains the happiness of union (yoga) which is the end of hardship, reaching it without exhaustion.

63. Not for the sake of desires, nor for misfortune, nor for any benefit,
Nor by discarding what has been achieved, should you fall away from the Dhamma.

He spoke this fourth verse.

Narada, Narada. It is not proper to fall away from the Dhamma out of desire for sensual objects. It is not proper to fall away from the Dhamma because of misfortune. It is not proper to fall away from the Dhamma for the sake of some perceived benefit, thinking, "Such and such a benefit will arise for me." It is not proper to fall away from the Dhamma by discarding and destroying the Jhana that has already been attained and perfected.

## Sensual Desire Causes Suffering
The teacher Sarabhaṅga arrived and, seeing the hermit Narada, realized, "He is following the will of his senses." He asked, "Narada, are you following the will of your senses?" Upon hearing these words, the hermit Narada stood up, paid respects, and said, "Teacher, I am following the will of my senses." Then the teacher said, "Narada, those who follow the will of their senses become withered in this current existence and suffer, and in their second existence, they are reborn in hell."

## The Nature of Sensual Suffering
Hearing this, the hermit Narada asked, "Teacher, the indulgence in sensual pleasure is called happiness. With what intention do you, Teacher, say that such happiness is suffering?" Then the teacher Sarabhaṅga said to the hermit Narada, "Narada, if that is so, then listen."

## Enduring Suffering
The hermit Narada said, "Teacher, this suffering is difficult to endure. I am unable to endure it."
442:
64. Skillfulness is good for a householder, as is sharing food.
Being unelated in gain, and undismayed in loss.

He spoke this fifth verse.

Narada, Narada. For householders living the home life, skillfulness—meaning the state of being diligent, clever, and proficient in order to produce wealth—is good. Sharing and consuming food together with virtuous monks and brahmins is also good. Being unelated—meaning not being frivolous or boastful by virtue of diligence when great power and wealth are obtained—is the third good thing. When there is a loss of benefit or a loss of reputation, being undismayed—meaning not being distressed—is the fourth good thing. Therefore, Narada, do not grieve thinking, "My Jhana has disappeared." If you do not go under the sway of the senses, your lost Jhana will surely become manifest again.

65. This much wisdom did Devila speak;
There is no one more wretched than he who goes under the sway of the senses.

He [the Buddha] spoke this sixth verse.

Monks, this much wisdom did that Devila speak. But there is no one else more wretched than one who goes under the sway of the senses through the power of defilements.

Then the Bodhisatta, intending to say to the hermit Narada, "Hardship that has arisen must indeed be endured," said:

## Dhamma Should Not Be Destroyed
The hermit Narada said, "Teacher, sensual pleasure is a supreme happiness. I am unable to give up that supreme happiness." Then the Bodhisatta said to the hermit Narada, "Narada, the Dhamma should not be destroyed for any reason whatsoever."

## The Four Good Points
After the teacher Sarabhaṅga had preached the Dhamma with these four verses, the hermit Kāḷadevila, wishing to admonish his younger brother, spoke.

Knowing that the hermit Kāḷadevila was admonishing the hermit Narada, the All-Knowing Blessed One, having become the Buddha, spoke again.

Then the teacher Sarabhaṅga called the hermit Narada and said, "Narada, listen first to these words: he who does not perform the tasks that should have been done beforehand, that person must grieve and weep like the young man who entered the forest." Thus, he brought forth the past story.

## Evidence Story
In the past, in a certain village of Kasi, there was a handsome young Brahmin. He was endowed with strength and could carry a bull elephant.

## The Great Human-Peta
That young man thought, "What use is it to me to support my parents by farming and such? What use is a wife and children? What use are meritorious deeds like giving (dana)? Without supporting anyone and without performing any good deeds, I will enter the forest, kill deer, and support only myself."
443:
Having thought thus, the young man, equipped with the five kinds of weapons, went to the Himavant. He lived there, killing various animals and eating them. He reached a great mountain-net (pabbata-jāla) surrounded by mountains on the banks of the river named Vidhavā in the Himavant. There, he killed animals and lived by eating meat roasted on embers.

The young man thought: "I will not be strong forever. When I am weak, I will not be able to roam the forest. Right now, I will drive various kinds of animals into this mountain-net, fix a gate, and without roaming the forest, I will kill and eat animals as I please." Having thought so, he did exactly as he planned.

Then, as time passed for the young man, that evil kamma reached its peak and bore fruit in this very life. He could not walk with his hands and feet; he could not move from here to there. He saw no food, no edibles, and no drinking water. His body withered. He became a human-peta. In the summer, his body cracked like the earth, and lines appeared. Having an ugly appearance and a deformed shape, he experienced great suffering.

## King Sivi Goes Hunting
When a long time had passed in this way, a king named Sivi in the Sivi kingdom, thinking "I will eat meat roasted on embers in the forest," handed over the kingdom to his ministers. Equipped with the five kinds of weapons, he entered the forest. Killing animals and eating their meat, he eventually reached that mountain-net region. Seeing that man, though afraid, he established mindfulness and asked: "O man, who are you?"

"Lord, I am a human-peta. I am experiencing the fruit of my own evil kamma. But who are you?" he asked. "I am King Sivi," the king replied. "Being a king, why have you come to this place?" the man asked. "I have come to eat venison," the king said.

## The State of the Human-Peta
Then the human-peta said to King Sivi: "Great King, I too came for this very reason—the desire to eat venison—and have become a human-peta." Explaining the whole matter in detail, and wishing to inform the king of his miserable state, he spoke the remaining verses:
444:
66. "Like one falling into the hands of enemies, O Sivi, I have come to ruin. Having neglected work, knowledge, skill, marriage, virtue, and gentleness—these things that bring glory—I am born [in this state] through my own deeds.
67. "I am like one who has lost a thousand, without kin or refuge. Having departed from the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, I am just like a peta.
68. "Having caused suffering to beings who desire happiness, I have reached this state. I find no happiness, standing as if surrounded by flames."
He spoke these remaining verses.

## Causes of Prosperity
*Sivi*: King Sivi. *Māmiva*: A person like me. *Amittānaṃ*: Of enemies. *Hatthatthaṃ*: Destruction in the hands [of enemies]. *Pappoti*: Reaches, as if reaching destruction. *Kamma*: Livelihood-completing work such as farming. *Vijjā*: Arts such as elephant-riding. *Dakkheyya*: Skill in producing wealth. *Vivāha*: Marriage. *Sīlamaddava*: The five precepts and associating with friends who speak gentle words. *Ete ca yase*: These qualities that bestow prosperity. *Hāpetvā*: Having neglected.

*Sehi kammehi*: Because of one's own evil deeds. *Nibbatto*: Became a human-peta. *So ahaṃ*: That 'I'. *Sahassajīno va*: Like a person who has lost a thousand [pieces of wealth]. *Abandhu*: Having no friends or relatives. *Aparāyaṇo*: Having no refuge. *Ariyadhammā*: From the practice of the virtuous. *Apakkanto*: Having departed. *Yathā*: In the manner that. *Mato*: A dead person. *Peto*: Becomes a peta. *Uppajjeyya*: Would be born. *Tatheva*: In that very same way. *Ahaṃ*: I. *Peto*: Am a human-peta while still alive.

*Sukhakāme*: Beings who desire happiness. *Dukkhāpetvā*: Having caused them suffering. *Imaṃ padaṃ*: This state of suffering. *Āpanno*: Have reached. *Asmi*: I am. *So ahaṃ*: That 'I'. *Bhāṇumatāmiva*: As if surrounded by embers. *Ṭhito*: Standing while being burned.
445:
I do not find happiness.

Having said this, he said, "Great King, I desired happiness but caused suffering to others, and thus I have become a human-ghost (manussapeta) in this very life. Therefore, O King, do not perform evil deeds. Return to your city and perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna)."

The King returned to his city, did as the human-ghost said, and filled the heavenly realm. The teacher Sarabhaṅga brought this matter to the attention of the ascetic Nārada.

## The Ascetic Nārada Gains Spiritual Urgency

The ascetic Nārada, moved by the Dhamma discourse of the teacher Sarabhaṅga, gained spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He paid homage to Sarabhaṅga, asked for forgiveness, practiced the preliminary exercises for the kasina (kasiṇa-parikamma), and restored his lost meditative absorption (jhāna). The teacher Sarabhaṅga did not allow the ascetic Nārada to remain in that cave but took him back to his own hermitage.

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching and explained the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). This is how he identified the Jātaka:

"At that time, the dissatisfied monk was the ascetic Nārada. The former wife was the courtesan. Sālissara was Sāriputta. Meṇḍissara was Kassapa. Pabbata was Anuruddha. The Elder Kaccāyana was Kāဠadevila. Ānanda was Anupiya. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was Kisavaccha. And I myself was the teacher Sarabhaṅga."

## Following the Senses Leads to Hell and Suffering Among Humans

The Indriya Jātaka is concluded.

## 8. Āditta Jātaka

## On the Merit of Choosing Where to Give Alms

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Āditta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Ādittasmiṃ,' concerning the Peerless Almsgiving (Asadisa-dāna).

The details of that Peerless Almsgiving should be understood as elaborated in the Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta.
446:
On the seventh day after the Peerless Almsgiving was given, the monks in the Dhamma Hall began a conversation: "Friends, the King of Kosala, having carefully investigated and knowing the field of merit, gave the Peerless Almsgiving to the Noble Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head."

The Fully Enlightened One arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such a subject," he said, "Monks, it is not surprising that the King of Kosala, having investigated, established his gift in the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head, which is the peerless field of merit. Wise men of old also gave great gifts after careful investigation." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, in the city of Roruva in the kingdom of Sivi, a king named Roruva ruled without violating the Ten Royal Virtues. He supported the people through the Four Bases of Sympathy (saṅgaha-vatthu) and, standing in the place of a father and mother to the people, he provided great alms to the poor, travelers, beggars, and mendicants.

The chief queen of King Roruva was named Samuddavijayā. She was wise and endowed with wisdom. One day, while the king was inspecting the alms-hall, he thought:

"Immoral and greedy beings eat my alms. This does not bring me joy. I wish to give to the virtuous Paccekabuddhas, the supreme recipients of offerings. They live in the Himalayan region. Who can invite them and bring them here? Whom shall I send?" Having thought thus, he informed the queen of this matter.
447:
69. When a house is burning, the vessel that is carried out is the one that is of use to the owner, not the one that is burnt there.

70. So too is the world ablaze with aging and death. One should carry out [wealth] by giving; what is given is well-carried out.

Great King. 'Ādittasmiṃ', in a house that is burning and blazing. 'Agārasmiṃ', in the house. 'Yaṃ bhājanaṃ', whatever vessel or utility. 'Nīharati', one carries out. 'Tattha', in that house. 'Yaṃ bhājanaṃ', whatever vessel. 'Neva ḍayhati', is not burnt. 'Taṃ bhājanaṃ', that vessel. 'Tassa', for that householder. 'Atthāya', for his benefit. 'Hoti yathā', just as it becomes.

'Evaṃ tathā', likewise. 'Loke', in the world. 'Jarāya ca', the fire of aging. 'Maraṇena ca', and the fire of death. 'Ādīpito', are burning and blazing. 'Dānena', through the volition of giving. 'Nīharetheva', one should indeed carry out the utilities. 'Yaṃ dānaṃ', whatever gift. 'Dinnaṃ', is given. 'Hoti', it is. 'Taṃ', that gift alone. 'Sunīhataṃ', is called wealth that is well-carried out. 'Hoti', it becomes.

At that time, the Queen said to King Roruva, "Great King, do not worry. By the power of our offerings, the power of our virtue, and the power of our truth, we shall send flowers to invite the Paccekabuddhas, and when they arrive, we shall give all the offerings."

## The Invitation of the Paccekabuddhas

The King agreed, saying "Very well," and had it proclaimed throughout the city by beat of drum, "Let all who dwell in the city undertake the precepts." He himself, along with his retinue, observed the Uposatha. Having prepared great offerings, he took a golden casket filled with jasmine flowers, descended from the palace, and stood in the royal courtyard. Placing his five limbs upon the ground (prostrating), he paid homage facing the East. Having paid homage to the Arahants in the Eastern direction, he said:

"If there be any merit in us, may you have compassion on us and accept our alms." He then threw seven handfuls of flowers toward the East. Because there were no Paccekabuddhas in the East, they did not come the next day.

On the second day, he paid homage to the South. From that direction too, no Paccekabuddhas came. On the third day, he paid homage to the West. From the West too, no Paccekabuddhas came. On the fourth day, he paid homage to the North.

After paying homage, he threw seven handfuls of flowers, saying, "May the Paccekabuddhas who dwell in the Northern Himavanta accept our alms." The flowers traveled and fell beside the seven Paccekabuddhas in the Nandamūla Cave.

When those Paccekabuddhas reflected, they realized the King had invited them. The next day, the Sanghatthera (the Elder of the group) called the other Paccekabuddhas and said, "Sirs, King Roruva invites you. Do a favor for the King." The seven Paccekabuddhas then traveled through the air and descended at the palace gate.
448:
71. He who gives a gift to one who has attained the Dhamma, to a person who has achieved it through effort and energy; that mortal, having crossed the Vaitaraṇī river of Yama, reaches the divine realms.

72. Giving and war are said to be equal; even a few who are virtuous can defeat many. If one gives even a little with faith, by that alone he becomes happy in the hereafter.

73. Giving with discrimination is praised by the Sugata; those who are worthy of offerings here in the world of living beings—gifts given to them are of great fruit, like seeds sown in a good field.

74. He who wanders without harming living beings, and does no evil out of fear of others' blame; the wise praise the 'fearful' (of sin) there, not the 'brave' (bold in sin). For the virtuous, out of fear [of sin], do no evil.

75. By a low holy life, one is reborn as a Khattiya. By a medium one, godhood is attained. By the highest, one is purified.

76. Indeed, giving is praised in many ways, but the path of Dhamma is better than giving. For in the past, and even earlier, the wise reached Nibbāna through wisdom.

Upon seeing the Paccekabuddhas, the King was filled with joy. He paid homage to them, invited them up to the palace, made great offerings, and served them food. At the end of the meal, he invited them for the next day, and the next, continuing this for six days.

On the seventh day, he prepared an offering of all the requisites (parikkhāra). He had couches and stools adorned with the seven kinds of gems laid out. He placed all the requisites used by monks, such as the triple robes and umbrellas, before the seven Paccekabuddhas and said, "We offer all these requisites to you, Bhantes." At the end of the meal, both the King and the Queen stood paying homage.

## The Sanghatthera Preaches

Then, wishing to give a blessing (anumodanā) to the King and Queen, the Sanghatthera spoke.

After the Sanghatthera had given the blessing and advised the King, "Great King, be heedful," he flew into the air, split the roof of the palace in two, and returned to the Nandamūla Cave. The requisites given to him also flew with him and descended at the Nandamūla Cave. The entire bodies of the King and Queen were filled with joy.

## The Dhamma of the Paccekabuddhas

After the Sanghatthera had departed, the remaining Paccekabuddhas gave their blessings with these verses [71-76] and departed with their requisites just as the Sanghatthera had done.

Great King. 'Jantu', a being. 'Yo macco', that mortal. 'Dhammaladdhassa', to a person who has attained the Dhamma, starting from an Arahant down to a practitioner of insight (vipassanā) who has attained the Dhamma.
449:
Taking the best of the wealth acquired through energetic effort, one gives a gift. That mortal, having crossed over the Vaitaraṇī of Yama—the eight great hells and sixteen prominent hells—reaches the divine realms, the abodes of the gods.
## Giving and War
Great King, the wise say that giving and war are similar. Just as a few soldiers, being brave, conquer many, so too a few volitions of relinquishment (muñca-cetanā), being present, conquer many defilements such as stinginess. If one gives even a small object, believing in kamma and its results, by that very gift, that person becomes happy in the next life.
## Giving with Discrimination
Great King, the Buddhas praise a gift given after careful selection of the object and the recipient. In this world of living beings, there are worthy recipients (dakkhiṇeyya) such as the Buddha. Gifts given to these worthy recipients are like seeds sown in a fertile field; they yield great fruit.
Great King, one who lives without harming living beings out of compassion does not commit evil for fear of the blame of others. The virtuous praise one who fears blame. They do not praise one who is bold in the face of such blame. Indeed, it is out of fear of the blame of others that the virtuous do not commit evil.
## Three Kinds of Giving and Three Kinds of Results
Great King, through low holy conduct (brahmacariya)—which is merely abstaining from sexual intercourse in the schools of outside sectarians, or virtue practiced while longing for sensual pleasures in the Dispensation—one is reborn in the warrior-noble (khattiya) class. Through middling brahmacariya—which is the access concentration of jhāna in the schools of outside sectarians...
450:
...one reaches the state of a deity (devatta). Through superior brahmacariya—which is the eight attainments in the schools of outside sectarians, or the development of insight (vipassanā) leading to the fruit of Arahantship in the Dispensation—one is purified, being cleansed from sensual desire and the suffering of the round of rebirths.
## Samatha and Vipassanā
Great King, giving is indeed praised in many ways. However, the Dhamma-factor known as Samatha and Vipassanā is superior to giving. This is true: in the beginning of this Bhadda-kappa, wise and virtuous ones like Kassapa Buddha, and even earlier, wise and virtuous ones like Vessabhū Buddha, having developed Samatha and Vipassanā, attained Nibbāna.
Thus, the seven Paccekabuddhas, having preached the noble deathless Nibbāna to the king and exhorted him to be heedful, returned to their dwelling place in the manner described. The king, along with his chief queen, gave gifts, remained steadfast throughout his life, and upon passing away from kingship, filled the heavenly realms.
Conclusion of the Jātaka: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Monks, thus in the past, the wise gave gifts after careful selection," and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Paccekabuddhas attained Parinibbāna; the mother of Rāhula was Queen Samuddavijayā; and I myself was King Mahāroruva."
## Giving to Noble Recipients Leads to the Heavenly Realm
The Āditta Jātaka is concluded.
## 9. Aṭṭhāna Jātaka
## On the Ingratitude of Women
The Present Story: While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Aṭṭhāna Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Gangā kumudinī," concerning a monk who had become dissatisfied.
The All-Knowing Buddha asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha asked, "For what reason?" and the monk replied, "Bhante, I am dissatisfied due to the power of defilements."
451:
“Monk, women are ungrateful, they betray their friends, and they are not to be trusted. In the past, even when wise men gave a thousand pieces of money every day to please a woman, they could not win her heart. One day, when she did not receive the thousand pieces, she had him seized by the neck and thrown out. Thus, women are ungrateful; do not fall under the power of defilements because of such a woman.” Having said this, the Teacher brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the King’s son, named Prince Brahmadatta, and the son of the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī, named Prince Mahādhana, were childhood friends who played in the dust together. They learned their arts from the same teacher’s family. When the King passed away, the Prince ascended to the throne. The Treasurer’s son also remained in the King’s presence.

## The Treasurer’s Son and the Courtesan

In Bārāṇasī, there was a beautiful courtesan. She had attained great beauty and charm. The Treasurer’s son would give her a thousand pieces of money every day and enjoy her company. Even after his father passed away and he attained the position of Treasurer, he did not leave her. He continued to give her a thousand pieces every day and took delight in her.

## The Treasurer’s Son is Driven Out

The Treasurer’s son went to serve the King three times a day. One day, while he was conversing with the King, the sun set and it became dark. Leaving the palace, he thought, “There is no time to go home and come back; I will go straight to the courtesan’s house.” He dismissed his attendants and entered her house alone.

When the courtesan saw him, she asked, “My lord, have you brought the thousand pieces?” He replied, “My lady, it is very late today. Therefore, I did not go home but dismissed my men and came here alone. Tomorrow, I will give you two thousand pieces.”

The courtesan thought, “If I allow him today, he will come empty-handed on other days as well. If he does so, my wealth will decrease. I will not give him an opportunity now.”
452:
She then said to him, “My lord, we are courtesans; without being given a thousand pieces, there is no such thing as play. Go and bring the thousand pieces.” He pleaded repeatedly, “My lady, I will bring double tomorrow.”

The courtesan ordered her maidservants, “Do not allow this man to stand here and look at me. Seize him by the neck, throw him out, and shut the door.” Hearing this, the maidservants did as they were told.

## He Becomes an Ascetic

Then the Treasurer’s son thought, “I have spent eighty crores of wealth with this woman. Yet, seeing me empty-handed for just one day, she had me seized by the neck and thrown out. Women are indeed wicked, shameless, ungrateful, and they betray their friends.”

Reflecting on the faults of women, he became disillusioned. He gained the perception of loathsomeness and became weary of household life. “What is the use of household life to me? I will go forth and become an ascetic this very day.” Without returning home or seeing the King, he left the city and entered the forest. Building a hermitage by the banks of the Ganges, he attained jhānas and abhiññās, and lived there subsisting on wild roots and fruits.

## The Courtesan Follows to Invite Him Back

When the King did not see the Treasurer’s son, he asked, “Where is my friend?” The deed done by the courtesan became known throughout the city. Therefore, they informed the King of the matter, saying, “Great King, your friend, out of shame, did not even return home but entered the forest and must have become an ascetic.”

Hearing this, the King summoned the courtesan and asked, “Is it true that because you did not receive a thousand pieces for one day, you had my friend seized by the neck and thrown out?” “It is true, O King,” she replied. “You wicked woman! Go quickly to where my friend has gone and bring him back. If you do not bring him, your life is forfeit.”

Terrified by the King’s words, she mounted a chariot and left the city with a large retinue. Searching for his dwelling place, she heard of it and went there. She bowed to him and pleaded, “Venerable sir, forgive the fault I committed out of foolishness. I will not do such a thing again.” When he said, “Very well, I forgive you; I have no malice toward you,” she said, “If you forgive me, please mount the chariot with me. We shall go to the city. When we arrive, I will give you all the wealth in my house.”

Hearing her words, he said, “My lady, it is impossible to go with you now. But when that which should not be in this world comes to pass, then perhaps I might go.” He then spoke this first verse:

77. When the Ganges is still and covered with lilies,
And cuckoos become the color of a conch shell,
When the rose-apple tree bears palm fruit,
Then, perhaps, that time might be.

[The meaning is:] My lady, just as lily ponds remain covered with lilies, if the entire Great Ganges were to abandon its swift current and become still and covered with lilies, and if all cuckoos were to become white like conch shells, and if every rose-apple tree were to bear palm fruit—then at such a time, our reunion might indeed take place.
453:
78. When there shall be a triple cloak made of tortoise hair, a winter garment to be worn, then indeed it might be.
79. When there shall be a well-built watchtower made of mosquito legs, firm and unshakable, then indeed it might be.
80. When there shall be a well-made ladder made of rabbit horns for the purpose of ascending to heaven, then indeed it might be.
81. When mice, having climbed that ladder, shall eat the moon and cause Rahu to fall, then indeed it might be.
82. When a swarm of flies, having drunk from a jar of liquor and becoming intoxicated, shall make their dwelling in hot coals, then indeed it might be.
83. When a donkey, endowed with lips like the bimba fruit and a beautiful face, shall be skilled in dancing and singing, then indeed it might be.
84. When crows and owls, meeting in secret, shall consult together and love one another, then indeed it might be.
85. When an umbrella made of lotus leaves shall be very strong for the purpose of warding off the rain, then indeed it might be.
86. When a small bird shall take Mount Gandhamādana in its beak and fly away, then indeed it might be.
87. When a boy shall take a sea-faring ship, together with its machinery and all its banners, and go away with it, then indeed it might be.

He spoke these verses.

Dear sister, when there shall be a triple cloak made of tortoise hair—one woven with tortoise-hair flowers, one with tortoise-hair wool, and one with both—capable of being worn in the winter season, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when there shall be a well-built watchtower made of mosquito legs, strong enough to support a hundred men fighting upon it, firm and unshakable, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when there shall be a well-made ladder made of rabbit horns for the purpose of ascending to heaven, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when mice, having climbed that ladder of rabbit horns, shall eat the moon and cause Rahu to flee, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when a swarm of flies, having drunk from jars of liquor and becoming intoxicated, shall be able to make their dwelling in hot coals, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when a donkey, endowed with lips like the ripe bimba fruit and a beautiful face like a golden mirror, shall be skilled in dancing and singing, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when crows and owls, having gone to a secluded place, shall consult together and love each other's prosperity, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when an umbrella made of lotus leaves shall be very strong for the purpose of warding off the rain, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when a small bird shall take Mount Gandhamādana in its beak and fly away, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Dear sister, when a boy shall take a sea-faring ship, together with its machinery and all its banners and structures, and go away with it in his hand, then indeed, at that time, my union with you would certainly be.

Having heard these words, the King summoned the courtesan and asked, "Is it true that one day, not receiving a thousand coins, you dragged your friend by the neck and cast him out?" "It is true, O Great King," she replied. "Vile servant! Go quickly to where your friend is and bring him back. If you do not bring him, your life shall be no more," said the King.

Hearing the King's words and being afraid, the courtesan rode in a carriage with a large retinue, left the city, and searched for the merchant son's dwelling. Hearing of his location, she went there, paid homage, and pleaded, "Venerable sir, please forgive the offense I committed out of great foolishness; I will not do such a thing again." When he said, "Very well, I forgive you; I hold no grudge against you," she said, "Venerable sir, if you forgive me, please ride in the carriage with me; when we reach the city, I will give you all the wealth in my house."

## The Ascetic Does Not Follow
The merchant's son, hearing the courtesan's words, intended to say, "Sister, now I cannot go with you; if an impossible thing should happen in this world, then I might come, though I do not know."

## Never Following
Even after he said this, the courtesan again said, "Venerable sir, come, let us go." When he said, "We shall go," and she asked, "At what time shall we go?", he intended to say, "We shall go at such a time as this:"
454:
Thus, the Bodhisatta, considering these impossible things, spoke these eleven verses. Having heard these words, the courtesan paid homage to the Bodhisatta, returned to the city, informed the King of the matter, and begged for her life.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher (the Buddha) said, "Monks, women are thus ungrateful and treacherous to their friends," and after declaring the Truths, He identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). To identify the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the King, and I myself was the ascetic."

## Vipassanā and the Dhamma alone lead to Nibbāna.
Thus ends the Aṭṭhāna Jātaka.
455:
## 10. Dīpi Jātaka
## Pleasant Words are Fruitless with Fault-finders

The Teacher, the Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Dīpi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Khamanīyaṃ yāpanīyaṃ," while staying at the Veluvana Monastery, concerning a certain she-goat.

On one occasion, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was staying at the Giribbaja monastery, which was surrounded by mountains and had a single gate. His walking path was near the gate.

## With Manly Effort

At that time, goat-herds, thinking "Let the goats graze here," drove the herd into the mountain enclosure and stayed there playing. One day, when they were leaving in the evening and taking the goats with them, a she-goat, grazing far away, did not see the others leaving and was left behind.

A panther saw the she-goat coming out later and stood at the gate of the mountain enclosure, thinking, "I will eat her." The she-goat looked here and there and saw the panther. She thought, "This panther stands there because he wants to kill and eat me. If I run away, I will not survive. Today, I must act with manly courage." She raised her horns and charged swiftly towards the panther. While the panther was struggling, thinking "I'll catch her from here, I'll catch her from there," she escaped his grasp, ran swiftly, and entered the midst of the herd.

## Safe from Danger

Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw the actions of the she-goat and the panther. The next day, he went and informed the Buddha. He said, "Venerable Sir, in this way, that she-goat escaped from the panther due to her skill in means and her effort." The Buddha said, "Moggallāna, that panther could not catch her now. But in the past, he killed and ate her while she was crying out." Having said this, at the request of the Elder, He brought forth the past.
456:
88. "Is it bearable? Is it supportable? Uncle, are you well? My mother told me to ask if you are well. We only wish for your happiness."

She spoke this first verse.

Uncle, are you well? Is it bearable? Is it supportable? My mother said, "Ask if you are well." We only desire your happiness.

89. "O she-goat, you came treading upon and striking my tail. Do you think that today you shall be released by calling me 'Uncle'?"

She spoke this second verse.

She-goat, you came treading upon and striking my tail. Do you think that today you shall be released by calling me 'Uncle'?

91. "As far as the four islands extend, with the oceans and mountains, so far does my tail encompass. How could you have avoided it?"

She spoke this fourth verse.

She-goat, as many as the four islands with the oceans and mountains there are, my tail encompasses and stays in that much space. How could you have avoided it?

In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy family. Upon reaching maturity, he renounced sensual pleasures, became an ascetic, attained jhānas and supernormal powers, and lived long in the Himalayas. He went to Rājagaha for salt and vinegar and lived in a leaf-hut in that same Giribbaja.

As before, while goat-herds were grazing the goats, one day a panther stood at the gate to eat a she-goat that came out late.

## Coaxing the Enemy

The she-goat saw the panther and thought, "Today my life is at an end. Indeed, I should make an effort for the sake of my life. By some means, I will exchange pleasant greetings with this panther, soften his heart, and protect my life." Thinking thus, she approached from afar, exchanging greetings with the panther:

## Finding Fault

Hearing those words, the panther thought, "This she-goat wants to deceive me by calling me 'Uncle'. She does not know my fierce nature."

## I Did Not Tread on Your Tail

Hearing his words, the she-goat said, "Uncle, do not say such a thing," and spoke the third verse:

90. "You are sitting facing the east, and I have come towards your face. Your tail is behind you; how then could I have trodden upon it?"

She spoke this third verse.

Uncle, you are sitting facing the east. I have come towards your face. How then could I tread upon your tail which is behind you?

## My Tail is Very Long

Then the panther said to the she-goat, "She-goat, what are you saying? There is no place where my tail does not reach."

## I Came from the Sky

Hearing this, the she-goat thought, "This wicked panther is not moved by pleasant words. I shall speak to him as an opponent."

## My Prey Has Fled

Then [the panther said], "She-goat, seeing you coming through the sky, all the beasts have fled. You have destroyed my food."
457:
92. "My mother, father, and brothers told me this before: 'The tail of the wicked leopard is long.' Thus, I have come through the air."

She spoke this fifth verse.

(In the past, my mother, father, and brothers told me this. Having heard from my relatives about the length of your tail, I, avoiding your tail, have come through the air, the sky.)

93. "Seeing you coming in the sky, O she-goat, the herd of deer fled; my prey has been ruined by you."

He spoke this sixth verse.

(O she-goat, seeing you coming in the sky, the herd of deer fled. You have ruined my food.)

94. "While the she-goat was thus wailing, the blood-drinker crushed her neck. There is no well-spoken word in the wicked."

95. "In the wicked, there is neither reason, nor Dhamma, nor well-spoken words. One should apply effort against the wicked; he does not delight in the virtuous."

He preached these two verses.

(Monks, the leopard, who drinks the blood and eats the flesh of beings, crushed the neck of the she-goat while she was thus wailing. In a person who is wicked, there is no benefit in well-spoken words. In a wicked person, reason does not exist. The nature of Dhamma does not exist. Good speech does not exist. Monks, one should apply effort against a wicked person. That wicked person does not delight in or love the well-spoken words of the virtuous.)

## Being Eaten

The she-goat, hearing those words and fearing death, was unable to find any other reason and lamented, "Uncle, do not do such a cruel deed; give me my life." But the leopard, while the she-goat was lamenting, seized her by the neck, killed her, and ate her.

The Omniscient Buddha, having attained Enlightenment, wishing to admonish the monks, said:

The ascetic saw all the actions of the she-goat and the leopard.
458:
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the she-goat was the same she-goat, the leopard was the same leopard, but the ascetic was I myself."

## Seeking Faults, Answering Him, No Excuses Should Be Made

The Dīpi Jātaka is finished.

Summary of the Jātakas:
Kaccāni, Aṭṭhasadda, Sulasa, Sumangala, Gangamāla, Cetiya, Indriya, Āditta, Aṭṭhāna, and Dīpi—these are the ten in the Eightfold Book (Aṭṭhakanipāta).

The commentary on the Aṭṭhakanipāta is finished.

## 1. Gijjha Jātaka
## Destruction due to Disobeying Parents' Words

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Gijjha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Pari-saṅkupatho nāma', concerning a certain monk who was difficult to admonish.

A certain young man of good family, having ordained in the Sasana that leads out of suffering, was admonished by his teachers, preceptors, and fellow practitioners who desired his welfare: 'You should advance in this way, retreat in this way, look ahead in this way, look aside in this way, bend your limbs in this way, stretch them in this way, dress in this way, robe yourself in this way, and hold the alms-bowl in this way. Having received only enough food for sustenance, you should consume it only after reflection. You should be one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, who knows moderation in eating, and who is devoted to wakefulness. You should know the duties for visitors (āgantuka-vatta), the duties for those departing (gamika-vatta), these fourteen Khandhaka duties, and the eighty great duties (mahāvatta). In those duties, you should conduct yourself well. These are the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga); you should undertake and practice these thirteen ascetic practices.' When thus admonished, he was difficult to speak to. He was impatient and did not accept the instruction respectfully.

'I do not speak to you; do not you speak to me. I alone shall know my own benefit or harm,' he said, making himself unadmonishable.

Then, knowing the state of that monk being difficult to admonish, the monks sat in the Dhamma Hall discussing his lack of virtue. The Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered here?' When they replied, 'We are gathered for such and such a discussion,' He had that monk summoned and asked:

'Monk, is it true that you are difficult to admonish?' When the monk replied, 'It is true,' the Buddha said, 'Monk, why do you not listen to the words of those who desire your welfare, having ordained in such a liberating Sasana? In the past also, by not following the words of the wise, you were ground to powder in the mouth of the Veramba wind.' Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a vulture on Mount Gijjhakūṭa. His son, named Supatta, the king of vultures, was the leader of many thousands of vultures and was possessed of great strength. He looked after his parents. Because of his strength, he flew very far. Then his father admonished him, 'Son, you must not go beyond such and such a place.' Although he said, 'Very well,' one day...
460:
1. The path called Parisaṅkupatha is the ancient vulture path. There lived a vulture who supported his aged parents. He brought them python fat in abundance.

2. The father spoke to the son, knowing he flew high—the one named Supatta, endowed with strength, majestic, and a far-flyer.

3. "When, dear son, you perceive the earth floating like a lotus leaf upon the water, encircled by the ocean like a circular wheel, then, dear son, turn back; do not go beyond that."

4. "You have flown up with speed, a strong bird, the best of winged ones. Looking down, with curved neck, you see mountains and forests."

5. The vulture saw the earth just as he had heard from his father, encircled by the ocean like a circular wheel.

6. But he, overstepping that, flew even higher. Then the sharp crests of the Veramba winds struck the strong bird.

7. The one who had gone too far was unable to return again. The bird met with destruction, falling under the power of the Veramba winds.

8. His children, his wife, and others who depended on him—all met with destruction because of the bird who did not follow advice.

9. Even so in this world, one who does not understand the words of elders, who wanders beyond limits, arrogant, like the vulture who transgressed the instruction, he indeed meets with destruction, having failed to follow the elders' teaching.

"In the past, you also did not listen to the words of the wise and were crushed to pieces in the crest of the Veramba winds," the Teacher said, and then he brought forth the past story.

In the past, the Bodhisatta was born in the vulture species on Mount Gijjhakūṭa. The Bodhisatta's son was a vulture king named Supatta. That vulture king had a following of over a thousand vultures. He was endowed with great strength and supported his parents. Because of his strength, he flew to very distant places.

## Disregarding the Parents' Words

At that time, the father admonished Supatta the vulture, saying, "Dear son, you must not go beyond such and such a place." Supatta the vulture agreed, saying, "Very well." One day, after it had rained, he flew up with the other vultures. Leaving the rest behind, he flew to an extremely high altitude, reached the crest of the Veramba winds, and was crushed to pieces.

The All-Knowing Buddha, wishing to illustrate this matter after becoming enlightened, said:

## The Veramba Winds

461:

## Follow the Words of Advice

"Monk, because of this, do not be like the vulture; listen to the words of those who desire your welfare," the All-Knowing Buddha admonished. From the time the Buddha admonished him, that monk became easy to speak to (obedient).

To conclude the Jātaka, the All-Knowing Buddha brought forth this Dhamma teaching and identified the birth: "At that time, the difficult-to-admonish vulture was this difficult-to-admonish monk. The father of the vulture was I, the Buddha."

## Desiring Welfare, Heed the Advice

The Gijjha Jātaka ends.
