## 2. Kosambiya Jātaka
## On Why One Should Not Engage in Quarrels and Disputes

**The Story of the Present**
While residing at the Ghositārāma monastery near the city of Kosambī, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, spoke this Kosambiya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Puthu saddo," concerning the monks of Kosambī who were engaged in quarreling.

The detailed account of this story is found in the Kosambaka-khandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga.

## Whether an Offense Was Committed
In this Kosambiya Jātaka, the summary is as follows: At that time, two monks lived in the same monastery—one was an expert in the Vinaya (Vinayadhara) and the other was an expert in the Suttas (Suttantika). One day, the Sutta expert, after attending to his bodily needs, left some leftover rinsing water in a vessel in the washroom.

Later, the Vinaya expert entered the washroom, saw the water, and upon coming out, asked the Sutta expert, "Friend, did you leave that water?" "Yes, friend," replied the Sutta expert. "Friend, do you not know that leaving leftover water in the vessel constitutes an offense?" asked the Vinaya expert.

"Friend, I did not know," said the Sutta expert. "Friend, whether you knew it or not, there is an offense in leaving this leftover rinsing water," said the Vinaya expert.

"Friend, if that is so, I shall atone for that offense," said the Sutta expert. The Vinaya expert then said, "Friend, if it was done without intention and through forgetfulness, there is no offense."

## The Monks Are Divided
The Sutta expert then held the view that it was "no offense." However, the Vinaya expert told his own disciples, "This Sutta expert monk does not even know when he has committed an offense." The disciples of the Vinaya expert, seeing the disciples of the Sutta expert, said, "Your preceptor has committed an offense and does not even realize it."

The disciples of the Sutta expert went and reported this to their preceptor. The Sutta expert said, "This Vinaya expert previously said it was 'no offense,' and now he says it is an 'offense.' This Vinaya expert is speaking a falsehood." The disciples of the Sutta expert then went and said, "Your preceptor is a liar."

In this way, they increased the quarrel among themselves. Later, the Vinaya expert, finding an opportunity, performed an act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) against the Sutta expert for his refusal to see the offense. From that time on, the lay donors of the four requisites for these two monks also split into two factions. The nuns who received their exhortations also split into two factions.
463:
The guardian deities also split into two factions. All the worldling deities up to the Brahma realm, who were friends and associates of those deities, also split into two factions. This commotion reached as far as the Akanittha Brahma realm.

## Even the Buddha Could Not Reconcile Them
Then, a certain monk approached the Buddha and reported the views of the monks: the view of the "suspenders" that "this Sutta expert monk was suspended by a legal act," and the view of the "followers of the suspended" that "he was suspended by an illegal act." He also reported how the followers of the suspended monk continued to surround him and follow him, even though they were forbidden by the suspenders.

The Omniscient Buddha sent word twice, saying, "Let them be united and harmonious." Hearing the reply, "Venerable Sir, they do not wish to be united," he went to those monks for the third time, knowing the Sangha was split. He explained the faults in performing the act of suspension to the suspenders and the faults in not seeing the offense to the suspended monks, and then he departed.

Again, hearing that they were performing the Uposatha and other rites within the same boundary in Kosambī while still living in a state of quarrel, the Buddha went there and said, "Enough, monks, do not quarrel," and gave further instructions.

A certain monk who was a speaker of Dhamma (Dhammavādī), not wishing the Buddha to be troubled, said, "Venerable Sir, let the Buddha, the Lord of Dhamma, wait. Venerable Sir, let the Buddha live unconcerned, devoted to the bliss of the present life. We shall be known by this quarrel, dispute, and contention."

When this was said, the Buddha said, "Monks, I shall tell you a story of the past."

**The Story of the Past**
In the past, there was a king of Kāsi named Brahmadatta in the city of Bārāṇasī. The Buddha told how King Brahmadatta seized the kingdom of King Dīghīti of Kosala, who lived in disguise and was eventually killed; and how Prince Dīghāvu, when he had the chance to take the king's life, spared him instead, and from that time on, King Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu became united and harmonious.

He exhorted them, saying, "Monks, even for those kings who carry weapons, such patience and gentleness existed. You, monks, have gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya. Therefore, you should truly be patient and gentle."

## The Teaching of Peace
For the second and third time, he forbade them, saying, "Enough, monks, do not quarrel." Seeing that the monks would not comply, he thought, "These empty men are completely possessed; it is not easy to convince them."

10. Much noise is made by the common folk; no one thinks himself a fool.
When the Sangha is being split, they do not think of anything else.

11. Forgetful of themselves, they pose as wise, speaking only what comes to their mouths.
They talk as much as they wish; they do not know by what they are led.

12. "He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me."
In those who harbor such thoughts, hatred is never appeased.

13. "He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me."
In those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred is appeased.

14. For never in this world is hatred appeased by hatred.
It is appeased by non-hatred; this is an eternal law.

Seeing the monks who did not practice accordingly, he said, "These monks, who are empty of the Path and Fruit, have minds that are overcome by unwholesome states."
464:
"...Like a king leaving a conquered kingdom,
One should wander alone like a Matanga elephant in the forest.
There is no companionship with a fool.
One should wander alone and do no evil,
Unconcerned like a Matanga elephant in the forest."
He preached these verses.

The assembly of monks (samajano), being of the same nature, has a loud noise (puthusaddo). Not a single monk (koci) thinks (na maññatha), "I am a fool (bālo)." While the Sangha (saṅghasmiṃ) is being greatly (bhiyyo) divided (bhijjamānasmiṃ), they do not consider (na amaññaruṃ) any other reason (aññaṃ), such as "The Sangha is divided because of me."

Those with lost mindfulness (parimuṭṭhā), pretending to be wise (paṇḍitābhāsā), whose range is only words (vācāgocarā)—not focusing on the noble Dhamma such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)—speak (bhāṇino) as much as they wish to open their mouths (mukhāyāmaṃ icchantī). They do not know (na vidū) that the quarrel (yena nītā) which leads to shamelessness is an evil.

"These men, empty of the Path and Fruit, are not easy to admonish." Having said this, he departed.

The next day, after returning from the alms-round in the village, he rested a little in the Gandhakuti, put away his bedding, took his bowl and robes, and standing in the air in the midst of the Sangha:

15. "Others do not realize that we here must perish. Those who realize this, their quarrels cease."

16. "Even those who cut bones, take life, steal cattle, horses, and wealth, and plunder the kingdom—even they can have concord.
Why should it not be so for you?"

17. "If one finds a prudent companion, a fellow-traveler who lives well and is wise, overcoming all dangers, one should wander with him, joyful and mindful."

18. "If one does not find a prudent companion, a fellow-traveler who lives well and is wise..."

19. "Wandering alone is better..."
465:
## One Should Not Retaliate

"He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me"—those who harbor such thoughts, their hatred is not stilled.

## No Hatred, Hatred Ceases

"He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me"—those who do not harbor such thoughts, their hatred is stilled.

Truly, in this world, hatred is never stilled by hatred. By non-hatred alone is it stilled. This is an eternal law.

Others (fools) do not realize in the midst of this Sangha while quarreling: "We are following the path to the realm of Yama (death)." Those who do realize this, their quarrels cease.

Even kings whose parents' bones were cut, whose parents' lives were taken, whose cattle, horses, and wealth were stolen, who plundered the kingdom—even they can have concord. Why should it not be so for you?
466:
"If one finds a prudent companion, a fellow-traveler who lives well and is wise, overcoming all dangers, one should wander with him, joyful and mindful."

"If one does not find a prudent companion, a fellow-traveler who lives well and is wise, like a king leaving a conquered kingdom, one should wander alone like a Matanga elephant in the forest."

## No Companionship with Fools

"Wandering alone is better; there is no companionship with a fool. One should wander alone and do no evil, unconcerned like a Matanga elephant in the forest."

The All-Knowing Buddha, having spoken thus, was unable to make those monks harmonious. Therefore, he went to the village of Bālakaloṇaka and taught the benefit of solitude to Elder Bhagu. From there, he went to the dwelling of the three clansmen and taught the benefit of living in harmony. Then he went to the Pālileyyaka forest and stayed for three months. Instead of returning to Kosambī, he went to Sāvatthī.

The lay devotees of Kosambī thought: "These monks of Kosambī have caused us much harm. The Blessed One left because he was harassed by them. We will not pay respects or give alms to them. Thus they will either leave, cease their enmity, or reconcile with the Blessed One." They acted accordingly.

The monks, oppressed by this punishment, went to Sāvatthī and asked for the Blessed One's forgiveness.

The All-Knowing Buddha identified the birth: "King Suddhodana was the father, Mahāmāyā was the mother, and I was Prince Dīghāvu."

## Many Monks, Split, Laypeople Should Guard

The Kosambiya Jataka is finished.
467:
## 3. Mahāsuva Jātaka

## Not Abandoning a Friend Even in Poverty

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Mahāsuva Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Dumo yadā hoti," concerning a certain monk.

That monk, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher, lived in a forest near an obscure border village in the Kosala country. The villagers of that border village were unable to offer him excellent alms-food.

Although he had a suitable lodging, he suffered due to the food and was unable to attain the Path or Fruition. Then, after three months had passed, he came to pay homage to the Fully Enlightened Buddha. The Teacher greeted him kindly and asked, "Monk, are you not suffering for lack of alms-food? Was your lodging suitable?" The monk informed Him of the matter.

## Be Content with Whatever is Received

The Fully Enlightened Buddha, knowing that the monk's lodging was suitable, said: "Monk, when a monk has a suitable lodging, he should abandon greedy behavior, consume whatever he receives, and practice the Dhamma of a recluse with contentment."

"Wise ones of old, even when born in the animal kingdom, when their dwelling tree became dry, they ate the wood dust, abandoned greedy behavior, and being content, did not break the law of friendship and did not go elsewhere. Why then did you abandon a suitable lodging because the alms-food was meager and coarse?" Having said this, at the monk's request, He brought forth the past.

In the past, in an Udumbara (fig) forest on the banks of the Ganges in the Himavanta, lived many hundreds of thousands of parrots. There, a certain parrot king, when the fruits of his dwelling tree were exhausted, would eat whatever remained—whether sprouts, leaves, bark, or rind—and drink the water of the Ganges. Being supremely few in wishes and content, he did not go elsewhere. Due to the power of his virtue of being few in wishes and content, Sakka's abode trembled. Sakka, reflecting and seeing him, dried up that tree with his power to test him. The tree became a mere stump, full of holes, and stood as if being struck when the wind blew. Wood dust came out of its holes. The parrot king ate that dust, drank the water of the Ganges, and without going elsewhere, sat on the Udumbara stump, disregarding the wind and heat. Sakka, knowing his supreme contentment, thought, "I will make him speak on the virtue of friendship, grant him a boon,
468:
and make the Udumbara tree bear immortal fruit before I return." He then took the form of a king of geese, with Sujā, the Asura maiden, preceding him. He went to that Udumbara forest, perched on a branch of a nearby tree, and, initiating a conversation with him, spoke the first verse:

20. Dumo yadā hoti phalūpapanno,
Bhuñjanti naṃ vihaṅgamā sampatantā.
Khīṇanti ñatvāna dumaṃ phalaccaye,
Disodisaṃ yanti tato vihaṅgamā.

He spoke this first verse. 

Suvarāja, O King of Parrots. Dumo, the tree. Yadā, when. Phalūpapanno, is full of fruit. Hoti, it is. Tadā, then. Vihaṅgamā, the birds. Naṃ, that tree. Sampatantā, flying from branch to branch. Bhuñjanti, they eat. Khīṇanti, that the fruit is exhausted. Ñatvāna, having known. Dumaṃ phalaccaye-phalaccayena, because the tree's fruit is gone. Vihaṅgamā, the birds. Tato, from that tree. Disodisaṃ, to various directions. Yanti, they fly away.

21. Cara cārikaṃ lohitatuṇḍa mā mari,
Kiṃ tvaṃ suva sukkhadumamhi jhāyasi.
Tadiṅgha maṃ brūhi vasantasannibha,
Kasmā suva sukkhadumaṃ na riñcasi.

He spoke this second verse.

Lohitatuṇḍa, you with the red beak. Suva, parrot. Cārikaṃ, travel to another place. Cara, go. Mā mari, do not die. Tvaṃ, you. Kiṃ, why. Sukkhadumamhi, at the dry tree. Jhāyasi, do you pine away? Vasantasannibha, you whose color is like the dark green forest in the rainy season. Suva, parrot. Taṃ, you. Iṅgha, I urge. Tvaṃ, you. Maṃ, to me. Brūhi, speak. Kasmā, why. Sukkhadumaṃ, the dry tree. Na riñcasi, do you not leave?

Wise ones of old, even when born in the animal kingdom, when their dwelling tree became dry, they ate the dust, abandoned greedy behavior, and being content, did not break the law of friendship and did not go elsewhere.
469:
22. Those who are truly friends to their friends, O Swan, in times of life-threatening danger, in sorrow and in joy, they do not abandon them whether their means are exhausted or not; for the virtuous follow the Dhamma of the righteous.

23. I am one of those righteous ones, O Swan; this tree is both my kinsman and my friend. I cannot bear to abandon it for the sake of my own life; knowing it is barren, to leave it would not be the Dhamma.

He spoke these two verses.

O Haṃsa, King of Swans. Those who are friends to their friends. That friend, in sorrow and in joy. Even at the cost of life. Remembering the Dhamma of the virtuous. The virtuous ones. That friend. Whether their wealth is exhausted. Or whether their wealth is not yet exhausted. They do not abandon.

O Haṃsa, King of Swans. I am one among those virtuous ones. This fig tree is my kinsman and my friend. I, who desire to sustain my life, knowing that the fruits are exhausted, am unable to abandon this fig tree. This abandonment is not the Dhamma of the virtuous.

24. Well done! Friendship has been proven; love, intimacy, and companionship. If you delight in this Dhamma, you are worthy of praise by the wise.

25. I grant you a boon, O Parrot, bird whose wings are your vehicle. Choose a boon, O curved-necked one, whatever your heart desires.

He spoke these two verses.

O Parrot. Being a friend is good. The state of living together as friends and companionship is good. If you delight in that nature of a beloved and respected friend. You are worthy of praise by the wise.

O bird whose wings are your vehicle, who travels through the sky. O Parrot with a curved neck. Whatever boon you desire in your mind. I shall give it to you. Ask for the boon you wish.

"Why do you, while consuming the alms-food, abandon the suitable monastery saying that the food is coarse?" Having said this, being entreated by that monk, the Teacher brought forth the past.

In the past, in a certain fig tree by the Ganges in the Himalayas, many hundreds of parrots lived. Among those parrots, one parrot king, when the fruits of the fig tree where he lived were exhausted, ate whatever shoots, leaves, bark, and crust remained. Drinking water from the Ganges, he remained there, content with supreme fewness of wishes, and did not go elsewhere. Because of the parrot king's virtue of having few wishes and being easily satisfied, Sakka's throne trembled.

## The Contented Parrot

When Sakka reflected, he saw the parrot king and, in order to test him, made the tree wither by his power. The fig tree became a mere stump. Having large and small holes, it made a sound like a musical instrument when struck by the wind. Dust came out from the holes of that fig tree.

Eating that dust and drinking water from the Ganges, the parrot king did not go elsewhere, but remained at the stump of the fig tree, regardless of wind, sun, or heat.

## The Tree is Dead

Sakka, knowing the parrot king's fewness of wishes, thought, "I will have him preach the virtues of the Dhamma of friends, grant him a boon, make the fig tree bear ambrosial fruit, and then return." Disguised as a swan, with the Asura maiden named Sujā in front, he went to the fig tree grove, perched on a branch of a nearby tree, and desiring to start a conversation with the parrot king—

Having said this, and then to urge the parrot king—

## One Should Not Abandon a Friend

Then, the parrot king, wishing to say, "I do not abandon this tree because I am grateful," said—

## I Shall Grant a Boon

Sakka, hearing the parrot's words, was pleased and, wishing to praise him and grant a boon, said—

## May This Tree Live Again

Hearing those words, the parrot king, wishing to accept the boon, spoke this seventh verse:

26. If you, O Swan, would grant me a boon, may this tree regain its life. May it stand beautiful, possessed of branches and fruit, flourishing with new leaves, and sweet for those who seek its honeyed fruit.

O Haṃsa, King of Swans. If you would grant me a boon. May this fig tree regain its life once more. May that fig tree, being endowed with branches, being endowed with fruit, having tender leaves flourishing all around, and having sweet fruit like honey for those who seek it, stand beautiful.
470:
27. "See this, friend, this magnificent fruiting tree;
May you be together with this Udumbara tree.
May it stand beautiful, possessed of branches,
Fruiting, flourishing, and having sweet fruits like honey."

Sakka spoke this eighth verse. 
Friend Parrot King, look at that noble Udumbara tree which is full of fruit. May your dwelling be together with this Udumbara tree. May that Udumbara tree stand beautiful, being possessed of branches, being full of fruit, being covered with lush new leaves on all sides, having sweet fruits like honey, and being graceful.

28. "Thus, Sakka, may you be happy,
Together with all your kinsmen,
Just as I am happy today,
Having seen the fruiting tree."

He spoke this ninth verse. 
King Sakka, just as I am happy today having seen the Udumbara tree full of fruit, in the same way, may you be happy together with all your kinsmen.

## The Udumbara Tree Flourishes Again
At that time, Sakka, wishing to grant a boon to the Parrot King—
Having spoken thus, he set aside his disguise as a goose, and showing his own power and that of Sujā, he took water from the Ganges with his hand and sprinkled it upon the Udumbara stump. At that moment, the Udumbara tree, well-covered with branches and twigs and bearing sweet fruit, arose and stood endowed with grace like a mountain of pure gems.

## May You Be Happy
The Parrot King, seeing that Udumbara tree, was filled with joy and, wishing to praise Sakka—
Sakka also, having granted the boon and made the Udumbara tree bear immortal fruits, went back to his own place together with Sujā.
To clarify this matter, the Blessed One, after attaining Enlightenment, spoke this final verse:

30. "Having given the boon to the parrot,
And having made the tree fruitful,
He departed with his wife,
To the Nandana Grove of the gods."

Monks, Sakka, having given the boon to the parrot and having made the Udumbara tree fruitful, departed with his wife to the Nandana Grove of the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

Conclusion: The Blessed One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, "Monks, in this way, the wise ones of old, even when born in the animal kingdom, were free from wandering out of greed. Why do you, having gone forth in such a Dispensation, wander out of greed? Go and live in that very place." Having thus spoken the meditation subject to that monk, He identified the Jātaka.
That monk went to that place, and while developing insight, he attained Arhatship.
As for how the Jātaka was identified: "At that time, Anuruddha was Sakka, and I myself was the Parrot King."

## Contentment and Patience bring True Happiness
Thus ends the Mahāsuvajātaka.
471:
30. There are trees with green leaves, many trees with various fruits.
Why does the parrot's mind delight in a dry, hollow tree?
31. We have enjoyed its fruits for many numerous years.
Even knowing it is fruitless, our love remains as before.

O bird, what fault do you see in leaving?
33. Those who associate for the sake of fruit and abandon it when it is fruitless,
They are wise only for their own benefit, unwise, and partial to themselves.
34. Good is the friendship made, the companionship, and the intimacy.
If you delight in this Dhamma, you are praiseworthy among the wise.

Like a poor man who has found a treasure, I would rejoice again and again.

Its branches grew, providing cool and delightful shade.

He departed with his wife to the Nandana Grove of the gods.

He spoke these verses.

While there are many trees that reach into the earth and are covered with dark green leaves and bear many fruits, why does the parrot's mind always delight in this dry Udumbara tree that makes a sound like a musical instrument when the wind blows?

For many years, numbering more than one, we have eaten the fruit of this Udumbara tree. Even knowing it is now without fruit, that same love exists just as it did before.

Birds, who are twice-born, leave and abandon an Udumbara tree that is dry, hollow, leafless, and fruitless. O Parrot King, what fault do you see in the act of leaving?

O King of Geese, those birds who associate with a place for the sake of fruit and abandon it saying it is fruitless, those birds are wise only for their own benefit and are not wise for the benefit of others; they fall only on their own side.

## 4. Cūḷasuvajātaka
## One Should Not Follow the Realm of Greed
Regarding the present story, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, taught this Cūḷasuvajātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Santi rukkhā," while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, concerning the Veranjā section.

When the All-Knowing Buddha, having spent the rainy season in Veranjā, gradually arrived at the city of Sāvatthī, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the All-Knowing Buddha, though a delicate noble and a delicate Buddha, and endowed with great psychic power, was invited by the Veranjā Brahmin. While staying there for the three months of the rainy season, being obstructed by Māra, he did not receive even a single day's alms from the Veranjā Brahmin. Yet, abandoning wandering out of greed, he sustained himself for the three months with a measure of ground barley and did not go elsewhere. Oh, how wonderful is the fewness of wishes and the contentment of the All-Knowing Buddhas!"

The All-Knowing Buddha came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," He said, "Monks, it is not wonderful that the Buddha has now abandoned wandering out of greed; in the past, even when born in the animal kingdom, I abandoned wandering out of greed." Having been requested by the monks, He brought forth the past.

The entire past story should be understood in the same way as the previous one.

## Not Abandoning a Friend
Parrot King, the love that exists among friends is good. Association through friendship and intimacy is good. If you delight in that Dhamma, you are indeed praiseworthy by the wise.

## I Will Give a Boon
O Parrot, who has wings as a vehicle, who travels through the sky, and has a curved neck, I give you a boon. Whatever boon you desire in your heart, ask for that boon.
472:
## May the Tree Flourish

O King of Swans! If I were to see that tree with leaves and fruit, I would rejoice again and again, just as a poor man rejoices upon finding a treasure.

Then Sakka, taking ambrosia, sprinkled the tree. Its branches flourished, and it provided cool and delightful shade.

## May You Also Be Happy

O Sakka, may you be happy along with all your kinsmen, just as I am happy today, having seen the tree bearing fruit.

Sakka, having granted a boon to the parrot and made the tree fruitful, departed with his wife to the Nandana Grove of the gods.
473:
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time Sakka was Anuruddha, and I myself was the Parrot King."

## Great Gratitude, Places, Should Not Be Shunned

The Cūḷasuva Jātaka ends.

## 5. Haritaca Jātaka

## Sensual Desire Destroys the Wise

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Haritaca Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sutaṃ metaṃ mahābrahme," concerning a dissatisfied monk.

Having seen an adorned woman, the monk became dissatisfied, with long hair, long nails, and body hair, wishing to return to lay life. When his teachers and preceptors brought him to the Buddha against his will, the All-Knowing Buddha asked, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?"

When the monk replied, "It is true, O Blessed One," the Buddha asked, "For what reason?" The monk answered, "Because of sensual desire after seeing an adorned woman, O Blessed One." The Buddha then said, "Monk, what is called sensual desire destroys virtue, is not delightful, and leads to rebirth in hell.

How could this sensual desire not defile someone like you? A great wind that can topple Mount Sineru has no shame before an old, withered leaf. Relying on this sensual desire, even great men who were following the ancient path of the Bodhisattas for the sake of Omniscience, and who had attained the five superknowledges and eight meditative attainments, were unable to maintain mindfulness and lost their jhāna." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in a Brahmin family with eighty crores of wealth in a certain market town.

## Haritaca the Hermit

Because of his golden complexion, they named the Bodhisatta "Haritaca Kumāra." When Haritaca Kumāra reached the age of maturity, he went to Takkasilā to learn the arts. After establishing his household and upon the death of his parents, he looked at his wealth and thought:

"Only the wealth is apparent; those who created the wealth are no longer seen. I too must eventually be crushed in the jaws of death."
474:
Fearing the danger of death, he gave great alms, entered the Himalayas, and became a hermit. On the seventh day, he attained the five superknowledges and eight meditative attainments. He lived there for a long time, subsisting on forest roots and fruits. Later, he descended from the mountains to seek salt and vinegar and eventually reached Vārāṇasī. He stayed in the royal garden and, the following day, while wandering for alms in Vārāṇasī, he arrived at the palace gate.

## Revered by the King

The King, seeing the hermit Haritaca, felt a heart full of faith. He invited him in, seated him on the royal throne under the white umbrella, and offered him various foods of excellent flavor. At the end of the appreciation talk, the King, being exceedingly pleased, asked, "Venerable Sir, where are you staying?"

When the hermit replied, "Great King, I am looking for a place to stay," the King said, "Very well, Venerable Sir." After breakfast, the King took the hermit Haritaca to the garden, had places for the night and day prepared, and appointed the gardener as his attendant. Then, having paid homage, the King departed.

## Wrongdoing with the Queen

From that time on, the Bodhisatta always ate at the King's palace and lived in that garden for twelve years. Then one day, the King, as he was going to suppress a rebellion in the border region, entrusted the Bodhisatta to the Queen, saying, "Do not neglect our field of merit."

From then on, the Queen served the Bodhisatta with her own hands. One day, the Queen had prepared the food, and as the Bodhisatta was late, she bathed in scented water, dressed in fine, smooth garments, and lay on a small couch near the lion-window, letting the breeze strike her body.

The Bodhisatta, properly dressed and carrying his alms bowl, arrived through the air at the lion-window. When the Queen heard the sound of the Bodhisatta's bark-cloth robe and rose quickly, her fine garment slipped from her body. The sight of the woman's body struck the Bodhisatta's eyes.
475:
40. "I have heard this, O Great Brahma: Harita enjoys sensual pleasures. Is this word empty, or do you live pure?"

He spoke this first verse. 

O Great Brahma, venerable one who is like a Great Brahma. Harita, the ascetic Haritaca. Do you live pure? I have heard this word that you enjoy sensual pleasures. Is that word false? How is it? Do you live pure?

41. "It is so, O Great King, just as you have heard. I have entered a wrong path, infatuated by delusive things."

He spoke this second verse.

Great King. Just as you have heard the word, it is true as heard. I, being infatuated by the sensual pleasures that cause delusion, have reached a wrong path.

42. "What is the use of subtle wisdom that thinks well, if it cannot dispel the lust that has arisen in the mind?"

He spoke this third verse.

Venerable sir. Why is the mind unable to dispel the lust that has arisen through such wisdom? If it is unable to dispel it, what is the use of that subtle wisdom which thinks of good benefits?

At that time, the defilements that had remained dormant within for a vast period of two hundred million years arose like a cobra sleeping in a basket and obscured the Bodhisatta's jhāna. Because the Bodhisatta was unable to maintain mindfulness, he took the Queen's hand. At that moment, they were screened by a curtain.

The Bodhisatta engaged in the ways of worldlings with the Queen, and after eating, he went to the park. From that day onwards, he did the same every day. Haritaca the ascetic's engagement in the ways of worldlings with the Queen became well-known throughout the city.

## The Ministers' Report
The ministers submitted a report to the King, saying, "Great King, the ascetic Haritaca acts in this manner."

## The King's Inquiry
The King, not believing them and thinking, "They say this because they wish to destroy the ascetic Haritaca," went to suppress the border unrest and returned to the city of Bārāṇasī. After circling the city clockwise, he went to the Queen and asked, "Is it true that my ascetic Haritaca engages in the ways of worldlings with you?"

When she replied, "It is true, Great King," the King still did not believe the Queen's words and thought, "I will ask the ascetic himself." He went to the park, sat in a suitable place, and desiring to ask the ascetic Haritaca—

## Confessing the Truth
The ascetic Haritaca thought, "Even if I say 'I do not enjoy sensual pleasures,' this King will surely believe my words. However, in this world, there is no refuge like truth. Those who abandon truth cannot reach omniscience even if they sit at the foot of the Bodhi tree. It is only proper that I speak the truth."

That word is true. For a Bodhisatta, there may be instances of taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants. But there is no such thing as telling a lie by prioritizing the intention to deceive or to destroy the welfare of others.

Therefore, desiring to speak only the truth—

## Extinguish Lust
The King, having heard those words—
476:
Then, Haritaca, showing the power of defilements to him, spoke the fourth verse:

43. "Great King, there are four very powerful things in the world where wisdom finds no footing: Lust, Hatred, Pride, and Delusion."

He spoke this fourth verse.

44. "We regarded you as an Arahant, endowed with virtue, living purely, wise and a scholar."

He spoke this fifth verse.

The ascetic Haritaca is worthy of receiving offerings. He is endowed with virtue. He lives purely. He has wisdom that destroys defilements. He has wisdom that knows cause and effect. Thus, we have regarded you, venerable sir.

45. "Evil thoughts, appearing beautiful and associated with lust, oppress even the wise sage who delights in the qualities of the Dhamma."

He spoke this sixth verse.

O King. Evil thoughts, which arise from taking objects as beautiful and are associated with lust, oppress even the wise who delight in the Dhamma-qualities of sages.

46. "This lust born of the body, which defiles your reputation, has arisen. Abandon it, may you be well. You were regarded as wise by many."

He spoke this seventh verse.

Venerable sir. This lust, born of the body, which destroys the beauty of your physical form and the beauty of your virtues, has arisen in you. Abandon that lust. May you be well. You were regarded as a wise man by many people.

47. "I will abandon those sensual pleasures that cause blindness, much suffering, and are great poisons. I will seek their root and cut off lust along with its bonds."

He spoke this eighth verse.

Great King. I will abandon those sensual pleasures that cause blindness, involve much suffering, and are the great poison of defilements. I will seek their root, which is improper attention. I will cut off lust along with its bonds.

At that time, the ascetic Haritaca, wishing to show the power of defilements to the King—

## The Four Powerful Things
Great King, in this world, wisdom finds no footing in these four things: Lust, Hatred, Pride (Intoxication), and Delusion. These four things are extremely powerful and intense.

The King, having heard those words—

Thereafter, the ascetic Haritaca—

At that time, the King, wishing to cause the ascetic Haritaca to make an effort in abandoning defilements—

## Regaining Mindfulness and Practicing Dhamma
Thereafter, the Bodhisatta, regaining mindfulness and noting the danger in sensual pleasures—
477:
48. "Having said this, Harita, the ascetic of true effort, having detached himself from sensual lust, reached the Brahma world."

He preached this verse.

"O monks, Harita the ascetic, who strove in speaking the truth, having said these words and having dispelled sensual lust, went to the Brahma realm; he was reborn there."

Having said this, he said, "Great King, please give me leave for a moment." Having obtained permission, he entered the leaf-hut, gazed at the Kasiṇa-maṇḍala, and regained his lost Jhāna. He then emerged from the hut, sat cross-legged in the air, and preached the Dhamma to the King. He said, "Great King, because I stayed in an improper place, I have reached a state of being censured among the people. May you be diligent. I shall now return to the forest where the scent of women does not reach." While the King was weeping and lamenting, he went to the Himālaya, and with his Jhāna unimpaired, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

The Teacher, having become fully enlightened, spoke this verse to show that matter:

[The Jātaka is concluded] The Teacher preached this verse, revealed the Truths, and identified the birth. At the end of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in Arahatship. As for the identification: "At that time, Ānanda was the King, and I myself was Harita the ascetic."

## Sensual pleasures, if craved, can lead to the wrong path.

The Haritaca Jātaka ends.

## 6. Padakusalamāṇava Jātaka

## Death due to deceiving the wisdom of others

The Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Padakusalamāṇava Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Bahussutaṃ," while staying at Jetavana Monastery, concerning a certain boy.

In the city of Sāvatthī, that boy, the son of a householder, was skilled in footprints even at the age of seven.

## The Art of Tracking Footprints

Then the boy's father, thinking "I will test him," went to a friend's house while the boy was unaware. Without asking where his father went, the boy followed his father's footprints and stood in his presence. Then one day, the father asked him, "Son, even though I went without letting you know, how do you know where I went?" The boy replied, "Father, I recognize your footprints; I am skilled in footprints."

Then, to test him, after eating his morning meal, the father left the house and went to the immediate neighbor's house, then to a second, then to a third house. Leaving the third house, he returned to his own house, then left by the north gate and went to Jetavana. There he worshipped the Buddha and sat listening to the Dhamma.

The boy asked, "Where has my father gone?" When told "We do not know," he followed his father's footprints starting from the neighbor's house, following the path his father took, went to Jetavana, worshipped the Buddha, and stood in his father's presence.
478:
When the father asked, "Son, how did you know I came here?" he replied, "I recognized your footprints and came by following them."

The Teacher asked, "Lay follower, what are you saying?" When told, "Venerable Sir, this boy is skilled in footprints. I came by this means to test him, and he, not seeing me at home, came by following my footprints," the Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not wonderful to know footprints on the ground; ancient wise ones knew footprints in the sky." Being requested by the lay follower, he told the story of the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, his Chief Queen committed adultery. When questioned by the King, she made an oath: "Great King, if I have committed adultery, may I become an Assāmukhī Yakkhinī (horse-faced ogress)." After passing away from that life, she became an Assāmukhī Yakkhinī at the foot of a mountain. Living in a cave, she caught and ate people traveling from the east to the west through the great forest.

## The Ogress and the Human Husband

That Assāmukhī Yakkhinī served the Great King Vessavaṇa for three years and obtained permission to eat humans in an area thirty leagues long and five leagues wide.

Then one day, a wealthy Brahmin of great possessions and beautiful appearance, surrounded by many people, set out on that road. Seeing the Brahmin, the Yakkhinī was pleased and ran towards him. Seeing her, the Brahmin's attendants fled.
479:
The Assamukhī Yakkhinī arrived with the speed of the wind, seized the Brahmin, and placed him on a rock to sleep. Upon reaching the cave, she felt the touch of a man and, through the power of passion, developed an affection for the Brahmin. Instead of eating him, she made him her husband. The two of them lived together in harmony.

From that time on, whenever the Yakkhinī captured humans, she would also take their clothes, rice, oil, and other goods. She would provide the Brahmin with various foods of excellent flavor, while she herself ate human flesh. When she went out, fearing the Brahmin might escape, she would block the entrance of the cave with a large stone before leaving.

While the two lived together in happiness, the Bodhisatta passed away from his previous place of existence and was conceived in the womb of the Assamukhī Yakkhinī, depending on the Brahmin.

## A Son is Born

After ten months, the Assamukhī Yakkhinī gave birth to a son. She felt great love for both her son and the Brahmin and nurtured them both. Later, when the son reached maturity, she would put him inside the cave along with his father and block the entrance.

One day, the Bodhisatta, knowing his mother had gone out, moved the stone and let his father outside the cave. When the Yakkhinī returned, she asked, "Who moved this stone?" The son replied, "Mother, I moved it. I cannot stay in the darkness." Out of love for her son, she said nothing.

On another day, the Bodhisatta asked his father, "Father, why is my mother's face of one kind, while your face is of another?" The father replied, "My son, your mother is a man-eating Yakkhinī, but we two are humans."

## The Escape

"Father, why then do we live in this place? Come, let us go to the world of men," the son said. The father replied, "My son, if we flee, your mother will eat us both." The Bodhisatta comforted his father, saying, "Father, do not fear. It is my responsibility to bring you to the world of men." The next day, when the mother had gone out, he took his father and fled.

When the Yakkhinī returned and did not see the father and son, she ran with the speed of the wind, caught them, and said, "Brahmin, why do you flee? What is lacking for you in this place?" The Brahmin replied, "Lady, do not ask me; your son took me and fled." Out of love for her son, she said nothing. She comforted them and brought them back to her dwelling. In this manner, when they fled again after a few days, she brought them back once more.

The Bodhisatta thought, "My mother's territory must have a limit. I should ask her the extent of the area where her authority holds sway, and then we shall flee beyond that limit." One day, while sitting in a suitable place with his mother, he said, "Mother, what belongs to a mother eventually passes to her sons. Please tell me the boundaries of the land that is your own."

The Yakkhinī described the landmarks such as mountains and rivers in all directions. She told her son that the area was thirty leagues in length and five leagues in breadth, saying, "My son, mark this area well."

After two or three days had passed, when the mother had gone into the forest, the Bodhisatta placed his father on his shoulders and, following the landmarks given by his mother, fled with the speed of the wind until he reached the bank of the river that formed the boundary.
480:
The Assamukhī Yakkhinī also arrived and, not seeing the father and son, pursued them. The Bodhisatta took his father and went into the middle of the river. The Yakkhinī arrived and stood on the riverbank. Realizing that they had crossed her boundary, she stood there and pleaded with her son and husband, "My son, take your father and come back. What fault is there in me? What desire of yours is not fulfilled by depending on me? Lords, please return!"

## Teaching the Mantra

Then the Brahmin crossed the river. The Assamukhī Yakkhinī, pleading only with her son, said, "My son, you should not do this. Please return!" The son replied, "Mother, we are humans, and you are a Yakkhinī. It is not possible for us to live with you forever."

"My son, will you truly not return?" the Yakkhinī asked. "Mother, I will not return," the Bodhisatta replied.

"My son, if you do not return, life in the world of men is difficult. Those who possess no skill cannot make a living. I know a mantra called the Cintāmaṇi. By the power of this mantra, one can track stolen goods by following their footsteps even after twelve years. This Cintāmaṇi mantra will be your livelihood. My son, learn this priceless mantra." Even though she was oppressed by such great sorrow, she gave him the mantra out of love for her son.

Standing in the river, the Bodhisatta paid homage to his mother, listened with great respect, and learned the mantra. Then, paying homage to his mother again, he said, "Mother, you may go now."

## The Ogress Dies

"My son, if you do not return, I have no life left," she said, and recited this verse:

"Come, my son, return to me,
Do not leave me helpless here.
Today, not seeing her dear son,
The Yakkhinī has come to death."

The Yakkhinī struck her breast, and at that very moment, her heart broke from grief for her son. She died and fell right there. The Bodhisatta, knowing his mother was dead, called his father and went to her. He built a pyre and performed the cremation. He honored her with flowers of various colors, paid his respects, and wept in lamentation. Then, taking his father, he went to the city of Bārāṇasī and stood at the palace gate.

## Serving the King

He sent word to the King, saying, "A youth skilled in footsteps stands at the gate." When the King said, "Then let him enter," the youth went in, paid homage to the King, and was asked, "My son, what skill do you possess?" He replied, "Great King, I can track stolen goods by following their footsteps even after twelve years."

When the King said, "In that case, serve me," the Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, if I receive one thousand pieces of money every day, I shall serve you." "Very well, my son, serve me," the King said, and he gave him one thousand pieces of money daily.

## Testing the Skill

Then one day, the Chaplain (Purohita) said to the King, "Great King, because we have not had to perform any task using this youth's skill, we do not know whether he truly possesses it or not. Let us test the youth."
481:
The King agreed, saying, "Very well." The two of them then gave a signal to the guards of the treasures, took the essence of the wealth, and descended from the palace. They circled the palace precincts three times, set up a ladder, and climbed over the wall to the outside. They entered the judgment hall and sat there. Then they went again, set up the ladder, climbed over the wall, and went to the edge of the royal pond. After circling the pond three times clockwise, they descended into it, placed the bundle of wealth inside, and ascended back to the palace.

The next day, a great uproar arose, with people saying, "Treasures have been stolen from the royal residence!" The King, acting as if he knew nothing, had the Bodhisatta summoned and said, "Son, many treasures have been stolen from the royal residence. It is now proper to search for that wealth."

The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, for me, who is capable of bringing back stolen goods by following the tracks of thieves even after twelve years, there is no difficulty in bringing back the wealth stolen today. I shall be able to do it; do not worry, Your Majesty."

"If that is so, then bring it," said the King.

## Being Able to Reveal Everything

The Bodhisatta said, "Very well, Great King." He paid respects to his mother, recited a mantra, and while standing on the palace terrace, said, "Great King, the footprints of two thieves are visible." Following the tracks of the King and the Chaplain, he entered the auspicious chamber, then exited and descended from the palace. He circled the palace precincts three times and, following the tracks, went near the wall. Standing at the wall, he said:

"Great King, at this spot, the tracks leave the wall and appear in the air. Provide a ladder." He had the ladder set up, climbed over the wall, and by following the tracks, went to the judgment hall. He then returned to the palace, had the ladder set up again, climbed over the wall, and went to the pond. After circling it three times clockwise, he said, "Great King, the thieves descended into this pond." He then took the bundle of wealth as if he had placed it there himself, gave it to the King, and said, "Great King, these two thieves are well-known great thieves. These thieves entered the royal residence by this path."
482:
## The People Rejoiced

The people were greatly delighted and snapped their fingers. There was a tossing of garments and turbans.

## Ordering the Capture of the Thieves

The King thought, "This youth, by following the tracks, only knows the place where the thieves placed the wealth; he is not able to catch the thieves." Having thought so, he then said to the youth, "Son, you have brought the stolen wealth to us, but the thieves have not yet been brought."

## Speaking Figuratively Due to Reluctance

"Great King, what benefit would there be in bringing the thieves? The thieves are right here; they are not far away," he said. "Son, point out who and who are the thieves of the wealth," the King said.

"Great King, whoever has the desire, that person is the thief. Since the time Your Majesty received the wealth, what benefit is there in catching the thieves? Your Majesty, do not be unmindful," said the Bodhisatta. "Son, I give you a thousand pieces of money every day. Catch the thieves and give them to me," the King said.

"Great King, having received the wealth, what will you do with the thieves?" the Bodhisatta asked. "Son, even more than the wealth, it is proper to get the thieves," the King replied.

"Great King, if that is so, I will not say to Your Majesty, 'These are the ones.' I will, however, bring an illustration of an event that occurred in the past for Your Majesty. If Your Majesty is wise, may you understand that reason," he said, and the Bodhisatta brought forth a story of the past.

## Story 1

In the past, not far from the city of Bārāṇasī, an actor named Pāṭali lived by the riverbank. On a festival day, he took his wife and entered Bārāṇasī. After dancing, playing the lute, and singing, he obtained wealth. When the festival ended, he took much liquor and food and was going to his village. Reaching the riverbank, he saw the new water rising. He sat eating food and drinking liquor. Becoming intoxicated and unaware of his own strength, he thought, "I will tie the great lute to my neck and cross the river." He took his wife and entered the river.

Water entered through the holes of the lute. Then, that lute caused the actor to sink in the water. The actor's wife, realizing her husband was sinking, let go of him, climbed out of the river, and stood on the bank. The actor Pāṭali surfaced once and sank once. Having swallowed water, his belly became bloated.

Then the actor's wife thought, "My husband will die now. I will ask for one song and, by singing that song in the midst of an audience, I will make a living." Having thought so, she said, "Lord, you are sinking in the water. Give me one song so that I may make a living."
483:
49. "O learned and eloquent one, the Ganges carries Pāṭali away. O venerable one being carried, give me one little verse."

He spoke this first verse. 

Bahussutaṃ: having much learning. Cittakathiṃ: one who speaks eloquently. Pāṭaliṃ: Pāṭali. Gaṅgā: the waters of the Ganges. Vahati: carries away. Vuyhamānaka: O Pāṭali, who is being carried away in the river. Te: to you. Bhaddaṃ: may there be goodness. Me: to me. Ekaṃ: one. Gāthakaṃ: little song/verse. Tvaṃ: you. Dehi: give.

50. "By that which they sprinkle the suffering, by that which they sprinkle the sick; in the midst of that I shall die; danger has arisen from my refuge."

He spoke this second verse.

Bhadde: O lady. Dukkhitaṃ: a person in suffering. Yena: by which water. Siñcanti: they sprinkle. Āturaṃ: a person in pain. Yena: by which water. Siñcanti: they sprinkle. Ahaṃ: I. Tassa: of that water. Majjhe: in the midst. Marissāmi: shall die. Me: to me. Saraṇato: from the water which is my refuge. Bhayaṃ: danger. Jātaṃ: has arisen.

51. "Where seeds grow, where beings are established; that very earth crushes my head; danger has arisen from my refuge."

He spoke this third verse.

Yattha: in which earth. Bījāni: seeds. Rūhanti: grow. Yattha: in which earth. Sattā: beings. Patiṭṭhitā: are established. Sā: that earth. Me: my. Sīsaṃ: head. Nipīḷeti: crushes/breaks. Me: to me. Saraṇato: from the earth which is my refuge. Bhayaṃ: danger. Jātaṃ: has arisen.

Meaning, "Give me a song."

At that time, the dancer named Pāṭali said to his wife, "O lady, how shall I give you a song? Now the water, which is the refuge of the multitude, is killing me."

The Bodhisatta recited this verse and said, "Great King, just as water is the refuge of the multitude, so too are kings the refuge of the people. If danger arises from the king, who shall be able to prevent that danger?" He continued, "Great King, I have spoken this hidden matter making it understandable to the wise. O Great King, may you understand it."

"Dear boy, I do not understand such hidden speech. Catch the thief and give him to me," the King said.

## Story 2

Then the Bodhisatta said to the King, "Great King, if that is so, then understand this matter," and he brought forth another example.

"Great King, in the past, in a gate-village of this very city of Bārāṇasī, a certain potter, while taking clay to make pots, dug a large pit with a cavern inside by repeatedly taking from the same spot.

Then one day, while the potter was digging clay, an unseasonable great storm arose and it rained heavily. The overflowing water caused the pit to collapse. The earth crushed the potter's head. The potter, lamenting, spoke this verse:"

The Bodhisatta spoke this verse and said, "Great King, just as the earth, which is the refuge of the multitude, crushed the potter's head, so too, when a King, who is like the earth and the refuge of all people, rises up and commits theft, who shall be able to prevent it? Great King, you will be able to know the thief who is spoken of in this hidden way."

"Dear boy, I have no need for hidden matters. Catch this thief and give him to me," the King said. Protecting the King, he did not say "You are the thief," but brought forth another example. "Great King, in the past, in this very city, a certain man's house caught fire."
484:
52. "By which meals are cooked, by which cold is dispelled; that very fire burns my limbs; danger has arisen from my refuge."

He spoke this fourth verse.

Bhattāni: meals. Yena: by which fire. Paccanti: they cook. Sītaṃ: cold. Yena: by which fire. Vihaññati: is dispelled. So: that fire. Maṃ-mama: my. Gattāni: limbs/body. Dahati: burns. Me: to me. Saraṇato: from the fire which is my refuge. Bhayaṃ: danger. Jātaṃ: has arisen.

The King said, "Dear boy, I have no desire for hidden speech. Catch the thief and give him to me, saying 'This person is the thief'."

## Story 3

Because the Bodhisatta wished to protect the King, he did not say "You are the thief," but brought forth another illustration.

"Great King, in this very city of Bārāṇasī, a certain man's house caught fire. That man entered the house and ordered another person, 'Go in and bring out the goods.' While that man was inside taking out the goods, the door of the house closed. That man, blinded by smoke and finding no way out, suffered great pain and, standing inside the house, lamented and spoke this verse:"

The Bodhisatta spoke this verse and said, "Great King, like fire, a certain person who is the refuge of the multitude has stolen a bundle of jewels. Do not ask me who the thief is." The King said, "Dear boy, give the thief to me."

## Story 4

Without saying "You yourself are the thief," the Bodhisatta brought forth another illustration.

"Great King, in the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, a certain man ate too much and, being unable to digest the food, fell into agony and lamented:"

53. "By which food many Brahmins and Khattiyas live; that food being eaten kills me; danger has arisen from my refuge."

He spoke this fifth verse.

Puthū: many. Brāhmaṇakhattiyā: Brahmins and Kings. Yena bhattena: by which food. Yāpenti: they live/sustain themselves. Bhutto: being eaten. So: that food. Maṃ: me. Vyāpādeti: kills. Me: to me. Saraṇato: from the food which is my refuge. Bhayaṃ: danger. Jātaṃ: has arisen.

The Bodhisatta spoke this verse and said, "Great King, like food, a certain person who is the refuge of the multitude has stolen the wealth. Once you have obtained that wealth, why do you still seek the thief?" The King said, "Dear boy, if you are able, give the thief to me."

## Story 5

The Bodhisatta brought forth another illustration. "Great King, in the past, in this very city of Bārāṇasī, the wind arose and broke a certain man's limbs. That man lamented:"

54. "In the last month of the summer, the wise desire the wind; that very wind breaks my limbs; danger has arisen from my refuge."

He spoke this sixth verse.

Paṇḍitā: the wise. Gimhānaṃ: of the summer seasons. Pacchime: in the last. Māse: month. Vātaṃ: wind. Icchanti: they desire. So: that wind. Maṃ-mama: my. Gattāni: limbs/body. Bhañjati: breaks. Me: to me. Saraṇato: from the wind which is my refuge. Bhayaṃ: danger. Jātaṃ: has arisen.

The Bodhisatta spoke this verse and said, "Great King, understand the reason that danger has arisen from the refuge." The King said, "Dear boy, give the thief to me."

## Story 6

To make the King understand, the Bodhisatta brought forth another illustration.

"Great King, in the past, in the Himālaya region, there was a great tree possessed of branches and twigs. That great tree was full of flowers and fruits. It was the dwelling place of birds. Two branches of that great tree rubbed against each other. From those branches, smoke arose. Sparks of fire fell. Seeing that fire, the king of birds spoke this verse:"

The Bodhisatta spoke this verse and said, "Great King, just as the tree is the refuge of the birds, so too is the King the refuge of the multitude. When that King commits theft, who shall be able to prevent it? Great King, please take note." The King said, "Dear boy, just give me the thief."
485:
55. The tree on which the birds relied,
That very tree now emits fire.
Seek the directions, O crooked-winged ones!
Danger has arisen from our refuge.

He spoke this seventh verse. 
(The meaning is:) The tree (*jagatiruhaṃ*) on which the birds relied (*nissitā*), that very tree (*svāyaṃ*) emits (*pamuñcati*) fire (*aggiṃ*). O birds (*vakkangā*), you (*tumhe*) should resort to (*bhajatha*) other directions (*disā*). For us (*no*), danger (*bhayaṃ*) has arisen (*jātaṃ*) from our refuge (*saraṇato*).

## Story 7
Then the Bodhisatta presented another example to the King.

Great King, in a certain village of Kāsi, behind a family's house, there was a river with a fierce crocodile. That family had an only son. When his father died, the son looked after his mother. Even though the son was unwilling, the mother brought a young woman from another family for him.

At first, the daughter-in-law loved her mother-in-law, but later, as her own children grew, she wanted to drive the mother-in-law out. The daughter-in-law's own mother also lived in that same house.

The daughter-in-law spoke various faults of the mother-in-law to her husband, trying to divide them, saying, "I cannot support your mother; kill her." When he said, "Lady, killing a human is a heavy burden, how can I kill her?", she replied, "When she falls asleep, we will take her along with her small bed and throw her into the crocodile-infested river; then the crocodiles will eat her."

The husband asked, "Where is your mother?" The wife replied, "My mother sleeps right next to yours." "In that case, go and tie a rope to your mother-in-law's bed as a sign," he said.

The woman did as her husband said and told him, "I have made the sign." The husband said, "Wait a little while, let the people fall asleep," and pretending to sleep, he went and tied that rope to his wife's mother's bed. Then he woke his wife, and both of them went, lifted the bed with the wife's mother, and threw it into the river. The crocodiles destroyed and ate the wife's mother who was thrown into the river.

The next day, realizing that her mother had been switched and killed, she said, "My lord, my mother has been killed; now kill your mother too." When the husband said, "Very well," she said, "Let us build a pyre in the cemetery, set it on fire, and kill her."
486:
56. The one whom I brought with joy,
Wearing garlands and anointed with sandalwood,
She now drives me out of the house.
Danger has arisen from my refuge.

He spoke this verse.
(The meaning is:) The woman (*yaṃ*) whom I brought (*ānayiṃ*) after making her happy (*somanassaṃ*), wearing garlands (*māliniṃ*) and anointed with sandalwood (*candanussadaṃ*), that woman (*sā*) now drives me out (*nicchubhati-nīharati*) of the house (*gharā*). For me (*me*), danger (*bhayaṃ*) has arisen (*jātaṃ*) from my refuge (*saraṇato*).

Then the couple took the husband's mother to the cemetery and left her there. At the cemetery, the husband asked the wife, "Lady, did you bring the fire?" "My lord, I forgot," the wife said. "In that case, go and get it," said the husband. "My lord, I cannot go alone, and if you go, I cannot stay here; let us both go," the wife said.

While the couple went to get the fire, the old mother was awakened by the cold wind. Realizing she was in a cemetery, she reflected, "These people want to kill me and have gone to get fire." Thinking, "They do not know my strength," she took a log, covered it with an old cloth, laid it on the bed, and fled into a cave in that cemetery.

The husband and wife brought the fire and, thinking it was the old woman, set the log on fire and left.

A certain thief had placed a bundle of treasure in that cave. He came to take the bundle, saw the old woman, and thought, "This must be an ogress; an ogress is guarding my treasure." He brought an exorcist. The exorcist entered the cave reciting mantras. Then the old woman said to the exorcist, "I am not an ogress; come, let us both divide this wealth."

When the exorcist asked, "How can I believe your words?", the old woman said, "Place your tongue upon my tongue." The exorcist did as she said. Then the old woman bit his tongue, causing it to fall. The exorcist cried out, "Truly, this is an ogress!" and fled with blood dripping from his tongue.

At dawn, the old woman dressed in fine clothes, took the bundle of various jewels, and went to the house. Seeing the mother-in-law, the daughter-in-law asked, "Mother, how did you get this wealth?" The mother-in-law said, "Daughter, by being burned on a pyre in that cemetery, I obtained wealth of this kind." "Mother, would I also be able to get it?" she asked. "Daughter, if you become like me, you will get it," said the mother-in-law.

## Story 8

The Bodhisatta, intending to protect the King, brought another example.

Great King, in the past, in this very city of Vārāṇasī, a certain man made a prayer and obtained a son. At the time of the son's birth, he was filled with joy, thinking, "I have obtained a son."

That father, living with great difficulty and hardship, lamented and spoke a stanza—

The Bodhisatta spoke this stanza and said, "Great King, just as an old man should be protected by a capable son, so too should all the country be protected by the King and the Chaplain. This danger has arisen from the King who protects all beings. By this reason, Great King, please know that 'such and such a person is the thief'."

"Young man, I do not know the reason; just give me the thief," the King urged the youth repeatedly.

## Catching the Thief in Front of the Crowd

Then the Bodhisatta said to the King, "Great King, do you truly desire the capture of the thief?" "Young man, it is as you say," the King replied.

"Great King, if that is so, I shall declare in the midst of the assembly that 'such and such a person is the thief'." "Young man, do so," said the King. Hearing the King's words, the Bodhisatta, thinking, "This King does not allow himself to be protected; I shall now catch the thief," addressed the assembled multitude and spoke these stanzas:

"The King is the refuge of the people, but from that King, danger has come to you. The King and the Chaplain are the ones who plunder. If you wish to catch the thieves, catch this King and this Brahmin and do what must be done."

## The King and the Chaplain Have Died

The assembled people, hearing the Bodhisatta's words, thought, "This King, though he should be our protector, now places blame on others, and having placed his own goods in the pond himself, makes us search for a thief. From now on, let us kill this wicked King so that he may not commit theft again." They rose up with sticks, clubs, and the like, and there and then beat the King and the Chaplain to death. They then anointed the Great Being and established him in the kingship.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Lay follower, knowing footprints on the ground is not wonderful; wise men of old knew footprints even in the sky." He then proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower and his son were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala).

How was the Jātaka identified? At that time, the father was Kassapa, and I myself was the youth Padakusala. Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## When Danger Arises from the Refuge, It Is Truly Fearful

The Padakusala-māṇava Jātaka is finished.

## 7. Lomasakassapa Jātaka

## Even Bodhisattas Become Negligent Because of Women

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Lomasakassapa Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Assa indasammo rājā," concerning a dissatisfied monk.

The All-Knowing Buddha asked, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true," the Buddha said, "Monk, how could a great wind capable of shaking Mount Sineru fail to shake old, withered leaves?"

"Even those endowed with fame fall into disrepute because of defilements; indeed, defilements stain even pure beings, let alone one like you." Having said this, being requested by that monk, he told the story of the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the King's son, Prince Brahmadatta, and the chaplain's son, named Kassapa, were two friends who learned all the arts in the house of the same teacher. Later, Prince Brahmadatta ascended the throne upon his father's death.

## The Chaplain's Son Becomes an Ascetic

Kassapa thought: "My friend has become king. Now he will give me great wealth. What use have I for wealth? I will ask permission from my parents and the king and go forth as a monk."

Having so thought, Kassapa asked permission from the king and his parents, entered the Himalayas, and became an ascetic. On the seventh day, he attained the five supernormal powers (abhiññā) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti). He lived by gathering gleanings. He became known as "Lomasakassapa."

## To Corrupt the Ascetic

Lomasakassapa had peaceful faculties and practiced fierce austerities. Due to the power of his practice, Sakka's throne trembled. Sakka, upon reflecting, saw Lomasakassapa and thought: "This ascetic has such fierce power he might even displace me from my position. I will unite with the King of Bārāṇasī to break his virtue."

Having so thought, Sakka, through his divine power, entered the King of Bārāṇasī's bedchamber at midnight, illuminating the entire room with his radiance. Standing in the air above the King, he woke him, saying, "O Great King, arise!" When asked, "Who are you?", he replied, "I am Sakka."

When asked, "For what purpose have you come?", he asked, "O Great King, do you desire to be the sole ruler of all Jambudīpa?" When the King replied, "Why would I not?", Sakka said to the King of Bārāṇasī, "O Great King, if that is so, invite Lomasakassapa and have him perform a sacrifice of slaughtered four-footed animals. You will become like Sakka, ageless and immortal, and rule as king over all Jambudīpa."

## Inviting for the Sacrifice

Hearing Sakka's words, the King agreed, saying, "Very well." Sakka said, "If so, do not delay," and departed. The next day, the King summoned the minister named Seyya and said, "Friend minister, go to my dear friend the ascetic Lomasakassapa and say in my name: 'The King will become the sole ruler of all Jambudīpa by having you perform a sacrifice of slaughtered four-footed animals. He will give you whatever region you desire. Come to perform the sacrifice with me.'"

Minister Seyya said, "Very well, O King." To find the ascetic's dwelling, he had a drum beaten in the city. When a hunter said, "I know the place," he put the hunter in the lead and went there with a large retinue. He paid homage to the sage, sat in a suitable place, and delivered the message.

## When the Ascetic Refused

Then the sage Lomasakassapa said to Minister Seyya, "What is this you are telling me?" and wishing to reject it, he spoke the verses.

## Tempting with a Princess to Perform the Sacrifice

Minister Seyya, having heard the words of the sage Lomasakassapa, went back to Bārāṇasī and informed the King. The King remained silent, thinking, "If he will not come, what can I do?"

Sakka came again at midnight, stood in the air, and asked, "O Great King, have you invited the sage Lomasakassapa to perform the sacrifice?" The King replied, "Though I sent for him, the sage Lomasakassapa will not come."

“Great King, having adorned your daughter Candavatī, send the minister Seyya as before and have him say, ‘O ascetic, if you go and perform the sacrifice, the King will give you this daughter.’ Without fail, the ascetic Lomasakassapa will become attached to the princess and come,” he said.

The King agreed, saying, “Very well.” The next day, he handed over the princess to the minister Seyya. The ascetic, breaking his sense-restraint, looked at the princess and immediately, with a mind filled with lust, fell away from his meditative absorption (jhāna). The minister, knowing the ascetic’s state of lust, said, “Venerable sir, if you perform the sacrifice, the King will give you this princess to be your attendant.”

Lomasakassapa, trembling by the power of defilements, asked, “Will the King really give me this princess?” “Yes, venerable sir, if you perform the sacrifice, the King will give you this princess,” the minister replied. The ascetic said, “Very well, if I obtain the princess, I will perform the sacrifice.” He then called the minister, ascended the chariot adorned with his matted hair, and followed him to Bārāṇasī. The King, hearing that the ascetic had arrived, initiated the work at the sacrificial pit.

Hearing the elephant's sound, the remaining elephants, horses, bulls, and others also cried out, terrified by the fear of death. The people also lamented.

## The Ascetic’s Remorse
The ascetic Lomasakassapa, hearing that tumultuous and loud outcry, was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and looked at his own matted hair and other features. Then, his matted hair, beard, and armpit hair became apparent to him. The ascetic Lomasakassapa became remorseful and, wishing to express his spiritual urgency, thought, “I have indeed committed an improper and evil deed.”

## The King Himself Urges Him
Then the King said to the ascetic Lomasakassapa, “O ascetic, do not fear; now I will give you Princess Candavatī as well as the seven kinds of treasures. Perform the sacrifice!”
