Aparūpaghātī: one who does not harm others. Assa: to that wise person. Balañca: strength. Vaṇṇo ca: and beauty. Hoti: occur. Hi saccaṃ: it is true. Sabbo vaṇṇo: all beauty. Āhāramayena: by various kinds of food alone. Na hoti: does not occur.

Ahosi: it was. Tato: from that food I thought of. Aññathā: otherwise. Ahosi: it became. Icceva: for this reason. Ettha: in this beauty of yours. Me: to me. Vimati: doubt. Jātā: has arisen.

Ahampi: I also. Loṇiyateliyāni: mixed with salt and oil. Maṃsāni ca: meats. Phalāni ca: fruits. Annāni ca: and rice. Bhuñje: get to eat. Sūro: a hero. Saṅgāmamukhaṃ: the front of the battle. Vijetvā: having conquered. Bhuñjati iva: as if he eats. Evaṃ tathā: in the same way. Ahaṃ: I. Manussesu: among humans. Rasaṃ: flavor. Bhottuṃ: to eat. Labhāmi: I get. Cakkavāka: O Cakkavāka. Tava yathā: like yours. Me: to me. Tādiso: of such a kind. Vaṇṇo: beauty. Na ca hoti: does not occur.

## Ugly Due to Reproach
Then, wishing to explain the reason for the crow's lack of beauty and the reason for his own beauty, the Cakkavāka said:
498:
“O crow, this thing called beauty does not arise from the cause of food alone; it also arises from the season (utu), the mind (citta), and kamma.” Thus the Cakkavāka rebuked the crow in many ways. The crow, being ashamed, said, “I have no need for your beauty,” and crying “Caw, caw,” he flew away.

To conclude the birth: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the fruit of Anāgāmi (Non-Returner). How was the birth identified? At that time, the greedy monk was the crow, the mother of Rāhula was the female Cakkavāka, and I, the Buddha, was the male Cakkavāka. Thus he identified the birth.

## Clothing, Greed, and Poverty
The Cakkavāka Jātaka ends.

## 9. Haliddirāga Jātaka
## On Avoiding Those Who Love and Hate Easily
The All-Knowing Buddha, who is the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Haliddirāga Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Sutitikkhaṃ,” concerning a monk tempted by a mature woman.

The present story will become clear in the Cūḷanārada Jātaka of the Terasa Nipāta.

As for the past story, it should be understood as follows:

## Inviting the Young Ascetic to the Human World
In the past, that girl, having broken the virtue of the young ascetic and knowing that he was under her influence, thought, “I will deceive this young ascetic and lead him to the human world.” She said, “The virtue guarded in the forest, which is devoid of sensual pleasures like sights and so on, is not of great fruit. The virtue guarded in the human world, where sensual pleasures like sights and so on are present, is of great fruit. Come, go with me to the human world and guard your virtue there. What is the use of the forest to you?” and spoke the first verse:
499:
78. "It is easy to endure in the forest, in a remote lodging; but those who endure in the village are much more noble than you."

In that verse, 'sutitikkhaṃ' means well-endured. 'Titikkhanti' means they endure cold and so on.

Having heard this, the young ascetic said, "My father has gone to the forest; when he returns, I will ask his permission and then go." The girl thought, "He says he has a father; if that father sees me, he might strike me with the end of his carrying pole and destroy me. I must go first." Then she said to him, "In that case, I will go first, marking the path; you come later," and she departed. After she had gone, he neither fetched wood nor water for drinking or use; he sat only brooding. When his father returned, he did not go out to meet him. Then the father, knowing "He has fallen under the power of a woman," asked, "My son, why have you not fetched wood? Why have you not provided water for drinking or use? Why do you sit only brooding?"

Then the young ascetic said, "Father, they say that virtue guarded in the forest is not of great fruit, but in the human world it is of great fruit. I will go there and guard my virtue. My companion told me 'You should come' and has gone ahead. I will go with that person. But what kind of man should I associate with while living there?" Asking this, he spoke the second stanza:

79. "Coming from the forest to the village, what kind of virtue and what kind of conduct should a man have for me to associate with him? Father, please tell me this when asked."

Then his father, explaining to him, spoke the remaining stanzas:

80. "Associate with one who inspires trust in you, my son, and who returns your trust; who is attentive and patient—associate with such a one after going from here.

81. "Associate with one in whose body, speech, and mind there is no wrongdoing; staying with him as if on a mother's breast, associate with such a one after going from here.

82. "Associate with one who lives by the Dhamma and, even while practicing, is not conceited; associate with that wise one of pure actions after going from here."

## Let us go when father returns
Upon hearing those words, the young ascetic said, "My father has gone to the forest. When he returns, I will ask his permission and then go." The girl also thought, "This young ascetic has a father. If that father sees me, he will strike me with the end of his carrying pole and bring me to ruin. I should go first." Having thought so, she said to the young ascetic, "Sir, in that case, I will go first, marking the path. You follow later," and she left.

## Asking permission from father
When the woman had gone, the young ascetic did not fetch wood. He did not draw drinking water. He remained only in a daze. When his father returned, he did not go to welcome him.

Then the father, realizing "This son of mine has followed the will of a woman," said, "Dear son, why have you not fetched wood? Why have you not drawn water for drinking and use? Why do you remain only in a daze?"

Thinking to ask, "Father, virtue guarded in the forest is not of great fruit; virtue guarded in the human world is of great fruit. I will go to the human world and guard my virtue. My companion said 'Come' and has gone ahead. I will follow that companion. What kind of person should I associate with while living in the human world?"

## The father ascetic's instructions
Then the father, wishing to inform the young ascetic, said:

## Associate with the trustworthy
Dear son, associate with one who is intimate with you and who appreciates your intimacy. One who listens to your words and is patient. After going from here, you should associate with such a person.

## Associate with the blameless
Dear son, associate with one who has no wrongdoing in body, speech, or mind. After going from here, you should associate with such a person, staying with them as if in a mother's bosom, regarding them like a mother.

## Associate with the humble
Dear son, associate with one who conducts their life according to the Dhamma of good conduct. Even while practicing the Dhamma, they do not take pride, thinking 'I alone practice the Dhamma.' After going from here, you should associate with such a wise person who habitually performs pure wholesome deeds.
500:
83. "Do not associate with a man of fickle affection, who has a mind like a monkey, who loves and hates easily, even if the whole world were empty of other people.

84. "Avoid from afar such a person, as one would avoid an angry venomous snake, or a great path smeared with dung, or as a vehicle avoids a rough road.

85. "Misfortunes grow for one who associates too much with a fool. Do not go with a fool; association with a fool is always like association with an enemy.

86. "I entreat you, my son, follow my words. Do not go with a fool; association with fools is suffering."

In those verses, 'yo te vissāsaye' means one who would trust you. 'Khameyya te' means one who would appreciate the trust you place in them. 'Sussūsī ca titikkhī ca' means one who is endowed with the desire to listen to your words and with patience toward your words. 'Urasiiva patiṭṭhāya' means just as a son stays on his mother's breast, so staying and regarding them like one's own mother, you should associate with them. 'Yo ca dhammena carati' means one who conducts themselves through the three-fold Dhamma of good conduct. 'Na maññati' means even while so conducting themselves, they do not take pride, thinking 'I am practicing the Dhamma.' 'Visuddhakāriṃ' means a performer of the pure ten courses of wholesome action.

'Rāgavirāginaṃ' means one who is both lustful and detached—having the nature of being attached and then immediately becoming detached. 'Nimmanussampi ce siyā' means even if the entire surface of Jambudīpa were empty of people and that person were the only human remaining, even then, do not associate with such a one. 'Mahāpathaṃ' means like a road smeared with excrement. 'Yānīva' means like one traveling by vehicle. 'Visamaṃ' means a rough path with hollows, elevations, stumps, and stones. 'Bālaṃ accupasevato' means for one who excessively associates with a fool or one of little wisdom. 'Sabbadā' means, my son, living with a fool is always suffering, just like living with an enemy. 'Taṃ tāhaṃ' means for that reason, I to you.

Being thus exhorted by his father, he said, "Father, if I go to the human world, I will not find wise ones like you. I am afraid to go there. I will live right here in your presence." Then, after giving him further exhortation, the father taught him the preliminary practices for kasiṇa meditation.

## Avoid the fickle-minded
Dear son, do not associate with a man who has fickle affection like turmeric-dye, who has a mind like a monkey, and who loves and hates easily. Even if the surface of Jambudīpa were empty of other humans, do not associate with such a person.

## Avoid the ill-tempered
Avoid such a person from afar, just as one traveling by vehicle avoids a rough road, or as one avoids an angry venomous snake, or a great path smeared with dung.

## Do not associate with fools
Dear son, misfortunes increase for one who excessively associates with a fool. Do not associate with a fool. Association with a fool is always like association with an enemy.

For that reason, dear son, I entreat you: follow my words. Do not associate with a fool. Association with fools brings about suffering.

When the young ascetic was thus exhorted by his father, he said, "Father, if I go to the human world, I will not find wise ones like you. Therefore, I am afraid to go to the human world. I will stay only here in my father's presence."

Then the father ascetic exhorted the young ascetic further and taught him the preliminary practices of kasiṇa meditation.
501:
The young ascetic soon attained the supernormal knowledges and meditative attainments, and along with his father, he was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. To identify the Birth: 'The dissatisfied monk at that time was the young ascetic, the young woman was the same woman, and I myself was the father ascetic.'

## He who is not with the fool, has few enemies, and is free from suffering

The Haliddirāga Jātaka is concluded.

## 10. Samugga Jātaka

## The Difficulty of Guarding a Woman

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Samugga Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with 'Kuto nu āgacchatha,' concerning a dissatisfied monk.

The Teacher asked that monk, 'Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?' When he replied, 'It is true, Venerable Sir,' the Teacher said, 'Monk, why do you long for a woman? Women are improper and ungrateful. In the past, even Dānavarakkhasas (ogres), though they swallowed a woman and carried her in their bellies, could not guard her or keep her devoted to one man. How will you be able to do so?' Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, renouncing sensual pleasures, entered the Himalayas and became an ascetic. Having attained the supernormal knowledges and meditative attainments, he lived subsisting on wild fruits.

## The Ogre Takes a Human Woman

A certain Dānavarakkhasa lived near the Bodhisatta's hermitage. From time to time, he would approach the Bodhisatta to listen to the Dhamma. However, he would stand on the road where people traveled in the forest and catch and eat those who passed by.

At that time, a daughter of a noble family in the kingdom of Kāsi, possessing supreme beauty, lived in a certain border village. One day, while she was returning from visiting her parents, the ogre saw the people in her retinue and rushed at them in a terrifying form. The people, terrified, threw down their weapons and fled. Seeing the beautiful woman sitting in the carriage, the ogre became infatuated, took her to his cave, and made her his wife.
502:
## Guarding Her in a Casket

From then on, he brought her ghee, oil, rice, fish, meat, and sweet fruits to nourish her. He adorned her with clothes and ornaments, and to protect her, he had her sleep in a casket, which he then swallowed and carried in his belly.

One day, desiring to bathe, the ogre went to a lake, vomited up the casket, took the woman out, let her bathe, anointed her with perfumes, and adorned her with ornaments. Saying, 'Let your body take some air for a while,' he left her near the casket and went down to the bathing place himself. Being unsuspicious of her, he went a little distance away to bathe.

## Misconduct with a Vidyādhara

At that time, a Vidyādhara named Vāyussaputta was traveling through the air with a sword girt to his side. The woman saw him and made a hand gesture, saying, 'Come here.' The Vidyādhara quickly descended. She put him in the casket and, watching for the ogre's return, sat near the casket.

Seeing the ogre returning, she showed herself to him, and before he reached the casket, she opened it, went inside, lay on top of the Vidyādhara, and covered herself with her robe.

The ogre came and, without inspecting the casket, thinking 'Only my wife is here,' swallowed the casket. While going back to his cave, he thought on the way, 'It has been a long time since I saw the ascetic; today I will go and pay respects to him.' He then went to the ascetic.

## Three People Coming

The ascetic, seeing the ogre approaching from afar and knowing that there were two people inside his belly, wished to speak and uttered the first stanza:

87. From where do you three come, sirs?
Welcome, sit on these seats.
Are you, sirs, well and healthy?
Indeed, it has been a long time since you came here.

O three people! From where do you come? Your coming is a welcome one. Come here and sit on these seats. Sirs, are you well and free from disease? Indeed, it has been a long time since you came here to my presence.

## Why Three?

Hearing these words, the ogre thought, 'I came to the ascetic alone, yet he says "three people." Why does he speak thus? Does he know the truth, or is he mad and babbling?' He approached the ascetic, paid respects, sat to one side, and wishing to converse with him, uttered the second stanza:
503:
89. "You are one, and your dear wife, cast into the casket and swallowed within; she is always protected, gone into your belly, yet there she delights with the son of Vāyu."

He spoke this third verse.

O Dānava, you are one. Your dear wife is swallowed and kept inside a casket. That wife, whom you always protect and keep within your belly, delights there with the Vidyādhara named Vāyussaputta.

88. "I alone have reached here today, and no second person is found with me. With what reference did you speak, O Sage? From where do these three people come, sir?"

He spoke this second verse.

O Sage, now I alone have arrived here before you. I have no companion whatsoever. O sirs, you three people, from where do you come? With what reference did you speak thus?

## You Three

The sage said, "O Dānava, is it not true that you have a woman?" "It is true, venerable sir," the Dānava replied. "If that is so, then listen," the sage said, and continued:

"O Dānava, thinking 'I will make this woman associate with only one man,' you carry her in your belly, yet you also carry the woman's lover as you go."

## Vomiting and Opening the Casket

Hearing these words, the Dānava thought, "Vidyādharas are full of deceit. If the Vidyādhara has a sword in his hand, he might rip open my belly and escape." Being greatly terrified, he quickly vomited the casket and placed it before him.
504:
90. "Agitated in form, as explained by the sage, that Dānava there vomited the casket; he saw his wife, wearing pure garlands, delighting there with the son of Vāyu."

He [the Buddha] spoke this verse.

Monks, when the sage had thus spoken, that Dānava, being terrified, vomited the casket in the presence of the sage. In that casket, he saw his wife, adorned with pure flowers, delighting with the Vidyādhara Vāyussaputta.

91. "This matter is well-seen by you who follow the ascetic practice. Lowly are the men who fall under the power of women. Indeed, just as my life is protected here, this wicked woman, while within me, delighted with another."

92. "Day and night she was served by me, like a forest-dwelling ascetic tending the fire. She, having transgressed the Dhamma, practiced what is not Dhamma; intimacy with women is of a nature that should not be done."

93. "I thought, 'She stays in the middle of my body, she is mine.' But she is unmindful and unrestrained. She, having transgressed the Dhamma, practiced what is not Dhamma; intimacy with women is of a nature that should not be done."

94. "How can one trust, thinking 'She is well-protected by me'? There is no protection for those of many minds. For they are like the pit of the infernal abyss; one who is negligent herein meets with ruin."

To show this matter after becoming the All-Enlightened Buddha:

## The Vidyādhara Escapes

The Vidyādhara, as soon as the casket was opened, recited a mantra, took his sword, and flew into the sky. Seeing that Vidyādhara, the Dānava was pleased with the Bodhisatta and spoke the remaining verses starting with praise.
505:
95. "Therefore, they are happy and free from sorrow, who live released from women. Desiring this supreme peace, one should not form an intimacy with women."

He spoke these verses preceded by praise.

Venerable Sage, this matter is well-seen by you who follow the austere practice. Men who fall under the power of women are base. Indeed, that woman whom I protected like my own life here within my belly—that woman, being wicked towards me, made another man delight.

Like an ascetic living in the forest tends the fire, I served that woman day and night. That woman, having overstepped the Dhamma, practiced what is not Dhamma. Intimacy with women is of a nature that should not be done.

I thought of this woman, who is endowed with the nature of the unrighteous and is unrestrained in body, speech, and mind, as 'She stays in the middle of my body' and 'She is mine.' That woman, having overstepped the Dhamma, practiced what is not Dhamma. Intimacy with women is of a nature that should not be done.

How can a wise man trust in a woman, thinking 'I have protected her well'? In this world, there is no such thing as protecting women who have many-faceted minds. Truly, these women are like the abyss called Valavāmukha in the ocean. A man who is negligent regarding women meets with ruin.

Therefore, those wise ones who live apart from women are happy and free from sorrow. One who desires that supreme peace, the bliss of Jhāna, should not form an intimacy with women.

Having said this, the Dānava ogre bowed at the feet of the Bodhisatta and praised him, saying, "Venerable sir, because of you I have gained my life. This woman of wicked conduct would have had the Vidyādhara kill me."

## Releasing the Woman

The Bodhisatta then preached the Dhamma to the Dānava, saying, "Do not do any evil to this woman. You should take the precepts," and established him in the Five Precepts.

The Dānava thought, "If I, even while carrying her in my belly, was unable to protect her, who else besides me will be able to protect her?" Thus, he released the woman and went back to his own forest.
506:
Having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. How did he identify the Jātaka? "At that time, I myself was the ascetic Dibbacakkhu." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Even while being guarded, women are many who desire evil.
The Samugga Jātaka is finished.

## 11. Pūtimamsa Jātaka
## Loss through looking when one should not look
The Present Story: The Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Pūtimamsa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na kho me ruccati," concerning the lack of restraint of the senses.

On one occasion, many monks had unguarded doors in their senses. The Omniscient Buddha, saying to the Venerable Ānanda Thera, "It is proper to admonish these monks," had the Saṅgha of monks assembled without distinction. Sitting in the midst of the adorned noble seat, he addressed the many monks:

"Monks, it is not proper for one called a monk to take up an object by way of the sign of beauty in forms and so forth. If one should die at the time of taking up an object by way of the sign of beauty, one will be reborn in hell and such. Therefore, do not take up the sign of beauty in forms and so forth. One called a monk should not be one who takes up objects in forms and so forth.

Monks who take up objects in forms and so forth reach great destruction in this very life. Therefore, monks, in this Dispensation, it is better to pierce the eye-sensitivity with a glowing, red-hot iron spike." Having elaborated in this manner, he continued:

"Monks, there is a time for you to look at forms, and a time not to look. When it is time to look, look by way of foulness (asubha). If you look by way of foulness, you will not fall away from your own domain.

What is your domain? It is the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the noble eightfold path, and the nine supramundane states. These are your domain.

To you who wander in this domain, Māra will find no opportunity. But if you look by way of the sign of beauty, following the power of defilements, you will fall away from your own domain like the jackal named Pūtimamsa." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, many hundreds of goats lived in a mountain cave in a forest region of the Himālaya.

## Jackals Eating Goat Meat
Not far from the dwelling place of those goats, in a certain cave, a jackal named Pūtimamsa lived with his wife named Veṇī. While wandering about, he saw those goats and thought, "It is proper to eat the meat of these goats by some means." By a trick, he killed one goat.
507:
96. "It does not please me, friend, to see Pūtimamsa.
From such a friend, one should keep far away."

He spoke this first verse. (Word-by-word explanation): Āḷi, friend. Pūtimamsassa, of the jackal Pūtimamsa. Pekkhanā, the looking. Me, by me. Na kho ruccati, is not liked. Etādisā, of such a nature. Sakhārasmā, from a friend. Ārakā, far away. Parivajjaye, one should avoid.

## To Eat the Wise She-Goat
Those two jackals, husband and wife, eating goat meat, became strong and had fat bodies. Gradually, the goats came to an end. Among those goats, there was a she-goat named Meṇḍakamātā who was wise and skilled in means.

The jackal Pūtimamsa, being unable to kill that she-goat named Meṇḍakamātā, consulted with his wife one day, "My dear, the goats are finished. It is proper to eat this she-goat named Meṇḍakamātā by some means. This is the plan for killing this she-goat:

You go alone and become friends with that she-goat. When you have become intimate with her, I will lie down pretending to be dead. You approach the she-goat and say, 'Friend she-goat Meṇḍakamātā, my husband is dead. I am without refuge. Apart from you, I have no other relative. Come, come,' and weeping, say, 'Let us perform the funeral rites for my husband's body.' Thus, bring that she-goat Meṇḍakamātā. Then I will jump up, bite her neck, and kill her."

The female jackal named Veṇī agreed, saying "Very well," and having formed a friendship and become intimate with the she-goat Meṇḍakamātā, she spoke to the she-goat as her husband had instructed. The she-goat said, "Friend female jackal, your husband has eaten all my relatives. I am afraid; I do not dare to go."

## Knowing by Following with Mindfulness
The female jackal named Veṇī said, "Friend she-goat, do not be afraid. What can a dead jackal do to you?" The she-goat said, "Friend female jackal, your husband is sharp in counsel; I am afraid." But being repeatedly entreated by the female jackal, she thought, "He must surely be dead," and went along with the female jackal.

As she went, she thought, "Who can know what he will do?" and being suspicious of that jackal, she kept the female jackal in front and went along while observing the jackal.
508:
97. "This Veṇī is mad; she praises her husband's friend. She grieves for Meṇḍakamātā, who came and is now going back."

He spoke this second verse. This female jackal named Veṇī is mad. In the presence of her husband, she praises the goat, who is her friend. Now, she grieves for the goat named Meṇḍakamātā, who had come but is now going back.

98. "Friend, you are indeed mad, foolish, and undiscerning, you who, having feigned death, look out at the wrong time."

He spoke this third verse. Friend Pūtimamsa, you who have feigned death and look out at the wrong time, you are indeed mad, foolish, and lacking in discernment.

Upon hearing the footsteps of the goat and the female jackal, the jackal raised his head and looked back, thinking, "Has the goat arrived?" Seeing the jackal act in such a way, the goat thought, "This wicked female jackal wants to deceive and kill me. Therefore, her husband is lying down feigning death," and she turned back.

When the female jackal asked, "Friend goat, why are you turning back?" she intended to explain the reason.

Having said this, the goat turned back and went to her own dwelling. Since the female jackal was unable to make the goat return, she became angry with the goat and went to her husband, sitting there brooding. Then, the jackal Pūtimamsa, wishing to reproach the female jackal, spoke.

Upon hearing those words, the female jackal spoke.

## Look Only When It Is Proper to Look

After becoming the Buddha, the Blessed One spoke this verse:

99. "One should not look at the wrong time; the wise should look at the right time. He who looks at the wrong time grieves like Pūtimamsa."

Monks, a wise person should not look at the wrong time—that is, when the mind arises with the aspect of beauty (subha) directed towards the strands of sensual pleasure. One should look at the right time—that is, when taking an object with the aspect of foulness (asubha), or by way of recollection (anussati), or by way of a kasina. He who looks at the wrong time, when the mind arises with the aspect of beauty directed towards sensual pleasures, suffers and grieves like the jackal Pūtimamsa.

## Another Deceptive Invitation

The female jackal named Veṇī comforted Pūtimamsa, saying, "Lord, do not worry. I will bring Meṇḍakamātā back again by a stratagem. When she comes, catch her without fail." She then went to Meṇḍakamātā and said, "Friend, our prosperity depends on your coming. My husband remembers you when you come. You have not yet exchanged pleasantries with my husband."

100. "Let there be friendship for me, O friend; give me a full bowl. My husband has come back to life; come as a dear visitor."

She spoke this fifth verse. Friend, let there be love for me. Give me my desired gift. My husband has revived; come with me to inquire after my husband's well-being.

## I Will Come with an Entourage

The goat thought, "This wicked female jackal wants to deceive me. It is not proper for me to act in direct opposition; I will deceive her by a stratagem."

## Who Are the Entourage?

Then, the female jackal named Veṇī, wishing to ask about the entourage, spoke this seventh verse:

102. "What is your entourage like, for whom I shall prepare food? What are all their names? Tell me this when asked."

Friend, what is that entourage of yours like, for whom I must prepare food? What are all their names? O friend, being asked, tell me about that entourage.

## Two Thousand Jackals

The goat, wishing to announce her entourage, said, "Among the four jackals starting with Māliya, each has an entourage of five hundred. I will come surrounded by these two thousand jackals." She added, "If those jackals do not get food, they will kill and eat both of you, husband and wife."

Hearing this, the female jackal became terrified and thought, "There is no benefit in this goat coming to our place. I will use a stratagem to prevent her from coming."

Having said this, fearing the danger of death, she went quickly to her husband, called him, and fled. Those two jackals, husband and wife, never dared to return to that place again.

Identifying the Birth: The Buddha concluded this Dhamma teaching and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I was the tree deity in that forest."

## One should deceive the deceiver and avoid them.

The Pūtimamsa Jātaka ends.

## 12. Tittira Jātaka
## About a Wicked Ascetic Lacking Compassion

While staying at Gijjhakūṭa Hill, the Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Tittira Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yo te puttake," concerning Devadatta's attempt to kill him.

At that time, monks in the Dhamma hall started a conversation: "Friends, Devadatta is shameless and not a good man. He has joined with Ajātasattu to try to kill the Buddha, who possesses such supreme virtues, by sending archers, rolling a rock, and releasing the elephant Nālāgiri."

The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing as you sit here?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are discussing such and such," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has made an effort to kill me; he did so in the past as well." Then he told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, a world-renowned teacher was teaching five hundred young students. One day, he thought, "Living in Vārāṇasī is an encumbrance for me. Before these students complete their education, I will go into the Himalayan forest and live in a hermitage not far from the road." Having thought so, he lived as planned. The students also built their own hermitages.

## Studying in the Forest

The relatives of the students sent rice and other provisions. People living in the country also sent rice and other things to the world-renowned teacher, saying, "The world-renowned teacher is living in such and such a place in the forest, teaching the students." Travelers through the wilderness also made offerings to the teacher. An obscure man offered a cow and her calf so that they might have milk to drink.

## Death of the Teacher

Near the teacher's hermitage lived a female iguana with her two young ones. Lions and tigers also came to pay respect to the teacher. A partridge also lived permanently in that place.

That partridge, by listening to the recitations of the teacher and the students, learned the three Vedas by heart. The students were very intimate with the partridge. Later, before the students had finished their studies, the teacher passed away. The students cremated the teacher's body, built a sand stupa, honored it with various flowers, and wept.

## The Partridge Continues the Teaching

Then the partridge asked the students, "Young men, why are you weeping?" The students replied, "The teacher died before our studies were completed. That is why we weep."

101. O friend Āḷi, may you have only what is dear. I give you a pleasing gift. I shall come with a great retinue; prepare the food.

She spoke this sixth verse. 

Āḷi, O friend. Te, to you. Piyam kho, only love/dearness. Hotu, may there be. Te, to you. Puṇṇapattaṃ, a pleasing gift. Dadāmi, I shall give. Mahatā, with a great. Parivārena, retinue. Essaṃ, I shall come. Bhojanaṃ, the food. Kayirāhi, please prepare.

"If this is so, do not worry; I will teach you the Vedas," said the partridge. "How did you become proficient in the Vedas?" the young men asked. "When a teacher taught you, I listened and mastered the Three Vedas," the partridge replied. "If that is so, let us know your proficiency," the young men said.

The partridge then recited the difficult passages for those young men as easily as river water flows from a mountain peak. The young men were greatly delighted and studied the arts under the wise partridge. The partridge, established in the position of a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha), taught the arts to those young men.

The young men made a golden cage for the partridge, hung a canopy above it, placed honey and parched rice in a golden bowl, and honored him with flowers of various colors. The fame that "a partridge is teaching the Vedas to five hundred young men in the forest" spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

## The Young Men Return to Their Towns and Villages

At that time, a great festival on the mountain top was proclaimed in Jambudīpa. The parents of the young men sent word, saying, "Let the young men come to see the festival." The young men informed the wise partridge of the matter, entrusted the entire monastery to him, and returned to their respective cities.

## The Wicked Ascetic Destroys

Then, a certain merciless, wicked ascetic wandered to that place and reached the monastery. A female lizard saw the ascetic, greeted him hospitably, and said, "There is rice in such a place, and oil and other things in such a place. Cook and eat," and then she went to search for food.

The ascetic cooked rice early, killed the lizard's two young ones, and ate them. During the day, he also killed and ate the wise partridge and a young calf.

In the evening, seeing the cow returning, he killed her too, ate the meat, and lay down at the foot of a tree, falling asleep with a loud snoring sound. When the female lizard did not see her young ones in the evening, she went searching for them.

## The Deity Speaks

A tree deity, seeing the lizard trembling because she could not find her young ones, stood by his divine power and said, "O lizard, do not tremble. This vile man has killed your young ones, the partridge, the calf, and the cow. Bite this wicked man on the neck and bring his life to an end." Intending this, he spoke this first verse:

105. Yo te puttake akhādi, dinnabhatto adūsake.
Tasmiṃ dāṭhaṃ nipātehi, mā te muccittha jīvato.

Godhe, O lizard. Dinnabhatto, to whom you gave food. Yo pāpapuriso, that vile man. Adūsake, who are innocent. Te, your. Futtake, little ones. Akhādi, has eaten. Tasmiṃ, upon that vile man. Tvaṃ, you. Dāṭhaṃ, your four fangs. Nipātehi, let fall (sink). Eso, this vile man. Jīvato, while living. Te, from your. Hatthatto, hand. Mā muccittha, do not let escape.

## The Lizard Does Not Wish to Kill

After that, the lizard spoke these two verses:

106. Ākiṇṇaluddo puriso, dhāticeleva makkhito.
Padesaṃ taṃ na passāmi, yattha dāṭhaṃ nipātaye.

107. Akataññussa posassa, niccaṃ vivaradassino.
Sabbaṃ ce pathaviṃ dajja, neva naṃ abhirādhaye.

Devate, O deity. Yattha, on which part of that vile man. Dāṭhaṃ, the fangs. Nipātaye, to sink. Taṃ padesaṃ, that spot. Ahaṃ, I. Na passāmi, do not see. So puriso, that man. Ākiṇṇaluddo, is filled with evil. Dhāticeleva, like a nurse's cloth. Makkhito, is smeared with evil.

Akataññussa, to the ungrateful one. Niccaṃ, who always. Vivaradassino, looks for faults/openings. Posassa, to the man. Sabbaṃ pathaviṃ, the whole earth. Ce dajja, even if one were to give. Naṃ, that man. Neva abhirādhaye, one could never satisfy.

The lizard said this and fled, wishing to protect her own life, thinking, "If this man wakes up, he might eat me too."

## The Tiger Arrives

The lion and the tiger were also friends of the partridge. Sometimes the lion and the tiger would come to visit the partridge. Sometimes the partridge would go to preach the Dhamma to the lion and the tiger and then return.

On that day, the lion said to the tiger, "Friend, it has been a long time since I saw the wise partridge; it has been seven or eight days now. Go and find out the news of the wise partridge and return."

The tiger agreed, and at the time the lizard fled, he arrived at that place. He saw the vile man asleep and noticed the feathers of the wise partridge in the man's matted hair. He also saw the bones of the cow and the calf.

The king tiger, seeing all this and not finding the wise partridge in the golden cage, realized, "This vile man has killed these creatures," and kicked the vile man with his foot to wake him. The treacherous ascetic saw the tiger and was terrified.

## The Tiger takes him to the Lion

Then the tiger asked the wicked ascetic, “You base man, did you kill and eat those creatures?” “Lord, I did not eat them,” the wicked ascetic replied. “You man of evil conduct, if you did not kill them, who else did? If you do not speak the truth, you shall not live,” the tiger said.

Fearing death, the wicked ascetic said, “Lord, I killed and ate the offspring of the iguana, the calves, and the cow. But I did not kill the partridge.”

Although the tiger said much, he did not believe the wicked ascetic’s words and asked, “Where did you come from?” The wicked ascetic replied, “I came from the kingdom of Kaliṅga, carrying the goods of merchants for my livelihood, doing this and that work, and have now arrived at this place.”

When the wicked ascetic had thus described all the deeds he had done, the tiger said, “You man of evil conduct, if you did not kill the partridge, who else would have? Come, I will take you to my friend, the King of Beasts,” and he drove the wicked ascetic before him, threatening him as they went.

## What is this man's business?

The Lion King, wishing to question the tiger who brought the wicked ascetic, spoke this fourth verse:

108. Subāhu, why have you returned in such haste
Together with this young man?
What business or purpose do you have here?
Tell me this matter when you are asked.

O friend tiger Subāhu, who has strong arms. Why have you returned in such haste together with this youth? What purpose or business do you have here with me? You who are asked, tell me that reason.

Having heard those words, the tiger spoke this fifth verse:

109. He who is your friend, the virtuous Daddara,
I suspect his death today.
Having heard this man’s occupations,
I do not think Daddara is safe today.

## Suspecting the partridge killer

O King of Beasts. There is your friend, the virtuous partridge named Daddara. Having heard the occupations by which this man makes his living, I suspect the death of that partridge today because of this man. I do not think the partridge is safe today.

## Why do you suspect?

Then the lion spoke this sixth verse to the Tiger King:

110. What were the occupations of this man,
In the summary of his livelihood?
Or what confession of the man did you hear,
That you suspect Daddara’s death because of this youth?

O friend tiger Subāhu. What occupations of this man did you hear as the summary of his livelihood? Or what confession of this man did you hear that makes you suspect the partridge is dead because of this youth?

## According to his behavior

Then the Tiger King, wishing to answer the Lion King, spoke these verses:

111. He has traversed Kaliṅga and practiced trade,
He has traveled the cane-path and the spike-path.
He has practiced with actors and with hunters,
And fought with sticks in the midst of festivals.

112. Birds were bound by him with a measured snare,
He has kept the winning dice, and transgressed self-control.
He was hired at midnight to carry those punished by the king,
Whose blood flowed from their wounds.
His hands were burnt by receiving hot food.

113. These were the occupations of this man,
In the summary of his livelihood.
As this mass of feathers is seen here,
He has killed cattle; why would he spare the partridge?

O King of Beasts. This man has carried the goods of merchants from the kingdom of Kaliṅga and practiced trade. He has traveled by cane-paths and spike-paths. He has associated with actors and with hunters and fishermen. He has fought with sticks in the midst of various festivals.

Birds were bound by him. Along with the work of measuring grain, he has kept the winning dice. He has transgressed the observance of virtue. At midnight, he went to the place where those punished by the king had their hands and feet cut off and were left in the rest-house, and he was hired to tend to their flowing blood. His hands have been burnt by receiving hot food.

I have heard these occupations as the summary of this man’s livelihood. Just as this mass of partridge feathers is seen within the matted hair of this base man, so it should be known that this base man alone is the cause of the partridge’s death. Since this base man has killed cattle, how could it be that he did not kill the partridge?

## The answer appears when the Lion asks

“Why would he not kill the partridge?” said the Tiger King. The Lion King then asked the man, “O man, did you kill the wise partridge?” “Lord, I killed him,” he replied. Then, having heard the true words of the wicked ascetic, the Lion King wished to let the man go.

## The wicked ascetic is dead

The Tiger King said, “This man must be killed,” and right there, he bit and killed the wicked ascetic with his fangs, dug a hole, and buried him. When the youths came and did not see the wise partridge, they wept and returned.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the All-Enlightened Buddha identified the Jātaka: “Monks, in this way Devadatta made efforts to kill me in the past.” Then he concluded the Jātaka: “At that time, Devadatta was the deceitful ascetic; Uppalavaṇṇā was the iguana; Moggallāna was the tiger; Sāriputta was the lion; Kassapa was the world-renowned teacher; and I, the Buddha, was the wise partridge.”

## When conduct is base, danger comes to those who possess it.

End of the Tittira Jātaka.
